title: The breakup nobody talks about: Losing a friend as you age
text:
(Aging Untold) — Some friendships are built over decades of shared memories, routines and common ground. But as politics shift, priorities change and people grow in different directions, even the closest bonds can quietly come apart.
“It’s not talked about a lot”
Losing a friend later in life can hit just as hard as any other breakup, but friendship loss is often grieved in silence, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said.
“I think people grieve over lost friendships, and they don’t talk about it because it seems bad or wrong or uncommon, or they discount it,” O’Rourke said.
During a dinner with friends, the conversation drifted toward politics, O’Rourke said.
“We all agreed that that was a topic we were not going to bring up because our friendship meant more than a topic,” O’Rourke said. “I love the maturity of the friendships that we acknowledged it so it could be sustained.”
Why losing a friend can feel like a broken heart
“I don’t think people realize that not every broken heart comes from romance,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “There are a lot of really deeply broken hearts from severed families and severed friendships. We don’t give enough credence to it, and we certainly don’t allow people to normally grieve it.”
When someone loses a spouse or goes through a divorce, people rally around them. That support often doesn’t show up the same way when a friendship ends.
“Nobody’s bringing you casseroles or sending you flowers usually, and it can be really tough,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
Don’t put all your friendship “eggs in one basket”
O’Rourke said she isn’t a fan of relying on a single best friend.
“I like the idea of having friendships broader — broader in age, broader in number — so that you’re enhanced in all areas of your life,” O’Rourke said. “And if one friendship changes, you’re not completely unraveled.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, agreed, comparing close friendships to relationships that end the way marriages sometimes do.
“I see people as they grow as kind of like people who get divorced,” Rogers said. “They grow apart for whatever reason.”
When a friendship is one-sided
O’Rourke described watching a friendship where one person consistently gave and the other consistently took — until the giver stopped.
“The giver kind of woke up and thought, ‘I’m not going to give anymore,’” O’Rourke said. “And it ended. Those that were watching it thought, ‘Oh, a sigh of relief.’ But they both went through grief.”
Moving forward after a friendship ends
Ambrose shared how a recent friendship breakup affected her personally, including during a family vacation.
“I was so shocked to have this end that it devastated me, and it ruined a vacation that was very important to me with my husband and son,” Ambrose said.
Her advice: don’t let the loss take over.
“Don’t let people ruin your day, your vacation,” Ambrose said. “Just accept it for what it is. Embrace it and get over it. They’re doing things for their reasons, and it’s maybe none of your business. Stay out of judgment. Don’t try to figure them out — go on and just say next.”
Ambrose added that picking yourself back up opens the door to new connections.
“It can be really tough grief, but pick yourself up because you have the opportunity to find new joy, new happiness,” Ambrose said. “You never know when you’re going to meet your next friends. So give yourself that gift and get back out there.”
Key takeaways
- Friendship loss deserves real grief. Losing a close friend can be as painful as a romantic breakup, but it rarely comes with the same outside support.
- Talk about it before it breaks. Setting boundaries, like agreeing not to discuss divisive topics, can help sustain long-term friendships.
- Diversify your friendships. Having a broad circle of friends across different ages and backgrounds can soften the blow if one relationship ends.
- Watch for one-sided dynamics. Friendships where one person always gives and the other always takes often end — and both people grieve, even if outsiders feel relief.
- Don’t let the loss take over your life. Accept the friendship for what it was, resist the urge to over-analyze the other person’s reasons and keep moving forward.
- Stay open to new connections. New friendships can bring new joy, even after a painful loss.

title: Dolly Parton's nephew wants more time to defend himself against restraining order from her estate
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Dolly Parton’s nephew wants more time to get a lawyer in place to defend himself against a temporary restraining order granted to her estate against him and his security company.
Representing himself, Bryan Seaver filed a motion Friday in a Tennessee court asking that a hearing on the order now set for Oct. 9 be delayed by about 10 days.
The serious rift in the country music legend’s circle opened and spilled into public view weeks after her Aug. 25 death. She’s Alive, the entity founded to manage and protect her estate, accused Seaver in a court petition of threatening to commit violence and destroy Parton’s legacy and business empire. She’s Alive is run by Parton’s longtime manager Danny Nozell.
The petition names Seaver — who was handpicked by the star to announce her death from cancer — and his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services.
Seaver’s new motion says “the defendants lack any legal knowledge or skills to proceed in this matter without retained counsel or what, if any, challenges can or should be raised.” It says the delay is necessary because the lawyer he wants to represent him cannot meet with him until Monday, and says he won’t object to the restraining order being extended until a new hearing date.
Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles, the judge overseeing the case, has not yet replied to Seaver’s motion. In granting the restraining order, she said the court took into account the repeated threats cited in the complaint, as well as the alleged demands for payment and Seaver’s “claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate.”
In the petition and other court documents filed by She’s Alive, Seaver is accused of sending increasingly threatening messages starting just before Parton’s death. She’s Alive terminated Seaver and SAPS in the week before the petition, saying his “terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable.”
Seaver has not responded to email and phone messages from The Associated Press seeking comment.
Parton was a widely beloved country music giant, philanthropist and cultural icon who wrote hundreds of songs, including classics like “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You,” that earned a total of more than 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams.

title: Norway to vote on lot rent stabilization ordinance Oct. 15
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Following a public hearing Oct. 1 , Norway’s Select Board approved a special town meeting warrant that paves the way for residents to vote on a proposed ordinance regulating how national corporations charge lot rent to mobile home owners.
The special town meeting will be held Oct. 15 at Oxford Hills Comprehensive High School’s Forum meeting room at 256 Main St. in Paris at 6 p.m.
Norway is the latest town to push back against what many say are predatory practices by out-of-state companies that buy mobile home parks and hike lot rents on residents through Maine state law loopholes.
The town previously adopted a moratorium on lot rent increases last March at a special town meeting attended by 160 voters, more than twice the number that would be at its annual town meeting three months later.
Communities, including Auburn, Jay, Old Orchard Beach, Saco, Sanford, Waterville and Brunswick, have taken or are considering similar actions.
The law, meant to prevent excessive rent and fee increases, passed in 2025 as LD 1723, created the opposite effect, allowing park owners to raise rents as often as every three months using formulas with vague, inflated data and no geographic basis.
Sun Communities, owner of the 55+ Norway Commons mobile home park at 99 Town and Country Drive, had previously planned to raise lot rents, using $741 as its basis of the average cost in the area. The park has more than 230 homesites, according to its website.
But no one in or around Norway, or even in coastal Maine towns, paid anywhere near that and Sun Communities refused to share the data it used to determine the figure, according to Norway park residents.
In Norway’s proposed ordinance, lot rent fees will be limited to the most recently posted annual percentage change in the consumer price index plus 1%, not to exceed 5%, and calculated against each resident’s existing rent or fee.
Some categories of parks would be exempt: 1. those owned by a cooperative of residents; 2. those parks with lots subject to any agreement that is more restrictive than the ordinance; and 3. those parks in which all lots are subject to an aggregate lot rent and fee amount or above the affordability threshold, defined as 20% of the current fair market rent for existing housing, based on the two-bedroom column for the relevant nonmetropolitan county (Oxford), as posted by the Maine State Housing Authority.
If passed on Oct. 15, the ordinance will go into effect immediately.

title: Cat food investigation finds heavy metals, pesticides and plastic chemicals
text:
Cat food investigation finds heavy metals, pesticides and plastic chemicals
Nearly all tested cat foods contain toxic plastic contaminants, the herbicide glyphosate and heavy metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic, according to a new investigation.
“Most cats eat the same foods nearly every day, with little variation,” said report author Molly Hamilton, executive director of the Clean Label Project, a Colorado nonprofit that tests consumer products for contaminants and certifies those meeting its standards.
“The contaminants are an ongoing exposure that may accumulate in cats’ bodies over their lifetimes,” Hamilton said. “For example, chronic kidney disease is among the most common causes of death in older cats — the kidneys play a major role in filtering heavy metals.”
Related video above | Cat stuck in home's wall for nearly a week: See the rescue
Toxins were found in all types of cat food — wet, dry and air- or freeze-dried — even in products labeled as natural and nutritionally superior, according to the analysis released Friday.
“Cat owners increasingly choose premium meats, organic vegetables and cleaner labels, assuming higher prices and quality ingredients mean healthier food,” Hamilton told CNN. “That’s not necessarily the case.”
Clean Label published a similar assessment of dog food in February that found three to 13 times more heavy metals than human food. Lead and cadmium exposure has been linked to canine cancer, a leading cause of death in dogs.
Heavy metals occur naturally in soil, water and air, but agricultural, industrial and mining pollution can increase and spread contamination. Plastics and other contaminants may also enter food during manufacturing, the report said.
“Overall, this appears to be a reasonably conducted analysis,” said Ryan Babadi, science director for Toxic Free Future, a nonprofit consumer product safety organization.
“Major retailers have the responsibility to require their suppliers to eliminate harmful chemicals from pet food and packaging — chemicals that are already being phased out or banned in many other products,” said Babadi, who was not involved in the investigation.
The Pet Food Institute, which represents manufacturers of cat foods, told CNN in an email that pet food manufacturers do implement comprehensive food safety and quality assurance programs.
Those include “ingredient specifications, supplier verification, testing protocols, traceability systems, and science-based preventive controls designed to ensure products are safe, nutritious, and consistent,” said Elise Fennig, the CEO for the Pet Food Institute.
“Cat owners should feel confident that the food they feed their pets is safe and produced according to rigorous regulatory and quality standards.”
Lead found in 99% of all samples
The investigation tested 100 top-selling cat foods for more than 122 contaminants, including lead, arsenic, cadmium, mercury, pesticides, herbicides and phthalates, the plastic chemicals linked to an increased risk of death in humans.
Lead was found in 99%, cadmium in 96% and arsenic in 94% of cat food samples across 62 brands. Contamination varied by product type — wet, dry, and air- or freeze-dried — and the type of protein, such as poultry, beef or fish.
Cadmium is classified as a human carcinogen and harms the kidneys and bones. A buildup of lead in the body damages nearly every major organ system. Inorganic arsenic — the type found in soil and water — is also a known human carcinogen.
Dry cat food contained roughly three times more lead than wet or air-dried products. No level of lead is safe for people, and children are most vulnerable: Their bodies absorb up to 50% of ingested lead, compared with about 10% for adults, which can cause stunted growth, decreased IQ, hyperactivity and irritability.
Cats and other small pets also absorb more than larger ones, yet few regulations control contaminants in pet food, Hamilton said. “The absence of safety standards does not mean a contaminant is safe. Most guidelines are designed for farm animals, not kittens or 15-year-old housecats.”
Fish and seafood — popular proteins for cats — had the strongest association with mercury and cadmium, the report found. Because microorganisms in water turn regular mercury into methylmercury, a toxic chemical form that binds tightly to fish tissue, the heavy metal accumulates to higher levels in aquatic animals.
Mercury is toxic to the nervous, digestive and immune systems, as well as the kidneys, lungs and skin, according to the World Health Organization.
Mercury levels were about 18 times higher and cadmium levels about 2.5 times higher in fish- or seafood-based cat foods than in foods made with other proteins. Wet versions of seafood products contained the most mercury — nearly 28 times as much as wet foods made with other meats, especially poultry.
“As the main protein, chicken was better when it came to mercury and cadmium, but we saw higher rates of lead and herbicides in chicken,” Hamilton said. “It’s a whack-a-mole situation — which contaminant do you want to whack?
“That doesn’t mean all fish options were high in mercury — levels depend on manufacturers’ quality-control testing,” she added. “We certified several fish-based foods.”
Nearly 85% of poultry-based foods met Clean Label Project’s purity standard compared with 25.7% of fish and seafood products.
“Every product in this study was purchased at retail, and no brand had any role in selecting products, conducting testing or analyzing the results. No brand saw the results before publication,” Hamilton said.
Glyphosate and phthalates
Although cats are carnivores, many manufacturers add produce to cat food for its antioxidants, minerals and vitamins. Unless grown organically, those plants may be exposed to pesticides. A national report found the vast majority of 100 popular fruits and vegetables tested positive for a wide variety of bug-killers.
The Clean Label investigation tested for glyphosate, which is agriculture’s most widely used herbicide. Glyphosate was found at detectable levels in 37% of products, and cat food with more plants in the first 10 ingredients had higher glyphosate levels.
The WHO’s International Agency for Research on Cancer classified glyphosate in 2015 as “probably carcinogenic to humans.” The US Environmental Protection Agency disagrees.
“On average, cat food with two plant ingredients among the top 10 on the label had roughly 40% more glyphosate than a similar food with one plant ingredient. Cat food with five plant ingredients had nearly four times as much,” Hamilton said.
Another “very concerning finding” was the widespread presence of di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate, or DEHP, a chemical used in PVC plastics and some food-contact materials that is linked to cancer, birth defects and other health concerns, Babadi said.
“It was detected in about half of the products tested, with the highest levels in canned and pouch products. DEHP contamination could potentially occur during food processing, including through contact with PVC tubing or other farm or food processing equipment,” he said.
“It is encouraging to see those harmful bisphenols, including BPA, were found less frequently, suggesting pet food can be produced and packaged without these endocrine-disrupting chemicals,” Babadi added.
The research did have limitations. Each product was tested from a single batch. Therefore, the study could not capture differences that might occur between batches of the same product.
“Brands that routinely screen for contaminants of concern tend to have more consistent results over time,” Hamilton said. “In addition, this study compares contaminant levels across products in each category of wet, dry and air- or freeze-dried. It does not determine whether a specific product will cause harm to a cat.”
What pet owners can do
If your cat favors seafood, vary its diet with chicken or other proteins to limit daily exposure to mercury and cadmium. Read the ingredient list carefully, however, as cat foods without fish in their name may still contain seafood ingredients and thus higher levels of mercury and cadmium.
According to the Clean Label report, wet or air-dried products are preferable to dry food for lower lead exposure, while avoiding foods with plants in the top 10 ingredients may lower pesticide exposure.
In addition, don’t rely on the first listed ingredient to gauge toxins. In more than a third of tested products, it didn’t tell the full story, Hamilton said.
“The first ingredient on a food label is often the biggest selling point because ingredients are listed by weight,” she said. “We tested and found the first ingredient is not always a reliable indicator of what the food contains, nor does it predict which contaminant may be present at the highest levels.”
One reason: Manufacturers need not disclose which part of a fish or other protein they use, Hamilton said. Wild salmon, for example, may sound healthier, but its liver, kidneys, intestines, head and skin store more chemical pollutants than the rest of the fish.
“Yet you have no idea what part of the fish is in cat food,” Hamilton said. “The best way to know what’s in your cat’s food is to contact the manufacturer and determine if they test the food – and how frequently they test.
“Because even if they were to tell you what part of the fish that they’re using, without testing, there’s no way to know how free of contaminants it really is.”
It’s also a good idea for consumers to reach out to the company making their cat’s favorite food brand and inquire about testing and quality control standards, experts say.
“Pet owners should take action and urge brands and retailers to ensure toxic chemicals and plastics are not hiding in cat food and its packaging,” Babadi said. “Pets, as part of our families, deserve food that is safe from toxic chemicals.”

title: Dupuis for Hancock County Sheriff
text:
To the Editor:
I believe going forward the election for Hancock County Sheriff is one of the most important elections in Hancock County this year. I am a lifelong Republican, but I have no problem voting for the Democratic candidate Dakota Dupuis.
I have worked with and for both candidates and Lieutenant Dupuis has the necessary skills and experience to successfully lead the sheriff’s department in the near and distant future.
The sheriff’s department has four core values: professionalism, courage, excellence and respect. Lt. Dupuis exemplifies each of these core values each day.
He has been leading the patrol/detective units for approximately three years. He has been actively involved in the budget process and the day-to-day operations of the sheriff’s department.
He is young (not inexperienced) and brings a fresh perspective to the management of the sheriff’s department.
Please join me in voting for Dakota Dupuis for Hancock County Sheriff.
Jon Mahon
Surry

title: USDA considers adapting farm-style safety net for fishermen
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Top federal agriculture officials visited Maine this week to evaluate whether crop insurance can be expanded to protect the state’s multimillion dollar lobster industry.
The visit by U.S. Department of Agriculture Undersecretary Richard Fordyce and Risk Management Agency Administrator Pat Swanson comes as the agency increasingly looks to integrate seafood producers into traditional agricultural safety nets.
Federal crop insurance allows farmers to buy government-subsidized policies that pay out in weeks to months after natural disasters or market drops cause severe revenue losses. In contrast, lobstermen rely on federal fishery disaster declarations that can take three to five years to distribute aid, which industry analysts call far too slow for small operators.
“We are a small-boat, owner-operated fishery made up of thousands of independent businesses, so programs designed for agriculture or other food-producing sectors will not necessarily translate neatly to lobster,” said Patrice McCarron, director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association.
However, McCarron called the visit “an important first step” toward determining whether existing USDA programs can be adapted or new approaches developed to better support Maine lobstermen in their role as food producers for the world.
During a dockside roundtable in Stonington on Tuesday, industry leaders emphasized that lobstermen face severe market swings and price crashes rather than physical catch loss alone. Fordyce, a corn and soybean farmer from Missouri, noted that lobstermen favored revenue protection over simple yield guarantees.
“Just talking with the lobstermen, I think they were probably more inclined to try to find a product or try to find a path forward that would be more supportive of total revenue,” Fordyce said. “I was quite surprised by the data that’s available as far as supporting catch numbers.”
Last year’s lobster catch was valued at $461.4 million — 7.5% below the 10-year average, and, when adjusted for inflation, 20% down from 2024, state data shows.
Curt Brown, president of Bold Coast Seafood in Prospect Harbor, hosted the delegation and highlighted the shared reality between ocean and land harvesters.
“I was struck by how many of the same challenges we face in seafood are also challenges that farmers across the country face every day,” Brown said. “There is a lot we can learn from each other.”
Seafood industry consultant Noah Oppenheim said bringing Midwest agricultural leaders to coastal Maine provided crucial perspective, especially the similarities between the rural fishing communities in Maine and the rural farming communities in the Midwest.
While the visit was focused on ways to manage the industry’s risks, representatives also used the time to drive home other ways the agency can help water-based food producers like they support land-based farmers, including equal access to loan, grant, purchasing and marketing programs.
“The agency seems wide open to focus on all of this at once,” Oppenheim said. “Congress knows this is a bipartisan feel-good issue. We need to be eating more domestic seafood. It’s the right thing to do to have seafood be an equal part of our food system.”
Oppenheim said opportunities for fishermen have expanded since the USDA created its Office of Seafood in April. One of its top priorities is to find ways for fishermen to tap into the same federal programs and safety nets as the nation’s potato and dairy farmers.
Addressing expectations regarding a timeline, Fordyce cautioned that any official expansion must ultimately be approved by the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation board. However, because local advocates have worked on the issue for several years, he said “a lot of that preliminary work has been kind of done.”
While a full rollout for lobster insurance remains down the road, Fordyce emphasized that establishing direct working relationships between Washington officials and Maine coastal leaders was the immediate, vital outcome of the trip.

title: Bowdoinham author publishes history of Texas’ longest river
text:
It makes sense that a river historian would choose live in a town at the confluence of six rivers. Bowdoinham’s rural character, and its many rivers, piqued Scot McFarlane’s interest before he’d ever seen the town.
McFarlane released his first book, “The River that Made Texas: A Forgotten History of the Trinity” on Sept. 29.
He grew up in rural Texas, along the Trinity River and became interested in river history. At 18, he made a documentary about a river, which was about to be dammed. He said he started the project expecting to focus on the loss of endangered plants, but quickly pivoted to the people who would be displaced.
McFarlane has been studying river history since he was an undergraduate student at Bowdoin College — his honors project focused on pollution in the Androscoggin River. As a doctorate student at Columbia University, he turned his attention back to Texas.
“We all just end up returning to the rivers of our youth, and the Trinity was my river,” McFarlane said.
Though the Trinity River is a key economic and recreational waterway that flows through Dallas-Fort Worth and near Houston, he said no one had previously written a comprehensive history. McFarlane said he thinks this is due to the river’s poor reputation, and some unsavory aspects of its history — for instance, pollution and slavery. The river, the longest to run entirely within Texas, is also shielded by infrastructure, including levees and high bridges.
“There are all these sort of actual physical things, in its history and in the landscape around it, that are hiding it from view,” said McFarlane.
Most of his research was conducted in archives — he went to over 40 of them — but he also talked with people who wanted to share family stories about the Trinity. Many of these concerned deaths that happened on the river. Despite the often dark accounts, McFarlane said hearing them was a highlight of the research process.
“People have felt compelled to share those stories, and they trust me with that,” he said. “Making those connections is a powerful feeling.”
He said he is drawn to studying the history of rivers because it often yields surprising results.
“They’re one of the more unpredictable forces of the natural world,” he said. “(They are) very much shaped by us, and shape us.”
McFarlane now lives on Merrymeeting Bay. He said that his favorite river in Maine is the Muddy River, the smallest and wildest of Bowdoinham’s six rivers.
“It’s so very small, but when you go back there, you feel more disconnected from everything … it’s a special spot,” he said.
McFarlane said that although the book was published by the academic University of North Carolina Press, is intended to be a “crossover book” — able to be used as a textbook, but also enjoyable for anyone who is interested in Texas history or rivers in general. So far, he said it’s selling well. As of Oct. 1, the paperback was the top new release seller in the Environmental Policy category.
“The River That Made Texas: A Forgotten History of the Trinity” is available online in Kindle or paperback form, and can be ordered from local bookstores.

title: Knox County administrator is resigning
text:
ROCKLAND — Knox County Administrator Amber Christie announced Wednesday that she was resigning her post effective Oct. 30.
The county commissioners met Thursday evening to formally accept the resignation.
“Stepping away from this role has been an incredibly difficult decision, and I want to sincerely apologize for any disruption or inconvenience my departure may cause the Commission, staff, and our community. The choice was not made lightly, but after much reflection and discussion, I have determined that it is necessary for me to step down at this time to focus on my personal health, family, and other commitments that require my full attention,” Christie said in her resignation letter.
Christie will remain available to assist with wrapping up ongoing projects and supporting a smooth transition, Commission Chair Ed Glaser said.
“The Commission, county leadership and county staff will be working to ensure that county services continue uninterrupted as we navigate the transition” the county said in a brief statement.
The Knox County Commission will begin discussing the long-term process and timeline for filling the Administrator position in the coming weeks.
Christie has served as county administrator since December 2024, succeeding Richard “Lance” Govang who served in the post for four months before being placed on paid leave and then resigning in September 2024. No reason was ever publicly released for his departure.
Christie was hired as human resources manager in February 2023.
Govang succeeded longtime Administrator Andrew Hart who resigned in January 2023.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: New Gloucester man in critical condition after striking tractor trailer in Auburn
text:
AUBURN — A New Gloucester man was left in critical condition Thursday night after slamming into a tractor-trailer at the corner of Washington Street and Kittyhawk Avenue.
Jonah King, 29, of New Gloucester, was traveling south on Washington Street when he went through a red light at the Kittyhawk Avenue intersection, Auburn police said in a statement on Facebook.
According to police, King struck a tractor-trailer operated by Peter Fontaine, 46, of North Waterboro, who was turning left from Kittyhawk Avenue through a green light.
King was transported to Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston with life-threatening injuries. He was later transferred to Maine Medical Center in Portland.
Auburn police said the department’s crash reconstruction team is investigating with help from the Maine State Police Commercial Vehicle Unit.

title: Obituary: Marie Dola Violette Shaw
text:
GROTON, Conn. – Marie Dola Violette Shaw, 85, of Groton, passed away peacefully with her family present on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026.
Born on Jan. 31, 1941, in Augusta, Maine, to the late George and Clemence (Dutil) Violette, Marie is survived by her loving husband of 67 years, Bill. Besides her husband Bill, she is survived by her daughters Nancy (Jeffrey) and Julie (Gary), her son Billy; grandchildren JoAnn, Melina, Celina, and Jacob; great-grandchildren Jonathan, Jacoby, Hayden, and Chloe; brother Roger, sisters Cecile, Mary Ann, and Linda, and the adopted Timothy Lehouillier family. She was preceded in death by her daughter, Dawna, and sister Constance.
Marie was raised in Hallowell, Maine on the family farm. Her chores were tending various animals and harvesting the yearly crops. She attended Hallowell schools. She met her future husband, Bill, at the local roller-skating rink. They started dating after Bill joined the US Navy, coming home each weekend and he soon won her heart. They were married at Sacred Heart Church in Hallowell on Thanksgiving Day, 1958. Marie became a proud Navy wife taking care of their children and becoming mom, dad, confidant and occasionally family peacemaker. She kept the family together during Bill’s many patrols protecting our country during the Cold War. There was a lot of moving around, seven times to be exact. She always had a positive attitude and looked forward to the new adventures while supporting family needs. The most difficult move was having to fly to Puerto Rico by herself with four young children, Billy being just two months old. She was a trooper and the travel happened without any hitches.
Marie always had a wish to do arts and crafts. She started with ceramics. Getting completely involved, she purchased her own oven and made nativity sets for her sisters. Everyone that saw them wanted one. So, we know how that goes, she made more. Also, she would make lamps, decorative figurines and Christmas decorations. Her favorite was the Christmas trees. Marie also took up sewing. She designed and made clothes for dolls, which again everyone wanted. Her reward was winning many blue ribbons at competitions.
Along with everything else, Marie decided to go back to work. She got a job at the Naval Submarine Base. She planned to work until the children finished school. Twenty-six years later she retired. Starting off at the Submarine Base Galley, she worked her way up to Supervisor. Her responsibilities included all versions of food preparation, serving and overall cleanliness of food preparation facilities. She was on the team that won the NEY award for the best shore activity galley, not once but twice. Marie was also awarded two “Outstanding Performance” awards for her efforts.
Marie’s family and friends always came first. She will be remembered for her genuine caring for others. Marie instilled faith and hope in all who knew her. Everyone came before her. If they were happy, she would be happy. There were many times when she would sit the children down and explain how growing up is not easy. She taught them to share with others.
Marie was deeply loved, and her absence will be felt in ways both large and small – in quiet moments, in familiar places, in stories told, and in the memories that continue to bring smiles through tears. We will miss her beyond words, but her love, her laughter, and the many moments she gave us will remain with us always.
The family would like to extend their appreciation and gratitude to the Yale-New Haven Healthcare team for their caring and professional services during Marie’s difficult times. We would like to give a special thanks to Dr. Charles Walcott and Dr Valarie Popkin for all their caring and support during this period.
Services will be private in the family plot at Riverside Cemetery, Pittston, Maine.
Byles Memorial Home, 99 Huntington Street, New London is assisting with the arrangements. Please visit http://www.byles.com to sign the guestbook.

name may be made to:

title: Susan Collins should give an interview to ProPublica
text:
I was a longtime Auburn resident and used to be a Republican.
As reported recently by ProPublica, a serious and potentially career-ending allegation was made against Sen. Susan Collins. Did she illegally channel government contracts to a Hawaiian defense contractor that paid her campaign through a fake company it concocted to hide what it was doing?
Will Sen. Collins agree to do a town hall or an interview with the ProPublica journalists to discuss the facts and points detailed in the ProPublica reporting? It appears her response thus far has been to have her staff blow smoke and for Collins to shoot the messenger, i.e., the journalists at ProPublica. She has essentially taken a clue from our president and yelled “fake news.”
But, ProPublica is a respected reporting source dedicated to holding government representatives to account. It report that it has reviewed thousands of emails never previously revealed, and it has interviewed many persons close to the case who have corroborated much of the reporting. It has the receipts, unfortunately for Collins.
Why did her campaign staff agree to accept $150,000 from a shell company hiding the source as a government contractor?
On the face of it, the ProPublica article is damning to Collins. Other than repeating “fake news,” how can she defend herself? I have no idea. But, for the first time in over 25 years, the public should hear from her live and in person. She should meet with voters. Failing her agreement to do so, she should sit for a thorough interview with ProPublica. Mainers deserve to know, to paraphrase Richard M. Nixon, if their U.S. senator is a crook.
Daniel Mawhinney
Portland

title: Maine State Archives launches expanded digital access
How geography plays a role in overwhelmed animal shelters
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (InvestigateTV) — Many animal shelters across America are overwhelmed, and where animals are located is a big reason why.
In regions like the South, shelters are under-resourced and over-capacity, packed with dogs and cats waiting for adoption. For many, that wait can be fatal. In 2024, U.S. shelters euthanized more than 600,000 animals.
Experts say homes often exist for these animals, but the animals are in the wrong place.
It’s a geographic mismatch the ASPCA and other groups are working to fix by moving pets hundreds of miles by land and air.
A new addition at home
Inside Johnny Hunter’s home, it’s clear he has a hobby. Over the years, he’s put together more than 100 Lego sets, with his apartment packed wall to wall.
Now he’s making room for someone new.
In early 2025, Hunter adopted a dog named Abby from Wayside Waifs in his hometown of Kansas City.
“It’s been awesome. I mean, she’s really changed my life,” Hunter said. “She’s kind of like a celebrity in my life.”
Abby, a 3-year-old pit bull mix, likely never would have become Hunter’s pet because she’s not from Missouri.
Abby ended up in Kansas City from Arkansas. The ASPCA brought her as part of a program that moves pets to places with more space and more adopters.
Hunter believes that relocating Abby “probably did” save her life.
How the program works
Casey Waugh has worked at Wayside Waifs for more than a decade and knows Abby’s story well.
“Her life completely changed because of this program and because of Wayside Waifs,” Waugh said.
Wayside Waifs has been part of the ASPCA’s national relocation network since 2010.
“We knew that there were homeless animals outside of Kansas City. We could reach our arms a little bit further and help those animals,” Waugh said.
Wayside Waifs is a destination shelter, meaning animals are transported from other shelters that may not have the resources to care for them.
In 2025, it took in about 850 animals through the program.
“Unfortunately, a lot of these animals wouldn’t make it,” Waugh.
While shelter euthanasia rates have declined over the last decade, shelters in many communities still take in more adoptable dogs and cats than they can place locally.
“There are often animals at source shelters that are at the end of opportunities that people have utilized all of the foster homes they can possibly utilize in their community,” said Karen Walsh, the ASPCA’s senior director of relocation.
Walsh said the relocation program has been operating since 2014 and partners with more than 140 shelters nationally.
She said shelters around the country are dealing with overpopulation, especially in the South and Midwest. Weather in those regions is more conducive to longer breeding seasons, and robust spay and neuter programs are less readily available.
“Our country is really out of balance in that area,” Walsh said.
Restoring that balance is a massive logistical challenge, according to Walsh.
It starts with more than 20 vehicles on the road seven days a week, along with locations across the country where animals can stay overnight during longer trips. Vehicles never travel more than 650 miles without stopping.
“We want to make sure that the drivers are safe and that the animals are safe,” Walsh said.
The program also relocates animals by plane. Flights take off weekly, sometimes carrying as many as 100 pets.
“I’ve never been on a runway where a flight was taking off where everybody wasn’t crying,” Walsh said.
Over the last decade, more than 300,000 animals have been moved through the program.
“This program absolutely saves lives,” Walsh said.
Health and safety standards
To ensure the health of the animals and prevent the spread of disease, Walsh said the ASPCA requires source and destination shelters to meet guidelines established by the Association of Shelter Veterinarians and the American Veterinary Medical Association.
“You always have to take the pet’s health and well-being in concern, no matter what you do,” said Dr. Michael Bailey, former president of the American Veterinary Medical Association.
The organization does not oversee relocation programs, but he said he believes the ASPCA is trying to carry out the work responsibly, and the details matter.
“Regular stops, making sure that they have time to exercise, that they have time to relieve themselves so that they do not get stressed in the movement so they do not become overheated,” Bailey said.
Bailey cautioned that moving animals can come with risks.
“The stress can lower their immune system. So, they are susceptible to new diseases,” Bailey said. “It also means that they can get hurt in the transport process themselves.”
He said veterinarian-issued health certificates can help confirm whether animals are healthy enough to travel, and many states require them across state lines. Beyond that, he said oversight varies widely.
Walsh has seen issues with some transfers conducted outside of the ASPCA’s program.
“We see some people driving from Texas to Canada and things like that, not being able to stop. Just switching over, switching over,” she said. “That’s so dangerous that we really try to encourage people not to do that.”
Walsh said the organization also educates on safe relocation and advocates for broader changes that address the root cause of shelter overpopulation.
“It’s just the beginning of a safety net program that allows the pop-off valve to open and the animals to leave so that people can be like, okay, now what are we doing this week to make a change?” Walsh said.
She stressed the importance of programs that prioritize low-cost spay and neuter practices, community engagement, and progressive adoption and foster services.
A new chapter
Since adopting Abby, Hunter has started volunteering at Wayside Waifs. “The more dogs we could save, the better.”
Hunter said he’ll always have a passion for building worlds, brick by brick, and now, one animal at a time.
“She really is my best friend. She’s just made every aspect of my life better,” Hunter said.
States are slowly adopting stricter regulations for animal shelters and rescue transfers.
In December 2025, New York began enforcing a law that requires licensing, health evaluations and transport safety standards for animal relocations into the state. Similar oversight exists in states including Oregon and Massachusetts.
The ASPCA said this relocation pipeline works because willing adopters are waiting at the other end.

title: UMaine football looking to snap 4-game losing streak
text:
The University of Maine’s struggling football team will try to end its four-game losing skid on Saturday when Coastal Athletic Association newcomer Sacred Heart ventures to Orono for a 3:30 p.m. contest.
It will be Military Appreciation Day for the Black Bears, who are 1-4 overall and 1-1 in the CAA. Sacred Heart is 1-3 and 1-2, respectively, but is coming off an impressive 20-13 victory over New Hampshire. UMaine will look to rebound from a 43-17 drubbing at the hands of Elon.
The Black Bears will try to provide a consistent performance after a loss that involved yet another inefficient offensive showing, back-to-back blocked punts and a defensive outing that was marred by explosive plays as Elon scored on plays of 57, 55 and 39 yards.
UMaine has played four of its first five games on the road, including Football Bowl Subdivision games at Appalachian State, a 55-3 loss, and Boston College (22-16).
FBS schools have many more resources than Football Championship Subdivision programs like UMaine.
UMaine head coach Jordan Stevens said it is “terrific” to be home and is looking for his team to “play to its identity.”
And he pointed out that his team will have its hands full against a Sacred Heart team that is not only coming off a win over New Hampshire, but it also battled Elon much more competitively than his team, losing 24-21 on a field goal with 1:19 left in its previous game.
“Sacred Heart is well-coached. They are competitive. They stay in games. We are going to have to do a great job controlling their quarterback (Poochie Snyder) and keeping him in check,” Stevens said. “His ability to scramble and get the ball downfield is really impressive.”
Snyder completed 8-of-10 passes for 95 yards and rushed for 67 yards and a touchdown against UNH.
Snyder has completed 67.95 percent of his passes for 558 yards and six touchdowns and has been intercepted just once. He is also the Pioneers’ second-leading rusher with 197 yards on 50 carries behind Chuck Webb’s 237 yards on 63 carries.
Snyder’s completion percentage is 13th best in the FCS and the team’s 179.5 rushing yards per game is second best in the CAA.
Jason Palmieri (17 catches-154 yards) and Dean Hangey (13-for-152) are their top receivers and the defense features linebacker Myles Hamilton (32 tackles, 2 pass breakups) and strong safety Kymari Latney (22 tackles).
Stevens said earlier in the week that he will re-evaluate the quarterback position and, based on the depth chart, Eddie Buehler has kept his starting job despite a 14-for-35 showing against Elon.
Buehler has completed 55.7 percent of his passes for 815 yards and four touchdowns with six interceptions.
One of the few bright spots at Elon was the running game, which churned out a season-best 167 yards on 34 carries behind Rashawn Marshall’s 105 yards on 14 carries.
He now has 281 yards on 64 carries.
Nick Laughlin (19 catches-189 yards) and Evan Wallace (17-for-148) are their top receivers and the defense features linebacker Sam Oppenheimer (49 tackles, 2 interceptions) and strong safety Jeremiah McGill (34 tackles) along with linebacker Noah Carpenter (33 tackles).
Oppenheimer is 13th in the nation among players at the 124 FCS schools with 49 tackles and his 32 tackles are fourth-best.
UMaine is last in the CAA in points per game (14.2) and next-to-last in yards per game (272.6) and rushing yards (94.2).
Sacred Heart is third in the CAA in total defense, allowing 325.5 yards per game.
Elsewhere in Maine
The state’s six Division III football schools are all winless heading into Saturday. They are a combined 0-17 on the season.
Bangor’s Husson University (0-4 and 0-1 in the Conference of New England) will entertain Western New England (2-2, 1-0) in a CNE game at 1 p.m. at the Winkin Sports Complex; Castine’s Maine Maritime Academy (0-3, 0-1 in CNE) will travel to Dudley, Massachusetts to take on Nichols College (1-3, 1-0) at 2 p.m. and the University of New England in Biddeford, 0-4 and 0-1, will host 15th ranked Endicott College (4-0, 1-0) at noon.
Maine Maritime Academy, which restored its football program in 2023 after it had been suspended for COVID-related issues and financial concerns in 2020, is looking to snap a 35-game losing streak.
The three New England Small College Athletic Conference schools will also be in action as 0-2 Bowdoin of Brunswick visits 2-0 Amherst at 1 p.m., Waterville’s Colby College (0-2) will trek to 1-1 Middlebury, also for a 1 p.m. kickoff, and 0-2 Bates will await 1-1 Tufts for a 7 p.m. game in Lewiston.

title: Court tosses manslaughter sentence after AI video of road-rage victim used in court
text:
CHANDLER, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) — A convict will have to be resentenced after the Arizona Court of Appeals vacated his sentence because an AI video of the victim affected the judge’s decision.
Gabriel Horcasitas was sentenced to 10 1/2 years in prison last year for the road-rage killing of Christopher Pelkey in November 2021.
The victim’s family created an AI video of Pelkey using a previously recorded video, a picture and a script written by his sister. That video was played during the sentencing.
The sentencing judge noted “obvious forgiveness” expressed in Pelkey’s AI statement before handing down the punishment to Horcasitas.
During the sentencing, the judge said he “loved” the video and that Pelkey was able “to speak from his heart” as the family envisioned.
In its decision announced Wednesday, the state Court of Appeals said the sentencing judge was prejudiced by the AI video, which made his decision fundamentally unfair.
The Court of Appeals said Horcasitas’ manslaughter conviction is upheld, but the 10 1/2-year sentence is vacated and he will be resentenced.

title: Cyclospora found at Mexican farmed linked to lettuce outbreak, FDA says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Food and Drug Administration said Friday that its inspectors detected cyclospora at the Mexican farm blamed for the largest foodborne illness outbreak of the parasite in U.S. history.
Despite the finding, the FDA said it’s unclear how the parasite got into lettuce at Taylor Farms’ facility. The agency said it has now closed its investigation into the outbreak, which led to nearly 13,000 cases of diarrhea and other illnesses across the U.S.
The announcement comes more than six weeks after the agency sent its investigators to the farm in Guanajuato, Mexico. The visit was the agency’s first time there in more than seven years following a steep drop in international food safety inspections after the COVID-19 pandemic.
FDA inspectors said Friday they found cyclospora in two places: a wastewater tank and a drainage ditch used for lettuce cultivation. While it’s unclear how the contamination took place, the FDA said the samples provide “strong epidemiological data” linking the outbreak to the Taylor Farms site.
U.S. officials last month declared the outbreak had ended.
Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that commonly causes watery diarrhea “with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements,” according to the CDC. The illness, called cyclosporiasis, is less common than foodborne illnesses caused by other germs, including salmonella and E. coli.
The parasite is spread through human feces, and it still isn’t clear how sewage could have contaminated enough food to sicken so many people.
Regulators from Mexico’s food safety authority announced in August that their own investigation did not detect cyclospora in the lettuce or water at the facility. That conclusion came days after the FDA was forced to retract a faulty test result that had incorrectly identified cyclospora in a sample of lettuce from Taylor Farms collected at the border.

title: Here’s how experts map Maine’s drought — and how you can help
text:
Do you know how to measure soil moisture levels or have a deep understanding of your region’s hydrology?
No?
Well, it doesn’t matter — if you want to help inform those responsible for analyzing drought conditions across Maine and the country, all you need is your own observations.
It doesn’t take a scientist to tell you that your lawn is turning brown, the pond you frequent is low, or your well is drying up. In fact, that’s where you’re the expert.
During a drought, one can’t help but feel a little helpless. It’s not like we can make it rain.
But you can help, because the public’s input is taken into account when the weekly U.S. Drought Monitor maps are put together. The maps and data are used to analyze drought impacts, and federal agencies consider them when they weigh whether to declare drought-related disasters.
Here’s how it all works — and where the average Mainer fits into the equation:
ONE NATION, UNDER DROUGHT
Those yellow, orange and red drought maps of Maine don’t really end at the state line.
The U.S. Drought Monitor was formed in 1999 by the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Meteorologists and climatologists from those entities take turns as the lead author of the national map, usually rotating every two weeks.
Precipitation is a major factor in analyzing a drought, but far from the only one. Streamflow, reservoir levels, temperatures, soil moisture, evaporation and vegetation health all play a role as well.
The author will compile that data (much of it obtained via satellite) and come up with a draft of that week’s map.
But numbers don’t tell the full story, nor can one meteorologist or climatologist. That’s where regional and local experts step in.
LOCAL EXPERTS
Sarah Jamison, senior service hydrologist with the National Weather Service office in Gray, is one of those experts.
Every week, she and other members of the Northeast Drought Early Warning System review the Drought Monitor’s draft and weigh in with their knowledge of the region.
“They’re getting not just their own assessment, not just the raw numbers, but they’re getting the more localized feedback,” Jamison said. “We don’t define what it should be for New England, but we recommend some changes.”
Local experts are necessary because the data isn’t one-size-fits-all.
“The same kind of dryness in Utah may reflect completely different impacts as it would to Cumberland County,” Jamison said. “There is climatology that’s also weighed into this.”
The Drought Monitor says it consults hundreds of regional and local experts. The weekly maps are, essentially, a (very) well-educated guess.
“It’s definitely a consolidation of a lot of contributors and a lot of information, balanced by the impact reports that they do solicit,” Jamison said.
HOW TO CONTRIBUTE
There’s no way for the experts who contribute to the weekly Drought Monitor maps to be everywhere at once, which is where Condition Monitoring Observer Reports come in. Anyone (18 or older, in most states) can find and fill out the form at droughtimpacts.unl.edu or drought.gov, or via the ArcGIS Survey123 app.
The observer report starts by asking for some basic information, like your location, familiarity with the area and general observations.
Then, there are over a dozen optional questions pertaining to a wide range of topics, from livestock and crop production to home and garden impacts. There are also questions on community health, water supply, hydropower, fish spawning and tourism impacts.
“My wetland pond has dried up, my well has gone dry, my lawn has turned brown, the trees are stressed and dropping acorns,” Jamison said, rattling off examples of various reports that help the experts. “It doesn’t matter exactly what magnitude of impact. Any kind of impacts that are driven by drought are all weighed.”
At the end, you can type in any additional comments and upload photos.
HOW THAT HELPS
The color of your backyard on the next week’s map isn’t just going to change because you made a submission. Conditions can vary from lawn to lawn and farm to farm, even in the same town or neighborhood.
“That’s one of the most unique things about drought,” Jamison said. “If we have a snowstorm with 8 inches, the impacts are relatively uniform across much of the area. With a drought … they’re going to vary, and that’s just natural.”
What can catch experts’ eyes are common reports that actually go against what the data is saying.
“If we believe, for example, it’s not a very significant drought, but then we start to see reports of ‘wells are going dry,’ ‘ponds are drying up,’ ‘crops are failing,’” Jamison said, “those kinds of things really can help be the checks and balances or the gut check on what we’re processing and evaluating.
“We don’t have people literally walking the area to make these designations,” Jamison added. “We have to rely on the tools in our arsenal, and then the reports that we get from people in the field.”

title: Bruins rally for overtime win
text:
WINNIPEG, Manitoba — Elias Lindholm tied it on a tip with 1:38 left in regulation and JJ Peterka scored at 3:21 of overtime to give the Boston Bruins a 4-3 victory over the Winnipeg Jets on Friday night.
David Pastrnak set up both late goals, with goalie Jeremy Swayman off for an extra attacker on Lindholm’s goal.
Peterka also had the winner Tuesday night against the New York Rangers in the Bruins’ opener.
Hampus Lindholm and James Hagens also scored, and Swayman made 30 saves.

title: Presenting community, convenience and affordability at any stage of life
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
• Two life-stage-appropriate communities make up one well-established and managed neighborhood.
• Today’s manufactured homes are modern, energy-efficient and spacious.
•Located just off Route 1 in Scarborough, the neighborhood has close access to restaurants, shopping, medical facilities, Portland’s art scene, I-295 and the turnpike.
For the past 83 years, State Manufactured Homes has been a fixture along Route 1, giving generations of people an affordable place to call home.
The company was founded by Bob and Agnes Desfosses and remains a locally owned and operated family business. What they started has now continued through four generations. The family has worked to maintain the reputation Bob and Agnes established, built around hard work, honesty and selling well-built, factory-made homes they stand behind.
That philosophy can be seen throughout the company’s two Scarborough communities: Pinecrest, an all-ages community, and Hillcrest, for residents 55 and older. Both are conveniently located just off Route 1 and have been continually updated over the years.
For families, Pinecrest offers the combination of neighborhood living, affordability and access to the Scarborough school district. It is also an attractive option for first-time homebuyers looking for a way to own a home without taking on the price tag that often comes with traditional housing in Greater Portland. With residents of all ages, Pinecrest provides a neighborhood where families can put down roots.
Nearby, the award-winning Hillcrest 55-plus community is tucked behind the State Manufactured Homes office at 126 U.S. Route 1. Designed with older adults in mind, Hillcrest combines attractive new and preowned homes with affordability, low-maintenance living and opportunities to stay active and connected.
Today’s manufactured homes feature modern building methods, including 2-by-6 wall construction, high levels of insulation, draft stops, programmable thermostats and Low-E argon tilt-in windows. Homes meet or exceed Energy Star certification requirements. Inside, the kitchens are spacious and designed for everyday living as well as entertaining. Storage can also be a pleasant surprise.
Residents of both communities have access to amenities. These include a recreation center, exercise equipment, a commercial kitchen, community garden and walking trails along the Nonesuch River. A full-time program director helps keep the calendar busy with bingo, potluck suppers, game nights, holiday activities and other events throughout the year.
Transportation is also available with a 24-passenger wheelchair-accessible bus. And because home would not be the same without four-legged family members, pets are welcome, too!
To take a tour and make Hillcrest or Pinecrest your home, call (207) 883-2512 to speak with Tina, Tracy or Alfie.

title: Tennessee's handling of the death penalty is again questioned after failed execution
text:
Christa Pike’s failed execution followed other death penalty miscues in Tennessee, which performs just a fraction of the nation’s executions but is now halting them for a second time since 2022, reigniting questions over the state’s handling of capital punishment.
Pike, 50, remained on a ventilator and unconscious at a Nashville-area hospital on Friday, according to her attorneys, who say she was poked with needles at least seven times in the state’s death chamber and then hospitalized with burned and blistered arms after being given two doses of lethal drugs.
The unsuccessful attempt was the second failed execution in four months in Tennessee. Since 2022, the state has carried out just four of the more than 140 executions that have taken place nationwide, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Republican Gov. Bill Lee paused executions in the state following the unsuccessful attempt to put Pike to death and ordered an independent investigation into what went wrong, as both critics and supporters of the death penalty called for changes.
“Number one, I think we need to get better people that are doing these executions because I don’t know that they’re trained well enough to be doing this on difficult patients,” said Republican state Sen. Joey Hensley, a family physician, adding that he suspects the IV line was not properly inserted.
Pike’s attorneys say executioners failed to properly set IV lines
Days after the attempt to execute Pike, who received two lethal doses of pentobarbital, she had blisters on her arms from the bleach-like, caustic substance that was injected into her body, her attorneys wrote in an emergency court filing on Friday.
Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” they wrote.
They wrote that instead of “remedying this failure” prison officials prepared and administered a backup set of pentobarbital syringes.
Tennessee has come under fire before
Pike’s case is not the first time Tennessee’s execution practices have drawn criticism.
Earlier this year, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after medical workers placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line, proceeding to attempt to place one into his other arm, his left hand and his left foot, then finally failing to establish a central line.
Lee ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute Carruthers again.
Four years before that, the governor ordered an independent review into capital punishment after abruptly stopping the April 2022 execution of Oscar Smith in the 11th hour when officials became aware of a mishandling of the drugs. Lee paused all executions over a week later after acknowledging the state had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were properly tested.
The report he ordered, released in late December 2022, found that the state hadn’t complied with its own lethal injection process since it was revised in 2018.
In that time period, Tennessee put seven inmates to death — two by injection and five in the electric chair. The report said that in none of those, nor in the execution Lee halted, did the pharmacy conduct the required test for endotoxins, and in one of the lethal injections, the drug midazolam was not tested for potency.
At the time, the state’s lethal injections were performed through a three-drug series of midazolam, vecuronium bromide and potassium chloride. The state later switched to using just pentobarbital.
The report, conducted by former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton, also found that the state’s unidentified executioner had no formal healthcare training and learned the role mainly through on-the-job experience.
After the release of the report, the Tennessee Department of Correction fired its longtime top attorney and another employee.
One of Pike’s attorneys, Steve Ferrell, was skeptical of the progress made since those revelations, saying the investigation resulted in “a less detailed protocol and more secrecy.”
Executioners often have little medical training, expert says
It’s not uncommon for executioners to have minimal medical training, according to Corinna Lain, a law professor at the University of Richmond and author of a book on lethal injections.
Lain said lethal injection has become more popular because it is considered less gruesome and hides the violence of state killing. But she said that, even when states follow protocol, the method still poses risks. A number of attorneys have echoed those concerns in lawsuits, arguing that the method is unconstitutional.
Lain said she has only found about 10 medically licensed doctors in the entire country who work with states on executions. Doctors she interviewed told her that they believed executions to be contrary to their oath to take care of people.
In many ways, executions are shrouded in secrecy. The identity of execution team members, the details about where and how lethal drugs are procured, and in some states even what happens in the death chamber is hidden from public view.
“Tennessee has botched executions so badly that two people this year have survived their own executions,” Lain said. “That’s quite something.”
Still, experts like Jordan Steiker, the co-director of the Capital Punishment Center at the University of Texas, say that the method is likely to continue to be an option for states with the death penalty.
That is in large part, Steiker said, because of a deferential judicial approach to the execution process, which has consistently empowered states to carry out executions.
“I think it gives states confidence that even if they take shortcuts, it’s unlikely that the courts will intervene in their ability to carry out executions,” Steiker said.

title: Secondhand shopping surge: More Americans are buying used clothing
text:
(Aging Untold) — Retail experts say many American consumers, including older shoppers, are seeking out pre-owned and sustainable products.
According to the 2025 Resale Report from ThredUp, the U.S. secondhand apparel market is growing at an average of about 9 percent each year.
The thrill of the hunt
For Stephanie Hernandez, a secondhand stylist based in Washington, D.C., thrift shopping is both a passion and a profession. Clients pay her to help them build a one-of-a-kind, sustainable wardrobe — because many want to shop more responsibly but don’t have the time to do it themselves.
“They want to be more sustainable, and they are kind of thinking about it more, but they don’t really have the time to go out to a thrift store and hunt for those amazing pieces,” Hernandez said.
Her motivation goes beyond fashion.
“I just feel like there’s already so much out there in the world, and buying new just creates more and more waste,” she said.
The Council for Textile Recycling estimates the average American throws away more than 70 pounds of clothing and other textiles each year. According to the United Nations Environment Programme, the equivalent of one garbage truck of textiles is landfilled or burned every single second globally.
“I’d see videos of clothes washing up on beaches in countries across the ocean and it breaks my heart. That’s kind of why I started the business, to educate people about that and show them that there are other options,” Hernandez said.
Sustainable fashion in the classroom
Mikki Taylor, a fashion design professor at Howard University’s Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, teaches a course on sustainable fashion and says she practices what she preaches.
In her class, students examine their own closets, choices and patterns of consumption.
“I let them know all the chemicals that are involved in just one item, one T-shirt, a pair of jeans. It is incredibly important to teach them that because our environment is definitely being affected,” Taylor said.
Her advice for those new to secondhand shopping: “I would say just dive in. I mean really, just look at how much you have, what is it that you can remake or reinvent, and then what I always advise is to get a solid staple piece, and then build around it.”
Start with what you have
Hernandez said every new client begins by shopping their existing wardrobe before ever setting foot in a thrift store.
“We literally go through everything in their closet,” she said. “And we put outfits together with things that they already own — so kinda showing them you can breathe new life into things you already have!”

title: Obituary: Ruth Anne Baker
text:
BATH – The world lost our dear Ruth Anne Baker, of Bath, Maine, on Sept. 16, 2026.
Ruth was born in Lowell, Mass., in 1953. She moved to Maine in 1975 and made it her home. A rare soul, Ruth made this world a better place for all who knew her. Ruth was always there for family and friends whenever she was needed.
Ruth’s professional life took many different and adventurous turns. Over the years, she worked in graphic design and real estate, started restaurants, ran her own cleaning business, and developed a real talent for horticulture. She had a natural eye for design, a remarkable green thumb, and a knack for seeing how a space — indoors or out — could be reorganized, improved, or made more beautiful.
She founded a number of eateries, designed elegant menus as a head chef and was the most welcoming, entertaining and caring expert waitron (Ruth’s title for waiters/waitresses) that a diner out could be blessed to spend wonderful time with.
For Ruth, work was never separate from the rest of her life – the people she worked alongside so often became lasting friends, and in many ways felt like family. It was one more way that her generosity and service carried through everything that she did, and her pool of grateful recipients of her special custom cheesecakes, delicious meals and love grew and grew.
Ruth was the most compassionate rescuer and adopter of animals in need, and her dogs Friendly, Blue, Jethro, Ellie May, Tzar, Tonka, Otto, Kayla, Rowdy, Birdie, along with her cats Les McLess and Lou McNally were deeply loved members of her family. Some of her favorite times were spent walking her dogs at Hermit Island, often in the company of friends.
Ruth enjoyed traveling and spending time with loved ones on her trips to Florida and California. She particularly loved camping in Maine.
Above all, Ruth was devoted to the people she loved. She was outspoken, funny, generous, and always ready to help. She could always be counted on to do everything in her power to make everyone’s lives around her better and more whole, and was forever an uplifting presence. She introduced others to recognizing and embracing their potential, and for more than a few people, she was a literal life saver.
Ruth is survived by her sister, Paige, her brother-in-law, Steve Russell, and her nephews Adam and Seth Russell.
She was predeceased by her mother, Doris Baker; her sister, Kathryn; and her bestest friend, Stephen Hay. She will forever be loved and missed.
Celebration of life details are not yet finalized; details will be shared later.
To share your thoughts and condolences with the family, please visit http://www.desmondfuneralhomes.com
