title: Sanford mayoral, City Council hopefuls weigh in on hot topics at candidate forum
text:
Sanford residents gathered at City Hall on Thursday night to meet the candidates for this fall’s mayoral and City Council elections.
The Meet the Candidates night was a question-and-answer style format and included every candidate for both races.
The questions focused on some particularly relevant topics in the city, including homelessness and a proposed biosolid waste manufacturing facility. Each candidate had 90 seconds to answer, plus two-minute introductory and closing statements. The discussion was moderated by York County Coast Star reporter Shawn P. Sullivan.
Mayor
The four candidates for mayor — Matthew Dupuis, Deputy Mayor Maura Herlihy, Peter Tranchemontagne and Daniel White — answered questions about the cost of living, public safety, industry developments in the city and more.
Two of the questions focused on the proposed Aries Clean Technologies biosolid gasification plan and the possibility of a data center development.
Both the Aries and the Sanford Woods Industrial and Technical Campus projects have generated heavy discussion in the city about possible environmental impacts.
The City Council established moratoriums earlier this year effectively pausing both projects to allow for a task force to research the impacts and the possible requirements they would need to meet.
Tranchemontagne, who currently serves on the City Council, said he believes voters should get to weigh in on such developments via referendums.
“My opinion on the data center, as a city councilor or as a mayor, shouldn’t matter,” he said. “You guys should go to the ballot box and vote if you want a data center in the city of Sanford or not.”
All four candidates seemed to agree that there was not enough information on either of these developments and their possible impacts to allow them to go forward at the moment. Dupuis said he also believed these issues should go to voters directly, but that he was against the ideas of both developments coming to Sanford.
White raised concerns about the data center’s technology and said the biosolid facility could have a “devastating” environmental impact on the city.
Herlihy agreed that more work needs to be done. She cited her work with the industrial development task force to work together to gather more information and encouraged residents to share their opinions with local officials.
City Council
The seven candidates for two positions on the City Council — Alex Clary, Meagan Crawford, Shawn Goodwin, Bryce Lambert, Jonathan Martell, Victoria Pariyar and Michael Perry — answered some of the same questions as the mayoral candidates, plus a few new ones.
The candidates touched on municipal budgets, city resources and community outreach. One question was about public safety, with candidates asked what they would tell residents who may feel unsafe in the city and what their solutions would be.
The discussion soon made its way to Sanford’s homeless population. Many candidates agreed that the topic is a complex one, suggesting that it won’t be resolved simply by increased policing but must also include a focus on rehabilitation and connecting homeless residents with resources.
“This is a complex problem,” Pariyar said. “You’ve got mental health, mixed with substance abuse, mixed with economic difficulties.”
Martell, a current member of the council, said he was glad when the body voted to end a syringe service program in the city, but he said needle waste is still a big issue, despite some improvements. He said the city needs to ensure the police department has the resources it needs to tackle the issue.
Perry said arresting people suffering with substance use disorders does nothing when the city doesn’t focus on education and rehabilitation. He also suggested safe-disposal kiosks throughout the city to keep needle waste down.
Clary said he believed shutting down the needle program was the wrong conclusion. He said even after the syringe program was shuttered, he’s still picked up thousands of needles throughout the city.
“You can buy (needles) in Hannaford, you can buy them at the pharmacy. … Shutting down the needle program is another example of our city council being short sighted on a complex issue,” he said. “We need policies that work.”
A recording of the event, with all the candidates’ full answers, is available on the city’s public access network’s YouTube channel.
A second Meet the Candidates night — for candidates running for school board, state House and state Senate — is scheduled for 6 p.m. Oct. 8, also in City Council chambers at City Hall.
Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: 'Exaltation of Parks': New book explores history, parallels of Acadia
text:
BAR HARBOR — When John D. Rockefeller Jr. began acquiring land for conservation, it took an actual act of Congress to turn those lands into national parks, an act that was met with degrees of pushback.
But the parks were also quickly beloved, so much so that even in the late 1800s and early 1900s, onlookers voiced concerns about overcrowding from the visitors who traversed trails and summited peaks to breathe in the country’s natural beauty.
This deep dive into history and the parallels it shares with the state of national parks today is explored in the new book “An Exaltation of Parks: John D. Rockefeller Jr.’s Crusade to Save America’s Wonderlands,” (The University of Utah Press, 2025) by writer and park ranger Steve Kemp.
“I’ve worked in national parks most of my adult life,” Kemp told the Islander. “The more time I spent in these parks, the more I realized they were all, except for Denali, influenced by John D. Rockefeller Jr.”
Whether he was working as a cook at Grand Teton, in maintenance at Yellowstone or as publications director, writer and editor for the Great Smoky Mountains Association (where he spent three decades of his career), Kemp always wanted to explore “Junior’s” connection to the parks.
He got the chance to do so a handful of years ago, when he began poring over documents at the Rockefeller Archive Center in Sleepy Hollow, N.Y.
“It was like being a bloodhound on the path of a really amazing story for six years,” Kemp recalled.
The published book is a testament to Kemp’s careful research, in which the use of keen details paints an intimate portrait and historical account of Junior, a man whose demeanor Kemp captured even though he died 66 years ago.
“They made it pretty easy in some ways in that the Rockefellers never threw away any paper,” Kemp said about how he conducted his research. “It was like a treasure hunt.”
That treasure hunt included going over hundreds of pages of documents just to find one quote, Kemp explained. He filled about 10 bankers boxes with documents from the National Archives and the National Park Service archives, going through them every other day.
Kemp used his research to show how Junior began purchasing large tracts of land, a process partially influenced by Junior’s alarm at the number of homes that had started to crop up within the rugged beauty of Mount Desert Island, including atop Cadillac Mountain. So Junior began acquiring land to conserve it, a movement that attracted supporters such as George B. Dorr and Charles W. Eliot, and culminated in the federal protection of lands and the creation of the National Park Service.
What also led to the federal protection of the parks was Junior’s disposition, Kemp found, including his modesty, his strong distaste for waste, his religious convictions and deep appreciation for nature and philanthropy.
Junior’s philanthropy, Kemp noted, could also have been sparked by Junior’s guilt from his family’s legacy and his father’s oil monopoly.
“He was just very gracious, very reserved, very professional,” Kemp said. “[The Rockefellers] would do things like give $10 million to a cause and not even put out a press release.”
Throughout his research, Kemp was reminded that national parks have been popular in the country since they were first established. “Going back in history, I really realized that national parks were a hit from the very beginning,” he said. American people have just always loved national parks.”
In fact, they were such a hit that high visitation numbers and overcrowding have been the double-edged sword poking at parks since their inception. “As soon as they opened — Yosemite, Yellowstone, Mount Rainier — people started complaining about them being too crowded … and how they were going to provide enough facilities for all these people,” Kemp said.
According to park data, 323 million recreation visits were recorded in 2025, down 2.7% from 2024’s record year.
It’s prompting park officials to look at ways of managing the large crowds. “I know Acadia is probably the most advanced as far as managing overcrowding, but I would say they still have their challenges,” Kemp said.
Some management strategies include public transportation and reservation systems, the latter of which was implemented in Acadia National Park in 2021 for vehicles summitting Cadillac Mountain. It prompted anecdotal frustration from locals and visitors at the time, but these types of strategies are necessary if parks are going to address issues from overcrowding, Kemp emphasized.
Additionally, in a full-circle moment like the one that confronted Junior, it may be time to expand park boundaries.
“We need to look at ways to expand the parks and to manage visitation in a much more organized fashion,” Kemp said. “To do that takes money.”
Kemp regularly experienced overcrowding while working in the Smokies, where he still volunteers.
Though expanding park boundaries may be necessary, there are other strategies that don’t have to require another act of Congress to help address crowd sizes.
This could include reworking existing trails that aren’t popular so that they become more desirable for visitors, helping to draw folks away from historically popular trails.
“We could be a lot more mindful of how we meet the public’s expectations, too,” he said. “Just doing that would solve a lot of problems.”
The silver lining, Kemp said, is that overcrowding proves that Junior and his colleagues built something people have cared about for generations.
“It’s a good problem to have,” Kemp said.

title: Shouldn’t it be easier to get to Canada from here?
text:
After a trip to Prince Edward Island a couple summers ago, seeing more of Canada rose among my travel priorities. The people are friendly, the exchange rate is favorable, and there’s a lot to explore. The only deterrent, for me, is the long drive.
Considering our proximity, geographically and culturally, it should be easier to get to some of our northern neighbor’s nearby destinations from southern Maine. Although our countries’ relationship might be strained, for travelers, it’s nothing a “Lake Ontario” hat can’t fix. After all, many Mainers now have an open invitation to become Canadian citizens.
At first glance, the prospect of the Scotia Prince bringing back its ferry service to Portland appeared to offer a potential option. Driving three hours to Bar Harbor to get on the CAT ferry for even longer has never tempted me, but the idea of traveling 10 minutes to go spend the night in a casino and wake up in Nova Scotia? Pretty appealing.
Reading more about what the Scotia Prince is considering, however, tamped my enthusiasm.
The nearly $1,000 one-way price tag (for two people, a car and a cabin) feels like a lot for a trip that, at 11 hours long, is no quicker than it would be by car at a fraction of the cost, regardless of dreaded gas prices. Being able to pass the time sleeping or playing blackjack doesn’t seem like enough of a selling point.
And while some describe the town of Yarmouth, where the ferry would land in Nova Scotia, as a hidden gem, the province’s most popular attractions are at least another couple hours away by car — in the direction of Maine — which again leads me back to sucking up the drive.
What about air travel, you ask? Flights from Portland to Halifax, with one layover, take nearly as long as the drive there and, most of the year, cost about as much as the ferry fee discussed. The same goes for Montreal and Quebec City, which are both about a five-hour drive and closer, as the crow flies, than Bridgeport, Connecticut.
If you’re hoping that direct flights to Canada are coming our way soon, you should know, at this point, that’s a pipe dream.
Toronto is the only city in the country to crack the top 15 international destinations of people flying out of the Portland International Jetport, then connecting through another domestic hub, coming in at No. 4 with just under 4,000 passengers in the past year.
The magic number for an airline to support a direct flight is 30,000 annual passengers, according to Airport Director Paul Bradbury.
Reviving rail service from Boston to Montreal, through Maine, is still being bandied about by state officials, though plans literally have had to change course since lawmakers decided last year to convert the St. Lawrence and Atlantic Rail corridor between Portland and Auburn into a multiuse trail.
The Maine-Canadian Legislative Advisory Commission in January presented a report to the Legislature’s transportation committee — with summarizes of several state-funded studies on the subject undertaken in the past 30 years — essentially recommending that the conversation continues.
In other words, don’t hold your breath.
Ditto for the possibility of an east-west highway being built, a concept first conceived when the country officially established its interstate system in the 1940s and last was seriously considered in Maine over a decade ago.
The amount of travel time that could save drivers would depend on the route, but one thing’s for sure, without it, bus companies aren’t going to start offering trips straight to Canada.
Now, you have to go down to Boston first, if not New York City, before heading north. Meaning, without a car, you really can’t get there from here.

title: 49ers owner Jed York suspended for 6 games after his arrest in prostitution sting
text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. (AP) — The NFL suspended San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York for six games Friday following his arrest earlier this year in a prostitution sting in Ohio.
The league announced that York was also fined $500,000 for violating the league’s personal conduct policy. York has not attended any games or league meetings so far this season and was credited with three games served. He is eligible to return on Oct. 20, following the team’s game the previous night against Washington.
York was arrested in a mobile home park by the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force after police said he was attempting to pay $160 for sex with a woman he believed to be a prostitute.
York was booked into jail and was released after posting a $5,000 bond. York was initially charged with engaging in prostitution, but prosecutors amended that to disorderly conduct. He pleaded no contest to that charge and to possessing criminal tools for using his phone to respond to an undercover online prostitution advertisement.
He was sentenced to one day in jail for both offenses to be served concurrently and was credited with one day served when he pleaded no contest. He was also fined $1,150. Police seized the $160 from York, and it was later given to the human trafficking task force as part of the plea. York also completed an online course.

title: Households will pay more for energy because of Trump's policy changes, think tank says
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Households in the contiguous United States will pay thousands of dollars more for energy through 2040 because of federal policy changes since President Donald Trump returned to office, according to modeling released Friday by a nonpartisan think tank.
The Energy Innovation analysis found that households will pay an average of $6,500 more for energy, cumulatively through 2040. In five states, households will pay roughly $9,000 more: Oregon, Mississippi, South Dakota, Virginia and Wyoming.
The California-based think tank said there will be more demand for natural gas for electricity because the administration is canceling new clean energy projects and there will be more demand for gasoline for transportation because Trump and Congress are revoking policies that encouraged or created incentives for more efficient and lower-emissions vehicles. Higher demand drives prices up.
Electricity bills are already rising faster than inflation in much of the U.S., which is being blamed in some areas on demand from data centers. The Iran war has sent oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, too.
Contrarily, Trump has said his administration’s energy policies will make bills more affordable for families and businesses. White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said Wednesday that lowering electricity prices remains a top priority and Trump is unleashing reliable energy like coal and natural gas to reverse the “catastrophic damage” Democrats did to the power grid by ramping up clean energy. A 2025 Department of Energy report, mandated by Trump, warned of increasing blackouts if the U.S. continued closing coal and natural gas plants.
“Joe Biden created a grid crisis; President Trump is fixing it,” Rogers wrote in an email. “If the Democrats had their way, these costly and unreliable renewable energy projects would still be failing our grid and our communities.”
The Republican president prioritizes fossil fuels to produce electricity, unlike Biden, who saw clean energy as a climate solution.
Analysis examined impact on states solely from federal policy changes
It focused on the sweeping package of tax breaks that slashed funding for clean energy tax credits, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump signed; environmental rollbacks, including clean air and power plant rules and the revocation of a scientific finding that underpinned the U.S. fight against climate change; the loosening of fuel economy standards and blocking of California’s novel rule banning the sale of new gas-powered cars by 2035; and federal actions to stop wind, solar and hydrogen projects.
These changes will result in annual household energy costs rising in every state in the contiguous U.S., plus job losses in 47 of 48 states and losses to the gross domestic product in 46 states, Energy Innovation said. It’s projecting 37,000 additional premature deaths from air pollution, $72 billion in additional healthcare costs and more than 9 billion tons of additional carbon pollution because of the environmental rollbacks. The analysis did not include Alaska or Hawaii because key federal data is not available for those two states, said Robbie Orvis, senior director for modeling and analysis.
Looking at the metrics, Orvis was hard-pressed to find a silver lining.
“Across pretty much every state, things are worse. The outlook now is worse for states and the affordability crisis will be worse because of the combined set of policies,” he said.
Climate Justice Alliance legislative director Mar Zepeda said her Washington, D.C., electric bill increased $200 in the past month. Zepeda said electricity demands from data centers are increasing energy rates, and federal “affordability” policies only exacerbate this.
“They may call it affordability, but affordable for whom and at what cost? Not for regular people,” Zepeda said in an email.
White House says the think tank is partisan
Rogers said it is “irresponsible” to classify Energy Innovation as nonpartisan because its employees have donated to Democrats and worked with Democrats on climate policy.
Spokesman Silvio Marcacci said they work with policymakers who want to cut emissions and lower bills, regardless of party. He said multiple states led by Republicans have used their tool designed to model policies affecting energy use and emissions. Much of their data comes from government sources, including the Energy Information Administration.
Rogers also said states led by Democrats that have embraced aggressive renewable mandates see higher energy costs, notably California and New York. She said this proves Republican policies are working. The conservative think tank, Institute for Energy Research, said in December that blue states have high rates.
However, in the Energy Innovation analysis, three of the five states facing the highest costs have Republican governors, and states that voted for Trump in 2024 will pay an average of $7,000 more in energy spending cumulatively per household, versus $5,800 on average per household in states that voted for Kamala Harris. Its research has found that states with high levels of wind and solar generation, including Republican-led Iowa and Oklahoma, have experienced the lowest rate increases.
The average price residential customers pay for electricity increased over the course of Biden’s term and has continued to rise since Trump returned to office, according to EIA data. Customers paid an average of about 12.6 cents per kilowatt-hour in January 2021 when Biden took office. In January 2025, when Trump returned to office, that price stood at nearly 16 cents per kilowatt-hour. It was 17.45 cents in January 2026 and 18.31 cents in July.
Oregon households’ annual energy spending slated to increase the most
The modeling projects federal policy changes will increase annual energy spending in Oregon by $840 per household in 2035 and $1,200 per household in 2040, with a cumulative $9,300 increase from 2026 to 2040 — the highest of any state.
The Oregon Citizens’ Utility Board advocates for residential utility customers. Executive Director Bob Jenks called those numbers “frightening” because Oregon already has an energy affordability problem. He cited steep rate increases as utilities make upgrades and data centers use more power.
As costs rise, Jenks expects utilities to disconnect more households because people won’t be able to afford their bills.
Jenks said wind and solar are essential for affordable electricity in Oregon, and he wants the federal government to partner with states to develop the energy they need.
“We’re trying to optimize among the resource options we have, and they’re trying to take things away and raise the costs,” he said.

title: Federal officials warn Maine of faulty sprinkler heads that may fail during a fire
text:
Federal officials warn Maine of faulty sprinkler heads that may fail during a fire
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission is asking Maine fire officials to help identify recalled sprinkler heads that may still be installed.
Federal officials warn Maine of faulty sprinkler heads that may fail during a fire
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission is asking Maine fire officials to help identify recalled sprinkler heads that may still be installed.
Federal safety officials are asking Maine fire officials to help identify recalled sprinkler heads that may still be installed in homes, businesses and other buildings more than two decades after the original recall.
In a Sept. 25 letter to Maine State Fire Marshal Shawn Esler, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission said approximately 35 million Central Sprinkler heads equipped with O-ring seals were recalled in 2001.
The agency said millions of the recalled sprinkler heads are believed to remain installed nationwide, creating a continuing risk of serious injury or death if they fail to operate during a fire.
The CPSC is asking Maine officials to alert fire departments, inspectors, building owners and facility managers about the recall and encourage property owners to determine whether the recalled sprinkler heads remain in use.
The renewed warning comes after a July 2025 fire at an assisted living facility in Fall River, Massachusetts that killed 10 residents and injured dozens.
According to the CPSC letter, recalled Central Sprinkler heads were later identified at that facility. The agency said one sprinkler in the room where the fire started failed to activate despite having previously been flagged as subject to the recall.
The state fire marshal has been contacted for comment.

title: New York's governor and AG set to give update on Cornell rape allegations
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New York’s governor and attorney general were set to give an update Friday morning about the investigation into a woman’s allegations that she was gang raped at a Cornell University fraternity house.
Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Thursday she appointed the office of Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the investigation, saying she had lost faith in the local district attorney’s ability to handle the case.
The investigation had initially been closed without charges in 2024.
Last month, the woman filed a civil lawsuit and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation. He has since been bombarded by criticism that he abandoned the original investigation too quickly.
The attorney general will oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury, Hochul said.
“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” she said in a statement Thursday.
Messages left for Van Houten were not immediately returned late Thursday.
The case has roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about its response and the larger issue of how sexual assaults are handled on college campuses.
The woman, identified only as Jane Doe in court documents, told campus police in November of 2024 that she was assaulted, then discussed it with the university’s internal investigators as part of Cornell’s disciplinary process.
The lawsuit against seven fraternity brothers, the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and others alleges that she was plied with drugs and alcohol, then subjected to sex acts by a group of men while she was partially or entirely incapacitated. One of the men sent a social media message to other fraternity members alerting them to what was happening, and inviting people to take part, according to the lawsuit.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they participated in a sexual assault. One said his client hadn’t touched the woman. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful.

title: Caribou council candidate wants to hold taxes down and bring business in
text:
A newcomer to municipal government is seeking election to the Caribou City Council because he wants the city to draw new businesses in while controlling the rise of property taxes.
George Joseph LaCasse Jr., 67, is running unopposed for a three-year council term.
This is LaCasse’s first run for public office. Joining him, also unopposed for the other two open seats, are Jeff Whitney and incumbent Tamara Lovewell.
“I would like to be involved with the community and try and bring new business to the area,” LaCasse said.
Born in Boston, LaCasse served in the U.S. Air Force and trained as a jet engine mechanic. He came to Maine in 1978, when he was stationed at Loring Air Force Base in Limestone.
He met his wife, Lisa Johndro of Limestone, there and the two married in 1979. They had two children and lived at Loring until 1984, when he was assigned to Okinawa, Japan, he said. He took his family with him, and they lived in Japan for five years. He was honorably discharged in May 1989.
He returned to Limestone, but jobs were scarce as the base prepared to close. So he sought work in Massachusetts, where the family lived for 17 years. They returned to Maine and finally moved to Caribou in 2008.
LaCasse worked for maintenance and repair firm Telford Aviation on the former Loring campus and also for the Loring Job Corps Center before his retirement, he said.
His education includes some college, and his party affiliation is independent, he said.
He and his wife still live in Caribou, where he is active in the Veterans of Foreign Wars and American Legion.
If elected, LaCasse would like to prioritize better control of taxes and learn what’s happening in the local schools. He also wants to explore operations of Caribou’s police and firefighters and determine what their needs are, he said.
A key step is to “gather information and see what needs to be done,” he said.
LaCasse believes the council could improve its work to draw new businesses to the area and improve the tax outlook for residents.
He knows there’ll be a learning curve since he’s new to municipal service, but wants to enjoy the process.
“I’m a veteran and retired, and [I’m] new to this,” he said. “I want to see if I can help.”

title: New York governor appoints special prosecutor to oversee Cornell University rape allegations
text:
New York's governor removes DA in Cornell rape allegations, appoints AG Letitia James to take over
New York’s governor appointed a special prosecutor Thursday to oversee an investigation into a woman’s allegations that she was gang raped at a Cornell University fraternity house, saying she had lost faith in the local district attorney’s ability to handle the case.
Video above: Cornell's student assembly plans a forum on sexual violence
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she had signed an executive order appointing the office of New York Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the investigation, which had initially been closed without charges in 2024.
The woman's allegations got a rush of new attention when she filed a civil lawsuit last month. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation Monday, but has been battered by criticism that he'd abandoned the original investigation too quickly.
“Newly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute an alleged sexual assault on Cornell University’s campus in October 2024,” Hochul said.
“This has, in turn, undercut my faith, and the public’s faith, in the District Attorney’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time."
Hochul said the attorney general would oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury.
“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued," Hochul said. "This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.”
Messages left for Van Houten were not immediately returned late Thursday. Hochul, James and Van Houten are all Democrats.
A campus roiled by continued revelations
Hochul's announcement came shortly after dozens of students and community members spent hours demanding transparency and accountability from university leaders at a forum sponsored by Cornell's student government. The case has roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about its response and the larger issue of how sexual assaults are handled on college campuses.
The woman, identified only as Jane Doe in court documents, reported the alleged assault to campus police in November of 2024, then discussed it with the university’s internal investigators as part of Cornell's disciplinary process.
Video below: Matthew Van Houten, District Attorney, Tompkins County, NY, on Cornell rape accusation
The lawsuit against seven fraternity brothers, the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and others, alleges that she was plied with drugs and alcohol, then subjected to sex acts by a group of men while she was partially or entirely incapacitated. One of the men sent a social media message to other fraternity members alerting them to what was happening, and inviting people to take part, according to the lawsuit.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they participated in a sexual assault. One said his client hadn’t touched the woman. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful.
When he reopened the investigation earlier this week, Van Houten said he would review new information in the woman's lawsuit. But he also issued a statement defending his initial decision not to prosecute, maintaining the woman’s first account to police didn’t include allegations that she was drugged against her will, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex.
Under pressure from the public and politicians, including Hochul, Cornell agreed Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations.
Students, community call for change
Over more than two-and-a-half hours Thursday, students and other members of the Cornell community expressed anger, frustration and grief over the school's handling of sexual assault allegations in general, with several speakers sharing their own experiences of sexual violence.
Many criticized Cornell President Michael I. Kotlikoff and the university’s administration, calling for greater transparency and accountability in the handling of the case, stronger sexual assault prevention efforts and changes to Greek life.
Jane Wang, a sophomore, said at the forum that when she reported being sexually assaulted on campus a year ago, she was met with a slew of paperwork and little guidance or follow-up. After an initial email chain about starting the investigation, she got few updates and had to prod for answers, she said. The process left her feeling an “overall sense of helplessness within a broader institution.”
“My main message for Cornell here is that we can’t be treating these cases only with care and attention after it catches national news,” Wang said, calling for the university to improve the “seriousness and timeliness” of its response to sexual assault allegations.
Video below: Attorney of the former student who alleges she was raped speaks to CNN
There was no immediate response to a message seeking comment about the forum and Wang's case sent to the university late Thursday.
Cornell has said it took a series of actions after the woman identifying as Jane Doe reported being raped at the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024.
It announced publicly that it had opened an investigation, condemned the alleged behavior, indefinitely suspended the fraternity, and convened a university task force to study ways to more effectively protect students against sexual assault.
It also conducted a monthslong investigation, which ended with some students being disciplined or expelled, though it has declined to provide specifics, citing student privacy rules. The university issued a statement Monday saying it supported reopening the criminal investigation.
“I think what happened here is an American problem,” said Hayden Watkins, an undergraduate and executive vice president of the Student Assembly, which hosted the forum.
“People kind of put Cornell on this pedestal because we are an elite institution,” he added. “But if it’s happening at places like Cornell, it’s happening on college campuses all across the country.”
Associated Press reporter Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this report.

title: What to know about Christa Pike and her failed lethal injection execution attempt
text:
(AP) - Tennessee’s failed attempt at executing Christa Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug in the state’s death chamber has left her in critical condition, according to her attorneys.
Pike, 50, was still in the hospital Thursday and her lawyers said they did not know her long-term chance for recovery. Tennessee went forward with the lethal injection Wednesday eight hours after it was originally scheduled to have taken place, a delay caused by a court ruling that temporarily paused the execution.
What happened to Pike is “singular and unparalleled,” said Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. She said Pike was the only person who has remained alive after lethal injection drugs were administered in an execution.
Here’s what to know about Pike’s failed execution:
An execution delayed, prolonged then failed
Pike’s execution was supposed to start at 10 a.m., but a federal appeals court stopped it about an hour before. The state appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, and it took eight hours for the conservative majority to overrule the lower court and let the lethal injection with the barbiturate pentobarbital to proceed.
About 90 minutes later, prison officials raised the curtain to the execution chamber, where media witnesses saw Pike strapped to a gurney with an IV in her arm. She said she was leaving the world with love.
“I’m ready to be free,” she said. “This is a happy day.”
She sang a song with her spiritual adviser, looked around and after several minutes said her arm was hurting or burning and asked if it was supposed to feel that way.
The curtain to the witnesses was closed then opened again around the time a second dose of pentobarbital would be administered. Pike appeared to lose consciousness, but she continued breathing and at times made snoring-like noises for the next hour.
Prison officials closed the curtain for good about 40 minutes after they first opened it. Pike’s attorney demanded a telephone to ask a court to stop the execution.
It’s unknown what was happening to Pike from the time the curtain closed for good at 8:06 p.m. until her attorney was told an ambulance was coming and witnesses were told to leave around 8:50 p.m.
“We at this point do not know the ramifications of the chemical torture that she has endured,” Pike’s attorney Randy Spivey said.
Prison officials have not said when their attempt to execute Pike turned into life-saving efforts. They have only released a statement saying their lethal injection protocols were followed.
Tennessee governor stops December execution to investigate
Within hours, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee canceled the state’s last execution of 2026, scheduled for Dec. 3, and ordered a comprehensive third-party investigation into what went wrong with Pike.
“It needs to be done thoroughly and however long that takes, whatever process is required to make sure we get to the very end of it and all the questions are answered,” Lee said.
It’s not the first time Lee has ordered an investigation into capital punishment in Tennessee. Four years ago, an independent review found the state didn’t follow its own execution rules and failed to properly test lethal injection drugs. That probe came after an April 2022 execution was stopped because of mishandling of drugs.
In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after medical workers who got an IV into his right arm couldn’t get a secondary IV line after trying his other arm, his left hand and his left foot, then failing to establish a central line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute Carruthers again.
Pike’s lawyers called for the governor to now spare her life.
“Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa’s sentence now,” Spivey said.
Pike’s lawyers warned of medical conditions
Pike’s legal team has previously told courts and Tennessee prison officials that she had medical conditions that would make death by lethal injection agonizing.
They said Pike suffered from a condition with elevated platelets known as thrombocytosis. They argued the condition could cause issues with blood clotting at injection sites or bleeding that could affect her lungs.
Medical workers also had trouble drawing blood from her, and setting an IV line is a harder process, her lawyers said. Spivey said he counted at least seven spots where needles were put into her left arm Wednesday and that at least one needle bent on an unsuccessful attempt.
Pike’s biggest fear from being executed wasn’t “a fear of dying. It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death. And that’s what happened minus the death,” said Stephen Ferrell, an attorney for Pike.
Pike killed 19-year-old job corps classmate
Pike didn’t deny she killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. The two were classmates at Knoxville Job Corps.
Prosecutors said Pike feared Slemmer was a romantic rival and lured her to a secluded area where she and her boyfriend slashed Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. The case got widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body.
Pike said she was sexually abused starting from when she was a toddler and that she was raped at ages 11 and 17. Her lawyers said her death sentence was unfair because she was 18 at the time of the crime and the jury wasn’t told about the abuse and how that might have affected her behavior.
Slemmer’s mother witnessed the execution attempt and said her daughter didn’t get justice.
“I watched the whole thing. She was awake. She was laughing. She was moving her head, moving her feet. She was trying to sit up. Didn’t work the first time they gave her a shot. It didn’t work the second time so she’s in the hospital and alive,” May Martinez said by telephone.
Tadaryl Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into her body. He was 17 at the time of the killing and was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age.
___
Kim Chandler in Nashville and Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: James “Jim” F. Mooney
text:
BOWDOINHAM – James “Jim” F. Mooney went home to be with his Lord and Savior on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026, following a brief illness.
He was born in Portland on April 9, 1953, to Frank C. Mooney Jr. and Elaine V. (Sullivan) Mooney. A 1971 graduate of Waterville High School, he went on to a variety of different careers, before finding his calling professionally as a personal financial planner.
To those that knew him best, Jim was a musician and an artist at heart. His art adorned the walls of many of his closest friends and family, and the medium that spoke to him was pen and ink. He was also a singer and songwriter who would always have his guitar handy at many social gatherings. He could usually be found strumming chords of his many songs that were inspired by his favorite folk singers like Jim Croce, Gordon Lightfoot, and Harry Chapin. Jim loved to host gatherings of friends and family for food, live music, and lots of laughs, and for many years hosted Fourth of July parties at his home, and enjoyed going “all out” preparing for the party.
Jim also was a lifelong golfer and appreciated the serenity and comradery that could be found sharing a round of golf and a few cold ones with his many friends throughout the years. Jim was also a family man, and he was very proud that he had raised two wonderful children. He also held a special place in his heart for his former wife and the mother of his children, June A. (LeGoff) Mooney. He will be sorely missed by the many lives that he touched, with his charming, quick smile and a spicy brand of Irish charm.
Jim is survived by his daughter Andrea Mooney (and spouse) of Augusta, his son Dylan Mooney of Augusta; sister Debbie (Mooney) Zorn of Bowdoinham; niece Sheri (Bartlett) Blackstone (and spouse) of Cundy’s Harbor, niece Shelley Zorn of Gardiner, and nephew Bob Cyr Jr.
He was reunited in peace with those who went before him, including Jim’s parents Frank and Elaine, his former wife, June, his sisters Pam (Mooney) Cyr and Sandee (Mooney) Bartlett.
Funeral services will be held Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, at 4 p.m. at Staples Funeral Home at 53 Brunswick Ave. in Gardiner.
Arrangements and guidance are in the care of Staples Funeral Home and Cremation Care, 53 Brunswick Avenue, Gardiner, Maine.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared with the family on the obituary page of the Staples Funeral Home website, http://www.staplesfuneralhome.com.

title: Woman gives birth to twins months after brutal dog attack
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW/Gray News) - Healing continues for Audrey Austin following a brutal dog attack back in July, when she was 24 weeks pregnant, that changed her life forever.
“I’m going to stay strong, and I’m going to keep moving, and it’s going to take time to forgive the person, but I forgave the dog,” Austin said.
On Thursday, Oct. 1, she wrapped up an eye appointment in Kansas City before making her way back to Topeka. It’s still one of many treatments Audrey is undergoing to regain her appearance.
“My first surgery for my nose—they’re going to do a forehead flip, where they’re going to take skin from my forehead and bring it to my nose,” she said.
But another thing added to her plate is caring for her newborn twins. Kasai and Kamyiah were born at just 38 weeks.
Audrey says because of the dog attack, her delivery wasn’t easy.
“My body has been under so much anesthesia and so much surgeries that I also think [it] put a strain on my babies,” Austin said.
The twins remain in the NICU, but it’s not stopping Audrey from being present.
“I see them in the mornings. [I see] them every day. I come up here, spend the night,” Austin said.
Alongside looking forward to bringing her babies home soon, Audrey is taking one step at a time in turning the page on this chapter of her life.
“It’s life. I mean, eventually, I’m going to grow from this. Eventually, I’m going to heal inside to not worry about what’s on the outside,” Austin said. “I’m still trying to get everything going for my babies when they come home.”
Audrey tells 13 NEWS that she has not been able to work since the dog attack. She’s currently seeking assistance from the community as she navigates this new chapter in her life. Her GoFundMe can be found here.

title: Many states have backup execution plans, but failures still happen
text:
(AP) - Long before Christa Pike was brought into Tennessee’s execution chamber, prison leaders reviewed and approved a backup plan detailing exactly what to do if the first attempt at lethal injection failed.
But the backup plan also failed, and Thursday — 24 hours later — Pike was still alive but in critical condition at a Tennessee hospital, though her prognosis remained uncertain. It’s not yet clear what went wrong.
Twenty-seven states have capital punishment, and they vary widely in how they administer the death penalty and just how much of that lethal process they keep hidden from public view, according to the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, a clearinghouse for information on U.S. executions.
Some states have extensive backup plans. Others don’t
Tennessee falls somewhere in the middle of the pack when it comes to contingency plans, with two redundancies built into its execution process.
First, inmates are supposed to have two intravenous lines placed. Thus, if the first IV site fails, the execution team can switch to the second one. A physician on the execution team can even insert a central line — which typically involves making an incision in a major blood vessel in the groin, neck or armpit in order to thread a catheter into the body to a spot near the heart — if needed.
Intravenous lines can fail for several reasons, like a needle and catheter not being properly placed in a vein or wiggling out of place — or a vein rupturing and letting blood and IV fluid leak into tissue surrounding the IV site.
Tennessee also allows for a second 100 mg dose of pentobarbital to be administered if the condemned person is still alive five minutes after the first dose was given.
Tennessee prison officials gave Pike a second dose, but it’s not clear if they used the primary IV site or the backup site to do so.
Little backup in Alabama, a lot in Idaho
Alabama has a three-drug lethal injection protocol. It allows for a backup dose of the first drug, the sedative midazolam, to be given if the inmate isn’t unconscious from the first dose. But the protocol doesn’t include additional instructions for what to do if the condemned person is still alive after the first dose of the next two drugs, rocuronium bromide and potassium chloride.
Idaho, meanwhile, has contingency plans for nearly every step of the execution process, with backup IV sites, allowances for administering a central IV line, and up to three full doses of any of the state’s four approved lethal injection drug cocktails.
Idaho recently made firing squad its primary execution method, though it has yet to kill someone by that method. Still, the state’s firing squad protocol also has a backup plan, with the prison director able to order a second volley of shots within a two-minute time span if she determines it is necessary to complete the execution.
Despite contingency plans, executions are still botched at times
Idaho called off the execution of Thomas Eugene Creech in 2024 after execution team members could not place a viable IV after eight attempts.
Tennessee also called off an execution earlier this year after failing to find a suitable vein for a secondary IV line.
In 2014, Arizona executioners injected Joseph Rudolph Wood with a lethal combination of drugs 15 times during the nearly two hours it took him to die. He gasped more than 600 times while he lay on the table.
Witnesses keep the public informed when executions succeed or fail
In many ways, executions are shrouded in secrecy. The identity of execution team members, the details about where and how lethal drugs are procured, and in some states even what happens in the death chamber is hidden from public view.
But executions, like all criminal sentences, are conducted by the state on behalf of its citizens, so it’s critical that members of the public understand exactly how that ultimate punishment is carried out.
Most death penalty states allow a few members of the media to witness executions on behalf of the public. Once the execution is over, those news representatives typically take part in a news conference, sharing exactly what they saw and heard with the rest of the world.
Access to executions varies by state, and limitations often lead to court battles
Only two states, Indiana and Wyoming, explicitly ban members of the press from witnessing executions. Wyoming, with no one currently on death row, hasn’t carried out an execution since 1992, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
A coalition of news organizations including The Associated Press sued Indiana last year for a seat in the witness room, but in June a federal appellate court upheld the state’s law barring media access.
In Idaho, media witnesses are allowed to watch as a condemned person is placed on a gurney, has IVs inserted and is put to death. Yet AP and other news organizations have sued for increased access. The news organizations asked a judge to allow them to watch via closed-circuit monitors as the drugs are pushed into the IV lines, which is currently shielded from public view in a private room beside the death chamber.
A federal judge ordered the state to provide that access, citing a 9th U.S. Circuit Court ruling that said the public should be able to view all critical parts of an execution via the press. But the state appealed, and the appellate court hasn’t yet ruled on the matter.
Media witnesses provided crucial details about Pike’s failed execution
When Pike’s first lethal injection dose failed to end her life, officials closed the curtains and administered a second dose of pentobarbital.
When the curtains reopened, Pike was making snoring sounds and was clearly alive, according to AP reporter Kim Chandler, who was one of the witnesses. Eventually the curtain was closed again and the microphone in the room was turned off, but Pike could still be heard making gasping or snoring sounds.
Nearly two hours after the execution began, media witnesses were escorted out, and Pike was taken to a hospital for treatment.
Many states, including Tennessee, keep the IV insertion hidden from public view, but allow witnesses to watch through a viewing window as the condemned person dies.
AP was part of a media coalition that previously sued Tennessee to see the IV insertion and to keep the viewing room curtains open until the pronouncement of death. But in April the Tennessee Supreme Court blocked a lower court’s order that would have allowed for increased access.
One of Pike’s attorneys, Steve Ferrell, said Pike feared that there could be complications because of a lifelong blood disorder that made it tough to get needles into her veins. Ferrell said it was possible that the IV did not enter Pike’s vein properly, and the drug may have filled her arm instead of entering her bloodstream.

title: Susan Collins should drop out and step down
text:
A million years ago, by which I mean this past June, Graham Platner called Sen. Susan Collins “corrupt.” He took a lot of flak for that. But new reporting from ProPublica seems to prove him right.
That Collins reportedly played “pay to play” with Navatek demonstrates a lack of judgment and ethics. Offering government contracts in return for a campaign contribution is the very definition of bribery. We should hope that the next Democratic administration pulls the files and reopens the investigation.
Collins must drop out of the Senate race and resign immediately. She is clearly not fit to serve. Self-dealing and insider trading have no place in the Senate. I feel she’s an embarrassment to Maine, and she has to go.
They said there was zero tolerance for sexual misbehavior when Senate candidate Graham Platner was accused (without further adjudication). Shouldn’t there be zero tolerance for plausible allegations of bribery and corruption by a sitting senator?
Wayne Clark
Durham

title: Jay generator journey loses steam as ‘super oversize’ load stops in Oxford
text:
Oxford became the focal point of local curiosity when a steam generator on a slow journey from Jay to South Portland using state routes had to pause in town and was parked at Call of the Wild RV Center on Main Street.
Employees at Call of the Wild said they had not been alerted that the 220-foot trailer load would be backed onto the property alongside its sales and service building.
They added that another business owner in the Route 26 neighborhood had refused to allow it on its property for the day.
The Maine Department of Transportation stipulated that the 20-foot-wide load and its accompanying vehicles can only travel public roads between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m.
The spectacle attracted a lot of curious locals who pulled into Call of the Wild’s parking lot during Thursday business hours to see what the hubbub was all about.
According to Facebook chatter, a large number of people parked at Oxford Plains Speedway Thursday evening to watch the trailer, attached to a tractor pulling it and another pushing it, hit the road for the next leg of its move, Route 117.
From there it is being taken over sections of Route 202, Route 22 and Route 1 to a location off Broadway in South Portland. The move, which began from Route 4 in Jay the evening of Sept. 29, was expected to take two days.
But after the trip began its duration was recalculated to last one week.
It is the first of nine “super oversize” equipment loads to be taken from the former Pixelle Specialty Solutions paper mill in Jay to the South Portland side of the Fore River in Casco Bay.

title: The best places to enjoy foliage in central Maine
text:
As the mornings grow crisper and fall color reaches its peak in the mountains, it’s time to start taking advantage.
While Maine forests continue to show off through a changing climate, and as we move toward peak foliage in early October, take advantage of the nice weather and enjoy the vibrant shades of red, orange and yellow peppering the tree line.
From hikes and walks to peaceful drives, here are some of the best places to see autumnal colors.
Mt. Pisgah
The tower trail up Mt. Pisgah, located in Winthrop and Wayne, requires just under a mile of hiking. Your reward? One of the best foliage views in central Maine. Journey among old sugar maples on your way to a 60-foot fire tower last used in 1991. From the top, you’ll get a first-hand look at 360 degrees of views.
Vienna Mountain Road
Vienna Mountain Road offers a plethora of scenery before you’re on your way up the mountain. From there, you’ll have access to plenty of trails. But if you don’t feel like a hike, the drive is well worth the views you’ll see along the way.
Kennebec River Rail Trail
This 6.5-mile path is an easy walk from Gardiner to Augusta with plenty of views of the Kennebec River. Enjoy autumnal scenes along the way, and take a break at the half-way point in Hallowell for a bite to eat or a seasonal drink.
Belgrade lakes
If you want a different kind of foliage view — perhaps one from the water — renting a boat on the Belgrade lakes is never a bad idea. Dress warmly and call any of the boat rental companies ahead of time, and then take in the seasonal view from a tranquil lake.
Old Canada Road National Scenic Byway
This drive will take you nearly 80 miles along U.S. Route 201, through forests and viewpoints for wildlife. Start your journey at the Robbins Hill Scenic Overlook in Solon and take your journey all the way to the Canadian border. Stops in Bingham and The Forks will give you an opportunity to see towns and stretch your legs along the way.
Moxie Falls
Head to Bingham via U.S. Route 201 toward The Forks for a scenic day trip full of vibrant leaves. The journey will take you through Moscow and Caratunk before veering toward Lake Moxie, where you can experience Moxie Falls. To extend that trip farther north, find a recommended route from the Visit Kennebec Valley guide.

title: NMMC emergency nurses blame toxic work environment for mass resignations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Emergency department registered nurses at Northern Maine Medical Center in Fort Kent said on Friday that six nurses resigned and more are actively seeking other employment because the “current atmosphere is not healthy to patients and puts their license at risk.”
The nurses, represented by the Maine State Nurses Association and National Nurses Organizing Committee, delivered a signed letter to CEO Jeff Zewe on Friday detailing reasons behind nurses seeking new employment, including a hostile work environment.
The letter to Zewe, obtained by the Bangor Daily News on Friday, was signed by the emergency department nurses, including the six who resigned, who said “nurses are walking out of the hospital and are not coming back.”
The emergency department resignations come just months after the union and administration signed a contract two years in the making.
Hospital spokeswoman Pam Sime said on Thursday that other opportunities and a move out of the area were behind the multiple nurse departures. Registered nurse Ami Maxwell, who still works at the hospital, said Sime’s account is accurate, but not complete.
The staffing loss was preventable. The nurses did not want to leave, but chose to look for new positions because it is an “awful toxic” work environment, Maxwell said.
“One of my co-workers has worked at the hospital for 39.5 years and is two years away from retirement,” Maxwell said. “He’s leaving the hospital he has always worked at but he’s leaving because he is fed-up and sad with how things are being run.”
The nurses bargaining unit and hospital administrators have been battling over issues for the past two years at both the Fort Kent facility and Houlton Regional Hospital, which fall under the same management team. As contract negotiations appeared to drag on, especially related to emergency department staffing and patient safety concerns, several nurses expressed frustrations with leadership during multiple strikes and other public actions.
The critical access 25-bed hospital’s emergency department treats approximately 7,000 patients annually, averaging 19 patient visits per day.
At issue for the emergency department nurses, as stated in the letter to Zewe, include a hostile work environment where staff do not feel valued, heard or respected; a lack of communication between administration and staff; high numbers of expensive traveling nurses; staff are pressured into working a shift rotation (a mix of day and night shifts); working short staffed; and changes to scheduling practices.
Sime said that the hospital regularly monitors patient volumes, quality indicators to ensure the emergency department continues to meet the healthcare needs of the community.
“[The hospital] has consistently been recognized for the quality of care provided to our patients and their families,” she said, adding that they have grown services that are needed in the community.
Registered nurse Kim Paradis worked her last shift at the hospital on Saturday. In her 24 years at the Fort Kent hospital, Paradis worked as a certified nursing assistant, a medical surgical registered nurse, manager of inpatient adult and child/adolescent psychiatric units, hospital supervisor and emergency department nurse.
Unfortunately, the communication and relationship between nursing staff and administration deteriorated to a point where communication no longer existed. When the voices of the nurses providing bedside care are no longer heard, patient care becomes vulnerable, Paradis said.
“Walking away from a place where I have invested so much of myself is not something I take lightly,” she said. “It is painful to leave. I cannot compromise my morals, my integrity, or my responsibility and accountability to the patients I serve.”
During union negotiations the hospital was limited by federal law in their ability to communicate with nurses, according to Sime.
“The law limits what management can say to employees during a union campaign and, after employees vote to be represented by a union, management is generally prohibited from discussing wages, hours and working conditions directly with the represented RNs,” she said.
Additionally, because the emergency department was more active in the union negotiations, they have been more “punished” than other departments, Maxwell said, adding that when they asked for resources, the nurses did not get them and other resources they had were taken away.
Maxwell and others who worked on the bargaining committee have been disciplined by administration and have open cases with the National Labor Relations Board because of some of these things, Maxwell said.
The loss of staff impacts patient care, and it also impacts the hospital’s bottom line as more money has to be spent on traveling nurses and on training new staff, according to the letter.
The hospital is offering the traveling nurses $50 an hour and $90 an hour for overtime as well as paid housing for a 16-week contract, according to Maxwell.
The previous administrator, Peter Sirois, was at the hospital for decades and was a part of the community, but things changed when he retired and the board hired Zewe, according to Maxwell and Paradis.
“Things have gotten a lot worse under his administration,” Maxwell said. “If half of the emergency department nurses are leaving, where is the board? Why are they not taking notice? We have reached out to them and have been met by silence. Are there no checks and balances or questioning when so many good people are leaving?”

title: The anti-bucket list: Why letting go might be a secret to aging well
text:
(Aging Untold) — A bucket list is about everything you still want to do. But what about an “anti-bucket list” — the things you’re finally ready to stop doing, stop caring about or stop apologizing for?
Saying no might be one of the most powerful tools for a freer, more joyful life after 60.
The problem with automatic “yes”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke kicked off the conversation with a true confession.
“I was asked to be on the HOA (homeowners association) board, and I said yes immediately,” O’Rourke said. “And then I went home and I was like, what did I say yes for? I don’t want to do that.”
O’Rourke said she had agreed out of guilt rather than genuine desire.
“I said it out of guilt that I should, that I can, that I would — afraid of what other people would think,” O’Rourke said. “So I reneged, and immediately I had better energy. I had better clarity. I got through the discomfort of saying no when I’m used to saying yes to everything.”
Subtraction as a privilege of aging
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose framed the shift as a kind of wisdom that comes with age.
“It’s a discernment. You hope as you get older, you become wiser and you make maybe more mature choices,” Ambrose said.
“One of the privileges of getting older is subtraction,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, added. “What can I do to subtract that’s going to give me more peace, more sleep, more joy. And it’s OK.”
Rogers said adding too many obligations creates stress that the body can’t distinguish from any other kind.
“Your body doesn’t realize the difference between types of stress, because it’s going to react the same,” Rogers said.
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck noted that saying yes isn’t always the wrong move.
“Sometimes yes is purpose,” Cradduck said. “Some people will say yes because it does give them the purpose, and we still need to feel that.”
Practicing the word “no”
Cradduck said the hardest habits to break are often the ones tied to people, boards and other obligations, like hosting Thanksgiving dinner year after year.
“I don’t want to fix Thanksgiving dinner anymore kind of thing,” Cradduck said, describing the kind of thought many people are afraid to say out loud. “I’ve done it for 35 years. Daughter, son, you can cook and it’s time for you to take it on.”
O’Rourke suggested starting small for anyone too anxious to say no to a big obligation right away.
“So maybe you start by saying something to someone other than a family member — say no and practice. Or if you’re really anxiety-ridden, say the words out loud to yourself. Kind of rehearse the conversation,” O’Rourke said.
Ambrose shared a story to illustrate the point, about a couple in their late 70s who had recently married.
“She was telling me about all the Thanksgivings and things that she’d hosted, what she could cook,” Ambrose said. “And he was so shocked. He said, ‘You told me you can’t cook.’ She said, ‘No, I didn’t say I can’t cook — I said I don’t cook.’”
“It can be very freeing,” Ambrose said. “I think as time becomes shorter, you start thinking about what I really want to do.”
Key takeaways
- An “anti-bucket list” is about subtraction, not addition.
- Guilt-driven “yes” answers can drain energy.
- The body reacts to different types of stress the same way.
- Not all “yes” answers are bad — some provide purpose.
- Practice saying no in low-stakes situations first.

title: Group of Seven to release barrels of stockpiled fuel
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The Group of Seven - a collection of some of the world’s largest economies - announced on Friday the release of 100 million barrels of fuel from its emergency stockpile following record-high fuel prices in September.
Oil prices have risen to record levels globally. The G7’s release of crude and diesel barrels marks a rare move intended to cap the cost of diesel.
The barrels come from the G7’s emergency stockpile, which is set aside for global supply shortages.
Wars in Ukraine and Iran have reduced the global fuel supply. Diesel has been particularly affected, with American farmers and the shipping industry facing a heavy impact.
With the midterm elections now days away, the Trump administration had considered restricting U.S. diesel exports, including a possible outright ban, to lower costs before November.
The G7’s release appears to end that possibility; the group’s statement said the release comes with an agreement among member nations not to limit energy exports to allied countries.
President Trump said in a Truth Social post the process will begin “immediately.” French President Emmanuel Macron said the release would happen over four months.
The move could reduce diesel prices by a few cents per gallon, according to experts, who added the effect would likely be temporary. Releasing stockpiled barrels does little to increase refinery capacity or production, experts said.

title: 911 call reveals concerns about well-being of 2 children found dead from starvation at home
text:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — Two children who were found dead in a home earlier this week in South Carolina have been identified, and authorities said this wasn’t the first time they had been called to the residence.
Emory Deacon, 2, and Harlow Deacon, 15 months old, died of starvation and dehydration due to neglect, Charleston County coroner Bobbi Jo O’Neal said.
Justine May, the children’s mother and described as their primary caregiver, has been charged in the case with two counts of homicide by child abuse.
According to the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office, deputies had responded to numerous calls at the Pinewood Drive residence before ultimately finding the two children dead during a welfare check at the home.
The previous calls to the home were said to have included welfare checks and visits coordinated with the South Carolina Department of Social Services and the South Carolina Department of Mental Health Mobile Crisis Unit.
Authorities said deputies made contact with May and the children in August and again several more times in September, noting they observed no signs of concern during those visits.
On Tuesday, authorities said they were called back to the home after a 911 call came through that morning asking deputies to conduct a welfare check on the two young girls after they had not been seen, with their mother acting differently while walking around the neighborhood by herself.
“I’m just concerned because she didn’t have her kids, and nobody has seen her kids,” the caller told the Charleston County 911 dispatcher. “She was walking down the road today, and she didn’t have her babies, and that’s not like her.”
When deputies arrived at the home that afternoon, they said May exited the house and was crying and speaking incoherently. Upon entering, that’s when they saw the two children dead.
May was taken into custody.
According to affidavits, after being read her Miranda rights, May told detectives that she had spent the previous two weeks in a “blur,” saying she could not remember the last time she fed Emory and Harlow or gave them anything to drink.
Authorities said May told detectives that she believed her children were dead because they did not eat. She reportedly told deputies that she knew that not feeding her children was neglectful and confirmed she had been the only one present at home and was the sole caregiver for the girls over the last few weeks.
May remains jailed at the Al Cannon Detention Center.

title: First National Bank partners with WindowDressers to support three community builds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WindowDressers, a nonprofit dedicated to warming homes, saving energy and building community, is excited to announce a partnership with First National Bank, which will be sponsoring three community builds in Orono, Rockland/Camden and Belfast. First National Bank will be providing both financial and volunteer support to each of these community builds.
This sponsorship will help sustain WindowDressers’ Special Rate Program, which offers low- or no-cost insulating window inserts to households who are struggling financially to afford their heating costs and other basic needs. In addition to their financial support, employees from First National Bank will participate as volunteers at the community builds, working alongside other community members to help assemble window inserts for households who have requested them. Last year, First National Bank employees participated in three local community builds as volunteers and WindowDressers is excited to continue this partnership.
“WindowDressers is deeply grateful for this partnership and the financial and volunteer support that First National Bank has provided us over the years. By working together, we can have a bigger impact in the communities we both serve,” Jessica Williams, executive director of WindowDressers, said.
Community members interested in volunteering or learning more about upcoming builds can visit https://windowdressers.org/community-builds-maine/.
Established in 1864 and headquartered in Damariscotta, First National Bank is a community bank and a subsidiary of The First Bancorp, Inc. (NASDAQ: FNLC). The full-service financial institution provides personal and business banking, mortgage and commercial lending, digital banking, and wealth management services through First National Wealth Management. With 18 banking offices, First National Bank serves communities throughout coastal and eastern Maine. The Bank also supports Maine communities through charitable giving and employee volunteerism. To learn more, call 1-800-564-3195 or visit www.thefirst.com.
WindowDressers is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that brings community volunteers of all economic and social situations together to improve the warmth and comfort of interior spaces, lower heating costs, and reduce pollution associated with burning fossil fuels, by producing low-cost insulating window inserts that function as custom, interior-mounted storm windows.

title: Obituary: Jonathan E. Helmreich
text:
MEADVILLE, Pa. – Prof. Jonathan E. Helmreich, 89, passed away peacefully in the early hours of Monday, Sept. 28, 2026 while visiting family in Pennsylvania. Son of Ernst C. and Louise R. Helmreich, he was born Dec. 21, 1936, in Brunswick, Maine. He graduated in 1958 from Amherst College and received a Ph.D. in history from Princeton University in 1961. In 1959 he wed Martha Schaff; they had three children together but later divorced. Jon married Nancy (Moyers) Ross in 1979.
In 1962 Dr. Helmreich joined the faculty at Allegheny College in Meadville, Pa. He taught European, Russian, and Soviet history and served as academic dean from 1966 through 1981. After retirement in 1998, he accepted the volunteer position of college historian. He was declared an honorary member of the Allegheny College Class of 2018 and awarded the College’s Alumni Medal.
Jonathan was an active community member in Crawford County, Pa. and in southwest Florida at both Sanibel and the Shell Point Retirement Community in Fort Myers, Fla. A member of Stone United Methodist Church in Meadville, Pa., he served on several committees and sang in the choir for 33 years. He was instrumental in founding the United Housing Corporation and the building of the Fairmont/Fairview low and moderate income apartments. He also served on the boards of the French Creek Valley Conservancy, Greendale Cemetery, the Erie Philharmonic, and the Crawford County Historical Society. He was a recipient of many service awards including the Robert T. Sherman Distinguished Service Award from Allegheny College and Meadville’s Raymond P. Shafer Award for Distinguished Community Service. Beyond that, Jon found exhilaration in hiking the Appalachian Trail and the Teton and Wind River ranges and sailing on any available body of water.
Above all, Jonathan took joy in his family. He was predeceased by his parents; and brother, Paul.
He is survived by his wife, Nancy; and by children Anne (Christian Wulffen), Dana (David Parfitt), Douglas (Julie), and stepchildren Michael Ross (Helen), James Ross (Darlene), Mary Miller (Kevin), Douglas Ross (Cheryl Hudson), and Susan Shrock (Larry Marsteller); and by four grandchildren; 10 step-grandchildren; and 10 step-great-grandchildren.
Internment will be at a private ceremony in Greendale Cemetery. Arrangements have been entrusted to Rose and Waid Funeral Home and Crematory, Inc., 581 Chestnut St., Meadville, Pa.
A celebration of life memorial service will take place at Allegheny College at a date and time to be arranged.
Memories and condolences may be shared at http://www.rosefh.com.
