title: Do you need to step back from caregiving? How to spot the signs
text:
(Aging Untold) — Caregiving is often called an act of love, but over time it can wear down your mind, your body and your relationships.
The Aging Untold experts explain the warning signs of caregiver burnout, why stepping back can actually be the safer choice and how to make the transition without falling into guilt.
“It’s OK if you’re even deliberating quitting”
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, says the first step is giving yourself permission to admit you’re struggling.
“The first thing I would say is, it’s OK if you’re even deliberating quitting. And it’s very understandable,” O’Rourke said. “If you’re really, really tired, you’re not sleeping, everybody’s making you mad, and you’re getting burnt out — the first thing I would do is do whatever you need to do to get unburned out. Don’t make a decision in the middle of that stress.”
O’Rourke recommends caregivers step back, let someone else fill in and let their nervous system settle before making any long-term decision.
“Get your central nervous system kind of dialed back a bit, and then make the decision,” she said. “If you’re going to make the decision — I want to quit — then have a plan. What’s the transition plan? Is it a community? Is it a relative? Is it a paid caregiver, whatever it is.”
Expect “buyer’s remorse” after the decision
O’Rourke said caregivers who do step back should prepare for a wave of conflicting emotions afterward.
“Be fully prepared to what I call buyer’s remorse,” O’Rourke said. “You make the decision and then you regret it, and you’re back and forth. ‘I’m a bad daughter.’ ‘I couldn’t do it.’ So there’s some back-and-forth emotions. I’ve had clients do this and they end up quitting. And then I have others — they got the rest they needed, and then they went back and did it differently.”
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, compared unmanaged caregiver stress to a fire waiting to happen.
“We often love to tell caregivers, don’t let yourself get burnout. But listen, guys — the match is lit, the kindling’s sitting there, and there’s literally gasoline on it,” Cradduck said. “And there’s not oftentimes water in the area to put the fire out. We fail to tell people how not to burn out.”
Respite care can offer a reset
Cradduck pointed to hospice respite care as one option for families whose loved one has reached that stage of care.
“If your loved one has reached the stage of hospice, hospice respite care is part of that program,” Cradduck said. “You can have your loved one, if they’re in the home, transported to a community for a week to 10 days. And they can do this every quarter. It can give you that reset and that break. And then you can go, ‘OK, I can do this a little longer.’ Or maybe you’re like, ‘You know what, I can’t.’”
O’Rourke added that respite care isn’t limited to hospice situations.
“If they’re not terminal, communities have respite care. Home health has respite care too,” O’Rourke said. “I love the idea of just saying, temporarily, I’m taking a leave of absence.”
Love doesn’t mean you have the ability to do the job
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said one of the hardest parts of caregiving is separating love for a person from the physical and emotional capacity to care for them.
“Being a caregiver takes away from your identity over time,” Rogers said. “One of the hardships is understanding that love doesn’t mean ability. When you recognize that you’re at a crossroad, I think that’s really empowering, because if you continue to do what you know is not working out, you’re going to take it out on your body physically as well. And then the resentment comes in, and then that fight-or-flight — you’re stuck in this mode and you just can’t heal. It becomes detrimental to both parties.”
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose shared what she has seen.
“I see people that say, ‘I loved my mom all the way to heaven. It was the greatest honor of my life,’” Ambrose said. “And then I see other people that say, ‘I can’t put my husband in a home. My children are ready to support me doing that, but I just can’t do it, and I don’t know what to do.’”
Ambrose noted that overwhelmed caregivers sometimes reach a point of hopelessness.
“Sometimes caregivers don’t outlive the person they’re caring for,” Ambrose said. “That’s sad when people are so overwhelmed that they may hope that they just pass away in their sleep, and that’s the way they see the burden being lifted.”
Caregiving doesn’t have to mean hands-on, 24/7 work
Ambrose said families should remind caregivers that stepping back from hands-on duties doesn’t mean stepping away from the relationship.
“Maybe mom needs even more than just, ‘Mom, we’re ready to support you when you’re ready,’” Ambrose said. “Maybe she needs to be rescued, because many caregivers do not outlive the spouse or the parent they’re caring for. But here’s the deal: Caregiving doesn’t have to be 24/7 hands-on. It can be advocacy and still being the spouse, still being the mom, still being the daughter.”
Ambrose described leverage as the key to sustainable caregiving.
“How can you use leverage? Leverage is three things: it’s systems, people and tools,” Ambrose said. “You may not know what those are, but you can reach out to people that work in home care, home health, the doctor’s office, the social worker at the hospital. Just keep asking questions, and you’ll find the resource to the resources. You’ll find your answers.”
Give yourself permission to get help
Cradduck said many caregivers stay in unsustainable situations because of a sense of duty tied to marriage vows or family roles.
“The problem that I see so frequently is the duty – It’s my duty. ‘Sickness and in health, better or worse — and this is the worst, and this is the sickness,’” Cradduck said. “I say you can still live those out as the spouse and not be the one that’s doing all the work. Try your darndest to find somebody that can help you out and give you that break. And then if that break’s what you need on a permanent level, go ahead and have somebody else step into the role. Give yourself permission. This is the hardest job you will ever do.”
Key takeaways
- Love doesn’t automatically equal capacity. Being the closest emotionally or geographically doesn’t mean you’re the one who has to have the skills or ability to provide hands-on care.
- Burnout harms both people — the caregiver and the person receiving care — through resentment, stress and physical health decline.
- Stepping away may be the healthiest choice.
- You can exit in planned stages — rest to clear your head, plan finances and arrange who will fill gaps in coverage.
- Caregiving can mean advocacy, not just hands-on labor. Using “leverage” — systems, people and tools — can let you stay involved without doing everything yourself.

title: Low-income Mainers auto-enrolled for electric discounts
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Up to 67,000 low-income Maine households will get discounts on their electric bills this year after an overhaul of a state assistance program.
People who already receive public health insurance or food and heating benefits will now also be automatically enrolled in the Low Income Assistance Program, or LIAP, that provides a percentage discount for eligible customers of Central Maine Power and Versant Power, according to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services.
Previously, eligible people had to enroll in LIAP separately by applying through their electric utility. The department estimates that tens of thousands of additional households will get into the program thanks to the system changes.
“Maine families are being pushed to the brink by the President’s whipsaw tariffs and his reckless war in Iran,” Gov. Janet Mills said in a Thursday press release. “At a time when every dollar matters, my administration is making it easier for vulnerable Mainers to lower their electric bills without unnecessary paperwork or bureaucratic hurdles.”
CMP customers could receive up to 81% off of their bill, and Versant customers could save up to 83%, depending on their income level, according to the Health and Human Services Department.
Funding for electric benefits nearly doubled this year, to about $40.5 million. The program is paid for through the state budget, a surcharge on utility bills and through a fund set up by developers of the New England Clean Energy Connect power line in western Maine.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Aging Untold: How to spot the signs you need to step back from caregiving
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, explore how to recognize when family caregiving demands have become too overwhelming and why stepping back can be the healthiest choice for everyone involved.
Plus, find out how to safely navigate physical intimacy and rebuild confidence after a serious health scare like a heart attack or stroke.
Then, we introduce a Virginia medical transport driver using line-dancing classes and community outreach to inspire local seniors.
Providing care for a loved one can be an honor, but it can also wear you down over time.
If you are experiencing caregiver burnout, it might be time to step back.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing how to admit you’re struggling, handle the conflicting emotions, get a break and find support.
Fear of another major health event like a heart attack or stroke can affect more than your routine — it can affect your relationship and your sex life.
“So many times people are so afraid of that fear of, if I do something, especially intercourse, I’m going to have another heart attack,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “You have to realize you’re going to have a new normal now. It’s not that you’re going back to where you were, but it’s a new norm, and you just have to talk with a physician. Cardiac rehab is a big deal.”
The Aging Untold experts are sharing how couples can navigate intimacy during recovery, from getting medical clearance and easing anxiety to finding a new normal together.
Many consumers, including older shoppers, are seeking out pre-owned and sustainable products, retail experts say.
Stephanie Hernandez, a secondhand stylist based in Washington, D.C., helps her clients build a one-of-a-kind, sustainable wardrobe — because many want to shop more responsibly but don’t have the time to do it themselves.
“I’d see videos of clothes washing up on beaches in countries across the ocean and it breaks my heart. That’s kind of why I started the business, to educate people about that and show them that there are other options,” Hernandez said.
Richard Caple says he didn’t want to teach the line-dancing class at Club 17, but he said yes. Now he’s attached to the seniors in his class, and it brings him joy when they share how it is helping them.
Caple has organized fashion shows to raise money for student scholarships and has raised money for the American Cancer Society. The group also helped one of its own members when she fell on hard times.
He does this while working full time as a medical transport driver for seniors in addition to leading the class.

title: Honeymooners among 4 Americans killed in Greece building collapse
text:
Honeymooners among 4 Americans killed in Greece building collapse
A newlywed couple, the bride's brother and his pregnant wife have been identified as the four Americans killed in a building collapse in Athens, Greece.
Alexander Kirkpatrick, 37, Florida Hoxha, 34, Florin Hoxha, 36, and Eris Cani were killed Sept. 25 when a two-story building collapsed in Athens’ historic Plaka district.
The four Americans were among the six killed in the blast, believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said.
Kirkpatrick and Florida Hoxha had married on Long Island the month before the blast and were ending their honeymoon in Athens, according to Newsday.
Florin Hoxha was the brother of the bride. Florin Hohxa accompanied the couple alongside his longtime partner, Cani, who was five months pregnant with their first child, according to media reports.
Video from the scene showed rubble strewn across the street and parked cars crushed by falling debris.
Neighboring buildings were damaged and evacuated.
Two women were injured in an adjacent building on Lysikratous Street, the fire department said. The search-and-rescue operation involved 30 firefighters and three dogs, and an investigation into the explosion was underway.
Plaka lies at the foot of the Acropolis, Greece’s most visited ancient monument.

title: This is why regular eye exams matter as vision changes with age
text:
(Aging Untold) — Vision changes can be easy to brush off until everyday tasks — such as reading small print or seeing clearly at night — become more difficult.
Changes may be common with age, but eye exams can reveal more than vision problems and protecting your eyesight can help preserve independence.
Night vision changes and glare can be early warning signs
“Some of the symptoms that people will get will be like changes in the vision at nighttime,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Others experience difficulty with reading or glare.
“Or they have to adjust the distance from which they’re reading, either too close or too far. And there’s something that’s changing.” Rogers said.
Rogers said people may assume these changes are simply a normal part of getting older, but don’t dismiss vision changes as an inevitable part of aging. Some eye diseases can offer early signs of what is happening elsewhere in the body.
Eye exams can offer clues about overall health
Rogers said the eyes are among the body’s most energy-demanding organs.
Conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure can increase oxidative stress, which Rogers described as damage to the mitochondria — the cells’ powerhouses.
Damage to mitochondria can contribute to deterioration in the eyes, Rogers said.
She recommends at least one regular eye exam once a year — at a minimum.
An exam might also reveal signs associated with diabetes, autoimmune diseases and blood pressure issues, gerontologist Sam Cradduck said. That means an exam is not only about checking whether someone needs a stronger prescription or reading glasses.
Amy shares a personal story
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a personal story of how an eye exam prompted by difficulty with headlights led doctors to find a mole in the back of her eye that they are monitoring.
“I would encourage anybody to get regular eye exams because you just don’t know what’s going on,” O’Rourke host said.
The major eye conditions
Rogers said glaucoma, cataracts and macular degeneration are three major eye conditions to watch for.
Medicare coverage for vision care can be limited, but cataract treatment is covered, O’Rourke said.
Family history can also be important, especially for people whose relatives have had macular degeneration or glaucoma.
“If you’ve got a family history, your eye issues like macular degeneration and glaucoma, then you for sure ought to be very active in your eye care,” O’Rourke said.
The potential consequences of losing vision make eye care an important investment.
“You lose so much if you lose your vision,” O’Rourke said.
Protecting vision can help preserve independence
Vision affects more than the ability to read a label or drive at night. Ambrose said losing vision can affect a person’s ability to remain in their own home as well as everyday independence.
“This is really about independence,” Ambrose said. “Because when you lose vision, it can affect your ability to stay in your own home. It can affect just absolutely everything.”
Ambrose encouraged people to consider what steps they can take when changes begin.
5 key takeaways about aging and eye health
- Do not assume every change is normal aging. Some changes in vision may be connected to broader health concerns.
- Schedule regular eye exams. Dr. Rhea Rogers recommends exams at least once a year, while noting that people with conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure may need particular attention to eye care.
- Know your family history. A family history of glaucoma or macular degeneration can make it especially important to be proactive about eye care.
- Think about independence. Protecting vision can help support everyday activities and the ability to remain in your own home.

title: Here’s what your state is doing to provide relief amid high fuel prices
text:
(AP) - High gasoline and diesel prices have prompted elected officials in many states to take actions providing relief to motorists.
Some governors and lawmakers have suspended motor fuel taxes. Others have reduced gas taxes. And still more have waived restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel typically used by farmers, foresters and others for off-road equipment.
The actions come as potential voters in the midterm elections have voiced widespread concern about high fuel prices and the general cost of living.
Average prices for regular gasoline have topped $4 a gallon while average diesel fuel prices have risen over $6 a gallon — both up substantially since the war with Iran began.
A growing number of governors and lawmakers have taken steps to provide fuel tax relief for at least some motorists. Here’s a look at some of those states:
- ALABAMA: Gov. Kay Ivey issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 120 days.
- ARKANSAS: Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
- CALIFORNIA: Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an order in September allowing a sooner switch to cheaper, winter-blends of fuel.
- GEORGIA: Gov. Brian Kemp resumed a 30-day fuel tax suspension in September, marking the second installment of the tax holiday that was first offered in the spring.
- ILLINOIS: The state budget delayed a 1.3 cent gas tax increase from July 1 to Jan. 1.
- INDIANA: Gov. Mike Braun has issued multiple extensions of a fuel tax holiday, which currently runs through Nov. 4. He also issued an executive order relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel.
- KENTUCKY: Gov. Andy Beshear in May temporarily reduced the gas tax by 10 cents. That has expired, but a freeze continues on a 0.6 cent increase that had been scheduled for July 1.
- LOUISIANA: Gov. Jeff Landry issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
- MISSOURI: Gov. Mike Kehoe issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
- NEBRASKA: Gov. Jim Pillen issued an executive order in September allowing people to seek refunds of state diesel taxes for transporting crops and livestock and relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 90 days.
- NORTH CAROLINA: Gov. Josh Stein in September ordered relaxed enforcement of restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel through the end of the year.
- NORTH DAKOTA: Gov. Kelly Armstrong issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for two months.
- OHIO: Legislation signed in October by Gov. Mike DeWine suspends state fuel taxes for 90 days.
- OKLAHOMA: Gov. Kevin Stitt in September ordered relaxed enforcement of restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 120 days.
- TEXAS: Gov. Greg Abbott issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
- UTAH: Legislation signed by Gov. Spencer Cox reduced the gas tax by 6 cents a gallon from July 1 through the remainder of the year.

title: Sally Cluchey cares about constituents
text:
I am writing to share my experience with my state representative, Sally Cluchey.
We recently moved to Bowdoinham, and it was starting to get into the cold months. We needed assistance navigating the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), which is a complicated process with lots of paperwork. I made an appointment with Bowdoinham Community Connections, a local organization that helps people in our community work through issues like this.
My appointment was with Sally Cluchey, who works for the program part-time when she is not in the Legislature. Sally spent a lot of time with us, working patiently until the whole process was completed. She really cared and did not judge our situation. We couldn’t have done it without her.
This experience gave me confidence that people really do care. I will be proud to support her reelection as my state representative.
Rebecca Cormier
Bowdoinham

title: Democrats launch $3.4M corruption-focused ad campaign against Susan Collins
text:
A Democratic super PAC launched a $3.4 million ad campaign on Friday to highlight a recent report that accused Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of steering millions of dollars to a defense contractor in exchange for campaign contributions.
The 30-second spot from WinSenate focuses on a recent ProPublica report about illegal campaign contributions made to a pro-Collins super PAC during her 2020 campaign.
The ad features local news reports about last week’s story. It includes an older-looking woman — a key swing demographic in the race — speaking directly to the camera.
“Susan Collins took illegal campaign money and steered millions in government contracts to the donor, but Donald Trump’s administration shut down the investigation,” the woman says. “Maybe there’s a reason Susan Collins does whatever Donald Trump wants her to.”
The big-dollar ad campaign shows how Democrats are looking to turn Collins’ central campaign argument into a liability in the closing month of Maine’s closely watched Senate race.
“Chuck Schumer is bringing his New York campaign tactics to Maine,” Collins campaign spokesperson Shawn Roderick said, referring to the Democratic leader in the Senate. “His ads keep getting fact-checked as false and now he is asking Mainers to believe someone who is doing hard time in federal prison for fraud. Mainers have never fallen for his tactics and they aren’t going to now.”
Polling leading up to ProPublica’s report had shown a tight race between Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president. Jackson holds a roughly two-point lead over Collins, according to polling averages from the election website FiftyPlusOne.
The ad comes after the Senate Majority PAC, which is aligned with WinSenate, issued a Sept. 29 memo outlining its plan to make corruption a key part of its closing message to midterm voters. The group said the message ties into voters’ concerns about rising prices.
The memo notes that invoking “corrupt” and “pay-to-play politicians” is particularly effective among swing voters — a group that has repeatedly sent Collins back to Washington, D.C., despite leaning Democratic in recent statewide elections.
Republican groups are also making corruption a central argument in attacks against Jackson. They’ve run ads that highlight Jackson’s expense reimbursements while maintaining a second home in Augusta, as well as his son Chace’s work as a lobbyist while his father was Senate president.
On the campaign trail and in ads, Collins has been touting her power as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee — the first Mainer to hold the post in 92 years. She says she’s been able to bring home $1.5 billion in federal earmarks over the last five years.
But Democrats are trying to flip the script to argue she’s using that position to benefit herself by pointing to ProPublica’s report.
Last week, the outlet reported that the FBI was preparing to open a sweeping corruption probe of Collins and other powerful politicians in 2024. But the probe was shut down after Trump returned to the White House in 2025 and disbanded the anti-corruption unit.
Collins, her campaign and her staff have all vigorously denied the allegations and called the report “outrageous” and a political hit job that’s based on the word of a convicted felon. They contend Collins was cleared of wrongdoing by the Biden administration, noting the defense contractor in question, Martin Kao, of the Hawaii-based firm Navatek, was implicating Collins to have his prison sentence reduced.
An FBI spokesperson is quoted in the story saying the bureau “ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign. Any suggestion otherwise is totally false.”
The WinSenate ad is part of a more than $32.7 million investment the Democratic super PAC is making in Maine, according to the media tracking firm, Ad Impact. The PAC has nearly $18.8 million in ads reserved between now and Election Day.
But Republican groups have a significant financial advantage in the race. Those groups have spent or reserved $100.5 million on ads this cycle — nearly $38 million more than Democrat-aligned groups, according to Ad Impact. Republican groups have reserved more than $37 million in ads leading up to the election.

title: Bangor Beautiful Commissioned A Community Mural Celebrating Local Artists On Hammond Street
text:
Another Massive Mural Is Coming Together In Downtown Bangor: Check This Out!
In 2022, a non-profit called Bangor Beautiful was started by a group of local artists and residents who wanted to find ways, through landscaping, gardens and art installations, to add a little beauty to the community around them.
Read More: Have You Seen These 9 Bangor Murals?
"We were founded by artists and community members who have volunteered for projects around the city over the last decade, from planting hundreds of flowers and trees to creating the popular 'Greetings from Bangor, Maine,' 'Paul B., Bangor Wants You,' and Kenduskeag Stream Trail murals."
If you've driven through downtown this week, you've probably seen their latest project, their "Community Mural."
Working with the Bangor Region Chamber of Commerce, Portland-based artist Rachel Gloria Adams has developed a piece that's enveloping the the side of the Hammond Street building in a painted patchwork quilt of sorts, incorporating artwork by Bangor artists, Juliana Cantreli, Nina Earley, Annette Dodd, Karen Nichols, Carile Deshane.
According to the folks at Bangor Beautiful, "She has developed a vibrant, graphic pattern-based visual language filled with references to the natural world and motherhood that possess an heirloom quality. "
Read More: Maine Fall Foliage Chairlift Rides: Last Chance This Weekend
They say the theme of Community was chosen in the hopes that it "gives people a sense of belonging and reminds us that we’re part of something larger than ourselves."
Besty Lundy, Executive Director of the Downtown Bangor Partnership says she's enjoyed seeing the mural take form.
"Downtown Bangor is excited to welcome another mural to our public art landscape. New public art continues to underscore Bangor's presence as an arts and culture destination for visitors from near and far."
Read More: Take a Maine Fall Foliage Train Ride on the Leaf Peeper
You can check out this mural, and more cool art features across Downtown Bangor. The Downtown Bangor website has an interactive map that shows the locations of different pieced. You can click here to see for yourself.
The project is being funded in part by sponsorships and donations. To contribute, you can click here.

title: Coming out later in life: Why more LGBTQ+ older adults are living openly
text:
(Aging Untold) — Aging brings changes beyond the physical — it can reshape courage, confidence and a sense of self. For some older adults in the LGBTQ+ community, that growth shows up as coming out later in life after decades of keeping part of who they are hidden.
The Aging Untold experts are exploring what shifts with age that make living openly feel possible, and what’s still at stake for couples who choose to stay private.
What finally makes it feel safe to come out
Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, opened the conversation by asking what changes as people get older that can make them feel safe enough to live more openly.
“I think the thing that changes the most is judgmental people pass away,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “I think if you’re trying to keep it from your own parents, and once they’re gone, you’re able to be who you are.”
Cradduck said the shift can also come from a child who wasn’t able to accept it, and later changes their mind — sometimes because someone else in their life has come out.
“It gives you an opportunity, plus the fear of your own mortality and not being able to end your life with the person you want to end your life with and having them beside you,” Cradduck said. “That can be very overwhelming. So you finally throw caution to the wind, and you no longer care what other people think. You care who’s beside you during those final moments. So you let the world know. And I see nothing wrong with that.”
A 50-year relationship kept secret
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a story from her own work: two women in their early 80s went into her office for help, and she could feel the love between them.
“I said, how long have you two been together? And they said, 50 years,” O’Rourke said. “Not married. And I said, ‘Does anybody in your family know?’ And they said, ‘No.’”
When O’Rourke asked the women what had stopped them from telling their families, they said they were too scared.
“They’re not going to accept it. We just kept everything the way it is,” they told O’Rourke.
“I felt sad. I would want them to have more, but I could tell that they had forged such a close bond that the decision worked for them,” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke said her advice for couples in that position is to be direct with family ahead of time.
“Let everybody know ahead of time, this is what we’re doing. This is who I am. This is what I want from you,” O’Rourke said. “These are the boundaries that I’m drawing for myself that I want you to abide by.”
Ambrose added that verbal wishes aren’t enough on their own.
“There’s some real nasty people when it comes to death and hospitals, etc., or who’s making decisions on the funerals,” Ambrose said. “It’s really important to have legal documents in place.”
When families shut partners out
Cradduck shared a story of a woman she provided care for.
The woman’s best friend was also her partner. During the woman’s final days in hospice care, her family forbade her partner from visiting — and wouldn’t let her attend the funeral to pay her respects, Cradduck saod.
“I’ve seen where families step in and they do the most horrific thing,” Cradduck said. “They’re protecting their own image of who this person was instead of accepting them.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said there is a physical toll that comes with hiding one’s identity for years.
“Once you become older, a lot of times I think people just own who they are. They’re authentic,” Rogers said. “When you’re living unseen and unheard, that’s an emotional burden, that’s loneliness, that’s stress. And that’s a whole bunch of physiology affecting your body.”
Cradduck also noted a gap in elder care options for LGBTQ+ seniors.
“We haven’t built enough communities for our aged population at all, but we don’t have enough LGBTQ-friendly companies and care companies,” Cradduck said.
She pointed to SAGE USA, which she described as an LGBTQ-friendly training program that helps communities, assisted living facilities and home care agencies work with elderly people in the community.
Coming out — or staying private — is a personal choice
O’Rourke said the decision to come out later in life comes with its own mix of emotions.
“You’re going to have grief associated with losing some people that might not accept it. You’ll have your own grief of changing from one identity to another,” O’Rourke said. “But you can have two feelings at the same time. You can feel sad. You can also feel celebratory. You can feel happy that you’re finally yourself.”
Cradduck said staying private can be the right call for some.
“If staying in the closet is what’s safest and what’s best, and what brings the least amount of stress and turmoil — then live your life that way,” Cradduck said.
O’Rourke added that religious beliefs are worth acknowledging as part of that decision as well.
“I think that’s important to acknowledge, but I’m with you — do whatever you feel comfortable with,” O’Rourke said.
Rogers also emphasized protecting those choices legally.
“Do whatever you feel comfortable with, but take the legal actions to protect,” Rogers said.
Ambrose added that younger generations may not fully grasp what older LGBTQ+ adults faced.
“Younger generations underestimate the amount of fear, stigma, pressure that was on us decades ago,” Ambrose said. “Some of the more controversial things that didn’t fit in the box, it was a really hard thing to live in. And I just believe we’re living in a more empowering age, and hopefully learning to act with a little more love and kindness.”

title: King co-sponsors bill to increase affordable housing construction
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
U.S. Sens. Angus King, I-ME and John Curtis, R-Utah, are introducing bipartisan legislation to help homebuilders reduce costs and avoid bureaucracy as they work to address the national housing shortage.
The bill is the “Build American Efficiency Act,” which is also being sponsored by U.S. Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and Peter Welch, D-Vt., and is designed to encourage the Department of Housing and Urban Development to share industry-led initiatives to certify products and facilities that comply with Build American Efficiency Act requirements.
“Despite our country’s desperate need for additional affordable housing options, American homebuilders face steep costs and bureaucratic red tape,” said King.
The Build American Efficiency Act was designed to streamline the process for builders to locate domestically sourced materials.
It would ease the restrictions of the Build America, Buy American law, which has been blamed for stalling building projects and driving up costs.
“The Build American Efficiency Act would empower the Department of Housing and Urban Development to share information to help builders, manufacturers, and housing providers navigate complicated compliance requirements and identify verified American-made products,” King said.
“Eliminating this time-consuming and costly additional step for homebuilders will allow them to build more homes faster. It’s a three-page bill that amounts to a common-sense helping hand.”
Maine supporters
In Maine, the Senate bill is supported by Avesta Housing and Evernorth.
“The Build American Efficiency Act is an important step forward that will help Avesta and creators of affordable housing everywhere, move ahead with creating desperately needed new homes for individuals and families,” noted Jennifer Hawkins, president and CEO of Avesta Housing.
“This bill removes a significant challenge to building housing that is now causing serious delays, increasing costs of construction, and putting the viability of needed developments at risk,” Hawkins added.
The bill has been supported by dozens of manufacturers, housing coalitions and contractors’ associations, including the Alliance for American Manufacturing, Associated General Contractors, the National Association of Manufacturers, the National Association of Realtors and the National Association of State Housing Agencies.

title: Former Maine judge and hot dog stand owner dies at 95
text:
Alan Crosby Pease, a former judge, hot dog stand owner, and active alumni of the University of Maine, died on Sept. 2 at the age of 95.
Pease was born to Harvey Roscoe Pease and Grace Crosby Pease on Oct. 11, 1930, on Water Street in Wiscasset. He attended elementary and middle school in Wiscasset and then Lincoln Academy.
To make money for college, Alan Pease had a “little trailer” he sold hot dogs in, according to his son, Daniel Pease. Alan Pease would take it to fairs and community baseball games.
At 19 years old, Alan Pease purchased a hot dog stand called The Little Trailer in Wiscasset from Stan and Velma Dodge. After switching hands a couple more times, it would go on to be known as Red’s Eats food stand.
Pease named the stand Al’s Eats and ran it singlehandedly seven nights a week, according to a history of Red’s Eats written by Virginia Wright and Deborah Gagnon. Daniel Pease said the operation was seasonal.
“They often talked about being open into the wee hours Saturday nights because the dance halls would get out and there was nothing else open,” Daniel Pease said. “So they had quite a business there on the Main Street in Wiscasset after midnight.”
In 1956, when Pease entered his last year of law school at the Boston University School of Law, he sold the stand to Frank Hammond.
Gagnon, who operates Red’s Eats, said she came to know Pease through exchanging letters about the stand. While operating the business, Pease created the “Sturdley,” a grilled hot dog with melted cheese, which remains on the Red’s Eats menu to this day.
“Alan wrote a letter to me congratulating us on Red’s Eats success and how happy it made him to see that the Sturdley was still on the menu,” Gagnon said in an email interview. “Alan named the grilled hot dog with melted cheese after a 1950s radio character, Sturdley. It’s still a customer favorite.”
Pease attended UMaine in Orono, graduating in 1952, the same year he married fellow graduate Margaret “Marnie” Murray. The couple later received the 2013 Block “M” Award for their leadership in their alumni class group.
University of Maine Alumni Association Director of Alumni Engagement Ashley Twombly said the Peases both felt it was important for the classmates to stay connected and stay engaged.
“I think they just felt like the university made them who they were and they wanted to make sure that they gave back,” Twombly said.
During his time at school, Pease served as class president, co-class president and class correspondent. He also created a website for the class. Twombly worked with him to host an annual reunion when she started her job in 2015.
“He was very kind, very patient,” Twombly said. “He just wanted to help and he understood that anytime that I was busy or that I just needed to take my time, he was just very gentle.”
After graduating, Pease enlisted in the U.S. Army and was stationed at Fort Benning in Georgia as a first lieutenant. Because of his experience at Al’s Eats, he oversaw the base commissary, an equipment and food supply store, and instructed other soldiers in military law.
“He had trouble telling right from left,” Daniel Pease said. “And that got him into some trouble, apparently, when he was leading some practice maneuvers at Fort Benning, and he would take his troop to the wrong place, and that didn’t work out too well. He claims that was why he didn’t get sent overseas.”
Alan Pease attended the Boston University School of Law, graduating with a Juris Doctor in 1957. While he was living in Boston, his daughter Kathryn Pease was born.
With his degree, he moved back to Wiscasset, where he started a legal practice and began serving on the newly established Wiscasset School District. His son, Daniel Pease, was born while they were living in Wiscasset.
The school district was established to take out loans to construct new buildings, according to a report written by Alan Pease at the time. Once the buildings were constructed, Pease resigned from the position.
“The people of Wiscasset have never ceased to do their part and this will be reflected in generations to come,” Pease said in the town report from 1973, his final year in the position.
In 1977, Pease began serving as a member of the Wiscasset Select Board. He stepped down in 1978 after being appointed to the Maine District Court as deputy chief judge and later chief judge.
Pease said at a December 1978 meeting of law enforcement officials he intended to be “tough but fair.”
John Atwood, who was the assistant attorney general at the time Pease sat as judge, said this was a fair assessment.
“Alan Pease was highly knowledgeable in the law,” Atwood said. “He kept up with all the research and trends and publications. He was always fair to all concerned, he didn’t have any favorites.”
Atwood said that Pease was widely admired at the time and was known to treat a case with the “dignity and gravity it deserved.” During the Vietnam War, many judges would offer defendants the choice of joining the military or going to jail, which Pease refused to do, instead treating them as “normal cases,” according to Atwood.
“He was everybody’s ideal of a judge,” Atwood said. “I never saw him lose his temper, although he certainly had cause from time to time.”
Former Maine District Court Judge Geoffrey Rushlau first saw Pease serve as a judge when he was a third-year law student at the prosecutor’s office. On first impression he said he thought Alan Pease was “composed” and “comfortable” on the bench. After finishing law school and witnessing more judges, Rushlau said his vision of Pease as an “excellent district court judge” was confirmed.
“He was extremely well organized,” Rushlau said. “He came to work early and stayed until all the work was done. He did not waste any time whatsoever as far as I can tell. His decisions were always very clear.”
During Pease’s time as judge, there was an unlimited possibility for “trial de novo,” according to Pierce Hasler wrote for the Maine Law Review. If a person was convicted at the district level, that person could appeal the decision to a superior court and have a new trial.
“It meant decisions by district court judges in some respect were like a practice round in golf or something like that,” Rushlau said. “I think it was probably difficult for a judge to do their job when they recognized that it might have very little significance, but I only ever saw him be perfectly respectful of the law in the process.”
The process was eliminated in the 1980s.
Rushlau said that Pease also did not tolerate alcohol consumption as an excuse for behavior during cases and his demeanor during those cases ensured it was treated in a serious manner.
Since the first Apple technology was released, Pease was interested in technology, Daniel Pease said.
“He was a source for us for years,” Daniel Pease said. “If we ever had a question about how to do something with the computer, he was the go-to guy.”
Alan Pease was the first chair of the Maine Court Technology Task Force, where he helped computerize the district court system. He taught adult education classes on computer science and maintained websites for several area nonprofits, Daniel Pease said.
Alan Pease also enjoyed woodworking and electronic building kits. Daniel Pease worked on several with him, he said. “I can’t think of any time he wasn’t helpful and encouraging,” Daniel Pease said.
Alan Pease retired in 1990 and moved with his wife to St. George and later to Camden, where Daniel Pease said they were able to be close to their four grandchildren. Margaret Pease died in 2021.

title: Maine man seriously injured in tractor-trailer collision
text:
A New Gloucester man was seriously injured Thursday evening when he collided with a tractor-trailer in Auburn.
Jonah King, 29, was driving south on Washington Street, near the intersection with Kittyhawk Avenue, about 7:29 p.m. when he collided with a turning tractor-trailer driven by 46-year-old Peter Fontaine of North Waterboro, according to the Auburn Police Department.
King suffered life-threatening injuries. He was taken to Central Maine Medical Center before being transferred to Maine Medical Center in Portland, Auburn police said Friday morning.
Fontaine had a green traffic signal for making a left-hand turn onto Washington Street from Kittyhawk Avenue, police said.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Kristi Noem posts from a Maine moose hunt
text:
Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem posted photos to Facebook on Thursday from a successful moose hunt in Maine.
Noem was accompanying her daughter Kassidy Noem Peters, who bagged a bull and described the outing on Instagram as a “once in a lifetime moose hunt.”
“After the hunt, we explored the surrounding conservation areas, habitat and Amish community,” wrote Kristi Noem, who now serves as special envoy for the Shield of the Americas.
Noem, who pioneered a fashion around tactical clothing before she was fired from her role as the head of Homeland Security, posted videos and photos from the hunt, including one in which she poked fun at herself for wearing ski pants and tagged a hunting apparel company to “make some pants to fit women!! Please.”
Another photo showed a sign marking the “Donald J. Trump Jr. Rifle Range.” The president’s son and his company, Trump Timberland and Wildlife Management, bought 3,900 acres from the family of former state Rep. Austin Theriault, R-Fort Kent, in Crystal and Island Falls in November 2024.
Some commenters noted that Peters’ name wasn’t on the list of permit holders from the 2026 moose lottery. But she could have obtained one through a lodge, which receives tags through a separate lottery and can then set its own price, often $15,000 to more than $30,000. Another option to purchase a moose permit is through the state’s annual auction of 10 tags.
Peters did not immediately respond to messages sent by the BDN to her Facebook and Instagram accounts.
BDN Outdoors Editor Susan Bard contributed reporting.

title: 3 teens injured in shooting after high school football game in Pittsburgh
text:
3 teens injured in shooting after high school football game in Pittsburgh
Police are searching for a gunman accused of shooting and injuring three teenagers outside of a high school football game in Pittsburgh on Thursday night, according to Pittsburgh Public Safety.
Officers are still searching for the shooter as of Friday morning, although officials have not released a description of the suspect.
Two male victims and one female victim, all believed to be teenagers, were taken to a hospital and are in stable condition, Pittsburgh Police Chief Jason Lando said.
The gunfire happened after an altercation outside George K. Cupples Stadium in Pittsburgh's South Side neighborhood following a high school football game between Westinghouse Academy and University Prep, officials said.
Police said the shots were fired as crowds were exiting the venue.
Video below: Pittsburgh police chief gives an update on the South Side shooting
"As the game ended, there was a large crowd out here on Carson Street. A couple of fights broke out. We had multiple officers from the city and Port Authority that were on the scene, helping to just facilitate people safely getting out, breaking up a couple fights, when suddenly, an individual pulled out a firearm and fired multiple rounds," Lando said.
Lando said there was already a hefty Pittsburgh Police and Port Authority Police presence inside and outside of the game. There are also metal detectors at the stadium. Police do not know if the shooter or the victims had been inside the stadium before the shooting.

title: The kindness of community
text:
To the Editor:
These days, I think a lot about what the word community actually means. One example might be in how we think about our Mount Desert Island community. Are we separate? Are we united? There are many real issues that potentially divide us in our public discourse, but when the unexpected tragedy strikes any one or several of us, how do we react? title: Halle Berry’s ex accuses her of child abuse
text:
LOS ANGELES (CNN) — Olivier Martinez, the ex-husband of actress Halle Berry, is accusing her of child abuse, according to court filings.
Martinez alleges Berry physically abused their 12-year-old son by jumping on him and choking him.
Martinez also filed for a temporary restraining order, adding there have been “other instances of abuse” over the years. He is asking for sole custody of the boy.
Berry’s attorney responded in a statement, calling the filing “entirely meritless and deliberately misleading.”
The attorney added that it was “not entirely unexpected from an individual with a well-documented history of erratic, possessive and violent behavior.”
Berry and Martinez divorced in 2015 after two years of marriage.

title: Head Start was there for my family. Maine children need it protected.
text:
Megan Newsome lives in Lisbon and is a Maine state parent ambassador.
When my son Brayden was born, our family was facing a lot at once.
I had been diagnosed with cancer while I was pregnant. He arrived about six weeks early and spent time in the NICU. By the time Brayden was about a year old, I was receiving WIC, the federally funded nutrition program for women, infants and children. WIC staff asked whether I had childcare and told me about Early Head Start.
I knew very little about the program then. It quickly became a godsend.
At the time, Brayden was not yet walking. He could not feed himself or hold his own cup. Within weeks of starting Early Head Start, he was pulling himself up, holding his cup and learning to use a spoon and pick up food on his own.
His teachers paid attention to who he was and how he learned.
Brayden is left-handed. When teachers recognized that and encouraged him to use the hand that came naturally to him, it showed me that they saw my son as an individual.
Head Start also gave me something I deeply needed while facing cancer: trusted people who could care for my child during the workday. Knowing my son was cared for and learning gave me comfort during an incredibly difficult time.
The support did not stop at the classroom door. Head Start connected us with mental health counseling, clothing, diapers, food banks and help during the holidays — all supports we needed to make sure Brayden had what he needed to learn and grow, at home and in the classroom. There was always someone I could turn to.
Brayden is now 3 and has moved from Early Head Start into Head Start. He is now on track developmentally, and this is a crucial moment in his learning. If he needs additional help before elementary school, I want us to recognize it early and have support in place.
That is why proposed changes to Head Start concern me so deeply. Families could lose developmental screenings, medical and dental services, counseling and other support that helps children grow and prepare for school.
For some children, Head Start may provide the only developmental screening they receive. It’s the front door to healthcare, dental care and mental health support. If those services disappear, important needs could go unnoticed until a child enters school and faces a harder path forward.
Larger classrooms and fewer teachers would also make it harder to provide the individual attention that helped Brayden. Teachers need time to know each child, understand how they learn and recognize when they may need additional support.
Head Start works because all these pieces work together. It is not simply a place where parents leave their children. It helps children build confidence and skills while connecting parents with trusted people and practical resources. Weakening any part of that model weakens the program families count on.
I know what Head Start made possible for my son and me. I also know other families rely on it for that same stability and partnership.
The public has only until Oct. 6 to comment on the proposed changes, but Congress can act even after that. I am asking Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King and Rep. Jared Golden, who represents Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, my home district, to listen to Maine families, oppose the proposed rule and protect the standards and services that make Head Start so effective.
Children deserve to enter school with their strengths recognized and the support they need already in place. Parents deserve trusted partners as they build strong futures for their families. Head Start gave my family both.

title: Maine Marathon: What to know for Sunday’s event in Portland
text:
The 35th edition of the Maine Community Bank Maine Marathon, Half Marathon and Marathon Relay takes place Sunday on the streets of Portland, Falmouth, Cumberland and Yarmouth, beginning at 7:45 a.m.
The largest marathon in Maine, the overall field is approaching 5,500 entries — well above last year’s record of 5,144.
“I’m limiting the growth to about 400 runners per year,” said Bob Dunfey, the volunteer race director.
The Maine Marathon and its participants have raised over $8,900,000 for charity. The event donates about 40% of revenue toward a variety of charities. Last year, donations totaled $793,285. Each year, the race picks three to five “designated charities.” This year’s beneficiaries are Nanna’s House, Day One, Camp No Limits, and the Pine Tree Society. Many other groups benefit from fundraising done by runners.
Here are key details about the Maine Marathon.
Start/finish: The marathon and half marathon start simultaneously on Baxter Boulevard in Portland. Both races also finish there.
Course: Essentially out-and-back. The course curls around Portland’s Back Cove, works it way to Route 1 North and then veers onto Route 88. The 26.2-mile marathon course goes through Falmouth and Cumberland before reaching the 12-mile mark in Yarmouth. Runners turn right onto Gilman Road, then another right onto Princes Point road to begin a roughly 3-mile loop to get back to Route 88, where they’ll head south on their return. The 13.1-mile half marathon follows the same route until it gets to a turnaround just past scenic Mussel Cove in Falmouth.
Event records: Men’s marathon — Ryan Eiler, Boston, 2 hours, 19 minutes, 19 seconds (2022); Women’s marathon — Abby Hamilton, Yarmouth, 2:39:38 (2021); Men’s half marathon — Colin Cernik, Portland, 1:04:39 (2025); Women’s half marathon, Cliodhna O’Malley, Windham, 1:15:06 (2025).
Prize money: The top male, female and non-binary runners earn $1,000 for the marathon and $500 for the half marathon, with cash through fifth place in each gender group if the runner meets the elite standard. Prizes are also available for a new event record in the marathon ($500) and half marathon ($250).
Top runners: The 2025 marathon winners, Sammy Mills of Portland and Emma Howe of Cambridge, Massachusetts, are not entered to defend their titles. The fastest local runners have migrated to the half marathon, including defending champions and event record holders Cernik and O’Malley. There are as many as 10 runners capable of challenging Cernik’s men’s record. The women’s half marathon features the past four winners — O’Malley, Phoebe Oehmig (2024), Veronica Graziano (2023) and Alyson Ursiny (2022). Megan O’Neil of Rochester, Michigan, is a serious threat. O’Neil ran a 2:31 at the Boston Marathon this spring, finishing 20th overall.
New this year: There will be lactation tents for the benefit of nursing mothers at the start/finish, and also near the 12- and 15-mile marks on the marathon course. … Instead of a starter’s gun or boat horn, the start of the chip-timed races will be signaled by a series of musical notes.
Race packet pickup: The runner’s expo on Saturday is at a new location. Runners can pick up their racing bib and T-shirt at Innovation Hall on the University of New England’s Portland campus from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Numerous vendors will be at the expo.
Race registrations: Dunfey said entries have come from 49 states (only North Dakota is missing), as well as Washington, D.C., the U.S. Virgin Island, Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, and 15 foreign countries. As of 3 p.m. Thursday, registration was still open but fast approaching the 5,500 cap.

title: Ken Urker, Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s ex-fiancé, found dead on his birthday, reports say
text:
RACELAND, La. (KPLC/Gray News) - Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s ex-fiancé Ken Urker was found dead in Louisiana, according to several reports.
He was 34.
A source close to the family confirmed his death to People. TMZ was first to report the news.
Urker’s brother Dylan found him unresponsive in his home on Thursday, which would have been his birthday, TMZ reported.
The Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Office said officers were called to a home in Raceland around 6:15 p.m. and found Urker dead, according to People.
According to People, Urker’s sister went live on TikTok Thursday night, confirming his death. She said his last words to her were “I love you,” People reported.
Urker and Blanchard were engaged from October 2018 to August 2019 while she was still in prison for her role in killing her abusive mother.
The two later rekindled their romance in April 2024. The two welcomed a daughter, Aurora Raina Urker, that same December.

title: Bernie Sanders to rally 3 times with Troy Jackson in Maine
text:
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders is heading to Maine next weekend for three rallies with Democrat Troy Jackson, marking a boost from a national progressive ally just three weeks before Jackson faces Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
The Vermont independent and two-time presidential candidate will join Jackson on stage in Bangor on Saturday, Oct. 10, along with two more get-out-the-vote rallies in Lewiston and Biddeford the following Sunday.
“We’re excited to welcome Bernie Sanders to Maine to rally with Troy Jackson,” Jackson campaign spokesman Dan Gottlieb said in a statement. “Bernie and Troy know that working people built this country and deserve a government that fights for them.”
The rallies with Sanders come ahead of an increasingly heated and tight race under the national spotlight as Democrats aim to deny Collins a historic sixth term and take back the Senate. Jackson has narrowly led most polls since he became the Democrats’ nominee in July. But Collins has led some, continuing to show strength among Democratic and independent voters who have helped her outperform Republicans and carry her to victories in the past.
The visit will be Sanders’ first public appearance in the state since he rallied in July in Bar Harbor with the man Jackson replaced on the ballot, Graham Platner, whose campaign collapsed after an ex-girlfriend accused him of rape.
Jackson, who was running for governor at the time, fired up the Bar Harbor crowd ahead of Sanders and Platner, who were also joined on stage by U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-California, and State Auditor Matt Dunlap, who faces former Gov. Paul LePage in the 2nd Congressional District matchup.
Jackson has been a longtime supporter of the Vermont progressive. The former Maine Senate president served as political director for Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign in Maine, and voted for him over Hillary Clinton as a superdelegate in that year’s Democratic National Convention.
Sanders, who had backed Platner before he was accused of sexual assault, told NBC’s “Meet the Press” in August that he’d endorse Jackson if he asked for it.
“You want a working-class voice in Washington, D.C., Troy is certainly that voice,” he said. “I have seen his platform. It is a strong platform, standing up for working families, taking on the oligarchs, fighting for Medicare for All.”
Sanders in May 2025 was one of Jackson’s first prominent endorsers in what became his third-place gubernatorial run this year. He appeared at multiple rallies with Jackson and Platner across the state. Collins recently received an endorsement from former independent Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia.
Next weekend’s rallies will come on the heels of the first two televised debates between Jackson and Collins, set for Tuesday and Thursday.
Jackson led Collins by 3 points in the latest AARP poll released Thursday. But no Republican in the group’s battleground Senate surveys is performing better with voters who split their tickets than Collins, who trailed every poll in 2020 before defeating former Maine House Speaker Sara Gideon by nearly 9 points.
Blake Kernen, a Collins campaign spokesperson, suggested the announcement of Sanders’ visit could be a bad sign for Jackson.
“If Troy Jackson needs help from one of the most partisan members of the Senate three weeks before Election Day, that’s a clear indication that Democrats don’t think they even have their base locked in,” she said.

title: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, a memo shows
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have been ordered not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training, under new internal guidance issued after several drivers were shot in encounters with ICE.
A memo sent to officers in ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division and obtained by The Associated Press warned they are not authorized to chase vehicles that fail to pull over under any circumstances. Instead, officers should take down the vehicles’ information for further investigation, according to the memo signed by ICE’s executive associate director Marcos D. Charles and dated Wednesday.
The new guidance comes after ICE-initiated vehicle stops have repeatedly escalated when drivers have refused to cooperate or tried to flee. ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen such encounters since last year, killing at least four people and wounding several others.
President Donald Trump’s administration has faced internal tension over how to handle traffic stops, which are seen as particularly high-risk encounters.
After fatal shootings of drivers in Maine and Texas in July, ICE officers were directed to temporarily pause most vehicle stops. But the next day, Trump went on social media to direct the agency to continue traffic stops, calling them “one of ICE’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools.”
ICE has faced intense pressure from the White House to deport more people who are in the country illegally, and its arrests have reached record numbers. At the same time, the agency’s rapid hiring spree last year resulted in some poorly vetted and trained officers hitting the streets.
In a statement, ICE downplayed the significance of the memo, which said the new guidance was intended to replace and amend prior directives issued earlier this year, last year and in 2018.
“Occasionally, ICE leadership issues guidance reminders to law enforcement officers,” the statement said. “Vehicle stops and arrests of illegal aliens continue.”
The new memo outlines steps intended to improve the safety of vehicle stops for ICE officers, drivers they are targeting, their passengers and the public.
The memo told ICE’s field office directors that they must ensure vehicles used for traffic stops have lights and sirens that let the public know they are law enforcement vehicles when activated. All officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras, under the guidance.
In addition, only officers who have completed one of five specific agency training courses can conduct vehicle stops. Officers who have not completed the training courses can only participate in vehicle stops “in a support capacity” as passengers and cannot be the drivers of any of the vehicles involved.
The guidance says ICE officers can continue to use a controversial technique known as pinning, which is defined as “using a vehicle or physical barrier to trap or stop a car,” but only if they have received special training. Similarly, only trained officers can use spike strips that deflate tires to prevent drivers from fleeing.
The memo came the day that courtroom testimony highlighted ways in which two ICE officers involved in a vehicle stop, pursuit and shooting that wounded a delivery driver in Austin last month would not have complied with the new guidance.
During a bond hearing for Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, testimony showed that the officer who shot him wasn’t wearing a body-worn camera. The ICE officer who did have a camera was driving in a separate car and turned it off during the pursuit.
Prosecutors presented surveillance video that showed an ICE agent chasing Garces Perez at high speeds through residential streets after he fled an initial traffic stop.
Garces Perez faces federal assault charges after investigators say he struck an ICE officer with his driver’s side mirror. That officer then shot into Perez’s vehicle, lodging a bullet in his back, officials say.
Attorneys for Garces Perez have called the charges against him “retaliation” and have argued that the camera footage was inconclusive because it didn’t fully capture the moment when he allegedly tried to flee.

title: University tests hot steam as alternative to farm fumigants
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
California university tests hot steam as alternative to farm fumigants
Researchers at UC Santa Cruz are exploring ways to help farmers go fully organic. A new steam technology could offer an alternative to pesticides and fumigants.
Researchers are testing whether hot steam can protect crops without relying on traditional pesticides or fumigants. The machine heats the soil to about 70 Celsius and holds it at that temperature for about 20 minutes.
“So it’s just water. It’s treating the soil only by heat,” Ryan Benson, lead engineer, said.
The process heats the ground enough to target pests, weeds and pathogens without chemicals, potentially giving organic farmers another tool.
“Soil fumigation has been traditional since 1950. That’s worked very well. This is just a look over the fence to see if an alternative works,” Mark Boulda, a farm advisor, said.
Pathogens can cause plant diseases and significant crop losses. Researchers say the steam treatment could help control soil-borne pathogens and extend the growing season, allowing farmers to keep working the land later into the fall.
The technology is being tested at organic berry farms across the Pajaro Valley, with a focus on farms near schools and neighborhoods.
Kathleen Kilpatrick, a member of the Santa Cruz County Safe Ag Safe Schools group, said, "The Pajaro Valley has some of the most concentrated use of fumigants in the state. We hope these pilot projects will provide tools for pesticide reduction and expansion of organic buffers."
Researchers say they will monitor the fields over time to assess the treatment’s long-term effectiveness.

title: Patriots defense loses Christian Gonzalez, Christian Barmore
text:
The Patriots will be without two of their top defensive players Sunday when they visit the Buffalo Bills.
Both cornerback Christian Gonzalez and defensive tackle Christian Barmore were ruled out Friday with shoulder injuries.
This will be the first game either has missed this season.
Gonzalez became the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history last month when he signed a four-year, $135 million contract. He has eight tackles on the season. Barmore has four tackles and one sack so far.
Quarterback Drake Maye is also dealing with a right shoulder issue, but participated in all practices this week.
Coach Mike Vrabel said Friday that Maye’s injury occurred sometime during the Week 3 loss at Jacksonville.
“There were no limitations, so he practiced full — he didn’t miss any reps,” Vrabel said. “But we just felt like it was best to list it just to make sure that we are doing everything that we’re supposed to do from a protocol standpoint.”
Vrabel acknowledged that not having Barmore as a pass rusher, nor Gonzalez to defend the Bills’ receivers, will be a challenge opposite Buffalo quarterback Josh Allen.
“That is just what the situation is. There’s nothing we can do about it,” Vrabel said. “We can make sure that the guys that are playing are ready and that we continue to do the things that we know are going to help us. But that happens every week in the National Football League. I’m looking forward to seeing the guys that are going to play in there.”

title: Babies after 40: How having babies later alters roles for parents, grandparents
text:
(Aging Untold) — More women are waiting until their 40s to have children, and the numbers show it.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, total U.S. births fell 14% from 1990 to 2023. During that same period, births among women 40 and older rose by more than 96,000 — a 200% increase.
The health risks are real, but manageable
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down why birth rates among women 40 and older have surged and what that shift means for health, family planning and the generations in between.
“It’s going to depend on the health state,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “At the foundation, it’s build your foundation, a healthy foundation, because they’re going to be more risks and complications in advanced maternal ages.”
Rogers said pregnancy after 40 is classified as advanced maternal age and can carry a higher risk for high blood pressure, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and chromosomal abnormalities. Physicians who specialize in high-risk pregnancies are available to help manage those risks, she added.
“With the resources that we have nowadays, it’s really, really important that you look at your foundation, your health, your sleep and all that,” Rogers said.
She added that paternal health matters just as much as maternal health.
“A lot of times we’re looking at the woman, but don’t forget the man,” Rogers said. “The fathers, their health as well has an influence on the sperm, just like the mothers on the egg.”
Why women are waiting longer
Rogers said many women now have more wisdom, resources and financial stability by the time they decide to have children.
“After age 40, for women, their wisdom is really leading their biology, but they’re doing it with intent,” she said. “They have better resources, more tools and probably are financially more stable.”
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, connected that shift to how this generation of women grew up.
“I think a lot of this age group grew up with single moms that were struggling because they didn’t put their education first, and they didn’t build those careers,” she said. “And so now they’re like, I’m not going to be in those shoes. I’m going to wait. I’m going to have all of that stability and all that financial security, and then I’m going to have my children.”
The trade-off: a changing generational gap
What’s lost when people wait longer to have children is time with grandparents, Cradduck said.
“My grandmother was my world,” Cradduck said. “I can’t imagine not having that in my life. Because of those influences, that’s how we build our empathy. So how are we reaching these smaller children when we’re losing that aged generation?”
Katherine Ambrose, an aging well coach, tied the concern back to the importance of healthy aging.
“That’s why healthy longevity is so important,” Ambrose said. “If you want to be around for grandchildren that are coming later, you’ve got to stay healthy and keep your energy up. So you can run around the theme parks with them.”
Older parents may bring more patience — and a new “sandwich generation”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared firsthand observations of children raised by older parents.
“My godson’s parents are older, and they were so much more patient,” she said. “They had less energy, so they asked for more help faster.”
O’Rourke said there was a crew of people, including herself, who helped.
The children were exposed to more people as a result and “seemed to mature faster,” she said.
O’Rourke also pointed to new financial and caregiving pressures that come with having children later in life.
“I would really put that thought in before I even had the child, because that’s a real concern,” O’Rourke said. “If you plan for it, it’s very, very possible. But it’s something to really think about.”
Cradduck said waiting to have kids can also mean caring for aging parents and raising children at the same time.
“There is that sandwich generation 2.0 that goes on here by being older,” Cradduck said. “You know your parents are in their 60s, likely by the time you’re having your children. So when your kids are teenagers, now your parents are in their advanced years. You may be caring for both at the same time, which we know is difficult.”
Wisdom over energy
Despite the challenges, the experts agreed that having children later in life comes with its own rewards.
“I’m so much calmer and wiser than I was as a young mom,” Cradduck said. “Maybe this waiting game — the wisdom replaces the energy. The patience replaces the frustration.”
“Every season of life has different strengths and trade-offs,” Ambrose said. “Every individual and family is different.”
Key takeaways
- Pregnancy after 40 carries a higher risk of high blood pressure, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and chromosomal abnormalities, Dr. Rhea Rogers said, so your health foundation matters.
- Paternal health and sperm quality matter just as much as maternal health when planning a pregnancy later in life.
- Women who wait often bring more financial stability, patience and life experience to parenting.
- Having children later can mean simultaneously caring for aging parents and raising kids — a “sandwich generation 2.0.”

title: Obituary: Linwood D. Libby
text:
SOUTH BERWICK – Linwood D. Libby, 91, of Berwick Estates and formerly of Lyman, passed away Thursday Sept. 24, 2026 at his residence.
He was born on Feb. 5, 1935 in Fort Fairfield, the son of Eldon and Vera Merrithew Libby. He attended local schools and graduated from Fort Fairfield High School.
Linwood later served in the National Guard and then served in the U.S. Army in Germany. Returning home, he attended USM in Portland.
Linwood was employed as a director for WCSH for 10 years. He was then employed at the South Portland Shipyard for 25 years. His latest employment was with Shields Meat and then the Maine Turnpike as a toll taker at the York Plaza.
He was predeceased by his wife, Patricia.
Survivors are a daughter, Denise Libby of Saco; and a brother, Beverly Libby of Caribou.
A graveside service with U.S. Military Honors will be held Friday, Oct. 9, at 1 p.m. at the Northern Maine Veterans Cemetery in Caribou.
Local arrangements are in the care of Dennett, Craig & Pate Funeral Home, Saco.
Memorial contributions in his name may be made to
Animal Welfare Society
