title: Many states have backup execution plans, but failures still happen
text:
(AP) - Long before Christa Pike was brought into Tennessee’s execution chamber, prison leaders reviewed and approved a backup plan detailing exactly what to do if the first attempt at lethal injection failed.
But the backup plan also failed, and Thursday — 24 hours later — Pike was still alive but in critical condition at a Tennessee hospital, though her prognosis remained uncertain. It’s not yet clear what went wrong.
Twenty-seven states have capital punishment, and they vary widely in how they administer the death penalty and just how much of that lethal process they keep hidden from public view, according to the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, a clearinghouse for information on U.S. executions.
Some states have extensive backup plans. Others don’t
Tennessee falls somewhere in the middle of the pack when it comes to contingency plans, with two redundancies built into its execution process.
First, inmates are supposed to have two intravenous lines placed. Thus, if the first IV site fails, the execution team can switch to the second one. A physician on the execution team can even insert a central line — which typically involves making an incision in a major blood vessel in the groin, neck or armpit in order to thread a catheter into the body to a spot near the heart — if needed.
Intravenous lines can fail for several reasons, like a needle and catheter not being properly placed in a vein or wiggling out of place — or a vein rupturing and letting blood and IV fluid leak into tissue surrounding the IV site.
Tennessee also allows for a second 100 mg dose of pentobarbital to be administered if the condemned person is still alive five minutes after the first dose was given.
Tennessee prison officials gave Pike a second dose, but it’s not clear if they used the primary IV site or the backup site to do so.
Little backup in Alabama, a lot in Idaho
Alabama has a three-drug lethal injection protocol. It allows for a backup dose of the first drug, the sedative midazolam, to be given if the inmate isn’t unconscious from the first dose. But the protocol doesn’t include additional instructions for what to do if the condemned person is still alive after the first dose of the next two drugs, rocuronium bromide and potassium chloride.
Idaho, meanwhile, has contingency plans for nearly every step of the execution process, with backup IV sites, allowances for administering a central IV line, and up to three full doses of any of the state’s four approved lethal injection drug cocktails.
Idaho recently made firing squad its primary execution method, though it has yet to kill someone by that method. Still, the state’s firing squad protocol also has a backup plan, with the prison director able to order a second volley of shots within a two-minute time span if she determines it is necessary to complete the execution.
Despite contingency plans, executions are still botched at times
Idaho called off the execution of Thomas Eugene Creech in 2024 after execution team members could not place a viable IV after eight attempts.
Tennessee also called off an execution earlier this year after failing to find a suitable vein for a secondary IV line.
In 2014, Arizona executioners injected Joseph Rudolph Wood with a lethal combination of drugs 15 times during the nearly two hours it took him to die. He gasped more than 600 times while he lay on the table.
Witnesses keep the public informed when executions succeed or fail
In many ways, executions are shrouded in secrecy. The identity of execution team members, the details about where and how lethal drugs are procured, and in some states even what happens in the death chamber is hidden from public view.
But executions, like all criminal sentences, are conducted by the state on behalf of its citizens, so it’s critical that members of the public understand exactly how that ultimate punishment is carried out.
Most death penalty states allow a few members of the media to witness executions on behalf of the public. Once the execution is over, those news representatives typically take part in a news conference, sharing exactly what they saw and heard with the rest of the world.
Access to executions varies by state, and limitations often lead to court battles
Only two states, Indiana and Wyoming, explicitly ban members of the press from witnessing executions. Wyoming, with no one currently on death row, hasn’t carried out an execution since 1992, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
A coalition of news organizations including The Associated Press sued Indiana last year for a seat in the witness room, but in June a federal appellate court upheld the state’s law barring media access.
In Idaho, media witnesses are allowed to watch as a condemned person is placed on a gurney, has IVs inserted and is put to death. Yet AP and other news organizations have sued for increased access. The news organizations asked a judge to allow them to watch via closed-circuit monitors as the drugs are pushed into the IV lines, which is currently shielded from public view in a private room beside the death chamber.
A federal judge ordered the state to provide that access, citing a 9th U.S. Circuit Court ruling that said the public should be able to view all critical parts of an execution via the press. But the state appealed, and the appellate court hasn’t yet ruled on the matter.
Media witnesses provided crucial details about Pike’s failed execution
When Pike’s first lethal injection dose failed to end her life, officials closed the curtains and administered a second dose of pentobarbital.
When the curtains reopened, Pike was making snoring sounds and was clearly alive, according to AP reporter Kim Chandler, who was one of the witnesses. Eventually the curtain was closed again and the microphone in the room was turned off, but Pike could still be heard making gasping or snoring sounds.
Nearly two hours after the execution began, media witnesses were escorted out, and Pike was taken to a hospital for treatment.
Many states, including Tennessee, keep the IV insertion hidden from public view, but allow witnesses to watch through a viewing window as the condemned person dies.
AP was part of a media coalition that previously sued Tennessee to see the IV insertion and to keep the viewing room curtains open until the pronouncement of death. But in April the Tennessee Supreme Court blocked a lower court’s order that would have allowed for increased access.
One of Pike’s attorneys, Steve Ferrell, said Pike feared that there could be complications because of a lifelong blood disorder that made it tough to get needles into her veins. Ferrell said it was possible that the IV did not enter Pike’s vein properly, and the drug may have filled her arm instead of entering her bloodstream.

title: I-95 bridge construction will close Broadway lane next week
text:
A lane closure is coming to Broadway in Bangor next week.
That will allow crews to complete work underneath the new bridge carrying Interstate 95 over Broadway, the city said Friday morning.
The southbound side of Broadway will be reduced to one lane where Broadway and I-95 meet from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Tuesday to Friday.
Drivers should avoid the area or expect delays because the lane closure will slow traffic through the area.
It’s the latest step toward the eventual replacement of the aging bridge carrying Interstate 95 traffic over Broadway. The 152-foot steel girder bridge, built in 1960, is crossed about 50,000 times daily and is in “poor condition,” transportation officials have told the Bangor Daily News. The Maine Department of Transportation expects to complete that work by late next year.
The project will cost more than $30 million.
In recent years other I-95 bridges in Bangor have been replaced, including the Ohio Street bridge in 2020 and the Union Street bridge in 2016, while a yearslong project is underway to redo the Hogan Road interchange.

title: Death Notice: David Willett
Portland code enforcement officer assaulted woman on the job, newly released reports show
text:
Editor’s note: This story contains language about sexual assault that may be upsetting to some readers.
A former Portland code enforcement officer and fire inspector is serving jail time for assaulting a woman while responding to a fire scene more than two years ago, according to newly released police reports.
Matthew Sarapas, 51, resigned in April 2025. He is in custody at the Cumberland County Jail after pleading guilty to Class D assault in August.
Since he was charged in March 2025, city officials have declined to share any information about what led to his arrest. But police reports, which the Portland Press Herald obtained this week through a public records request, show that the charge stemmed from Sarapas’ presence at the scene of a building fire on Brighton Avenue in April 2024.
A woman living in the building, who was 20 at the time, told police that Sarapas came into her apartment because she was worried about a gas smell, according to police reports provided by the Cumberland County District Attorney’s Office. When she let him in to check the smoke detectors, she said, he began rubbing her shoulders and fondling her breasts. She said he also licked her breast and made her touch his penis without her consent, records show.
She reported the assault shortly after Sarapas left. When police interviewed Sarapas later that day, he denied allegations of any sexual contact, detectives wrote in their reports.
Sarapas agreed to a DNA swab for a sexual assault evidence collection kit. Once the DNA analysis was completed nearly a year later, in February 2025, reports show investigators determined that Sarapas’ saliva had been found on the woman’s breast.
Portland police again interviewed Sarapas in March 2025, at the department’s headquarters on Middle Street. He admitted to touching and kissing the woman’s breasts and told a detective “there was nothing that was not consensual,” according to a police report.
Sarapas’ attorney Daniel Wentworth said Friday that his client acknowledges he had a lapse in judgment during what he thought was a consensual encounter.
Sarapas was arrested immediately after the interview at police headquarters and taken to the Cumberland County Jail on charges of unlawful sexual touching and assault, both Class D crimes. He was banned from accessing all city-owned residential buildings, as well as the property on Brighton Avenue where the woman lived, according to bail conditions in court paperwork. The assault did not happen on city property.
He was put on administrative leave for about a month between his arrest and his resignation. He was paid $5,847 during that time, city spokesperson Jessica Grondin said Thursday.
In August, Sarapas was convicted of one count of Class D assault as part of a plea deal in which prosecutors dismissed the unlawful sexual touching charge against him. Sarapas’ attorney said he took the deal because he didn’t want to put his family or the victim through a trial.
Sarapas was ordered to pay a $300 fine and turn himself in at the jail on Sept. 11 for a 90-day sentence, according to court documents. Cumberland County Jail staff confirmed Thursday that Sarapas was still in custody.
HOW TO GET HELP
IF YOU or someone you know has experienced sexual violence, you can call the statewide Sexual Assault Crisis and Support Line at 1-800-871-7741 for free and confidential help 24 hours a day.

title: You asked, Maine’s candidates answered
text:
The BDN Editorial Board operates independently from the newsroom, and does not set policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com.
This year, the BDN opinion page is taking a different approach to our assessment of Maine’s candidates for office. Rather than having the editorial board drive the discussion, we want to put the focus on the topics and concerns that matter most to you. We hope to help you cut through the political rancor to focus on the kitchen table issues that matter most to Mainers.
So, we put you, our readers — specifically BDN subscribers — in the driver’s seat to focus on the issues that were most important to you.
Over the last few weeks, we asked our subscribers to submit questions. You did! We received nearly 100 questions for the candidates for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House. Several key concerns emerged. Health care was at the top of the list, with both access and affordability on your minds. Numerous people focused on Social Security: Will it remain available? Will benefits be cut or delayed? Candidates’ plans to address climate change was also a concern, especially to readers from coastal Maine.
You asked how candidates for governor will keep taxes in check without gutting government services. You asked how they’d work with people with different, even opposing views.
You also wanted to know about priorities and accomplishments, about ethics, trust and bipartisan cooperation. Many people expressed fears about the future of our democratic norms and how they can best be preserved. You also wanted to know if candidates shared these concerns.
A special shout out to Stu Kantor for a question that really captures the angst of this election: Why should we trust you?
We combined and narrowed down your questions to a manageable number, and asked candidates to keep their responses brief.
Today, we begin sharing their responses. We start with the race for governor. We’ll continue to share more questions and answers in the coming days and weeks.
You’ll see some common themes, but also stark differences, particularly when it comes to health care and climate change. You may also see some surprises.
Some candidates offered detailed plans, others provided generalities (to be fair, we limited how long their responses could be). Some candidates make pledges they can’t fulfill, such as saying they’ll make decisions that rest with the Maine Legislature, not the governor.
Some touted their own plans and goals. Others criticized their opponent.
We’re thankful that every candidate responded.
Thank you to everyone who sent in questions. Thank you to the candidates (and their staffs) who took the time to offer thoughtful answers. Thank you all for your support of this project, which puts the focus on you, our valued readers and subscribers.
We hope this information, which you asked for, helps you decide who you will vote for in the Nov. 3 election. Visit www.bangordailynews.com/candidates-questions/ to see the responses.

title: Energy Department employee arrested on charge of trying to support Iran-backed Houthis
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A Department of Energy electrical engineer has been arrested on charges of providing support to the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, including by buying materials for homemade explosives and drones and traveling to Yemen, the Justice Department said Thursday.
Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, of Richland, Washington, was arrested Thursday and is due to make his first court appearance Friday. Court records do not list an attorney available to speak on his behalf.
The FBI says Ellaboudy had a goal of helping the Houthis improve their communications capabilities and traveled last September to Yemen, where the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces are now engaged in renewed violence that has killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands. The conflict began in 2014 when the Iran-backed rebels took over the capital, Sanaa, forcing the country’s government to settle into exile in Saudi Arabia.
Upon his return to the United States, authorities say, Ellaboudy told Customs and Border Protection officials that he was traveling back from Oman on a work trip and was part of a U.S. government mission to inspect missile defense systems. But investigators interviewed Ellaboudy’s supervisor, who reported having no knowledge of any international travel or of an Energy Department missile inspection program that Ellaboudy would have been assigned to, an FBI affidavit said.
Ellaboudy himself was recorded telling FBI informants, whom officials had introduced into the investigation, that he had to be smuggled into and out of Yemen and that he had hoped to reach the country’s capital to make government-level connections, the affidavit says. He was ultimately unable to make it to Sanaa, the FBI said.
The FBI says investigators began looking into Ellaboudy after learning that he had purchased precursor chemicals commonly involved in the construction of homemade explosive devices, including acetone and sodium bisulfate, as well as parts used for drones.
During the course of the investigation, the FBI says, he communicated with multiple informants — including one who purported to be a Houthi colonel — and provided advice and assistance on communications equipment.
Ellaboudy is charged under a law that makes it a crime to provide material support to a group designated by the United States as a foreign terrorist organization, of which the Houthis are one.
“These allegations are so deeply disturbing that they almost defy imagination,” John Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department’s National Security Division, said in a statement.

title: What a swim! Harp seal swims thousands of miles from Maine to the Arctic
text:
What a swim! Harp seal tracked from Maine to the Arctic
A young harp seal that needed some special care in Maine earlier this year after getting stranded here has now made an incredible swim.
Marine Mammals of Maine says the yearling stranded in Midcoast Maine in May and was treated for severe dehydration and a respiratory infection.
After making a full recovery, she was released on May 29 in Phippsburg, outfitted with a non-invasive satellite tracking tag that is still recording.
The tracking shows that on June 17, she was off the coast of Cape Breton Island. By July 4, she was off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador before heading up through Baffin Bay and into the Arctic. On August 17, she was along the northwest coast of Greenland in the northern end of Baffin Bay and has been hanging out in the Queen Elizabeth Islands in the arctic part of the Canadian territory of Nunavut. On Sept. 30, she was near Grise Fiord on Inuit-owned land. The track from Phippsburg to there shows a journey of roughly 4,500 miles.
According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, full-grown harp seals are about 5 to 6 feet long, weigh about 260 to 300 pounds and can live up to 30 years.
Harp seals gather on pack ice in large groups during breeding and molting seasons. These groups can contain up to several thousand seals. Harp seals also feed and travel in large groups during seasonal migrations. They often travel away from the pack ice during the summer and follow the ice north to feed in the Arctic. Annual migrations can be more than 3,100 miles roundtrip.
Harp seals can dive up to 1,300 feet below the surface and remain underwater for about 16 minutes.

title: Maine Coastal Program announces $299,057 in Habitat Restoration Planning Grants to communities
text:
AUGUSTA – The Maine Office of Community Affairs’ Maine Coastal Program awarded $299,057 to four municipalities and service providers for projects to develop habitat restoration plans in support of community resilience.
Communities depend on healthy coastal habitats to buffer storm surge, maintain clean water and absorb rising seas. The funded projects demonstrate how coastal communities across Maine are prioritizing habitat restoration for ecological and community resilience.
The funding for these grants comes from a one-time Habitat Restoration Planning opportunity through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Office of Coastal Management. The grants will support projects focused on tidal marsh restoration design, road crossing assessments and prioritization, and natural resource inventories. Projects will begin in the fall.
The four selected projects are:
- Town of Gouldsboro: “Preliminary Natural Resource Inventory and Infrastructure Vulnerability Assessment of the Sand Cove area in Gouldsboro, ME.” The town will hire a consultant to map sea level rise, storm surge threats, basic infrastructure, and natural resources of Grand Marsh. These data and calculations will enable the town to assess how proposed coastal transportation improvements interact with the protection of the existing dune, freshwater, and intertidal wetlands in the study area.
- Downeast Salmon Federation (DSF): “Point Street Resilient Crossing Design Supplement.” DSF will work with a consultant to improve habitat resiliency through infrastructure upgrades. This work includes culvert replacement design, geotechnical assessments, and improvements to water infrastructure at the Point Street crossing of the West Branch Pleasant River (WBPR) in Addison, Maine.
- Town of Boothbay: “Town-wide Crossing Assessment and Prioritization.” The town will hire a consultant to conduct road crossing assessments and evaluate every crossing in Boothbay for coastal habitat restoration potential and climate hazard vulnerability. With this evaluation, the Town of Boothbay will have the tools available to prioritize projects to create a resilient coastal community.
- Kennebec Estuary Land Trust (KELT): “Planning for the restoration and enhancement of resilience of Popham area tidal marshes.” KELT will hire a consultant to evaluate the Popham marshes’ vegetation and existing conditions to understand its resiliency to changing water levels. Developing a plan for marsh rehabilitation and evaluating its potential absorption capability can help prepare the Phippsburg area and its associated infrastructure for future flood events.
For inquiries about the Habitat Restoration Planning Grant Program, contact Erin Campbell at erin.grace.campbell@maine.gov.

title: City of Portland begins ‘daylighting crosswalks’ as part of Vision Zero commitment
New York’s governor says Cornell rape accuser was ‘failed’ by people obligated to protect her
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Friday that the woman who accused members of a Cornell University fraternity of gang rape was “failed” by people obligated to protect her, including police and the county prosecutor.
Hochul’s claim came during a news conference in which she gave details on her decision to turn the case over to a special prosecutor, the state Attorney General Letitia James.
The governor said she made the decision after learning “troubling details” about how authorities have handled the woman’s claims thus far, including that the district attorney closed the case without having anyone interview the victim or anyone else involved in the alleged attack.
“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?” Hochul said. “This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”
She also assailed the Cornell University Police Department for not fully conveying the woman’s story to prosecutors.
“After this young woman came forward, she spoke to the police. She sat for hours and told them exactly what happened to her. And according to new reports, she could not have been clearer that she was 100% confident that she had been raped,” the governor said. ”Yet, shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors.”
Hochul said Thursday that she appointed James to oversee the case because she had lost faith in the local district attorney’s ability to handle it.
The investigation initially was closed without charges in 2024.
Last month, the woman filed a lawsuit and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation. He has since been bombarded by criticism that he abandoned the original investigation too quickly.
The attorney general will oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury, Hochul said.
“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” she said in a statement Thursday.
Van Houten didn’t immediately respond to Thursday messages seeking comment.
The case has roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about its response and the larger issue of how sexual assaults are handled on college campuses.
The woman, identified only as Jane Doe in court documents, told campus police in November of 2024 that she was sexually assaulted, then discussed it with the university’s internal investigators as part of Cornell’s disciplinary process.
The lawsuit against seven fraternity brothers, the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and others alleges that she was plied with drugs and alcohol, then subjected to sexual acts by a group of men while she was partially or entirely incapacitated. One of the men sent a social media message to other fraternity members alerting them to what was happening, and inviting people to take part, according to the lawsuit.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they participated in a sexual assault. One said his client hadn’t touched the woman. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful.
New York governors have turned to attorneys general to oversee important cases in the past.
In 2018, then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo appointed then-Nassau County District Attorney Madeline Singas as a special prosecutor to investigate Eric Schneiderman, who resigned as New York attorney general after women accused him of violent slapping, choking and other abuse.
In 2021, James oversaw a non-criminal investigation into sexual harassment allegations against then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo, leading to his resignation. Cuomo initially tried to choose who would lead the investigation into the allegations. He then allowed James to choose two independent attorneys to lead it instead.
James’ office also handles other criminal work and has the power under state law to investigate every death involving law enforcement in the state. But, typically, she can’t initiate criminal investigations without a referral from a local district attorney, the governor or a state agency, or an appointment like the one Hochul made Thursday.

This story was updated to correct the spelling of Letitia James’ name.

title: Mobile outreach meets people with substance use disorders where they are
text:
Adam Bloom-Paicopolos, MPP, is the executive director at the Alliance for Addiction & Mental Health Services, Maine’s statewide association for community behavioral health providers serving over 120,000 Mainers annually.
Most communities share a common goal: to care for one another, especially during times of vulnerability. Today, many individuals face complex challenges related to substance use, mental health and housing instability. While there are no simple answers, there are thoughtful, practical approaches that can make a meaningful difference, one person at a time.
One approach to substance use that has been gaining momentum across the country is secondary prevention.
At its core, secondary prevention is not about enabling harmful behavior. It is about preserving life, reducing immediate risk and creating pathways to recovery when individuals are ready. It recognizes that no two people are the same and that progress often begins with trust, respect and individualized support.
As part of this programming, mobile outreach units offer a flexible way to deliver that support directly to individuals who may not otherwise access care. Instead of requiring people to navigate complex systems on their own, trained professionals meet them where they are, physically and emotionally, with services tailored to their specific needs and circumstances.
This model prioritizes individualized intervention. Some individuals may be ready for immediate connection to detox or treatment, while others may need time, information or basic support before taking that step. Mobile outreach allows for real-time assessment and response, offering health screenings, referrals and rapid connections to care based on each person’s readiness.
Peer support is a critical component of this approach. Specialists with lived experience bring credibility and empathy that help build trust quickly. Their presence can turn a moment of hesitation into a moment of possibility, offering not just guidance but hope grounded in personal experience.
In addition to connection and counseling, mobile outreach provides practical, life-saving
resources. These include naloxone to reverse overdoses, wound assessment and basic first aid and crisis support. Just as important, individuals can be connected to housing assistance, social services and behavioral healthcare, because recovery is not just about treatment, but about stability and the opportunity to rebuild.
This work is not done in isolation. Mobile outreach is designed to coordinate with existing providers, healthcare systems and first responders, strengthening, not duplicating, the services already in place. By filling gaps and improving access, it helps create a more responsive and effective system overall.
There is also a practical benefit for the broader community. Early, individualized intervention often reduces reliance on emergency services. When people receive timely support, communities frequently see fewer emergency room visits, hospitalizations and crisis calls. This not only improves outcomes for individuals but also helps manage public resources more effectively.
Across the country, programs like this are demonstrating measurable results: reductions in overdose deaths, increased engagement in treatment and stronger connections between individuals and care providers. These outcomes are not the result of a single solution, but of a consistent commitment to meeting people as individuals, with dignity and without judgment.
That principle matters. Every person’s path is different, shaped by their history, circumstances, and readiness for change. A one-size-fits-all approach cannot fully address such complexity. What can make the difference is a model that is flexible, responsive and grounded in human connection.
Supporting secondary prevention and mobile outreach is a person-centered and practical step forward. It reflects a balanced approach. One that values safety, responsibility and compassion equally. It is not about lowering expectations, but about removing barriers so that individuals can take meaningful steps toward stability and recovery.
In the end, community well-being is built not only through systems, but through moments of connection. A conversation. A referral. A life saved. A path forward. Sometimes the most effective solutions begin by simply meeting people where they are and walking alongside them from there.

title: Patriots defense loses Christian Gonzalez, Christian Barmore
text:
The Patriots will be without two of their top defensive players Sunday when they visit the Buffalo Bills.
Both cornerback Christian Gonzalez and defensive tackle Christian Barmore were ruled out Friday with shoulder injuries.
This will be the first game either has missed this season.
Gonzalez became the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history last month when he signed a four-year, $135 million contract. He has eight tackles on the season. Barmore has four tackles and one sack so far.
Quarterback Drake Maye is also dealing with a right shoulder issue, but participated in all practices this week.
Coach Mike Vrabel said Friday that Maye’s injury occurred sometime during the Week 3 loss at Jacksonville.
“There were no limitations, so he practiced full — he didn’t miss any reps,” Vrabel said. “But we just felt like it was best to list it just to make sure that we are doing everything that we’re supposed to do from a protocol standpoint.”
Vrabel acknowledged that not having Barmore as a pass rusher, nor Gonzalez to defend the Bills’ receivers, will be a challenge opposite Buffalo quarterback Josh Allen.
“That is just what the situation is. There’s nothing we can do about it,” Vrabel said. “We can make sure that the guys that are playing are ready and that we continue to do the things that we know are going to help us. But that happens every week in the National Football League. I’m looking forward to seeing the guys that are going to play in there.”

title: Recycling facility helps police catch suspect after 77 fire hydrants damaged
text:
ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) - Scrap yards are usually full of metal and hidden treasures, but this week, one of those yards helped police haul in something else - a scrap thief.
“Naturally, when they approached me, I was very happy to help and do anything I could and step forward and give them the information they needed,” Phillip Harbison, general manager at SA Recycling in St. Louis, exclaimed.
The recycling facility, located off of the Broadway, helped find the man who put countless lives in jeopardy.
“I genuinely just dislike thieves; I’m not a fan of thieves at all,” Harbison stated. “So it’s very important to me to get them off the street, and especially when they’re doing things that can harm our community.”
Over the past week, police have been searching for a suspect accused of damaging and stealing the components off of 77 fire hydrants across the City of St. Louis.
On Thursday, police arrested 65-year-old Harry Farmer in connection with that vandalism after they said surveillance video caught him sawing off the hydrants’ brass valves.
“We had a citizen who came forward. We were able to get video of this individual. We were able to obtain a name, but we had to do a case to make sure that we got it right, got the evidence, and then we had to track down video at each one of these known locations,” Chief Robert Tracy, St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department, said.
Farmer allegedly went to SA Recycling to sell the valves, which is when Harbison got him on camera and a picture of his ID.
“All the way from the second they pull onto this lot, they’re on camera,” he explained. “We have pictures of their ID; everything is stored in our database, so every transaction will have a picture of the material they brought in, of their ID, license plate, all of that.”
When police came to ask if they had any information about these incidents, Harbison said they were happy to cooperate.
“You don’t want those types of people out in the city and I want to stop the bad name that’s being given to scrap yards, and that’s why we keep the records we do and are able to help when the police do come and ask for help,” he stated.
Farmer has now been charged with eight felonies.
“Damaging fire hydrants creates a major public safety risk,” Chief Tracy said. “Firefighters depend on working hydrants to protect lives and property - interfering with that access puts residents, businesses and first responders in danger.”
“I’ve been Fire Chief for 19 years, been in this city for 48 with the fire department. I’ve never, ever seen anything like this. Traveled around the country, I’ve never seen hydrants vandalized like this intentionally,” Chief Dennis Jenkerson, St. Louis Fire Department, stated.
For recycling facilities like Harbisons, they just have one message to other scrap thieves.
“I will not buy it; don’t bring it to SA Recycling. SA Recycling does not want stolen scrap… some of us will absolutely do our part and help the community and put criminals behind bars," he said.
As of Friday evening, Farmer is in custody, but police still have to extradite him back to Missouri from Illinois.
The investigation remains ongoing. Police want anyone with more information on the damaged hydrants to contact 314-444-2500 and talk to District 4 detectives.

title: Maine's heating oil prices are 80% higher than a year ago
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s heating oil prices are about 80% higher than those seen a year ago.
The statewide average price for a gallon of heating oil is $5.96, down slightly from last week’s record high of $6.02, according to a Maine Department of Energy Resources survey.
Prices range from a statewide low of $5 a gallon to as high as $6.30 in parts of eastern and Down East Maine, where the average rests at $6.
This time last year heating oil went for an average of $3.33 a gallon, and this same time in 2024 it went for $3.34.
That means it will cost Mainers an additional $725 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank, the Department of Energy Resources said Thursday afternoon.
That’s raising concerns among lower-income homeowners in a state heavily reliant on heating oil to stay warm during the winter. Mainers already have empty fuel tanks, according to the community action program serving Aroostook, Hancock and Washington counties. But the Trump administration has rebuffed calls to release federal heating assistance early.
“With oil prices setting record highs, this is likely to be a very tough winter for many Maine families,” said Maine Public Advocate Heather Sanborn, who encouraged Mainers to check their eligibility for rebates or programs to reduce their energy bills.
The higher cost to stay warm is driven by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s more than 4-year-old war in Ukraine and President Donald Trump’s war in Iran, which effectively halted maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s natural gas and oil passes.
The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier and 9,000 additional troops into the Middle East, a move that comes after Republican President Donald Trump threatened more airstrikes against Iran, according to The Associated Press.
Adding to the complex global picture, Iran-aligned Houthis seized key territory at the mouth of the Red Sea, another vital global shipping route, and attacked energy sites in Saudi Arabia, Reuters reported.
“Maine’s reliance on imported heating fuels means our households remain exposed to volatility in global oil markets, putting added pressure on families as we head into winter with record high prices,” said Celina Cunningham, acting state energy commissioner.

(Gray News) - Former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo will no longer work for CBS Sports, according to reports.
Sportswriter Richard Deitsch posted a statement from CBS Sports on X that said the network and Romo “mutually agreed to part ways.”

“None of this is an excuse. These are my failures, and I take full responsibility for them,” Romo continued.

title: Lewiston PAC formed to support conservative candidates in local campaigns
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- Save Lewiston, a PAC formed over the summer, has generated promotional materials supporting at least eight conservative candidates running for Lewiston City Council, mayor and state House and Senate seats.
- Candidates garnering the PAC’s support have said they are not working with the PAC and continue to carry out traditional grassroots campaigning.
- Opponents have said voters deserve to know who is behind the PAC and its AI-generated promotional materials.
LEWISTON — Social media has been aflutter with campaign images promoting local candidates that originate from a political action committee whose mission is to elect Republican and conservative candidates to municipal and state office.
“Our fight is with Augusta, not our neighbors! One vote can change Maine!” one image says in big, bold letters situated next to Ward 7 Councilor Bret Martel who is running for Maine State House District 95. “The humiliation of Lewiston and our citizens must end! Vote for change in November!” another image says next to mayoral candidate Rick LaChapelle, who along with three other candidates is running to unseat incumbent Carl Sheline.
At the very bottom of the image a disclaimer reads: “Paid for by Save Lewiston PAC, 937 Main St. Lewiston ME 04240. Not paid for or authorized by any candidate. This communication contains audio, video and/or images that have been manipulated or altered.”
The image is one of over 90 on Save Lewiston PAC’s Facebook page promoting eight candidates for public office, many for municipal offices such as City Council and the School Committee.
The PAC — which has raised over $50,000 and spent about $4,100 — supports “Republicans and candidates who support conservative policies seeking election for any State or Lewiston Municipal position or office,” according to position statements in its filing.
The filing also says the PAC opposes “Democrats and candidates (with) liberal, leftist, and/or liberal policies seeking election for any State or Lewiston Municipal position or office.”
Filings list three officers responsible for committee business: Principal Officer Thomas Peters III, Treasurer Shane Bouchard and authorized agent Mitchel Roberge. Peters and Roberge are attorneys and Bouchard was Lewiston’s mayor for just over a year, from January 2018 to March 2019. Bouchard stepped down as mayor following a controversy involving private texts.
The PAC’s physical address, 937 Main St. in Lewiston, matches Peters & Roberge Attorneys at Law. Peters, Bouchard and Roberge did not reply to questions.
‘LEWISTON NEEDS TO BE SAVED’
In addition to LaChapelle, when it comes to city races, images generated by the PAC promote Susan Longchamps, running against Rebecca J. Long to retain her seat as Ward 2 councilor; Chandra Sasseville, who faces incumbent Michael Roy and resident Matthew Agren in Ward 4; Robert Glaspy Jr., who is running against Hollie Anne Niemi to replace outgoing Ward 6 Councilor David Chittim; and Marcel Leclair, who is running against Nicole Johnson for Lewiston School Committee’s Ward 5 seat.
Alongside Martel, for State House candidates, the PAC is also promoting Longchamps, a Republican, for House District 93 against incumbent Democrat Julia McCabe; Republican Lee Clement, who faces Democrat Luke Jensen for the House District 96 seat; and unenrolled candidate Eryn Soule, who faces Democrat Shanna Cox for Maine Senate District 21.
The Sun Journal reached out to the eight candidates featured in Save Lewiston’s images. Martel and Soule said they are not receiving any financial contributions from the PAC and have not had any communication with it.
Though he has not worked with the Save Lewiston organization, Martel said he knows some of those who are involved with it and has had ordinary conversations with them as he has many in the community.
“Those conversations did not concern the PAC’s support for me, its advertisements, expenditures, priorities, decisions or campaign strategy,” Martel said. “I have not requested, suggested, approved or coordinated any of the PAC’s activities, and neither I nor my campaign has received any contribution or funding from the PAC.”
The Save Lewiston PAC’s decision to support Martel was theirs alone, Martel said, adding that he appreciates lawful support, but did not request, approve or coordinate the PAC’s activities.
“Its activities will not change how I conduct my campaign,” Martel said. “I remain focused on running my own local, grassroots campaign and speaking directly with the people of District 95.”
Soule, too, says she had no involvement with the PAC, though the sentiment in its name is something she strongly identifies with.
“My assumption is that the PAC believes Lewiston is going in the wrong direction and needs to be saved,” Soule said. “Whether you are looking at drugs, violence, homelessness, property taxes or education, Lewiston’s current policies and leadership, including those representing us in Augusta, have taken us in the wrong direction and Lewiston needs to be saved with a reversal in policies and approach.”
Identifying as a fiscal conservative supporting smaller government, lower taxes and less regulation, Soule said the election should be about Lewiston and the problems facing its residents. If Save Lewiston makes more people pay attention to those problems, it’s a good thing, she said.
“More people paying attention means more feedback and input and more people getting involved. Lewiston needs some wins!” Soule said.
‘VOTERS SHOULD KNOW’
Cox, Soule’s opponent, said the U.S. Supreme Court made outside money a fact of life in politics with its Citizens United decision. But, she said, PACs don’t win elections.
“Knocking on doors does,” Cox said. “I have been to over 7,000 of them, and what I hear from neighbors about wages, housing, heating their homes this winter and the cost of living matters a lot more to me than who’s spending what on TV ads.”
Though Cox said her campaign has benefited from PACs coming from “more seasoned electeds as well as organized labor,” she said her concern about Save Lewiston is that it uses AI-generated images and slogans to tell voters who to support — and that it is taking a nonpartisan municipal election and making it highly partisan.
“(The ads) say very little about what those candidates would actually do for Lewiston,” Cox said. “Voters should know who is behind those messages and who is accountable for them. I expect candidates and elected officials to be clear about their positions and answer for what they say.”
Brendan Fischer, director of strategic investigations for the Campaign Legal Center, a nonpartisan organization focused on improving democratic participation, said PAC spending at the municipal level may be less common than at the state or federal level, but is not unprecedented.
“Particularly when wealthy interests have an interest in the outcome of the race,” Fischer said. “In some cases, super PAC spending can come from local races becoming nationalized, but here campaign finance reports indicate that the funding is coming from local interests.”
Fischer said that the “seemingly AI-generated ads” may simply reflect the growing availability of AI tools.
Martel’s Democratic opponent, Kiernan Majerus-Collins, said he was not aware of any spending by outside PACs in support of his campaign and considers Save Lewiston “bad news” for the city and its residents. Given Bouchard’s history as mayor, he said, the PAC is problematic as much for who is running it as the “corporate money and AI slop.”
Majerus-Collins said PACs are “a symptom of a broken campaign finance system” that considers political spending protected free speech. He said he is used to PACs spending money against him.
“In my primary, an out-of-town PAC used out-of-state corporate money from the gambling industry to try to defeat me,” Majerus-Collins said. “That effort failed, and I am confident this one will too.”
Sheline, who has been a target of the PAC’s promotional materials, said Save Lewiston is “propping up candidates and talking points” that voters have rejected in previous elections.
“Their abundance of AI-generated graphics doesn’t make them or their positions any more appealing,” Sheline said. “The vast majority of people in Lewiston support our local schools, value the library and don’t want to see our neighbors kidnapped by masked government thugs. Lewistonians care deeply about each other. It’s what makes this city great and it’s why I love being mayor.”

title: Obituary: Joseph L.A. Cyr
text:
AUBURN – Joseph Louis Alphee Cyr, 88, passed away peacefully on Sept. 28, 2026, at his home, surrounded by the loved ones that meant so much to him. In his final days, Joseph was showered with love, comfort, and care. His daughter-in-law, Judy Cyr, devoted this past year to caring for him, showing him the same respect, kindness, and compassion that she so freely gives to everyone in her life. Because of her, his final year and his final days were filled with dignity, love, and the comfort of being surrounded by family.
Joseph was a beloved son, brother, father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and friend to many. Born in Canada, he was a true French-speaking Canuck who carried his heritage with him throughout his life.
He graduated from Lewiston High School in 1961 and, after becoming a naturalized American citizen, proudly served in the United States Army. Following his time in the military, Joseph traveled to Grover, Texas, where he worked on a cattle ranch. Although he already knew how to ride, life on a 4,000-head cattle ranch quickly taught him that he needed to learn how to rope as well. He embraced the challenge and became a true cowboy in every sense of the word.
Joseph returned home in 1962 and married, beginning a life centered around his family. Together, they raised four loving children who would become the heart of his life.
He worked for many years in the shoe industry, beginning as a hand sewer at Belgrade Shoe before continuing his career at Sabotage Moc and later Billings. In total, Joseph spent 29 years as a hand sewer. A man of many trades, he also worked as a farrier and a as a floor installer throughout the Lewiston, Auburn, and Rumford areas. He was hardworking, dependable, and never afraid to learn a new skill or lend a helping hand.
But above all of his many accomplishments, Joseph’s greatest joy was his family. His happiest moments were found around the table and surrounded by the people he loved. Holidays meant steak, mashed potatoes, and his famous cornbread. Christmas meant a new sweater – usually purchased with so much love and enthusiasm that it somehow ended up being three sizes too small. And birthdays and special occasions meant a card signed simply, “Love, Pépère.”
Joseph was a deeply devoted Catholic. His faith was an important part of who he was. He faithfully attended Mass, often sitting quietly in the back in his best suit, and carried his faith with him throughout his life. His devotion to God and his Catholic faith remained a constant source of strength and guidance.
Those who knew Joseph will remember the little things that made him unmistakably himself. They will remember seeing him driving down the road, easily spotted by the cowboy hat he wore so proudly. They will remember his stories, his traditions, his sense of humor, and the countless ways he showed his love without always needing to say it.
Joseph was truly one of a kind. We were blessed to have him in our lives, and although his absence will leave a space that cannot be filled, the memories he gave us will remain for generations to come.
Joseph is survived by his daughter, Tina Cyr (Tina Church) of Auburn; his sons, Tim Cyr (Judy Cyr), Tom Cyr (Darcey Cyr), and Tony Cyr (Wanda Berube) of Auburn; and his grandchildren, Amber Binnington (Jonathan Binnington), Megan Cyr (Floyd Goding), Samantha Fecteau (Gabriel Fecteau), Reese Cyr (Haley Leighton), and Josh Cyr (Stephanie Cyr).
He is also survived by his 13 great-grandchildren, Adyson, Calvin, Beckett, Timmothy, Cecelia, Noah, Benjamin, Ryker, Alana, Easton, Vivian, Avery, and Gracelynn, who were surely among his greatest joys.
Joseph is also survived by his sister, Andrina Leger of Arizona; his brothers, Rene (Flora) of Turner and Jude (Joan) of Auburn; and his sisters-in-law, Judy Cyr of Sabattus and Rachelle Cyr of Lewiston, as well as many extended family members and dear friends.
In addition to his parents, Joseph was predeceased by his sister and brother-in-law, Priscilla (Cyr) and Rene Gagne; his brothers, Normand, Robert “Moe,” and Aurele Cyr; and his brother-in-law, Edward Leger.
He will be deeply missed by the family he loved so dearly, but his memory will live on in the stories, traditions, lessons, and love he leaves behind.
The world lost a good man, but heaven gained a cowboy.
Online condolences and sharing of memories may be expressed at http://www.albert-burpee.com
Visitation will be held at Albert & Burpee Funeral Home on Monday, October 5, 2026, from 9-10:30 a.m., followed by a Mass of Christian Burial at 11 a.m., at Sacred Heart Church, 8 Sacred Heart Place, Auburn. Committal prayers with military honors will follow in the Large Chapel of the Mausoleum at St. Peter’s Cemetery, Deer Road, Lewiston.

title: This grocery store employee makes sure every customer finds what they’re looking for
text:
WAUSAU, Wis. (InvestigateTV) - For almost three decades, Greg Atchison has been a friendly face in the grocery business.
“It’s greeting people. Meeting people, seeing people, it’s therapeutic,” Atchison said.
Atchison has worked 28 years in customer service. Twenty years at Festival Foods, formerly Trig’s, and eight at County Market. His approach extends beyond typical customer interactions.
Jake Sischo, store director at Festival Foods, said customers recognize Atchison immediately when they enter the store.
“It’s almost like ‘Cheers.’ Instead of yelling ‘Norm,’ they walk in and they’re like ‘Greg! How’s it going?’” Sischo said.
Dana Glaser, a Festival Foods customer, said Atchison consistently provides helpful service.
“He just always has a smile. If you can’t find what you need he’ll go in the back and get it for you and wrap it up,” Glaser said.
Atchison said his approach centers on genuine enthusiasm for the work.
“Come to work. You’re happy to be here. You’re happy to serve people. People see that. They pick up on it. It’s a 2-edge sword,” Atchison said.
His service earned him the company’s all-star boomerang award, which recognizes employees who encourage customer loyalty.
“It’s about bringing the guest back. Doing something that will make sure the guest comes back and enjoys shopping with us. That is what Greg does,” Sischo said.
Atchison was the second person in the store to receive the award and among the first 10 in the company, according to Sischo.
Customer Jerry Schroeder said Atchison consistently helps other shoppers.
“Always helping somebody. See. He’s down there helping somebody now,” Schroeder said.
Now in his early 70’s, his work schedule has been scaled back from full-time hours.
“Full-time retirement is full-time work to find yourself busy. To keep yourself busy. Especially when you don’t have hobbies,” Atchison said.
Customers continue to seek him out during his shifts.
“Because he’s always so cheerful. You’ve had a bad day, come in, and he’s happy. Smiling,” Schroeder said.
Sischo said the store will accommodate Atchison’s continued employment.
“We will take him for as long as he wants to be here,” Sischo said.
Atchison said he plans to continue working because of his passion for customer service.
“If you love what you do, it’s not work. And I love doing this. I really do,” Atchison said.
Festival Foods has a 10-tile policy requiring employees to greet customers within 10 tiles and offer assistance. Atchison extends that range, greeting customers from 20 or 30 tiles away.

title: Energy Department employee arrested on charge of trying to support Iran-backed Houthis
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A Department of Energy electrical engineer has been arrested on charges of providing support to the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, including by buying materials for homemade explosives and drones and traveling to Yemen, the Justice Department said Thursday.
Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, of Richland, Washington, was arrested Thursday and is due to make his first court appearance Friday. Court records do not list an attorney available to speak on his behalf.
The FBI says Ellaboudy had a goal of helping the Houthis improve their communications capabilities and traveled last September to Yemen, where the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces are now engaged in renewed violence that has killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands. The conflict began in 2014 when the Iran-backed rebels took over the capital, Sanaa, forcing the country’s government to settle into exile in Saudi Arabia.
Upon his return to the United States, authorities say, Ellaboudy told Customs and Border Protection officials that he was traveling back from Oman on a work trip and was part of a U.S. government mission to inspect missile defense systems. But investigators interviewed Ellaboudy’s supervisor, who reported having no knowledge of any international travel or of an Energy Department missile inspection program that Ellaboudy would have been assigned to, an FBI affidavit said.
Ellaboudy himself was recorded telling FBI informants, whom officials had introduced into the investigation, that he had to be smuggled into and out of Yemen and that he had hoped to reach the country’s capital to make government-level connections, the affidavit says. He was ultimately unable to make it to Sanaa, the FBI said.
The FBI says investigators began looking into Ellaboudy after learning that he had purchased precursor chemicals commonly involved in the construction of homemade explosive devices, including acetone and sodium bisulfate, as well as parts used for drones.
During the course of the investigation, the FBI says, he communicated with multiple informants — including one who purported to be a Houthi colonel — and provided advice and assistance on communications equipment.
Ellaboudy is charged under a law that makes it a crime to provide material support to a group designated by the United States as a foreign terrorist organization, of which the Houthis are one.
“These allegations are so deeply disturbing that they almost defy imagination,” John Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department’s National Security Division, said in a statement.

title: Outdoor Leadership Conference challenges Maine educators’ wilderness skills
text:
ROME, Maine (WABI) - Dozens of Maine teachers traded the classroom for the Pine Tree Camp in Rome Friday for the 2026 Outdoor Leadership Conference.
Hosted by Teens to Trails—a non-profit helping Maine schools create and foster student outdoor clubs—the event gives educators tools to lead outside the classroom.
With a focus on connection and community, morning sessions paired an inclusivity panel with hands-on practice starting wilderness campfires.
Bucksport teacher and coach Miles Bisher leads a middle school outdoor club, attempting to bring new skills and outdoor resources back to his students.
“If we can make the outdoors feel like it’s the thing to do and the place to be, that’s going to get them outside and get excited... laying that foundation at a middle school level, I think, can make a huge difference in the people that they will become and the communities they will create,“ said Bisher.
Bisher shared his excitement about pairing with local gear shares and statewide partners to help ensure every kid can participate, regardless of financial background or experience.
To help lead those outdoor adventures, educators also spent the afternoon out on the water brushing up on skills like canoeing, kayaking and fly fishing.

title: Assault charges will be dropped against former Maine Capitol Police Chief in plea agreement
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The former Maine Capitol Police chief could pay a $300 fine following an altercation outside a Hallowell bar last year.
Matthew Clancy, 63, of Sidney, reached a nine-month informal deferred disposition agreement with prosecutors Tuesday.
Clancy was originally charged with assault, refusing to submit to arrest, and disorderly conduct. Police say he fought with patrons after taking photos of them at The Quarry Tap Room last August, then struck an officer after being kicked out.
Clancy was placed on administrative leave immediately after and resigned as chief two months later.
Under the agreement, Clancy remains on bail, must undergo substance abuse counseling, and cannot possess alcohol or return to the bar.
If he complies, Clancy will plead guilty to a misdemeanor disorderly conduct charge and pay a $300 fine.
Clancy’s lawyer confirmed to Central Maine that the assault and refusing to submit charges will be dropped as part of the agreement.
He is due back in court in July.

title: Friday Food Insider: From cider donuts to cotton candy, Maine's fall fairs are back
text:
Beyond the food, Maine’s fall calendar is packed with pumpkin-powered celebrations, apple-themed festivities and agricultural fairs featuring local producers, live entertainment and family activities.
Nothing says fall in Maine quite like a trip to the fair, where the food is as much of an attraction as the rides and entertainment. From warm cider donuts and fried dough to fluffy cotton candy and sticky caramel apples, fairgrounds offer no shortage of favorites.
Beyond the food, Maine's fall calendar is packed with pumpkin-powered celebrations, apple-themed festivities and agricultural fairs featuring local producers, live entertainment and family activities.
Here is a list of the Maine fall fairs
Cumberland Fair at Cumberland Fairgrounds ends on Saturday, Oct. 3.
Freeport Fall Festival, in downtown Freeport, runs from Oct. 2-4. The three-day festival features more than 200 New England artists, makers and local food producers.
Fryeburg Fair, at 1154 Main St., runs from Oct. 4-11. The agricultural fair features livestock, competitions, rides, food, entertainment and traditional fair activities.
Damariscotta Pumpkinfest & Regatta runs from Oct. 1-12 in downtown Damariscotta and Newcastle. Events include giant-pumpkin competitions, a pumpkin parade, a food court, a dessert contest, a pumpkin derby and a pumpkin boat regatta.
Fall Fest, at Sunday River in Newry, runs from Oct. 10-11. The festival features fall foliage, arts and crafts, live music, food and family activities.
Great Maine Apple Day, at the Common Ground Education Center on Oct. 25, 294 Crosby Brook Road in Unity. The event celebrates Maine apples with seasonal activities and food-related programming.

title: Bangor Beautiful Commissioned A Community Mural Celebrating Local Artists On Hammond Street
text:
Another Massive Mural Is Coming Together In Downtown Bangor: Check This Out!
In 2022, a non-profit called Bangor Beautiful was started by a group of local artists and residents who wanted to find ways, through landscaping, gardens and art installations, to add a little beauty to the community around them.

"We were founded by artists and community members who have volunteered for projects around the city over the last decade, from planting hundreds of flowers and trees to creating the popular 'Greetings from Bangor, Maine,' 'Paul B., Bangor Wants You,' and Kenduskeag Stream Trail murals."
If you've driven through downtown this week, you've probably seen their latest project, their "Community Mural."
Working with the Bangor Region Chamber of Commerce, Portland-based artist Rachel Gloria Adams has developed a piece that's enveloping the the side of the Hammond Street building in a painted patchwork quilt of sorts, incorporating artwork by Bangor artists, Juliana Cantreli, Nina Earley, Annette Dodd, Karen Nichols, Carile Deshane.

title: Line-dance instructor builds community while inspiring students
text:
PETERSBURG, Va. (Aging Untold) — Richard Caple leads a line dancing class at Club 17 in Petersburg, and he also gives back to the community through scholarships and fundraisers.
How the class started
Caple said he did not initially want to lead the class.
“So, a year ago, we had contemplated on him becoming a line dance instructor. And I asked him, would he do it? And he said yes,” Adrianne Green, a member of the group, said.
“And they set me up. I didn’t want to do it. I really didn’t want to do it. But after the response, I got twisted, twisted my arm,” Caple said.
Participants and the class
Most participants are members of Mount Olivet Baptist Church.
Caple said the class gives him joy when participants share their experiences.
“It gives me joy when I when they give me their testimonies like they’ve been to the doctor. The doctor said they have lost weight. They are doing good,” Caple said.
“I don’t know why I’m attached to them seniors, but them seniors, they got my heart, they got it and they know it too,” Caple said.
Community outreach
Caple has organized fashion shows to raise money for student scholarships. He keeps company with the sick and shut-in and raises money for the American Cancer Society. The group also helped one of its own members when she fell on hard times.
“Last week, one of the club members here asked up to help in a donation because a lady’s house was being condemned. So we were able to raise $500 that same evening,” Caple said.
Full-time job
Caple works a full-time job as a medical transport driver for seniors in addition to leading the class.
“I was told about it by a senior. She said, never change what you’re doing. You just ask God to give you the strength to make time to do what you like to do,” Caple said.

title: Rockland sees uptick in liens for unpaid taxes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — The number of liens placed on properties by the city this year increased from last year.
There were 121 liens filed Sept. 30 in the Knox County Registry of Deeds. This is up from 106 filed last year, but slightly less than in 2024 when 123 were filed.
The fewest liens filed in Rockland for a year came in 2021 when there were 71. The most ever filed was 387 in 1992 during a deep nationwide recession. Since the early 1990s, the taxes for properties with mortgages are rolled into mortgage payments and the financial institution will pay the taxes if the property owner is unable and the property is at risk of being foreclosed.
Property taxes unpaid as of Sept. 30 amounted to $501,397. The liens are for taxes billed in September 2025.
The property owners have 18 months to pay off the liens or the properties will automatically be foreclosed on by the city in March 2028 as is dictated by state law.
The largest liens were placed on 500 Main St. and 497 Main St. which each owe about $20,000 in unpaid property taxes.

title: Renewed scrutiny of laws on intoxication and consent amid Cornell allegations
text:
Cornell rape allegations lead to renewed scrutiny of laws on intoxication and consent
A woman's account of being sexually assaulted at a Cornell University fraternity house has advocates and lawmakers renewing their criticism of a New York law that makes it more difficult to prosecute people who have taken advantage of others too intoxicated to consent to sex.
Video above: Attorney of the former student who alleges she was raped speaks to CNN
Under state law, rape charges generally need to involve force or a clear refusal of sex, unless the victim is physically helpless due to being unconscious, or mentally incapacitated due to being drugged without their consent.
Those limitations have led to something nicknamed the “voluntary intoxication loophole.” Prosecutors can't easily bring charges against someone who engaged in sex with someone who voluntarily became intoxicated to the point where their ability to say “yes” or “no” to sex was compromised.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited that law as he defended his office's initial decision not to file criminal charges against any of the men sued by a woman who says she was the victim of a gang rape at Cornell in 2024.
Video below: Cornell's student assembly plans a forum on sexual violence
Van Houten said that in her sworn statement to campus police in 2024, the woman didn't allege that she became intoxicated against her will, or was physically forced into sex or was unconscious when it happened.
“That’s victim blaming, straight up,” in state law, said Stefan Turkheimer, vice president of public policy for RAINN, the largest anti-sexual violence organization in the U.S. “It prevents a lot of cases from coming forward, where prosecutors are reluctant to try to push forward on a case where the person is incapacitated due to voluntary intoxication.”
New York lawmakers renew push to change the law
New York state lawmakers have considered bills to change the law over the years, though the proposals have stalled, despite support from prominent district attorneys and advocates.
Jeffrey Dinowitz, a state Assembly member who has sponsored such measures starting back in 2019, said the Cornell case is “exactly the type of situation this legislation would address” and hoped that there would be additional urgency in the coming legislative session to change the law.
“It’s just outrageous and it makes me angry that we haven’t passed this yet,” he said, adding that “it would at least ensure that the survivor would get justice.”
The woman, identified only by a pseudonym in the civil lawsuit, filed the complaint Sept. 16, saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house on the Ivy League campus in October 2024 after being pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol. She became completely incapacitated while frat members were sexually assaulting her, the lawsuit alleges.
Van Houten has since reopened the investigation, saying he would consider presenting the case to a grand jury for their consideration. But in a written statement issued Monday, he said his initial decision not to charge relied heavily on a statement the woman gave to police that was given to his office, in which he said she had described some of the male students exhibiting incapacitation but not herself.
Police have not released that document, and the prosecutor's statement only included sparse redacted pieces of that document in his explanation.
Other states with intoxication laws are moving to change them
New York is one of 19 states with rape or sexual assault laws that consider intoxicated victims to be mentally incapacitated only if they became drunk or were drugged without their knowledge or consent, according to research by The Associated Press and a report published in The Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law.
Many of those laws have been in place for a long time. But states have been gradually moving to change them.
After the Minnesota Supreme Court overturned a sexual misconduct conviction in 2021 because the incapacitated victim had voluntarily become intoxicated, the state legislature revised its laws later that year to allow charges to be brought no matter whether an incapacitated victim had voluntarily or involuntarily become intoxicated. Michigan made a similar revision to its sexual assault laws in 2023, and Texas followed in 2025.
“That business of whether the victim was voluntarily intoxicated or involuntarily intoxicated should really not matter in the vast majority of cases, if not all of them,” said Chinmoy Gulrajani, a psychiatry professor at the University of Minnesota who has researched state sexual assault laws. That’s because “the assailant should have known that this is not a person who is in their right state of mind.”
Turkheimer said these laws can have a disproportionate effect on campuses, where people may be experiencing alcohol or drugs in social settings for the first time. He said mental incapacitation laws aren’t about someone having just a few drinks, but about situations in which a person has lost the capacity to consent.
“The movement is, to look at a person who is incapacitated, regardless of how they got there, and actually give that person protection," he said. “This is a situation where a person has reached a state where they lack the capacity to consent. And in that situation, the law should be protecting those people because they simply can’t protect themselves.”
Associated Press reporter Anthony Izaguirre in New York contributed to this report.

Customer Jerry Schroeder said Atchison consistently helps other shoppers.
“Always helping somebody. See. He’s down there helping somebody now,” Schroeder said.
Now in his early 70’s, his work schedule has been scaled back from full-time hours.
“Full-time retirement is full-time work to find yourself busy. To keep yourself busy. Especially when you don’t have hobbies,” Atchison said.
Customers continue to seek him out during his shifts.
“Because he’s always so cheerful. You’ve had a bad day, come in, and he’s happy. Smiling,” Schroeder said.
Sischo said the store will accommodate Atchison’s continued employment.
“We will take him for as long as he wants to be here,” Sischo said.
Atchison said he plans to continue working because of his passion for customer service.
“If you love what you do, it’s not work. And I love doing this. I really do,” Atchison said.
Festival Foods has a 10-tile policy requiring employees to greet customers within 10 tiles and offer assistance. Atchison extends that range, greeting customers from 20 or 30 tiles away.
