title: 5 large whales found entangled off the Maine coast in 2025
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Five large whales were found entangled in heavy ocean ropes off the coast of Maine last year, but new federal data carries a vital silver lining for the state’s multimillion-dollar lobster fleet: not a single one was a North Atlantic right whale.
Rescue teams and aerial surveyors documented three humpback whales, one fin whale, and one minke whale caught in ropes off Maine’s coast in 2025. The complete absence of right whales in Maine gear last year arrives at a high-stakes moment for coastal communities.
A report released this week by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration lists only one right whale entanglement in U.S. waters in 2025, and it occurred in the calving grounds off the coast of Georgia.
North Atlantic right whales are critically endangered, with about 380 individuals believed to be alive today. Because the dwindling species teeters near extinction, federal regulators have spent years imposing strict rules on how Maine lobstermen set their gear.
Regulators have targeted seabed-to-surface buoy ropes — the long lines connecting ocean floor traps to floating buoys — which can wrap tightly around migrating whales, causing injuries and death. Heavy ropes can drag for months, inflicting painful wounds and hindering reproduction.
Tensions escalated dramatically after regulators confirmed a young female right whale known as No. 5120 died in early 2024 from entanglement in Maine lobster rope. It was the first right whale death tied directly to Maine gear, sparking industry fears of a federal crackdown.
On a national level, entanglement numbers dropped last year. NOAA documented 76 confirmed large whale entanglements in U.S. waters in 2025, a sharp decline from the 95 confirmed cases in 2024 but a minor increase over the 18-year annual average of about 73 cases.
Humpbacks made up the vast majority of national entanglements in 2025, with 65 reported cases.
Regionally, the year-to-year and long-term entanglement numbers were even better. Confirmed entanglements in New England waters dropped to their lowest since 2013, showing a big regional decline even as West Coast cases surged.
The encouraging numbers align with hopeful news from southern calving grounds, where scientists recorded 23 newborn right whale calves last winter — the species’ most successful calving season since 2009.
The federal report comes at the perfect time for Maine’s multimillion-dollar lobster industry.
The U.S. House recently passed the Northeast Lobstermen Protection Act, co-sponsored by Rep. Jared Golden of Maine, D-2nd District. If passed by the Senate, it would extend a current congressional pause on new whale regulations from 2028 until 2035.
The industry and its supporters, including Gov. Janet Mills and President Donald Trump, argue that because right whale entanglements are not happening in Maine waters, new restrictions are unnecessary and would needlessly cripple a historic industry.
Federal officials say rising birth rates combined with lower regional entanglements may give regulators greater flexibility when drafting future whale protection rules, but conservationists caution that right whales remain in peril from vessel strikes and heavy ropes.
“We’re utterly failing to solve this deadly problem,” said Rachel Rilee, oceans policy specialist at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Pop-up fishing gear could help end this gruesome problem. Federal officials and the fishing industry need to stop making excuses.”
Still, for Maine fishermen defending their livelihoods, last year’s whale entanglement figures demonstrate that working waterfronts and endangered wildlife can coexist with just the right mix of ocean safeguards in place.

title: Man accused of murder dies more than a week after he was shot by police in Portland
text:
Man accused of murder dies more than a week after he was shot by police in Portland, Maine
A man accused of murdering another man has now died, more than a week after he was shot by police in Portland.
The Portland Police Department said it was notified on Thursday, Oct. 1, that Brian Oliver, 41, of Portland, died at MaineHealth Maine Medical Center, where he had been receiving treatment since he was shot by police on Sept. 21.
Police were called to 27 Colonial Road at about 8:16 p.m. on Sept. 21 for a reported disturbance.
When police arrived, a tenant took them inside an apartment but then ran back toward the officers screaming.
Officer Joseph Lowe and Officer David Moore then entered the apartment and said they found Oliver assaulting 69-year-old Mark Tschamler.
Police say Oliver was shot after refusing to drop his weapon.
Tschamler was pronounced dead at the scene.
A longtime friend of Tschamler told Maine's Total Coverage that Tschamler had been diagnosed with throat cancer.
Police say Oliver was going to be charged with murder, but formal charges were never filed due to his medical condition following the incident.

title: Here’s what your state is doing to provide relief amid high fuel prices
text:
(AP) - High gasoline and diesel prices have prompted elected officials in many states to take actions providing relief to motorists.
Some governors and lawmakers have suspended motor fuel taxes. Others have reduced gas taxes. And still more have waived restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel typically used by farmers, foresters and others for off-road equipment.
The actions come as potential voters in the midterm elections have voiced widespread concern about high fuel prices and the general cost of living.
Average prices for regular gasoline have topped $4 a gallon while average diesel fuel prices have risen over $6 a gallon — both up substantially since the war with Iran began.
A growing number of governors and lawmakers have taken steps to provide fuel tax relief for at least some motorists. Here’s a look at some of those states:
- ALABAMA: Gov. Kay Ivey issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 120 days.
- ARKANSAS: Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
- CALIFORNIA: Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an order in September allowing a sooner switch to cheaper, winter-blends of fuel.
- GEORGIA: Gov. Brian Kemp resumed a 30-day fuel tax suspension in September, marking the second installment of the tax holiday that was first offered in the spring.
- ILLINOIS: The state budget delayed a 1.3 cent gas tax increase from July 1 to Jan. 1.
- INDIANA: Gov. Mike Braun has issued multiple extensions of a fuel tax holiday, which currently runs through Nov. 4. He also issued an executive order relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel.
- KENTUCKY: Gov. Andy Beshear in May temporarily reduced the gas tax by 10 cents. That has expired, but a freeze continues on a 0.6 cent increase that had been scheduled for July 1.
- LOUISIANA: Gov. Jeff Landry issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
- MISSOURI: Gov. Mike Kehoe issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
- NEBRASKA: Gov. Jim Pillen issued an executive order in September allowing people to seek refunds of state diesel taxes for transporting crops and livestock and relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 90 days.
- NORTH CAROLINA: Gov. Josh Stein in September ordered relaxed enforcement of restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel through the end of the year.
- NORTH DAKOTA: Gov. Kelly Armstrong issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for two months.
- OHIO: Legislation signed in October by Gov. Mike DeWine suspends state fuel taxes for 90 days.
- OKLAHOMA: Gov. Kevin Stitt in September ordered relaxed enforcement of restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 120 days.
- TEXAS: Gov. Greg Abbott issued an executive order in September relaxing restrictions on tax-exempt diesel fuel for 30 days.
- UTAH: Legislation signed by Gov. Spencer Cox reduced the gas tax by 6 cents a gallon from July 1 through the remainder of the year.

title: Houlton asks court to dismiss public records case over surveillance cameras
text:
The town of Houlton asked the Aroostook County Superior Court this week to dismiss a recently filed Freedom of Access Act lawsuit, claiming it has complied with Maine law. The petitioner disputed the claim Friday.
Resident Craig Harriman sued Houlton in September, claiming officials did not release all the public documents he requested related to the town’s controversial facial recognition surveillance cameras that were removed earlier this year.
Houlton is no stranger to resident lawsuits alleging the town “cherry picks” documents for FOAA requests while withholding or remaining silent about others. Harriman’s Friday response is the latest chapter in the years-long saga surrounding the town’s surveillance cameras.
The town alleged this week that it never denied Harriman’s request, that it has supplied him with all requested documents and that any omissions were inadvertent.
The suit was Harriman’s third Rule 80B appeal, which is a Superior Court filing to challenge actions taken by government agencies. He alleged that each time he sought to enforce his right to inspect government records under Maine law, the town gave no lawful reason for failing to produce data he had requested multiple times.
The town’s document denials do not cite a lawful exemption as required by Maine law, demonstrating a pattern of noncompliance, he said.
In his most recent court action, Harriman specifically directed his public records request to Police Chief Tim DeLuca. He sought all 2021 electronic communications between DeLuca and former town information technology employee Scott Rossignol concerning the purchase, testing and installation of town surveillance cameras and school cameras.
The town omitted DeLuca’s responsive emails to Rossignol, never provided a written exemption explanation and never confirmed in writing that DeLuca’s account, servers and archives were searched, according to Harriman.
“On August 26, 2026, the town wrote that ‘the request was fulfilled.’ That is a written refusal of the remaining statutory demands,” Harriman said.
In addition to Maine law, the town is held under a more stringent public records obligation to Harriman, bound by a 2025 settlement agreement between Harriman, Mark Lipscombe and Patrick Bruce.
After months of negotiation, the Houlton Town Council approved the agreement in October 2025 regarding the removal of controversial surveillance cameras equipped with facial recognition technology.
The three men alleged the town unlawfully possessed and used facial recognition technology in violation of Maine law and were prepared to sue the town seeking a temporary restraining order and permanent injunctive relief regarding the town’s use of the technology, the settlement alleges.
Prior to the settlement, Harriman, Lipscombe and Bruce each filed multiple Freedom of Access Act requests related to the cameras. Bruce told the Town Council in January 2025 that the use of facial recognition technology violated Maine’s strict facial surveillance law.
As part of the settlement agreement, the town was required to produce documents related to all outstanding public records requests from the men, which included Harriman’s, within 30 days. For any documents not produced, the town was mandated to accompany the response with an affidavit detailing a diligent search for the record requested.
The town did not produce all of Harriman’s requested documents and they did not supply search documentation, he said.
“Calling omitted records ‘inadvertent’ does not convert that refusal into compliance,” Harriman said. “Chief DeLuca’s November 24, 2025, statement that all responsive documents had been provided cannot be treated as a completed search.”
The town claimed it has given Harriman all the documents. Harriman disagreed, saying he repeatedly wrote to DeLuca and Interim Town Manager Nancy Ketch requesting the missing documents and received none.
Additionally, Harriman attended several Town Council meetings to express his frustration and request the missing documents. He shared his FOAA requests and town response with each councilor.
Ketch told Harriman in an Aug. 26 email that he had received all the documents related to his request.
“I am sorry if some items you previously received from the first distribution were not included in the second distribution,” she wrote. “As I previously stated, all records were reviewed internally and in good faith to obtain the requested documents. Any missing documents provided from the second request were inadvertent. Again, you have received all documents from the Town, so the request was fulfilled.”
Harriman is asking the court to declare that Houlton violated the Maine Freedom of Access Act and order the immediate production of all the remaining records he has requested.
He is also asking the court to order the town to confirm in writing that they completed a thorough search of DeLuca’s email account, relevant town and police servers and archives related to the documents he requested.

title: Obituary: Carol Anne Doele
text:
BRUNSWICK – Carol Anne Doele, 88, died Sept. 26, 2026 at Maine Medical Center, Portland. She was born April 18, 1938 in Brooklyn, N.Y., the daughter of Henry and Adele Stewart Ahnemann. She married Donald C. Doele on Feb. 25, 1956. They remained married until his death on Aug. 9, 2022, enjoying 66 years together.
Carol’s passion was music. She found herself a part of her church choirs, including at Trinity United Methodist, Ewing, N.J.; Lawrenceville Presbyterian Church, New Jersey; and First Parish Church, Brunswick. She had also been a member of the Princeton Pro Musica, with whom she performed at Carnegie Hall and traveled to perform in Ireland, Canada, and Ecuador. Every Christmas her family gathered around her at the piano as she played and led holiday carols.
She worked as a bookkeeper at First Methodist Church in Trenton, N.J. Then as the office manager for over 25 years at the Nassau Club in Princeton, N.J. After retiring and moving to Maine in 2003, she was the bookkeeper for a number of years at First Parrish Church, Brunswick.
She was predeceased by her husband, Donald; and her son, Bruce Doele.
She is survived by her brother, Donald (Ann) and sons Donald, Jr. of Damariscotta, David (Jody) of Easthampton, Mass. and Bradley (Cindy) of Palmyra, N.J. She is also survived by six grandchildren, Ryan (Kayle) Doele, Ashlee (Carlos) Ochoa, Tara (Matthew) Leise, James Doele, Lauren (Phillip) Akins, Jeremy Doele; five great-grandsons, Wyatt and James Akins, Hank and Bruce Doele, and Jack Leise; and her great-granddaughter, Scottie Leise.
A memorial service will be held 10 a.m. Monday, Nov. 2, at First Parish Church, Cleaveland Street, Brunswick. With her wishes, she will be interred into the First Parish Memorial Garden, Brunswick.
Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.
Memorial donations
may be made to:
First Parish Church, Brunswick and The Muscular Dystrophy Association (www.mda.org/disease/polymyositis) designated for Polymyositis research.

title: James Gunn to Remain in Charge of DC Under Skydance
text:
James Gunn and Peter Safran Will Remain DC Studios Co-CEOs at Skydance
The final legal hurdles have been cleared and in a matter of months, Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Skydance will be no more, replaced by a combined corporation known simply as Skydance.
Smooshing two film studios into one will result in massive changes in Hollywood; we only know of a few of them for sure at this point. The heads of Paramount, Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, look to oversee the combined film production at both Paramount and Warner Bros., meaning the current heads of Warners, Micael De Luca and Pam Abdy will likely be in search of new jobs elsewhere.
But two of De Luca and Abdy’s key lieutenants are staying — as the co-CEOs of DC Studios, James Gunn and Peter Safran, are set to stay on and continue overseeing DC movies and shows for the new Skydance regime.
Earlier today, Gunn posted a promotional video hyping the new soon-to-be-merged Skydance company and all of its brands. Frankly, it’s an alarming amount of film companies, TV networks, and intellectual property. It feels like half of Hollywood when it’s laid out this way.
Gunn’s video included the caption: “What once was the peak, is now just the beginning.”
READ MORE: 12 DC Comics That Can Never Become DC Movies
According to Deadline, Gunn and Safran had a meeting with Skydance overseer David Ellison and “it went well.”
Even if you wanted to dismiss Gunn and Safran, even if you felt they had done a poor job relaunching DC’s combined fictional universe in the last few years, now would probably be a bad time to do it. Gunn directed the first film in the current DC Universe, Superman, and he’s in production now on its sequel, Man of Tomorrow. You could dump him as an executive, but that would just make releasing the sequel, Man of Tomorrow, infinitely more difficult.
The next DC Studios movie, Clayface, opens in theaters on October 23. Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow follows on July 9, 2027.

title: Letter: Reject Penobscot County jail question
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Our jail system in Penobscot County costs taxpayers millions but does not seem to make us safer. And now county commissioners want to build a new jail outside Bangor. A question will be on the Nov. 3 ballot just for Penobscot County asking to move the jail location out of Bangor. This will raise taxes even higher. It seems commissioners only know how to spend our tax dollars, not how to save them. It’s time to say “No!”
I don’t believe we need a new jail. We can renovate the one we have for much, much less. We can use diversion and not arrest so many, so that people who need mental health or substance use programs can get the treatment they need, which they often can’t get if they’re locked up.

Larry Dansinger
Bangor

title: Head Start was there for my family. Maine children need it protected.
text:
Megan Newsome lives in Lisbon and is a Maine state parent ambassador.
When my son Brayden was born, our family was facing a lot at once.
I had been diagnosed with cancer while I was pregnant. He arrived about six weeks early and spent time in the NICU. By the time Brayden was about a year old, I was receiving WIC, the federally funded nutrition program for women, infants and children. WIC staff asked whether I had childcare and told me about Early Head Start.
I knew very little about the program then. It quickly became a godsend.
At the time, Brayden was not yet walking. He could not feed himself or hold his own cup. Within weeks of starting Early Head Start, he was pulling himself up, holding his cup and learning to use a spoon and pick up food on his own.
His teachers paid attention to who he was and how he learned.
Brayden is left-handed. When teachers recognized that and encouraged him to use the hand that came naturally to him, it showed me that they saw my son as an individual.
Head Start also gave me something I deeply needed while facing cancer: trusted people who could care for my child during the workday. Knowing my son was cared for and learning gave me comfort during an incredibly difficult time.
The support did not stop at the classroom door. Head Start connected us with mental health counseling, clothing, diapers, food banks and help during the holidays — all supports we needed to make sure Brayden had what he needed to learn and grow, at home and in the classroom. There was always someone I could turn to.
Brayden is now 3 and has moved from Early Head Start into Head Start. He is now on track developmentally, and this is a crucial moment in his learning. If he needs additional help before elementary school, I want us to recognize it early and have support in place.
That is why proposed changes to Head Start concern me so deeply. Families could lose developmental screenings, medical and dental services, counseling and other support that helps children grow and prepare for school.
For some children, Head Start may provide the only developmental screening they receive. It’s the front door to healthcare, dental care and mental health support. If those services disappear, important needs could go unnoticed until a child enters school and faces a harder path forward.
Larger classrooms and fewer teachers would also make it harder to provide the individual attention that helped Brayden. Teachers need time to know each child, understand how they learn and recognize when they may need additional support.
Head Start works because all these pieces work together. It is not simply a place where parents leave their children. It helps children build confidence and skills while connecting parents with trusted people and practical resources. Weakening any part of that model weakens the program families count on.
I know what Head Start made possible for my son and me. I also know other families rely on it for that same stability and partnership.
The public has only until Oct. 6 to comment on the proposed changes, but Congress can act even after that. I am asking Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King and Rep. Jared Golden, who represents Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, my home district, to listen to Maine families, oppose the proposed rule and protect the standards and services that make Head Start so effective.
Children deserve to enter school with their strengths recognized and the support they need already in place. Parents deserve trusted partners as they build strong futures for their families. Head Start gave my family both.

title: Cause of death revealed for Chad Lowe’s 13-year-old daughter Fiona

Cause of death revealed for Chad Lowe’s 13-year-old daughter Fiona
The cause of death has been revealed for Chad Lowe's 13-year-old daughter Fiona.
Fiona Lowe was pronounced dead at 1:14 a.m. on Sept. 29 at a Los Angeles-area hospital.
Her manner of death was ruled a suicide Thursday, according to the medical examiner’s office.
Fiona Lowe was the daughter of actor Chad Lowe and producer Kim Painter, who announced their daughter’s death on Tuesday.
In a statement to People magazine, the couple said, "We are deeply heartbroken by the loss of our beloved Fiona."
The family said Fiona was smart, creative and loved to dance.
"She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents," the family said. "In fact, she was the light of our lives."
In the statement, the family also shared the national suicide and crisis helpline. "Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time. If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988."
Fiona was born on Nov. 16, 2012. Lowe and Painter share two other daughters together, 17-year-old Mabel Painter Lowe and 10-year-old Nixie Barbara Lowe.
Lowe, the younger brother of actor Rob Lowe, won an Emmy Award for his supporting role in "Life Goes On" as a young man living with HIV.

title: Collins’ record on military affairs is distressing
text:
While the abandoned FBI investigation into Sen. Susan Collins — as reported by ProPublica and carried by this publication on Sept. 23 — is dismaying enough, there is considerably more reason to be dismayed by Collins’ record on military affairs.
Throughout the disastrous 2003-2011 Iraq War, Collins was a staunch supporter of the war, which, according to a Brown University report, will end up costing U.S. taxpayers a total of $2.9 trillion. That’s a staggering $8,457 for every man, woman and child in the country — and that’s about $12 billion right from the pockets of Maine taxpayers. All the while, 14 million American children face food insecurity.
In an emailed Sept. 22 “Tuesday Report,” Collins touted her having secured $42 million in Maine heating assistance. Not bad for one Tuesday Report, but at $42 million per year, Collins would need 285 years of heating assistance to equal the amount Maine taxpayers spent on her disastrous Iraq War — which killed 4,492 Americans and at least 733,000 Iraqis, and destabilized the entire Middle East.
Heating assistance for 285 years. Even Susan Collins would struggle to serve in Congress that long.
Lawrence Reichard
Belfast

title: 49ers owner Jed York suspended for 6 games after his arrest in prostitution sting
text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. (AP) — The NFL suspended San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York for six games Friday following his arrest earlier this year in a prostitution sting in Ohio.
The league announced that York was also fined $500,000 for violating the league’s personal conduct policy. York has not attended any games or league meetings so far this season and was credited with three games served. He is eligible to return on Oct. 20, following the team’s game the previous night against Washington.
York was arrested in a mobile home park by the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force after police said he was attempting to pay $160 for sex with a woman he believed to be a prostitute.
York was booked into jail and was released after posting a $5,000 bond. York was initially charged with engaging in prostitution, but prosecutors amended that to disorderly conduct. He pleaded no contest to that charge and to possessing criminal tools for using his phone to respond to an undercover online prostitution advertisement.
He was sentenced to one day in jail for both offenses to be served concurrently and was credited with one day served when he pleaded no contest. He was also fined $1,150. Police seized the $160 from York, and it was later given to the human trafficking task force as part of the plea. York also completed an online course.

title: 20 people take US citizenship oath in Bangor
text:
The first thing Marvis Zou did after becoming a naturalized citizen on Friday was register to vote.
Zou, who immigrated from China 16 years ago at age 16, said that the privilege to vote is of utmost importance.
“It feels complicated to become a citizen under this administration,” Zou, who lives in Freedom, said. “It feels really heavy and light at the same time.”
Twenty people from 12 different countries became naturalized citizens on Friday morning at a citizenship ceremony in U.S. District Court of Maine in Bangor. The right to vote is what many of the United States’ newest citizens are most excited for — especially as the November midterms approach.
Administering the Naturalization Oath of Allegiance to the United States is a good reminder that the country is strengthened by immigrants, Judge Stacey Neumann said. Immigrants help grow the country’s conscience and creativity.
“Today you join a community bound not by a single language, ethnicity, or religion, but by a shared promise that a free and democratic nation can be strengthened by the talents, dreams, and hard work of people from all over the world,” Neumann said. “Your presence here shows that this promise endures.”
Barbara Ann Lewis has lived in the U.S. for 35 years, coming to the country from New Brunswick. She met her husband at the Loring Air Force Base around that time. Lewis, a nurse in Fort Fairfield, wanted to become a citizen because her children, grandchildren and immediate family are citizens.
Registering to vote was also her first step after the ceremony. She said she’s excited to vote, as is Jack Truong, who worked for five years to become a citizen.
The new citizens can run for local office and serve on a jury, but most importantly, they carry the demand to be informed and speak up to ensure others are treated with dignity and respect, Neumann said.
Immigrants have shaped the country and the newest citizens get to join those ranks, she said.
“Our history includes painful chapters, the exclusion of Chinese laborers, the incarceration of Japanese-American families, and the many moments when newcomers meet with suspicion instead of open doors,” Neumann said. “Yet again and again, America has returned to its core promise. We grow morally, economically, culturally when we choose inclusion over exclusion, hope over fear, and community over isolation.
“We become stronger when we recognize the dignity and potential of those who arrived at our shores.”

title: GRAPHIC: Video inside Flydubai flight shows moment passengers seize control
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — A dentist and other passengers wrestled with a violent copilot. A plumber seized the controls as the plane plunged towards the desert. And the captain, despite being stabbed, managed to open the cockpit door — helping save all 182 people aboard the Israel-bound flight.
“Hollywood isn’t creative enough to come up with stories like this!” said Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel.
Although major questions remained unanswered on Thursday about the attacker and his motive, the story of ordinary passengers saving the FlyDubai flight from disaster has quickly become the stuff of legend.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warmly embraced plumber Yaniv Hayoun shortly after the passengers arrived in Tel Aviv late on Wednesday. He later posted a five-star review of Hayoun’s professional services, calling him “a hero who has saved many lives.”
“He can help you too — I highly recommend him!” Netanyahu added on X.
Hayoun was among several Israelis recommended for the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, while Indian Capt. Smit Machchhar was called “a HERO” by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
One met the prime minister wearing a bloody shirt
Many of the details emerged in a rush shortly after the passengers, most of them Israeli, landed back home to cheers and waving flags.
Hayoun, apologizing for his bloody shirt, within minutes was telling the prime minister and journalists what happened.
There had been little time for him and the others to think. Passengers screamed after spotting the copilot stabbing the captain, and the flight from Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates, to the Israeli city of Tel Aviv began a steep dive. Some believed they were about to die.
A handful of Israelis reacted, hurtling up the aisle after the badly wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door. That was crucial, as cockpit doors are typically locked to prevent hijackings.
They had to struggle, Hayoun said, with the captain’s body resting against it.
The plumber seized the controls, just like in the movies
Hayoun said the copilot appeared to be trying to damage the plane’s controls. He grabbed the copilot, and others began struggling with the man.
Hayoun then tackled the controls. He had no training, but he remembered what he had seen in movies.
“I asked him, how did you know how to do that? And he said, ‘Well, I, I watched these air disaster films,’” Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday.
It was not clear who among the passengers had security experience, though military service is compulsory for most men and women in Israel.
Soon, crew who had been traveling on the plane stepped in to stabilize it, issuing a mayday call and seeking a place to land.
“He managed to stabilize the plane by the skin of his teeth,” another Israeli praised for intervening, Asaf Rajuan, told journalists. Aviation experts have marveled that the plane didn’t crash after a descent so sharp that the rudder was torn away.
A dentist treated the wounded pilot
The handful of Israeli passengers grappled with the copilot for several minutes before subduing him and binding his hands with the cord from a set of headphones.
One of them, Dr. Shota Musayev, a dentist, also attended to the captain, who appeared to have lost a lot of blood. “He was just praying the whole time and was in contact with me, and I was afraid we would really lose him,” Musayev said.
In video that Musayev shot and shared with The Associated Press, the captain lay on the floor of the cabin, saying his head was in pain.
Musayev later told journalists he and the other responders knew they’d had just seconds to act before a “critical event.”
But even with the copilot bound and subdued, they were scared that other attackers might be on the plane. They sent other people around the cabin to stand by.
“We didn’t know where we were going to land. Underneath us there was only desert. We were afraid that they were taking us to a hostile country,” Rajuan said. “We didn’t know who to trust. We didn’t know if the pilot was with us or not … We started suspecting the flight attendants, too.”
Finally, just about an hour after the plane issued a distress call, it made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Now, investigators from across the region are working to understand what led to the attack. The copilot still has not been publicly identified.
As of Thursday evening, the world had not yet heard from the central hero, the captain, who India’s Embassy in the United Arab Emirates said was “in good health and recovering well.”
___
Associated Press reporter Areej Hazboun in Jerusalem contributed.

title: Reports: Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s partner, Ken Urker, dies at 34
text:
Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s partner, Ken Urker, dies at 34
Ken Urker, Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s partner and father of her child, died Thursday on his 34th birthday, according to multiple media reports.
Video above: Gypsy Rose Blanchard released from prison in 2023
His cause of death is not known at this time.
Urker was found unresponsive at his Louisiana home on Thursday by a family member, according to People. Officers were called to the home at around 6:15 p.m., and Urker was found "dead upon arrival," the Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Office confirmed to People.
His death is under investigation.
"I’m in disbelief. I can’t think," Blanchard told People magazine Friday. "I've screamed until my throat burns."
"There are no words that can express the depth of this loss," she added. "I ask for privacy and compassion for our daughter, our families, and everyone grieving Ken during this incredibly painful time."
Blanchard became infamous due to her role in the killing of her abusive mother. She was released from prison in December 2023 after serving more than seven years of a 10-year prison sentence. Blanchard was the victim of Munchausen syndrome by proxy, in which a caregiver fakes their child’s illness or induces symptoms to make their child ill.
Blanchard met Urker while she was in prison. Urker had written a "supportive letter, not on any kind of romantic level" to Blanchard, and included his phone number, after watching "Mommy Dead and Dearest," which was released in 2017, Blanchard said on the "We Need to Talk" podcast in June.
She added that she gave Urker a call and "within five minutes of talking on the phone, I felt like we had known each other our whole lives." After two years of dating, the couple got engaged while she was in prison, but Urker split up with her months later, she said.
Blanchard went on to marry Louisiana teacher Ryan Anderson in a prison wedding ceremony in July 2022, but they parted ways in 2023, and she rekindled her romance with Urker.
Urker and Blanchard share a daughter together named Aurora Raina Urker. The couple got engaged in October 2018 and then broke up. They reunited in April 2024, shortly after Blanchard's divorce from Ryan Anderson, and their daughter was born Dec. 28, 2024.
CNN contributed to this report.

title: Edward Little football outlasts Scarborough in double overtime thriller
text:
AUBURN — No one on the Edward Little football team was alive when the Red Eddies won their last state championship in 1977, or when they made their last title game appearance in 2002 for that matter, but the players are still aware of the program’s decades-long drought.
And while their 27-21 double overtime win over Scarborough on Friday doesn’t fix things, it proved to be a step in the right direction — one that was on full display as quarterback Logan Stout rushed 9 yards into the end zone to clinch a Week 5 thriller for his team.
“(This win) means the world to us and our program,” said Stout, a sophomore. “And our program had been looking for a team like this for so long, and it means so much for us to keep bringing it on and on and on, and bringing it up and up and up for the next few years — and even right now, just bringing it up from here.”
Stout had already thrown a touchdown and rushed for another in regulation. In overtime, he doubled his total, scoring on both of Edward Little’s drives.
“Coach (Brian Jahna) is like …‘Can you get this (touchdown)?’” Stout said. “I’m like, ‘Yes Coach, I got this.’ First play, it was the wedge, it wasn’t the best. We didn’t get much. But then second play, I knew it was coming. I knew he would give me that sweep to the outside, and just took it from there.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
In the first quarter, Edward Little (2-2) showed it was ready for a fight against a Scarborough (0-5) team that had faced a gauntlet of a schedule, with losses against Thornton Academy, Portland, South Portland and Bonny Eagle in the first four weeks of the season.
The Red Eddies struck first on a 7-yard touchdown pass from Stout to Ashton Sullivan, and they kept the Red Storm out of the end zone in the first half. Scarborough’s best chance at scoring came with the ball inside the Edward Little 5-yard line, but Sullivan sacked quarterback Oscar Goss to force a turnover on downs.
The Red Storm scored on their first drive of the second half — a 16-yard touchdown pass from Goss to Jackson Leahy — which tied the game, 7-7. On the ensuing Red Eddies drive, Ozzie Bodah returned a fumble for 22 yards for a score, putting Scarborough ahead by a touchdown with under five and half minutes to play in the third quarter.
Edward Little bounced back quickly. On its next drive, Stout had a 26-yard touchdown run negated by a holding penalty, but just under two and half minutes into the fourth quarter, he found the end zone on a 1-yard rush.
Stout scored in the same way on the Red Eddies’ first overtime drive. Scarborough then answered with a 2-yard pass from Goss to Brandon Brady. The Red Storm had the ball first in the second overtime, but missed a field goal. That opened the door for Stout, who rushed for his third touchdown of the game to lift Edward Little to victory.
UNSUNG HERO
Edward Little’s Adonis Bailey-Curry intercepted two passes late in the fourth quarter. These game-saving plays helped the Red Eddies survive to win the game in overtime.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “They grew up with not seeing a whole lot of wins, so to establish that themselves, it’s a really big deal. And a night like tonight could go either way, right? So to have it fall on our side of things, I think it was really big in terms of their confidence and their belief in themselves.” — Edward Little coach Brian Jahna
• “I was honest with them just now: ‘We need to grow up.’ And I don’t question their effort, but poise in big moments is important, and that was the difference in the game. So we’re going to keep working, keep moving forward. We’re passionately invested in these young guys. These lessons are tough. They played very, very hard tonight, but it wasn’t enough.” — Scarborough coach Michael Vance
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Edward Little: Logan Stout (4 for 6 passing, 38 yards, TD; 3 rushing TDs); Ashton Sullivan (TD reception; sack); Adonis Bailey-Curry (2 interceptions)
• Scarborough: Oscar Goss (9 for 20 passing, 125 yards, two touchdowns)

title: Shouldn’t it be easier to get to Canada from here?
text:
After a trip to Prince Edward Island a couple summers ago, seeing more of Canada rose among my travel priorities. The people are friendly, the exchange rate is favorable, and there’s a lot to explore. The only deterrent, for me, is the long drive.
Considering our proximity, geographically and culturally, it should be easier to get to some of our northern neighbor’s nearby destinations from southern Maine. Although our countries’ relationship might be strained, for travelers, it’s nothing a “Lake Ontario” hat can’t fix. After all, many Mainers now have an open invitation to become Canadian citizens.
At first glance, the prospect of the Scotia Prince bringing back its ferry service to Portland appeared to offer a potential option. Driving three hours to Bar Harbor to get on the CAT ferry for even longer has never tempted me, but the idea of traveling 10 minutes to go spend the night in a casino and wake up in Nova Scotia? Pretty appealing.
Reading more about what the Scotia Prince is considering, however, tamped my enthusiasm.
The nearly $1,000 one-way price tag (for two people, a car and a cabin) feels like a lot for a trip that, at 11 hours long, is no quicker than it would be by car at a fraction of the cost, regardless of dreaded gas prices. Being able to pass the time sleeping or playing blackjack doesn’t seem like enough of a selling point.
And while some describe the town of Yarmouth, where the ferry would land in Nova Scotia, as a hidden gem, the province’s most popular attractions are at least another couple hours away by car — in the direction of Maine — which again leads me back to sucking up the drive.
What about air travel, you ask? Flights from Portland to Halifax, with one layover, take nearly as long as the drive there and, most of the year, cost about as much as the ferry fee discussed. The same goes for Montreal and Quebec City, which are both about a five-hour drive and closer, as the crow flies, than Bridgeport, Connecticut.
If you’re hoping that direct flights to Canada are coming our way soon, you should know, at this point, that’s a pipe dream.
Toronto is the only city in the country to crack the top 15 international destinations of people flying out of the Portland International Jetport, then connecting through another domestic hub, coming in at No. 4 with just under 4,000 passengers in the past year.
The magic number for an airline to support a direct flight is 30,000 annual passengers, according to Airport Director Paul Bradbury.
Reviving rail service from Boston to Montreal, through Maine, is still being bandied about by state officials, though plans literally have had to change course since lawmakers decided last year to convert the St. Lawrence and Atlantic Rail corridor between Portland and Auburn into a multiuse trail.
The Maine-Canadian Legislative Advisory Commission in January presented a report to the Legislature’s transportation committee — with summarizes of several state-funded studies on the subject undertaken in the past 30 years — essentially recommending that the conversation continues.
In other words, don’t hold your breath.
Ditto for the possibility of an east-west highway being built, a concept first conceived when the country officially established its interstate system in the 1940s and last was seriously considered in Maine over a decade ago.
The amount of travel time that could save drivers would depend on the route, but one thing’s for sure, without it, bus companies aren’t going to start offering trips straight to Canada.
Now, you have to go down to Boston first, if not New York City, before heading north. Meaning, without a car, you really can’t get there from here.

title: Experts say now is an ideal time to protect yourself from flu. Here’s why
text:
(AP) - It’s October and time for flu shots.
Medical experts urge getting a flu vaccination soon, before influenza starts spreading widely — and to get up to date on protection against other fall respiratory viruses, too. Updated COVID-19 shots are available now, plus shots for people especially vulnerable to another winter risk called RSV.
While these infections make many people feel miserable for a few days before they recover, every year flu alone causes hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations in the U.S. and kills tens of thousands.
Vaccination isn’t “a guarantee that we’re going to prevent illness. But just like the seat belt in your car, it decreases risk” of the worst outcomes, said Dr. Ryan Stanton of the American College of Emergency Physicians.
Fall vaccine advice usually comes from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and its independent advisory panel. But this year that panel, which influences state and insurance vaccine policies, is caught in a court battle and the CDC hasn’t updated its advice.
Now doctors’ groups are filling the gap: the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America have posted vaccination guidelines for their patient populations plus the scientific evidence behind them.
Here’s what to know:
Just about everyone should get vaccinated against flu
Just about everybody starting at age 6 months needs flu vaccination, the medical societies agree. But flu is particularly dangerous for people 65 and older, pregnant women, young children and people of any age who have chronic health problems, including asthma, diabetes, heart disease and weak immune systems. The last two flu seasons brought unusually high numbers of child deaths, the vast majority of them in unvaccinated kids.
The vaccines don’t block all flu infections, but they do help prevent the worst outcomes, decreasing older adults’ hospitalizations by 31% last year, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project, a public health group based at the University of Minnesota.
Here’s how to pick from the multiple flu vaccine options
Three “enhanced” flu vaccines are designed to better protect seniors. The American Academy of Family Physicians urges them to choose one — “but do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available,” said AAFP’s Dr. Sarah Nosal.
The Food and Drug Administration recently approved a new choice for people ages 50 and older, the first flu vaccine made with the same mRNA technology that was key to ending the COVID-19 pandemic. One study found Moderna’s mFlusiva was 27% more effective against symptomatic illness among 50- to 64-year-olds than a standard shot.
The shot-averse could choose a nasal spray, FluMist, if they’re ages 2 to 49 and meet other health criteria.
The latest on COVID-19 vaccines
COVID-19 shots once were recommended for just about everyone by federal health agencies, but like last year, the FDA has only formally approved them for higher-risk people — those ages 65 and older or younger people with at least one health condition that increases their risk.
Still, the family physicians recommend all adults get a COVID-19 vaccination, especially seniors and those with other risk factors. Adults 65 and older should get a fall dose and then a second dose six months later, as immunity wanes over time, Nosal said.
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a COVID-19 shot for all children ages 6 months to 23 months, and for older kids with high-risk conditions. It also supports vaccination for any child whose parent wishes it.
With millions of shots administered, there’s no evidence that coronavirus vaccination during pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage or other problems, “so please get the vaccine,” said ACOG’s Dr. Christina Davidson.
Depending on age, people can choose a shot from Moderna, Pfizer, or the only non-mRNA version from Novavax and Sanofi.
Just like with flu vaccines, these shots are better at preventing severe disease than mild cases. The Vaccine Integrity Project said last fall’s COVID-19 shots cut the risk of hospitalization by 53% in seniors and slashed emergency room visits for very young children.
Common side effects for flu and COVID-19 vaccines are mild and temporary, such as sore arms, fatigue, headaches, muscle aches, and mild fever. They occurred somewhat more often with the new mFlusiva than with standard flu shots.
Here’s where you can get vaccinated
While pediatricians and some clinics offer both flu and coronavirus shots, they’re most common in pharmacies.
For COVID-19 shots, states have more pharmacy rules. For example, Walgreens says it offers those shots without a prescription in all but two states, Arizona and Oregon, but can provide doses for children as young as 3 in some states while others have higher age limits.
Medicare covers the fall shots and most private health insurers say they plan to continue doing so through 2027. If you want to choose mFlusiva, the new Moderna flu option, make sure to double check that your insurance covers it.
When to get vaccinated
Flu experts say October is best, although vaccinations will remain available through the fall — just remember it can take two weeks for protection to kick in. COVID-19 cases rose in the late summer and usually do again around the winter holidays. Some experts say it’s also OK to time the coronavirus shot a few weeks ahead of an event you wouldn’t want to miss because of illness, like a special trip or get-together.
RSV is a nuisance for many, but it can be deadly for some
RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, typically is a cold-like nuisance during the fall, winter and early spring. But it can be severe, even life-threatening, for infants and older adults.
The family physicians recommend a one-time vaccination for adults 75 and older, people 50 to 74 who are at increased risk, or younger people with weak immune systems.
It’s also recommended during late pregnancy to protect infants born during RSV season. Separately, the pediatricians recommend a vaccine-like medication for those infants whose moms weren’t vaccinated and some other high-risk babies.

title: Lebanon, Sanford firefighters rescue skydiver stuck in tree
text:
Firefighters rescued a skydiver who got stuck in a tree in Lebanon on Thursday.
The Lebanon Fire-EMS was dispatched to the scene at about 4:45 p.m., the department said in a news release.
Responding crews located the skydiver with Skydive New England about 50 to 60 feet above the ground and observed that he was awake and alert, the department said. A Sanford Fire Department tower ladder was called to the scene due to the height.
Once on scene, Sanford firefighters extended the ladder, positioning it beneath the skydiver before safely bringing him into the tower’s bucket, according to the news release. They disconnected him from his parachute equipment before lowering him to the ground.
Lebanon Fire-EMS personnel transported the skydiver to a local hospital with minor injuries to his face and leg, the department said.
“Incidents such as this demonstrate the importance of strong mutual aid relationships and cooperation between neighboring fire and emergency medical services,” the department stated. “Access to specialized equipment and trained personnel allows departments to work together to manage unusual and technically challenging incidents safely and effectively.”`

title: More than 100 pet rats found living in parked cars, police say
text:
EUGENE, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - More than 100 pet rats were found in two parked cars in Eugene last month, according to the police department.
At about 10:30 a.m. on Sept. 23, officers and animal welfare were called to help with two cars being towed. Police said one of the cars, a blue Saturn, was covered by tarp and, when removed, officers could see several rats inside.
According to police, there were rat feces throughout the car, along with chewed-up seat cushions, trash, no food, and very little water.
More rats were found in a nearby gold Suburban.
Police said the owner of the rats claimed to have rescued them. The owner tried to help capture the rats and get them out of the cars using yogurt, but the rats were hard to catch.
Fifty-two rats in eight cages were taken to Greenhill Humane Society. Three of the rats reportedly gave birth to 18 newborn rats after arriving.
The cars were taken to a towing yard with rats still inside. Police said animal welfare was going to continue to provide food and water for the rats until Greenhill had room to take more.
Police said the case remains open under a neglect investigation.

title: Obituary: Joanna “Jo” Tibby
text:
MOUNT VERNON – Joanna “Jo” Tibby, 82, died unexpectedly at her home in Mount Vernon, Maine, on August 3, 2026.
Born Jan. 27, 1944, in Washington, D.C., Jo grew up in Port Washington, NY, with her parents John and Emily, her sister, Ellen, and brother, William “Wil”. After high school, her life took her to many places, including New York City, California, Montreal, Vermont, and abroad before she eventually found her way to Maine. When Jo arrived here, she told people she knew she had “come home.” Jo spent more than half of her life in Mount Vernon, with the help of neighbors and friends, she designed and built the house that became her home.
There is no short obituary that can hold an entire 82-year life—the places traveled, work done, meals prepared, causes supported, cats rescued, friendships made, and all the ordinary moments that become precious once someone is gone. What remains are the stories, the connections, and the many traces of a life lived across many places before Jo found the place she called home.
Jo’s working life was wonderfully varied. She worked in bookstores and restaurants, ran a small graphic arts print shop, dispatched ambulances, baked bread and desserts, and worked as a conductor on the Belfast and Moosehead Lake Railroad. Her travels and many occupations became part of the long and interesting path that eventually brought her home to Mount Vernon.
Jo also gave her time and talents to the community around her. She helped develop Neighbors Driving Neighbors and designed its icon. She participated in Mount Vernon’s Community Partnership Corporation and its work toward affordable senior housing. Again and again, as a neighbor and friend, she offered support, transportation, diabetes education, a warm listening presence, and with the years the increasingly thoughtful observations she called “quack therapy” and others called wisdom. At Bearnstow, where she was a longtime member of the community, Jo served as a local liaison, helped with publicity, and prepared family-style meals during the summer season. She helped bring Bearnstow dancers to Mt. Vernon’s annual early summer crafts fair and helped make it a parade.
Perhaps one of the most enduring parts of Jo’s legacy is her love for cats. Cats in need found a friend in Jo. She rescued homeless cats, cared for them, and worked to find them safe and loving homes. Her home on Bean Road became part of that effort, and over the years cats who might otherwise have been without a home were given another chance because Jo was willing to help. Those cats went on to become beloved companions in other homes and families. In that way, Jo’s kindness to them traveled farther than she may ever have known. Every cat she helped rescue and every home she helped find became another small continuation of something she cared deeply about. Jo leaves behind her own beloved feline family, Honeylee, Sullivan “Sully,” and Phoebe. They, too, are part of Jo’s story.
Jo is remembered by her sister, Ellen; her brother, Wil and his longtime partner Gaye; and the many friends, neighbors, and members of the Mount Vernon and Bearnstow communities whose lives crossed paths with hers.
Jo’s inspirational spirit lives on. Celebrating Jo’s Life – Family, friends, neighbors, and community members are invited to gather in remembrance of Jo on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026, from 12 to 2 p.m. at the Mount Vernon Community Center, Main Street, Mount Vernon, Maine.
Those wishing to honor Jo’s memory with a donation are invited to consider:
PALS in Manchester, Maine or
any no-kill animal shelter Helping another cat find safety, care, and a home would be a meaningful way to carry forward a part of Jo’s legacy

title: Mother charged with capital murder in deaths of 2 sons
text:
WAXAHACHIE, Texas (KWTX/Gray News) — A Texas mother is facing two counts of capital murder after authorities said she shot and killed her sons Thursday morning.
Forty-two-year-old Colleen Nichole Lemmon of Waxahachie was booked into the Wayne McCollum Detention Center following treatment at a local hospital for non-life-threatening injuries.
Deputies respond to 911 call
Ellis County Sheriff’s Office deputies responded around 4:13 a.m. Thursday to a 911 call reporting an unknown emergency at a home in the 900 block of Big Sky Drive in Waxahachie.
Deputies entered the home and discovered two male victims suffering from gunshot wounds.
One victim, identified by authorities as 21-year-old Christopher Scott Pitre of Waxahachie, was pronounced dead at the scene.
The second victim, a 15-year-old boy, was rushed to a local hospital in critical condition, where he later died from his injuries. The sheriff’s office said the teenager’s identity is being withheld.
Investigation and statement
Detectives developed probable cause through corroborating evidence recovered during the investigation that Lemmon was responsible for shooting both of her sons, the sheriff’s office said.
The victims’ father has been notified of both deaths.
“My deepest sympathies go out to the victims’ father, family members, and loved ones involved in this tragic incident,” Ellis County Sheriff Brad Norman said in a statement. “They will remain in our prayers during this difficult time.”
Jail records show Lemmon is charged with two counts of capital murder. Her bond is pending arraignment.

title: More than 100 pet rats found living in parked cars, police say
text:
EUGENE, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - More than 100 pet rats were found in two parked cars in Eugene last month, according to the police department.
At about 10:30 a.m. on Sept. 23, officers and animal welfare were called to help with two cars being towed. Police said one of the cars, a blue Saturn, was covered by tarp and, when removed, officers could see several rats inside.
According to police, there were rat feces throughout the car, along with chewed-up seat cushions, trash, no food, and very little water.
More rats were found in a nearby gold Suburban.
Police said the owner of the rats claimed to have rescued them. The owner tried to help capture the rats and get them out of the cars using yogurt, but the rats were hard to catch.
Fifty-two rats in eight cages were taken to Greenhill Humane Society. Three of the rats reportedly gave birth to 18 newborn rats after arriving.
The cars were taken to a towing yard with rats still inside. Police said animal welfare was going to continue to provide food and water for the rats until Greenhill had room to take more.
Police said the case remains open under a neglect investigation.

title: ‘I was fighting for my life.’ Flydubai pilot recounts moments when he was attacked
text:
NEW DELHI (AP) — The Indian airline captain who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a FlyDubai flight described Friday how he fought for his life in the minutes after his co-pilot stabbed him and the plane began a steep descent.
Capt. Smit Machchhar, recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a televised video call that he knew he had to get back on his feet to save his passengers.
“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” he said from the hospital, his head bandaged and tubes in his nose, before breaking down as he recalled the attack.
“I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realized that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives,” he told Modi.
Machchhar, who is from Mumbai, was seriously injured in Wednesday’s attack but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and restrain the attacker as the Boeing 737 descended sharply, witnesses and Israeli authorities said. He has been hailed as a hero, with world leaders saying he helped avert a disaster.
The flight, carrying 182 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was diverted to Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia for an emergency landing. FlyDubai said Wednesday that the jet was secured by on-duty crew members “who diverted and landed the aircraft safely.” A regional official said the crew members were pilots in training.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the attacker, an Omani national, was arrested in Saudi Arabia and was undergoing interrogation there. The motive for the attack was not immediately clear.
Modi told Machchhar his “courage, patience, and presence of mind” saved many lives.
Machchhar said his flying experience allowed him to sense the plane’s steep descent even after he was knocked down by the attacker.
“I have been flying planes for 17 years and serving as a captain for the last 11 years. I can sense exactly what is happening with the aircraft even with my eyes closed. When I was down, I could feel that the aircraft was plummeting,” he said.
Machchhar said that during those difficult moments, he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a Hindu devotional hymn dedicated to Lord Hanuman, the monkey god, and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” he told Modi.
Machchhar, who is married and has two children, has worked for FlyDubai for about four years, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before joining the airline, he spent 11 years with SpiceJet, an Indian low-cost carrier, where he served as a senior commander and line training captain. He logged more than 9,750 flying hours with SpiceJet.
Philip Kean, CEO of Mainland Air, the New Zealand flight school where Machchhar trained, said pilots are taught how to take over if a fellow crew member becomes incapacitated. But the training does not typically prepare them for a stabbing attack by a colleague, he told The Associated Press on Friday.
“I don’t think there’s much in the handbook for being stabbed,” Kean said.
“You’re friends and you’re flying together,” he said. “Nobody would expect … a person to have a go at you like that.”
___
Associated Press journalist Charlotte Graham-McLay in Wellington, New Zealand, contributed to this report.

title: Massabesic football’s defense stymies Noble
text:
WATERBORO — Mark it down. Massabesic High’s football team is a tough defensive nut to crack.
The Mustangs held high-powered Noble to one score, 28 rushing yards and 147 total yards, one week after the Knights scored 51 points and rushed for 381 yards against Marshwood. Massabesic sacked Noble quarterback Mark LaPointe four times and blocked a field goal.
That defense, plus a grinding offense powered by fullback Alex Harriman and two big-play scores, produced a 14-7 win Friday night, giving the Mustangs a 4-1 record in Class A South.
“It just starts with Day 1 in practice. If we’re physical on offense, it’s going to translate to defense,” said inside linebacker Nolan Pomerleau. “Me and Dustin (Maley) are awesome backers, but it’s the people up front that help us get so many tackles. And our secondary does its job. It’s 11 men trusting in each other.”
Noble slipped to 2-3. Defending state champ Thornton Academy (4-0) and Bonny Eagle (5-0) are chugging along, as usual, at the top of the league. Massabesic and South Portland (3-2), who meet next Friday, are in good positions to earn one of Class A South’s four playoff berths.
Noble’s uphill continues next week when it hosts Thornton.
“We move forward. We continue to work on what we do well, and we come out at Homecoming next week versus TA and give it our best shot and try to get a win and get back on the right track,” said Noble coach Keenon Blindow.
KEY PLAYS
Noble had three excellent chances to score. Early in the second quarter, the Knights had first-and-goal at the 5 but went backwards, as Maley stopped Knights running back Tristan Miniutti in the hole, Pomerleau ran down LaPointe for a 1-yard loss on a sweep, and Pomerleau’s twin brother, Gavin, sacked LaPointe. Tyler Gray’s 29-yard field goal was good but was nullified by an illegal block. Gray then missed from 39 yards.
In the third quarter, Massabesic turnovers gave Noble the ball in Mustangs territory at the 25 (four-and-out) and 33 (blocked field goal by Maley).
Massabesic took advantage of a break when its own poor punt skimmed off a Noble player and was recovered by Pomerleau near midfield. Harriman started to find some creases with four straight runs for 31 yards.
On a third-and-11, Ayden Kirk — who alternated throughout the game with Cooper Smith at quarterback — floated a high lob to the sideline. Gavin Jipson won a jump ball, then kept his balance and scored easily for a 25-yard touchdown that gave the Mustangs a 6-0 lead with 28 seconds left in the first half.
Massabesic upped its lead to 14-0 on a 75-yard sprint after a toss sweep to Maley in the third quarter, followed by a Kirk-to-Hunter Cormier 2-point conversion pass.
Noble’s defense was also strong, with end Jacob Provencher repeatedly making plays in the Mustangs’ backfield or right at the line. Getting inside linebackers Carter Ouellette and Caiden Barnes back from injury also helped fortify a group that gave up 52 points in its loss at Marshwood.
Noble scored with 10:53 to play on a 27-yard pass from LaPointe to Bryson McCormack, cutting the lead to 14-7.
After Massabesic chewed up seven minutes but botched a good chance to regain a two-score lead, Noble had a final possession with 2:58 to play. Three LaPointe completions moved the ball to midfield before Nolan Pomerleau and defensive end George Wehrman had consecutive sacks. On fourth-and-27, LaPointe’s scramble was stopped a yard short by Harriman.
“The mental toughness is definitely on our team,” Maley said. “We love to hit and we love to be physical, and I feel like that’s where we beat a lot of teams.”
STATISTICS
• Noble: Mark LaPointe (13 of 18 passing, 119 yards, TD; 10 carries, minus-12 yards), Tristan Miniutti (8 carries, 19 yards), Bryson McCormack (5 catches, 61 yards, TD)
• Massabesic: Alex Harriman (21 carries, 113 yards), Ayden Kirk (1 of 2 passing, 25 yards, TD, INT), Cooper Smith (2 of 2 passing, 13 yards), Dustin Maley (6 carries, 77 yards, 75-yard TD)

title: Obituary: Burton Wakeman Taylor Jr.
text:
CUNDY’S HARBOR – “Burr” Taylor died Sept. 19, 2026 at home in Cundy’s Harbor.
Born in Syracuse, N.Y., Burr grew up in Maine, started a family in Long Island, N.Y. and then happily moved back full-time to Harpswell. Burr was best known by his family for his blueberry pancakes and devil’s advocacy in all matters – sometimes more devilish, sometimes more advocate.
Burton Wakeman Taylor, Jr. was born April 8, 1939 to Claire May and Burton Wakeman Taylor. He attended school in Brunswick, worked at Skillins Boatyard on Orr’s Island, and set up some lobster traps for his parents’ dinners. He attended Deerfield Academy for high school where he joined the swim team yet pined for Maine. In short order, he attended Wesleyan University, married Frances Miller, volunteered for the draft and was honorably discharged from the Army, finished his BA and MAT and settled in Brookhaven, N.Y. In 1985, Burr married his longtime partner, Carol Duron.
In New York, Burr taught Social Studies and served as a representative for the teachers’ union at Middle Island School District. He became treasurer and general fixer/ problem solver for various justice-seeking, try-a-different-way organizations including Bay Community School, Bay Food Co-op, and South Country Peace Group. Each summer he sailed Downeast with Carol and they gardened and readied his parents’ cottage for four- season living.
Once a Maine resident again, Burr worked part-time at St. John’s School in Brunswick. He jumped into countless local organizations, working to understand the intricacies of state and local laws and regulations to best support and advocate for the preservation of the Maine waterfront and communities he loved and respected deeply. Among the organizations he volunteered with were: Harpswell Islands School and Harpswell Historical Society, Curtis Library, Beacon Schools Project, and Midcoast Hunger Prevention. He was on many local boards, including MidCoast Literacy Volunteers, and the Harpswell Harbor and Waterfront Committee, Heritage Land Trust, Planning Board, Conservation Commission, Historical Society, Budget Advisory Committee, Comprehensive Plan Implementation Committee and Cundy’s Harbor Fire Department.
Burr is survived by his wife, Carol Duron Taylor; children Brenda, Sam, and Amy; seven grandchildren; and two great-grandchildren.
Memories and condolences may be shared with family at http://www.FuneralAlternatives.net.
A private service will be held Summer of 2027.
To commemorate Burr, make a donation to the Cundy’s Harbor Fire Department, question authority and yourself, do a chore for someone else, consider others’ opinions.

title: NY governor says Cornell rape accuser was 'failed' by people obligated to protect her
text:
NY governor says Cornell rape accuser was 'failed' by people obligated to protect her
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Friday that the woman who accused members of a Cornell University fraternity of gang rape was “failed” by people obligated to protect her, including police and the county prosecutor.
Hochul’s claim came during a news conference in which she gave details on her decision to turn the case over to a special prosecutor, the state Attorney General Letitia James.
The governor said she made the decision after learning “troubling details” about how authorities have handled the woman’s claims thus far, including that the district attorney closed the case without having anyone interview the victim or anyone else involved in the alleged attack.
“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?" Hochul said. "This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”
She also assailed the Cornell University Police Department for not fully conveying the woman’s story to prosecutors.
“After this young woman came forward, she spoke to the police. She sat for hours and told them exactly what happened to her. And according to new reports, she could not have been clearer that she was 100% confident that she had been raped," the governor said. "Yet, shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors.”
Hochul said Thursday that she appointed James' office to oversee the case because she had lost faith in the local district attorney’s ability to handle it.
The investigation initially was closed without charges in 2024.
Last month, the woman filed a lawsuit and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation. He has since been bombarded by criticism that he abandoned the original investigation too quickly.
The attorney general will oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury, Hochul said.
“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued," she said in a statement Thursday.
Van Houten didn't immediately respond to Thursday messages seeking comment.
The case has roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about its response and the larger issue of how sexual assaults are handled on college campuses.
The woman, identified only as Jane Doe in court documents, told campus police in November of 2024 that she was sexually assaulted, then discussed it with the university’s internal investigators as part of Cornell’s disciplinary process.
The lawsuit against seven fraternity brothers, the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and others alleges that she was plied with drugs and alcohol, then subjected to sexual acts by a group of men while she was partially or entirely incapacitated. One of the men sent a social media message to other fraternity members alerting them to what was happening, and inviting people to take part, according to the lawsuit.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they participated in a sexual assault. One said his client hadn’t touched the woman. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful.
New York governors have turned to attorney generals to oversee important cases in the past.
In 2018, then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo appointed then-Nassau County District Attorney Madeline Singas as a special prosecutor to investigate Eric Schneiderman, who resigned as New York attorney general after women accused him of violent slapping, choking and other abuse.
In 2021, James oversaw a non-criminal investigation into sexual harassment allegations against then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo, leading to his resignation. Cuomo initially tried to choose who would lead the investigation into the allegations. He then allowed James to choose two independent attorneys to lead it instead.
James’ office also handles other criminal work and has the power under state law to investigate every death involving law enforcement in the state. But, typically, she can’t initiate criminal investigations without a referral from a local district attorney, the governor or a state agency, or an appointment like the one Hochul made Thursday.

title: Portland Trail Blazers fire new play-by-play broadcaster hours after hiring announced
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - The Portland Trail Blazers have fired newly hired play-by-play broadcaster Braiden Bell.
According to a statement from the team, Bell’s termination stemmed from social media posts that violated team and league policies about racist, sexist and harmful comments.
“The Portland Trail Blazers have zero tolerance for racist, sexist or harmful comments,” the team said with the announcement. “The play-by-play role carries a long legacy of excellence ... and we hold that standard without exception.”
Bell had been announced as the team’s new play-by-play announcer just hours before his firing.
“We did not meet our own bar in this process, and for that we apologize to Blazers fans and Rip City,” the team continued. “We will make sure that our new broadcaster reflects our values.”
Bell graduated from Arizona State University, where he called games for the basketball team.
Before his brief stint with the Trail Blazers, Bell also called games for California Baptist University, as well as being the play-by-play announcer for the Phoenix Mercury and working games in the NBA G League.
Bell said he was “deeply sorry” for the language that he used in previous posts on social media following his dismissal from the team.
“Those tweets, while wrong, were written by me 14 years ago while I was only 15 years old and have no reflection of who I am today. I do not take lightly any harm it causes now,” Bell’s message read. “I’d like to apologize to anyone who was hurt by my words and will continue to always treat people with kindness and respect.”
The 2026-27 NBA regular season begins on Oct. 20, with the Trail Blazers’ first preseason game scheduled for Oct. 7.
