title: Death Notice: Ruth Baker
Lewiston’s Alter L/A warming center prepares for winter, gets $300K grant
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In preparation for the colder months, MaineHousing has awarded over $300,000 to Alter L/A, Lewiston’s 24/7 warming center, which continues to work toward becoming a homeless shelter.
Alter L/A is one of 12 organizations MaineHousing donated upward of $2.7 million to across the state to prepare for the winter and rising heating costs, a recent news release said.
It’s the only warming center in the Twin Cities open 24/7. It’s been a service for the community over the last four years in various locations across Lewiston. The center receives money from the city to operate. Last year it served over 700 individuals, with a 24-hour average of 112 people.
The grant money will primarily go toward staffing, Kevin Boilard, the executive director, said Thursday.
“The intention is not just to house them, but to bring them in, make them warm and connect them to stability and the structure that most (people) are looking for,” Boilard said
Alter L/A is the only Lewiston-Auburn organization that received money through the grant.
The center at 70 Horton St. currently operates as a 24/7 warming and cooling center. Boilard and his organization received a license from the city in June to turn the former funeral home building into the city’s only 24-hour low-barrier homeless shelter, but necessary changes to the building and licensing requirements have delayed the effort.
Boilard said they continue to working toward opening as a full homeless shelter. To check off the final boxes toward the license, the center is adding showers and a sprinkler system that Boilard hopes to complete in the next two months to meet the Nov. 15 warming center opening date.
A warming center is different from a homeless shelter. A homeless shelter provides temporary housing among other services, while a warming center is meant to be a place for people to stop in to warm up, though Alter L/A is currently also providing some support services.
Lewiston has six shelters, including one for youth and another for victims of domestic violence, but none are open 24 hours a day and have a low barrier, as Alter L/A plans to have.
The money from MaineHousing comes as the cost of fuel to heat homes is high, and Boilard expects to see more sporadic drop-ins because of it. People may come in if they lose heat in their apartment or are not able to afford heat after prioritizing other important costs.
“The assumption that warming centers are for the unhoused battling drug addictions really works against the true realities of the conversations where people have roofs over their heads, but no heat in their homes,” Boilard said.
Boilard categorized the homelessness problem in the Lewiston and Auburn area as chronic.
Most individuals who visit the center do so in multiple stints, or for 12 months or more, said Boilard, who ran warming centers at other locations before Alter L/A. The average guest age is 52 years old, he said, and people can range in age up to their 80s.
Anyone can seek help at any point in their life, Boilard said, and he wanted people to know that Alter L/A offers more than just a space to get warm.
Last year, staff helped 40 people get connected to housing services, he said. The staff also try to connect individuals to primary health care providers and help them with paperwork necessary to obtain government support or a job.
“Often, they are looking for it, but they are disconnected from resources and it’s hard for them to see reality. Our goal is to bring that vision back to them and bring their hope back,” Boilard said.

title: Susan Collins should give an interview to ProPublica
text:
I was a longtime Auburn resident and used to be a Republican.
As reported recently by ProPublica, a serious and potentially career-ending allegation was made against Sen. Susan Collins. Did she illegally channel government contracts to a Hawaiian defense contractor that paid her campaign through a fake company it concocted to hide what it was doing?
Will Sen. Collins agree to do a town hall or an interview with the ProPublica journalists to discuss the facts and points detailed in the ProPublica reporting? It appears her response thus far has been to have her staff blow smoke and for Collins to shoot the messenger, i.e., the journalists at ProPublica. She has essentially taken a clue from our president and yelled “fake news.”
But, ProPublica is a respected reporting source dedicated to holding government representatives to account. It report that it has reviewed thousands of emails never previously revealed, and it has interviewed many persons close to the case who have corroborated much of the reporting. It has the receipts, unfortunately for Collins.
Why did her campaign staff agree to accept $150,000 from a shell company hiding the source as a government contractor?
On the face of it, the ProPublica article is damning to Collins. Other than repeating “fake news,” how can she defend herself? I have no idea. But, for the first time in over 25 years, the public should hear from her live and in person. She should meet with voters. Failing her agreement to do so, she should sit for a thorough interview with ProPublica. Mainers deserve to know, to paraphrase Richard M. Nixon, if their U.S. senator is a crook.
Daniel Mawhinney
Portland

title: El Niño expected to drive up the cost of coffee and some other foods
text:
(Gray News) - Economists expect some food costs could go up soon due to the near-record-strong super El Niño still strengthening in the Pacific Ocean.
El Niño is forecast to peak this fall and winter.
It’s expected to combine with pre-existing global supply chain pressures to drive up prices on tropical products. That includes things like coffee, chocolate, some fruits and nuts and palm oil.
According to Reuters, El Niño typically brings droughts in regions such as Southeast Asia, Australia and southern Africa and heavy rainfall in other parts of the world like the southern parts of South America and the United States. These conditions can impact various crops that grow in those areas, such as coffee beans and cacao.
El Niño comes at an already challenging time for food prices, given supply chain pressures from geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and Black Sea.

title: Obituary: Dorothy Claire (Freeman) Corkhill
text:
BRUNSWICK – Dorothy Claire (Freeman) Corkhill, 92, died peacefully Sept. 27, 2026 surrounded by her family after a period of declining health. She was a devoted wife, mother, grandmother, and friend whose life was marked by curiosity, generosity, and a deep love of family.
Dorothy was born Aug. 20, 1934 in Yonkers, N.Y., to Mary (Farrell) Freeman and Raymond Freeman. She graduated from Gorton High School and went on to receive her R.N. from Johns Hopkins University, followed by a B.S. in Nursing from Teachers College, Columbia University. After graduation, she worked as a public health nurse in Manhattan and was subsequently awarded a full scholarship to Boston University to pursue a master’s degree in nursing.
Dorothy met William “Bill” at a Fourth of July party in Quogue, Long Island, in 1963, where she and a friend took note of the affable, outgoing young man who was on a fishing trip with friends. They promptly dubbed him “the jolly fisherman.” Eight weeks later, on the night before Dorothy was to leave for Boston, Bill asked her to stay and marry him. She did, and that decision began a marriage of more than 60 years filled with love, laughter, adventure, and family.
Dorothy and Bill were married on Feb. 8, 1964, in Bronxville, N.Y., and settled in Sea Cliff, N.Y., where they raised their three children. After the birth of their first child, Dorothy chose to devote herself full-time to her family. She was a constant presence in the lives of her children, attending their many sporting events, music performances, dance recitals, and other pursuits.
In 1985, Dorothy and Bill painstakingly restored an old farmhouse on Merrymeeting Bay in Bowdoinham, Maine, working with talented local tradespeople and coming to cherish the slower pace, natural beauty, and people of Maine. When Bill retired in 1994, they moved to Maine full-time, settling in Mill Cove in Harpswell. There, their lives settled into a happy rhythm of travel, tennis, golf, reading, walking, boating, volunteering, time with friends, and an ever-growing family.
As two only children themselves, Dorothy and Bill were especially overjoyed by the growing family they created together. They found immense happiness in their grandchildren and took great interest in their individual personalities, pursuits, and accomplishments.
Books were a lifelong source of comfort and companionship for Dorothy. She had experienced the early, heartbreaking deaths of her young sister and baby brother. Reading became a constant in her life, providing both refuge and joy. She was particularly drawn to books about real people and events rather than fiction, reflecting her enduring interest in the world and the lives of others. She later shared that love of books with her community by volunteering at Curtis Memorial Library (often getting lost in the pages of the books she was supposed to be sorting for the library’s annual sale).
In her later years, Dorothy faced the challenges of Parkinson’s disease with quiet strength. In December 2025, Dorothy and Bill moved to Thornton Hall in Brunswick, where Dorothy was lovingly cared for by Bill and the wonderful staff there. She spent the final months of her life in hospice care.
Her family is deeply grateful to CHANS Hospice and to everyone at Thornton Hall for the compassion, dignity, and kindness they showed Dorothy and her family during this time. They are also grateful for the many friends and neighbors who were part of their lives and offered friendship, kindness, and support, especially in the later years.
Dorothy is survived by her husband, Bill; her son, William Corkhill, Jr., of Wellesley, Mass., his wife, Sheila, and their children, Fiona, Willie, Iain, and Duncan; daughter, Lee Corkhill, of Portland, her partner, Rushmore DeNooyer, and her son, Charlie Graffius; and daughter, Monica Davis, of Bar Harbor, her husband, Scott, and their children, Simon and Ella.
Dorothy’s family will remember her for her warmth, quiet strength, faith, wit, and devotion to those she loved. They will also remember the remarkable partnership she shared with Bill. Dorothy will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered by all who were fortunate enough to have known her.
A private family service will be held. Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.funeralalternatives.net.
In lieu of flowers, donations in Dorothy’s memory may be made to Curtis Memorial Library in Brunswick, Maine, or CHANS Hospice in gratitude for the care and comfort they provided to Dorothy and her family.

title: Maine credit unions kick off $100K challenge to support hunger relief
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine credit unions are seeking to raise $100,000 this month to help fund 200,000 healthy meals for people in need across the state.
Anyone can donate to the seventh annual Ending Hunger Challenge, including individuals and businesses, and credit union membership is not required.
“Maine credit unions always step up when our neighbors need help,” said Elise Baldacci, president of the Westbrook-based Maine Credit Union League.
The campaign kickoff comes a few months after credit unions donated $100,000 to Good Shepherd Food Bank through another initiative.
“Demand for food assistance continues to grow and every donation our campaign receives this month will help put food on the table for more people in need,” Baldacci noted.
Food insecurity remains a serious concern across Maine, with 14.5% of households struggling to consistently put food on the table. Maine also has New England’s highest rate of childhood food insecurity.
Funds raised in October will support hunger-relief efforts across Maine, with 25% of online donations directly benefiting Good Shepherd Food Bank. The remaining funds will support local food pantries, meal programs, schools and other organizations.
“I’m incredibly proud of the way Maine’s credit unions carry out our ‘people helping people’ philosophy through this campaign,” Baldacci said. “They see the impact of hunger in their communities every day, and that makes this work personal.”
How to donate
Those interested in donating can make an online contribution at www.campaignforendinghunger.org or check with any credit union branch.

title: Houlton council candidate wants to balance town services with affordability
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Houlton man who was Town Council chairman when he termed out two years ago brings a business focus as he runs to continue his work on the council.
Chris Robinson, 60, who has served as the sales manager for Carroll’s Auto Sales in Presque Isle for nearly two decades, is seeking a three-year seat as a declared write-in candidate.
“I thought I was fairly effective the last time I was a councilor and chair and because of that I thought I could do it again,” Robinson said. “There were some key deciding votes I made as chair.”
Also on the ballot for the one of three open three-year terms are councilors Sue Tortello and J.J. Schools. Declared write-in Matt Carr is also vying for the seat.
Coming in on the heels of a two-year period of upheaval, with multiple town managers leaving the post, Robinson believes that with a strong council and a strong town manager things can be leveled out and corrected.
“We need to be able to find a balance between administering goods and services and attending to the people who pay the taxes,” he said. “It’s a hard, hard thing.”
An increasing demand for town services alongside a large number of residents on fixed incomes is a big challenge. Take for example, if you have a retired couple on a fixed income and their property assessment keeps going up or their taxes keep going up, their monthly income doesn’t. The number one priority is “budgeting the budget,” trying to find the balance between goods and services and taxpayer burden.
“If you budget the budget the rest all fall in line,” he said.
Robinson said that the spending decisions cannot be short-sighted, giving the example of small county towns deciding to eliminate essential services like police. Washburn is one such town that did so, and now is patrolled alternately by sheriff’s deputies and Maine State Police.
People often don’t realize what happens when you do that, Robinson said. That expense may no longer be in the town budget, but the county tax increases because the Aroostook County Sheriff’s office now covers the town.
Robinson, who describes himself as an advocate for taxpayers and a strong police department, does not favor eliminating police because “there will be more problems than ever.”
“It’s a very complicated web we weave here,” Robinson said. “And every little thing we do affects part of it. It goes back to everybody wanting goods and services but can’t afford to pay for it.”
For example, he pointed to a diminishing population base and dwindling school enrollment, and wonders if the town is at a level where there needs to be serious talk of school consolidation.
The most important issues for the town to address are the budget, affordable housing and homelessness, Robinson said.
“Affordable housing — what’s the rent in Houlton, $1,000 or $1,500?” he asked. “That’s more than a mortgage.”
The housing issue and homelessness tie together, and town leaders have to examine it. They shouldn’t ignore it, he said.
Robinson, who has served multiple terms on the council, said he absolutely believes in term limits. It’s the right thing because it forces change and other people to come forward, he said.
“I believe in the charter that was created, [which says] after two consecutive three-year terms you have to get off for two years,” he said. “I am a strong believer in that system.”
Robinson holds a bachelor of science in environmental studies from the University of Maine System and lives in Houlton with his wife, Vicki. They have two daughters. He also runs a nonprofit, Wilderness Walk for Warriors, with his brother.
“My hands are full, but I always feel like part of me wants to try and give back, and [that’s[ why we started the nonprofit,” Robinson said. “I like giving back.”

title: This family bought a Bangor home after 15 years of renting in the city
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This story is part of the BDN’s Home Buying series that shares stories of Mainers who became homeowners despite the state’s volatile real estate market. Want to share your experience buying a home in Maine? Email kobrien@bangordailynews.com.
After more than a decade of renting in Bangor, this couple decided it was time to buy a home when they realized rental prices were equal to, or more than, what monthly mortgage payments would be.
LaRae LaBouff and her husband, Jordan, were preparing to return home to Bangor in July after traveling for six months during his sabbatical from work. They had given up their apartment while traveling and planned to stay with friends while searching for a new unit to rent, as they had for the last 15 years.
However, their plans changed when they realized Bangor rents were equal to or more than what a mortgage payment would be, LaRae LaBouff said.
“Rather than take that risk of renting from someone else, the price going up and maybe having to move again, we decided that it was time to go ahead and buy a house,” she said.
The couple’s decision points to how rental prices in Bangor have risen significantly in recent years to the point where buying property can be more advantageous for those who are looking to put down roots and can handle the upfront costs, even though home prices have soared as well.
A housing study performed in Bangor last year found median rental fees in the city rose by $110 from 2020 to 2022 when they had jumped by only $80 over the seven years prior to that. Today, average rental prices for a unit in Bangor have surpassed $1,500 a month, according to Zillow.
The family also decided to pursue homeownership when they noticed the market shifting to favor buyers rather than sellers, as had been the case for years since the pandemic when prices shot up and availability was slim.
Now, home prices have remained steady in recent months and Maine saw healthy inventory through much of the summer and into the fall. This gives prospective buyers more choices and the leverage to negotiate more favorable prices and agreement terms.
“That’s one of the reasons why I said we should go ahead and do this now is because I knew that markets are volatile and things change really quickly,” LaRae LaBouff said.
The family looked for only a few weeks before finding their future home, which is tucked away in the lower portion of Bangor’s Little City neighborhood. However, LaRae LaBouff said she had been browsing Zillow in her free time for about two years despite not being interested in buying.
Built in 1880, the 1,700-square-foot house fit the couple’s size needs, as they didn’t want a home larger than 2,000 square feet, she said. They also wanted three bedrooms and a spacious backyard that was preferably already fenced in, so their dog could have space to run without a leash. The home even has a deck, which was on the couple’s wish list.
“We got exactly what we wanted,” LaRae LaBouff said. “It just turned out to be the right time for the sellers and us.”
Their realtor and a trusted friend guided them on a virtual tour of the home while they were out of town and pointed out any appealing features as well as anything that would need to be addressed immediately.
The family closed on July 13, two days after they returned to Bangor, and began moving in that day, LaRae LaBouff said.
It was listed in late May for just under $275,000 and the couple snatched it up less than two months later for $267,500, well below their $300,000 limit.
The home last sold in 2015 for $112,500 before it was listed again in July 2024 for nearly $280,000, according to Zillow records. It bounced on and off the market for roughly the same price for several months until the LaBouffs found it.
The family previously bought a home in Waco, Texas, in 2007, which they owned for nearly a decade before moving to Maine. This is their first time owning a house in Maine.
Aside from the space the property offers, LaRae LaBouff said she and her husband were drawn to the home’s layout and the touches of character that can be found in a nearly 150-year-old building, such as crown and baseboard moulding.
Meanwhile, Jordan LaBouff was drawn to the home’s “warm and welcoming” atmosphere as well as the entryway and staircase, he said. The family is also looking forward to cooking in the large kitchen and hosting friends and family in the dining room.
“I also realized recently that it looks a little bit like the Anne of Green Gables house on Prince Edward Island,” LaRae LaBouff said. “It just felt like our style.”
For those who are interested in becoming homebuyers soon, LaRae LaBouff recommended finding an experienced and trustworthy real estate agent to work with.
“They’re going to be able to give you information and advice that you might otherwise not even think about,” she said. “If you tell them exactly what you’re looking for, they know the market really well and can help you find something that you may not be able to find on your own.”

title: Trial set to decide whether undue influence was used in making Maine man's will
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — A two-day trial is scheduled for next month on the request of the daughter of a deceased Washington man who wants the Knox County Probate Court to remove the personal representative of her late father’s estate.
Cynthia MacPherson of Middleboro, Massachusetts, has asked the court to remove Kristen Redman as the personal representative of the estate of her late father, Robert Allen Hanson, who died July 20, 2025, at the age of 90. Hanson had lived in both Washington and Warren.
MacPherson hired a lawyer who filed a petition in August 2025 to remove Redman as the personal representative of her father’s estate. She has argued that the Searsmont woman used undue influence on him in the final months of his life to benefit herself.
Redman has said she did nothing wrong.
Probate Judge Carol Emery has scheduled a hearing on the motion on Nov. 17 and 18.
There is a medium probability of a settlement, according to Emery’s scheduling order.
The issues to be heard at the hearing are whether the will is valid, whether undue influence was involved, the disposition of the estate, the accounting of estate assets, and the final administration and distribution of the estate.
The daughter’s lawyer plans to call five witnesses and Redman’s lawyer plans to call six witnesses.
“The current Personal Representative used undue influence on Decedent (Hanson) to have herself named as Personal Representative. The Last Will and Testament was executed only 11 days prior to Decedent’s death and lists the Personal Representative and an acquaintance of hers as one-third beneficiaries of his estate, despite not knowing either of these individuals well. Upon information and belief, the current Personal Representative has mismanaged decedent’s assets under a power of attorney prior to decedent’s death and has acted in her self-interest to convey estate assets to herself knowing that her actions are not benefiting the estate,” stated the petition filed last year from attorney Catherine Gamache on behalf of the daughter.
Hanson’s estate is valued at up to $250,000, based on the filing fee in the estate file.
Hanson signed a document on Feb. 19, 2025, that gave Redman a limited power of attorney and to serve as his agent, according to a document filed in the Knox County Registry of Deeds. Hanson sold his home in Washington on April 4, 2025.
Hanson signed a will on July 9, 2025, that named Redman, MacPherson, and William Bernardo Jr. of Warren as equal beneficiaries of his estate.
MacPherson said in a telephone interview last year that she was unaware that her father had signed a power of attorney with anyone or named Redman to be the personal representative of his estate until after her father died. She questioned why Redman was in the will and also asked why Bernardo, who she said Redman had arranged to help with Hanson’s move, was named in the will. The daughter said Redman had her name put on Hanson’s bank accounts prior to his death.
Redman said she had no idea that she was included in Hanson’s will until after his death. She also denied having any role in Bernardo being named in the will.
Redman said she helped Hanson out after his wife died because the wife had always paid the bills. She said Hanson and his wife had taken out a home equity loan and Hanson had not been making payments. She helped him write the checks so that he would not lose the home.
What makes this matter more unusual is that Redman has been listed in two other wills to serve as personal representatives of estates for people who are not related to her.
When contacted last year by the Midcoast Villager, retired Register of Probate Elaine Hallett, who served in the office for 45 years, said she can not recall any instance in which a non-relative, who wasn’t an attorney, had been personal representative over more than one estate at a time. There is no legal prohibition on serving as personal representatives on multiple estates at the same time.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: In a 99-cent AriZona Iced Tea can, echoes of childhood autonomy and fleeting freedoms
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Four quarters used to buy a can of AriZona Iced Tea. You’d crack it open and savor the artificially flavored, high-fructose-corn-syrup-sweetened drink between fits of giggling on the walk home from school.
For some, the can symbolized childhood autonomy. It was among the first solo purchases a kid made or a reward for satisfactorily completed chores.
With inflation, a 99-cent thirst-quencher is a matter of nostalgia for adults with matured beverage tastes. An AriZona “tallboy” — the printed price on the can serving as a measuring stick for the value of a dollar — remains especially affordable and instructive for American youth with allowance, disposable income from part-time wages or birthday money.
Founded in 1992, AriZona Beverage Company first launched drinks in Brooklyn, New York. The 99-cent cans launched in 1997. Popularity — and profitability — of the drink came soon after. But it was the price sticker that promoted a kind of utilitarianism — a warning to shop owners looking for a higher profit margin.
Countless American preteens and teenagers across class have paired AriZona drinks with their bagged snack of choice and candy — a trifecta downed before reaching the front door and discovering … dinner. Allowance and childhood disposable income, however, have never been universal. Some could count on receiving a few dollars irregularly or not at all.
Still, when most other prices went up, the AriZona drink’s price permanence was something that didn’t necessitate debit cards or parental approval. Coins and dollar bills sweetened the experience of forging friendships on the journey home.
Just who gets the privilege of experiencing money as freedom makes the AriZona can more than just a bodega staple. It shows how much culture can be concealed in ordinary consumer transactions.
On Feb. 26, 2012, 17-year-old Trayvon Martin left the gated residential community in Sanford, Florida, where his father lived en route to a 7-Eleven. The hoodie-wearing Black teenager was filmed on surveillance purchasing a watermelon-flavored AriZona drink and a pack of Skittles. When he discovered he was being tailed by a neighborhood watch volunteer, Trayvon confronted him. The teen didn’t survive the encounter; George Zimmerman shot him in the chest.
The AriZona drink and Skittles became evidence in a homicide investigation, and soon after became one of the earliest protest symbols in the Black Lives Matter movement sparked by Zimmerman’s acquittal. More than 13 years later, some still associate these items with questions of who in the U.S. is truly free to move through public spaces without being regarded as suspicious.
____
Aaron Morrison is the race and ethnicity news editor at AP. This story is part of a recurring series, “ American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. For more stories on the anniversary, click here.

title: Rescue dog gets job helping children
text:
Rescue dog gets a special job helping children
Meet Hanalei, a certified therapy dog and rescue, joining a Treasure Coast nonprofit in its work helping child victims of sexual exploitation and trafficking. 
Rescue dog gets a special job helping children
Meet Hanalei, a certified therapy dog and rescue, joining a Treasure Coast nonprofit in its work helping child victims of sexual exploitation and trafficking. 
A Florida nonprofit is adding a new four-legged resource to its work helping child victims of sexual exploitation and trafficking.
Video above: Dog missing for 30 days rescued from storm drain
Catch the Wave of Hope is an anti-exploitation and anti-trafficking organization focused on awareness, education and survivor support. The organization works with children, parents, law enforcement, and other community professionals while also connecting survivors with therapy and other resources.
Now, Hanalei, a certified therapy dog, is joining that effort. Hanalei was rescued from Big Dog Ranch Rescue at 3 months old. She is a Labrador-Boxer mix and will turn two in November.
Sarah Marie Henry, the executive director, is Hanalei's owner and handler.
"We have just kind of heard this overwhelming need for more therapeutic options, especially for children," Henry said.
Hanalei will work with children at the Treasure Coast Child Advocacy Center, where some children go through the forensic interview process. She will also be available during therapy sessions and potentially during court proceedings.
"She is there to be a support to really help them feel safe and comforted," Henry said.
Henry said Hanalei was a natural fit for the role because she has always responded well to children. She was trained and assessed before becoming certified through the Alliance of Therapy Dogs.
Henry said children have already responded positively to Hanalei, including children with different learning disabilities.
"It's almost instilled in them that she knows and is excited to see them and really gets down on their level and is just available," she said.
Hanalei is also a rescue, something Henry said gives her story another meaningful connection to the children she serves.
"I think that she just has a different understanding because of where she came from and what she's overcome to now be here," Henry said.
The organization plans to add two more therapy dogs, with one already in the process.
For Henry, the goal is to give children another source of comfort as they work through difficult experiences.
"She'll be there to help encourage communication when kids are having a harder time articulating what maybe happened to them," she said.
And while the work can be difficult, Henry said the message behind Hanalei's role is simple:
"What's happened has happened, but there is hope," she said.
Catch the Wave of Hope has a list of educational resources on their website, along with ways for people to seek help.
People can also follow Hanalei's journey through an Instagram page.

title: Jay-based school district sees rise in special education referrals
text:
JAY — Regional School Unit 73 is seeing greater demand for special education services, particularly among prekindergarten and kindergarten students, with 340 districtwide.
Special Services Director Cherie Parker told the RSU 73 board of directors Sept. 24 that the district has 26 open referrals for special education evaluation, including 19 at Spruce Mountain Primary School in Livermore.
The number of students receiving special education services has increased by 11 since the start of the school year. The primary school serves 90 students, also an increase of 11, and accounts for much of the districtwide growth.
Parker said prekindergarten and kindergarten students account for much of the increase in referrals.
“The scary part is we’ve had such an influx of referrals at this age group, they’ve assigned us a second case manager,” Parker said. “So, it’s definitely a high-need group.”
Spruce Mountain Elementary School in Jay has 72 students with individualized education programs, while the Spruce Mountain Middle School in Jay has 74 and Spruce Mountain High School, also in Jay, has 104. Fourteen students with individualized education programs are placed in day treatment programs or special-purpose private schools outside the district.
The district also has several open special education positions, including an educational technician II at the high school, a special education social worker serving kindergarten through grade 5 and a half-time educational technician I supporting prekindergarten students.
Parker said contracted remote special education teachers are providing case management and supporting staff working directly with students.
“This year has started off to be a challenge for many of our staff members, veteran or novice, pre-K to grade 12,” Parker said.

title: A closer look at the candidates for the Portland City Council District 5 race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A crowded field has emerged to take Councilor Kate Sykes’ place in Portland’s District 5, which includes Riverton and portions of North Deering.
The Portland Press Herald spoke to each candidate ahead of the Nov. 3 election to ask why they are running and what their priorities are.
This is the third of three previews for Portland City Council races. Read the preview of the at-large race here, and the preview of the District 4 race here. Early voting in the state of Maine begins Oct. 5. For polling locations, or to request an absentee ballot, go to portlandmaine.gov/elections-voting.
MICHAEL TODD CHRETIEN
Michael Todd Chretien has some ambitious goals. He’s knocked on 2,500 doors so far, and wants to get to 4,000. Part of his campaign platform calls for producing 5,000 new housing units in the next five years in order to build a tax base to sustain a growing city.
Chretien, 57, lives on outer Washington Avenue. He’s a Spanish interpreter for Portland schools, and runs an organic farm.
On the campaign trail, he said District 5’s diverse mix of seniors, young families and new Mainers have pride in Portland. But they’re concerned about rising property taxes and the cost of housing.
He believes climate change and other factors will lead to a “bloom of growth” over the next few years, and Portland needs to be ready.
“Either we figure out how to plan a city that’s affordable, welcoming and safe and secure for everybody, or we’re going to become a city of haves and have-nots,” he said.
In 2025, Chretien served as co-chair of the Maine Democratic Socialists of America, and has been endorsed by Troy Jackson, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate. He also has the support of the councilor he hopes to succeed.
When residents tell him property taxes are “getting out of control,” he responds that Portland is getting “taken to the cleaners” by the state of Maine’s school funding formula, and he wants officials to press the Legislature to change that.
On housing, Chretien said officials need to do a better job coordinating with developers in order to get new housing built. When asked if the current inclusionary zoning policy, which requires that large developments include at least 25% affordable units, should be reconsidered, he said he’s “open for negotiations.”
As long as new development includes workforce and affordable housing, he’s in favor of market-rate and luxury units as well, he said.
Chretien works out of the school department’s central office on Cumberland Avenue and frequently sees Portland’s issues with homelessness and substance use. Due to the location of the city-run homeless shelter off Riverside Street, he said District 5 residents are also more in tune with the problem, which he believes has reached a “crisis” level.
But, he said, city staff and social service programs are doing “an incredible job holding back an economic tide of poverty.”
“What we see on the street is a small number of people in open crisis. But what we don’t often see are the thousands of people who have gotten to recovery or to a shelter and then found a place to live,” he said.
Chretien thinks the city can maintain its needle exchange policies while also having “zero tolerance” for needles on the streets. He’s “not against” using involuntary commitment to remove people from the streets, but doesn’t believe removing chronically homeless people from downtown will suddenly bring businesses back.
He said the combination of remote work and where people live has changed downtowns, and the city needs housing and jobs to rebuild community.
“There are some signs of life,” he said. “It’s in a tough spot right now, we can have policies that bring development back, bring businesses back, and help the people living on our streets to get the help they need.”
JAKOBI DELGADO
If successful this November, Jakobi Delgado would be the youngest person ever elected to the City Council.
Delgado, a Portland High School graduate and economics student at the University of Southern Maine, turns 19 this month. But he doesn’t believe his age should impact how voters view him.
“I care equally about the young people in my district as I do about the retired people struggling to live off Social Security,” he said. “I may be the youngest person on the ballot, but that doesn’t make me any less qualified to represent them.”
When he’s not studying, Delgado manages a Dollar Tree. While others his age pursue a range of hobbies, his is politics and being involved in the community.
When asked what he’s hearing from residents, he said concerns over property taxes and public safety.
“People can not take any more property tax increases,” he said, adding that District 5 has the largest proportion of working-class homeowners in the city. “They’ve been pushed to the limit.”
Delgado said he won’t vote for a budget that raises taxes, and would “work day and night” on the budget to scale back or condense programs.
He agrees with Mayor Mark Dion’s recent proposal to work with the county to establish a secure treatment sentencing option.
“I’ve had family members who dealt with addiction and it takes control of you,” he said. “Sometimes as a society we need to step in and say you’re no longer medically able to make a decision.”
He also favors Dion’s proposal to ban standing in certain medians.
As a college student, he said Portland needs solutions to the high cost of housing, and said early career jobs don’t pay enough to afford the average apartment in the city.
Referring to Chretien’s goal of producing 5,000 new housing units, Delgado said, “I think the job of a councilor is to create the environment for housing to be built.” That means streamlining permitting, he said.
When asked what he’d change about how government operates, he said he’d add a sixth council district in the city and remove an at-large seat. He believes the number of at-large seats means the council often gets caught up in national politics rather than addressing the things that directly impact residents.
He said in his experience, city councilors are not approachable.
“My goal is to be the most approachable on the council,” he said.
KEVIN GARDELLA
Kevin Gardella has lived in Portland for 27 years, and while he recognizes the city’s housing crisis, he has mixed feelings about a changing Portland.
He called the coming 30-story Old Port Square tower on Union Street “loathsome” and said ReCode has given the planning board “carte blanche” to approve projects that are out of character with the city.
To address affordability, Gardella believes underutilized buildings and vacant office space should be redeveloped into affordable housing, and the city should make it easier to build accessory dwelling units.
He’s hearing the same concerns about homelessness and public safety, both downtown and in District 5 areas near Riverside Street, and over rising property taxes.
Voters tell him there’s “a lot of waste going on” and he agrees with them.
“It’s gotten worse and they kind of want to see some accountability and some new approaches,” he said.
He previously described himself as “socially liberal and fiscally concerned.”
Like Delgado, he agrees with forcing certain people into a secure detox facility when appropriate, but recognizes the wide range of needs among the unhoused in Portland. He’d like to see more healthcare professionals on the streets to ensure that basic health needs are met.
He praised the city and its operation at the Homeless Services Center on Riverside Street, which he toured recently.
“I was very impressed by the level of care,” he said.
Gardella, 49, has worked the majority of his life in eldercare, but is currently helping to open a health practice. He ran for the school committee in 2006 but lost.
While going door-to-door, he’s tried to seek out neighbors who might be more conservative in order to get a “better cross section” of views.
He said his two “non-negotiables” are opposing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and police surveillance, and above all he wants officials to do a better job representing constituents.
“Currently, I do not see City Hall representing constituents,” he said.
ILMA LÓPEZ
Ilma López and her family live in the Riverton neighborhood, but as the co-owner of two downtown restaurants, she’s intimately aware of the challenges facing small-business owners due to the economy and public safety factors.
Last week, her West End restaurant Ugly Duckling was vandalized and broken into while staff were still there. In an Instagram post following the incident, López said, “This is not okay. And it cannot be something we simply learn to accept. We can have compassion and still expect accountability.”
She said this week that the ordeal reinforced what she has been speaking with voters about: the need for enforcement and accountability.
“(There’s) a lack of clear consequences,” she said, adding that Portland’s government entities are working separately rather than together to solve the city’s problems.
As a business owner, she said it’s often difficult to believe that all city councilors “have our back.” She said it often feels like Portland business owners are viewed as “privileged” but said 80% of small businesses are struggling.
López said her restaurants “kill it in the summer” but that it’s the result of a lot of hard work, and then the reality of increased costs, social issues and winter set in. She said customers tell her they’re now avoiding certain areas because of the homelessness issue. Her businesses now leave the lights on overnight.
“No one deserves to be on the street,” she said, but she believes Portland and the county need to cater services to better help unhoused people find stability and jobs.
López, 44, was born and raised in Venezuela but has lived in Portland for 14 years. She has children in Portland schools, and hears the concerns over city and school budgets and taxes.
“For the money we’re spending, it’s not fair,” she said. “My kids’ teachers have second jobs.”
When asked about the housing crisis, López said the city should be more mindful of where projects are placed and its communication with neighborhoods. Referring to Belfort Landing in Riverton, she said, “I don’t think the neighborhood had a fighting chance to say something.”
She also called Chretien’s 5,000-unit goal “unattainable,” and similar to Gardella, believes there needs to be a mix between new buildings and redeveloping underused property.
“Portland is not broken, it just needs some tweaks,” she said. “I always tell my kids, ‘You have a voice, use it.’ Stand up for what you think is right. That’s why I’m running. I plan to do what’s right.”

title: Friday’s high school football: Oxford Hills tops Lewiston, stays unbeaten
text:
Toby Oufiero passed for three touchdowns and ran for another, leading Oxford Hills to a 35-6 win over Lewiston in a Class A North football game Friday night in Lewiston.
After a scoreless first quarter, the Vikings (4-0) took control with three touchdowns in the second, starting with a 6-yard run by Keegan Ridley. That score was set up by Gunner Truman’s 49-yard reception on third-and-13 on the opening play of the quarter.
Oufiero then threw a 15-yard TD pass to Truman and a 21-yarder to Tucker Hilden, giving the Vikings a 21-0 halftime lead.
Oufiero’s third TD pass was a 16-yard to Carter Davis. The Vikings’ quarterback put running time into effect with a 6-yard touchdown run late in the third quarter.
Lewiston (0-5) scored on a 69-yard run by Kevin Mahon in the fourth quarter.
ORONO 36, SPRUCE MOUNTAIN 34: The Red Riots (2-3) stopped the Phoenix (3-2) on a two-point conversion with 18 seconds left to secure an eight-man football victory in Orono.
Spruce Mountain scored on a 34-yard pass from Dylan Jewett to Levi Richards, but Orono pressured Jewett on the conversion attempt and the ball slipped out of the Phoenix quarterback’s hands.
Orono took a 36-28 lead with less than two minutes to play on Cooper Brown’s 2-yard pass to Eli Schaff on fourth down. That was Brown’s second fourth-down TD pass of the game. In the third quarter, he tossed a 17-yarder to Richie Watson on fourth-and-long.
Brown and Eli Schaff connected on a 5-yard touchdown in the third, and Watson ran for two scores in the first half.
Jewett scored two touchdowns for Spruce Mountain, a 75-yard kickoff return and an 18-yard run, and he threw two TD passes, both to Richards. Owen Kelvey scored the Phoenix’s other touchdown on a 9-yard run.

title: Marquee field hockey matchup between Mt. Ararat and Camden Hills suspended by rain
text:
ROCKPORT — It’s one of the season’s most intriguing field hockey matchups, but it will have to wait.
The matchup between Mt. Ararat and Camden Hills, two of the top contenders in Class A North, was suspended Friday after a scoreless quarter because of rain. The plan is for the game to be resumed at a date to be determined, depending on officials’ availability.
Rain began drenching the field in Rockport five minutes into the game, sparking concerns about player safety. On one of Camden Hills’ four corners, the player inserting the ball fell on her follow through because of the slippery ground.
“We were really excited to play and have a good game and see what we could put together,” Mt. Ararat coach Krista Chase said. “(But) we want to play a good game with them, and keep everybody safe and be able to showcase both teams. It’s always harder to do that in the rain and the wet.”
Mt. Ararat is 8-0 and ranked fourth in the Varsity Maine Top 10. Camden Hills is 9-1 and ranked sixth in the Varsity Maine poll, but first in the Class A North Heal point standings, two spots ahead of Mt. Ararat.

title: Obituary: Joanna “Jo” Tibby
text:
MOUNT VERNON – Joanna “Jo” Tibby, 82, died unexpectedly at her home in Mount Vernon, Maine, on August 3, 2026.
Born Jan. 27, 1944, in Washington, D.C., Jo grew up in Port Washington, NY, with her parents John and Emily, her sister, Ellen, and brother, William “Wil”. After high school, her life took her to many places, including New York City, California, Montreal, Vermont, and abroad before she eventually found her way to Maine. When Jo arrived here, she told people she knew she had “come home.” Jo spent more than half of her life in Mount Vernon, with the help of neighbors and friends, she designed and built the house that became her home.
There is no short obituary that can hold an entire 82-year life—the places traveled, work done, meals prepared, causes supported, cats rescued, friendships made, and all the ordinary moments that become precious once someone is gone. What remains are the stories, the connections, and the many traces of a life lived across many places before Jo found the place she called home.
Jo’s working life was wonderfully varied. She worked in bookstores and restaurants, ran a small graphic arts print shop, dispatched ambulances, baked bread and desserts, and worked as a conductor on the Belfast and Moosehead Lake Railroad. Her travels and many occupations became part of the long and interesting path that eventually brought her home to Mount Vernon.
Jo also gave her time and talents to the community around her. She helped develop Neighbors Driving Neighbors and designed its icon. She participated in Mount Vernon’s Community Partnership Corporation and its work toward affordable senior housing. Again and again, as a neighbor and friend, she offered support, transportation, diabetes education, a warm listening presence, and with the years the increasingly thoughtful observations she called “quack therapy” and others called wisdom. At Bearnstow, where she was a longtime member of the community, Jo served as a local liaison, helped with publicity, and prepared family-style meals during the summer season. She helped bring Bearnstow dancers to Mt. Vernon’s annual early summer crafts fair and helped make it a parade.
Perhaps one of the most enduring parts of Jo’s legacy is her love for cats. Cats in need found a friend in Jo. She rescued homeless cats, cared for them, and worked to find them safe and loving homes. Her home on Bean Road became part of that effort, and over the years cats who might otherwise have been without a home were given another chance because Jo was willing to help. Those cats went on to become beloved companions in other homes and families. In that way, Jo’s kindness to them traveled farther than she may ever have known. Every cat she helped rescue and every home she helped find became another small continuation of something she cared deeply about. Jo leaves behind her own beloved feline family, Honeylee, Sullivan “Sully,” and Phoebe. They, too, are part of Jo’s story.
Jo is remembered by her sister, Ellen; her brother, Wil and his longtime partner Gaye; and the many friends, neighbors, and members of the Mount Vernon and Bearnstow communities whose lives crossed paths with hers.
Jo’s inspirational spirit lives on. Celebrating Jo’s Life – Family, friends, neighbors, and community members are invited to gather in remembrance of Jo on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026, from 12 to 2 p.m. at the Mount Vernon Community Center, Main Street, Mount Vernon, Maine.
Those wishing to honor Jo’s memory with a donation are invited to consider:
PALS in Manchester, Maine or
any no-kill animal shelter Helping another cat find safety, care, and a home would be a meaningful way to carry forward a part of Jo’s legacy

title: How to make Food Network Magazine’s brownie chunk cookies
text:
How to make Food Network Magazine’s brownie chunk cookies
Looking for a fun way to get kids into the kitchen this fall? Food Network Magazine’s new cookbook, The Big, Fun Kids Cookie Book, features more than 100 easy recipes created with young bakers in mind.
Editorial director Maile Carpenter demonstrated one of the cookbook’s featured recipes: brownie chunk cookies.
The recipe puts a twist on a classic chocolate chip cookie by swapping the chocolate chips for pieces of fudgy brownies. Carpenter said store-bought brownies work just fine, or families can use leftover homemade brownies.
The cookies take about 30 minutes of active preparation and make approximately 16 cookies.
Carpenter said recipes like this can help children build confidence in the kitchen because the ingredients and steps are simple. Parents can also involve kids in measuring ingredients, stirring in the brownie pieces and adding extra chunks to the tops of the cookies.
Brownie Chunk Cookies
Active time: 30 minutes
Total time: 1 hour, 15 minutes, plus cooling
Makes: About 16 cookies
Ingredients
- 2 ¼ cups all-purpose flour
- 1 teaspoon salt
- ¾ teaspoon baking soda
- 2 sticks unsalted butter, at room temperature
- ¾ cup packed light brown sugar
- ¾ cup granulated sugar
- 2 large eggs, at room temperature
- 1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
- 2 ½ cups cubed fudgy brownies, cut into approximately ½-inch cubes
Directions
- Whisk together the flour, salt and baking soda in a medium bowl.
- In a large bowl, combine the butter, brown sugar and granulated sugar. Beat with a mixer on medium speed until light and fluffy, about 5 minutes. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then beat in the vanilla.
- Reduce the mixer speed to low and beat in the flour mixture until combined. Stir in 1 cup of the brownie cubes with a wooden spoon.
- Position racks in the upper and lower thirds of the oven and preheat to 400 degrees. Line three baking sheets with parchment paper.
- Scoop ¼ cupfuls of dough onto one baking sheet. Press the remaining 1 ½ cups of brownie cubes into the tops of the cookies, flattening them slightly. Refrigerate the cookies until firm, about 20 minutes.
- Divide and space the cookies among the prepared baking sheets, placing five or six cookies on each sheet.
- Bake two pans at a time, switching the pans halfway through, until the cookies are golden brown around the edges and set in the centers, 12 to 16 minutes.
- Let the cookies cool on the baking sheets for 10 minutes, then transfer them to racks to cool completely.
Recipe courtesy of Food Network Magazine’s The Big, Fun Kids Cookie Book.

title: Janet Mills urges action on heating assistance as Maine braces for cold
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gov. Janet Mills wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation Friday demanding more money from the federal government for heating assistance, a measure that she said is necessary to “ensure the safety and comfort of Maine people” amid record high heating oil prices.
The Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) currently provides about $40 million in assistance to qualifying households in Maine. Those funds are usually sent out in late November and applications are now open.
The governor’s request came as heating oil prices hit a record high in Maine last week, averaging $6.02 per gallon, the Department of Energy Resources said. This week, prices dropped slightly, to $5.96 per gallon — still above the previous record of $5.92 set in 2022.
Those prices were driven in large part by the continued constriction of the Strait of Hormuz, which, prior to the start of the war in Iran, carried about a quarter of the world’s oil shipments.
In her letter, Mills placed blame on President Donald Trump.
“Maine people should not be forced to choose between staying warm and putting food on the table because the president chose to drag the country into a needless war,” she wrote.
Prices that high demand an additional congressional allocation to the LIHEAP program, Mills said. Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, could be particularly hard-hit if LIHEAP funds aren’t increased, she said.
She encouraged Mainers to apply for LIHEAP funding as soon as possible. Applications and income limits can be found on MaineHousing’s website.
“Federal funding levels appropriated for LIHEAP this winter did not fully consider the drastic impacts of the president’s war that has sent fuel prices skyrocketing and are now insufficient for the circumstances that Maine and other cold-climate states now face,” Mills said.
Meanwhile, the Group of Seven wealthy democracies said Friday that they plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel also recently hit record high prices in the U.S.
Gas prices in the U.S. and abroad have soared during the eight-month war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22. Maine diesel prices averaged $6.47.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, lauded the G7 announcement Friday. She said the release should put “immediate downward pressure on energy prices and helping to lower the cost of producing and transporting goods.”
This story contains reporting from The Associated Press.

title: Quicksand won’t swallow you whole, here’s how to escape
text:
(InvestigateTV) — As kids playing outside, a lot of us were afraid of running into quicksand. But as it turns out, quicksand is not a bottomless pit like in the movies. It is a mixture of sand and water that appears solid.
According to Scientific American, quicksand can look solid, but the moment a person steps on it, the sand grains lose their grip and the ground turns “soupy.”
Quicksand then flows like liquid, and sand starts sinking to the bottom. The more a person struggles, the more fluid quicksand becomes. Research shows it will not swallow a person whole.
Matt Bloomfield, a professional guide based in Phoenix, got stuck in quicksand last year during a canyoneering trip with friends at Grand Staircase Escalante in Utah.
“It’s one of my favorites, for sure,” Bloomfield said.
In Bloomfield’s videos, the canyon floor becomes bouncy, like jello.
“So then we started to, like, kind of squish around in it and noticed that there was a lot of quicksand around,” Bloomfield said.
Bloomfield said he recognized the quicksand immediately because he had encountered it before.
“No, that was a big surprise,” Bloomfield said. “It kind of shocked me at first because it was up to my waist when I first fell in. But then once you start to struggle a little bit more, you start to sink. You can get stuck if you don’t know the proper way to free yourself. It can be very, very difficult to pull your legs out.”
In quicksand, the more a person struggles, the deeper they sink.
Bloomfield sank to his chest at one point.
“At this point, I had been, like, struggling to keep my cameras out of the mud,” Bloomfield said. “So I was staying upright, which is exactly what I shouldn’t have been doing. So I was sinking in a little bit deeper.”
Bloomfield said he flattened himself and leaned forward to get his arms out in front of him.
“I was able to kind of wiggle my legs and get them closer to the surface and then just kind of army crawl my way out,” Bloomfield said.
The current quicksand alert applies just south of the Grand Staircase Escalante area at the Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. The area spans more than a million acres of Arizona and Utah and includes Lake Powell, where dropping water levels are exposing more areas to explore on foot.
The quicksand alert is intended to raise awareness rather than alarm. The danger comes from getting stuck for hours and becoming exhausted, rather than from sinking completely underground.
Bloomfield said sinking stops before a person goes fully underwater.
“Yeah, it feels like that’s going to happen, but generally I think you get to like your lungs and you have more buoyancy where you actually can’t go any further,” Bloomfield said.
Bloomfield was with other people during his encounter. Park rangers recommend hiking with someone else in case of encountering quicksand in the area.
If a person gets stuck, officials recommend staying calm and applying the methods described to escape.

title: Christa Pike on ventilator and unconscious after failed execution, her lawyers say
text:
Christa Pike on ventilator and unconscious after failed execution, her lawyers say
Christa Pike remained in a hospital where she was on a ventilator and unconscious after her failed execution in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.
Video above: How can a lethal injection go wrong?
Hospital staff were working to save Pike's life and "clear the pentobarbital she was administered from her system" as of late Thursday, the attorneys said.
Pike was given two doses of the drug in a failed attempt Wednesday to execute her.
In the court filing, Pike's attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body," they wrote.
They wrote that instead of "remedying this failure," they prepared and administered a backup set of pentobarbital syringes.
State officials have not offered any explanation about what went wrong during the execution attempt
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee demanded a review of the state’s execution procedures and indefinitely postponed Pike’s execution and another one slated for this year. Other Republican political leaders in Tennessee said the state should review whether to stop single-drug lethal injections and consider other options to carry out death sentences.
The execution team worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs, said Pike's defense lawyer Randy Spivey, who counted at least seven needles in her left arm.
Neither the initial nor the backup dose of pentobarbital worked. Pike was still snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt.

title: New York’s governor says state’s AG will oversee Cornell rape investigation
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) — New York’s governor appointed a special prosecutor Thursday to oversee an investigation into a woman’s allegations that she was gang raped at a Cornell University fraternity house, saying she had lost faith in the local district attorney’s ability to handle the case.
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she had signed an executive order appointing the office of New York Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the investigation, which had initially been closed without charges in 2024.
The woman’s allegations got a rush of new attention when she filed a civil lawsuit last month. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation Monday, but has been battered by criticism that he’d abandoned the original investigation too quickly.
“Newly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute an alleged sexual assault on Cornell University’s campus in October 2024,” Hochul said.
“This has, in turn, undercut my faith, and the public’s faith, in the District Attorney’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time.”
Hochul said the attorney general would oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury.
“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said. ”This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.”
Messages left for Van Houten were not immediately returned late Thursday. Hochul, James and Van Houten are all Democrats.
A campus roiled by continued revelations
Hochul’s announcement came shortly after dozens of students and community members spent hours demanding transparency and accountability from university leaders at a forum sponsored by Cornell’s student government. The case has roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about its response and the larger issue of how sexual assaults are handled on college campuses.
The woman, identified only as Jane Doe in court documents, reported the alleged assault to campus police in November of 2024, then discussed it with the university’s internal investigators as part of Cornell’s disciplinary process.
The lawsuit against seven fraternity brothers, the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and others, alleges that she was plied with drugs and alcohol, then subjected to sex acts by a group of men while she was partially or entirely incapacitated. One of the men sent a social media message to other fraternity members alerting them to what was happening, and inviting people to take part, according to the lawsuit.
When he reopened the investigation earlier this week, Van Houten said he would review new information in the woman’s lawsuit. But he also issued a statement defending his initial decision not to prosecute, maintaining the woman’s first account to police didn’t include allegations that she was drugged against her will, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex.
Under pressure from the public and politicians, including Hochul, Cornell agreed Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations.
Students, community call for change
Over more than 2 1/2 hours Thursday, students and other members of the Cornell community expressed anger, frustration and grief over the school’s handling of sexual assault allegations in general, with several speakers sharing their own experiences of sexual violence.
Many criticized Cornell President Michael I. Kotlikoff and the university’s administration, calling for greater transparency and accountability in the handling of the case, stronger sexual assault prevention efforts and changes to Greek life.
Jane Wang, a sophomore, said at the forum that when she reported being sexually assaulted on campus a year ago, she was met with a slew of paperwork and little guidance or follow-up. After an initial email chain about starting the investigation, she got few updates and had to prod for answers, she said. The process left her feeling an “overall sense of helplessness within a broader institution.”
“My main message for Cornell here is that we can’t be treating these cases only with care and attention after it catches national news,” Wang said, calling for the university to improve the “seriousness and timeliness” of its response to sexual assault allegations.
There was no immediate response to a message seeking comment about the forum and Wang’s case sent to the university late Thursday.
Cornell has said it took a series of actions after the woman identifying as Jane Doe reported being raped at the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024.
It announced publicly that it had opened an investigation, condemned the alleged behavior, indefinitely suspended the fraternity, and convened a university task force to study ways to more effectively protect students against sexual assault.
It also conducted a monthslong investigation, which ended with some students being disciplined or expelled, though it has declined to provide specifics, citing student privacy rules. The university issued a statement Monday saying it supported reopening the criminal investigation.
“I think what happened here is an American problem,” said Hayden Watkins, an undergraduate and executive vice president of the Student Assembly, which hosted the forum.
“People kind of put Cornell on this pedestal because we are an elite institution,” he added. “But if it’s happening at places like Cornell, it’s happening on college campuses all across the country.”
___
Associated Press reporter Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this report.

title: Maine Menu: Chicken Cordon Bleu Casserole
text:
Maine Menu: Chicken Cordon Bleu Casserole
Maine Menu: Chicken Cordon Bleu Casserole
Maine Menu: Cumberland Fair 2026
This week's Maine Menu took us to the Cumberland Fair.
This year's theme is poultry, so chicken is on the menu.
We are back for our annual tradition. The Cumberland Fair with my former classmate from Thornton Academy, Margaret Arsenault is here to whip something up for us today. What are you going to make? Going to make Chicken Cordon Bleu Casserole. Sounds good. I love chicken Cordon Bleu but it's hard to roll. So, no rolling. No Rolling.
So, we're going to start with some butter to coat the pan.
Now we'll take out chopped up chicken. I use a rotisserie chicken. One rotisserie chicken. This is the most requested chicken dish in my house.
Spread it out.
Jim if you don't mind taking the diced ham and pouring that on top.
I use a combination of Swiss cheese and Harvarti cheese.
Do two layers of each.
We going to take the vest of one lemon and put it in two cups of water. This is going to make the gravy that goes on top.
And then we're going to take our special gravy. Actually the flavor in this is the best.
We're going to pour the gravy on and let it seep in.
Jim, I'm going to have to do the hard part. Crush up the crackers and then add the butter.
Baked at 375-degrees for 35 minutes.
"Delicious. We came back for it. She told us at one o'clock to come back at 1:30 and you can try. It's very good," said Meg Quilty of Wells.
RECIPE: Chicken Cordon Bleu
5 cups rotisserie chicken, chopped or shredded
2 cups ham, cubed
8 oz Havarti cheese, sliced or shredded (about 2 cups)
8 oz Swiss cheese, sliced or shredded (about 2 cups)
1 packet country gravy mix
(use 2 cups water - half the usual amount) Zest of 1 lemon
1 tablespoon Dijon mustard (optional)
2 cups crushed Ritz crackers
(about 40-45 crackers)
2-3 tablespoons melted butter
¼ teaspoon black pepper
(optional)
Preheat oven to 375°F. Grease a 9 × 13-inch casserole dish.
Spread the rotisserie chicken evenly in the dish, then scatter the ham cubes over the top.
Prepare 1 packet of country gravy mix using 2 cups water (half the usual amount).
Whisk until thickened.
Stir in the lemon zest, black pepper, and Dijon mustard (if using).
Pour the warm gravy evenly over the chicken and ham. (Use all or reserve a little if it looks too saucy.) Layer the Havarti cheese, then the Swiss cheese over the top.
Mix the crushed Ritz crackers with melted butter and sprinkle evenly over the casserole.
Bake uncovered for 25-30 minutes, until hot, bubbly, and golden brown.
Let rest for 5-10 minutes before serving.
