title: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, a memo shows
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have been ordered not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training, under new internal guidance issued after several drivers were shot in encounters with ICE.
A memo sent to officers in ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division and obtained by The Associated Press warned they are not authorized to chase vehicles that fail to pull over under any circumstances. Instead, officers should take down the vehicles’ information for further investigation, according to the memo signed by ICE’s executive associate director Marcos D. Charles and dated Wednesday.
The new guidance comes after ICE-initiated vehicle stops have repeatedly escalated when drivers have refused to cooperate or tried to flee. ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen such encounters since last year, killing at least four people and wounding several others.
President Donald Trump’s administration has faced internal tension over how to handle traffic stops, which are seen as particularly high-risk encounters.
After fatal shootings of drivers in Maine and Texas in July, ICE officers were directed to temporarily pause most vehicle stops. But the next day, Trump went on social media to direct the agency to continue traffic stops, calling them “one of ICE’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools.”
ICE has faced intense pressure from the White House to deport more people who are in the country illegally, and its arrests have reached record numbers. At the same time, the agency’s rapid hiring spree last year resulted in some poorly vetted and trained officers hitting the streets.
In a statement, ICE downplayed the significance of the memo, which said the new guidance was intended to replace and amend prior directives issued earlier this year, last year and in 2018.
“Occasionally, ICE leadership issues guidance reminders to law enforcement officers,” the statement said. “Vehicle stops and arrests of illegal aliens continue.”
The new memo outlines steps intended to improve the safety of vehicle stops for ICE officers, drivers they are targeting, their passengers and the public.
The memo told ICE’s field office directors that they must ensure vehicles used for traffic stops have lights and sirens that let the public know they are law enforcement vehicles when activated. All officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras, under the guidance.
In addition, only officers who have completed one of five specific agency training courses can conduct vehicle stops. Officers who have not completed the training courses can only participate in vehicle stops “in a support capacity” as passengers and cannot be the drivers of any of the vehicles involved.
The guidance says ICE officers can continue to use a controversial technique known as pinning, which is defined as “using a vehicle or physical barrier to trap or stop a car,” but only if they have received special training. Similarly, only trained officers can use spike strips that deflate tires to prevent drivers from fleeing.
The memo came the day that courtroom testimony highlighted ways in which two ICE officers involved in a vehicle stop, pursuit and shooting that wounded a delivery driver in Austin last month would not have complied with the new guidance.
During a bond hearing for Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, testimony showed that the officer who shot him wasn’t wearing a body-worn camera. The ICE officer who did have a camera was driving in a separate car and turned it off during the pursuit.
Prosecutors presented surveillance video that showed an ICE agent chasing Garces Perez at high speeds through residential streets after he fled an initial traffic stop.
Garces Perez faces federal assault charges after investigators say he struck an ICE officer with his driver’s side mirror. That officer then shot into Perez’s vehicle, lodging a bullet in his back, officials say.
Attorneys for Garces Perez have called the charges against him “retaliation” and have argued that the camera footage was inconclusive because it didn’t fully capture the moment when he allegedly tried to flee.

title: Maine must not bring back Paul LePage
text:
Paul LePage is back, but there’s nothing new about him we haven’t already seen and nothing we want to revisit. He’s grossly insulting (believing he’s funny), calling himself “Trump before Trump,” making blatantly racist and sexist comments that don’t belong in political campaigns or polite conversations.
LePage was always an embarrassment for Maine, and he’d be happy to embarrass it again. I’ll never forget visiting friends in Massachusetts who were ready with cringeworthy questions about Maine’s infamous governor. (“Did he really say that?”) But, we’re never going back there.
LePage got into office by finding a third-party candidate who’d split the vote for him. A dishonest tactic, it drove Maine to embrace ranked-choice voting, which increases our choices and our power as voters. In Maine, our votes really do matter!
It’s highly ironic, but it’s thanks to Paul LePage’s awful record that we use RCV and why we’re not going to be cheated out of our best choice for Maine’s 2nd District: Matt Dunlap.
Toni Seger
Lovell

title: Here’s how experts map Maine’s drought — and how you can help
text:
Do you know how to measure soil moisture levels or have a deep understanding of your region’s hydrology?
No?
Well, it doesn’t matter — if you want to help inform those responsible for analyzing drought conditions across Maine and the country, all you need is your own observations.
It doesn’t take a scientist to tell you that your lawn is turning brown, the pond you frequent is low, or your well is drying up. In fact, that’s where you’re the expert.
During a drought, one can’t help but feel a little helpless. It’s not like we can make it rain.
But you can help, because the public’s input is taken into account when the weekly U.S. Drought Monitor maps are put together. The maps and data are used to analyze drought impacts, and federal agencies consider them when they weigh whether to declare drought-related disasters.
Here’s how it all works — and where the average Mainer fits into the equation:
ONE NATION, UNDER DROUGHT
Those yellow, orange and red drought maps of Maine don’t really end at the state line.
The U.S. Drought Monitor was formed in 1999 by the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Meteorologists and climatologists from those entities take turns as the lead author of the national map, usually rotating every two weeks.
Precipitation is a major factor in analyzing a drought, but far from the only one. Streamflow, reservoir levels, temperatures, soil moisture, evaporation and vegetation health all play a role as well.
The author will compile that data (much of it obtained via satellite) and come up with a draft of that week’s map.
But numbers don’t tell the full story, nor can one meteorologist or climatologist. That’s where regional and local experts step in.
LOCAL EXPERTS
Sarah Jamison, senior service hydrologist with the National Weather Service office in Gray, is one of those experts.
Every week, she and other members of the Northeast Drought Early Warning System review the Drought Monitor’s draft and weigh in with their knowledge of the region.
“They’re getting not just their own assessment, not just the raw numbers, but they’re getting the more localized feedback,” Jamison said. “We don’t define what it should be for New England, but we recommend some changes.”
Local experts are necessary because the data isn’t one-size-fits-all.
“The same kind of dryness in Utah may reflect completely different impacts as it would to Cumberland County,” Jamison said. “There is climatology that’s also weighed into this.”
The Drought Monitor says it consults hundreds of regional and local experts. The weekly maps are, essentially, a (very) well-educated guess.
“It’s definitely a consolidation of a lot of contributors and a lot of information, balanced by the impact reports that they do solicit,” Jamison said.
HOW TO CONTRIBUTE
There’s no way for the experts who contribute to the weekly Drought Monitor maps to be everywhere at once, which is where Condition Monitoring Observer Reports come in. Anyone (18 or older, in most states) can find and fill out the form at droughtimpacts.unl.edu or drought.gov, or via the ArcGIS Survey123 app.
The observer report starts by asking for some basic information, like your location, familiarity with the area and general observations.
Then, there are over a dozen optional questions pertaining to a wide range of topics, from livestock and crop production to home and garden impacts. There are also questions on community health, water supply, hydropower, fish spawning and tourism impacts.
“My wetland pond has dried up, my well has gone dry, my lawn has turned brown, the trees are stressed and dropping acorns,” Jamison said, rattling off examples of various reports that help the experts. “It doesn’t matter exactly what magnitude of impact. Any kind of impacts that are driven by drought are all weighed.”
At the end, you can type in any additional comments and upload photos.
HOW THAT HELPS
The color of your backyard on the next week’s map isn’t just going to change because you made a submission. Conditions can vary from lawn to lawn and farm to farm, even in the same town or neighborhood.
“That’s one of the most unique things about drought,” Jamison said. “If we have a snowstorm with 8 inches, the impacts are relatively uniform across much of the area. With a drought … they’re going to vary, and that’s just natural.”
What can catch experts’ eyes are common reports that actually go against what the data is saying.
“If we believe, for example, it’s not a very significant drought, but then we start to see reports of ‘wells are going dry,’ ‘ponds are drying up,’ ‘crops are failing,’” Jamison said, “those kinds of things really can help be the checks and balances or the gut check on what we’re processing and evaluating.
“We don’t have people literally walking the area to make these designations,” Jamison added. “We have to rely on the tools in our arsenal, and then the reports that we get from people in the field.”

title: Patriots defense loses Christian Gonzalez, Christian Barmore
text:
The Patriots will be without two of their top defensive players Sunday when they visit the Buffalo Bills.
Both cornerback Christian Gonzalez and defensive tackle Christian Barmore were ruled out Friday with shoulder injuries.
This will be the first game either has missed this season.
Gonzalez became the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history last month when he signed a four-year, $135 million contract. He has eight tackles on the season. Barmore has four tackles and one sack so far.
Quarterback Drake Maye is also dealing with a right shoulder issue, but participated in all practices this week.
Coach Mike Vrabel said Friday that Maye’s injury occurred sometime during the Week 3 loss at Jacksonville.
“There were no limitations, so he practiced full — he didn’t miss any reps,” Vrabel said. “But we just felt like it was best to list it just to make sure that we are doing everything that we’re supposed to do from a protocol standpoint.”
Vrabel acknowledged that not having Barmore as a pass rusher, nor Gonzalez to defend the Bills’ receivers, will be a challenge opposite Buffalo quarterback Josh Allen.
“That is just what the situation is. There’s nothing we can do about it,” Vrabel said. “We can make sure that the guys that are playing are ready and that we continue to do the things that we know are going to help us. But that happens every week in the National Football League. I’m looking forward to seeing the guys that are going to play in there.”

title: Bangor police arrest man accused of nearly running over Maine Wire reporter
text:
Bangor police on Friday announced they had arrested a man in connection with an incident Thursday morning in which a driver went onto the grass and nearly hit a reporter from The Maine Wire.
The incident happened just before 8 a.m. on Odlin Road. In video footage filmed by The Maine Wire, the media arm of the conservative Maine Policy Institute, the reporter, Joe Sokol, is speaking to the camera when a driver backs onto the grass next to him and confronts him. After a brief exchange, the driver pulls away and Sokol continues recording.
That footage, along with surveillance video posted by The Maine Wire, shows a driver then cut across grass toward Sokol from the direction in which the car had just left, appearing to hit the camera that was filming Sokol.
Sokol was standing outside an addiction treatment center working on a report, according to a statement from the Maine Wire. As the vehicle nears, the video shows Sokol move toward the vehicle, in what The Maine Wire said was him trying to preserve evidence.
Bangor police investigated and identified the driver as Ryan Hayward, 38, of Bangor.
He was arrested and is charged with reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon, driving to endanger, and violating conditions of release.

title: Bucksport Town Council advances proposed 180-day moratorium on commercial data centers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BUCKSPORT, Maine (WABI) - The Bucksport Town Council voted to advance a proposed 180-day moratorium on commercial data centers following a public discussion at its Sept. 24 meeting.
Bucksport’s Community and Economic Development Director confirmed to WABI that an interested developer recently toured the former paper mill site.
Backers of the moratorium argue the temporary freeze is essential to study energy, water, and environmental impacts before any formal proposal is filed.
One councilor cast the sole opposing vote, contending that the town should encourage smaller data centers to rebuild the industrial tax base.
The proposed ordinance moves to a second reading and formal public hearing on Oct. 8.

title: USDA considers adapting farm-style safety net for fishermen
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Top federal agriculture officials visited Maine this week to evaluate whether crop insurance can be expanded to protect the state’s multimillion dollar lobster industry.
The visit by U.S. Department of Agriculture Undersecretary Richard Fordyce and Risk Management Agency Administrator Pat Swanson comes as the agency increasingly looks to integrate seafood producers into traditional agricultural safety nets.
Federal crop insurance allows farmers to buy government-subsidized policies that pay out in weeks to months after natural disasters or market drops cause severe revenue losses. In contrast, lobstermen rely on federal fishery disaster declarations that can take three to five years to distribute aid, which industry analysts call far too slow for small operators.
“We are a small-boat, owner-operated fishery made up of thousands of independent businesses, so programs designed for agriculture or other food-producing sectors will not necessarily translate neatly to lobster,” said Patrice McCarron, director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association.
However, McCarron called the visit “an important first step” toward determining whether existing USDA programs can be adapted or new approaches developed to better support Maine lobstermen in their role as food producers for the world.
During a dockside roundtable in Stonington on Tuesday, industry leaders emphasized that lobstermen face severe market swings and price crashes rather than physical catch loss alone. Fordyce, a corn and soybean farmer from Missouri, noted that lobstermen favored revenue protection over simple yield guarantees.
“Just talking with the lobstermen, I think they were probably more inclined to try to find a product or try to find a path forward that would be more supportive of total revenue,” Fordyce said. “I was quite surprised by the data that’s available as far as supporting catch numbers.”
Last year’s lobster catch was valued at $461.4 million — 7.5% below the 10-year average, and, when adjusted for inflation, 20% down from 2024, state data shows.
Curt Brown, president of Bold Coast Seafood in Prospect Harbor, hosted the delegation and highlighted the shared reality between ocean and land harvesters.
“I was struck by how many of the same challenges we face in seafood are also challenges that farmers across the country face every day,” Brown said. “There is a lot we can learn from each other.”
Seafood industry consultant Noah Oppenheim said bringing Midwest agricultural leaders to coastal Maine provided crucial perspective, especially the similarities between the rural fishing communities in Maine and the rural farming communities in the Midwest.
While the visit was focused on ways to manage the industry’s risks, representatives also used the time to drive home other ways the agency can help water-based food producers like they support land-based farmers, including equal access to loan, grant, purchasing and marketing programs.
“The agency seems wide open to focus on all of this at once,” Oppenheim said. “Congress knows this is a bipartisan feel-good issue. We need to be eating more domestic seafood. It’s the right thing to do to have seafood be an equal part of our food system.”
Oppenheim said opportunities for fishermen have expanded since the USDA created its Office of Seafood in April. One of its top priorities is to find ways for fishermen to tap into the same federal programs and safety nets as the nation’s potato and dairy farmers.
Addressing expectations regarding a timeline, Fordyce cautioned that any official expansion must ultimately be approved by the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation board. However, because local advocates have worked on the issue for several years, he said “a lot of that preliminary work has been kind of done.”
While a full rollout for lobster insurance remains down the road, Fordyce emphasized that establishing direct working relationships between Washington officials and Maine coastal leaders was the immediate, vital outcome of the trip.

title: 30 condo units coming to Gorham
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A 30-unit condominium development off County Road (Route 22) was approved in Gorham this week after a year and a half long review process.
Thistlewood Petit Condominiums, located behind a commercial building owned by the Gorham landscaping company Bee and Eez at 34 County Road, will reserve 75% of its 31 one-bedroom units for residents older than 55. One of the condos is already built and for sale, and the landowner, Christina Mitchell, lives in another home on the 15.4 property with her handicapped sister.
Developer Susan Duchaine said she and Mitchell want the neighborhood to be for older Mainers who are not ready to move into an assisted living facility or can’t afford the high cost of living in one.
“Our thought process is, if they’re in Florida half the year, maybe they still want a place to come home to and not be on their kid’s couch,” Duchaine said. “Maybe they want to be in a community where there’s people nearby of similar age groups.”
The neighborhood will consist of a roadway loop called Thistle Drive with 10 buildings containing three “tiny houses” in each. Prices will start at $350,000, Duchaine said.
About half of the condos will be one story and 400 square feet, and the other half will be two stories and 600 square feet. Each will have a 200 square foot front porch, 12-by-24 foot finished garage, kitchen, living room, bathroom, and the two-story units will have office space.
The neighborhood will also have sidewalks and 10 acres of woods behind the condos.
Duchaine will build a westbound left turning lane on County Road in front of the property to accommodate additional traffic before building the complex. She said she hopes to list the condos for sale immediately, begin construction in the next few weeks and be ready for buyers to move in come February.
A number of issues caused delay in the approval process, including the neighborhood layout needing reconfiguration due to problems with emergency vehicle access and disagreements over how to best adjust for added traffic. While Duchaine and Andy Morrell, the engineer representing the project with BH2M, wanted the entrance and exit of the neighborhood to be right-in and right-out to ensure safety, the town engineer said the added the left turning lane is necessary.

title: Steven Juskewitch for District Attorney
text:
I’m running for District Attorney in Hancock and Washington counties because justice has to mean something on both sides of the courtroom — and it has to arrive in time to matter.
For 28 years I served as an Army officer in positions of leadership — 82nd ABN Div., command of two drill sergeant companies, battalion staff, and teaching leadership and problem-solving at Fort Leavenworth. That service taught me a simple standard: you don’t send people into a fight you haven’t prepared them to win, and you don’t put people in harm’s way without a clear, defensible reason.
I’ve spent years since then as a prosecutor and a defense attorney. I successfully tried sexual assaults, shaken baby cases, and other serious felony cases as assistant District Attorney and Deputy DA in Hancock and Washington Counties after prosecuting in Cumberland County. I’ve also stood on the other side of the table successfully defending people accused of crimes. That combination is not common, and it matters.
The District Attorney is not a scorekeeper. The DA is a minister of justice. The job is to protect the rights of everyone involved — victims, the accused, witnesses and the public.
One of the core duties of that office is knowing the law well enough to guide the people who gather the facts. Police should not have to guess what will hold up in court. The DA’s office should help officers understand what evidence needs to be collected, how it needs to be collected so it is admissible, what questions will actually reveal what happened, and whether the facts support pursuing a case at all. Early, clear guidance produces stronger cases against the guilty and reveals cases which should not have been prosecuted.
Like continuances, dismissals are unacceptable to the criminal justice process. Losing a criminal trial is even more unacceptable; an innocent person was tried and that failure cuts two ways, and both are unjust. Sometimes it means real criminals walk because the case wasn’t ready. Victims are left without accountability.
Sometimes it means the office takes people to trial who are innocent, or who may have done something but against whom the evidence was never strong enough to know. The law says a person is innocent until proven guilty. The community often does not treat them that way. An arrest and a trial brands someone. Jobs, families, reputations, and peace of mind cause damage that a later “not guilty” does not fully repair.
Part of why weak cases keep moving forward is how the grand jury is used. In current practice, police officers are typically the ones who testify. Victims often never speak for themselves at that stage. Hearing from a victim in a controlled, respectful setting can give a grand jury more confidence that a case should go forward. It can also surface problems early. Tough questions asked there — not in front of a trial jury — can show that a case should not proceed. When that step is skipped, cases that should have been stopped still go to trial. That wastes time, energy, and taxpayer dollars. It also puts an accused person through a public process without a sufficient reason.
Delay makes all of this worse.
Justice delayed is not a slogan. It is about a person sitting in jail 522 days waiting for trial who, even though he did not believe he was guilty, pleaded guilty for time served so he could get out and care for his dying mother. That is not a system doing its job. That is a system forcing a choice no person should have to make.
It is also rape cases taking more than five years to reach court because of backlog. Victims wait. Memories fade. Evidence gets harder to use. The public loses confidence that the most serious crimes will be handled with urgency.
Part of the backlog is not a mystery. Lower-priority cases — things like fishing with an expired license and other far less significant matters — are taking time, staff, and courtroom space that should be reserved for violence, sexual assault, and other cases that actually threaten public safety. A District Attorney has to set priorities. Not every case deserves the same place in line. Plea bargains should not be a bargain.
I have tried serious felony cases from both sides. I know what a winnable case looks like and what a case that should never have been filed looks like. Leadership in this office means training and coordinating with law enforcement from the first interview, using the grand jury as a real screening tool, moving serious cases first, resolving minor matters without letting them choke the docket, and having the courage to say “not this one” when the evidence does not support putting a person’s life through the system.
That is why I am running. Experience on both sides of the aisle. A lifetime of command and accountability. A commitment to protect victims without sacrificing the rights of the accused or the integrity of the process. Thousands of dismissals and victims not timely informed should not be happening.
I am asking for your support, your questions, and your vote. Hancock and Washington Counties deserve a District Attorney who treats every case as a matter of justice, not just a matter of volume.
Steven Juskewitch is a candidate for District Attorney, District 7.

title: Janet Mills calls on Congress to approve more funding for heating assistance
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gov. Janet Mills is calling on Congress to approve more funds for heating assistance.
In a Friday letter to U.S. Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King and U.S. Reps. Chellie Pingree and Jared Golden, Mills wrote that congressional appropriations for the Low-Income Heating Assistance Program didn’t account for the impact of President Donald Trump’s war in Iran, which effectively halted shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas passes.
“Maine people should not be forced to choose between staying warm and putting food on the table because the President chose to drag the country into a needless war,” Mills wrote.
The statewide average price for a gallon of heating oil this week is $5.96, down slightly from last week’s record high of $6.02 but nearly 80% higher than the same last year, according to a Maine Department of Energy Resources survey.
Prices range from a low of $5 a gallon to as high as $6.30 in parts of eastern and Down East Maine, where the average rests at $6.
This time last year heating oil went for an average of $3.33 a gallon, and this same time in 2024 it went for $3.34.
That means it will cost Mainers an additional $725 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank, the Department of Energy Resources said Thursday afternoon.
That’s raising concerns among lower-income homeowners in a state heavily reliant on heating oil to stay warm during the winter. Mainers already have empty fuel tanks, according to the community action program serving Aroostook, Hancock and Washington counties. But the Trump administration has rebuffed calls to release federal heating assistance early.
“As a large, rural state with an older housing stock, Maine people are especially vulnerable to spikes in the cost of heating fuel,” Mills wrote.
Her administration has moved to assist low-income Mainers with energy costs, including $300 relief checks in the supplemental state budget earlier this year and this week automatically enrolling Mainers who receive public health insurance and food or heating assistance in a program to discount electric bills. Under that latter move, CMP customers could see their bills cut up to 81% and Versant Power customers up to 83%, depending on their income levels.

title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: Sacrificing Safety?
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A crash can change a life in seconds and in many American cars, a safety feature designed to keep front-seat passengers from hitting each other is still missing.
Plus, when deadly crashes keep happening, families want more than promises — they want safer streets before another life is lost.
Sacrificing Safety?
They’re an auto safety innovation in cars around the world: airbags that can protect you and your front-seat passenger from hitting each other in a side-impact crash. When drivers and front-seat passengers collide, the result can be serious head injuries or death. But even though those airbags were first introduced in the U.S., many cars here don’t have them. Why?
Crash tests in Europe in 2020 drove the adoption of those airbags, but the U.S. doesn’t do that type of testing. Authorities here question whether the airbags are necessary – but the world’s largest auto safety equipment supplier tells us lives are being lost unnecessarily due to the lack of airbags that manufacturers already know how to incorporate into their vehicles.
We’ll speak with one accident victim who says a front-center airbag could have prevented her from suffering a devastating head injury and the lifelong consequences.
A goal to end traffic deaths by 2050. Is it working?
More than 36,000 people were killed on American roads last year — according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration — a reminder that for too many families, a routine drive can end in tragedy.
In Phoenix, city leaders are trying to reduce deadly crashes — but acknowledge the work is far from done. Reporter Amy Cutler looks at the city’s safety plan, the gaps that remain, and one family’s loss.
Loud car modifications: What’s legal, what’s not
For many people, a quiet night at home or a meal outside can be interrupted in an instant by the roar of a revving engine or a backfiring exhaust.
In North Carolina — as in many states — vehicles must meet muffler and exhaust requirements. But police say catching violators can be difficult. Reporter Jamie Boll in Charlotte explains what’s legal, what isn’t, and why neighbors want action.
How ‘convenient spending’ could drain your budget
We all do it from time to time – shell out money to save a little time or make life easier. It’s called convenient spending.
In this Watching Your Wallet, Consumer Investigator Rachel DePompa shows us why convenience can act like a monthly trap, silently draining your budget.

title: Christa Pike is on a ventilator and unconscious after failed Tennessee execution, attorneys say
text:
NASHVILLE (AP) — Christa Pike remained in a hospital where she was on a ventilator and unconscious after her failed execution in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.
Hospital staff was working to save Pike’s life and “clear the pentobarbital she was administered from her system” as of late Thursday, the attorneys said.
Pike was given two doses of the drug in a failed attempt Wednesday to execute her.
In the court filing, Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” they wrote.
They wrote that instead of “remedying this failure,” they prepared and administered a backup set of pentobarbital syringes.
State officials have not offered any explanation about what went wrong during the execution attempt
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee demanded a review of the state’s execution procedures and indefinitely postponed Pike’s execution and another one slated for this year. Other Republican political leaders in Tennessee said the state should review whether to stop single-drug lethal injections and consider other options to carry out death sentences.
The execution team worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs, said Pike’s defense lawyer Randy Spivey, who counted at least seven needles in her left arm.
Neither the initial nor the backup dose of pentobarbital worked. Pike was still snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt.
In directly communicating with WVLT8, attorneys wrote:
“Christa remains critically ill and is receiving medical care for the devastating effects of Wednesday night’s events. As detailed in today’s filing, Christa remains hospitalized following Wednesday night’s failed execution attempt. She is critically ill, unconscious, intubated and receiving breathing assistance through a ventilator. She is being treated for the serious effects of the pentobarbital administered during the execution attempt, including significant injuries to both arms.”

title: ‘A psychopath’: Professional boxer arrested after 2-year-old dies, 1-year-old hurt in alleged abuse
text:
MESA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A professional boxer is facing a first-degree murder charge after police say he beat and killed his girlfriend’s 2-year-old son and abused his own 1-year-old child.
Mesa police said the situation started Tuesday when paramedics responded to an apartment for a child in medical distress. First responders rushed the toddler to a hospital, where he died from his injuries.
Doctors noted suspicious bruising was found across the child’s body and contacted police, triggering a homicide investigation.
Investigators identified Kishawn Porter, 23, a professional fighter, as the suspect in the case.
Authorities said that while Porter is a professional fighter, bruising found across his knuckles did not come from training or competition, but rather from fatal child abuse.
Porter was taken into police custody on Tuesday.
“Mr. Porter hit and punched the 2-year-old victim multiple times with either his hands and/or a sandal,” a prosecutor with the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office said during Porter’s initial court appearance.
During Porter’s court appearance, prosecutors outlined a violent juvenile history, telling the judge Porter has prior adjudications for child molestation and aggravated assault involving a restrained victim.
An autopsy conducted Wednesday by the Maricopa County medical examiner revealed catastrophic internal trauma on the child that included healing and acute rib fractures, a lacerated liver and a lacerated stomach, with blood found pooling in the abdomen.
“It takes a substantial amount of force to lacerate the stomach, and the injuries were all consistent with child abuse,” court records stated. “Based on the injuries, no one could have survived the severity.”
Forensic experts noted that the child’s healing rib fractures pointed to a pattern of ongoing violence in the home rather than an isolated incident.
“That means this wasn’t the only attack,” Dr. Roy Lubit, a forensic psychiatrist who specializes in child abuse cases, said. “The idea of beating and killing an infant indicates an almost basic lack of humanity. An individual who would do the acts that are alleged would almost be overwhelmingly likely to be a psychopath.”
Detectives said Porter also abused his own 1-year-old child by spanking him, hitting him in the mouth and slapping his torso and rib cage.
Formal charges regarding the allegations involving the 1-year-old have not yet been submitted to prosecutors.
Following his arrest, two combat sports promotions announced they had cut ties with Porter due to the severity of the charges.
A judge set Porter’s bond at $1.5 million.

title: Secondhand shopping surge: More Americans are buying used clothing
text:
(Aging Untold) — Retail experts say many American consumers, including older shoppers, are seeking out pre-owned and sustainable products.
According to the 2025 Resale Report from ThredUp, the U.S. secondhand apparel market is growing at an average of about 9 percent each year.
The thrill of the hunt
For Stephanie Hernandez, a secondhand stylist based in Washington, D.C., thrift shopping is both a passion and a profession. Clients pay her to help them build a one-of-a-kind, sustainable wardrobe — because many want to shop more responsibly but don’t have the time to do it themselves.
“They want to be more sustainable, and they are kind of thinking about it more, but they don’t really have the time to go out to a thrift store and hunt for those amazing pieces,” Hernandez said.
Her motivation goes beyond fashion.
“I just feel like there’s already so much out there in the world, and buying new just creates more and more waste,” she said.
The Council for Textile Recycling estimates the average American throws away more than 70 pounds of clothing and other textiles each year. According to the United Nations Environment Programme, the equivalent of one garbage truck of textiles is landfilled or burned every single second globally.
“I’d see videos of clothes washing up on beaches in countries across the ocean and it breaks my heart. That’s kind of why I started the business, to educate people about that and show them that there are other options,” Hernandez said.
Sustainable fashion in the classroom
Mikki Taylor, a fashion design professor at Howard University’s Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, teaches a course on sustainable fashion and says she practices what she preaches.
In her class, students examine their own closets, choices and patterns of consumption.
“I let them know all the chemicals that are involved in just one item, one T-shirt, a pair of jeans. It is incredibly important to teach them that because our environment is definitely being affected,” Taylor said.
Her advice for those new to secondhand shopping: “I would say just dive in. I mean really, just look at how much you have, what is it that you can remake or reinvent, and then what I always advise is to get a solid staple piece, and then build around it.”
Start with what you have
Hernandez said every new client begins by shopping their existing wardrobe before ever setting foot in a thrift store.
“We literally go through everything in their closet,” she said. “And we put outfits together with things that they already own — so kinda showing them you can breathe new life into things you already have!”

title: Obituary: George Adams Gilmore
text:
BRUNSWICK – George Adams Gilmore, a resident of Thornton Oaks, passed away on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026 at Mid Coast Hospital.
George was born in Portland, Maine on April 15, 1935, the son of Martha Senter Gilmore, of Brunswick and David William Gilmore, a professor of European Languages at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, N.J., and a summer resident on Birch Island in Maine.
George grew up in Highland Park, N.J., a suburb of New Brunswick, and graduated from Highland Park High School in 1952, and was president of his class. George then attended Webb Institute of Naval Architecture in Glen Cove, Long Island, N.Y., where he graduated in 1957 with a B.S. in Naval Architecture and Marine Engineering.
George worked in the marine field until 1958 when he joined the U.S. Navy and was Brigade Commander at Naval Officer Training Command in Newport, R.I. He served as a submarine repair coordinator for two years at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard in Hawaii, and then two years as the Damage Control Officer on the USS Colahan, (a Bath built destroyer), in the Pacific Ocean during the Vietnam War.
George then attended Harvard Business School, graduating in 1964. He then worked in various marine design and management positions with locations in Bethesda, Md., Washington, D.C., and New York City, N.Y. In NYC, at Energy Transportation Corporation, he was co-author with two others in 1980 of the Society of Naval Architects and Marine Engineers technical paper “Service Experience with 125,000-m3 LNG Vessels of Spherical Tank Design.” George moved to Brunswick, Maine in 1985 where he became the manager of Senter’s Department Store, founded by his grandfather, until it closed in 1992.
After moving to Brunswick, he married Martha Kendall Gilmore. They were active members of the Maine State Music Theatre community. They also enjoyed time on Casco Bay and summers at Mere Point. While in Brunswick, George participated in several organizations including The Brunswick Rotary Club, Maine Merchants Association, Independence Association, and Brunswick-Topsham Land Trust. He was a member of First Parish Church.
George was predeceased by his wife, Martha Kendall Gilmore.
George is survived by three stepchildren, Kent (Lisa) Black, Daphne Brenner, Elizabeth Shortsleeve; step-grandchildren; and numerous cousins from the Senter Family.
Friends and family are invited to visit 10 a.m. Saturday Oct. 17, at First Parish Church, Maine Street, Brunswick. A funeral service will follow at 11 a.m. at the church. Committal will reunite him with his wife, Martha in Riverside Cemetery, Brunswick. Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.

title: Biddeford-area legislative candidates talk housing, affordability and immigration
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BIDDEFORD — Five candidates for Maine legislative seats took the stage Thursday night to let voters hear candidates’ views on important issues facing the city.
The candidates appearing were: Sen. Henry Ingwersen, the incumbent Democrat in Senate District 32, and independent challenger Jason Litalien; Rep. Marc Malon, the incumbent Democrat in House District 133, and independent challenger Marc Lessard; and Rep. Traci Gere, the incumbent Democrat for House District 134.
Gere’s independent opponent, Alan Daggett, was invited to the forum but did not attend. Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, a Democrat who is running for reelection unopposed in House District 132, had a prior commitment and was not present.
The forum was hosted at Biddeford High School by Heart of Biddeford, was led by Biddeford-Saco Chamber of Commerce Director Alex MacPhail and featured questions asked by members of four local news organizations, including the Portland Press Herald.
EDUCATION IN MAINE
The first question of the evening asked the candidates if the current Legislature is adequately supporting Maine education.
Gere said she has helped to make significant investments in Maine students during her time in Augusta — including increasing teacher salaries and championing the new statewide cellphone ban — and plans to continue that work if reelected.
“I want to see Maine students’ reading and math scores improve,” she said.
Malon also said he’d like to see test scores improve and wants to make sure the state is investing in students and teachers.
“Everyone deserves a quality public education in Maine,” he said.
But while Ingwersen agreed with Gere and Malon, Lessard and Litalien — the two independent challengers — said the current Legislature needs a change.
“We could do everything opposite of what we’ve been doing,” Lessard said.
COST OF LIVING
The issue of affordability is top of mind for many Mainers in this election cycle. Litalien said people are struggling to stay afloat, citing record heating oil prices and high taxes.
Lessard pledged to work hard to keep taxes low, pointing to his record as a member of the Biddeford City Council for over 30 years and the York County Budget Committee for almost a decade.
“I will be a wall in Augusta,” he said. “This wall will not crumble.”
Housing — or the lack thereof — is one of the most important issues related to affordability, said Malon. a member of the state Housing and Economic Development Committee.
The solution, he said, is building more housing of all kinds. The state needs to make smart investments in housing, he added, and needs to reform regulations that make it difficult for the state to build.
“This is personal to me. I want my daughters to be able to live here,” Malon said. “We need to do more.”
IMMIGRATION IN MAINE
After Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was shot and killed by a federal immigration officer in Biddeford over the summer, immigration has been widely discussed throughout the state.
The Biddeford community is heartbroken, Ingwersen said, adding that he voted for laws to limit U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in Maine. While the state can’t keep ICE out completely, it can limit how local officials interact with the agency, he said.
“Immigration is part of the history of the United States,” Gere added. “No one should be shot in the streets.”
Litalien, who is a lawyer, said that while Durán Guerrero’s death was a tragedy, immigration is a federal issue, not a state issue.
“I have no issue at all with legal immigration,” he said. “We need law and order and to make sure things are legal.”
THE OPIOID CRISIS
Some Biddeford residents have expressed increasing concerns about needle waste and the handling of the opioid crisis. Litalien and Lessard both said free needle exchange programs are a problem, and that the state needs to look for other solutions.
Malon, on the other hand, said those programs are saving lives.
“People have access to safe supplies and a connection to community,” he said.
Gere added that she has seen a steep decline in opioid deaths when programs like free needle exchanges are available, but she’s always open to improvements.
FINAL STATEMENTS
At the end of the forum, each candidate had the opportunity to give closing remarks. Litalien said the election comes down to one thing: Are Mainers happy with how things are going?
“I’m really frustrated at this point,” he told voters. “You have a simple choice.”
Lessard reiterated that he would be the person to keep finances in check in Augusta.
Malon and Gere said legislating is a “team sport,” and that legislators need to know how to work together to get things done.
Ingwersen is proud of his record, he said, and he wants to continue the work he’s been doing in Augusta.
In-person early voting begins Monday; Biddeford voters can cast ballots at the city clerk’s office in City Hall from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. Mondays and Tuesdays and 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Wednesdays and Thursdays. Election Day voting will take place from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. at Biddeford High School’s Tiger Gym.

title: Experts say now is an ideal time to protect yourself from flu. Here’s why
text:
(AP) - It’s October and time for flu shots.
Medical experts urge getting a flu vaccination soon, before influenza starts spreading widely — and to get up to date on protection against other fall respiratory viruses, too. Updated COVID-19 shots are available now, plus shots for people especially vulnerable to another winter risk called RSV.
While these infections make many people feel miserable for a few days before they recover, every year flu alone causes hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations in the U.S. and kills tens of thousands.
Vaccination isn’t “a guarantee that we’re going to prevent illness. But just like the seat belt in your car, it decreases risk” of the worst outcomes, said Dr. Ryan Stanton of the American College of Emergency Physicians.
Fall vaccine advice usually comes from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and its independent advisory panel. But this year that panel, which influences state and insurance vaccine policies, is caught in a court battle and the CDC hasn’t updated its advice.
Now doctors’ groups are filling the gap: the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America have posted vaccination guidelines for their patient populations plus the scientific evidence behind them.
Here’s what to know:
Just about everyone should get vaccinated against flu
Just about everybody starting at age 6 months needs flu vaccination, the medical societies agree. But flu is particularly dangerous for people 65 and older, pregnant women, young children and people of any age who have chronic health problems, including asthma, diabetes, heart disease and weak immune systems. The last two flu seasons brought unusually high numbers of child deaths, the vast majority of them in unvaccinated kids.
The vaccines don’t block all flu infections, but they do help prevent the worst outcomes, decreasing older adults’ hospitalizations by 31% last year, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project, a public health group based at the University of Minnesota.
Here’s how to pick from the multiple flu vaccine options
Three “enhanced” flu vaccines are designed to better protect seniors. The American Academy of Family Physicians urges them to choose one — “but do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available,” said AAFP’s Dr. Sarah Nosal.
The Food and Drug Administration recently approved a new choice for people ages 50 and older, the first flu vaccine made with the same mRNA technology that was key to ending the COVID-19 pandemic. One study found Moderna’s mFlusiva was 27% more effective against symptomatic illness among 50- to 64-year-olds than a standard shot.
The shot-averse could choose a nasal spray, FluMist, if they’re ages 2 to 49 and meet other health criteria.
The latest on COVID-19 vaccines
COVID-19 shots once were recommended for just about everyone by federal health agencies, but like last year, the FDA has only formally approved them for higher-risk people — those ages 65 and older or younger people with at least one health condition that increases their risk.
Still, the family physicians recommend all adults get a COVID-19 vaccination, especially seniors and those with other risk factors. Adults 65 and older should get a fall dose and then a second dose six months later, as immunity wanes over time, Nosal said.
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a COVID-19 shot for all children ages 6 months to 23 months, and for older kids with high-risk conditions. It also supports vaccination for any child whose parent wishes it.
With millions of shots administered, there’s no evidence that coronavirus vaccination during pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage or other problems, “so please get the vaccine,” said ACOG’s Dr. Christina Davidson.
Depending on age, people can choose a shot from Moderna, Pfizer, or the only non-mRNA version from Novavax and Sanofi.
Just like with flu vaccines, these shots are better at preventing severe disease than mild cases. The Vaccine Integrity Project said last fall’s COVID-19 shots cut the risk of hospitalization by 53% in seniors and slashed emergency room visits for very young children.
Common side effects for flu and COVID-19 vaccines are mild and temporary, such as sore arms, fatigue, headaches, muscle aches, and mild fever. They occurred somewhat more often with the new mFlusiva than with standard flu shots.
Here’s where you can get vaccinated
While pediatricians and some clinics offer both flu and coronavirus shots, they’re most common in pharmacies.
For COVID-19 shots, states have more pharmacy rules. For example, Walgreens says it offers those shots without a prescription in all but two states, Arizona and Oregon, but can provide doses for children as young as 3 in some states while others have higher age limits.
Medicare covers the fall shots and most private health insurers say they plan to continue doing so through 2027. If you want to choose mFlusiva, the new Moderna flu option, make sure to double check that your insurance covers it.
When to get vaccinated
Flu experts say October is best, although vaccinations will remain available through the fall — just remember it can take two weeks for protection to kick in. COVID-19 cases rose in the late summer and usually do again around the winter holidays. Some experts say it’s also OK to time the coronavirus shot a few weeks ahead of an event you wouldn’t want to miss because of illness, like a special trip or get-together.
RSV is a nuisance for many, but it can be deadly for some
RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, typically is a cold-like nuisance during the fall, winter and early spring. But it can be severe, even life-threatening, for infants and older adults.
The family physicians recommend a one-time vaccination for adults 75 and older, people 50 to 74 who are at increased risk, or younger people with weak immune systems.
It’s also recommended during late pregnancy to protect infants born during RSV season. Separately, the pediatricians recommend a vaccine-like medication for those infants whose moms weren’t vaccinated and some other high-risk babies.

title: They were born on the same day in the same hospital. Now they’re getting married
text:
CRANE, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - Inside of Crane High School, home of the Pirates, scavenging through decades of student pictures are Principal Tara Mease and science teacher Karen Faucett.
Their own children, Brayden Faucett and Lorene Mease, are included on the wall of graduates.
“Kind of a big year coming up,” reporter Chad Plein asked the women.
“Our kids are getting married,” Tara answered.
It’s not out of the ordinary for high school sweethearts to get married. It’s also not too unusual that both of their moms also graduated from the same school.
So, what is so unusual about this love story?
“I was born on July 7th, 2006,” Lorene said.
“[I was born on] July 7th, 2006,” Brayden said.
Lorene and Brayden were born on the same day, minutes apart, with Lorene being a bit older. In the same hospital. By the same doctor.
“When I got to the hospital, they were like, ‘We’re gonna have to try and delay. He’s in a C-section right now,’” Karen recalled.
“They’d gotten [Lorene] out, and a nurse stuck her head in the door and said, ‘Dr. Ting, those twins are coming right now,’” Tara continued.
“He came rushing in, and immediately they performed my C-section,” Karen said.
“Then found out later that it was the Faucett boys, that Karen was in the hospital, and he was rushing out of my C-section to go deliver her twins,” Tara said.
“We put it together that I had interrupted Lorene’s delivery,” Karen said.
Doing the math, the odds of a soon-to-be married couple being born on the same day, minutes apart, in the same hospital, by the same doctor, are 1 in 514 billion.
Lorene has a memory from the day she was born written inside her baby book.
“[My mom] wrote, ‘Mommy’s friend Karen Faucett had twin boys on the same day I was born,’” Lorene read from the book.
“We were around each other a little bit as kids, because our moms were friends from high school,” Lorene said about their childhood. “But Brayden and his brother never wanted me to hang around with them.”
Brayden recalled never hanging out with her as children. “But I guess, from what she tells me, me and my brother always told her it was our birthday and not hers.”
They started dating after their 16th birthday and haven’t looked back. Brayden popped the question earlier this year on a piece of land where they’ll one day build their home and live happily ever after.
“I just feel like it is so important to find someone who’s truly your best friend,” Lorene said. “I mean, we’ll be joking around sometimes, and then I’ll just kind of sit there like, ‘Wow, we’re going to get married.’ Like, we’re going to get to spend the rest of our lives together.”
“She always says it’s like we’re just best friends,” Brayden said. “And I said, ‘Well, there’s nothing wrong with that.’”
Lorene and Brayden have their date set and it’s not on their birthday in July. Lorene said she doesn’t want a summer wedding.
They’re getting married on October 3rd.

title: Catering business shut down after football team suffers food poisoning before game
text:
ROCK ISLAND, Ill. (KWQC/Gray News) - An unlicensed home-based catering business in Illinois has been ordered to cease operations after dozens of people were sickened at a football team dinner.
According to the Rock Island Health Department, it was notified of a foodborne illness outbreak that stemmed from a Rock Island football team dinner that took place on Sept. 24 in the school cafeteria.
Health department officials said the dinner was catered by a home-based business called Sunshine and Spice.
Players, coaches and parents who attended the dinner were served fajita chicken, seasoned taco beef, cheese, flour taco shells, cheesy pepper beans, cilantro corn rice and Pico de Gallo salsa.
Seventy-five people were served the meal, and at least 45 were reported sick, causing the team to postpone its homecoming football game.
Just hours after the dinner, 23 players, five coaches and three parents reported symptoms, which included vomiting and diarrhea.
Officials said no one was hospitalized, but one player did have to visit a doctor.
The health department reported that most symptoms were over within 24 hours.
Health department officials noted that they met with the owner of Sunshine and Spice and learned the business was unlicensed and not food-safety certified. They then ordered the business to shut down, with the option of getting properly certified.
Officials said the owner told the health department that all ingredients were purchased from the Moline Walmart, Spotted Apron in Geneseo and farmers’ markets in Davenport and Coal Valley.
Joshua Harris, owner of Sunshine and Spice, released the following statement regarding the situation:
“First, Sunshine and Spice wants to sincerely apologize and send even more prayers to anyone affected by last week’s Rock Island football team meal.
We provided a taco bar-style potluck before the team was dismissed to prepare for their homecoming game. All of the food purchased from Walmart was fully cooked. We put all of the leftovers in plastic bags provided by the team parents for anyone to take home.
We have cooked for numerous parents of the team/school in the past and have no reason ever to provide a sub-standard meal or purposely attempt any tampering shenanigans. We are saddened by this whole situation.
We have been working side by side with the Rock Island County Health Department and Rock Island City/County Law Enforcement Agencies to be a part of their continuing investigations.
Again, we want to extend our deepest apologies and continued prayers to those affected.”
The investigation into the food poisoning remained active pending test results for pathogens in the food seized by the county, health officials said.

title: Divers find body of person missing from California helicopter crash that killed 2 others
text:
Police divers have found the body of a patient who went missing after a medical helicopter crashed into the Pacific Ocean off Catalina Island near Los Angeles, bringing the death toll to three while two other people were recovering from their injuries, authorities said Friday.
Divers with the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department found the victim’s body Thursday in the wreckage of the helicopter after searching more than 156 square miles (404 square kilometers) over 23 hours, the Coast Guard said in a statement.
Relatives of the missing person told ABC7 that the woman was being transported from Catalina Island to the mainland for medical care after having an allergic reaction. They also said her 20-year-old son went with her in the helicopter to help translate.
The helicopter with five people aboard went down shortly after takeoff and hit the water not far from the island, officials said. The cause is not clear and the National Transportation Safety Board is investigating.
First responders pulled four people from the water on Wednesday night.
Los Angeles County Sheriff Robert Luna said that authorities were not yet identifying the victims by name. But he described the two people who died as the male pilot and a female nurse. He also said another medic and a fourth person, a man, were hospitalized.
Luna said the helicopter wreckage was about 200 feet (60 meters) deep in the water.
The helicopter’s operator, REACH Air Medical Services of Sacramento, confirmed that two of its crew members died and a third was recovering at a hospital. The company declined to provide more details.
“In the days ahead, our focus will remain on caring for our people, supporting their families and honoring the lives and service of those we have lost,” REACH said in a statement.
A memorial service was held on the island to honor the victims.
The crash came 11 days after a firefighting helicopter went down, killing two pilots in Yosemite National Park in California, and two weeks after a news helicopter crashed in Los Angeles, killing two people.
Emergency personnel were called to the Catalina crash shortly before 8 p.m. on Wednesday. Two people were pronounced dead at the scene, and two, in stable condition, were brought to hospitals on the mainland, the Los Angeles County Fire Department said.
The helicopter landed on the island shortly after 7 p.m., following a 24-minute flight from an airport in Oceanside, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24.
The NTSB identified the aircraft as a Eurocopter EC-135-P2 and said it would be brought to a secure facility for evaluation, a board spokesperson said.
Los Angeles County Supervisor Janice Hahn called the crash a terrible tragedy.
“The people who were on board dedicated their careers to saving lives. They are heroes,” she said in a social media post.

title: Janet Mills urges action on heating assistance as Maine braces for cold
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gov. Janet Mills wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation Friday demanding more money from the federal government for heating assistance, a measure that she said is necessary to “ensure the safety and comfort of Maine people” amid record high heating oil prices.
The Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) currently provides about $40 million in assistance to qualifying households in Maine. Those funds are usually sent out in late November and applications are now open.
The governor’s request came as heating oil prices hit a record high in Maine last week, averaging $6.02 per gallon, the Department of Energy Resources said. This week, prices dropped slightly, to $5.96 per gallon — still above the previous record of $5.92 set in 2022.
Those prices were driven in large part by the continued constriction of the Strait of Hormuz, which, prior to the start of the war in Iran, carried about a quarter of the world’s oil shipments.
In her letter, Mills placed blame on President Donald Trump.
“Maine people should not be forced to choose between staying warm and putting food on the table because the president chose to drag the country into a needless war,” she wrote.
Prices that high demand an additional congressional allocation to the LIHEAP program, Mills said. Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, could be particularly hard-hit if LIHEAP funds aren’t increased, she said.
She encouraged Mainers to apply for LIHEAP funding as soon as possible. Applications and income limits can be found on MaineHousing’s website.
“Federal funding levels appropriated for LIHEAP this winter did not fully consider the drastic impacts of the president’s war that has sent fuel prices skyrocketing and are now insufficient for the circumstances that Maine and other cold-climate states now face,” Mills said.
Meanwhile, the Group of Seven wealthy democracies said Friday that they plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel also recently hit record high prices in the U.S.
Gas prices in the U.S. and abroad have soared during the eight-month war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22. Maine diesel prices averaged $6.47.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, lauded the G7 announcement Friday. She said the release should put “immediate downward pressure on energy prices and helping to lower the cost of producing and transporting goods.”
This story contains reporting from The Associated Press.

title: Happy to be ‘stuck’ in central Maine, thanks
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I was disappointed by a recent news report (“As life in Maine gets more expensive, young people struggle to keep up,” Sept. 18). As a proud Augusta resident who left Portland years ago due to — go figure — rising costs and lack of opportunity, I thought it quite rich to ascribe to my neighbor the feeling that he was “stuck in central Maine.”
The report itself makes clear my neighbor was attributing that sentiment to his friends in — I guess, to the reporter — more desirable locales, not necessarily speaking about his own feelings.
Some people want to live in Maine, even up here in the scary boondocks of central Maine, because it’s a great place to live, with great people. It’s disappointing that the reporting ignores that possibility.
Honestly, that last line (“Maybe, for now, he is [stuck].”) angered and offended me.
“Maybe,” indeed.
Stanley Abraham
Augusta

title: ‘A psychopath’: Professional boxer arrested after 2-year-old dies, 1-year-old hurt in alleged abuse
text:
MESA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A professional boxer is facing a first-degree murder charge after police say he beat and killed his girlfriend’s 2-year-old son and abused his own 1-year-old child.
Mesa police said the situation started Tuesday when paramedics responded to an apartment for a child in medical distress. First responders rushed the toddler to a hospital, where he died from his injuries.
Doctors noted suspicious bruising was found across the child’s body and contacted police, triggering a homicide investigation.
Investigators identified Kishawn Porter, 23, a professional fighter, as the suspect in the case.
Authorities said that while Porter is a professional fighter, bruising found across his knuckles did not come from training or competition, but rather from fatal child abuse.
Porter was taken into police custody on Tuesday.
“Mr. Porter hit and punched the 2-year-old victim multiple times with either his hands and/or a sandal,” a prosecutor with the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office said during Porter’s initial court appearance.
During Porter’s court appearance, prosecutors outlined a violent juvenile history, telling the judge Porter has prior adjudications for child molestation and aggravated assault involving a restrained victim.
An autopsy conducted Wednesday by the Maricopa County medical examiner revealed catastrophic internal trauma on the child that included healing and acute rib fractures, a lacerated liver and a lacerated stomach, with blood found pooling in the abdomen.
“It takes a substantial amount of force to lacerate the stomach, and the injuries were all consistent with child abuse,” court records stated. “Based on the injuries, no one could have survived the severity.”
Forensic experts noted that the child’s healing rib fractures pointed to a pattern of ongoing violence in the home rather than an isolated incident.
“That means this wasn’t the only attack,” Dr. Roy Lubit, a forensic psychiatrist who specializes in child abuse cases, said. “The idea of beating and killing an infant indicates an almost basic lack of humanity. An individual who would do the acts that are alleged would almost be overwhelmingly likely to be a psychopath.”
Detectives said Porter also abused his own 1-year-old child by spanking him, hitting him in the mouth and slapping his torso and rib cage.
Formal charges regarding the allegations involving the 1-year-old have not yet been submitted to prosecutors.
Following his arrest, two combat sports promotions announced they had cut ties with Porter due to the severity of the charges.
A judge set Porter’s bond at $1.5 million.

title: Kennedy Center Honors to be held at Capital One Arena amid fight over adding Trump's name
text:
This year’s Kennedy Center Honors will be held at Washington’s Capital One Arena, not the riverfront building that’s been at the center of a legal fight over adding President Donald Trump’s name to the building.
The 49th annual awards are set to take place at Washington’s downtown arena, a Kennedy Center spokesperson said Friday. Few other details were immediately available, and an explanation for the change wasn’t given.
The center’s board voted last month to close the iconic performing arts venue along the Potomac River waterfront after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning Trump’s name to the building.
Trump has said in social media posts that the center needed to close for safety repairs. But he said the repairs would only happen if the board was allowed to move forward with plans to add his name to the building.
A federal judge has twice said that can’t happen without the approval of Congress, which has allocated $257 million for repairs.
The president hosted the 2025 awards, whose honorees included Sylvester Stallone and George Strait. He said at the time that he would rename the facility the “Trump Kennedy Center,” and not long after workers began adding his name to the building.
The board of trustees, named by Trump, voted unanimously for the change, which has been challenged in court since.
Congress named the performing arts center as a living memorial to John F. Kennedy in 1964, the year after he was assassinated.
The law explicitly prohibits the board of trustees from making the center into a memorial to anyone else, and from putting another person’s name on the building’s exterior.
The Kennedy Center Honors, which recognize people for lifetime contributions to American culture through the performing arts, was established in 1978. The 2026 honorees are set to be named at a later day, the center’s spokesperson said. The event will take place on December 7.

title: Former GOP Rep. David Rivera sentenced to 10 years for secret Venezuela lobbying
text:
MIAMI (AP) — A former Miami congressman and longtime friend of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was sentenced Friday to 10 years in prison in connection with a secret $50 million lobbying campaign on behalf of Venezuela during the first Trump administration.
Republican David Rivera has been jailed since jurors found him guilty in May on all counts, including failing to register as a foreign agent and conspiracy to commit money laundering as part of his work for former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro ’s government.
The Republican stalwart’s seven-week trial included testimony by Rubio and offered a rare glimpse into Miami’s role as a crossroads for foreign influence campaigns aimed at shaping U.S. policy toward Latin America. President Donald Trump’s secretary of state testified during the trial that he had no idea about the lobbying and felt betrayed.

title: 🍂🏰 LAST CALL, MAINE! Visit Fort Knox & the Penobscot Narrows Bridge Before the Season Ends! 🌉
text:
Visit Fort Knox & Penobscot Narrows Bridge Before the Season Ends
This is something that every Mainer should do, but do it soon, before the 2026 season is over!
Just across the Penobscot River from Bucksport, the town of Prospect is home to the historic Fort Knox. Built between 1844 and 1869, it was the first fort in Maine built entirely of granite, most previous forts used wood, earth, and stone.
The Fort Knox Historic Site and the Penobscot Narrows Observatory Bridge, opens up to the public for the season, at the beginning of each May, and wraps up at the end of October. Both make for a really fun day of exploring for the whole family, not to mention of near perfect view of the fall foliage in the area.
The final chance to visit for the 2026 season, will be on Halloween Day, Saturday, October 31st, so make your plans now!
Read More: Bangor Waterfront Concerts 2027: Must-See Artists On Our Wishlist
The grounds will be open daily during the offseason from 9am to sunset. Dogs are welcome if they are on a 4'-6' leash, cleaned up after and not a nuisance to other guests.
The Penobscot Bridge and Penobscot Narrows Observatory, is one of the coolest experiences you can have in the state of Maine. It is the first bridge observation tower in the United States and the tallest public bridge observatory in the entire world.
The tower reaches 420 feet into the air and allows visitors to view the bridge, the nearby Fort Knox State Historic Site, the Penobscot River, and Bay, with spectacular, mind-blowing 360-degree views.
In fact, believe it or not, it is taller than the Statue of Liberty! The PNO is the tallest bridge observatory open to the public in the world. Visitors to the observatory ride Maine's fastest elevator all the way to the top.
Check out the Fort Knox website for more information, or give them a call at 207-469-6553

title: Kennebec county grand jury indictments
Democrats launch $3.4M corruption-focused ad campaign against Susan Collins
text:
A Democratic super PAC launched a $3.4 million ad campaign on Friday to highlight a recent report that accused Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of steering millions of dollars to a defense contractor in exchange for campaign contributions.
The 30-second spot from WinSenate focuses on a recent ProPublica report about illegal campaign contributions made to a pro-Collins super PAC during her 2020 campaign.
The ad features local news reports about last week’s story. It includes an older-looking woman — a key swing demographic in the race — speaking directly to the camera.
“Susan Collins took illegal campaign money and steered millions in government contracts to the donor, but Donald Trump’s administration shut down the investigation,” the woman says. “Maybe there’s a reason Susan Collins does whatever Donald Trump wants her to.”
The big-dollar ad campaign shows how Democrats are looking to turn Collins’ central campaign argument into a liability in the closing month of Maine’s closely watched Senate race.
“Chuck Schumer is bringing his New York campaign tactics to Maine,” Collins campaign spokesperson Shawn Roderick said, referring to the Democratic leader in the Senate. “His ads keep getting fact-checked as false and now he is asking Mainers to believe someone who is doing hard time in federal prison for fraud. Mainers have never fallen for his tactics and they aren’t going to now.”
Polling leading up to ProPublica’s report had shown a tight race between Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president. Jackson holds a roughly two-point lead over Collins, according to polling averages from the election website FiftyPlusOne.
The ad comes after the Senate Majority PAC, which is aligned with WinSenate, issued a Sept. 29 memo outlining its plan to make corruption a key part of its closing message to midterm voters. The group said the message ties into voters’ concerns about rising prices.
The memo notes that invoking “corrupt” and “pay-to-play politicians” is particularly effective among swing voters — a group that has repeatedly sent Collins back to Washington, D.C., despite leaning Democratic in recent statewide elections.
Republican groups are also making corruption a central argument in attacks against Jackson. They’ve run ads that highlight Jackson’s expense reimbursements while maintaining a second home in Augusta, as well as his son Chace’s work as a lobbyist while his father was Senate president.
On the campaign trail and in ads, Collins has been touting her power as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee — the first Mainer to hold the post in 92 years. She says she’s been able to bring home $1.5 billion in federal earmarks over the last five years.
But Democrats are trying to flip the script to argue she’s using that position to benefit herself by pointing to ProPublica’s report.
Last week, the outlet reported that the FBI was preparing to open a sweeping corruption probe of Collins and other powerful politicians in 2024. But the probe was shut down after Trump returned to the White House in 2025 and disbanded the anti-corruption unit.
Collins, her campaign and her staff have all vigorously denied the allegations and called the report “outrageous” and a political hit job that’s based on the word of a convicted felon. They contend Collins was cleared of wrongdoing by the Biden administration, noting the defense contractor in question, Martin Kao, of the Hawaii-based firm Navatek, was implicating Collins to have his prison sentence reduced.
An FBI spokesperson is quoted in the story saying the bureau “ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign. Any suggestion otherwise is totally false.”
The WinSenate ad is part of a more than $32.7 million investment the Democratic super PAC is making in Maine, according to the media tracking firm, Ad Impact. The PAC has nearly $18.8 million in ads reserved between now and Election Day.
But Republican groups have a significant financial advantage in the race. Those groups have spent or reserved $100.5 million on ads this cycle — nearly $38 million more than Democrat-aligned groups, according to Ad Impact. Republican groups have reserved more than $37 million in ads leading up to the election.

title: Christa Pike was on a ventilator and unconscious after failed Tennessee execution, attorneys say
text:
Christa Pike was placed on a ventilator and unconscious in a hospital in the hours after her failed execution in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.
Hospital staff, her lawyers said, were working to save Pike’s life and clear the two doses of the drug that the state uses to execute prisoners.
The stunning failure in Tennessee’s execution chamber on Wednesday has left both sides on the death penalty debate demanding answers. The state’s governor has ordered an independent review.
In the court filing, Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the lethal drug pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” they wrote.
Instead of “remedying this failure,” they prepared and administered a backup set of pentobarbital syringe, her lawyers said.
State officials have not offered any explanation about what went wrong during the execution attempt
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee demanded a review of the state’s execution procedures and indefinitely postponed Pike’s execution and another one slated for this year. Other Republican political leaders in Tennessee said the state should review whether to stop single-drug lethal injections and consider other options to carry out death sentences.
The execution team worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs, said Pike’s defense lawyer Randy Spivey, who counted at least seven needles in her left arm.
Neither the initial nor the backup dose of pentobarbital worked. Pike was still snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt.
