Gem hunter finds Arkansas diamond he claims could be worth $1 million
text:
Arkansas gem hunter finds a diamond he claims could be worth $1 million
Jack Pearadin is the first to admit that his diamond-hunting hobby hasn't paid off, despite sifting rocks for more than a dozen years.
But earlier this year, the Navy reservist and his friend shoveled a six-carat diamond from a field in Arkansas where he's found over 300 gems so far. And this one is like nothing he's dug up before — Pearadin claims collectors have told him it could be worth $1 million.
At least one experienced appraiser told The Associated Press that a diamond of such size and quality could be worth a fourth of that — still an impressive find.
“Oh my God! Oh my God!” Pearadin said as he livestreamed the discovery on TikTok. “Holy crap, we got a big one!” he yelled after rinsing gravel from a bucket and then flipping the pile onto a table to expose the shiny facets of a 6.03-carat diamond.
Roughly the size of a fingernail, it’s the largest diamond found this year at Crater of Diamonds State Park. More than 37,000 diamonds have been discovered since the former open-pit diamond mine became part of a state park in 1972.
The largest diamond found at the park, 'Uncle Sam,’ weighed 40 carats
The park charges a $15 entry fee to fill a 5-gallon bucket with rocks, and people can keep any gemstones they find. Most are small and worth maybe a few hundred dollars. The largest diamond ever unearthed in the United States, a 40.23-carat stone called the Uncle Sam, was found at the park in 1924, before it became a state park in 1972.
Pearadin, originally from Missouri, has been trying his luck at the park since 2013, even moving to nearby Murfreesboro to support his hobby — “I love it that much,” he told The Associated Press. He's sold most of his diamonds online.
Most of the 400 to 800 diamonds found at the park annually weigh about a quarter of a carat, according to park interpreter Sarah Bivens. But there have been some bigger ones, said park assistant superintendent Waymon Cox: In 2020 a 9-carat diamond was found by an Arkansas bank manager, and in 2024 a French man unearthed a 7-carat diamond.
Diamonds are found in few places in the US
Diamonds are crystallized under tremendous pressure and heat deep inside the Earth and then thrust to the surface through volcanic activity before they’re scattered by water or wind. These natural diamonds are often cloudy and oddly shaped, and lose about 25% of their weight as they're cut and polished into what a jeweler would sell, according to Nathan Renfro, senior manager at the Gemological Institute of America.
Renfro said the U.S. has only two known primary deposits of diamonds — places where columns of once-molten volcanic rock have reached the surface — Crater of Diamonds and Colorado’s Kelsey Lake, where the land was reclaimed after a commercial mining operation went out of business years ago.
Today, that leaves the Arkansas park as one of the only places in the world where anyone can hunt for diamonds and take their finds with them.
“It’s a pretty remarkable operation that that’s available to the public,” Renfro said. “Most diamond mines are super high security.”
So can Jack finally get a big payday?
A typical .17-carat diamond from the park can sell for around $700, said certified gem appraiser Laura Stanley in Little Rock. But a high-quality six-carat yellow diamond from the park can sell for about $250,000, she said, partly because of their origin.
“They are their own entity,” Stanley said. “It’s the only place in America where you can go find your own diamond and you can’t compare that to a diamond from anywhere else.”
The Uncle Sam crystal was cut and polished into a 12.42-carat diamond gifted to the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, where it's on view in the “Great American Diamonds” exhibit.
Pearadin named his latest and biggest find the “American Dream.”
“It’s just this massive, gorgeous yellow diamond,” Pearadin said. He plans to split the profits with fellow gem hunter Michael Schumacher of Wisconsin, who helped dig the gravel that produced the stone, and open his own crystal mine.

title: Maine author releases psychological thriller ‘The Golden House’
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Jonathan McCarthy is returning to the WABI Book Club with his latest novel, a psychological thriller titled “The Golden House.”
Book Summary
“This is the first book in a trilogy centered around a powerful Maine family beginning in 1939. The Golden House (a private psychiatric hospital) promises healing, discretion—and a cure for those society considers unfit. When Oliver Orwell and his troubled mother, Anna, become patients, they discover that compassion can conceal cruelty and trust can become obsession. Behind the institution’s elegant gates, some secrets are never meant to escape.”
Author draws on decades in the field
McCarthy draws on his career as inspiration.
“I have worked in or around psychiatric hospitals for much of the past 30 years and during that time learned of antiquated laws that allowed people to be committed based on the word of a family member. Like a husband having his wife committed,” he said. “The real-life challenge of psychiatric care at that time was that we didn’t have medications that were effective in treating mental illness. That led to marginalized people in society being subject to admission at facilities who were not really capable of effective treatment.”
McCarthy said this book started out as a short story for a weekly contest back in 2023. He said it did not win, but it was well received and readers wanted to know what happened.
“The Golden House” is available on Amazon and is included as part of the Kindle Unlimited plan.

title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: Sacrificing Safety?
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A crash can change a life in seconds and in many American cars, a safety feature designed to keep front-seat passengers from hitting each other is still missing.
Plus, when deadly crashes keep happening, families want more than promises — they want safer streets before another life is lost.
Sacrificing Safety?
They’re an auto safety innovation in cars around the world: airbags that can protect you and your front-seat passenger from hitting each other in a side-impact crash. When drivers and front-seat passengers collide, the result can be serious head injuries or death. But even though those airbags were first introduced in the U.S., many cars here don’t have them. Why?
Crash tests in Europe in 2020 drove the adoption of those airbags, but the U.S. doesn’t do that type of testing. Authorities here question whether the airbags are necessary – but the world’s largest auto safety equipment supplier tells us lives are being lost unnecessarily due to the lack of airbags that manufacturers already know how to incorporate into their vehicles.
We’ll speak with one accident victim who says a front-center airbag could have prevented her from suffering a devastating head injury and the lifelong consequences.
A goal to end traffic deaths by 2050. Is it working?
More than 36,000 people were killed on American roads last year — according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration — a reminder that for too many families, a routine drive can end in tragedy.
In Phoenix, city leaders are trying to reduce deadly crashes — but acknowledge the work is far from done. Reporter Amy Cutler looks at the city’s safety plan, the gaps that remain, and one family’s loss.
Loud car modifications: What’s legal, what’s not
For many people, a quiet night at home or a meal outside can be interrupted in an instant by the roar of a revving engine or a backfiring exhaust.
In North Carolina — as in many states — vehicles must meet muffler and exhaust requirements. But police say catching violators can be difficult. Reporter Jamie Boll in Charlotte explains what’s legal, what isn’t, and why neighbors want action.
How ‘convenient spending’ could drain your budget
We all do it from time to time – shell out money to save a little time or make life easier. It’s called convenient spending.
In this Watching Your Wallet, Consumer Investigator Rachel DePompa shows us why convenience can act like a monthly trap, silently draining your budget.

title: Supreme Court preview: New term brings Second Amendment, voting rights cases
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A new term at the U.S. Supreme Court begins Monday.
The term follows a session in which the Supreme Court struck down the president’s tariffs and his executive order on birthright citizenship. Justices this term are set to hear a number of notable cases.
Among the cases on the docket is Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to bans on AR-15-style rifles.
Georgetown Law professor Michele Goodwin said the case is significant.
“Well, this is an important case because we see the Supreme Court’s efforts to give life to individual liberties associated with the Second Amendment and gun rights,” Goodwin said. “You see that further cemented in this challenge. We don’t know how the Supreme Court would rule, but, you know, there are some tea leaves that we could follow. The Second Amendment has truly gained speed, if you will, before the United States Supreme Court.”
Also on the docket is Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota. The case concerns whether the National Voter Registration Act or a federal consent decree takes precedence over state documentary proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registration.
“What this case is ultimately about is whether the Voter Registration Act would prohibit what is basically, in essence, happening in Arizona,” Goodwin said.
The court is also likely to hear cases from the so-called shadow docket, or emergency docket, which lets parties seek expedited Supreme Court intervention before a case completes the ordinary appeals process.
“But the argument has been that the Supreme Court that the Trump administration has been able to have a speed pass jump its way to the Supreme Court, which has meant that the lower courts have not been able to actually deal with these cases,” Goodwin said.
During his second term, President Trump has appealed to the shadow docket more than any other president. According to both the White House and the Department of Justice, that will likely continue.

The generous collective support of five prestigious Maine organizations on the cusp of October’s Domestic VIolence Awareness Month will help us continue to provide essential resources and support to our sister survivors in every county in our state, as well as expand our impactful survivor-informed educational program in middle schools and high schools.”

title: The Most Overrated Horror Movies Of All Time
text:
The 10 Most Overrated Horror Movies Of All Time
The great thing about horror movies is that there are tons of them out there, and a lot of them are great. If you’re a horror fan, you’ve probably seen the classics, movies like The Thing or The Exorcist or Rosemary’s Baby or Scream or Hereditary or Dracula that have stood the test of time and are basically regarded by most people as straight up good movies. No arguments there. (All movies have their detractors, but, by and large, the canon is the canon.)
And then there are movies regarded as classics that absolutely do not deserve that honor at all. Crowd-pleasing blockbuster sensations they may have been in their time, but some beloved horror movies are vastly overrated, to the point where we wonder why we’re all kidding ourselves. Every genre has its share of overrated entries, but, for some reason, horror has tons of them. These movies aren’t necessarily bad — we even like some of them!— they’re just not that good, or not good enough to warrant all the praise that’s been heaped upon them over the years.
So, it’s time to set the record straight. All of the movies on this list are movies we’d call overrated for a lot of different reasons. Maybe they made a splash when they first came out and the effect has diminished over the years. Maybe the crazy gross-out effects just don’t hit like they should. Maybe the violence is the only notable thing about them. Maybe the plot is just kind of disappointing compared to the hype. Whatever the reason, we’re un-canonizing these horror favorites starting today.

title: Freeport football dominates possession in win over Morse
text:
FREEPORT — The Freeport football team understood it needed long drives on offense and to dominate on defense against Morse.
The Falcons put together a drive of nine-plus minutes in the fourth quarter to secure a 20-6 win Friday in a game between Class D South contenders.
Sam Willard, a senior who replaced injured starting quarterback Andrew Thomas, ran for 101 yards on 21 carries a touchdown. He also had a touchdown pass.
“Sam’s been playing varsity football since he was a freshman, he always grinds it out and works hard,” said Freeport coach Paul St. Pierre. “He was excited, enthusiastic, and worked hard all week.”
Thomas, who injured his throwing hand in a 14-6 loss to Winslow last week, played defense for the Falcons (4-1) on Friday.
Leading 14-6 entering the fourth quarter, Freeport put together a 10-play drive that burned 9:13 off the block. The Falcons didn’t score, but they used up enough time to prevent a Morse comeback.
The Shipbuilders (3-2) played without starting quarterback Dylan Root and running back Junuh Hays.
Freeport held Morse to 91 yards.
“We did a rush a little bit (early),” Willard said. “But in the second half, we chilled a little bit, chewed up the clock a little bit, and used that to our advantage.”
Willard scored on a 13-yard run with 1:32 left.
Top of the standings
With the win, Freeport has a tight hold on the No. 1 seed in the D South Crabtree standings. The Falcons beat defending state champion Winthrop 29-28 on Sept. 11.
“This is huge,” said Freeport senior running back Keegan Haveran, who rushed for 66 yards and scored a touchdown. “Just coming back from a loss, getting this big win, we needed it. It secured a good position in the playoffs.”
The Falcons still have a tough final stretch of the season, including a Class C battle on the road next week against Wells, before finishing with divisional opponents Dirigo and Lisbon.
Run, run, run
There were just eight passing attempts between the teams. Willard was 3 of 5 for 20 yards, including a 13-yard touchdown pass to Bryson Jack in the second quarter that gave the Falcons a 14-6 lead.
Freeport didn’t need to pass because it had so much success on the ground, rushing for 200 yards.
The clock also ran. Due the high volume of rushing and disciplined play, the game lasted just 95 minutes.
Standouts for the Shipbuilders
Senior running back Caden Wells ran for 68 yards on 17 carries and scored the Shipbuilders’ lone touchdown.
“It was an incredible effort from our kids tonight, I’m so proud of them and their resilience,” Morse coach Jason Darling said. “Their adaptability was fantastic.”
On defense, the duo of Olliver Roderiques and Clay Plummer made multiple stops in Freeport’s backfield. Plummer, a defensive lineman, lined up as a fullback at times.
Special mark for Paul St. Pierre
St. Pierre, who was hired as Freeport’s head coach in April 2015, earned his 50th victory with the program.
“I’ll be honest, it’s not something I ever thought about before (Friday night),” St. Pierre said. “My first year, we were 0-8. I couldn’t imagine 10 wins. To get 50, that’s pretty sweet, but it just means I’m getting older.”
Players greeted him in the postgame huddle with a sign celebrating the occasion, which he ran through before the team broke the huddle.
“They deserve (the success),” St. Pierre said. “Some of these guys have worked their butts off for four years, they went through some adversity. To see them get rewarded for their hard work, it’s worth it.”
Statistical leaders
• Freeport: Sam Willard (21 carries, 101 yards; 3 of 5 passing, 20 yards, 2 TDs), Keegan Haveran (8 carries, 68 yards, TD)
• Morse: Caden Wells (17 carries, 68 yards, TD), Logan True (7 carries, 33 yards)

title: Jury acquits fired Florida sheriff's deputy in killing of Black U.S. Airforce Airman Roger Fortson
text:
A former Florida sheriff’s deputy has been found not guilty of manslaughter with a firearm in the killing of a Black U.S. Air Force airman fatally shot at his apartment during a domestic disturbance call.
An Okaloosa County jury acquitted Eddie Duran, 38, on Thursday. Duran had faced up to 30 years in prison.
Duran, who is Hispanic, worked for the Okaloosa County sheriff’s department in May 2024 when he responded to Roger Fortson’s Fort Walton Beach apartment near Hurlburt Field, where the airman was stationed.
The sheriff’s office had said the deputy “reacted in self-defense after he encountered a 23-year-old man armed with a gun.” The shooting was captured on the deputy’s body camera.
The video shows the deputy banging on the door and stepping aside, seemingly out of view of the door. Twice he shouted: “Sheriff’s office! Open the door!”
Fortson opened the door and could be seen holding what appeared to be a handgun pointed down toward the floor. The deputy shouted, “Step back!” and fired off shots. He then shouted, “Drop the gun! Drop the gun!”
“It’s over there,” Fortson said.
“Drop the gun!” the deputy yelled back.
“I don’t have it,” Fortson said, lying on the ground.
The deputy then called paramedics on his radio.
Fortson later died at a hospital. The domestic disturbance report that led Duran to Fortson’s apartment turned out to be false.
After the shooting, authorities said Fortson was alone in the apartment and on the phone with his girlfriend.
Fortson was assigned as a missions operator to the 4th Special Operations Squadron at Hurlburt Field. He was a member of the squadron’s AC-130J Ghostrider aircrew, which loads the gunship’s 30 mm and 105 mm cannons during missions.
The State Attorney’s office prosecuted Duran and said in a news release that it accepts the jury’s verdict, which means the state “did not prove the criminal charge beyond a reasonable doubt to the satisfaction of every juror.”
“We understand that this verdict will cause pain, anger, or disappointment for many people, particularly some members of the community who view Senior Airman Fortson’s death within a context of encounters nationally involving law enforcement,” the State Attorney’s office said. “Those reactions should not be dismissed.”
Duran was fired after an internal sheriff’s office investigation later determined his life was not in danger when he shot Fortson.
Duran’s attorney, Rod Smith, said the shooting was a police officer safety issue and that Duran went to Fortson’s apartment “to find out what was going on based on a complaint from a neighbor.”
“None of this needed to happen,” Smith told The Associated Press on Friday. “(Fortson) absolutely knew a police officer was at the door. Deputy Duran, himself, was also a victim of a terrible tragedy. He had followed his training. The guy answered the door with a semiautomatic pistol in his hand.”
It is highly unusual for Florida law enforcement officers to be charged for an on-duty killing — it has only happened four times in the last 35 years before Fortson’s killing. Even then, only one of those officers was convicted.
“Deputies perform essential and often dangerous work every day, and are entitled to the same presumption of innocence and fair process as everyone else accused of a crime,” the State Attorney’s office said. “At the same time, the authority to use deadly force must remain subject to independent review. Presenting disputed evidence to a jury is part of that accountability and is essential to public trust.”
Fortson’s killing renewed looks at controversial “Stand Your Ground” laws in Florida and some other states where gun owners can claim self-defense after carrying out shootings. Critics have denounced them as “shoot first” laws that have created a climate of vigilantism in which gun owners operate with impunity in largely killing Black people.
Fortson carried his legally owned handgun to the door of his apartment after hearing banging noises that ended up being a sheriff’s deputy. It was the deputy who opened fire, not Fortson.
A federal civil rights lawsuit was filed last year by Fortson’s family against Duran, Sheriff Eric Aden and others, according to Ben Crump, a prominent attorney who represents the family in the lawsuit.
“This is a painful moment for everyone who loved Roger Fortson, and his family is heartbroken,” Crump said in a statement. “His family has lived with that loss every day for more than two years, and this verdict is incredibly hard for them.”
___
Williams reported from Detroit.

title: Mobile outreach meets people with substance use disorders where they are
text:
Adam Bloom-Paicopolos, MPP, is the executive director at the Alliance for Addiction & Mental Health Services, Maine’s statewide association for community behavioral health providers serving over 120,000 Mainers annually.
Most communities share a common goal: to care for one another, especially during times of vulnerability. Today, many individuals face complex challenges related to substance use, mental health and housing instability. While there are no simple answers, there are thoughtful, practical approaches that can make a meaningful difference, one person at a time.
One approach to substance use that has been gaining momentum across the country is secondary prevention.
At its core, secondary prevention is not about enabling harmful behavior. It is about preserving life, reducing immediate risk and creating pathways to recovery when individuals are ready. It recognizes that no two people are the same and that progress often begins with trust, respect and individualized support.
As part of this programming, mobile outreach units offer a flexible way to deliver that support directly to individuals who may not otherwise access care. Instead of requiring people to navigate complex systems on their own, trained professionals meet them where they are, physically and emotionally, with services tailored to their specific needs and circumstances.
This model prioritizes individualized intervention. Some individuals may be ready for immediate connection to detox or treatment, while others may need time, information or basic support before taking that step. Mobile outreach allows for real-time assessment and response, offering health screenings, referrals and rapid connections to care based on each person’s readiness.
Peer support is a critical component of this approach. Specialists with lived experience bring credibility and empathy that help build trust quickly. Their presence can turn a moment of hesitation into a moment of possibility, offering not just guidance but hope grounded in personal experience.
In addition to connection and counseling, mobile outreach provides practical, life-saving
resources. These include naloxone to reverse overdoses, wound assessment and basic first aid and crisis support. Just as important, individuals can be connected to housing assistance, social services and behavioral healthcare, because recovery is not just about treatment, but about stability and the opportunity to rebuild.
This work is not done in isolation. Mobile outreach is designed to coordinate with existing providers, healthcare systems and first responders, strengthening, not duplicating, the services already in place. By filling gaps and improving access, it helps create a more responsive and effective system overall.
There is also a practical benefit for the broader community. Early, individualized intervention often reduces reliance on emergency services. When people receive timely support, communities frequently see fewer emergency room visits, hospitalizations and crisis calls. This not only improves outcomes for individuals but also helps manage public resources more effectively.
Across the country, programs like this are demonstrating measurable results: reductions in overdose deaths, increased engagement in treatment and stronger connections between individuals and care providers. These outcomes are not the result of a single solution, but of a consistent commitment to meeting people as individuals, with dignity and without judgment.
That principle matters. Every person’s path is different, shaped by their history, circumstances, and readiness for change. A one-size-fits-all approach cannot fully address such complexity. What can make the difference is a model that is flexible, responsive and grounded in human connection.
Supporting secondary prevention and mobile outreach is a person-centered and practical step forward. It reflects a balanced approach. One that values safety, responsibility and compassion equally. It is not about lowering expectations, but about removing barriers so that individuals can take meaningful steps toward stability and recovery.
In the end, community well-being is built not only through systems, but through moments of connection. A conversation. A referral. A life saved. A path forward. Sometimes the most effective solutions begin by simply meeting people where they are and walking alongside them from there.

title: Thousands of US troops heading to Mideast amid uncertainty about war's direction
text:
Thousands of US troops heading to Mideast amid uncertainty about war's direction
President Donald Trump told voters Thursday that the conflict with Iran would end quickly, after previously suggesting that he might ramp up strikes following midterm elections.
Thousands of US troops heading to Mideast amid uncertainty about war's direction
President Donald Trump told voters Thursday that the conflict with Iran would end quickly, after previously suggesting that he might ramp up strikes following midterm elections.
The U.S. military is deploying roughly 9,000 troops to the Middle East aboard a group of ships, including a third aircraft carrier, according to The Associated Press. The move will bring the American naval presence in the region to more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, an unusually high number.
It comes after President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s latest peace proposal. He also told Time Magazine in an interview published Thursday that he might ramp up strikes after November’s midterm elections.
However, during campaign stops in Texas and Oklahoma on Thursday, Trump told voters that the conflict would be over soon.
"Just as I promised, I'm sure that Iran will be very quickly ended. I will tell you, the energy prices are going to be rapidly, rapidly come down," Trump said.
Trump initially predicted that the war, which began Feb. 28, 2026, would last for a matter of weeks.
A new AP-NORC Center poll shows that about half of U.S. adults are "extremely" or "very" concerned about affording gas in the coming months. The survey also found that 69% believe the war has not been worth fighting.
Trump acknowledged that the war could hurt Republicans during the midterm elections while speaking to reporters Thursday.
"Well, it's possible," Trump said. "It should help because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon. So when you say, 'Is it OK for Iran to have a nuclear weapon?' I would say 100% of the people say no, including worldwide. So, when you say it that way, it would help. If you don't say that, it could hurt, yeah."
Trump was also asked about possible Iranian involvement in the recent attempted crash of an Israel-bound flight.
"I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes, but we're working on it right now," Trump said.
Trump added that, if Iran was involved, the Islamic Republic would be hit "very hard" in retaliation for the incident, which endangered the lives of more than 180 passengers aboard the jet.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News earlier Thursday that it was too early to determine Iran’s involvement but noted that investigators believe the suspect was radicalized.
Some worry Tehran may be turning to asymmetrical tactics as part of a strategy shift since the U.S. has had greater success opening up the Strait of Hormuz to shipping traffic.

title: Midcoast Victorian inn sells for $3.3M
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A stately Victorian inn on Talbot Avenue in Rockland has been sold to a new owner.
An entity named EJ Estates LLC, which has a local address, purchased the inn for $3.3 million.
The transaction closed on Sept. 21, according to a transfer tax declaration form filed with the state.
The company that sold the inn, Maude & Dixie LLC, was the second owner of the business, which originally was built as a private home in the 1890s, according to the city’s assessing records. The original owner, Charles H. Berry, was a prominent local merchant who had the 6,000-square-foot structure built as a home for his new wife, MaineBiz reported in 2020.
“Renowned for its homemade pies, grand hospitality with a Victorian flair, luxurious comfort and genuine hospitality, our romantic Rockland, Maine inn offers the ideal mid-coast location for exploring Maine’s arts, heritage, lighthouses and coastal sights,” the inn’s website says.
The business has 12 guest rooms, each with either a queen- or king-sized bed, an en-suite bathroom and a working fireplace. The property is one of several in the Rockland Residential Historic District, which is listed in the National Register of Historic Places.
Previous owners Cheryl Michaelsen and Michael LaPosta opened the inn in 1999, a year after they purchased the property for $300,000, city records indicate. The current assessed value of the property, which includes a 0.6-acre parcel of land the inn sits on, is $1.2 million.
Maude & Dixie LLC also owned the neighboring Talbot House inn, but sold that property earlier this year, according to Midcoast Villager. Katie Witt and James Wood, doing business as Wittwood Estates LLC, purchased Talbot House in late May for $1.3 million, the Villager reported.
Additional information about the company that purchased the inn was unavailable Friday afternoon.

title: Florida woman accused of telling Claude AI she was going to 'shoot up the sheriff's office'
text:
Florida woman accused of telling Claude AI she was going to 'shoot up the sheriff's office'
A woman from Bonita Springs, Florida, was arrested after she was accused of using an artificial intelligence platform to make violent threats against the Lee County Sheriff's Office.
According to investigators, Carli Michelle Heller, 30, reportedly wrote a threat on Anthropic's Claude AI platform. The platform auto-flagged the messages and escalated them to a human review team, which then notified law enforcement.
The arrest report states that on Sept. 26 at approximately 5:10 a.m., Heller reportedly wrote, "I'm going to shoot up the sheriff's right the [expletive] now." The following day, at approximately 1:07 a.m., she was accused of posting, "This is 100% last chance I'm done. I got a new [expletive] gun today. [Expletive] you."
Deputies responded to Heller's residence, where she was detained without incident. She's facing a charge of written threats of violence.
In the same week, deputies also arrested a man who they said posted a threat targeted at Sheriff Carmine Marceno in an AI-generated image showing him running away and injured as two people shoot at him.
Legal analyst and attorney Michael Raheb explained the challenges of proving such threats in court.
"They're going to argue that is a direct threat because you have the individual person and you show a violent act towards that individual. And that may be their theory. I would tell you, it's not going to be easy," Raheb said.
Raheb also highlighted the complexities of hate speech on AI platforms.
"This is a very slippery slope. We gotta remember the First Amendment, a right to free speech," he said. "As long as it doesn't cross that threshold, like I said, and harm someone."
Dr. Chrissann Ruehle, assistant professor of AI ethics at Florida Gulf Coast University, emphasized the responsibility of technology developers in preventing harmful applications.
"The technology developers have a responsibility to develop some guardrails around how the AI is being developed, and if some harmful applications are developed, they have a responsibility for flagging those," Ruehle said.
Marceno issued a statement warning about the risks of anonymity in AI platforms, saying, "Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool, and like any technology, it can be misused. When someone uses AI to make or facilitate a threat, we have to take that threat seriously. Users need to understand that you are never truly anonymous."
These cases highlight concerns about how artificial intelligence is changing the way threats are identified and addressed.

title: Maine Marathon: What to know for Sunday’s event in Portland
text:
The 35th edition of the Maine Community Bank Maine Marathon, Half Marathon and Marathon Relay takes place Sunday on the streets of Portland, Falmouth, Cumberland and Yarmouth, beginning at 7:45 a.m.
The largest marathon in Maine, the overall field is approaching 5,500 entries — well above last year’s record of 5,144.
“I’m limiting the growth to about 400 runners per year,” said Bob Dunfey, the volunteer race director.
The Maine Marathon and its participants have raised over $8,900,000 for charity. The event donates about 40% of revenue toward a variety of charities. Last year, donations totaled $793,285. Each year, the race picks three to five “designated charities.” This year’s beneficiaries are Nanna’s House, Day One, Camp No Limits, and the Pine Tree Society. Many other groups benefit from fundraising done by runners.
Here are key details about the Maine Marathon.
Start/finish: The marathon and half marathon start simultaneously on Baxter Boulevard in Portland. Both races also finish there.
Course: Essentially out-and-back. The course curls around Portland’s Back Cove, works it way to Route 1 North and then veers onto Route 88. The 26.2-mile marathon course goes through Falmouth and Cumberland before reaching the 12-mile mark in Yarmouth. Runners turn right onto Gilman Road, then another right onto Princes Point road to begin a roughly 3-mile loop to get back to Route 88, where they’ll head south on their return. The 13.1-mile half marathon follows the same route until it gets to a turnaround just past scenic Mussel Cove in Falmouth.
Event records: Men’s marathon — Ryan Eiler, Boston, 2 hours, 19 minutes, 19 seconds (2022); Women’s marathon — Abby Hamilton, Yarmouth, 2:39:38 (2021); Men’s half marathon — Colin Cernik, Portland, 1:04:39 (2025); Women’s half marathon, Cliodhna O’Malley, Windham, 1:15:06 (2025).
Prize money: The top male, female and non-binary runners earn $1,000 for the marathon and $500 for the half marathon, with cash through fifth place in each gender group if the runner meets the elite standard. Prizes are also available for a new event record in the marathon ($500) and half marathon ($250).
Top runners: The 2025 marathon winners, Sammy Mills of Portland and Emma Howe of Cambridge, Massachusetts, are not entered to defend their titles. The fastest local runners have migrated to the half marathon, including defending champions and event record holders Cernik and O’Malley. There are as many as 10 runners capable of challenging Cernik’s men’s record. The women’s half marathon features the past four winners — O’Malley, Phoebe Oehmig (2024), Veronica Graziano (2023) and Alyson Ursiny (2022). Megan O’Neil of Rochester, Michigan, is a serious threat. O’Neil ran a 2:31 at the Boston Marathon this spring, finishing 20th overall.
New this year: There will be lactation tents for the benefit of nursing mothers at the start/finish, and also near the 12- and 15-mile marks on the marathon course. … Instead of a starter’s gun or boat horn, the start of the chip-timed races will be signaled by a series of musical notes.
Race packet pickup: The runner’s expo on Saturday is at a new location. Runners can pick up their racing bib and T-shirt at Innovation Hall on the University of New England’s Portland campus from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Numerous vendors will be at the expo.
Race registrations: Dunfey said entries have come from 49 states (only North Dakota is missing), as well as Washington, D.C., the U.S. Virgin Island, Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, and 15 foreign countries. As of 3 p.m. Thursday, registration was still open but fast approaching the 5,500 cap.

title: Group of Seven to release barrels of stockpiled fuel
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The Group of Seven - a collection of some of the world’s largest economies - announced on Friday the release of 100 million barrels of fuel from its emergency stockpile following record-high fuel prices in September.
Oil prices have risen to record levels globally. The G7’s release of crude and diesel barrels marks a rare move intended to cap the cost of diesel.
The barrels come from the G7’s emergency stockpile, which is set aside for global supply shortages.
Wars in Ukraine and Iran have reduced the global fuel supply. Diesel has been particularly affected, with American farmers and the shipping industry facing a heavy impact.
With the midterm elections now days away, the Trump administration had considered restricting U.S. diesel exports, including a possible outright ban, to lower costs before November.
The G7’s release appears to end that possibility; the group’s statement said the release comes with an agreement among member nations not to limit energy exports to allied countries.
President Trump said in a Truth Social post the process will begin “immediately.” French President Emmanuel Macron said the release would happen over four months.
The move could reduce diesel prices by a few cents per gallon, according to experts, who added the effect would likely be temporary. Releasing stockpiled barrels does little to increase refinery capacity or production, experts said.

title: Putin warns Russia will use 'all weapons,' including nuclear, if any of its territory is attacked
text:
Putin warns Russia will use 'all weapons,' including nuclear, if any of its territory is attacked
President Vladimir Putin on Thursday reiterated Moscow's long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries but will respond to aggression with “all weapons" in its arsenal.
In remarks at a foreign policy forum, Putin accused the West and Europe of escalating tensions by talking about preparing for a war with Moscow in the coming years, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea, and seizing Russian vessels.
His remarks followed Moscow's warning to NATO that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad should any members of the military alliance try to cut off the Baltic exclave from the rest of Russia.
Several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that NATO is preparing (an) air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and (the) Kaliningrad region.”
They accused European leaders of “playing a dangerous game” by saying Russia might attack another country or ramp up a campaign of destabilizing attacks with drones and sabotage. Moscow has called the allegations absurd.
Video below: On campaign trail, Trump says politics is like war, look at Putin
“There should be no mistake — Russia would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate (the) Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country,” the Russian Embassy in Ireland said in its statement on Tuesday.
Asked at the Valdai Club forum Thursday whether Russia was on the cusp of a war with NATO or whether both were trying to intimidate each other, Putin said: “It's not intimidation, it’s a response to an attempt to intimidate us.”
Putin said that “everything is written correctly” in the earlier warning to NATO.
“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case we mean Kaliningrad, or maybe some other territories — of course, inevitably and immediately the question of Russian Federation using all weapons at the disposal of our country will appear on the agenda,” he said.
Putin didn’t specify whether Moscow would use nuclear weapons but said it has arms that “no one else has” and would determine which to use in case of an attack.
NATO pushed back against Russian nuclear rhetoric
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed Wednesday that Russia had sent a written message to the U.S.-led military alliance. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” she said in a statement.
Hart insisted NATO is not targeting Kaliningrad and had sent a reply noting that “NATO is a defensive alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia.”
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Wednesday the bloc's response to the message was “short and concise."
“Basically what we said is, ‘Hey, listen, we are defensive alliance, and stop the nuclear threat. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful,’” Rutte told Euronews.
NATO's response also urged Russia to stop its “unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine,” now in its fifth year.
The Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad sits between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. It is home to Russia’s main Baltic navy base and other military assets, and nuclear-capable Iskander missiles are deployed there.
Western military officers have said that key military installations in Kaliningrad would be a likely first target should Russia ever attack any NATO ally.
NATO allies have conducted military exercises in the Baltic Sea region in recent months. More are planned in October. It launched Operation Baltic Sentry there last year to protect communication cables and pipelines.
On Aug. 18, NATO held an exercise over northern Poland and the Baltic region involving several aircraft, including an EA-37B Compass Call — a sophisticated American plane that can jam communications and radar, the U.S. Air Forces in Europe said.
Defense analysts believe the unannounced, large-scale exercise would not have been welcomed by the Kremlin.
Rutte urges continued focus on supporting Ukraine
European leaders and intelligence services have warned that Russia could be ready to strike at another country within a few years, especially if it wins its war on Ukraine.
Rutte told Euronews that Russia is trying “to divide us and lose the focus” on defending Ukraine.
“We will not,” he said, adding that the best way to respond is to provide Kyiv with more support.
“That’s the message. Calm, carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going. That’s how we deal with it," Rutte said.

title: A look at the work of CMP's troubleshooters as Public Utilities Commission considers rate hikes
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A look at the work of Central Maine Power's troubleshooters as Public Utilities Commission considers rate hikes
Central Maine Power says the money would go toward upgrading infrastructure, which would ease the burden for troubleshooters.
A look at the work of Central Maine Power's troubleshooters as Public Utilities Commission considers rate hikes
Central Maine Power says the money would go toward upgrading infrastructure, which would ease the burden for troubleshooters.
Troubleshooters, as Central Maine Power calls them, are essentially the first responders of the electrical grid. They are the first to respond to calls as mundane as reconnecting electrical boxes to cleaning up downed trees on power lines.
The Portland district has two troubleshooters who are on during the day.
"During a blue sky day like today, perhaps we could be out there within ten minutes, depending on where it is," said Cameron Goodhart, a manager of operations at Central Maine Power.
Maine's Total Coverage followed one of Central Maine Power's troubleshooters named Kevin Wedgewood. Typically, he drives around solo.
His day started responding to a customer who needed to be reconnected to the grid. Wedgewood said calls like this are some of the easiest he gets. While Friday was a slower day for Wedgewood, storms or intense heatwaves can slow troubleshooters down with several calls.
After his first call, he responded to a report of a downed tree branch on power lines in Westbrook.
Wedgewood said, typically a downed branch touching multiple lines would've meant a power outage for thousands of customers. However, the power lines in this area have been upgraded to "tree wire," which allows the branch to rest there safely.
"If we didn't have tree wire up here, it would have caused an outage on both circuits, probably affecting about half of Westbrook," Wedgewood said.
It also would have been an emergency call, rather than something they respond to days later on a slower day.
Central Maine Power's proposed rate hike
CMP is requesting a $189 million increase to rates in order to help upgrade equipment that failed or got close to failing this summer. The staff at the Maine Public Utilities Commission recently recommended the agency deny the rate hike, and most recently Central Maine Power filed exceptions in response to the recommendation.
All of those documents, along with hundreds of public comments, will be considered by the Public Utilities Commission next week.
Central Maine Power said the money would go toward upgrading infrastructure.
"A lot of the calls that we do have are from the aging infrastructure. So, that plays a big part in the calls that we get on a day-to-day basis," Goodhart said.
For example, tree wire to replace bare wire, which is susceptible to falling branches. Central Maine Power said that 90% of its distribution systems use bare wire.
The electric company has also said that the temporary hike would cover infrastructure that has already been built.
The Public Utilities Commission said the rate hike would result in a $11.06 monthly increase to the average residential customer.
Many public comments have been made against the rate hike, citing issues with affordability.
The Office of the Public Advocate has also objected to the rate increase.
The rate increase would go into effect May 1, 2027, if it is approved.

title: Christa Pike was on a ventilator and unconscious after failed Tennessee execution, attorneys say
text:
NASHVILLE (AP) — Christa Pike remained in a hospital where she was on a ventilator and unconscious after her failed execution in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.
Hospital staff was working to save Pike’s life and “clear the pentobarbital she was administered from her system” as of late Thursday, the attorneys said.
Pike was given two doses of the drug in a failed attempt Wednesday to execute her.
In the court filing, Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” they wrote.
They wrote that instead of “remedying this failure,” they prepared and administered a backup set of pentobarbital syringes.
State officials have not offered any explanation about what went wrong during the execution attempt
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee demanded a review of the state’s execution procedures and indefinitely postponed Pike’s execution and another one slated for this year. Other Republican political leaders in Tennessee said the state should review whether to stop single-drug lethal injections and consider other options to carry out death sentences.
The execution team worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs, said Pike’s defense lawyer Randy Spivey, who counted at least seven needles in her left arm.
Neither the initial nor the backup dose of pentobarbital worked. Pike was still snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt.
In directly communicating with WVLT8, attorneys wrote:
“Christa remains critically ill and is receiving medical care for the devastating effects of Wednesday night’s events. As detailed in today’s filing, Christa remains hospitalized following Wednesday night’s failed execution attempt. She is critically ill, unconscious, intubated and receiving breathing assistance through a ventilator. She is being treated for the serious effects of the pentobarbital administered during the execution attempt, including significant injuries to both arms.”

title: What kind of Maine do you wish to help create?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sondra Shapiro has more than 40 years of experience in mature-market publishing. She is the former executive editor of the award-winning 50+ Advocate Newspaper in Massachusetts. She lives in Ogunquit.
When you walk into the voting booth, what kind of future are you voting for?
Ask yourself: What do I want for my own life, and for the lives of the people I care about?
I don’t have children or grandchildren of my own, but most of my friends do. Watching them babysit, spend time with their families and talk endlessly about the people they love, their devotion is unmistakable. Because I love my friends, I want the exact same things for them that they want for their families: happiness, security and a better tomorrow.
But this question is not only about parents or grandparents. It is about every Mainer. It is about the young adult trying to build a life here, the working family trying to keep up with rising costs, the older neighbor relying on Social Security or Medicare and anyone who wants to feel secure in the place they call home.
So when I enter the voting booth, I try to think beyond the candidate or the party. I think about the country and the state we are creating.
Right now we are watching the boundaries of executive power being tested in Washington. We have seen the federal government attempt to exert control over aspects of how states conduct elections, including voting by mail. Maine fought back, joining a coalition of states to challenge those rules in court; a legal battle that culminated in the U.S. Supreme Court upholding our voting rights. Our state also successfully blocked a federal lawsuit attempting to force the release of Mainers’ private voter data.
Is that federal overreach the direction we want our country to take?
If so, we should be honest with ourselves about it. If not, we need to think seriously about the importance of checks and balances. No president should have unchecked power. The protections built into our system are there precisely because power changes hands.
Whoever represents Maine in the Senate will also have a constitutional role in confirming Supreme Court nominees if vacancies occur. The president nominates them, but the Senate provides advice and consent. Those decisions can affect our country for decades.
But this isn’t only about government and institutions. It is about our everyday lives.
I think about Social Security. Medicare. The cost of living. Housing. Healthcare.
Maine is not a state where most families have unlimited financial cushions. For many people, the cost of housing, food, healthcare and raising children is not an abstract economic discussion. It is the arithmetic of everyday life.
Some Mainers are worried about whether they can afford to stay in the communities they love. Others are trying to buy a first home, pay for college, care for an aging parent or manage medical bills. Many are simply wondering whether the next generation will have the same opportunities they had.
These concerns belong to all of us, regardless of our age or family situation. They are about whether people can live with dignity, find stability and build a future here in Maine.
Maybe you are tired of politics. Maybe you’ve tuned it out. Maybe you believe your one vote won’t change anything.
But your vote is one of the few opportunities you have to say, in a very concrete way, this is the future I want.
Before you mark that ballot, don’t vote by reflex or party habit. Stop for a moment, look closely at the future you are choosing, and ask yourself: Is this the country, and the Maine, I want to help create?

title: Lawrence football outlasts Cony in battle of B North unbeatens
text:
FAIRFIELD — You would have expected it from the Cony Rams. But from the Lawrence football team? Airing it out? Blasphemy.
Well, not Friday night. Sure, Lawrence’s running game put up gaudy numbers, as usual, but it was the passing game that made the difference in the Bulldogs’ 35-27 victory over Cony.
Jackson Dangler threw four touchdown passes as Lawrence won a battle of unbeaten Class B North teams at Keyes Field. The outcome sent the Bulldogs to the top of the region and snapped the Rams’ streak of 12 straight Pine Tree Conference wins.
“Like I said at the beginning of the season, I’ll pass when I need to, and tonight was one of those nights, I guess,” Dangler said. “I just threw it when I needed to against a team with good (defensive backs in) Cony. … We all stepped up, and it was great.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
Lawrence (5-0) ran the ball at will on the opening drive, which culminated in a 37-yard touchdown run by Keegan Littlefield. The Bulldogs then snuffed out a Cony fake punt, after which Dangler found Miles Provost for a 23-yard touchdown pass to make it 14-0 midway through the first quarter.
Dangler’s second touchdown pass, a 9-yarder to Provost, put Lawrence up 21-0 with 6:40 left in the half.
Drew Lindquist threw a 5-yard pass to Jacob Fifield to put Cony (4-1) on the board with 1:31 left, but Lawrence answered on the final play of the half, as Dangler found Hunter Curtis for an 11-yard score.
Cony began to stuff the Lawrence run game in the second half, and a huge third quarter from Lindquist — 172 yards passing — included two more touchdown passes to Fifield. Those plays bookended another passing score for the Bulldogs — 60 yards from Dangler to Littlefield.
“We’ve been practicing that all year,” Lawrence coach Pete Curtis said of the final touchdown pass, a beautifully executed wheel route. “We haven’t had to throw the ball much during a game, but we knew we could. We have a capable quarterback in Jackson, and he was on tonight.”
Cony got back within one score on the second play of the fourth quarter, as Lindquist scrambled 11 yards into the end zone on third-and-goal. The Rams got the ball back late with a chance to tie, but Lawrence forced a three-and-out before running out the clock.
WHAT IT MEANS
• Lawrence has the inside track for the No. 1 seed in Class B North. That was always the likely outcome of Friday’s game, and wins next week at Brunswick, at Camden Hills on Oct. 17 and at home against Messalonskee on Oct. 24 would clinch the top spot for the Bulldogs.
• Cony hadn’t lost against a PTC opponent since a 28-18 defeat to Lawrence in the 2024 North semifinals. Still, Cony coach B.L. Lippert was pleased his young team didn’t wither in the face of adversity — and with Kingston Cox, one of its top players, sidelined because of an injury.
“We played hard all night long; we just got off to a bad start,” Lippert said. “We’ve seen it all year. (We won late) at Fryeburg, and we won against Skowhegan late. This team’s got some grit and some toughness. … When we get (Anderson Noyes) back (from injury), we’re going to be even more dangerous.”
UNSUNG HERO
Lawrence’s Brady Richards. It’s hard to call Provost “unsung” given that the junior caught two touchdown passes. So, the nod goes (again) to Richards, who was massively disruptive on defense and notched a strip-sack on special teams on Cony’s fake punt in the first quarter.
“He’s always been there, ever since he stepped in in the state game his freshman year,” Dangler said. “He’s definitely one of the best players I’ve ever seen and one of the best I’ll ever play with.”
NOTABLE QUOTABLE
“I think it’s very special (to get a big homecoming win), but we can’t get ahead of ourselves. We’ve got to come back to practice and work, and when we see those guys again, it’ll be a different game.” — Miles Provost
STAT LEADERS
• Cony: Drew Lindquist (15 of 28, 279 passing yards, three touchdowns), Jacob Fifield (four catches, 69 yards, three touchdowns), Landen Perry (six catches, 119 yards)
• Lawrence: Jackson Dangler (5 of 12, 116 yards, four touchdowns), Keegan Littlefield (19 carries, 136 yards, touchdown; 60-yard receiving touchdown), Miles Provost (three catches, 45 yards, two touchdowns; sack, fumble recovery)
UP NEXT
• Cony: vs. Camden Hills (1-3), 7 p.m. Thursday
• Lawrence: at Brunswick (1-3), 7 p.m. Friday

title: Robot Safety Program
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Teaching young children about safety can be a challenge, but some folks found a way to make the message a little more memorable. It’s the focus of this week’s Throwback Thursday with Brian Bouchard.
Getting kids to remember an important lesson can sometimes come down to how you deliver it. In this week’s Throwback Thursday, we dial the time machine back to 1984 where WAGM report Frank Graff takes us to Ashland Elementary School where a traveling safety robot stopped by to teach students.
This is K24, a robot who, with his human companion, travels around the country teaching children about safety. Today K24 found himself at the Ashland Elementary School, teaching the children in kindergarten through 4th grade his list of safety do’s and don’ts. Today’s topics included bicycle, crosswalk, and school bus safety. K24 also addressed the dangers of children talking to strangers, and he taught the youngsters how to avoid strangers and how to give descriptions of people bothering them to police, issues that have received a lot of publicity lately. The children seem to get the message.
“Never take rides from strangers.”
“When somebody comes and tries to take you away, you run away.”
“Never go into strangers’ cars and that.”
K24 is the brainchild of the Creative Safety Products Company. Its home office is in New Jersey. For the past eight years, the company has been taking its robots to schools and anywhere else they’re hired to perform, teaching small children about safety. Besides K24, the company also boasts a talking dog and a Volkswagen. They have other creations due out soon. A company representative was in Ashland last year discussing the program with schools, businesses and police officials. Several firms in Ashland got together and raised the almost $2000 needed to bring the program to Ashland. Teachers and police officials alike say the program strength lies in taking serious subjects like teaching children not to talk to strangers and discussing it in a way that children will understand.
“I believe it’s something that the children will remember more than just hearing it from a person”
“These days of, You know, Star Wars and and robots. The kids really identify with these with these types of people or... or creatures.”
K24 – Safety Robot
“If you stood up in front of the boys and girls, they wouldn’t listen to you too much. But when I thought they listened because they know I’m a safety robot. That’s why ”

title: Court tosses manslaughter sentence after AI video of road-rage victim used in court
text:
CHANDLER, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) — A convict will have to be resentenced after the Arizona Court of Appeals vacated his sentence because an AI video of the victim affected the judge’s decision.
Gabriel Horcasitas was sentenced to 10 1/2 years in prison last year for the road-rage killing of Christopher Pelkey in November 2021.
The victim’s family created an AI video of Pelkey using a previously recorded video, a picture and a script written by his sister. That video was played during the sentencing.
The sentencing judge noted “obvious forgiveness” expressed in Pelkey’s AI statement before handing down the punishment to Horcasitas.
During the sentencing, the judge said he “loved” the video and that Pelkey was able “to speak from his heart” as the family envisioned.
In its decision announced Wednesday, the state Court of Appeals said the sentencing judge was prejudiced by the AI video, which made his decision fundamentally unfair.
The Court of Appeals said Horcasitas’ manslaughter conviction is upheld, but the 10 1/2-year sentence is vacated and he will be resentenced.

title: InvestigateTV+: A conservation success story
text:
(InvestigateTV) — An American symbol once on the brink of extinction, the bald eagle is considered a conservation success story. InvestigateTV+ explores its decades-long journey to recovery.
Then, we uncover the paper trail leading to a Russian citizen in Texas and why Medicare recipients should take a second look at their statements.
Plus, a father honors his son by teaching young drivers about the dangers on the road.
An American success story
A bald eagle sits atop a Louisiana cypress tree in Lake Palourde near Morgan City, a scene that would have been inconceivable a few short decades ago.
“We can see up to 60 eagles in a tour,” said Billy Gaston, who makes a living largely off providing eagle sightseeing tours in and near the lake.
The government removed the eagle from the Endangered Species List in 2007, widely regarded as one of conservation’s great success stories.
Investigation reveals Medicare billing scheme
A WSMV4 investigation has uncovered a Medicare fraud scheme that billed the federal program tens of thousands of dollars for medical supplies that Tennessee recipients never needed or received.
Our investigation found the billing is connected to a Russian citizen living in Texas, accused in a $3 billion Medicare fraud scheme.
Encouraging safe-driving
Mike Lutzenkirchen is sharing his son’s story with teens and young adults in hopes of preventing fatal crashes caused by unsafe driving.
Lutzenkirchen’s son, Philip, died in a car accident in 2014. Philip, a former Auburn football player, had been drinking with friends before getting into a car. Investigators said the car was speeding and ran a stop sign, killing both Philip and the driver.
Helping every customer he sees
For almost three decades, Greg Atchison has been a friendly face in the grocery business.
“It’s greeting people. Meeting people, seeing people, it’s therapeutic,” Atchison said.
Atchison has worked 28 years in customer service. Twenty years at Festival Foods, formerly Trig’s, and eight at County Market. His approach extends beyond typical customer interactions.

title: House fire shuts down Christian Ridge Road in Ellsworth
text:
Christian Ridge Road, which Ellsworth commuters use to get between Bangor and Bucksport roads without having to drive through downtown, is partially shut down Friday afternoon as firefighters work to put out a fire at a local house.
The fire involved a Christian Ridge Road home, about a mile from Bucksport Road, with blue shingles and a trailer in its front yard.
It was not immediately clear at around 2 p.m. if there were any injuries or what caused the fire.
A section of Christian Ridge Road was completely closed from Red Bridge Road to Higgins Way.
At least eight firetrucks and two ambulances were spotted at the scene. Firefighters strapped with hoses were seen climbing up ladders, positioning their hoses through broken windows. Just before 2:30 p.m., firefighters had ascended the home’s roof.
Emergency vehicles from Ellsworth, Hancock, Orland and Southwest Harbor were on scene. A Maine Forest Ranger was also on scene.
Firetrucks were still arriving on scene by 2:30 p.m.
The Ellsworth Fire Chief did not immediately respond to inquiries from the Bangor Daily News, and the Ellsworth Police Department couldn’t provide any details on the blaze.
A thick cloud of smoke was seen billowing from the home’s roof. A sheet of smoke covered the surrounding area.

title: What's next for Christa Pike after surviving lethal injection
text:
What's next for Christa Pike after surviving lethal injection
Christa Pike survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her via lethal injection on Wednesday, but her medical and legal future remains remarkably unclear.
Video above: How could a lethal injection go wrong?
Pike is in critical condition and receiving life-saving medical care after being injected with two ostensibly fatal doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said Thursday. They declined to offer further details on her health.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years. Now, her legal case will be at a standstill.
Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, announced he would call off the state's last remaining execution this year while a third-party review takes place to "determine what exactly occurred" in Pike's case, according to The Associated Press. CNN has reached out to the governor’s office for comment.
"The Governor has appropriately called for an investigation," the office of Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti said in a statement. "We need to know what happened."
The moratorium is part of the stop-and-start use of executions in Tennessee over the last few years. Lee similarly paused executions in 2022 for a review, and earlier this year the state failed to carry out a lethal injection on a death-row inmate after struggling to find a vein.
Attorneys call for commutation
Pike was initially scheduled to be executed on Wednesday morning, but last-minute legal appeals delayed the execution to later in the day.
The execution protocol began in the early evening, and she gave her last words at 7:26 p.m., according to media witnesses. Yet after two doses of the drug cocktail, she was snoring and appeared to be alive, the witnesses said.
"None of it was normal," said Catherine Sweeney, a reporter for WPLN. "I covered all the executions last year, and most of the ones this year. We haven’t seen anything like it. It went really poorly."
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it acted according to its protocol throughout the failed execution.
"The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office," the department said in a statement Wednesday. "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."
Randy Spivey, one of Pike’s attorneys, said the governor's call for a review of the execution protocol doesn't go far enough. He called for Lee to commute her sentence, saying she had endured punishment "greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty."
The attorneys said they had warned the court beforehand that Pike's vein issues would make it difficult to carry out the lethal injection.
"We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy," attorneys Spivey and Kelly Gleason said in a statement.
But what happened Wednesday was essentially her "biggest fear," attorney Stephen Ferrell said.
"It was not a fear of dying. It was a fear of prolonged, painful, traumatic death. That's what happened, minus the death," he said.
Precedent for surviving an execution
While it's not uncommon to have a "botched" execution – when something differs from official protocol – it’s exceedingly rare for an execution to simply fail, said Austin Sarat, an Amherst College professor and author of several books on the death penalty and lethal injection.
"Those cases where people survive an execution create a real dilemma for the legal system. Now what?" he said.
Sarat said there is some legal precedent for inmates who survived an execution being put to death again.
In a case 80 years ago, 16-year-old Willie Francis survived an execution via the electric chair in Louisiana due to a malfunction. He appealed his case to the U.S. Supreme Court, saying a second execution would violate the double jeopardy clause of the Constitution and the protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
The Court rejected his appeal, and he died in a second electric chair execution.
Similarly, in a 2009 case, Ohio personnel attempted to execute Romell Broom by lethal injection, but they were unable to access a vein and establish an IV line. Afterward, he argued that a second execution attempt would violate the double jeopardy clause and protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
The Ohio Supreme Court ruled against him in 2016, saying that setting the IV line was only a "preliminary step" to an execution, so a second execution attempt would not be considered a violation of the double jeopardy clause.
Broom ultimately died of Covid-19 in 2020 while still on death row, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Still, Pike’s case is unique because the lethal drugs actually entered her system, Sarat said.
"So we're in kind of unprecedented territory with Pike in the sense of she survived her execution," he said.

title: Coming out later in life: Why more LGBTQ+ older adults are living openly
text:
(Aging Untold) — Aging brings changes beyond the physical — it can reshape courage, confidence and a sense of self. For some older adults in the LGBTQ+ community, that growth shows up as coming out later in life after decades of keeping part of who they are hidden.
The Aging Untold experts are exploring what shifts with age that make living openly feel possible, and what’s still at stake for couples who choose to stay private.
What finally makes it feel safe to come out
Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, opened the conversation by asking what changes as people get older that can make them feel safe enough to live more openly.
“I think the thing that changes the most is judgmental people pass away,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “I think if you’re trying to keep it from your own parents, and once they’re gone, you’re able to be who you are.”
Cradduck said the shift can also come from a child who wasn’t able to accept it, and later changes their mind — sometimes because someone else in their life has come out.
“It gives you an opportunity, plus the fear of your own mortality and not being able to end your life with the person you want to end your life with and having them beside you,” Cradduck said. “That can be very overwhelming. So you finally throw caution to the wind, and you no longer care what other people think. You care who’s beside you during those final moments. So you let the world know. And I see nothing wrong with that.”
A 50-year relationship kept secret
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a story from her own work: two women in their early 80s went into her office for help, and she could feel the love between them.
“I said, how long have you two been together? And they said, 50 years,” O’Rourke said. “Not married. And I said, ‘Does anybody in your family know?’ And they said, ‘No.’”
When O’Rourke asked the women what had stopped them from telling their families, they said they were too scared.
“They’re not going to accept it. We just kept everything the way it is,” they told O’Rourke.
“I felt sad. I would want them to have more, but I could tell that they had forged such a close bond that the decision worked for them,” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke said her advice for couples in that position is to be direct with family ahead of time.
“Let everybody know ahead of time, this is what we’re doing. This is who I am. This is what I want from you,” O’Rourke said. “These are the boundaries that I’m drawing for myself that I want you to abide by.”
Ambrose added that verbal wishes aren’t enough on their own.
“There’s some real nasty people when it comes to death and hospitals, etc., or who’s making decisions on the funerals,” Ambrose said. “It’s really important to have legal documents in place.”
When families shut partners out
Cradduck shared a story of a woman she provided care for.
The woman’s best friend was also her partner. During the woman’s final days in hospice care, her family forbade her partner from visiting — and wouldn’t let her attend the funeral to pay her respects, Cradduck saod.
“I’ve seen where families step in and they do the most horrific thing,” Cradduck said. “They’re protecting their own image of who this person was instead of accepting them.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said there is a physical toll that comes with hiding one’s identity for years.
“Once you become older, a lot of times I think people just own who they are. They’re authentic,” Rogers said. “When you’re living unseen and unheard, that’s an emotional burden, that’s loneliness, that’s stress. And that’s a whole bunch of physiology affecting your body.”
Cradduck also noted a gap in elder care options for LGBTQ+ seniors.
“We haven’t built enough communities for our aged population at all, but we don’t have enough LGBTQ-friendly companies and care companies,” Cradduck said.
She pointed to SAGE USA, which she described as an LGBTQ-friendly training program that helps communities, assisted living facilities and home care agencies work with elderly people in the community.
Coming out — or staying private — is a personal choice
O’Rourke said the decision to come out later in life comes with its own mix of emotions.
“You’re going to have grief associated with losing some people that might not accept it. You’ll have your own grief of changing from one identity to another,” O’Rourke said. “But you can have two feelings at the same time. You can feel sad. You can also feel celebratory. You can feel happy that you’re finally yourself.”
Cradduck said staying private can be the right call for some.
“If staying in the closet is what’s safest and what’s best, and what brings the least amount of stress and turmoil — then live your life that way,” Cradduck said.
O’Rourke added that religious beliefs are worth acknowledging as part of that decision as well.
“I think that’s important to acknowledge, but I’m with you — do whatever you feel comfortable with,” O’Rourke said.
Rogers also emphasized protecting those choices legally.
“Do whatever you feel comfortable with, but take the legal actions to protect,” Rogers said.
Ambrose added that younger generations may not fully grasp what older LGBTQ+ adults faced.
“Younger generations underestimate the amount of fear, stigma, pressure that was on us decades ago,” Ambrose said. “Some of the more controversial things that didn’t fit in the box, it was a really hard thing to live in. And I just believe we’re living in a more empowering age, and hopefully learning to act with a little more love and kindness.”

title: Supreme Court preview: New term brings Second Amendment, voting rights cases
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A new term at the U.S. Supreme Court begins Monday.
The term follows a session in which the Supreme Court struck down the president’s tariffs and his executive order on birthright citizenship. Justices this term are set to hear a number of notable cases.
Among the cases on the docket is Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to bans on AR-15-style rifles.
Georgetown Law professor Michele Goodwin said the case is significant.
“Well, this is an important case because we see the Supreme Court’s efforts to give life to individual liberties associated with the Second Amendment and gun rights,” Goodwin said. “You see that further cemented in this challenge. We don’t know how the Supreme Court would rule, but, you know, there are some tea leaves that we could follow. The Second Amendment has truly gained speed, if you will, before the United States Supreme Court.”
Also on the docket is Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota. The case concerns whether the National Voter Registration Act or a federal consent decree takes precedence over state documentary proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registration.
“What this case is ultimately about is whether the Voter Registration Act would prohibit what is basically, in essence, happening in Arizona,” Goodwin said.
The court is also likely to hear cases from the so-called shadow docket, or emergency docket, which lets parties seek expedited Supreme Court intervention before a case completes the ordinary appeals process.
“But the argument has been that the Supreme Court that the Trump administration has been able to have a speed pass jump its way to the Supreme Court, which has meant that the lower courts have not been able to actually deal with these cases,” Goodwin said.
During his second term, President Trump has appealed to the shadow docket more than any other president. According to both the White House and the Department of Justice, that will likely continue.

title: Portland Trail Blazers fire new play-by-play broadcaster hours after hiring announced
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - The Portland Trail Blazers have fired newly hired play-by-play broadcaster Braiden Bell.
According to a statement from the team, Bell’s termination stemmed from social media posts that violated team and league policies about racist, sexist and harmful comments.
“The Portland Trail Blazers have zero tolerance for racist, sexist or harmful comments,” the team said with the announcement. “The play-by-play role carries a long legacy of excellence ... and we hold that standard without exception.”
Bell had been announced as the team’s new play-by-play announcer just hours before his firing.
“We did not meet our own bar in this process, and for that we apologize to Blazers fans and Rip City,” the team continued. “We will make sure that our new broadcaster reflects our values.”
Bell graduated from Arizona State University, where he called games for the basketball team.
Before his brief stint with the Trail Blazers, Bell also called games for California Baptist University, as well as being the play-by-play announcer for the Phoenix Mercury and working games in the NBA G League.
Bell said he was “deeply sorry” for the language that he used in previous posts on social media following his dismissal from the team.
“Those tweets, while wrong, were written by me 14 years ago while I was only 15 years old and have no reflection of who I am today. I do not take lightly any harm it causes now,” Bell’s message read. “I’d like to apologize to anyone who was hurt by my words and will continue to always treat people with kindness and respect.”
The 2026-27 NBA regular season begins on Oct. 20, with the Trail Blazers’ first preseason game scheduled for Oct. 7.
