title: Wellness Hub opens in Rumford as a place for healing, connection, community
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
RUMFORD — 1.4.3. Wellness Hub, a new nonprofit wellness space created for healing, connection and community, officially opened its doors Sept. 24 at 119 Congress St.
Prior to a ribbon-cutting ceremony with the River Valley Chamber of Commerce, business owner Courtney McPherson told people attending, “143 means I love you and the lotus is a flower that grows from the mud and rises to the surface to the light. So the meaning behind all of this is love and growth.”
Located on the first floor at the former KeyBank building, DeCourcy related how this wellness space came to light.
“From 2019 into 2020, I went through a really dark time, and I could not find community modalities and I had to drive a long ways, and I don’t like driving,” she said. “So I found all these things that helped me feel better and kind of came home to myself and found true love for me. And after I got out of my hole, I said, ‘We need this in Rumford. We need something people can come to that’s local. We need community. We need a safe space to take our masks off and be OK to be in the dark or in the light.'”
They offer classes, including a child and me yoga class, from ages 12 months to 18. And they have a woman who does chair yoga up to age 100 or so. There are also group dance classes.
“There’s a lot of different things in here like the salt vault and some saunas,” McPherson said. “And we have massage therapists and energy workers, and there’s a movement space.”
McPherson stressed that their services are for all genders and all ages, all walks. It’s a “mind, body and soul connection.”
“There’s a place to sit and lounge, and I’ll have tea and coffee every day. You don’t have to come and buy anything. Just come and chill,” she said.
McPherson said, “I have my dream team, a lot of girls behind me, and my family. We’re all a team. We work off each other.”
Among those she thanked were her investors, including her grandparents, who left her money when they passed. “I decided a good way to use their money was to build something for the community.”
Refreshments were provided by the Region 9 School of Applied Technology in Mexico, and prepared and served by the school’s Culinary Arts students Peyton Richard, Adriana Navarro and Brooklynn Webster.

title: Obituary: David C. Burton
text:
BELGRADE – Surrounded by loving family in the home he built himself, David “Dave” Burton passed away peacefully on Sept. 22, 2026, after a long, courageous struggle with multiple health conditions. He was 78 years old.
Dave was born in Waterville, Maine on Jan. 16, 1948, the first of seven children born to Donald and Leora (Edith) Burton (Williams). He was a lifelong resident of Belgrade and graduated from Belgrade High School as salutatorian in 1966.
After attending SMVTI and earning an associate’s degree in electrical technology, Dave voluntarily enlisted in the Army and proudly served as a ‘missile man’ with the 65th Artillery from 1968 to 1971. Later, as a patient at the Togus VA hospital, Dave met a pleasant young hospital employee from ‘The County’ who would turn out to be his lifelong love and partner. David and Carolyn (Barnes) Burton were married on August 3, 1974, and through all the ups and downs, shared 52 wonderful years together.
A licensed master electrician for 35 years, Dave was employed by various companies, but his longest tenure was working for Digital Equipment in Augusta where he met many good friends. Later, his passion for hunting, fishing and the outdoors would lead him to attend schools in Iowa and Montana to learn the art of taxidermy, and he brought those skills home to operate his own business for 10 years until his declining health forced him to retire. An interest in giving back to the town he loved led him to be trained as an EMT and he spent 10 years with Belgrade Fire and Rescue, earning Rescue Person of the Year in 1999.
Dave was happiest spending time with his family and in the outdoors. He loved his wife, his two boys and (especially) his grandchildren fiercely and never let his health issues interfere with him being present for them with a smile on his face. He was a huge fan of the Red Sox and Patriots, enjoyed gardening and spending quiet time on his land, often just looking at the trees. He was also thrilled to see his lifelong dream of having a camp on the water come to fruition and spent as much time as possible there with Carolyn and his family.
David was predeceased by his parents Donald and Leora; a sister Brenda (Burton) Hilliker, and a brother Brandon Burton.
He is survived by his wife Carolyn; son Ryan and his wife Amanda of Mount Vernon, son Travis and his wife Bethany of Belgrade; and four very special grandchildren, Nathaniel, Silas, Eliana and Blake. Also surviving are a sister, Bonnie Burton of Winslow, a brother Terry and his wife Claudia of Belgrade, a brother Michael of Belgrade, a brother Wayne and his wife Shirley of Chicopee, Mass.; and several nieces and nephews.
The family would like to thank the staff at Fresenius Kidney Care in Augusta and MaineGeneral Homecare and Hospice for the wonderful care that Dave received.
Dave’s funeral service will be held at 11 a.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, at Veilleux Funeral Home, 8 Elm Street in Waterville followed by a reception. An internment at Pine Grove Cemetery will be held later that afternoon.

title: Former Maine Capitol Police chief given chance to avoid most serious charges after bar fight
text:
The former Maine Capitol Police chief may avoid the most serious charges after he allegedly assaulted a Hallowell police officer who tried to break up a bar fight last year.
Under deferred disposition, Matthew Clancy must seek counseling and treatment for substance use and provide the court with proof of that by Oct. 20, according to ABC affiliate WMTW.
Clancy must then provide evidence every three months that he’s continuing that treatment, WMTW reported.
He also is prohibited from possessing or consuming alcohol.
If he abides by the terms of the deal through July 6, 2027, Clancy will face just a disorderly conduct charge and a fine up to $300. But if he fails to satisfy those conditions, he will face, in addition to disorderly conduct, charges of assault and refusing to submit to arrest, according to WMTW.
Clancy allegedly got into an altercation with other patrons at the Quarry Tap Room on Water Street in Hallowell during the early morning hours of Aug. 2. That spilled out into the street, and when a city police officer intervened, Clancy allegedly assaulted the officer.
He was placed on leave after his arrest, and then resigned two months later.
Clancy took over the Maine Capitol Police, which patrols and protects the state government in Augusta, in 2021 after its previous chief, Russell Gauvin, resigned amid an uproar over social media posts promoting falsehoods about the 2020 presidential election, expressing sympathy for a former Maine police officer who called for violence against Black Lives Matter protesters, and mocking people who wore masks to prevent the spread of COVID-19.
Before coming to the state capital, Clancy led police departments in Plympton and Duxbury, Massachusetts, taught at Bridgewater State University and served more than a decade on the board of directors of the Massachusetts Police Accreditation Commission.
The Maine Capitol Police is now gradually being absorbed by the Maine State Police.

Jay plans workshop on Walden solar project, possible TIF
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — The Jay Select Board plans to hold a separate workshop on Walden Renewables’ proposed solar development as board members seek more information about potential tax revenue, a possible tax increment financing agreement and questions raised during earlier public hearings.
The workshop is expected to include a general overview of tax increment financing, discussion of Walden Renewables’ proposal and the potential impact on local taxes.
Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere told the board Sept. 28 that discussions about a tax increment financing, or TIF, agreement would typically involve the town assessor, town attorney, Walden and members of the Select Board before a proposal would return to the full board for consideration.
“Ultimately, any TIF is approved by the residents,” LaFreniere said. “It has to go to a vote anyways.”
Board members debated whether those discussions should take place before voters decide the future of the project or afterward. Some questioned whether the town should devote time to developing a financial arrangement before knowing whether residents support the project, while others said voters should have more information about potential revenue before casting ballots.
LaFreniere said Walden has discussed using a structure modeled on a TIF in Sanford. Under her understanding of that arrangement, a TIF district would capture the project’s added taxable value so it would not count against the municipality in calculations involving state revenue sharing and school funding, while payments from the developer would provide revenue to the town.
“I don’t even want to say this because I don’t know enough to make sure that this is correct,” LaFreniere said before explaining her understanding of the Sanford arrangement.
Questions at the meeting included whether payments would be based on the project’s proposed generating capacity or its actual annual production, along with the eventual number of solar panels, acreage involved, buffer zones and screening.
“And that’s part of those discussions,” LaFreniere said. “These are important questions.”
In a follow-up email Wednesday, LaFreniere said she expects the workshop to cover TIFs more broadly as well as the Walden proposal.
“I believe the workshop will be a complete overview of TIFs in general as well as the Walden proposal,” she said.
The board ultimately favored a separate workshop rather than adding the discussion to a regular Select Board meeting. It was noted that a dedicated workshop would be more beneficial to the public.
No date has been set. LaFreniere said Walden is coordinating possible dates with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection and an attorney.
Separately, Walden Renewables will hold a public informational meeting from 5:30-7 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 13, at LaFleurs Restaurant, 224 Main St. The meeting is intended for residents who want information about the proposed solar project directly from the developer.

title: Gem hunter finds a diamond he claims could be worth $1 million
text:
LITTLE ROCK, Ark. (AP) — Jack Pearadin is the first to admit that his diamond-hunting hobby hasn’t paid off, despite sifting rocks for more than a dozen years.
But earlier this year, the Navy reservist and his friend shoveled a six-carat diamond from a field in Arkansas where he’s found over 300 gems so far. And this one is like nothing he’s dug up before — Pearadin claims collectors have told him it could be worth $1 million.
At least one experienced appraiser told The Associated Press that a diamond of such size and quality could be worth a fourth of that — still an impressive find.
“Oh my God! Oh my God!” Pearadin said as he livestreamed the discovery on TikTok. “Holy crap, we got a big one!” he yelled after rinsing gravel from a bucket and then flipping the pile onto a table to expose the shiny facets of a 6.03-carat diamond.
Roughly the size of a fingernail, it’s the largest diamond found this year at Crater of Diamonds State Park. More than 37,000 diamonds have been discovered since the former open-pit diamond mine became part of a state park in 1972.
The largest diamond found at the park, ‘Uncle Sam,’ weighed 40 carats
The park charges a $15 entry fee to fill a 5-gallon bucket with rocks, and people can keep any gemstones they find. Most are small and worth maybe a few hundred dollars. The largest diamond ever unearthed in the United States, a 40.23-carat stone called the Uncle Sam, was found at the park in 1924.
Pearadin, originally from Missouri, has been trying his luck at the park since 2013, even moving to nearby Murfreesboro to support his hobby — “I love it that much,” he told The Associated Press. He’s sold most of his diamonds online.
Most of the 400 to 800 diamonds found at the park annually weigh about a quarter of a carat, according to park interpreter Sarah Bivens. But there have been some bigger ones, said park assistant superintendent Waymon Cox: In 2020 a 9-carat diamond was found by an Arkansas bank manager, and in 2024 a French man unearthed a 7-carat diamond.
Diamonds are found in few places in the US
Diamonds are crystallized under tremendous pressure and heat deep inside the Earth and then thrust to the surface through volcanic activity before they’re scattered by water or wind. These natural diamonds are often cloudy and oddly shaped, and lose about 25% of their weight as they’re cut and polished into what a jeweler would sell, according to Nathan Renfro, senior manager at the Gemological Institute of America.
Renfro said the U.S. has only two known primary deposits of diamonds — places where columns of once-molten volcanic rock have reached the surface — Crater of Diamonds and Colorado’s Kelsey Lake, where the land was reclaimed after a commercial mining operation went out of business years ago.
Today, that leaves the Arkansas park as one of the only places in the world where anyone can hunt for diamonds and take their finds with them.
“It’s a pretty remarkable operation that that’s available to the public,” Renfro said. “Most diamond mines are super high security.”
So can Jack finally get a big payday?
A typical .17-carat diamond from the park can sell for around $700, said certified gem appraiser Laura Stanley in Little Rock. But a high-quality six-carat yellow diamond from the park can sell for about $250,000, she said, partly because of their origin.
“They are their own entity,” Stanley said. “It’s the only place in America where you can go find your own diamond and you can’t compare that to a diamond from anywhere else.”
The Uncle Sam crystal was cut and polished into a 12.42-carat diamond gifted to the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, where it’s on view in the “Great American Diamonds” exhibit.
Pearadin named his latest and biggest find the “American Dream.”
“It’s just this massive, gorgeous yellow diamond,” Pearadin said. He plans to split the profits with fellow gem hunter Michael Schumacher of Wisconsin, who helped fill the bucket that held the stone, and open his own crystal mine.
___
Turbay is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Learn about e-bikes at Westbrook’s BikeFest
text:
Whether you’ve never ridden a bike or you’re an expert cyclist, prefer road or mountain bikes, bike as your mode of transportation or just do it for fun, Westbrook’s BikeFest is for everyone who wants to learn more about biking.
The annual festival is returning to Rock Row from noon to 6 p.m. Saturday to increase awareness and involvement in bike culture.
Hosted by the oldest bike shop in Maine — Ernie’s Cycle Shop — the festival began as an appreciation party for employees. It quickly grew into a fun festival for the entire biking community with live music, guided bike rides and food trucks.
This year’s festival features an educational forum on e-bikes, hosted by Vision Zero Maine, a citizen-led group of Mainers committed to creating safe streets. Industry experts, law enforcement and elected officials will speak about the difference between e-bikes and e-motos and how each should be used.
Vision Zero Maine’s Paul Drinan, who helped organize BikeFest, hopes to spread awareness that while bikes, including e-bikes, can be used for fun, they’re also a legitimate form of transportation. Many people don’t have a car, including children, seniors, and others who just can’t afford one, he said, and bikes can give them the independence and freedom that other modes of transportation provide. And e-bikes can help people who might need a little extra assistance or aren’t as physically able.
“E-bikes have really been transformative for a lot of people,” Drinan said.
People will be able to try e-bikes at BikeFest.
The rise of e-bikes has created controversy, as people are concerned about speed and safety. But the real issue, Drinan said, is e-motos. E-motos are often labeled as e-bikes, but they can go much faster than an electric bicycle and have more powerful motors. E-bikes are classified into three categories based on features like speed and motor type, but even the fastest can’t exceed 28 mph, while e-motos can reach speeds up to 60 mph.
“It’s a high-powered device that is much more like a motorcycle than a bicycle,” Drinan said.
But people often confuse the two, leading to calls to restrict or ban e-bikes. Those unfair laws or ordinances stem from a lack of education about e-bikes and e-motos, Drinan said, and that’s why he wants to educate parents, children and lawmakers about e-bikes.

title: Ex-sports doctor Larry Nassar removed from Michigan’s sex offender registry
text:
Larry Nassar among 20,000 offenders removed from Michigan’s sex offender registry due to recent state Supreme Court ruling
Disgraced sports doctor Larry Nassar, who was convicted of sexually abusing Olympic and college female gymnasts, is among thousands of other offenders who have been removed from Michigan's sex offender registry.
On Sept. 9, the Michigan Supreme Court ruled that the state cannot retroactively apply current registration requirements to people who committed sex offenses before July 2011, per amendments made in 2021 to the Sex Offender Registration Act (SORA).
Nassar and more than 20,000 other offenders whose crimes occurred prior to July 1, 2011, have been removed from the state's sex offender registry as a result of the ruling, according to the Eaton County Prosecuting Attorney's Office.
"The Michigan Supreme Court’s decision to eliminate SORA requirements for these offenders is deeply concerning," the attorney's office wrote in a social media post on Sunday. "Our community, along with the victims of these crimes, expected the registry to provide a measure of protection and awareness—assurances that have now been removed by the Court’s ruling."
Nassar, 63, was sentenced in state court in 2018 to 40 to 175 years in prison. He admitted to sexually assaulting athletes when he worked at Michigan State University and at USA Gymnastics in Indianapolis, which trains Olympians. Nassar was also handed a 60-year federal sentence for child pornography crimes.
The ruling does not change Nassar's prison sentences.

Skydiver rescued after getting stuck 50 to 60 feet up in Lebanon tree

Firefighters rescued a skydiver who became stuck 50 to 60 feet up in a tree in Lebanon on Thursday, according to the Lebanon fire chief.
Lebanon Fire-EMS responded with an engine and ambulance before requesting mutual aid from Sanford Fire Department because Lebanon did not have a ladder capable of reaching the skydiver, the chief said.
Sanford firefighters brought the man down after he had been stuck in the tree for approximately 30 to 40 minutes.
He was evaluated by Lebanon Fire-EMS personnel and transported to a local hospital with minor injuries according to the chief.
Lebanon Fire-EMS thanked Sanford Fire for its assistance, saying the incident highlighted the importance of mutual aid between neighboring departments.
"We may have different names on our trucks and serve different communities, but when help is needed, we work together," the department wrote.

title: El Niño expected to drive up the cost of coffee and some other foods
text:
(Gray News) - Economists expect some food costs could go up soon due to the near-record-strong super El Niño still strengthening in the Pacific Ocean.
El Niño is forecast to peak this fall and winter.
It’s expected to combine with pre-existing global supply chain pressures to drive up prices on tropical products. That includes things like coffee, chocolate, some fruits and nuts and palm oil.
According to Reuters, El Niño typically brings droughts in regions such as Southeast Asia, Australia and southern Africa and heavy rainfall in other parts of the world like the southern parts of South America and the United States. These conditions can impact various crops that grow in those areas, such as coffee beans and cacao.
El Niño comes at an already challenging time for food prices, given supply chain pressures from geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and Black Sea.

title: G7 nations to release ‘substantial’ amounts of diesel as prices hover near record highs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Group of Seven industrial nations said they agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel recently hit record prices in the United States, where President Donald Trump said the diesel release would happen “immediately.”
Trump and his Republican Party face pressure to address surging prices ahead of November’s midterm elections. Trump announced the action Friday on social media, saying, “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately.”
The president faces lagging approval ratings as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods.
Gas prices in the U.S. and abroad have soared during the eight-month-long war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. Trump has insisted prices will come down after the war, though there’s no end in sight.
The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.
Trump had a conversation overnight with French President Emmanuel Macron, the chair of the G7, about the need to address rising fuel prices and the availability of petroleum products, according to the French Embassy in the U.S. Macron on Friday then chaired a videoconference of G7 leaders to discuss the issue.
France holds the rotating presidency of the G7 group and made the announcement in a statement released after video-conference talks that Macron presided over. The International Energy Agency will coordinate the effort to combat soaring fuel prices. “We will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels (MB) to begin immediately over 4 months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners,” the statement said.
A new AP-NORC poll found that a majority of U.S. adults blame Trump for higher prices, and approval on his handling of the economy hit a new low.
Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a disconnect between his achievements and the public’s view of his work. Trump this week gave himself an A-plus for his work on the economy but said “we’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion.”

title: MLB won't consider game at Grand Teton National Park, says was only conducting initial due diligence
text:
MLB won't consider game at Grand Teton National Park, says was only conducting initial due diligence
Major League Baseball won't consider staging a game in western Wyoming’s Grand Teton National Park.
Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred sent a letter Thursday to Teton County Commissioner Chair Mark Newcomb, Jackson Mayor Arne Jorgensen and Jackson Hole Chamber of Commerce President Rick Howe, who wrote to Manfred voicing objections on Monday following a report in The Washington Post that Grand Teton was under consideration.
Related video above: The Must-See National Parks in America
Manfred sent a similar letter to U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico.
“MLB has no formal plan to play a game in Grand Teton National Park,” Manfred wrote. “Our team was conducting initial due diligence on many potential sites when this story was reported and we had made no decision of the feasibility of staging a game in Grand Teton National Park. We also had not reached the stage in our due diligence in which we evaluated the environmental impact or spoke to members of the community to solicit their views — steps that would have certainly been a part of any process should it have moved forward.”
Manfred then said Grand Teton wouldn't remain under consideration.
“Since the story was reported, it has become clear the local community does not want us to continue evaluating Grand Teton National Park as a potential site,” Manfred wrote. “We obviously would not bring a game to a community that has concerns about the venue and will not continue to evaluate Grand Teton National Park as a potential site."
MLB and the players’ association have played a handful of regular-season games away from the 30 big league ballparks in recent years, including in the Iowa cornfields made famous by the movie “Field of Dreams.”
Grand Teton includes a commercial airport — the busiest in Wyoming — and a vast expanse of Jackson Hole bottomlands with spectacular views of the Teton Range.
“We are grateful that Major League Baseball heard the roar of the crowd and rightfully recognized that Grand Teton is already a field of dreams, filled with mountains, forests, wild nature and wildlife that attracts millions of dedicated fans each year," Allison Michalski, Grand Teton senior program manager for National Parks Conservation Association, said in a statement. “The bases were loaded with opposition, and this news is a grand slam for Teton county communities and the enduring legacy of Grand Teton National Park.”

title: Final jobs report released before midterms: What does it mean for your wallet?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Final jobs report released before midterms: What does it mean for your wallet?
The Labor Department's latest jobs report shows slower hiring and a slight rise in unemployment, as economic concerns take center stage ahead of the midterms.
Final jobs report released before midterms: What does it mean for your wallet?
The Labor Department's latest jobs report shows slower hiring and a slight rise in unemployment, as economic concerns take center stage ahead of the midterms.
The Labor Department released its final jobs report before the midterm elections, showing slower-than-expected job growth and a slight increase in unemployment.
Samuel Taube, an analyst at NerdWallet, said, "One thing that investors may have noticed that might seem a little strange at first glance is that the stock market actually rose on this news of a weaker-than-expected jobs report and a slight uptick in the unemployment rate."
The report revealed that U.S. employers added 29,000 jobs, significantly lower than the 90,000 jobs economists had predicted. The unemployment rate climbed by 0.1 percentage point to 4.2%, which is still considered relatively low.
Taube noted that the report decreases the odds of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates again at the end of October.
The hiring data comes as Republicans work to maintain control of Congress amid growing concerns about affordability. A recent Associated Press poll found that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of President Donald Trump's handling of the cost of living, while 26% approve of his overall handling of the economy.
In response to economic concerns, Trump is hitting the campaign trail. He is scheduled to deliver a speech in Alabama today.
Thad Kousser, a professor of political science at UC San Diego, said, "President Trump has been very consistent in his messaging, focusing on the policy wins, what was in the big beautiful bill last year that Republicans in Alabama should be excited about. He'll probably talk about immigration. That has been his signature issue."
Trump's 32-day campaign blitz will continue in Vandalia, Ohio, over the weekend and Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday.

title: Susan Collins should give an interview to ProPublica
text:
I was a longtime Auburn resident and used to be a Republican.
As reported recently by ProPublica, a serious and potentially career-ending allegation was made against Sen. Susan Collins. Did she illegally channel government contracts to a Hawaiian defense contractor that paid her campaign through a fake company it concocted to hide what it was doing?
Will Sen. Collins agree to do a town hall or an interview with the ProPublica journalists to discuss the facts and points detailed in the ProPublica reporting? It appears her response thus far has been to have her staff blow smoke and for Collins to shoot the messenger, i.e., the journalists at ProPublica. She has essentially taken a clue from our president and yelled “fake news.”
But, ProPublica is a respected reporting source dedicated to holding government representatives to account. It report that it has reviewed thousands of emails never previously revealed, and it has interviewed many persons close to the case who have corroborated much of the reporting. It has the receipts, unfortunately for Collins.
Why did her campaign staff agree to accept $150,000 from a shell company hiding the source as a government contractor?
On the face of it, the ProPublica article is damning to Collins. Other than repeating “fake news,” how can she defend herself? I have no idea. But, for the first time in over 25 years, the public should hear from her live and in person. She should meet with voters. Failing her agreement to do so, she should sit for a thorough interview with ProPublica. Mainers deserve to know, to paraphrase Richard M. Nixon, if their U.S. senator is a crook.
Daniel Mawhinney
Portland

title: Tony Romo, CBS Sports part ways months after ex-quarterback’s arrest
text:
Tony Romo, CBS Sports part ways months after ex-quarterback’s arrest
Tony Romo and CBS Sports have parted ways, the network announced, months after the former quarterback's July arrest for driving while intoxicated.
“CBS Sports and Tony Romo have mutually agreed to part ways. We thank Tony for his contributions over the past nine years and wish him the best moving forward," a statement from CBS reads in part.
Related video above | Tony Romo pleads no contest to OWI after Milwaukee arrest
The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback was arrested in Milwaukee on July 23 after a traffic stop. Court records showed that one of the arresting officers said he detected a “strong odor of an alcoholic beverage” on Romo.
Romo pleaded no contest, and issued a statement apologizing for his actions.
According to Milwaukee County court records, Romo lost his driving privileges for six months and was ordered to complete an alcohol assessment program.
Romo also owes $834. An interlock device must be installed on any vehicle owned or operated by Romo or registered to his name, and that order will remain in effect for at least one year after he is issued a license.
“The past month has been difficult, but it has also been personally significant,” Romo said in a statement on Instagram. “It has required me to confront and own my mistakes fully — to the Lord, to myself, to my family and now to the public.”
Romo said the multiple back surgeries that led to his retirement as a player “left me with constant, debilitating pain.” He noted that the pain “led to a dependence on pain medication, and my efforts to get off those medications led to an over-reliance on alcohol.”
“None of this is an excuse,” Romo said. “These are my failures and I take responsibility for them.”
CBS Sports coverage moving forward will not be impacted, the network said, adding, "JJ Watt will continue to partner with Jim Nantz and Tracy Wolfson on our lead NFL announce team for the rest of the season. All other teams remain the same, including Ian Eagle, Ross Tucker and Evan Washburn.”
The Associated press contributed to this report.

title: Ken Urker, Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s ex-fiancé, found dead on his birthday, reports say
text:
RACELAND, La. (KPLC/Gray News) - Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s ex-fiancé Ken Urker was found dead in Louisiana, according to several reports.
He was 34.
A source close to the family confirmed his death to People. TMZ was first to report the news.
Urker’s brother Dylan found him unresponsive in his home on Thursday, which would have been his birthday, TMZ reported.
The Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Office said officers were called to a home in Raceland around 6:15 p.m. and found Urker dead, according to People.
According to People, Urker’s sister went live on TikTok Thursday night, confirming his death. She said his last words to her were “I love you,” People reported.
Urker and Blanchard were engaged from October 2018 to August 2019 while she was still in prison for her role in killing her abusive mother.
The two later rekindled their romance in April 2024. The two welcomed a daughter, Aurora Raina Urker, that same December.

title: How Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike unfolded, minute-by-minute
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike was scheduled to be executed. But after two injections, she kept breathing. She made snoring sounds, she talked, she said her arm was hurting.
Pike, sentenced to die for torturing and killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995, said as her scheduled lethal injection began that she was at peace.
Strapped to a gurney around 7:30 p.m. Wednesday, Pike, who was allowed to give a final statement, said she was leaving the world with love.
“I’m ready to be free,” she said. “This is a happy day.”
Leaving prison in an ambulance, not a hearse
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she committed the murder and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
But instead she survived two doses of the pentobarbital meant to kill her. She left the prison in an ambulance instead of a hearse.
The Associated Press was among those who witnessed her failed execution. She was already strapped to the gurney, with IV inserted in her arm, when prison officials raised the curtain to the execution room at 7:27 p.m.
Her spiritual adviser was standing beside the gurney near her head. He spoke to her. They sang a song. The lyrics were not audible, but included repeating the phrase — “I love you.” The spiritual adviser stroked her forehead.
Minutes ticked by. She raised her head and looked around; she smiled. Then she said her arm was hurting and asked a prison official in the room if it was supposed to feel that way.
Ten minutes in, at 7:37 p.m., she sighed, the IV in her arm fed from a control room adjacent to the death chamber, separated by a ledge. At 7:41 p.m., a rock or paper weight about the size of a golf ball was placed on the ledge. Prison officials have not confirmed what it means, but its placement appeared to coincide with a direction in the protocol that says after the drugs are administered, a five-minute countdown begins until the curtain is closed.
At 7:46 p.m., officials closed the curtain, blocking the witnesses’ view of the death chamber. Pike’s spiritual adviser left the chamber and sat briefly with her attorney in the media witness room.
The curtain rose again three minutes later. The Tennessee lethal injection protocol calls for a second round of pentobarbital if the inmate is not deceased after the first round.
An hour-plus of what sounded like snoring
Her spiritual adviser returned to the chamber and stood beside Pike with his hands folded. Pike appeared to begin to lose consciousness at some point and started making a sound like snoring. She continued to do so for the next hour, a sign that she was alive long after she was expected to be dead.
Her head raised slightly off the gurney and turned to the side at about 7:56 p.m. She kept breathing.
Officials closed the curtain again at 8:06 p.m.
For the next 40 minutes, Pike could be heard from behind the curtain. She sounded like she was snoring, a rhythmic, regular breathing pattern.
Inside the prison, Pike’s attorney, Randy Spivey, later told the media that at about 8:22 p.m. he demanded access to a telephone to contact other lawyers on the team. He said he demanded the execution be halted and that life-saving medical care be given to Pike. He said he received confirmation at about 8:50 p.m. that an ambulance was on the way.
At 8:53 p.m., an announcement came: “Will witnesses please exit the area.” The media was escorted out, and a prison spokesperson said she had no information to provide about what had happened.
Fire trucks and ambulances arrived in front of the prison at around 9:14 p.m. Pike’s attorneys later issued a statement that she had been taken to a hospital and was being treated, though they did not know the specifics of her condition. On Thursday afternoon, they said she was in critical condition receiving medical care.
Governor orders a review
The Tennessee Department of Correction issued a statement saying the department followed protocol.
“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening,” the agency wrote. “Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”
The agency has not said what went wrong. It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to complete an execution, though in the other case, officials couldn’t find a suitable vein for an IV line so the drugs weren’t administered.
Gov. Bill Lee ordered a review and postponed another execution scheduled for later this year, calling what happened in the death chamber “deeply disturbing.”
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, had traveled to Nashville to see the sentence carried out.
“I didn’t get justice for my daughter,” Martinez told the AP by telephone.
“I watched the whole thing. She was awake,” Martinez said. ”She was moving her head, moving her feet. She was trying to sit up. Didn’t work the first time they gave her a shot. It didn’t work the second time so she’s in the hospital and alive.”
“This isn’t justice for Colleen.”
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

title: AARP survey finds most older adults lack confidence in online privacy
text:
Maine (WABI) - A new survey from AARP highlights how artificial intelligence is changing the online safety landscape.
The survey of more than 600 older adults, conducted by Senior Planet from AARP, found just 7% feel very confident about protecting their data online.
The survey also found 70% are not very confident or not at all confident about what they should or should not share with AI tools.
“We don’t want people to stop using technology. It’s really important for us to stay part of the mainstream and learn these tools, but we do want people to become informed, we use them and just be a little bit more cautious and use that common sense we all have,” said Tom Kamber, executive director of Older Adults Technology Services, AARP.
AARP has unveiled a new guide for privacy and security best practices. Recommendations include limiting what apps can access, regularly checking privacy settings on devices and accounts, and staying mindful of what you share on the web.
People can visit seniorplanet.org/privacy-and-security to better understand how to protect their privacy and security while using the internet.

title: AARP supports veterans
text:
To the Editor:
As veterans continue to face challenges related to health, connection and well-being, it is important they know that AARP is in their corner with free resources designed to support them and their families.
A recent AARP report found that 38% of U.S. veterans age 45 and older are lonely — more than 4.8 million people nationwide. The study also found that many veterans have fewer friends than they did five years ago and wish they were more socially connected. These findings underscore the need for practical tools that help veterans access care, build connections, and remain engaged in their communities.
One such resource is a new free tool from AARP’s Veterans and Military Families initiative. Through Health.Vet, veterans can enter their ZIP code and receive a personalized report identifying nearby eligible VA community care providers, helping them find care closer to home without lengthy travel.
AARP also recently partnered with Dogs Inc. to offer a free dog-training video series for veterans, military families, caregivers and pet owners. The program provides practical training tips that can strengthen the bond between people and their dogs while promoting routine, companionship and connection.
Veterans in Maine can find information, benefits, programs and support through the AARP Maine Online Veterans Resource Guide at aarp.org/veteransME, a convenient one-stop resource. In honor of America's 250th birthday, AARP Maine volunteers and friends also wrote 250 letters for veterans traveling with Honor Flight Maine, helping ensure each participant receives a heartfelt message of thanks for their service.
Veterans have served our country with dedication. Ensuring they have access to care, companionship, and trusted resources is one way we can serve them in return.
Sincerely,
Tim Gudridge, U.S. Air Force, retired AARP Maine veteran outreach volunteer lead
Sumner

title: Jay generator journey loses steam as ‘super oversize’ load stops in Oxford
text:
Oxford became the focal point of local curiosity when a steam generator on a slow journey from Jay to South Portland using state routes had to pause in town and was parked at Call of the Wild RV Center on Main Street.
Employees at Call of the Wild said they had not been alerted that the 220-foot trailer load would be backed onto the property alongside its sales and service building.
They added that another business owner in the Route 26 neighborhood had refused to allow it on its property for the day.
The Maine Department of Transportation stipulated that the 20-foot-wide load and its accompanying vehicles can only travel public roads between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m.
The spectacle attracted a lot of curious locals who pulled into Call of the Wild’s parking lot during Thursday business hours to see what the hubbub was all about.
According to Facebook chatter, a large number of people parked at Oxford Plains Speedway Thursday evening to watch the trailer, attached to a tractor pulling it and another pushing it, hit the road for the next leg of its move, Route 117.
From there it is being taken over sections of Route 202, Route 22 and Route 1 to a location off Broadway in South Portland. The move, which began from Route 4 in Jay the evening of Sept. 29, was expected to take two days.
But after the trip began its duration was recalculated to last one week.
It is the first of nine “super oversize” equipment loads to be taken from the former Pixelle Specialty Solutions paper mill in Jay to the South Portland side of the Fore River in Casco Bay.

title: Ice Cream, Foliage and 80-degree temperatures hit Maine in October
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ice Cream, Foliage and 80-degree temperatures hit Maine in October
When it's 82-degrees out, what do you do?
You head to Red's Dairy Freeze in South Portland as last days of ice cream are being served up.
"It's wonderful. When it's 82. You eat ice cream and go to the beach. We're full of sand," said Julie and Philip Lamson of Standish.
Teacher Elaine Brassard was caught eating an ice cream cone while taking a break from school.
"I'm off school right now but I'm going back to school in the next five minutes. I had to get a quick ice cream. I'm actually between USM and Cape High School," Brassard said.
The owner Red's Dairy Freeze said the popular ice cream stand will remain open until they run out of ice cream before closing up for the season.
"It could be today, could be tomorrow. Anytime this weekend is what we are thinking," said Laura Gregoire.
At Portland Head Light, tourists were taking in the sights and snapping pictures. Tour buses were pulling and out of the Fort Williams Park in Cape Elizabeth.
License plates in the parking lot came from all over, New Jersey, Ohio, New York and Louisiana.
WMTW asked some of the drivers if gas prices were keeping them away.
"In Pittsburgh is $4.79 a gallon. Diesel is seven, almost $7 a gallon in diesel. We are still traveling. We're travelers. We like to travel," said Lisa Kreuzer of Pittsburgh.
"It is gorgeous here. It is beautiful. The colors are changing. Highlight with the bike tours today with Lighthouse Bike Tours," said Debbie White of San Francisco, California
"I think before we left it was $6.49, $6.59 for regular leaded. I was like - oh my goodness, what a deal it's like $4.19 here," White said.
Enjoy the warm weather while it lasts because we all know what's around the corner - cooler temperatures and Halloween.

Third place primary finisher to continue to invest in "common sense" candidates
Former Republican gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Bush plans to invest six figures in Bangor, Waterville and Lewiston to support city councils.
Former Republican gubernatorial primary candidate Jonathan Bush may not have become his party's nominee, but he said he still wants to invest in Maine.
He is investing six figures in a political campaign for what he calls "common sense candidates," no matter their party affiliation.
This will work on things like local accountability and voter education.
Bush said there will be television ads and other campaign materials in Bangor, Lewiston and Waterville.
"I think that there's lots of people in places like Bangor and Waterville and Lewiston that are pillars of their community, but don't think of politics as their lot that have suddenly realized, geez, I better make it my lot because my city is literally emptying out, and being refilled by tweakers from other states," Bush said.
Bush finished third in the June primary but said he is not ruling out another run for "something" in four years.

title: Edward Little football outlasts Scarborough in double overtime thriller
text:
AUBURN — No one on the Edward Little football team was alive when the Red Eddies won their last state championship in 1977, or when they made their last title game appearance in 2002 for that matter, but the players are still aware of the program’s decades-long drought.
And while their 27-21 double overtime win over Scarborough on Friday doesn’t fix things, it proved to be a step in the right direction — one that was on full display as quarterback Logan Stout rushed 9 yards into the end zone to clinch a Week 5 thriller for his team.
“(This win) means the world to us and our program,” said Stout, a sophomore. “And our program had been looking for a team like this for so long, and it means so much for us to keep bringing it on and on and on, and bringing it up and up and up for the next few years — and even right now, just bringing it up from here.”
Stout had already thrown a touchdown and rushed for another in regulation. In overtime, he doubled his total, scoring on both of Edward Little’s drives.
“Coach (Brian Jahna) is like …‘Can you get this (touchdown)?’” Stout said. “I’m like, ‘Yes Coach, I got this.’ First play, it was the wedge, it wasn’t the best. We didn’t get much. But then second play, I knew it was coming. I knew he would give me that sweep to the outside, and just took it from there.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
In the first quarter, Edward Little (2-2) showed it was ready for a fight against a Scarborough (0-5) team that had faced a gauntlet of a schedule, with losses against Thornton Academy, Portland, South Portland and Bonny Eagle in the first four weeks of the season.
The Red Eddies struck first on a 7-yard touchdown pass from Stout to Ashton Sullivan, and they kept the Red Storm out of the end zone in the first half. Scarborough’s best chance at scoring came with the ball inside the Edward Little 5-yard line, but Sullivan sacked quarterback Oscar Goss to force a turnover on downs.
The Red Storm scored on their first drive of the second half — a 16-yard touchdown pass from Goss to Jackson Leahy — which tied the game, 7-7. On the ensuing Red Eddies drive, Ozzie Bodah returned a fumble for 22 yards for a score, putting Scarborough ahead by a touchdown with under five and half minutes to play in the third quarter.
Edward Little bounced back quickly. On its next drive, Stout had a 26-yard touchdown run negated by a holding penalty, but just under two and half minutes into the fourth quarter, he found the end zone on a 1-yard rush.
Stout scored in the same way on the Red Eddies’ first overtime drive. Scarborough then answered with a 2-yard pass from Goss to Brandon Brady. The Red Storm had the ball first in the second overtime, but missed a field goal. That opened the door for Stout, who rushed for his third touchdown of the game to lift Edward Little to victory.
UNSUNG HERO
Edward Little’s Adonis Bailey-Curry intercepted two passes late in the fourth quarter. These game-saving plays helped the Red Eddies survive to win the game in overtime.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “They grew up with not seeing a whole lot of wins, so to establish that themselves, it’s a really big deal. And a night like tonight could go either way, right? So to have it fall on our side of things, I think it was really big in terms of their confidence and their belief in themselves.” — Edward Little coach Brian Jahna
• “I was honest with them just now: ‘We need to grow up.’ And I don’t question their effort, but poise in big moments is important, and that was the difference in the game. So we’re going to keep working, keep moving forward. We’re passionately invested in these young guys. These lessons are tough. They played very, very hard tonight, but it wasn’t enough.” — Scarborough coach Michael Vance
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Edward Little: Logan Stout (4 for 6 passing, 38 yards, TD; 3 rushing TDs); Ashton Sullivan (TD reception; sack); Adonis Bailey-Curry (2 interceptions)
• Scarborough: Oscar Goss (9 for 20 passing, 125 yards, two touchdowns)

title: Susan Collins should drop out and step down
text:
A million years ago, by which I mean this past June, Graham Platner called Sen. Susan Collins “corrupt.” He took a lot of flak for that. But new reporting from ProPublica seems to prove him right.
That Collins reportedly played “pay to play” with Navatek demonstrates a lack of judgment and ethics. Offering government contracts in return for a campaign contribution is the very definition of bribery. We should hope that the next Democratic administration pulls the files and reopens the investigation.
Collins must drop out of the Senate race and resign immediately. She is clearly not fit to serve. Self-dealing and insider trading have no place in the Senate. I feel she’s an embarrassment to Maine, and she has to go.
They said there was zero tolerance for sexual misbehavior when Senate candidate Graham Platner was accused (without further adjudication). Shouldn’t there be zero tolerance for plausible allegations of bribery and corruption by a sitting senator?
Wayne Clark
Durham

text:
FlyDubai pilot hailed hero after onboard attack: 'I couldn't let everybody else die'
Smit Machchhar, the hero FlyDubai captain who fought off a savage attack by his copilot, kept fighting because he could not "let everybody else die," he said in his first public remarks since Wednesday's suspected hijacking attempt.
Related video: Brother of FlyDubai passenger speaks about flight where captain was stabbed
"In that moment, I was fighting for my life," Machchhar told India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a video call on Friday. "Because I had fallen down… I was so severely wounded that I had fallen down… at that time, I was thinking, what if I don't get up?
A horrific mid-air catastrophe on a plane heading to Tel Aviv was averted in a stunning turn of events on Wednesday when passengers and crew bravely rushed into the cockpit and regained control of the aircraft.
Machchhar said he was on the ground in the cockpit when he realized the plane was going down.
"And I knew in that moment – one last push, Smit! Just do it. The door is right there," he told Modi. "And even at that time, he was beating me up."
"And then I just opened it … and then everybody came," he said, referring to several other passengers who then rushed into the cockpit and restrained his attacker.
"I was doing this for my life, but at the same time, I knew that I couldn't let everybody else die."

title: InvestigateTV+: A conservation success story
text:
(InvestigateTV) — An American symbol once on the brink of extinction, the bald eagle is considered a conservation success story. InvestigateTV+ explores its decades-long journey to recovery.
Then, we uncover the paper trail leading to a Russian citizen in Texas and why Medicare recipients should take a second look at their statements.
Plus, a father honors his son by teaching young drivers about the dangers on the road.
An American success story
A bald eagle sits atop a Louisiana cypress tree in Lake Palourde near Morgan City, a scene that would have been inconceivable a few short decades ago.
“We can see up to 60 eagles in a tour,” said Billy Gaston, who makes a living largely off providing eagle sightseeing tours in and near the lake.
The government removed the eagle from the Endangered Species List in 2007, widely regarded as one of conservation’s great success stories.
Investigation reveals Medicare billing scheme
A WSMV4 investigation has uncovered a Medicare fraud scheme that billed the federal program tens of thousands of dollars for medical supplies that Tennessee recipients never needed or received.
Our investigation found the billing is connected to a Russian citizen living in Texas, accused in a $3 billion Medicare fraud scheme.
Encouraging safe-driving
Mike Lutzenkirchen is sharing his son’s story with teens and young adults in hopes of preventing fatal crashes caused by unsafe driving.
Lutzenkirchen’s son, Philip, died in a car accident in 2014. Philip, a former Auburn football player, had been drinking with friends before getting into a car. Investigators said the car was speeding and ran a stop sign, killing both Philip and the driver.
Helping every customer he sees
For almost three decades, Greg Atchison has been a friendly face in the grocery business.
“It’s greeting people. Meeting people, seeing people, it’s therapeutic,” Atchison said.
Atchison has worked 28 years in customer service. Twenty years at Festival Foods, formerly Trig’s, and eight at County Market. His approach extends beyond typical customer interactions.

title: Wife hid husband’s remains in freezer for up to 7 years to collect benefits, police say
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska. (KTUU/Gray News) - A woman in Alaska hid her late husband’s remains in a freezer for years in order to collect benefits, according to authorities.
Juneau police found the remains of Ross Pasquan inside a chest freezer on July 19. Police said he would have been 74 years old at the time of the discovery of his remains.
A family member had been cleaning out the property following the death of Pasquan’s wife, Sheryl Ann McDonald-Pasquan, who died on July 14, 2025, from natural causes.
Inside a storage shed, a family member discovered a locked freezer.
Police said the person found the key, opened the freezer and found a tarp-wrapped object that appeared to contain human remains. They closed the freezer and went directly to Juneau police.
The State Medical Examiner’s Office determined that Pasquan died of natural causes related to severe cardiovascular disease. Investigators believe Pasquan’s remains were placed in the freezer sometime between 2018 and 2025.
The investigation found that McDonald-Pasquan concealed his death and continued applying for and receiving benefits in his name until her death. Those benefits included Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend checks, Social Security benefits and retirement benefits.
Investigators also learned that a retirement benefit provider had not been notified of his death and was still depositing monthly payments into Pasquan’s account up until July 2026.
Investigators found no evidence that another person caused Pasquan’s death or helped McDonald-Pasquan in concealing his remains or collecting his benefits.
Witness interviews indicated that Pasquan had a history of significant health problems and that McDonald-Pasquan served as his primary caregiver. Witnesses said she explained his absence by telling them he had been moved to a care facility outside Juneau.
The investigation is now closed due to McDonald-Pasquan’s death.

title: Radio signal detected from exoplanet for the first time
text:
(CNN) - For the first time, astronomers say they have detected radio waves from a planet outside our solar system.
The planet, about 63 light-years away, is producing a radio signal that’s linked to an enormous magnetic field.
Scientists say the signal is not evidence of intelligent life.
Researchers believe that the field is at least 200 times stronger than Jupiter’s.
More observations are planned as scientists try to understand why the magnetic field is so powerful.

Police bodycam footage of Luigi Mangione’s arrest released
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Police bodycam footage released Friday shows the moment officers located and arrested Luigi Mangione at a Pennsylvania McDonald’s in connection with the shooting death of United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in Manhattan.
In one video, officers ask Mangione to lower the face mask he was wearing to hide his identity.
“That’s 100% him,” one officer says eagerly as they step outside to speak out of Mangione’s earshot.
“I told you, man,” another responds off camera.
Later, an officer searches Mangione’s belongings and smiles widely as she pulls out a gun cartridge, seemingly confirming they’d found their suspect.
The trove of videos comes from Mangione’s Dec. 9, 2024, arrest in Altoona, five days after Thompson, a 50-year-old Minnesota executive, was gunned down as he walked to a midtown Manhattan hotel for his company’s annual investor conference.
A Manhattan judge unsealed the recordings Friday after CNN petitioned for their release. Parts of the videos were shown during a December court hearing as Mangione’s lawyers unsuccessfully sought to get key evidence thrown out, including his initial statements to police and items seized at the time of his arrest.
Mangione pleaded guilty in August to federal stalking charges and faces life in prison when he’s sentenced in December. He also faces murder charges in New York state court, though those proceedings have been postponed indefinitely as his lawyers seek to have the case thrown out.
The videos released Friday begin as officers descend on the McDonald’s in central Pennsylvania, nearly 300 miles (483 kilometers) from Manhattan.
They find Mangione, the Ivy League-educated scion of a wealthy Maryland family, seated at a table wearing a ski hat, surgical face mask and winter coat. The officers say they’re responding to a call about a suspicious person and ask for his name and identification.
“You’re a little nervous right now. Why are you nervous?” an officer asks at one point.
They order him to put his hands on his head and ask him if he’s been in New York recently. They confront him about a phony New Jersey driver’s license he offers up bearing the name Mark Rosario.
“You’re under official police investigation right now,” one officer warns. “You give a false name to us again, you’re gonna be arrested for false ID.”
When Mangione finally comes clean, they ask why he had lied.
“I clearly shouldn’t have,” he responds as he’s asked to write his real name and spell it aloud.
Other videos show officers patting Mangione down, reading him his rights, placing him in cuffs and taking him to the police station.
As an officer searches him more thoroughly at the station, another officer goes through his backpack.
The officer finds the 9 mm handgun authorities would later confirm was used in the killing, as well as a silencer and another ammo magazine. They also recover the journal that prosecutors would later say revealed Mangione’s intent to “wack” a health insurance executive, as well as his other handwritten notes.
“He has a checklist for today,” another officer says, ticking off the seized items to someone on the phone. “Tomorrow he’s supposed to do an intel check-in and get a survival kit.”

title: Europe bows to US pressure to release diesel reserves in boost for Trump
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Europe bows to US pressure to release diesel reserves in boost for Trump
U.S. President Donald Trump announced that Europe has agreed to release "a massive amount of their heavily stocked diesel oil," following days of pressure to take action to cool surging fuel prices.
"The process will begin immediately," Trump posted on Truth Social Friday.
European officials held crisis talks earlier on Friday after the U.S. piled pressure on the region to tap into its emergency stocks of diesel – or face a possible ban on U.S. exports of the fuel.
France released a statement announcing the drawdown after chairing a videoconference of G7 leaders.
In a statement, G7 leaders said that they "will implement our commitments" by releasing 100 million barrels over four months, beginning immediately. This includes a "frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners," the statement read.
The ultimatum from the U.S. administration marked an escalation in pressure on Europe as Trump attempts to bring down U.S. fuel prices ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Diesel is the workhorse fuel for the global economy, powering trucks, tractors, freight trains and other commercial vehicles. The U.S. is the world's largest exporter of the fuel and Trump has touted a ban on diesel exports as a way to boost domestic supplies – and, in turn, bring down prices.
A U.S. diesel export ban would hit Europe – a net importer of the fuel – hard. But tapping into its emergency reserves risks leaving Europe exposed should supply disruptions from the war in the Middle East and Ukraine continue.
Both U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright urged European countries this week to release diesel from their stockpiles.
"This is a time for a coordinated release of diesel stores as we go into harvest season, and we go into winter heating oil season. Now is the time to bring more diesel to the market," Wright told Fox News on Thursday.
The U.S.-Iran war – now in its eighth month – has disrupted flows of crude and refined oil products from the Middle East. While Europe is not currently grappling with outright shortages, global supplies are tight and prices have soared.
U.S. diesel prices have also shot up since the start of the war and, last month, topped $6 a gallon for the first time, according to data from AAA. The average price stood at $6.40 a gallon on Friday morning. Prices fell 5% on Friday in response to news of the coordinated release of reserves.
'Grappling and fighting'
The threat of a ban on U.S. diesel exports meant Europe had little choice but to comply with U.S. demands, analysts said.
The U.S. is such a critical supplier of diesel to the international market that any ban on its exports would see countries "grappling and fighting over what remains," said Richard Bronze, Energy Aspects’ co-founder.
Europe's benchmark diesel prices have more than doubled since the start of the U.S.-Iran war in late February, according to Intercontinental Exchange data.
Worsening the picture is a ban on diesel exports from Russia – which Moscow recently extended until the end of October – following Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries. As are indications from China that it may tighten restrictions on its oil product exports, said Bronze.
EU member states are required to hold oil stocks equal to 90 days of net imports, but the Commission does not specify how those stocks should be divided between crude oil, jet fuel, kerosene and diesel.
Matt Stanley, head of market engagement at Kpler, highlighted Europe's dilemma and the risks posed by dipping into emergency reserves in an uncertain geopolitical environment.
"If the underlying disruption continues, you cannot keep drawing inventories indefinitely without eventually creating a much bigger supply problem," he told CNN.
In March, member countries of the International Energy Agency agreed to release 400 million barrels of oil into the global market – the largest release of emergency oil stocks in history – in response to the U.S.-Iran war.
But the U.S. argued that Europe has not fulfilled its side of the bargain.

title: Maine Marathon: What to know for Sunday’s event in Portland
text:
The 35th edition of the Maine Community Bank Maine Marathon, Half Marathon and Marathon Relay takes place Sunday on the streets of Portland, Falmouth, Cumberland and Yarmouth, beginning at 7:45 a.m.
The largest marathon in Maine, the overall field is approaching 5,500 entries — well above last year’s record of 5,144.
“I’m limiting the growth to about 400 runners per year,” said Bob Dunfey, the volunteer race director.
The Maine Marathon and its participants have raised over $8,900,000 for charity. The event donates about 40% of revenue toward a variety of charities. Last year, donations totaled $793,285. Each year, the race picks three to five “designated charities.” This year’s beneficiaries are Nanna’s House, Day One, Camp No Limits, and the Pine Tree Society. Many other groups benefit from fundraising done by runners.
Here are key details about the Maine Marathon.
Start/finish: The marathon and half marathon start simultaneously on Baxter Boulevard in Portland. Both races also finish there.
Course: Essentially out-and-back. The course curls around Portland’s Back Cove, works it way to Route 1 North and then veers onto Route 88. The 26.2-mile marathon course goes through Falmouth and Cumberland before reaching the 12-mile mark in Yarmouth. Runners turn right onto Gilman Road, then another right onto Princes Point road to begin a roughly 3-mile loop to get back to Route 88, where they’ll head south on their return. The 13.1-mile half marathon follows the same route until it gets to a turnaround just past scenic Mussel Cove in Falmouth.
Event records: Men’s marathon — Ryan Eiler, Boston, 2 hours, 19 minutes, 19 seconds (2022); Women’s marathon — Abby Hamilton, Yarmouth, 2:39:38 (2021); Men’s half marathon — Colin Cernik, Portland, 1:04:39 (2025); Women’s half marathon, Cliodhna O’Malley, Windham, 1:15:06 (2025).
Prize money: The top male, female and non-binary runners earn $1,000 for the marathon and $500 for the half marathon, with cash through fifth place in each gender group if the runner meets the elite standard. Prizes are also available for a new event record in the marathon ($500) and half marathon ($250).
Top runners: The 2025 marathon winners, Sammy Mills of Portland and Emma Howe of Cambridge, Massachusetts, are not entered to defend their titles. The fastest local runners have migrated to the half marathon, including defending champions and event record holders Cernik and O’Malley. There are as many as 10 runners capable of challenging Cernik’s men’s record. The women’s half marathon features the past four winners — O’Malley, Phoebe Oehmig (2024), Veronica Graziano (2023) and Alyson Ursiny (2022). Megan O’Neil of Rochester, Michigan, is a serious threat. O’Neil ran a 2:31 at the Boston Marathon this spring, finishing 20th overall.
New this year: There will be lactation tents for the benefit of nursing mothers at the start/finish, and also near the 12- and 15-mile marks on the marathon course. … Instead of a starter’s gun or boat horn, the start of the chip-timed races will be signaled by a series of musical notes.
Race packet pickup: The runner’s expo on Saturday is at a new location. Runners can pick up their racing bib and T-shirt at Innovation Hall on the University of New England’s Portland campus from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Numerous vendors will be at the expo.
Race registrations: Dunfey said entries have come from 49 states (only North Dakota is missing), as well as Washington, D.C., the U.S. Virgin Island, Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, and 15 foreign countries. As of 3 p.m. Thursday, registration was still open but fast approaching the 5,500 cap.

title: Here’s why some southern Maine towns haven’t considered pausing data centers — yet
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Local moratoriums on data centers popped up across Maine this summer, following Gov. Janet Mills’ veto of a bill temporarily restricting their permitting statewide. Some municipalities did so in the face of data center proposals in their communities, others did so preemptively.
There are other towns with similar demographics and geography that haven’t made that move — at least not yet — deeming it not necessary at this time for a mixture of reasons.
Towns including Brunswick, Bangor, Westbrook, Gorham, Gray, Sanford, Scarborough and Saco have approved temporary moratoriums since May, intended to give them time to address concerns about the facilities and potentially adjust their zoning ordinances accordingly. Other municipalities, including North Berwick, Buxton and Wells, are set to let voters decide on either moratoriums or outright bans on data center developments, with more southern Maine communities in the early phases of considering halts.
On the other hand, some towns, including Yarmouth, have not taken action regarding data centers and are taking a “wait-and-see” approach, said town staff.
“I think it’s a community-by-community decision,” said Yarmouth Planning and Development Director Erin Zwirko.
Zwirko said she reviewed the data center moratoriums of neighboring municipalities and their ordinances in the spring. She concluded that a data center likely wouldn’t be an allowed use under Yarmouth’s land use ordinances, though they don’t explicitly mention data centers and she’s aware that ambiguity could be exploited.
“An attorney working for a data center could interpret it differently,” said Zwirko.
Zwirko consulted with the town manager, code enforcement officer and the town’s legal counsel, who together determined it was not necessary for Yarmouth to pursue a moratorium. If conditions change — such as a data center proposal for the community, which has minimal space where such a project could even fit — the Town Council could then enact a data center moratorium, said Zwirko.
Zwirko said she hasn’t heard concerns about data centers from Yarmouth residents, but has a sense of how they would respond to a proposed plan based on the public discussions about the town’s future when Yarmouth updated its comprehensive plan in 2024.
“I don’t believe that that type of use is something that would fit into the goals of the community,” said Zwirko.
In other towns, there is also little urgency to address data centers, but it’s a long-term consideration. In Falmouth, the Town Council has yet to consider action related to data centers, as the topic didn’t make it onto the council’s annual work plan development meeting in the summer, said Town Manager Nathan Poore. It’s on the agenda for the mid-year progress meeting in January. Then, councilors will discuss if a data center moratorium or ban is something they want to set as a priority for the next six months, said Poore.
In neighboring Cumberland, which has not been approached with a data center proposal, a moratorium or ban has not been considered, said Town Manager Matthew Sturgis. Likewise in South Portland, city staff determined that a policy addressing data centers is not currently necessary, and no councilors have proposed a workshop on the topic.
Sturgis said that rather than taking local action at this time, Cumberland is closely following how the state is pursuing policies regarding data centers. Sturgis said the Legislature passing the bill that would temporarily ban new data center development in Maine, despite it being shot down by Mills, indicates that data center development wil be raised again as a statewide issue.
“(W)e anticipate the Legislature will address it again in the first term,” wrote Sturgis in an email.

text:
Panda diplomacy family tree: Here's every pair loaned to the US by China
