Panda diplomacy family tree: Here's every pair loaned to the US by China
China first gifted giant pandas to the U.S. in 1972. Now, they are on loan to American zoos.
Zoo Atlanta has two new residents from China.
Giant pandas Fu Shuang, a female panda, and Ping Ping, a male panda, arrived at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on Sunday aboard the FedEx Panda Express. They are the third pair of giant pandas loaned to the U.S. by China as a form of diplomacy over the past two years.
These pandas were sent one day after President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met during a state visit. 
China first gifted pandas to the U.S. in 1972 following President Richard Nixon's visit to Beijing. First Lady Patricia Nixon mentioned her fondness for giant pandas to Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai, and so two giant pandas were gifted to the American people as a form of diplomacy.
Since then, the Chinese government has been loaning pandas to American zoos in exchange for an annual base fee of $1 million for research and conservation.
The Get the Facts Data Team went through the reports of the National Zoo, San Diego Zoo, Memphis Zoo and Zoo Atlanta and created a family tree from the giant panda pairs that were loaned to the U.S. This does not include short-term exhibition loans, such as the giant pandas loaned for the 1984 Olympic Games.
Nine giant panda pairs have been brought to the country since 1972, and around 25 cubs have been born on U.S. soil. Of these cubs, eight did not survive.
Panda cubs are traditionally named around 100 days after birth. Unnamed cubs died before their naming ceremony.

title: Country star diagnosed with rare blood cancer after health scare: ‘One day at a time’
text:
Country star diagnosed with rare blood cancer after health scare: ‘One day at a time’
Charles Kelley, the singer and songwriter best known as a founding member of the country trio Lady A, revealed he’s been diagnosed with a rare blood cancer.
The 44-year-old Grammy winner shared the news on Instagram this week, saying that doctors have diagnosed him with multiple myeloma – a rare blood cancer in which abnormal plasma cells grow in the bone marrow.
Kelley said it started with him going to the doctor to address a few “random” rib fractures, which prompted several blood tests from doctors.
Related video above | Lady A’s Charles Kelley talks touring with his son
"And one of the blood tests we did, they found a blood cancer in there called multiple myeloma and it's rare," he said.
Despite his diagnosis, Kelley said he’s hopeful.
"I'm young. I feel healthy. The treatments, I will have to say, have just come so far, even in the past five years that, even life expectancy just far exceeds what it used to be," Kelley said.
His diagnosis does not mean an end to the music.
"I can still work. I think physically I will feel like myself,” he said. “I'll have tough days, but you know, I want to keep working.”
"I need to be happy and doing what I love to do and spending and soaking up as much time with my family as I can,” he added. “I'm hopeful, I really am. We just want to let you all know and I'll try to let you in when I feel like it's appropriate throughout the journey and it's just another hurdle and you know I'm pretty confident that we're going to get through it."
Kelley, along with longtime friend Dave Haywood and singer Hillary Scott, formed Lady Antebellum in 2006.
The group’s polished blend of country, pop and rock helped it reach a broad audience, led by hits including “Need You Now” and “I Run to You.”
“Need You Now” won the Grammy for song of the year in 2011, and the trio has earned seven Grammy Awards.
The band changed its name to Lady A in 2020.
Kelley has also released solo music, including the 2016 album “The Driver,” and has co-written songs for other artists.

title: Mobile outreach meets people with substance use disorders where they are
text:
Adam Bloom-Paicopolos, MPP, is the executive director at the Alliance for Addiction & Mental Health Services, Maine’s statewide association for community behavioral health providers serving over 120,000 Mainers annually.
Most communities share a common goal: to care for one another, especially during times of vulnerability. Today, many individuals face complex challenges related to substance use, mental health and housing instability. While there are no simple answers, there are thoughtful, practical approaches that can make a meaningful difference, one person at a time.
One approach to substance use that has been gaining momentum across the country is secondary prevention.
At its core, secondary prevention is not about enabling harmful behavior. It is about preserving life, reducing immediate risk and creating pathways to recovery when individuals are ready. It recognizes that no two people are the same and that progress often begins with trust, respect and individualized support.
As part of this programming, mobile outreach units offer a flexible way to deliver that support directly to individuals who may not otherwise access care. Instead of requiring people to navigate complex systems on their own, trained professionals meet them where they are, physically and emotionally, with services tailored to their specific needs and circumstances.
This model prioritizes individualized intervention. Some individuals may be ready for immediate connection to detox or treatment, while others may need time, information or basic support before taking that step. Mobile outreach allows for real-time assessment and response, offering health screenings, referrals and rapid connections to care based on each person’s readiness.
Peer support is a critical component of this approach. Specialists with lived experience bring credibility and empathy that help build trust quickly. Their presence can turn a moment of hesitation into a moment of possibility, offering not just guidance but hope grounded in personal experience.
In addition to connection and counseling, mobile outreach provides practical, life-saving
resources. These include naloxone to reverse overdoses, wound assessment and basic first aid and crisis support. Just as important, individuals can be connected to housing assistance, social services and behavioral healthcare, because recovery is not just about treatment, but about stability and the opportunity to rebuild.
This work is not done in isolation. Mobile outreach is designed to coordinate with existing providers, healthcare systems and first responders, strengthening, not duplicating, the services already in place. By filling gaps and improving access, it helps create a more responsive and effective system overall.
There is also a practical benefit for the broader community. Early, individualized intervention often reduces reliance on emergency services. When people receive timely support, communities frequently see fewer emergency room visits, hospitalizations and crisis calls. This not only improves outcomes for individuals but also helps manage public resources more effectively.
Across the country, programs like this are demonstrating measurable results: reductions in overdose deaths, increased engagement in treatment and stronger connections between individuals and care providers. These outcomes are not the result of a single solution, but of a consistent commitment to meeting people as individuals, with dignity and without judgment.
That principle matters. Every person’s path is different, shaped by their history, circumstances, and readiness for change. A one-size-fits-all approach cannot fully address such complexity. What can make the difference is a model that is flexible, responsive and grounded in human connection.
Supporting secondary prevention and mobile outreach is a person-centered and practical step forward. It reflects a balanced approach. One that values safety, responsibility and compassion equally. It is not about lowering expectations, but about removing barriers so that individuals can take meaningful steps toward stability and recovery.
In the end, community well-being is built not only through systems, but through moments of connection. A conversation. A referral. A life saved. A path forward. Sometimes the most effective solutions begin by simply meeting people where they are and walking alongside them from there.

title: Recycling facility helps police catch suspect after 77 fire hydrants damaged
text:
ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) - Scrap yards are usually full of metal and hidden treasures, but this week, one of those yards helped police haul in something else - a scrap thief.
“Naturally, when they approached me, I was very happy to help and do anything I could and step forward and give them the information they needed,” Phillip Harbison, general manager at SA Recycling in St. Louis, exclaimed.
The recycling facility, located off of the Broadway, helped find the man who put countless lives in jeopardy.
“I genuinely just dislike thieves; I’m not a fan of thieves at all,” Harbison stated. “So it’s very important to me to get them off the street, and especially when they’re doing things that can harm our community.”
Over the past week, police have been searching for a suspect accused of damaging and stealing the components off of 77 fire hydrants across the City of St. Louis.
On Thursday, police arrested 65-year-old Harry Farmer in connection with that vandalism after they said surveillance video caught him sawing off the hydrants’ brass valves.
“We had a citizen who came forward. We were able to get video of this individual. We were able to obtain a name, but we had to do a case to make sure that we got it right, got the evidence, and then we had to track down video at each one of these known locations,” Chief Robert Tracy, St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department, said.
Farmer allegedly went to SA Recycling to sell the valves, which is when Harbison got him on camera and a picture of his ID.
“All the way from the second they pull onto this lot, they’re on camera,” he explained. “We have pictures of their ID; everything is stored in our database, so every transaction will have a picture of the material they brought in, of their ID, license plate, all of that.”
When police came to ask if they had any information about these incidents, Harbison said they were happy to cooperate.
“You don’t want those types of people out in the city and I want to stop the bad name that’s being given to scrap yards, and that’s why we keep the records we do and are able to help when the police do come and ask for help,” he stated.
Farmer has now been charged with eight felonies.
“Damaging fire hydrants creates a major public safety risk,” Chief Tracy said. “Firefighters depend on working hydrants to protect lives and property - interfering with that access puts residents, businesses and first responders in danger.”
“I’ve been Fire Chief for 19 years, been in this city for 48 with the fire department. I’ve never, ever seen anything like this. Traveled around the country, I’ve never seen hydrants vandalized like this intentionally,” Chief Dennis Jenkerson, St. Louis Fire Department, stated.
For recycling facilities like Harbisons, they just have one message to other scrap thieves.
“I will not buy it; don’t bring it to SA Recycling. SA Recycling does not want stolen scrap… some of us will absolutely do our part and help the community and put criminals behind bars," he said.
As of Friday evening, Farmer is in custody, but police still have to extradite him back to Missouri from Illinois.
The investigation remains ongoing. Police want anyone with more information on the damaged hydrants to contact 314-444-2500 and talk to District 4 detectives.

title: What kind of Maine do you wish to help create?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sondra Shapiro has more than 40 years of experience in mature-market publishing. She is the former executive editor of the award-winning 50+ Advocate Newspaper in Massachusetts. She lives in Ogunquit.
When you walk into the voting booth, what kind of future are you voting for?
Ask yourself: What do I want for my own life, and for the lives of the people I care about?
I don’t have children or grandchildren of my own, but most of my friends do. Watching them babysit, spend time with their families and talk endlessly about the people they love, their devotion is unmistakable. Because I love my friends, I want the exact same things for them that they want for their families: happiness, security and a better tomorrow.
But this question is not only about parents or grandparents. It is about every Mainer. It is about the young adult trying to build a life here, the working family trying to keep up with rising costs, the older neighbor relying on Social Security or Medicare and anyone who wants to feel secure in the place they call home.
So when I enter the voting booth, I try to think beyond the candidate or the party. I think about the country and the state we are creating.
Right now we are watching the boundaries of executive power being tested in Washington. We have seen the federal government attempt to exert control over aspects of how states conduct elections, including voting by mail. Maine fought back, joining a coalition of states to challenge those rules in court; a legal battle that culminated in the U.S. Supreme Court upholding our voting rights. Our state also successfully blocked a federal lawsuit attempting to force the release of Mainers’ private voter data.
Is that federal overreach the direction we want our country to take?
If so, we should be honest with ourselves about it. If not, we need to think seriously about the importance of checks and balances. No president should have unchecked power. The protections built into our system are there precisely because power changes hands.
Whoever represents Maine in the Senate will also have a constitutional role in confirming Supreme Court nominees if vacancies occur. The president nominates them, but the Senate provides advice and consent. Those decisions can affect our country for decades.
But this isn’t only about government and institutions. It is about our everyday lives.
I think about Social Security. Medicare. The cost of living. Housing. Healthcare.
Maine is not a state where most families have unlimited financial cushions. For many people, the cost of housing, food, healthcare and raising children is not an abstract economic discussion. It is the arithmetic of everyday life.
Some Mainers are worried about whether they can afford to stay in the communities they love. Others are trying to buy a first home, pay for college, care for an aging parent or manage medical bills. Many are simply wondering whether the next generation will have the same opportunities they had.
These concerns belong to all of us, regardless of our age or family situation. They are about whether people can live with dignity, find stability and build a future here in Maine.
Maybe you are tired of politics. Maybe you’ve tuned it out. Maybe you believe your one vote won’t change anything.
But your vote is one of the few opportunities you have to say, in a very concrete way, this is the future I want.
Before you mark that ballot, don’t vote by reflex or party habit. Stop for a moment, look closely at the future you are choosing, and ask yourself: Is this the country, and the Maine, I want to help create?

title: How Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike unfolded, minute-by-minute
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike was scheduled to be executed. But after two injections, she kept breathing. She made snoring sounds, she talked, she said her arm was hurting.
Pike, sentenced to die for torturing and killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995, said as her scheduled lethal injection began that she was at peace.
Strapped to a gurney around 7:30 p.m. Wednesday, Pike, who was allowed to give a final statement, said she was leaving the world with love.
“I’m ready to be free,” she said. “This is a happy day.”
Leaving prison in an ambulance, not a hearse
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she committed the murder and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
But instead she survived two doses of the pentobarbital meant to kill her. She left the prison in an ambulance instead of a hearse.
The Associated Press was among those who witnessed her failed execution. She was already strapped to the gurney, with IV inserted in her arm, when prison officials raised the curtain to the execution room at 7:27 p.m.
Her spiritual adviser was standing beside the gurney near her head. He spoke to her. They sang a song. The lyrics were not audible, but included repeating the phrase — “I love you.” The spiritual adviser stroked her forehead.
Minutes ticked by. She raised her head and looked around; she smiled. Then she said her arm was hurting and asked a prison official in the room if it was supposed to feel that way.
Ten minutes in, at 7:37 p.m., she sighed, the IV in her arm fed from a control room adjacent to the death chamber, separated by a ledge. At 7:41 p.m., a rock or paper weight about the size of a golf ball was placed on the ledge. Prison officials have not confirmed what it means, but its placement appeared to coincide with a direction in the protocol that says after the drugs are administered, a five-minute countdown begins until the curtain is closed.
At 7:46 p.m., officials closed the curtain, blocking the witnesses’ view of the death chamber. Pike’s spiritual adviser left the chamber and sat briefly with her attorney in the media witness room.
The curtain rose again three minutes later. The Tennessee lethal injection protocol calls for a second round of pentobarbital if the inmate is not deceased after the first round.
An hour-plus of what sounded like snoring
Her spiritual adviser returned to the chamber and stood beside Pike with his hands folded. Pike appeared to begin to lose consciousness at some point and started making a sound like snoring. She continued to do so for the next hour, a sign that she was alive long after she was expected to be dead.
Her head raised slightly off the gurney and turned to the side at about 7:56 p.m. She kept breathing.
Officials closed the curtain again at 8:06 p.m.
For the next 40 minutes, Pike could be heard from behind the curtain. She sounded like she was snoring, a rhythmic, regular breathing pattern.
Inside the prison, Pike’s attorney, Randy Spivey, later told the media that at about 8:22 p.m. he demanded access to a telephone to contact other lawyers on the team. He said he demanded the execution be halted and that life-saving medical care be given to Pike. He said he received confirmation at about 8:50 p.m. that an ambulance was on the way.
At 8:53 p.m., an announcement came: “Will witnesses please exit the area.” The media was escorted out, and a prison spokesperson said she had no information to provide about what had happened.
Fire trucks and ambulances arrived in front of the prison at around 9:14 p.m. Pike’s attorneys later issued a statement that she had been taken to a hospital and was being treated, though they did not know the specifics of her condition. On Thursday afternoon, they said she was in critical condition receiving medical care.
Governor orders a review
The Tennessee Department of Correction issued a statement saying the department followed protocol.
“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening,” the agency wrote. “Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”
The agency has not said what went wrong. It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to complete an execution, though in the other case, officials couldn’t find a suitable vein for an IV line so the drugs weren’t administered.
Gov. Bill Lee ordered a review and postponed another execution scheduled for later this year, calling what happened in the death chamber “deeply disturbing.”
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, had traveled to Nashville to see the sentence carried out.
“I didn’t get justice for my daughter,” Martinez told the AP by telephone.
“I watched the whole thing. She was awake,” Martinez said. ”She was moving her head, moving her feet. She was trying to sit up. Didn’t work the first time they gave her a shot. It didn’t work the second time so she’s in the hospital and alive.”
“This isn’t justice for Colleen.”

title: Cape Elizabeth rolls Waterville
What’s next for Lindsay Clancy after judge denies motion for not guilty verdict
text:
What’s next for Lindsay Clancy after judge denies motion for not guilty verdict
The judge overseeing Lindsay Clancy’s murder case denied one of her motions aimed at avoiding a retrial.
Clancy still has another motion to dismiss the case that’s pending in court, and the district attorney in Plymouth County, Massachusetts, hasn’t committed to pursuing a retrial against her.
Clancy’s post-trial motion – typical in criminal trials – asked the judge to enter a finding of not guilty, arguing prosecutors didn’t present enough evidence to convince a jury beyond a reasonable doubt that she killed her children.
Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington filed the motion after her seven-week trial ended in a mistrial over a hung jury last month. The jury reported they were deadlocked 11-1 after deliberating for six days.
The trial garnered national attention, sparking discussion about maternal mental health and postpartum resources available to women. Clancy had supporters clad in pink each day at court and a widespread following online.
Reddington and prosecutors argued the motion before Judge William Sullivan at a hearing Tuesday.
Reddington said at trial prosecutors did not prove Clancy killed her three children – Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan in January 2023 – a statement that appeared to contradict statements he made while trying the case.
Clancy never actually admitted to the killings, but still there was not a full investigation into the deaths of the Clancy children, Reddington told the court Tuesday. “They just immediately assumed that this woman was guilty.”
He also said, if that wasn’t enough, the Commonwealth didn’t sufficiently prove Clancy should be held criminally responsible for the killings because of her mental state at the time.
A prosecutor called the defense argument “laughable.”
Defense had high bar to reach
Judge Sullivan didn’t rule from the bench at the time but issued a written order Thursday denying the defense motion.
“With respect to the elements of murder and the identity of who committed the alleged crimes, the evidence presented by the Commonwealth in its case in chief … was sufficient to satisfy any rational trier of fact beyond a reasonable doubt,” Sullivan wrote.
A motion for a required finding of not guilty in Massachusetts is a defense request to the judge to enter a finding of not guilty because the prosecution’s evidence is legally insufficient for a juror to convict on.
The bar for granting one is high, so they’re typically denied.
The judge must view the trial evidence in a light most favorable to the prosecution, and the defense must show the court that prosecutors failed to present enough evidence for a reasonable juror to find the prosecution proved every element of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt.
At trial, Reddington argued that Clancy was in a state of postpartum psychosis when she killed her children and should not be held criminally responsible for their deaths.
After killing her children, prosecutors allege, she then tried to kill herself, slashing her neck and wrists, then jumping from a window.
When asked Tuesday after the hearing if he’s now asserting that Clancy did not kill her children, Reddington said his arguments weren’t new, and he’s questioned the prosecution’s evidence in the case.
“It’s not new rocket science by any means. It’s the fact that they cannot prove probable cause.”
At trial, Reddington told the jury Clancy should not be held criminally responsible for killing her children because she was in a state of postpartum psychosis.
Earlier this week, Sullivan said he’d hear arguments at the next hearing set for Nov. 2 on the outstanding defense motion to dismiss the case over double jeopardy and other issues related to the holdout juror.
The judge also said he wants to schedule a date for the second trial.
If they do agree on a retrial date, Reddington said he’s not available for a trial before June because of his caseload.
Both Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz and Clancy’s defense team have declined to speak publicly about any ongoing plea negotiations.

title: Catering business shut down after football team suffers food poisoning before game
text:
ROCK ISLAND, Ill. (KWQC/Gray News) - An unlicensed home-based catering business in Illinois has been ordered to cease operations after dozens of people were sickened at a football team dinner.
According to the Rock Island Health Department, it was notified of a foodborne illness outbreak that stemmed from a Rock Island football team dinner that took place on Sept. 24 in the school cafeteria.
Health department officials said the dinner was catered by a home-based business called Sunshine and Spice.
Players, coaches and parents who attended the dinner were served fajita chicken, seasoned taco beef, cheese, flour taco shells, cheesy pepper beans, cilantro corn rice and Pico de Gallo salsa.
Seventy-five people were served the meal, and at least 45 were reported sick, causing the team to postpone its homecoming football game.
Just hours after the dinner, 23 players, five coaches and three parents reported symptoms, which included vomiting and diarrhea.
Officials said no one was hospitalized, but one player did have to visit a doctor.
The health department reported that most symptoms were over within 24 hours.
Health department officials noted that they met with the owner of Sunshine and Spice and learned the business was unlicensed and not food-safety certified. They then ordered the business to shut down, with the option of getting properly certified.
Officials said the owner told the health department that all ingredients were purchased from the Moline Walmart, Spotted Apron in Geneseo and farmers’ markets in Davenport and Coal Valley.
Joshua Harris, owner of Sunshine and Spice, released the following statement regarding the situation:
“First, Sunshine and Spice wants to sincerely apologize and send even more prayers to anyone affected by last week’s Rock Island football team meal.
We provided a taco bar-style potluck before the team was dismissed to prepare for their homecoming game. All of the food purchased from Walmart was fully cooked. We put all of the leftovers in plastic bags provided by the team parents for anyone to take home.
We have cooked for numerous parents of the team/school in the past and have no reason ever to provide a sub-standard meal or purposely attempt any tampering shenanigans. We are saddened by this whole situation.
We have been working side by side with the Rock Island County Health Department and Rock Island City/County Law Enforcement Agencies to be a part of their continuing investigations.
Again, we want to extend our deepest apologies and continued prayers to those affected.”
The investigation into the food poisoning remained active pending test results for pathogens in the food seized by the county, health officials said.

title: Mickey Gasper has surgery after Red Sox season ends
text:
BOSTON — Boston Red Sox first baseman and catcher Mickey Gasper has undergone what the team says was a successful repair of his right biceps tendon.
The club made the announcement on Friday. The procedure was performed by Dr. Matthew Leibman at MassGeneral Brigham in Boston.
Gasper started Boston’s final regular-season series against the Chicago Cubs on Sept. 25 at catcher but was replaced in the sixth inning after experiencing discomfort in his biceps.
He was placed on the injured list and was not on the Red Sox’s roster for their AL Wild Card Series loss to the New York Yankees.
The 30-year-old New Hampshire native played a career-high 67 games in his third major league season, batting .251 with 10 home runs and 24 RBI.

title: 🍂🏰 LAST CALL, MAINE! Visit Fort Knox & the Penobscot Narrows Bridge Before the Season Ends! 🌉
text:
Visit Fort Knox & Penobscot Narrows Bridge Before the Season Ends
This is something that every Mainer should do, but do it soon, before the 2026 season is over!
Just across the Penobscot River from Bucksport, the town of Prospect is home to the historic Fort Knox. Built between 1844 and 1869, it was the first fort in Maine built entirely of granite, most previous forts used wood, earth, and stone.
The Fort Knox Historic Site and the Penobscot Narrows Observatory Bridge, opens up to the public for the season, at the beginning of each May, and wraps up at the end of October. Both make for a really fun day of exploring for the whole family, not to mention of near perfect view of the fall foliage in the area.
The final chance to visit for the 2026 season, will be on Halloween Day, Saturday, October 31st, so make your plans now!
Read More: Bangor Waterfront Concerts 2027: Must-See Artists On Our Wishlist
The grounds will be open daily during the offseason from 9am to sunset. Dogs are welcome if they are on a 4'-6' leash, cleaned up after and not a nuisance to other guests.
The Penobscot Bridge and Penobscot Narrows Observatory, is one of the coolest experiences you can have in the state of Maine. It is the first bridge observation tower in the United States and the tallest public bridge observatory in the entire world.
The tower reaches 420 feet into the air and allows visitors to view the bridge, the nearby Fort Knox State Historic Site, the Penobscot River, and Bay, with spectacular, mind-blowing 360-degree views.
In fact, believe it or not, it is taller than the Statue of Liberty! The PNO is the tallest bridge observatory open to the public in the world. Visitors to the observatory ride Maine's fastest elevator all the way to the top.
Check out the Fort Knox website for more information, or give them a call at 207-469-6553

title: Shouldn’t it be easier to get to Canada from here?
text:
After a trip to Prince Edward Island a couple summers ago, seeing more of Canada rose among my travel priorities. The people are friendly, the exchange rate is favorable, and there’s a lot to explore. The only deterrent, for me, is the long drive.
Considering our proximity, geographically and culturally, it should be easier to get to some of our northern neighbor’s nearby destinations from southern Maine. Although our countries’ relationship might be strained, for travelers, it’s nothing a “Lake Ontario” hat can’t fix. After all, many Mainers now have an open invitation to become Canadian citizens.
At first glance, the prospect of the Scotia Prince bringing back its ferry service to Portland appeared to offer a potential option. Driving three hours to Bar Harbor to get on the CAT ferry for even longer has never tempted me, but the idea of traveling 10 minutes to go spend the night in a casino and wake up in Nova Scotia? Pretty appealing.
Reading more about what the Scotia Prince is considering, however, tamped my enthusiasm.
The nearly $1,000 one-way price tag (for two people, a car and a cabin) feels like a lot for a trip that, at 11 hours long, is no quicker than it would be by car at a fraction of the cost, regardless of dreaded gas prices. Being able to pass the time sleeping or playing blackjack doesn’t seem like enough of a selling point.
And while some describe the town of Yarmouth, where the ferry would land in Nova Scotia, as a hidden gem, the province’s most popular attractions are at least another couple hours away by car — in the direction of Maine — which again leads me back to sucking up the drive.
What about air travel, you ask? Flights from Portland to Halifax, with one layover, take nearly as long as the drive there and, most of the year, cost about as much as the ferry fee discussed. The same goes for Montreal and Quebec City, which are both about a five-hour drive and closer, as the crow flies, than Bridgeport, Connecticut.
If you’re hoping that direct flights to Canada are coming our way soon, you should know, at this point, that’s a pipe dream.
Toronto is the only city in the country to crack the top 15 international destinations of people flying out of the Portland International Jetport, then connecting through another domestic hub, coming in at No. 4 with just under 4,000 passengers in the past year.
The magic number for an airline to support a direct flight is 30,000 annual passengers, according to Airport Director Paul Bradbury.
Reviving rail service from Boston to Montreal, through Maine, is still being bandied about by state officials, though plans literally have had to change course since lawmakers decided last year to convert the St. Lawrence and Atlantic Rail corridor between Portland and Auburn into a multiuse trail.
The Maine-Canadian Legislative Advisory Commission in January presented a report to the Legislature’s transportation committee — with summarizes of several state-funded studies on the subject undertaken in the past 30 years — essentially recommending that the conversation continues.
In other words, don’t hold your breath.
Ditto for the possibility of an east-west highway being built, a concept first conceived when the country officially established its interstate system in the 1940s and last was seriously considered in Maine over a decade ago.
The amount of travel time that could save drivers would depend on the route, but one thing’s for sure, without it, bus companies aren’t going to start offering trips straight to Canada.
Now, you have to go down to Boston first, if not New York City, before heading north. Meaning, without a car, you really can’t get there from here.

title: Kennedy Center Honors to be held at Capital One Arena amid fight over adding Trump's name
text:
Kennedy Center Honors to be held at Capital One Arena amid fight over adding Trump's name
This year's Kennedy Center Honors will be held at Washington's Capital One Arena, not the riverfront building that's been at the center of a legal fight over adding President Donald Trump's name to the building.
Related video above: Judge blocks Trump name plan as Kennedy Center board votes to close
The 49th annual awards are set to take place at Washington's downtown arena, a Kennedy Center spokesperson said Friday. Few other details were immediately available, and an explanation for the change wasn't given.
The center's board voted last month to close the iconic performing arts venue along the Potomac River waterfront after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning Trump's name to the building.
Trump has said in social media posts that the center needed to close for safety repairs. But he said the repairs would only happen if the board was allowed to move forward with plans to add his name to the building.
A federal judge has twice said that can't happen without the approval of Congress, which has allocated $257 million for repairs.
The president hosted the 2025 awards, whose honorees included Sylvester Stallone and George Strait. He said at the time that he would rename the facility the "Trump Kennedy Center," and not long after workers began adding his name to the building.
The board of trustees, named by Trump, voted unanimously for the change, which has been challenged in court since.
Congress named the performing arts center as a living memorial to John F. Kennedy in 1964, the year after he was assassinated.
The law explicitly prohibits the board of trustees from making the center into a memorial to anyone else, and from putting another person's name on the building's exterior.
The Kennedy Center Honors, which recognize people for lifetime contributions to American culture through the performing arts, was established in 1978. The 2026 honorees are set to be named at a later date, the center's spokesperson said. The event will take place on Dec. 7.

title: Scammers are using everyday tech tools to flood your phone
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Scam calls and texts have become the top way scammers reach their victims, outpacing overall scam growth, according to a new report from the Better Business Bureau.
Josh Planos, a spokesperson for the Better Business Bureau, said the scale of the problem continues to grow.
“This is a very lucrative industry for scammers, and they really seem to be interested in growing and scaling their efforts in ways that we’ve never seen before,” Planos said.
The BBB’s International Investigations Initiative analyzed nearly 440,000 Scam Tracker reports since 2022. Planos said scammers are frequently relying on legitimate digital services to reach victims.
“In a lot of cases, they are exploiting legal services like virtual or VOIP phone numbers, bulk texting platforms, website builders, AI voice and video generation and social media ad platforms, all of which have very low barriers to entry,” Planos said.
Planos said the report found regulators are struggling to keep up with how scammers operate.
“The study really does argue that the current telecom rules were written for the landline era of phones,” Planos said. “We outline a number of fixes. We should expand two existing FCC rules, which are the telemarketing sales rule and the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, that limit telemarketing calls. We would recommend that it be brought in to explicitly cover text messages, which currently have weaker protection than calls.”
Planos said there is one simple step every consumer can take immediately: turning on a phone’s spam filter.
He also noted that a new or unfamiliar phone number does not necessarily mean a new scam. Scammers can change phone numbers quickly and often do so as part of the same ongoing scheme.
The BBB also recommends being suspicious of texts offering jobs or loans that were never applied for. If such a text arrives, the BBB recommends ending the conversation and avoiding any links sent by an unknown sender.

title: Sheriff's race heating up as endorsement crosses party lines
text:
ELLSWORTH — In an unusual twist in local politics, three of Hancock County’s Democratic state legislators endorsed the Republican candidate for sheriff, Corey Bagley of Hancock, over Democratic candidate Dakota Dupuis of Ellsworth.
Whoever wins will replace Hancock County Sheriff Scott Kane, who is not seeking a fourth term.
Sen. Nicole Grohoski (D-Ellsworth), on behalf of herself and state Reps. Nina Milliken (D-Blue Hill) and Gary Friedmann (D-Bar Harbor), submitted an opinion piece to the Islander on Sept. 25 titled, “Party labels aren’t enough: Why we’re crossing lines for sheriff.”
“While the two candidates touched on many of the same themes, we left those conversations with a clear conclusion: Corey Bagley gave stronger, more credible, and more experienced answers to our questions,” the letter stated. “His decades of law enforcement experience gave weight to his proposals in a way that Dakota Dupuis, at this stage in his career, simply could not match.”
However, the Dems appear to be a house divided.
“This letter signed by the three legislators is unfortunate,” said Hancock County Dem chairwoman Marcia Myers. “He [Dupuis] is not Scott Kane.”
“We are 100% behind Dakota,” said Myers. “It’s not just because he’s the Democratic candidate. We have had hours of discussion with him about management of the sheriff’s office. He brings care and confidence and rigorous fiscal responsibility.”
Crossing party lines to publicly support an opposing party’s candidate isn’t routine.
“For another party to cross party lines and endorse another candidate, it’s a huge deal,” said Bagley, who is currently an Ellsworth Police detective. “I hope people realize that. They [the three legislators] think I’m the best candidate for the job.”
Bagley said the endorsement isn’t anything he “went out and sought. I’m very grateful for their endorsement.”
Dupuis, who is currently a lieutenant at the Sheriff’s Office, said he respects Milliken, Grohoski and Friedmann’s right to their opinions.
“That said, when an opinion is presented alongside a number of questionable assertions, I believe voters deserve complete context,” Dupuis said. “My intention is not to tell anyone who to support but to provide additional facts and circumstances so voters can make that decision for themselves.”
The legislators’ letter states that “the sheriff’s budget increased by more than $700,000 from 2024 to 2025,” Dupuis said. The actual increase was approximately $430,000. “Of that approximate $430,000 increase, $278,000 were in wages and fringe benefits, which are controlled by the county commissioners and ultimately decided by their approval, not the sheriff’s office.” The commissioners must comply with wages and benefits as negotiated with the unions.
Dupuis said the letter criticized his role in purchasing Axon tasers, but that when Bagley was working for the sheriff’s office, Axon tasers were also purchased.
The Democratic candidate said he also took issue with the characterization of the purchase of Chevrolet Tahoes as “frivolous spending.” These models were built as “police pursuit vehicles,” which are designed and equipped for law enforcement use, Dupuis said. “These features include upgraded brakes, suspension, reinforced mechanical components and specialized wiring to support equipment typically installed in police vehicles.”
“I believe in strong law enforcement, but law enforcement cannot solve every public safety problem alone,” Dupuis said. “Mental health services, substance-use treatment, domestic violence resources and community partnerships are all important.”
“Another recurring theme [in the letter] is Sheriff Scott Kane’s support for my campaign,” Dupuis said. “Sheriff Kane and I are two different people. I respect Sheriff Kane and appreciate his years of public service. That does not mean I agree with every decision, policy or position he has taken.”
Kane is a Republican. Dupuis said he was previously a registered Republican but changed parties to become a Democrat in 2024, in part due to his family’s experiences with the healthcare system.
Dupuis said that because of his interest in running for sheriff, he has taken on more leadership responsibilities than would be typical for a lieutenant.
However, “many of the issues cited in the article occurred before I assumed an administrative role,” Dupuis said. “Conversely, many occurred while Corey [Bagley] held an administration position within the same organization.”
Both candidates have said the position of county sheriff should not be about politics.
Maine has had two unsuccessful efforts in recent history to end party affiliations for county sheriffs. In 2007, the bill LD 953, “An Act to Provide for Nonpartisan Elections for Sheriffs,” proposed barring candidates from filing through party primaries or listing an affiliation.
A similar effort in 2015, “An Act to Make Certain Primaries Non-Partisan,” sponsored by former State Rep. Walter Kumiega (D-Deer Isle), would have created a nonpartisan primary process for sheriffs and other county offices. But that also failed to come to fruition.
“This is the kind of change that requires a number of cosponsors and a parade of passionate speakers at the public hearing,” Kumiega said on Tuesday. “I still think it’s a good idea. An open June primary and a two-person November runoff for seats like sheriff, district attorney and judge of probate will yield better results. Party politics aren’t very relevant to these posts.”
Maine’s county sheriffs were once appointed. A Sept. 10, 1855, amendment to the Maine Constitution changed that to elected county officers.
Bagley, who worked at the sheriff’s office for 31 years, including roles as lieutenant and chief deputy, said he wants voters to consider each candidate.
“I want them to look at both candidates, their history, the law enforcement career and supervisory experience and make a well-informed decision from that,” said Bagley. “This should not be about politics.”

title: UN Human Rights Office calls botched lethal injection of Christa Pike ‘abhorrent’ and ‘cruel’
text:
NASHVILLE (WSMV/Gray News) — The failed execution of Tennessee’s only woman on death row, 50-year-old Christa Pike, is ringing alarm bells for one of the most prominent international human rights organizations.
The United Nations Human Rights Office is condemning Tennessee’s failed attempt at an execution on Wednesday night.
“The prolonged suffering – physical and mental – arising from multiple failed execution attempts is abhorrent and cruel. And there are key fair trial questions still unresolved,” a post from the organization said.
Witnesses said that, after receiving two doses of pentobarbital, Pike did not die. Her breathing was labored and sounded like “snoring,” they said, and at one point she asked prison staff “if it was supposed to feel that way.”
An ambulance responded to Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville following the botched lethal injection.
United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk is now calling for Tennessee to no longer pursue executing Pike.
The UN office pointed to a larger trend in the U.S., saying it is “troubled” by an uptick in executions.
“The death penalty has no place in any society,” the UN Human Rights Office said.
Pike was still in the hospital Thursday, and her lawyers said they did not know her long-term chance for recovery.
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate. The killing stoked fears of Satan worship because of a pentagram carved on Slemmer’s body.
She did not dispute that she helped kill Slemmer, but supporters argued that her mental illness and allegations of severe sexual abuse should be considered. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder after the killing.

title: Susan Collins votes conscientiously and gets results
text:
Sen. Susan Collins has taken years of criticism for her vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh. What her critics rarely mention is that she also voted to confirm Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan, nominated by President Obama, and Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, nominated by President Biden.
That record isn’t a contradiction. It reflects a principle. The Constitution gives senators the job of advising and consenting on a president’s nominees, and Sen. Collins has consistently treated that as a question of qualifications, character and respect for the law, not whether she agrees with a nominee’s politics. Voting only for judges who share your views would turn every confirmation into a partisan brawl. She has refused to do that, whether the president was a Republican or a Democrat, and she has refused to be moved by political campaigns built on accusations rather than evidence.
That same practical, steady approach shows up here at home. Sen. Collins secured $4.7 million in federal funding for a new Belgrade Fire and Rescue Station. For a small town like ours, that kind of investment would be nearly impossible to raise on our own. It means our firefighters and rescue personnel will have a safe, modern facility to serve residents and the thousands of visitors who come to the lakes every summer.
Mainers deserve a senator who does her homework, votes her conscience and gets results for our communities. Sen. Collins has done all three, and she has my support.
Penny Morrell
Belgrade

title: Peak foliage from flight: how one Maine pilot takes leaf-peeping to new heights
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BINGHAM, Maine (WABI) - This week’s foliage report shows northern and western parts of the state nearing peak color.
One of the best ways to see the colors is from above.
Kevin Dauphinee is a commercial sea plane pilot based in Bingham.
“The colors are much more pronounced this year,” Dauphinee said.
According to our First Alert Weather Team, you first want steady rainfall in the spring and summer to keep the trees healthy. Leaves start to change color as photosynthesis (production of sugar) slows down. For vibrant colors in the fall, you want bright, sunny days to boost photosynthesis in the leaves and cooler nights to trap in the sugar. An early frost will ruin the color-making process.
A view from above
The seaplane trip covered nearly 100 miles over the Kennebec Valley, offering views of the western mountains, including Katahdin, Mount Kineo, Bigelow and Sugarloaf.
“I guess just a little bit of freedom and quietness and get away from the world, and it’s nice up there,” Dauphinee said.
Dauphinee said he works with clients to make sure they get the flight they want.
“I’ll ask them if there’s something they want to see or, you know, some people just want to go for a ride,” Dauphinee said. “So, we kind of pick where we’re going to fly. I might sit down with them with a map and kind of say, these are the areas that we can fly in and they’ll pick something out. And then as we get going, they might change their mind. Hey, let’s go look at that, and they just go wherever they want to go.”
Dauphinee said he likes when clients have new ideas for their flight path.
“Some operators like to have their own route and they take that route every time, but I like to be different,” Dauphinee said. “I want to see different things too, it’s kind of nice when somebody wants to go off the path.”
Dauphinee said flying gives you views of the mountains without having to exhaust yourself climbing them.
“We can change our altitude to look at different things and fly by the mountains,” Dauphinee said. “We don’t get out of breath flying by the mountains, so that’s good.”
Dauphinee said he flies over wildlife on almost every flight.
“Moose, bear, deer, all the animals, we see them quite often,” Dauphinee said.
For nervous fliers, Dauphinee offers advice.
“I always tell them it’s kind of like a river, with the wind going over the mountains and the land,” Dauphinee said. “You just kind of gotta ride it, and just breathe and take it easy and enjoy the view. That usually helps.”
Dauphinee said flights can be booked on his Facebook page year-round.

title: Former chief of Maine Capitol Police reaches deal to settle bar fight charges
text:
Former chief of Maine Capitol Police reaches deal to settle bar fight charges
The former chief of the Maine Capitol Police has reached a deal regarding charges related to an altercation at a pub in Hallowell.
Matthew Clancy resigned his post, effective October 8, 2025. He had been placed on paid administrative leave in August of 2025.
The video in the media player above is from our reporting following Clancy's arrest.
According to court documents, Clancy agreed to a deferred disposition. Under the deal, he will remain on bail until July 6, 2027, and cannot have or drink alcohol during that time. He must also get substance use counseling or treatment and provide proof that he is doing so by Oct. 20, 2026. He must then provide written proof of counseling every three months.
If there have been no bail violations by July 6 and he meets all the conditions, court documents say prosecutors will "file an information alleging Count 3 disorderly conduct with an agreed upon $300 fine."
If any of the terms are not met, Clancy will be able to enter a plea to charges of assault and refusing to submit to arrest, or to go to trial.
Clancy was charged after the incident in August 2025, when he was accused of assaulting a police officer who responded to the scene.
The head of security for The Quarry Tap Room, Rob McGee, told Maine's Total Coverage that Clancy was taking pictures of people inside the pub. A fellow patron told Clancy to stop taking pictures, and when he did not stop, the patron grabbed Clancy's phone out of his hand.
According to McGee, a fight then broke out inside the pub and then spilled out onto the sidewalk in front of the establishment.
Police said a responding officer was allegedly assaulted by Clancy, who resisted arrest.
Clancy was sworn-in as the Maine Capitol Police chief in 2021.

title: Many states have backup execution plans, but failures still happen
text:
Long before Christa Pike was brought into Tennessee’s execution chamber, prison leaders reviewed and approved a backup plan detailing exactly what to do if the first attempt at lethal injection failed.
But the backup plan also failed, and Thursday — 24 hours later — Pike was still alive but in critical condition at a Tennessee hospital, though her prognosis remained uncertain. It’s not yet clear what went wrong.
Twenty-seven states have capital punishment, and they vary widely in how they administer the death penalty and just how much of that lethal process they keep hidden from public view, according to the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, a clearinghouse for information on U.S. executions.
Some states have extensive backup plans. Others don’t
Tennessee falls somewhere in the middle of the pack when it comes to contingency plans, with two redundancies built into its execution process.
First, inmates are supposed to have two intravenous lines placed. Thus, if the first IV site fails, the execution team can switch to the second one. A physician on the execution team can even insert a central line — which typically involves making an incision in a major blood vessel in the groin, neck or armpit in order to thread a catheter into the body to a spot near the heart — if needed.
Intravenous lines can fail for several reasons, like a needle and catheter not being properly placed in a vein or wiggling out of place — or a vein rupturing and letting blood and IV fluid leak into tissue surrounding the IV site.
Tennessee also allows for a second 100 mg dose of pentobarbital to be administered if the condemned person is still alive five minutes after the first dose was given.
Tennessee prison officials gave Pike a second dose, but it’s not clear if they used the primary IV site or the backup site to do so.
Little backup in Alabama, a lot in Idaho
Alabama has a three-drug lethal injection protocol. It allows for a backup dose of the first drug, the sedative midazolam, to be given if the inmate isn’t unconscious from the first dose. But the protocol doesn’t include additional instructions for what to do if the condemned person is still alive after the first dose of the next two drugs, rocuronium bromide and potassium chloride.
Idaho, meanwhile, has contingency plans for nearly every step of the execution process, with backup IV sites, allowances for administering a central IV line, and up to three full doses of any of the state’s four approved lethal injection drug cocktails.
Idaho recently made firing squad its primary execution method, though it has yet to kill someone by that method. Still, the state’s firing squad protocol also has a backup plan, with the prison director able to order a second volley of shots within a two-minute time span if she determines it is necessary to complete the execution.
Despite contingency plans, executions are still botched at times
Idaho called off the execution of Thomas Eugene Creech in 2024 after execution team members could not place a viable IV after eight attempts.
Tennessee also called off an execution earlier this year after failing to find a suitable vein for a secondary IV line.
In 2014, Arizona executioners injected Joseph Rudolph Wood with a lethal combination of drugs 15 times during the nearly two hours it took him to die. He gasped more than 600 times while he lay on the table.
Witnesses keep the public informed when executions succeed or fail
In many ways, executions are shrouded in secrecy. The identity of execution team members, the details about where and how lethal drugs are procured, and in some states even what happens in the death chamber is hidden from public view.
But executions, like all criminal sentences, are conducted by the state on behalf of its citizens, so it’s critical that members of the public understand exactly how that ultimate punishment is carried out.
Most death penalty states allow a few members of the media to witness executions on behalf of the public. Once the execution is over, those news representatives typically take part in a news conference, sharing exactly what they saw and heard with the rest of the world.
Access to executions varies by state, and limitations often lead to court battles
Only two states, Indiana and Wyoming, explicitly ban members of the press from witnessing executions. Wyoming, with no one currently on death row, hasn’t carried out an execution since 1992, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
A coalition of news organizations including The Associated Press sued Indiana last year for a seat in the witness room, but in June a federal appellate court upheld the state’s law barring media access.
In Idaho, media witnesses are allowed to watch as a condemned person is placed on a gurney, has IVs inserted and is put to death. Yet AP and other news organizations have sued for increased access. The news organizations asked a judge to allow them to watch via closed-circuit monitors as the drugs are pushed into the IV lines, which is currently shielded from public view in a private room beside the death chamber.
A federal judge ordered the state to provide that access, citing a 9th U.S. Circuit Court ruling that said the public should be able to view all critical parts of an execution via the press. But the state appealed, and the appellate court hasn’t yet ruled on the matter.
Media witnesses provided crucial details about Pike’s failed execution
When Pike’s first lethal injection dose failed to end her life, officials closed the curtains and administered a second dose of pentobarbital.
When the curtains reopened, Pike was making snoring sounds and was clearly alive, according to AP reporter Kim Chandler, who was one of the witnesses. Eventually the curtain was closed again and the microphone in the room was turned off, but Pike could still be heard making gasping or snoring sounds.
Nearly two hours after the execution began, media witnesses were escorted out, and Pike was taken to a hospital for treatment.
Many states, including Tennessee, keep the IV insertion hidden from public view, but allow witnesses to watch through a viewing window as the condemned person dies.
AP was part of a media coalition that previously sued Tennessee to see the IV insertion and to keep the viewing room curtains open until the pronouncement of death. But in April the Tennessee Supreme court blocked a lower court’s order that would have allowed for increased access.
One of Pike’s attorneys, Steve Ferrell, said Pike feared that there could be complications because of a lifelong blood disorder that made it tough to get needles into her veins. Ferrell said it was possible that the IV did not enter Pike’s vein properly, and the drug may have filled her arm instead of entering her bloodstream.

title: ‘Learn from Lutz’: Sharing his son’s traffic death to encourage safe-driving
text:
GEORGIA (InvestigateTV) — Mike Lutzenkirchen is sharing his son’s story with teens and young adults in hopes of preventing fatal crashes caused by unsafe driving.
Lutzenkirchen’s son, Philip, died in a car accident in 2014. Philip, a former Auburn football player, had been drinking with friends before getting into a car. Investigators said the car was speeding and ran a stop sign, killing both Philip and the driver.
Both had blood alcohol levels above the legal limit.
“It’s just like that. There’s a crash last night. Your son is dead,” Mike Lutzenkirchen said, recalling a conversation with a coroner the day after Philip’s death.
“We went to a black hole for two weeks. We’re trying to figure out what do you do in life,” Lutzenkirchen said.
A new foundation
Lutzenkirchen created the Lutzie 43 Foundation after his son’s death. The foundation works with schools, government agencies and law enforcement to address the more than 42,000 annual traffic deaths in the United States.
The foundation holds summits, including one at Georgia Military College, where students take part in breakout sessions.
The foundation’s message asks drivers to take 43 seconds when they get in a car — a reference to Philip’s jersey number at Auburn — to make sure they have a clear head, clear hands, clear eyes, and to buckle their seat belt.
The summit also covers sharing the road with truckers and demonstrates how state transportation professionals and first responders work the scene of a crash.
School and law enforcement response
Georgia Military College Assistant Principal Jennifer Deason said students attending the summit are distracted by their phones and the freedom of driving, which leads them to ignore safety.
“Every student that attends here, I see them as my children. And so to know that they are in danger, if every time they get on the highway, whether or not they are distracted or not,” Deason said.
Capt. Maurice Raines, deputy director of the Georgia Governor’s Office of Highway Safety, said fatal crashes are 100% preventable.
“Hopefully by educating, the word will get out that we need to change our behavior. And if that doesn’t work, law enforcement will work to try to change that behavior,” Raines said.
Raines said more than 200 traffic deaths have occurred in Georgia so far this year.
Nationwide goal
Lutzenkirchen’s goal is a recognizable nationwide campaign sharing his son’s story.
“We’re trying to take the mistakes that Philip and his friend made that weekend and just make a difference. Live like Lutz, love like Lutz, and learn from Lutz,” Lutzenkirchen said.
The Lutzie 43 Foundation’s safe driving summit also demonstrates how state transportation professionals and first responders work a crash scene, allowing students to learn from multiple perspectives why driving is both dangerous and a privilege.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports seat belts can reduce the risk of death or injury by nearly half.

title: Here’s why Troy Jackson speaks the way he does
text:
Mary M. Drymon, Ph.D., lives in Winslow.
I have been an avid supporter of Troy Jackson since I first heard him speak at the 2016 Maine State Democratic Party Convention. I believe strongly in the message that he has been articulating for years: support for Medicare for all, defending Social Security and protecting working-class values.
I not only support what he is saying, I love the way he says it.
What some see as not being “polished” enough, and speaking haltingly, I see as authenticity. As a historian specifically focused on the Scottish and Irish diaspora, I appreciate his “Allagash accent” and consider his patterns of speech unique. I couldn’t resist a bit of research into where it originates by looking at some of the surnames in his family.
Troy Jackson’s mother is a McBreairty. That surname may have origins on the islands of Arran and Bute in Western Scotland. The surname comes from the Gaelic Mac Muircheartaigh, which translates roughly to “son of the navigator or mariner.” This highlights their early history as skilled sea captains and sailors.
One branch of the McBreairtys migrated across the Irish Sea into the Ulster Plantations in Ireland. They concentrated in the seaport of Killybegs in the precinct of Boylagh and Bannagh in County Donegal, where they became deeply integrated into local Irish culture. During the early 1600s time period, the British fortified and planned the port town of Killybegs to prevent invasion by Spanish forces.
In around 1618, King James I also granted vast territories — which included the town of Killybegs as well as Kilcar, Ardara, the island of Inishkeel and Killymard — to John Murray. The McBreairtys were likely tenants of Murray.
By the mid-1700s, some McBreairtys were part of a group that migrated from Ireland to Nova Scotia, where they met and intermarried with people of French Canadian descent, creating an early fusion culture. Eventually some McBreairtys moved into Maine — lured by the abundantly available wood resources of the Allagash Valley. The residents of Allagash lived in deep geographical isolation at the edge of the Maine North Woods. This isolation created a linguistic time capsule. They retained a Donegal cadence of speech.
The Donegal accent belongs to the northern province of Ulster, which is heavily influenced by Scottish rhythms and vocabulary. The Allagash brogue mirrors this, sounding noticeably different from both the classic nasal “Boston/coastal Maine” accent and the neighboring Acadian French inflections. Listeners often note that the Allagash dialect features a distinct rhythmic “lilt,” clipped vowel sounds and subtle sentence-ending pitch changes reminiscent of the Ulster-Scots speech patterns found across County Donegal.
The speech pattern that is found deep within the Allagash Valley stands out as a unique, highly localized linguistic pocket that retains the speech patterns of its original settlers. Modern connectivity and standardized education have softened the accent.
Troy Jackson uses his accented speech to describe how we can navigate a better future together — not from the left or right but from the bottom up. He articulates new ideas with a very old way of speaking that unmistakably echoes history. It’s worth a listen.

title: New Gloucester man in critical condition after striking tractor trailer in Auburn
text:
AUBURN — A New Gloucester man was left in critical condition Thursday night after slamming into a tractor-trailer at the corner of Washington Street and Kittyhawk Avenue.
Jonah King, 29, of New Gloucester, was traveling south on Washington Street when he went through a red light at the Kittyhawk Avenue intersection, Auburn police said in a statement on Facebook.
According to police, King struck a tractor-trailer operated by Peter Fontaine, 46, of North Waterboro, who was turning left from Kittyhawk Avenue through a green light.
King was transported to Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston with life-threatening injuries. He was later transferred to Maine Medical Center in Portland.
Auburn police said the department’s crash reconstruction team is investigating with help from the Maine State Police Commercial Vehicle Unit.

title: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, a memo shows
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have been ordered not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training, under new internal guidance issued after several drivers were shot in encounters with ICE.
A memo sent to officers in ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division and obtained by The Associated Press warned they are not authorized to chase vehicles that fail to pull over under any circumstances. Instead, officers should take down the vehicles’ information for further investigation, according to the memo signed by ICE’s executive associate director Marcos D. Charles and dated Wednesday.
The new guidance comes after ICE-initiated vehicle stops have repeatedly escalated when drivers have refused to cooperate or tried to flee. ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen such encounters since last year, killing at least four people and wounding several others.
President Donald Trump’s administration has faced internal tension over how to handle traffic stops, which are seen as particularly high-risk encounters.
After fatal shootings of drivers in Maine and Texas in July, ICE officers were directed to temporarily pause most vehicle stops. But the next day, Trump went on social media to direct the agency to continue traffic stops, calling them “one of ICE’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools.”
ICE has faced intense pressure from the White House to deport more people who are in the country illegally, and its arrests have reached record numbers. At the same time, the agency’s rapid hiring spree last year resulted in some poorly vetted and trained officers hitting the streets.
In a statement, ICE downplayed the significance of the memo, which said the new guidance was intended to replace and amend prior directives issued earlier this year, last year and in 2018.
“Occasionally, ICE leadership issues guidance reminders to law enforcement officers,” the statement said. “Vehicle stops and arrests of illegal aliens continue.”
The new memo outlines steps intended to improve the safety of vehicle stops for ICE officers, drivers they are targeting, their passengers and the public.
The memo told ICE’s field office directors that they must ensure vehicles used for traffic stops have lights and sirens that let the public know they are law enforcement vehicles when activated. All officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras, under the guidance.
In addition, only officers who have completed one of five specific agency training courses can conduct vehicle stops. Officers who have not completed the training courses can only participate in vehicle stops “in a support capacity” as passengers and cannot be the drivers of any of the vehicles involved.
The guidance says ICE officers can continue to use a controversial technique known as pinning, which is defined as “using a vehicle or physical barrier to trap or stop a car,” but only if they have received special training. Similarly, only trained officers can use spike strips that deflate tires to prevent drivers from fleeing.
The memo came the day that courtroom testimony highlighted ways in which two ICE officers involved in a vehicle stop, pursuit and shooting that wounded a delivery driver in Austin last month would not have complied with the new guidance.
During a bond hearing for Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, testimony showed that the officer who shot him wasn’t wearing a body-worn camera. The ICE officer who did have a camera was driving in a separate car and turned it off during the pursuit.
Prosecutors presented surveillance video that showed an ICE agent chasing Garces Perez at high speeds through residential streets after he fled an initial traffic stop.
Garces Perez faces federal assault charges after investigators say he struck an ICE officer with his driver’s side mirror. That officer then shot into Perez’s vehicle, lodging a bullet in his back, officials say.
Attorneys for Garces Perez have called the charges against him “retaliation” and have argued that the camera footage was inconclusive because it didn’t fully capture the moment when he allegedly tried to flee.

title: Former Maine Capitol Police chief agrees to deal over Hallowell bar scuffle
text:
AUGUSTA — The former chief of the Maine Capitol Police, who was arrested last year after a scuffle with a Hallowell police officer outside a bar, has reached a deal with prosecutors that could mean his punishment will be a $300 fine.
Matthew M. Clancy, 63, of Sidney, entered into the agreement with prosecutors Tuesday, court records show.
Under the deal, which Superior Court Justice Deborah P. Cashman summarized in an order, Clancy and prosecutors agreed to a nine-month “informal deferred disposition.”
During that time, Clancy is to remain released on bail, with conditions that he not use or possess alcohol and that he not return to The Quarry Tap Room in Hallowell, where the August 2025 scuffle took place.
Clancy is also to engage in substance abuse counseling and treatment to the satisfaction of his provider, Cashman wrote. He must provide proof to prosecutors by Oct. 20 that he has sought that treatment. He then must continue in whatever treatment the provider recommends, providing proof of counseling to prosecutors in January 2027 and April 2027.
If Clancy complies and otherwise does not violate his bail conditions or the law, prosecutors intend to file a new misdemeanor-level charge of disorderly conduct, with Clancy agreeing to plead guilty and pay a $300 fine, according to Cashman’s order.
The order does not explicitly say what would happen to the current misdemeanor-level charges of assault and refusing to submit to arrest or detention, but Clancy’s lawyer David J. Bobrow confirmed they would be dismissed as part of the agreement.
If he does not comply with the terms, the resolution of the case goes back to square one: Clancy can either plead guilty to the two current charges or proceed to trial, Cashman wrote.
Clancy is due back in court July 6, 2027.
Bobrow, reached via email Thursday, declined to comment on the informal structure of the deal and the negotiations that led to it.
In an email, District Attorney Natasha Irving did not answer why her office chose to structure the deal informally. She wrote that in a typical, formal deferred disposition, a defendant enters a guilty plea at the beginning and is given terms to comply with for six months to three years.
“With an informal, no plea is entered, so the matter could still go to trial if it is a bad outcome,” Irving wrote.
Irving, the elected top prosecutor for Knox, Lincoln, Sagadahoc and Waldo counties, was assigned to handle the case because Maeghan Maloney, the district attorney for Kennebec and Somerset counties, determined her office had a conflict of interest.
The Capitol Police is a bureau of the Maine Department of Public Safety tasked with security and other policing responsibilities at the state government buildings in Augusta, which is in Maloney’s prosecutorial district.
Clancy, who resigned Oct. 8, 2025, was in charge of the agency at the time of the Aug. 2, 2025, incident.
Hallowell police Officer Johnny Narvaez wrote in a report that at 11:58 p.m. on Aug. 1, he was parked outside The Quarry Tap Room on Water Street in Hallowell, when he saw a man, later identified as Clancy, in a verbal argument with security staff and other patrons. Hallowell police released the full report about a month after Clancy’s arrest, in response to a records request under Maine’s Freedom of Access Act.
When Narvaez asked Clancy to leave, Clancy said he did not have to do so, grabbed Narvaez’s shoulder and struck him on the forehead with an open palm, according to the report.
Narvaez began to escort him away, but Clancy pulled his arm away and the two got into a “brief physical struggle,” his report says.
A security guard assisted Narvaez with holding Clancy’s arms, and Clancy continued to resist, Narvaez wrote. The two then brought Clancy to the ground.
While doing so, Clancy struck and injured his head on the pavement, the report says.
Narvaez was eventually able to put Clancy in handcuffs, he wrote. While on the ground, Clancy said to Narvaez, “You are f—d now, do you know who I am?” the report says.
Narvaez learned from bar security guards that they had tried to kick Clancy out after he got into arguments with other customers, who were complaining he was taking photos without permission.
Clancy, after being taken to MaineGeneral Medical Center via ambulance, told hospital staff he had drunk two beers, but had consumed a few drinks somewhere else before going to The Quarry Tap Room.
Clancy was placed on administrative leave the same day as the arrest, a Department of Public Safety spokesperson confirmed four days later, despite multiple inquiries before then about his status.
He resigned two months later, submitting a one sentence letter to Public Safety Commissioner Michael Sauschuck. The state paid out $2,442 and any unused time off, per a separation agreement signed the same day, released in response to a public records request.
Clancy earned about $107,000 in regular wages in 2024, state payroll records available online show. He also earned just more than $3,000 in overtime pay and collected about $24,000 in insurance and retirement benefits.
He had been chief of the Capitol Police since 2021. Before coming to Maine, Clancy was a police officer in Massachusetts for 39 years, including 20 years as a chief in two municipalities, according to information previously published on the Capitol Police website.
Officials in three of the Massachusetts towns that employed Clancy for most of his career — Plympton, Duxbury and Mashpee — said they had no records of any disciplinary actions or complaints regarding Clancy.
But Clancy had faced discipline in Maine before the arrest, public records show.
A 2023 disciplinary investigation found that Clancy requested a subordinate state employee to perform services of a personal nature using a Capitol Police vehicle while on the clock, failed to report an interaction with local police, and on one occasion drove his state vehicle after drinking at the Augusta Country Club, prompting Sauschuck to propose a 40-hour unpaid suspension. A separate Waterville police report from July 2023 described Clancy appearing intoxicated and being picked up by a Capitol Police officer.
