title: What kind of Maine do you wish to help create?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sondra Shapiro has more than 40 years of experience in mature-market publishing. She is the former executive editor of the award-winning 50+ Advocate Newspaper in Massachusetts. She lives in Ogunquit.
When you walk into the voting booth, what kind of future are you voting for?
Ask yourself: What do I want for my own life, and for the lives of the people I care about?
I don’t have children or grandchildren of my own, but most of my friends do. Watching them babysit, spend time with their families and talk endlessly about the people they love, their devotion is unmistakable. Because I love my friends, I want the exact same things for them that they want for their families: happiness, security and a better tomorrow.
But this question is not only about parents or grandparents. It is about every Mainer. It is about the young adult trying to build a life here, the working family trying to keep up with rising costs, the older neighbor relying on Social Security or Medicare and anyone who wants to feel secure in the place they call home.
So when I enter the voting booth, I try to think beyond the candidate or the party. I think about the country and the state we are creating.
Right now we are watching the boundaries of executive power being tested in Washington. We have seen the federal government attempt to exert control over aspects of how states conduct elections, including voting by mail. Maine fought back, joining a coalition of states to challenge those rules in court; a legal battle that culminated in the U.S. Supreme Court upholding our voting rights. Our state also successfully blocked a federal lawsuit attempting to force the release of Mainers’ private voter data.
Is that federal overreach the direction we want our country to take?
If so, we should be honest with ourselves about it. If not, we need to think seriously about the importance of checks and balances. No president should have unchecked power. The protections built into our system are there precisely because power changes hands.
Whoever represents Maine in the Senate will also have a constitutional role in confirming Supreme Court nominees if vacancies occur. The president nominates them, but the Senate provides advice and consent. Those decisions can affect our country for decades.
But this isn’t only about government and institutions. It is about our everyday lives.
I think about Social Security. Medicare. The cost of living. Housing. Healthcare.
Maine is not a state where most families have unlimited financial cushions. For many people, the cost of housing, food, healthcare and raising children is not an abstract economic discussion. It is the arithmetic of everyday life.
Some Mainers are worried about whether they can afford to stay in the communities they love. Others are trying to buy a first home, pay for college, care for an aging parent or manage medical bills. Many are simply wondering whether the next generation will have the same opportunities they had.
These concerns belong to all of us, regardless of our age or family situation. They are about whether people can live with dignity, find stability and build a future here in Maine.
Maybe you are tired of politics. Maybe you’ve tuned it out. Maybe you believe your one vote won’t change anything.
But your vote is one of the few opportunities you have to say, in a very concrete way, this is the future I want.
Before you mark that ballot, don’t vote by reflex or party habit. Stop for a moment, look closely at the future you are choosing, and ask yourself: Is this the country, and the Maine, I want to help create?

title: Popular frozen pasta sold nationwide at Walmart recalled. Here’s why
text:
(Gray News) - More frozen pasta sold at Walmart stores nationwide is being recalled over listeria concerns, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
Last month, the company announced it was recalling two lots of Bettergoods Authentic Italian Lemon Alfredo Fettuccine because they may be contaminated with listeria.
That recall now includes all lots of the pasta.
Listeria is a harmful bacterium that can cause serious and sometimes fatal illness in some people, including children, older adults and pregnant people.
The frozen pasta was sold at Walmart stores nationwide in 22-ounce, yellow plastic packages with UPC number 194346442706.
So far, no illnesses have been reported.

title: Janet Mills urges action on heating assistance as Maine braces for cold
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gov. Janet Mills wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation Friday demanding more money from the federal government for heating assistance, a measure that she said is necessary to “ensure the safety and comfort of Maine people” amid record high heating oil prices.
The Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) currently provides about $40 million in assistance to qualifying households in Maine. Those funds are usually sent out in late November and applications are now open.
The governor’s request came as heating oil prices hit a record high in Maine last week, averaging $6.02 per gallon, the Department of Energy Resources said. This week, prices dropped slightly, to $5.96 per gallon — still above the previous record of $5.92 set in 2022.
Those prices were driven in large part by the continued constriction of the Strait of Hormuz, which, prior to the start of the war in Iran, carried about a quarter of the world’s oil shipments.
In her letter, Mills placed blame on President Donald Trump.
“Maine people should not be forced to choose between staying warm and putting food on the table because the president chose to drag the country into a needless war,” she wrote.
Prices that high demand an additional congressional allocation to the LIHEAP program, Mills said. Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, could be particularly hard-hit if LIHEAP funds aren’t increased, she said.
She encouraged Mainers to apply for LIHEAP funding as soon as possible. Applications and income limits can be found on MaineHousing’s website.
“Federal funding levels appropriated for LIHEAP this winter did not fully consider the drastic impacts of the president’s war that has sent fuel prices skyrocketing and are now insufficient for the circumstances that Maine and other cold-climate states now face,” Mills said.
Meanwhile, the Group of Seven wealthy democracies said Friday that they plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel also recently hit record high prices in the U.S.
Gas prices in the U.S. and abroad have soared during the eight-month war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22. Maine diesel prices averaged $6.47.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, lauded the G7 announcement Friday. She said the release should put “immediate downward pressure on energy prices and helping to lower the cost of producing and transporting goods.”
This story contains reporting from The Associated Press.

title: Democrats launch $3.4M corruption-focused ad campaign against Susan Collins
text:
A Democratic super PAC launched a $3.4 million ad campaign on Friday to highlight a recent report that accused Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of steering millions of dollars to a defense contractor in exchange for campaign contributions.
The 30-second spot from WinSenate focuses on a recent ProPublica report about illegal campaign contributions made to a pro-Collins super PAC during her 2020 campaign.
The ad features local news reports about last week’s story. It includes an older-looking woman — a key swing demographic in the race — speaking directly to the camera.
“Susan Collins took illegal campaign money and steered millions in government contracts to the donor, but Donald Trump’s administration shut down the investigation,” the woman says. “Maybe there’s a reason Susan Collins does whatever Donald Trump wants her to.”
The big-dollar ad campaign shows how Democrats are looking to turn Collins’ central campaign argument into a liability in the closing month of Maine’s closely watched Senate race.
“Chuck Schumer is bringing his New York campaign tactics to Maine,” Collins campaign spokesperson Shawn Roderick said, referring to the Democratic leader in the Senate. “His ads keep getting fact-checked as false and now he is asking Mainers to believe someone who is doing hard time in federal prison for fraud. Mainers have never fallen for his tactics and they aren’t going to now.”
Polling leading up to ProPublica’s report had shown a tight race between Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president. Jackson holds a roughly two-point lead over Collins, according to polling averages from the election website FiftyPlusOne.
The ad comes after the Senate Majority PAC, which is aligned with WinSenate, issued a Sept. 29 memo outlining its plan to make corruption a key part of its closing message to midterm voters. The group said the message ties into voters’ concerns about rising prices.
The memo notes that invoking “corrupt” and “pay-to-play politicians” is particularly effective among swing voters — a group that has repeatedly sent Collins back to Washington, D.C., despite leaning Democratic in recent statewide elections.
Republican groups are also making corruption a central argument in attacks against Jackson. They’ve run ads that highlight Jackson’s expense reimbursements while maintaining a second home in Augusta, as well as his son Chace’s work as a lobbyist while his father was Senate president.
On the campaign trail and in ads, Collins has been touting her power as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee — the first Mainer to hold the post in 92 years. She says she’s been able to bring home $1.5 billion in federal earmarks over the last five years.
But Democrats are trying to flip the script to argue she’s using that position to benefit herself by pointing to ProPublica’s report.
Last week, the outlet reported that the FBI was preparing to open a sweeping corruption probe of Collins and other powerful politicians in 2024. But the probe was shut down after Trump returned to the White House in 2025 and disbanded the anti-corruption unit.
Collins, her campaign and her staff have all vigorously denied the allegations and called the report “outrageous” and a political hit job that’s based on the word of a convicted felon. They contend Collins was cleared of wrongdoing by the Biden administration, noting the defense contractor in question, Martin Kao, of the Hawaii-based firm Navatek, was implicating Collins to have his prison sentence reduced.
An FBI spokesperson is quoted in the story saying the bureau “ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign. Any suggestion otherwise is totally false.”
The WinSenate ad is part of a more than $32.7 million investment the Democratic super PAC is making in Maine, according to the media tracking firm, Ad Impact. The PAC has nearly $18.8 million in ads reserved between now and Election Day.
But Republican groups have a significant financial advantage in the race. Those groups have spent or reserved $100.5 million on ads this cycle — nearly $38 million more than Democrat-aligned groups, according to Ad Impact. Republican groups have reserved more than $37 million in ads leading up to the election.

title: Mother accused of letting 7-year-old daughter’s teeth decay, leaving her unable to eat solid food
text:
(Gray News) - A mother in Pennsylvania is accused of allowing her 7-year-old daughter’s teeth to decay so badly that the girl could not eat solid food or live without pain.
Maria Lopez-Paz, 39, was charged with endangering the welfare of a child.
On Sept. 10, Scranton police responded to reports of a child not being fed, as well as possible drug use in the home, according to the Scranton Times Tribune.
Officers spoke with a county Office of Youth and Family Services case manager, who reported the child was not attending school because she was not vaccinated.
Police scheduled an emergency interview and medical assessment with the child.
During the interview, the 7-year-old told officers the only time she was without pain was when she was asleep. She also raised concerns about cockroaches, rats and bugs in the home, according to the complaint.
The child said when she was hungry, she drank milk.
On Sept. 14, caseworkers took the girl to the dentist, where staff determined the girl had never had any dental care.
The girl suffered from 10 cavities and large areas of decay and needed multiple extractions and procedures.
Investigators also noted the juvenile had not seen a doctor since 2024, when the family moved to Pennsylvania.

title: Obituary: Stephen T. Hughes
text:
AUBURN / NEW YORK CITY, N.Y. – Stephen T. Hughes passed away on Aug. 17, 2026. He was 83.
Steve lived a life marked by service to others — as an elected official, a trustee of the University of Maine, and an active member of several Episcopal parishes, most notably St. Bartholomew’s Church in New York City, N.Y. where he lived for the last 40 years of his life.
Born on July 26, 1943 to Albert W. “Beau” Hughes and Edith Bivens Hughes, Steve grew up in Auburn and graduated from Edward Little High School. He went on to attend Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, a state where members of his extended family lived. After being drafted, Steve served for two years in the United States Army before enrolling at the University of Maine.
At UMaine, Steve made many lifelong friends and served as president of the student body during a tumultuous era when the Vietnam War and the national debate surrounding it profoundly affected campus life. While still an undergraduate, he gained statewide recognition when Gov. Kenneth M. Curtis appointed him as the first student to serve as a trustee of the University of Maine.
Steve graduated from UMaine in 1970 and, while continuing his service as a trustee, attended the University of Maine School of Law. In 1974, voters in Auburn elected him to the Maine House of Representatives. He was reelected in 1976.
During his legislative career, Steve became closely identified with two landmark environmental measures. He sponsored legislation establishing Maine’s beverage-container deposit law, commonly known as the “Bottle Bill,” and championed the successful effort to eliminate most roadside billboards. Both measures helped shape Maine’s approach to environmental protection and preservation of its landscape and remain the law today. Steve was also a strong advocate for civil rights, reproductive freedom, and the rule of law.
After serving four years in the Legislature, Steve left Maine for New York City, N.Y. where he pursued a life of ministry. He enrolled at Union Theological Seminary and spent 15 years leading programs at the Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine. He later became deeply involved with St. Bartholomew’s Church, known as St. Bart’s, where he served in a variety of leadership roles for 25 years. His activities there were curtailed in later years by health issues related to COVID-19.
Throughout his life, Steve maintained a deep love of music, culture, and the arts. Blessed with an extraordinary tenor voice, he sang with numerous choirs in both Maine and New York. He also loved to travel and, over the years, explored much of the United States and Europe with his many friends.
Steve will be remembered for his lively conversation, intellectual curiosity, commitment to public and community service, love of music and the arts, and devotion to a wide circle of friends and an extended network of cousins scattered across the country.
Steve was predeceased by his parents, Albert W. “Beau” Hughes and Edith Bivens Hughes; and his brother, Nick Hughes.
A gathering of Steve’s Maine family and friends will be held 2 p.m., Sunday, Oct. 11, at Maple Hill Farm in Hallowell. A service celebrating Steve’s life will be held at 2 p.m. Nov. 6 at St. Bartholomew’s Church in New York City, N.Y. Interment will be in the Hughes family plot in Eno Presbyterian Church in Cedar Grove, N.C.
In lieu of flowers please donate to be made to the University of Maine Alumni Association. https://www.umainealumni.com/

title: UN Human Rights Office calls botched lethal injection of Christa Pike ‘abhorrent’ and ‘cruel’
text:
NASHVILLE (WSMV/Gray News) — The failed execution of Tennessee’s only woman on death row, 50-year-old Christa Pike, is ringing alarm bells for one of the most prominent international human rights organizations.
The United Nations Human Rights Office is condemning Tennessee’s failed attempt at an execution on Wednesday night.
“The prolonged suffering – physical and mental – arising from multiple failed execution attempts is abhorrent and cruel. And there are key fair trial questions still unresolved,” a post from the organization said.
Witnesses said that, after receiving two doses of pentobarbital, Pike did not die. Her breathing was labored and sounded like “snoring,” they said, and at one point she asked prison staff “if it was supposed to feel that way.”
An ambulance responded to Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville following the botched lethal injection.
United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk is now calling for Tennessee to no longer pursue executing Pike.
The UN office pointed to a larger trend in the U.S., saying it is “troubled” by an uptick in executions.
“The death penalty has no place in any society,” the UN Human Rights Office said.
Pike was still in the hospital Thursday, and her lawyers said they did not know her long-term chance for recovery.
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate. The killing stoked fears of Satan worship because of a pentagram carved on Slemmer’s body.
She did not dispute that she helped kill Slemmer, but supporters argued that her mental illness and allegations of severe sexual abuse should be considered. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder after the killing.

New synthetic opioid up to 10 times more potent than fentanyl detected in Maine
text:
MAINE (WABI) - A newly emerging synthetic opioid called cychlorphine is turning up in fatal overdoses nationwide.
Dr. Barry Logan, chief scientist at NMS Labs and CFSRE, analyzes data from drug seizures, ER visits and autopsies. He warns cychlorphine’s extreme potency sets it apart, with six cases already detected in Maine this year.
“About seven and a half to 10 times more potent than fentanyl,” Logan said.
Cychlorphine binds tightly to brain receptors, causing rapid respiratory depression. To make matters worse, standard test strips and hospital screens can’t detect it.
NMS toxicology shows cychlorphine has so far been co-ingested with other drugs—most often fentanyl, methamphetamine and cocaine.
In rural Maine, where volunteer EMS crews face longer drive times, seconds count. Logan says these stronger drugs create new hurdles.
“That’s definitely more of a risk in rural jurisdictions than in urban,” Logan said. “Narcan is going to work on any drug that binds to the opioid receptors. Because some of these are more potent and more tightly bound, somebody may have to administer more Narcan to reverse the effects of it than they would, say, for fentanyl.”
Logan says cychlorphine is just the latest in an ongoing cycle: once regulators ban a compound, illicit chemists resurrect old, uncommercialized patents to replace it.
“After the drugs are scheduled, the markets do change quite quickly. The drug will disappear and a new drug or new family of drugs will appear,” Logan said. “In our experience, about six months after something is scheduled, there’s already something starting to replace it in drug markets.”
Experts say staying ahead of that cycle requires updated toxicology testing and keeping overdose reversal tools widely available.
The Maine Drug Enforcement Agency said that though labs have detected it, MDEA has not been notified of any specific Maine case in which cychlorphine was determined to be the cause of death.
The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner has not yet responded to a request for comment.

title: Nonprofit dental clinic in Belfast closes temporarily amid PCHC’s financial crisis
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A nonprofit dental clinic that opened in Belfast this spring to make dental care more widely available has temporarily closed.
Seaport Dental Center, which is owned and operated by Penobscot Community Health Care, hopes to resume service in about a month, the not-for-profit healthcare agency posted Friday morning on Facebook.
“We anticipate resuming limited dental services two Fridays per month beginning in late October or early November, once provider scheduling is finalized,” the post said. “This limited schedule is expected to continue through spring 2027 as we continue recruitment efforts.”
The temporary closure of the clinic is the latest hurdle confronting PCHC, which is facing a financial crisis that agency officials say could result in it having to declare bankruptcy.
The crisis has resulted in planned layoffs amid the pending closure of an adult wellness clinic in Bangor, and has been complicated by a decision by Bangor officials to exercise the city’s right of first refusal on a Maine Avenue property that PCHC had been hoping to sell quickly to a private healthcare provider.
Asked Friday to elaborate on the reasons for the temporary closure of the Belfast dental clinic, PCHC President and CEO Lori Dwyer said only that it “is a temporary closure driven by hiring challenges.”
She declined further comment.
PCHC officials said in May, when the clinic opened, that they hoped to address a shortage of dental care services in the Belfast area. Waldo County has just one dentist per nearly 6,000 residents — about half as many as the state average, state statistics show.
“It’s pretty startling how poor oral health care is in the state,” Dwyer said at the time.
The clinic is not yet scheduling appointments for its anticipated reopening, the agency’s Facebook post said. Patients already on the clinic’s waitlist will be able to schedule appointments. New patients are not being accepted for the time being.
Anyone needing urgent dental care should call PCHC’s Bangor clinic at 207-992-2152 to schedule an emergency visit.

title: Happy to be ‘stuck’ in central Maine, thanks
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I was disappointed by a recent news report (“As life in Maine gets more expensive, young people struggle to keep up,” Sept. 18). As a proud Augusta resident who left Portland years ago due to — go figure — rising costs and lack of opportunity, I thought it quite rich to ascribe to my neighbor the feeling that he was “stuck in central Maine.”
The report itself makes clear my neighbor was attributing that sentiment to his friends in — I guess, to the reporter — more desirable locales, not necessarily speaking about his own feelings.
Some people want to live in Maine, even up here in the scary boondocks of central Maine, because it’s a great place to live, with great people. It’s disappointing that the reporting ignores that possibility.
Honestly, that last line (“Maybe, for now, he is [stuck].”) angered and offended me.
“Maybe,” indeed.
Stanley Abraham
Augusta

title: Trump tried to make an ally out of fishermen. Some have started to turn on him.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — John Evich, a commercial fisherman in Washington and Alaska, has voted for President Donald Trump three times, viewing him as someone who would fight for his industry.
But these days, Evich is weary of the high cost of doing business at sea, with fuel prices rising and trade hostilities with Canada jeopardizing markets for the crabs that he pulls off the ocean floor.
“If somebody came along that was going to do a better job, I would vote for them in a heartbeat,” he said.
Evich’s sentiment, echoed throughout the U.S. seafood industry, is another piece of a political puzzle that is working against Trump in the midterm elections. Dissatisfaction among commercial fishermen could cause collateral damage for Republicans in competitive races in Washington, Alaska and Maine.
“Having those costs be so much higher this year has really undermined the viability of some of our fisheries,” Alaska fisherman Linda Behnken said.
Trump sought to make an ally out of fishermen during his first term with expanded fishing territory, aggressive trade moves and cutting down regulations on the water. He did so again after his second election.
But one of Trump’s government cutback efforts, cuts to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which regulates fisheries, has left the agency slower to respond to the industry’s needs, fishermen said. Staff cutbacks also resulted in the agency reducing weather balloons used to gather data fishermen rely on.
Fuel costs have also crept up during the war with Iran, pushing diesel fuel into the $6-per-gallon range when it was less than $4 per gallon a year ago — a major burden for a diesel-dependent industry. And the trade war with Canada has complicated the American seafood industry’s relationship with a country it has long been interconnected with, fishermen said.
The Trump administration has continued trying to win the hearts of fishermen with industry-friendly moves, including an early September promise to reduce more regulatory burdens in response to a 2025 executive order. And some of the industry’s key states, such as Alaska, Washington and Maine, are important to Trump politically this year because of competitive House and Senate races. But support on the water could be waning.
“I’m for whatever has to happen for the greater good in the long run for my family and my country,” Evich said.
Trump has cozied up to the fishing industry for years
Trump has positioned himself as a pro-fishing president since his first term, when one of his major moves to impact the fishing industry was the rollback of Obama-era fishing restrictions for Northeast Canyons and Seamounts National Monument off the New England coast. Biden later restored the protections, and then Trump removed them again.
The fishing industry is potentially a natural ally for Trump. A 2026 NOAA survey of commercial fishing crews found that 70% thought fishing rules were too restrictive, and Trump has fashioned himself as an enemy of bureaucracy and red tape.
But in recent months, Trump has brought disruption to the fishing industry in a time when it can ill afford it, said John Sackton, founder of SeafoodNews.com and a longtime industry analyst. He said he sees an industry that is eager to “turn the page” on the Trump administration.
“Now what’s happened is that there has been this unbelievable wave of disruption from everything — targeting NOAA and fisheries, science and even weather reporting that people rely on,” said Sackton, who also cited tariffs and the rising cost of doing business as problems Trump brought to the industry.
Fuel costs and tariffs are huge concerns for fishermen
The high price of fuel is “one of the most immediate pressures on us as commercial fishermen,” said Bonnie Brady, executive director of the Long Island Commercial Fishing Association in New York.
Nearly all of the U.S.’s commercial fishing fleet uses marine diesel fuel, which makes soaring fuel costs a burden they can’t avoid. Sometimes fuel prices are so high right now that fishermen can’t afford to leave the dock at all, she said.
“Actual dockside marine-fuel prices vary, but the magnitude of the increase is undeniable. It determines whether a trip is economically viable, what the crew earns and whether necessary vessel maintenance can be performed,” Brady said.
In Rhode Island, fisherman Chris Brown, who targets species such as fluke and squid out of Point Judith, puts it more bluntly.
“It’s huge. It’s crazy. Thank you, Donald Trump,” he said sarcastically.
Trump’s trade war with Canada is a more complicated matter because Canada exempted U.S. fish and seafood products from its counter-tariffs that followed the U.S. placing tariffs on Canadian goods. Prior to the exemption, Patrice McCarron, executive director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, said U.S. lobstermen risked becoming “collateral damage in a broader trade dispute.”
But unease among fishermen remains, in part because Canada is the U.S.’s largest seafood trading partner. The U.S. also relies on Canada for seafood processing and manufacturing of fishing gear. For some species, such as lobster and salmon, American and Canadian fishermen fish very close to each other or even in the same waters.
A trade war with such a key partner could have negative consequences for the fishing industry, said Steve Train, a lobster fisherman from Long Island, Maine, who described himself as a “right-leaning centrist” who has voted Republican more than Democrat.
“I get the standing up to a bully concept, but too many people will be caught in the middle of this,” Train said. “Both sides need to reconsider these tariffs, and they need to reconsider soon.”
Cuts to NOAA are troubling to fishermen
NOAA Fisheries, the arm of NOAA tasked with overseeing commercial fishing, is facing a budget cut of more than 40% in the fiscal 2027 budget proposal. That would result in cuts to science programs, fisheries management and data collection.
Those cutbacks trickle down to the fishermen and result in a lack of fishing opportunities, Sackton said. Some in the fishery also have the impression NOAA is too understaffed to regulate fisheries in a timely fashion, he said.
In Sitka, Alaska, Behnken said the Trump administration’s cutbacks at NOAA have made it more difficult for her and others who rely on the agency. She said she has a lot of empathy for the workers left at the agency, who she said are “doing the work of three people, particularly at the weather service,” but it is still frustrating for fishermen.
“It’s hard to retain good people when their future at the organization is that uncertain,” said Behnken, who is executive director of the Alaska Longline Fishermen’s Association.
Story by Patrick Whittle, Associated Press

title: Maine heating costs expected to spike: How to apply for energy assistance
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - With cold weather approaching, Maine energy officials are urging residents to prepare now as heating fuel costs remain elevated across the state.
According to a newly released heating guide from the Maine Department of Energy Resources, Maine continues to be the most heating oil-dependent state in the country, with roughly half of all households relying on oil to heat their homes.
Prices at the pump and terminal are putting significant strain on budgets. Heating oil currently averages $5.96 per gallon, meaning Mainers can expect to pay approximately $725 more to fill a typical home tank compared to this time last year.
To help residents navigate changing prices, energy alternatives, and weatherization improvements, state energy officials recently hosted an informational community webinar outlining available resources and programs.
Applying for Home Energy Assistance
State officials recommend applying for the Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) as early as possible. Sarah Johnson, manager of Home Energy Assistance Programs, outlined the documentation households need to have ready before their appointment:
“All household members must provide proof of citizenship. Acceptable documentation includes a U.S. passport, a REAL ID, and birth certificates with required information,” Johnson said. “There are other ways to prove citizenship if an applicant does not have these items. The primary applicant must also provide an unexpired photo ID, and Social Security cards must be provided for all household members.”
Officials noted that application calendars fill quickly, and scheduling an appointment into late October or early November is typical.
Emergency Fuel Assistance and Resources
For residents facing an immediate heating crisis or who cannot afford a scheduled delivery, state officials advise calling 2-1-1. Operators can connect households directly with local Community Action Agencies to access emergency fuel assistance funds.
Residents can review the complete state heating guide and find additional weatherization tools by visiting the Department of Energy Resources link.

title: Tony Romo out at CBS Sports following his arrest
text:
(Gray News) - Former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo will no longer work for CBS Sports, according to reports.
Sportswriter Richard Deitsch posted a statement from CBS Sports on X that said the network and Romo “mutually agreed to part ways.”
“We thank Tony for his contributions over the last nine years and wish him the best moving forward,” the statement said.
Romo, 46, was arrested on July 23 on suspicion of operating a vehicle while under the influence. He was placed on indefinite leave from his role as CBS’ lead NFL analyst shortly after.
Romo joined CBS Sports in 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during a playing career that ran from 2004-16 and was spent entirely with Dallas.
His arrest followed a traffic stop on Interstate 43 in Wisconsin. The Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office reported he was spotted unsafely passing cars.
The sheriff’s office said Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests and was arrested, booked and released. An open bottle of an alcoholic beverage was also found in the passenger seat of his Jeep.
He pleaded no contest to a civil offense for driving under the influence on Sept. 1.
“I own this completely,” Romo wrote on Instagram.
He said multiple back surgeries left him with constant pain, which led to a dependence on pain medication. While trying to get off those medications, Romo said he became dependent on alcohol.
“None of this is an excuse. These are my failures, and I take full responsibility for them,” Romo continued.
CBS Sports said in the statement that JJ Watt will continue his role as lead analyst on CBS Sports’ lead NFL team for the rest of the season, alongside play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson.

title: Woman gives birth to twins months after brutal dog attack
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW/Gray News) - Healing continues for Audrey Austin following a brutal dog attack back in July, when she was 24 weeks pregnant, that changed her life forever.
“I’m going to stay strong, and I’m going to keep moving, and it’s going to take time to forgive the person, but I forgave the dog,” Austin said.
On Thursday, Oct. 1, she wrapped up an eye appointment in Kansas City before making her way back to Topeka. It’s still one of many treatments Audrey is undergoing to regain her appearance.
“My first surgery for my nose—they’re going to do a forehead flip, where they’re going to take skin from my forehead and bring it to my nose,” she said.
But another thing added to her plate is caring for her newborn twins. Kasai and Kamyiah were born at just 38 weeks.
Audrey says because of the dog attack, her delivery wasn’t easy.
“My body has been under so much anesthesia and so much surgeries that I also think [it] put a strain on my babies,” Austin said.
The twins remain in the NICU, but it’s not stopping Audrey from being present.
“I see them in the mornings. [I see] them every day. I come up here, spend the night,” Austin said.
Alongside looking forward to bringing her babies home soon, Audrey is taking one step at a time in turning the page on this chapter of her life.
“It’s life. I mean, eventually, I’m going to grow from this. Eventually, I’m going to heal inside to not worry about what’s on the outside,” Austin said. “I’m still trying to get everything going for my babies when they come home.”
Audrey tells 13 NEWS that she has not been able to work since the dog attack. She’s currently seeking assistance from the community as she navigates this new chapter in her life. Her GoFundMe can be found here.

title: Mother accused of letting 7-year-old daughter’s teeth decay, leaving her unable to eat solid food
text:
(Gray News) - A mother in Pennsylvania is accused of allowing her 7-year-old daughter’s teeth to decay so badly that the girl could not eat solid food or live without pain.
Maria Lopez-Paz, 39, was charged with endangering the welfare of a child.
On Sept. 10, Scranton police responded to reports of a child not being fed, as well as possible drug use in the home, according to the Scranton Times Tribune.
Officers spoke with a county Office of Youth and Family Services case manager, who reported the child was not attending school because she was not vaccinated.
Police scheduled an emergency interview and medical assessment with the child.
During the interview, the 7-year-old told officers the only time she was without pain was when she was asleep. She also raised concerns about cockroaches, rats and bugs in the home, according to the complaint.
The child said when she was hungry, she drank milk.
On Sept. 14, caseworkers took the girl to the dentist, where staff determined the girl had never had any dental care.
The girl suffered from 10 cavities and large areas of decay and needed multiple extractions and procedures.
Investigators also noted the juvenile had not seen a doctor since 2024, when the family moved to Pennsylvania.
A preliminary hearing is scheduled for 11 a.m. Oct. 14 before District Judge Laura Turlip.

title: 911 call reveals concerns about well-being of 2 children found dead from starvation at home
text:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — Two children who were found dead in a home earlier this week in South Carolina have been identified, and authorities said this wasn’t the first time they had been called to the residence.
Emory Deacon, 2, and Harlow Deacon, 15 months old, died of starvation and dehydration due to neglect, Charleston County coroner Bobbi Jo O’Neal said.
Justine May, the children’s mother and described as their primary caregiver, has been charged in the case with two counts of homicide by child abuse.
According to the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office, deputies had responded to numerous calls at the Pinewood Drive residence before ultimately finding the two children dead during a welfare check at the home.
The previous calls to the home were said to have included welfare checks and visits coordinated with the South Carolina Department of Social Services and the South Carolina Department of Mental Health Mobile Crisis Unit.
Authorities said deputies made contact with May and the children in August and again several more times in September, noting they observed no signs of concern during those visits.
On Tuesday, authorities said they were called back to the home after a 911 call came through that morning asking deputies to conduct a welfare check on the two young girls after they had not been seen, with their mother acting differently while walking around the neighborhood by herself.
“I’m just concerned because she didn’t have her kids, and nobody has seen her kids,” the caller told the Charleston County 911 dispatcher. “She was walking down the road today, and she didn’t have her babies, and that’s not like her.”
When deputies arrived at the home that afternoon, they said May exited the house and was crying and speaking incoherently. Upon entering, that’s when they saw the two children dead.
May was taken into custody.
According to affidavits, after being read her Miranda rights, May told detectives that she had spent the previous two weeks in a “blur,” saying she could not remember the last time she fed Emory and Harlow or gave them anything to drink.
Authorities said May told detectives that she believed her children were dead because they did not eat. She reportedly told deputies that she knew that not feeding her children was neglectful and confirmed she had been the only one present at home and was the sole caregiver for the girls over the last few weeks.
May remains jailed at the Al Cannon Detention Center.

title: Head Start was there for my family. Maine children need it protected.
text:
Megan Newsome lives in Lisbon and is a Maine state parent ambassador.
When my son Brayden was born, our family was facing a lot at once.
I had been diagnosed with cancer while I was pregnant. He arrived about six weeks early and spent time in the NICU. By the time Brayden was about a year old, I was receiving WIC, the federally funded nutrition program for women, infants and children. WIC staff asked whether I had childcare and told me about Early Head Start.
I knew very little about the program then. It quickly became a godsend.
At the time, Brayden was not yet walking. He could not feed himself or hold his own cup. Within weeks of starting Early Head Start, he was pulling himself up, holding his cup and learning to use a spoon and pick up food on his own.
His teachers paid attention to who he was and how he learned.
Brayden is left-handed. When teachers recognized that and encouraged him to use the hand that came naturally to him, it showed me that they saw my son as an individual.
Head Start also gave me something I deeply needed while facing cancer: trusted people who could care for my child during the workday. Knowing my son was cared for and learning gave me comfort during an incredibly difficult time.
The support did not stop at the classroom door. Head Start connected us with mental health counseling, clothing, diapers, food banks and help during the holidays — all supports we needed to make sure Brayden had what he needed to learn and grow, at home and in the classroom. There was always someone I could turn to.
Brayden is now 3 and has moved from Early Head Start into Head Start. He is now on track developmentally, and this is a crucial moment in his learning. If he needs additional help before elementary school, I want us to recognize it early and have support in place.
That is why proposed changes to Head Start concern me so deeply. Families could lose developmental screenings, medical and dental services, counseling and other support that helps children grow and prepare for school.
For some children, Head Start may provide the only developmental screening they receive. It’s the front door to healthcare, dental care and mental health support. If those services disappear, important needs could go unnoticed until a child enters school and faces a harder path forward.
Larger classrooms and fewer teachers would also make it harder to provide the individual attention that helped Brayden. Teachers need time to know each child, understand how they learn and recognize when they may need additional support.
Head Start works because all these pieces work together. It is not simply a place where parents leave their children. It helps children build confidence and skills while connecting parents with trusted people and practical resources. Weakening any part of that model weakens the program families count on.
I know what Head Start made possible for my son and me. I also know other families rely on it for that same stability and partnership.
The public has only until Oct. 6 to comment on the proposed changes, but Congress can act even after that. I am asking Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King and Rep. Jared Golden, who represents Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, my home district, to listen to Maine families, oppose the proposed rule and protect the standards and services that make Head Start so effective.
Children deserve to enter school with their strengths recognized and the support they need already in place. Parents deserve trusted partners as they build strong futures for their families. Head Start gave my family both.

title: Mickey Gasper has surgery after Red Sox season ends
text:
BOSTON — Boston Red Sox first baseman and catcher Mickey Gasper has undergone what the team says was a successful repair of his right biceps tendon.
The club made the announcement on Friday. The procedure was performed by Dr. Matthew Leibman at MassGeneral Brigham in Boston.
Gasper started Boston’s final regular-season series against the Chicago Cubs on Sept. 25 at catcher but was replaced in the sixth inning after experiencing discomfort in his biceps.
He was placed on the injured list and was not on the Red Sox’s roster for their AL Wild Card Series loss to the New York Yankees.
The 30-year-old New Hampshire native played a career-high 67 games in his third major league season, batting .251 with 10 home runs and 24 RBI.

title: Mother charged with capital murder in deaths of 2 sons
text:
WAXAHACHIE, Texas (KWTX/Gray News) — A Texas mother is facing two counts of capital murder after authorities said she shot and killed her sons Thursday morning.
Forty-two-year-old Colleen Nichole Lemmon of Waxahachie was booked into the Wayne McCollum Detention Center following treatment at a local hospital for non-life-threatening injuries.
Deputies respond to 911 call
Ellis County Sheriff’s Office deputies responded around 4:13 a.m. Thursday to a 911 call reporting an unknown emergency at a home in the 900 block of Big Sky Drive in Waxahachie.
Deputies entered the home and discovered two male victims suffering from gunshot wounds.
One victim, identified by authorities as 21-year-old Christopher Scott Pitre of Waxahachie, was pronounced dead at the scene.
The second victim, a 15-year-old boy, was rushed to a local hospital in critical condition, where he later died from his injuries. The sheriff’s office said the teenager’s identity is being withheld.
Investigation and statement
Detectives developed probable cause through corroborating evidence recovered during the investigation that Lemmon was responsible for shooting both of her sons, the sheriff’s office said.
The victims’ father has been notified of both deaths.
“My deepest sympathies go out to the victims’ father, family members, and loved ones involved in this tragic incident,” Ellis County Sheriff Brad Norman said in a statement. “They will remain in our prayers during this difficult time.”
Jail records show Lemmon is charged with two counts of capital murder. Her bond is pending arraignment.

title: Maine’s candidates for governor answer your questions
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
To put the focus on the topics and concerns that matter most to you, the BDN opinion section asked subscribers for their questions for the candidates for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House. In coming days, we’ll share their answers. We start today with the three candidates for governor.
What are the first 3 things you would do if you are elected?
Bobby Charles, Republican
Lower electric bills, cut waste, cut taxes.
Hannah Pingree, Democrat
First, I’d build a great team. That’s how I’ve led throughout my career: surround yourself with smart, talented, hardworking people and trust them to deliver. Good government starts with good people.
Then I’d get to work on a balanced budget focused on our most urgent needs: lowering costs, building more housing, strengthening health care and education, and providing immediate relief, including heating help this winter.
I’d move aggressively to build more homes by cutting barriers to construction and investing in housing Mainers can afford. On health care, I’d begin work on a public option, protect rural hospitals, and lower prescription drug costs. And I’d strengthen public education from early childhood through higher education, investing in proven programs like the science of reading and evidence-based math.
I’d work with legislators from both parties. But we also have to be clear-eyed: the Trump Administration will make the next governor’s job harder, with federal cuts that threaten Maine’s budget, economy, health care system, and people’s rights. On day one, I’ll use the full authority of the governor’s office to protect Mainers’ rights and freedoms, push back against harmful federal overreach, and address emerging challenges, from threats to reproductive and civil rights to the risks posed by AI.
And I’d fulfill a campaign promise: working with the Wabanaki Nations to pass legislation in my first 100 days advancing full tribal sovereignty and ensuring the Wabanaki have the same rights as other federally recognized tribes.
This moment demands a governor who can do many things at once, and deliver.
Rick Bennett, independent
My first three actions all serve one goal: Making Maine affordable again.
First, cut the costs crushing Mainers. I will apply the Property Tax Fairness Credit, up to $1,500 for most households and $2,000 for Mainers 65 and older, directly to property tax bills, so relief arrives when the bill arrives, not months later at refund time. I will reduce down payments for first-time home buyers, reduce utility profits to lower delivery costs, and make child care affordable by unifying Maine’s birth to five systems under one roof.
Second, restore accountability in state government. I will create an Office of Inspector General reporting to the governor, publish the budget in plain language online so any Mainer can follow it, subject every agency program to a biennial review that justifies its cost and results, and require the state to pay its own bills, including hospital and nonprofit provider claims, within 30 days.
Third, grow Maine’s economy. I will give job seekers and employers one “front door” instead of a maze of agencies, negotiate special energy rate contracts for manufacturers tied to job commitments, and expand Career and Technical Education and paid apprenticeships so young Mainers can build a career and a life here.
Mainers are doing everything right and still falling behind. Government’s job is to make the math work again.
Health care costs are rising, yet many Maine hospitals are struggling to stay open. What specifically would you do to lower health care costs in Maine? To increase access to care? How would you help Maine health care facilities improve their financial stability?
Pingree
Health care costs are out of control, and many Maine people can’t get the care they need. Rural hospitals are under enormous financial pressure, services are disappearing, and families are waiting longer, traveling farther, and paying more. Federal cuts to Medicaid and other health care funding will make those pressures worse.
Congress should pass universal health care, but Maine families can’t wait. As governor, I’ll act.
First, I’ll create a public health insurance option: a state-backed plan that gives individuals and small businesses another affordable choice. It won’t replace anyone’s current coverage. It will compete with private insurers, put patients before profits, and be accountable to Maine people — not corporate shareholders.
I’ll also attack the underlying costs driving premiums and medical bills. I’ll use Maine’s purchasing power to lower prescription drug costs, limit restrictive prior authorizations, strengthen oversight of excessive price increases, demand greater transparency from insurers and health systems, and push back against corporate consolidation that raises costs without improving care.
And we have to protect access, especially in rural Maine. I’ll work to stabilize rural hospitals while expanding primary care, home care, maternity, reproductive, mental health, and substance-use care closer to home. That means investing in our health care workforce, investing in community-based care, and creating a systems approach to ensure that everything from rural hospitals to nursing homes are accessible for Mainers when they need it most, regardless of what county you live in.
Maine shouldn’t accept a system where families can’t afford care and the providers they depend on can’t afford to stay open. My plan tackles both affordability and access, building a health care system strong enough to serve every community.
Bennett
Yes, health care costs keep rising while rural hospitals strain to keep their doors open, and we have to be honest about why. Right now we are subsidizing a failed system in the least efficient way possible.
First, pay providers fairly and on time. Maine hospitals and nonprofit providers wait months for the state to pay legitimate claims, and some borrow thousands in interest just to keep operating. As governor, I will require clean claims to be paid within 30 days, set MaineCare rates that reflect the actual cost of care, and stop shifting costs onto hospitals and local property taxpayers.
Second, invest in prevention first. States that invested in coordinated primary and behavioral health care saw hospital and emergency spending fall dramatically. That means telehealth so geography is not a barrier, mobile crisis teams, and supportive housing so people stop cycling through emergency rooms and jails.
Third, protect financial stability against what is coming from Washington. The federal reconciliation law will change how nearly 400,000 Mainers access coverage and could cost Maine 4,300 jobs and $749 million in economic activity. I will defend MaineCare, expand telehealth, and fight to keep rural hospitals and clinics open.
Fourth, launch a Medical Debt Relief Program to reduce crushing debt, protect family finances, and help Mainers get care.
Finally, I commit Maine to a path to universal care, because coverage that is not affordable is not coverage.
Charles
By simply living up to our fiscal responsibilities.
Affordability is my number one concern, and it’s the number one concern of most Mainers. That includes health care.
Gov. Janet Mills’ first act in office was to expand MaineCare to able-bodied, childless adults without a plan to pay for it. Working, taxpaying Mainers have been footing the bill ever since.
Mills and Hannah Pingree, her top policy advisor, mismanaged Maine’s health care system. Mostly on their watch, Maine lost 12 birthing units, 15 nursing homes, 24 assisted living facilities and 75 home care agencies. Providers were paid late and reimbursed at rates that don’t cover the cost of care.
This must be reversed. As governor, I will restore proper management to MaineCare, pay providers on time and at fair rates, and make sure Mainers have high-quality health care that is accessible and affordable.
Maine has one of the highest tax burdens in the country. What would you do to lower taxes? To increase incomes? Do you believe that lowering taxes will draw businesses to Maine? What government programs, if any, would you cut to lower state spending to reduce taxes? Will you push for government and school consolidation to lower property taxes?
Bennett
Maine’s tax burden is high because state spending grows faster than paychecks, and the state keeps shifting its own costs onto property tax bills. The state budget grew 77% over the past decade, from $8.2 billion to $14.5 billion, more than twice the rate of inflation, while most of it renews on autopilot with limited scrutiny.
I will lower taxes by lowering the cost of government and going after what drives property taxes up. Every program must justify its cost and results each biennium; every tax expenditure must show measurable public benefit; no more contracts without competitive bidding; and an Inspector General to find waste and corruption.
On property taxes, I will apply the Property Tax Fairness Credit directly to tax bills, expand the homestead exemption frozen since 2020, move toward income sensitive property tax caps like Vermont’s so no one is taxed out of their home, and pay the state’s share: full revenue sharing and the 55% school funding commitment, instead of unfunded mandates. I support regionalizing services like EMS, dispatch, and public works when towns choose to partner, with incentives, not consolidation forced from Augusta.
Lower taxes alone will not draw businesses; lower costs will. Energy, housing, health care, and child care, along with a skilled workforce, decide where employers go. That is how incomes rise.
Charles
I will launch a full-scale audit of state government on day one to root out the waste, fraud and abuse that has become so common in Augusta. That starts with the large number of reckless no-bid, sole-source contracts that this administration’s own state auditor has flagged. It includes the $45 million in improper spending that federal auditors found in just one Medicaid program. This audit will be run by career, civil service bean counters, not political operatives.
State government can and must lower the tax burden, starting with property taxes. As governor, I will raise the Homestead Exemption to $100,000. I will raise the state’s reimbursement to towns to 100%, so that relief doesn’t get shifted onto other local taxpayers. And I will roll back the unfunded mandates Augusta keeps passing down to our towns and school districts, which drive up property taxes every year.
I will also roll back hundreds of burdensome regulations that hold back economic growth, and I will work to cut and ultimately eliminate the individual income tax to spur growth and bring new investment to Maine.
Between last year and this year alone, total state spending jumped by about $1.3 billion, nearly half of what Maine collects in income tax. Since 2016, total state spending has grown by roughly $7 billion, about 80%. We will cut $1 billion in the first year and keep reducing the income tax in the years that follow.
Pingree
Maine’s tax system has asked too much of people who can afford it least, while working families fall further behind. I want to rebalance that: reward work, tax wealth fairly, and give middle- and low-income Mainers real relief, starting with property taxes.
I’ll double the Homestead Exemption, expand the Property Tax Fairness Credit so more households qualify, increase the benefit, and simplify the application so seniors and renters can access it. I’ll also work with bipartisan lawmakers and local leaders on a constitutional proposal to ensure non-resident owners of high-value second homes contribute fairly to the communities they impact.
With 482 municipalities, we need more regional cooperation to reduce costs and improve services. I’ll support new partnerships for EMS, public safety, and homeless services, while maintaining the state’s commitment to fund 55% of K-12 education so local property taxpayers aren’t left with the bill.
Maine took an important step with the new millionaire’s tax. I’ll build on that through a transparent process examining additional reforms to provide relief for working families.
Tax policy alone won’t grow Maine’s economy. Employers tell me they need skilled workers, housing, reliable infrastructure, and affordable energy. That’s why my economic plan invests in housing, workforce development, and industries that have long sustained Maine, including fishing, forestry, and farming, while supporting innovation and clean energy.
As governor, I’ll build a balanced budget that protects seniors, kids, and working families from Washington’s cuts to health care and food programs while being honest about the fiscal challenges ahead.
Do you believe climate change is real and made worse by burning fossil fuel? Would you encourage the development of more renewable energy in Maine? If so, what specific measures do you support? Do you support net energy billing? Should it be changed?
Pingree
Yes. Climate change is real, burning fossil fuels makes it worse, and Mainers are already paying the price through extreme storms, rising costs, threats to our farms, forests, and working waterfronts.
As speaker of the Maine House of Representatives, I took on the fossil fuel and chemical industries and won, passing Maine’s first meaningful greenhouse gas reduction targets and laws like the Kid Safe Products Act. As co-chair of the Maine Climate Council, I led Maine Won’t Wait and we delivered real results: more than 100,000 heat pumps installed two years ahead of schedule, and a Community Resilience Partnership that’s helped over 250 towns prepare for extreme weather. Energy experts rated Maine most improved in the country on efficiency.
So yes, I’ll keep pushing hard on affordable renewable energy and efficiency as governor: expanding heat pumps and weatherization, growing clean energy projects in our towns and schools, investing in resilient infrastructure before the next storm hits rather than after, and holding utilities and polluters accountable so families aren’t footing the bill.
Maine’s dependence on heating oil and natural gas leaves families vulnerable to volatile prices. Producing our own clean energy means independence, good Maine jobs, and keeping energy dollars here at home.
I support net energy billing, but it must be structured fairly so families who don’t have solar aren’t subsidizing overly generous contracts. Maine has already reformed the program. Going forward, I’ll prioritize community projects that benefit ratepayers as well as competitive, large-scale clean-energy procurements that deliver lower-cost power for all ratepayers, create Maine jobs, provide real support for host communities, and are responsibly sited. We can cut emissions, strengthen our economy, and lower energy costs at the same time.
Bennett
Yes. Climate change is real, and burning fossil fuels is making it worse. I trust science, and in Maine we can see the evidence: The Gulf of Maine is among the fastest warming water bodies in the world, and the January 2024 storms devastated harbors and working waterfronts.
Yes, I would encourage renewable energy development, but it must lower costs for Mainers, not just add generation. My plan: Create a Maine Generation Authority to build renewable energy and storage that Maine owns, stabilize supply costs, and sell excess power to the region at a profit, using the revenue to lower rates for Maine families instead of enriching out of state shareholders. I will reduce utility profits to lower delivery costs, modernize the grid for reliability, and fund $30 million in weatherization bonds, because the cheapest energy is the energy we don’t waste: every dollar through Efficiency Maine returns $3.70 to our economy. Renewable projects should be built here, owned here, and sited with real input from host communities and Wabanaki Nations.
On net energy billing: yes, with reform. I sponsored legislation to reform net energy billing tariff rates to protect ratepayers from cost shifting, and I was lead cosponsor of a bill to create a Net Energy Billing Cost Stabilization Fund to shield households and businesses from price spikes. Clean energy should mean cheaper energy. If we are going to power the region, Maine people should finally get the benefit.
Charles
Climate change is real.
But the most urgent question is how Mainers will pay their electric bills. Under a flawed and uncoordinated set of Mills-Pingree energy policies, electricity [supply] prices have gone from about 6 cents per kilowatt-hour to 19 cents in just eight years. Maine families cannot afford this.
We were promised these policies would cut carbon emissions and lower energy costs. Neither happened. Maine’s carbon emissions have grown at four times the national rate, and some energy costs have tripled.
Mainers are being crushed by energy policy malpractice, and our economy is paying the price. Maine now ranks 47th in the nation for economic growth, due in large part to unaffordable energy.
Much of what ratepayers pay has gone straight to Wall Street and global investors, including Goldman Sachs, Mitsubishi, the Carlyle Group and BlackRock, the world’s largest investment firm.
My 12-point plan will restore accountability, affordability and reliability for Maine ratepayers. To the extent the law allows, we will put the failed net energy billing program behind us for good. We will also: Expand access to affordable natural gas; end the subsidies that have driven up electricity costs; lift the cap on hydropower; save our dams and the Sappi mill; review the roughly 400 laws that have driven prices sky high; put competent leaders on the Public Utilities Commission; put Maine ratepayers and affordability first; and explore greater use of biomass and small modular reactors.
Can you give examples of specific times when you have stood up to or voted against your political party or people with views similar to yours? Why did you do this? How did you decide to take a different position? What will you do to diminish the political partisanship that has divided Maine?
Charles
My campaign, and my time as governor, will be about solving problems and fixing what has made life in Maine unaffordable, unpredictable and, in too many places, unsafe.
I have always been an independent thinker. In Congress, I led a bipartisan drug policy working group with Democrats like Elijah Cummings of Maryland and Charlie Rangel of New York, alongside Republicans. I reach my positions based on facts and logic, not party.
That is why I have disagreed with the president on several issues. I oppose rolling back coal plant regulations, because coal emissions put mercury in Maine’s lakes. I oppose new tariffs on Canada, because 41% of Maine’s trade is with Canada. And having spent time in Iraq and Afghanistan, I do not favor a prolonged military engagement with Iran.
But Maine is where I can make a difference. As governor, I will work tirelessly with Republicans, independents and Democrats to make Maine more affordable and safer, to strengthen addiction treatment and recovery, and to end eight years of waste, fraud and abuse in Augusta.
Pingree
Yes. I’ve never believed my job is to follow a party line. My job is to do what’s right for Maine.
As House speaker, I led the fight to pass marriage equality, even when that meant pushing members of my own party who weren’t ready. I listened to the people whose lives were affected and worked to bring people along.
I was proud to be elected speaker unanimously, by Republicans, Democrats and independents. I worked with Republican Leader Josh Tardy to negotiate balanced bipartisan budgets and bond packages. We disagreed on plenty, but we trusted each other enough to negotiate honestly.
From my local school board to state government, I’ve worked with Republican leaders on everything from climate action and housing to economic recovery. I’ve learned you don’t have to agree on everything to get important things done.
That’s how I’ll govern. I’ll start with what’s best for Maine people, not which party gets credit. I’ll bring Democratic, Republican, and independent leaders to the table early and seek common ground without abandoning my values.
Maine is too small, and the challenges we face too serious, to govern by partisan warfare. That’s how things work in towns across Maine, where people don’t give up on their neighbors. We all want the same things for our families: housing and health care we can afford, good jobs, decent schools, and safe communities.
My record shows I can stand my ground when it matters, work across the aisle when we find common purpose, and get things done.
Bennett
As an independent governor, under my leadership it will never be about what’s best for Republicans, or best for Democrats. It will be about what’s best for Maine.
I will build two-thirds consensus budgets, open closed-door party caucuses to Maine’s Freedom of Access Act, and make all appointments on competence and character rather than party.
I was unanimously elected president of the Maine Senate under a bipartisan power sharing agreement, and we passed major legislation. I championed opening Maine’s primaries to unaffiliated voters, enfranchising roughly one third of the electorate. I introduced truth and disclosure legislation to unmask dark money, and I chaired the effort to ban foreign governments from spending in our elections. All efforts that have significant bipartisan support.
But independence is not just about standing up to your own side. It is about bringing people along to do the right thing. I helped bring my former caucus to support funding for community substance use recovery centers, because that work saves lives. On environmental issues, I worked across party lines and helped bring my former caucus to support major environmental bills. I also fought to expand broadband, because in rural Maine that is not a luxury. It is how people work, learn, and get health care.
I have always made those decisions the same way: not by asking what is best for a party, but what is best for Maine.
Why should we trust you?
Bennett
Because my record and my plan say the same thing, and because I will let Mainers verify it.
I served in the Maine House, spent four terms in the Maine Senate, including as president of the Senate elected unanimously by both parties, and returned to the Senate in 2020 after a career in business. My family has lived in Oxford County for more than 200 years. I have fought dark money, expanded broadband, and taken on the utilities.
I tell Mainers the truth even when it costs me. I won’t promise to slash taxes while defending a budget that grew 77% in a decade, and I won’t pretend that taxing someone else is the same as lowering your bill. Relief has to be the point of the policy, not a byproduct.
Trust is also about competence. The governor is chief executive of an organization with more than 13,500 employees and a $14.5 billion budget. I will publish what the state spends in plain language online, create an Office of Inspector General, pay Maine’s bills on time, and measure results publicly, so you can check my word against the record.
I am not running to protect the system. I am running to take it on. And I invite Mainers to hold me to that standard from day one.
Charles
Trust is earned. It comes from telling people the truth, caring about them and doing the job well. That is the standard I have held myself to all my life, and it is the standard I will bring to the Blaine House. As an Eagle Scout in Maine in my youth, a federal investigator, a Naval officer for 10 years, and someone who has worked for three presidents, two secretaries of state and two speakers of the House, my reputation is built on trust and getting things done.
Mainers deserve to know how their government spends their money. On day one, I will order a full, independent audit of state government and make the findings public, good and bad. I have pledged to take no campaign money from lobbyists, law firms that lobby, Central Maine Power or data centers, so I will owe no one a favor.
I grew up in Wayne. My mother taught public school for 40 years. I know what it means to stretch a paycheck, and after more than 17 months on the road across Maine, I have met families stretching further than ever. One of the finest leaders I ever served, Secretary of State Colin Powell, taught me that if you care about your people, they will care about you. He knew their names, their families and their dreams. I intend to govern the same way. Kindness is not weakness.
My mother made education the foundation of my life. It carried me from Maranacook High School to Dartmouth, to Oxford University on scholarship to study economics, and to Columbia Law School.
My life has been about earning and keeping trust. I clerked on a U.S. Court of Appeals, held the highest-level clearances as a Navy intelligence officer, served as a federal investigator, and conducted oversight of the largest departments of the federal government. I have always tried to live by the Scout Law, which begins with the word “trustworthy.”
As assistant secretary of state under Secretary Powell, I managed billions of dollars and thousands of people. I ran the department’s air wing, stood up police training in Iraq and Afghanistan, and oversaw law enforcement programs from Colombia to Kosovo. I cut costs and demanded results. Maine urgently needs that kind of seasoned, competent management, and it has not had it.
My word is my bond. Mainers deserve the truth, and that is what I will deliver as governor.
Pingree
You should trust me because you know me. I’m a lifelong Mainer — born in a rural community, where everyone cares about their neighbors and now raising my own teenage kids here. I’ve spent nearly 25 years of my life in public service because I care deeply about Maine people and our future.
Throughout my career, I’ve focused on getting things done to improve people’s lives. In the Legislature, I worked with Democrats, Republicans, and independents to tackle challenges like health care costs, housing, environmental protection, broadband expansion, and protecting our working waterfronts. As speaker, I earned the trust of colleagues across the aisle by showing up, listening, and bringing people together to solve problems.
When Gov. Janet Mills needed a leader to start the new “Office of the Future” to tackle housing, workforce challenges, economic recovery, and climate resilience, she trusted me with that responsibility. Whether in the State House or chairing my local school board, I’ve always believed leadership means showing up, listening to everyone, and staying at the table until the work is done.
At a time when so much of our politics is driven by division and anger, I think Mainers are looking for something different. Our kids deserve something different. They want leaders who will tell the truth, work hard, and put people ahead of politics. That’s how I’ve tried to lead throughout my career, and it’s how I’ll lead as governor: rolling up my sleeves, working with anyone willing to move Maine forward, and never forgetting who this work is for.

title: GRAPHIC: Video inside Flydubai flight shows moment passengers seize control
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — A dentist and other passengers wrestled with a violent copilot. A plumber seized the controls as the plane plunged towards the desert. And the captain, despite being stabbed, managed to open the cockpit door — helping save all 182 people aboard the Israel-bound flight.
“Hollywood isn’t creative enough to come up with stories like this!” said Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel.
Although major questions remained unanswered on Thursday about the attacker and his motive, the story of ordinary passengers saving the FlyDubai flight from disaster has quickly become the stuff of legend.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warmly embraced plumber Yaniv Hayoun shortly after the passengers arrived in Tel Aviv late on Wednesday. He later posted a five-star review of Hayoun’s professional services, calling him “a hero who has saved many lives.”
“He can help you too — I highly recommend him!” Netanyahu added on X.
Hayoun was among several Israelis recommended for the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, while Indian Capt. Smit Machchhar was called “a HERO” by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
One met the prime minister wearing a bloody shirt
Many of the details emerged in a rush shortly after the passengers, most of them Israeli, landed back home to cheers and waving flags.
Hayoun, apologizing for his bloody shirt, within minutes was telling the prime minister and journalists what happened.
There had been little time for him and the others to think. Passengers screamed after spotting the copilot stabbing the captain, and the flight from Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates, to the Israeli city of Tel Aviv began a steep dive. Some believed they were about to die.
A handful of Israelis reacted, hurtling up the aisle after the badly wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door. That was crucial, as cockpit doors are typically locked to prevent hijackings.
They had to struggle, Hayoun said, with the captain’s body resting against it.
The plumber seized the controls, just like in the movies
Hayoun said the copilot appeared to be trying to damage the plane’s controls. He grabbed the copilot, and others began struggling with the man.
Hayoun then tackled the controls. He had no training, but he remembered what he had seen in movies.
“I asked him, how did you know how to do that? And he said, ‘Well, I, I watched these air disaster films,’” Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday.
It was not clear who among the passengers had security experience, though military service is compulsory for most men and women in Israel.
Soon, crew who had been traveling on the plane stepped in to stabilize it, issuing a mayday call and seeking a place to land.
“He managed to stabilize the plane by the skin of his teeth,” another Israeli praised for intervening, Asaf Rajuan, told journalists. Aviation experts have marveled that the plane didn’t crash after a descent so sharp that the rudder was torn away.
A dentist treated the wounded pilot
The handful of Israeli passengers grappled with the copilot for several minutes before subduing him and binding his hands with the cord from a set of headphones.
One of them, Dr. Shota Musayev, a dentist, also attended to the captain, who appeared to have lost a lot of blood. “He was just praying the whole time and was in contact with me, and I was afraid we would really lose him,” Musayev said.
In video that Musayev shot and shared with The Associated Press, the captain lay on the floor of the cabin, saying his head was in pain.
Musayev later told journalists he and the other responders knew they’d had just seconds to act before a “critical event.”
But even with the copilot bound and subdued, they were scared that other attackers might be on the plane. They sent other people around the cabin to stand by.
“We didn’t know where we were going to land. Underneath us there was only desert. We were afraid that they were taking us to a hostile country,” Rajuan said. “We didn’t know who to trust. We didn’t know if the pilot was with us or not … We started suspecting the flight attendants, too.”
Finally, just about an hour after the plane issued a distress call, it made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Now, investigators from across the region are working to understand what led to the attack. The copilot still has not been publicly identified.
As of Thursday evening, the world had not yet heard from the central hero, the captain, who India’s Embassy in the United Arab Emirates said was “in good health and recovering well.”
___
Associated Press reporter Areej Hazboun in Jerusalem contributed.
