title: Gem hunter finds a diamond he claims could be worth $1 million
text:
LITTLE ROCK, Ark. (AP) — Jack Pearadin is the first to admit that his diamond-hunting hobby hasn’t paid off, despite sifting rocks for more than a dozen years.
But earlier this year, the Navy reservist and his friend shoveled a six-carat diamond from a field in Arkansas where he’s found over 300 gems so far. And this one is like nothing he’s dug up before — Pearadin claims collectors have told him it could be worth $1 million.
At least one experienced appraiser told The Associated Press that a diamond of such size and quality could be worth a fourth of that — still an impressive find.
“Oh my God! Oh my God!” Pearadin said as he livestreamed the discovery on TikTok. “Holy crap, we got a big one!” he yelled after rinsing gravel from a bucket and then flipping the pile onto a table to expose the shiny facets of a 6.03-carat diamond.
Roughly the size of a fingernail, it’s the largest diamond found this year at Crater of Diamonds State Park. More than 37,000 diamonds have been discovered since the former open-pit diamond mine became part of a state park in 1972.
The largest diamond found at the park, ‘Uncle Sam,’ weighed 40 carats
The park charges a $15 entry fee to fill a 5-gallon bucket with rocks, and people can keep any gemstones they find. Most are small and worth maybe a few hundred dollars. The largest diamond ever unearthed in the United States, a 40.23-carat stone called the Uncle Sam, was found at the park in 1924.
Pearadin, originally from Missouri, has been trying his luck at the park since 2013, even moving to nearby Murfreesboro to support his hobby — “I love it that much,” he told The Associated Press. He’s sold most of his diamonds online.
Most of the 400 to 800 diamonds found at the park annually weigh about a quarter of a carat, according to park interpreter Sarah Bivens. But there have been some bigger ones, said park assistant superintendent Waymon Cox: In 2020 a 9-carat diamond was found by an Arkansas bank manager, and in 2024 a French man unearthed a 7-carat diamond.
Diamonds are found in few places in the US
Diamonds are crystallized under tremendous pressure and heat deep inside the Earth and then thrust to the surface through volcanic activity before they’re scattered by water or wind. These natural diamonds are often cloudy and oddly shaped, and lose about 25% of their weight as they’re cut and polished into what a jeweler would sell, according to Nathan Renfro, senior manager at the Gemological Institute of America.
Renfro said the U.S. has only two known primary deposits of diamonds — places where columns of once-molten volcanic rock have reached the surface — Crater of Diamonds and Colorado’s Kelsey Lake, where the land was reclaimed after a commercial mining operation went out of business years ago.
Today, that leaves the Arkansas park as one of the only places in the world where anyone can hunt for diamonds and take their finds with them.
“It’s a pretty remarkable operation that that’s available to the public,” Renfro said. “Most diamond mines are super high security.”
So can Jack finally get a big payday?
A typical .17-carat diamond from the park can sell for around $700, said certified gem appraiser Laura Stanley in Little Rock. But a high-quality six-carat yellow diamond from the park can sell for about $250,000, she said, partly because of their origin.
“They are their own entity,” Stanley said. “It’s the only place in America where you can go find your own diamond and you can’t compare that to a diamond from anywhere else.”
The Uncle Sam crystal was cut and polished into a 12.42-carat diamond gifted to the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, where it’s on view in the “Great American Diamonds” exhibit.
Pearadin named his latest and biggest find the “American Dream.”
“It’s just this massive, gorgeous yellow diamond,” Pearadin said. He plans to split the profits with fellow gem hunter Michael Schumacher of Wisconsin, who helped fill the bucket that held the stone, and open his own crystal mine.
___
Turbay is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

title: Warming center leaders fear people will freeze to death after 2 shelters are denied funding
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bangor’s warming center providers are scrambling to determine how they’ll shelter homeless residents this winter after learning that two of the centers were denied state funding.
“It’s going to be a tough year for the unhoused community if we don’t have some additional beds,” Joe Hartel, executive director of the Together Place recovery center, said.
He and other service providers worry that there won’t be enough warming center space available this year and people will be left out in the cold as the city struggles to address its homelessness crisis.
“My fear is that we see more people with cases of hypothermia, it leads to more isolation, which creates overdose deaths, and then we see people dying because of freezing to death,” Hartel said. His organization ran a warming center for the first time last year, and its application to MaineHousing this year was denied.
The Mansion Church has run a warming center for years but was also denied state funding this year. Terry Dinkins, the church’s pastor, said he was shocked to hear the news.
“I think we need the three warming centers,” he said, estimating that the level of need this year will be similar to last year, if not more. Last year, the city’s warming centers served about 80 to 90 people per night, Bruce Hews, the city’s homeless response coordinator, told the homelessness advisory committee last week.
MaineHousing awarded funding this week for 65 warming center beds at the Brick Church and five at the Bangor Area Homeless Shelter.
The Mansion Church’s application was denied because it didn’t meet the funding requirements, since the church said it planned to stay open until March and the funding is for programs operating through the end of April, according to MaineHousing spokesperson Scott Thistle.
The Together Place was denied funding because of its limited experience operating a warming shelter and because its application was more expensive per bed than others, according to Thistle.
“We understand the need for overnight shelter will be high this winter in Bangor and across Maine. Our role is to award scarce public resources fairly and equitably to organizations that can make the greatest impact,” Thistle said.
Although two shelters were denied funding, Bangor overall is getting far more money than in years past — and more than any other city — because the Brick Church was awarded $427,650 in addition to the homeless shelter’s $10,000. Bangor warming centers only got $67,000 total from MaineHousing last year.
The city stepped in to provide emergency funding during a similar scramble last year when the Brick Church’s funding request was denied by MaineHousing. That money allowed the Brick Church to continue operating, and it also allowed the Together Place to open an overnight warming center for the first time.
Leon Licata, pastor of the Brick Church, said he asked for more funding than usual this year, and that the shelter has always had to rely on donations to supplement the funding it was able to get.
“We’re really excited about it, and on the other hand, we’re really stressed out about it, because none of the other shelters got funded,” Licata said.
He plans to use the funds to pay off costs associated with the building, pay for electricity, heating oil and other essentials, and give small stipends to some of his warming center staff, which wasn’t possible before.
The Brick Church serves multiple meals for its warming center visitors and will open Nov. 15 this year with a maximum capacity of 70 people. It’s in need of more volunteers to staff nighttime shifts, Licata said.
“My biggest fear right now is that there’s not going to be enough room to house everybody that wants to come in out of the cold,” Licata said. “That’s your son, your daughter, your mother, your father, or one of your grandparents that are going to be left out in the cold because I don’t have enough room.”
He expects this could be the first year he has to turn someone away.
Beyond the need for more capacity, the concentration of state funding mostly to one shelter disrupts the collaboration that warming center leaders say made the network operate effectively last year.
For example, if a visitor at the Mansion Church became agitated or broke the rules last winter, Dinkins said he’d call Licata or Hartel and send the person their way. That flexibility is no longer available.
“Last year was pretty beautiful, the way these organizations worked together” to make sure there was space for everyone who needed it, Hartel said.
Hartel said his organization requested about $300,000 for 40 warming center beds. The Together Place will be unable to open a warming center again without funding, he added.
Dinkins still plans to open the Mansion Church and has pulled it off in past years just with help from church members and other supporters — but it’s unclear when it’ll be able to open or what limitations it’ll have.
Even with the state funding his church received last year, it still wasn’t enough on its own, Dinkins said. This year, he requested $80,000 knowing the total costs would likely be closer to $120,000.
The Mansion Church has space for 30 people, or 50 with enough staff to open up the basement.
“Whatever it takes. We need to open up because I don’t think that the Brick [Church] can handle it by themselves,” Dinkins said.
The group of warming center leaders plans to meet all together with city staff on Friday, according to Licata.
“The city’s going to have to step up and somehow dish out some money,” he said.

title: Public service announcements or propaganda? Experts weigh in on new Trump ads
text:
Public service announcements or propaganda? Experts weigh in on new Trump ads
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
Weeks before the midterm elections, the Trump administration released a series of taxpayer-funded ads prominently featuring President Donald Trump promoting his agenda, and Democratic lawmakers called them illegal propaganda.
One of the ads plays black-and-white footage of Trump with a voiceover of him saying, “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America.” Photos of him as president and during the 2024 campaign flash onscreen as the song “Love Me” by JMSN plays in the background. This ad aired Sept. 23 on Fox News and Newsmax, Politico reported.
A group of Democratic lawmakers wrote a Sept. 24 letter to Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, saying the ad violates federal law and should be taken off the air.
“This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars,” the letter said.
“This is the final battle,” Trump said in another ad. “With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state” and “expel the warmongers from our government.”
A third ad is a minute-long clip of him speaking at Mount Rushmore in July for the 250th celebration of the country’s independence, praising the U.S. as “the most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history.”
“Paid for by the U.S. government,” text on the ads says.
The New York Times reported that more than $1 million likely has been spent on airing the ads, according to an estimate from AdImpact, an ad tracking service. It’s unclear which government agency is paying.
The White House defended the videos, saying they are not campaign ads but public service announcements and that past administrations have similarly used PSAs “to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction.” It compared Trump’s videos with President George W. Bush’s national television campaign about Medicare; an Obama administration national ad to promote Affordable Care Act subsidies; and a Biden-era ad to encourage COVID-19 vaccination.
But experts in campaign and government law told PolitiFact they are not convinced the Trump ads are public service announcements.
Experts express doubt about the ads
Trump’s ads do not inform citizens about how to access, benefit from or understand government programs, which is what differentiates public announcements from campaign ads, said Samuel Bagenstos, a University of Michigan law professor.
“By paying for the ads with government funds, the Trump administration is violating the statute imposing a government-wide prohibition on using federal funds to pay for ‘publicity or propaganda,’” Bagenstos said. “It’s basically impossible to come up with a respectable argument to the contrary. All these ads do is aggrandize Donald Trump.”
Federal law does not define “publicity or propaganda,” but the phrase is included in the omnibus appropriations bills Congress passes every year. Without a definition for the phrase, the Government Accountability Office says it has identified three activities banned by the publicity or propaganda prohibition: self-aggrandizement, covert propaganda and purely partisan materials.
Brett Kappel, an attorney and expert on government ethics law, also does not think the Trump ads qualify as PSAs.
Kappel said whether the ads are illegal depends on which federal agency’s money is being used and whether the appropriations legislation for that agency prohibits using appropriated funds for “publicity or propaganda.”
One ad is repurposed from 2024 campaign
The black-and-white “Final Battle” ad, which features Trump walking toward the camera, aired Sept. 26 and 27 during football games and TV programs. It is not new. Trump released nearly identical ads in January 2024 and October 2024 during his presidential campaign. The 2024 ads ended with a call to text or vote for Trump.
The Hatch Act limits certain political activities of federal employees. Whether the ads violate that law is harder to prove since Trump is not a candidate for the midterm elections, even though his party has much at stake, Bagenstos said.
For the Hatch Act, the key issue is whether these ads constitute “propaganda,” a term that is not defined in the law, said Stanley Brand, a Penn State Dickinson Law distinguished fellow in law and government.
As a practical matter, with the Trump administration in charge of enforcing the laws, including the Hatch Act, there is little to no likelihood of enforcement, experts said.
PolitiFact Researcher Caryn Baird contributed to this report.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com. It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Letter: Further research needed on offshore wind in Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
In a Sept. 22 story on Maine’s lawsuit challenging the U.S. Department of the Interior’s buy-out termination of Gulf of Maine offshore wind leases, WMTW reports: “The lawsuit also argues that the cancellations could negatively impact Maine’s plans for future offshore wind development and other renewable energy goals.”
So just what are Maine’s plans for future offshore wind development? Now is exactly the right time to explore that question.
Previous to the Trump administration holding offshore wind hostage, Maine announced plans to develop an offshore wind manufacturing, assembling and launching facility on Sears Island. Those plans failed to adequately consider a number of other, viable options and failed to generate sufficient funding.
During today’s offshore wind pause, even as Clearway Energy pursues an 800-megawatt onshore wind project in Aroostook County, Maine needs to consider the least environmentally damaging and most economically beneficial offshore wind development strategy.
Developing two currently industrialized ports for offshore wind that would coordinate manufacturing, assembly and launching, a strategy used elsewhere and for the Aqua Ventus quarter-scale turbine now operating near Castine, almost certainly would reduce environmental harm, save costs and spread development’s fiscal benefits across a greater segment of the Maine coast than the previously failed offshore plan.
Climate change poses a clear and present threat to Maine’s future. Clean, renewable energy production helps reduce climate change impacts. Prudence points to further research now into whether offshore wind can be part of Maine’s adaptation.
Stephen Miller
Islesboro

title: Judge blocks Trump from firing Seattle US attorney who had job for an hour
text:
Judge blocks Trump from firing Seattle US attorney who had job for an hour
A judge on Thursday overturned President Donald Trump's decision to fire the court-appointed top U.S. prosecutor in Seattle, the latest development in a legal tug-of-war over the administration’s efforts to control who occupies the powerful Justice Department posts.
Video above: Will more firings at independent federal agencies follow Supreme Court ruling?
The 17 active and senior judges in the Western District of Washington unanimously named Roger Rogoff, a former judge and veteran prosecutor, U.S. attorney in July, after Trump failed to fill the post with a nominee confirmed by the U.S. Senate.
The president fired Rogoff less than an hour later. Rogoff sued, and in a ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Stanley Bastian found the termination unlawful and reinstated him.
Bastian noted that when presidents fail to fill a U.S. attorney post with a nominee confirmed by the Senate, federal law authorizes the judges of that district to appoint someone “until the vacancy is filled.”
“It does not say ‘until the president fires the person selected,’” Bastian said.
He concluded: “Mr. Roger Rogoff is the United States attorney for the Western District of Washington and has been the rightful holder of that office since July 15, 2026, when he took the oath of office.”
The Justice Department said in a written statement it disagreed with the decision and would appeal.
Rogoff is the latest in a series of judicially appointed U.S. attorneys to be ousted by the Trump administration, and he is believed to be the first to sue over the removal, setting up a direct legal battle over the issue.
Presidents normally appoint U.S. attorneys, the top federal prosecutor in each judicial district. The positions require Senate confirmation, except in temporary appointments, which can last up to 120 days. When temporary appointments expire before a nominee is confirmed, the judges in a judicial district can name a U.S. attorney.
But under Trump, the Justice Department has sought to leave unconfirmed prosecutors in their positions indefinitely, often through novel personnel maneuvers. Trump named Charles Neil Floyd, who previously served as an immigration judge, interim U.S. attorney in Seattle in October 2025 but never forwarded his nomination to the Senate.
When Floyd’s time as interim U.S. attorney expired, Trump simply shifted his title, a tactic the administration has also tried in other federal judicial districts: It named him first assistant U.S. attorney, while leaving the top post empty.
Trump last month nominated Pete Serrano, the first assistant U.S. attorney in eastern Washington, to be the U.S. attorney in Seattle. But Serrano has not been confirmed, and his nomination is opposed by Washington's senior Democratic senator, Patty Murray.
"Today’s ruling is an important victory for the rule of law and the people in Western Washington who deserve a U.S. attorney that answers to the law, not Donald Trump,” Murray said in a written statement Thursday.
Bastian is the chief judge in eastern Washington. He heard the case because the judges in western Washington were recused.
In December, Alina Habba resigned as the top federal prosecutor for New Jersey after an appeals court said she had been serving in the post unlawfully.
Lindsey Halligan, who pursued indictments against a pair of Trump’s adversaries, left her position as an acting U.S. attorney in Virginia after a judge concluded her appointment was unlawful and that indictments she brought against James and former FBI Director James Comey must be dismissed.
The judges there named James Hundley, who had handled criminal and civil cases for more than 30 years, but the administration fired him. It also fired a court-appointed U.S. attorney in northern New York.

title: New York’s governor says Cornell rape accuser was ‘failed’ by people obligated to protect her
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Friday that the woman who accused members of a Cornell University fraternity of gang rape was “failed” by people obligated to protect her, including police and the county prosecutor.
Hochul’s claim came during a news conference in which she gave details on her decision to turn the case over to a special prosecutor, the state Attorney General Letitia James.
The governor said she made the decision after learning “troubling details” about how authorities have handled the woman’s claims thus far, including that the district attorney closed the case without having anyone interview the victim or anyone else involved in the alleged attack.
“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?” Hochul said. “This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”
She also assailed the Cornell University Police Department for not fully conveying the woman’s story to prosecutors.
“After this young woman came forward, she spoke to the police. She sat for hours and told them exactly what happened to her. And according to new reports, she could not have been clearer that she was 100% confident that she had been raped,” the governor said. ”Yet, shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors.”
Hochul said Thursday that she appointed James to oversee the case because she had lost faith in the local district attorney’s ability to handle it.
The investigation initially was closed without charges in 2024.
Last month, the woman filed a lawsuit and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation. He has since been bombarded by criticism that he abandoned the original investigation too quickly.
The attorney general will oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury, Hochul said.
“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” she said in a statement Thursday.
Van Houten didn’t immediately respond to Thursday messages seeking comment.
The case has roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about its response and the larger issue of how sexual assaults are handled on college campuses.
The woman, identified only as Jane Doe in court documents, told campus police in November of 2024 that she was sexually assaulted, then discussed it with the university’s internal investigators as part of Cornell’s disciplinary process.
The lawsuit against seven fraternity brothers, the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and others alleges that she was plied with drugs and alcohol, then subjected to sexual acts by a group of men while she was partially or entirely incapacitated. One of the men sent a social media message to other fraternity members alerting them to what was happening, and inviting people to take part, according to the lawsuit.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they participated in a sexual assault. One said his client hadn’t touched the woman. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful.
New York governors have turned to attorneys general to oversee important cases in the past.
In 2018, then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo appointed then-Nassau County District Attorney Madeline Singas as a special prosecutor to investigate Eric Schneiderman, who resigned as New York attorney general after women accused him of violent slapping, choking and other abuse.
In 2021, James oversaw a non-criminal investigation into sexual harassment allegations against then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo, leading to his resignation. Cuomo initially tried to choose who would lead the investigation into the allegations. He then allowed James to choose two independent attorneys to lead it instead.
James’ office also handles other criminal work and has the power under state law to investigate every death involving law enforcement in the state. But, typically, she can’t initiate criminal investigations without a referral from a local district attorney, the governor or a state agency, or an appointment like the one Hochul made Thursday.
___
This story was updated to correct the spelling of Letitia James’ name.

title: They were born on the same day in the same hospital. Now they’re getting married
text:
CRANE, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - Inside of Crane High School, home of the Pirates, scavenging through decades of student pictures are Principal Tara Mease and science teacher Karen Faucett.
Their own children, Brayden Faucett and Lorene Mease, are included on the wall of graduates.
“Kind of a big year coming up,” reporter Chad Plein asked the women.
“Our kids are getting married,” Tara answered.
It’s not out of the ordinary for high school sweethearts to get married. It’s also not too unusual that both of their moms also graduated from the same school.
So, what is so unusual about this love story?
“I was born on July 7th, 2006,” Lorene said.
“[I was born on] July 7th, 2006,” Brayden said.
Lorene and Brayden were born on the same day, minutes apart, with Lorene being a bit older. In the same hospital. By the same doctor.
“When I got to the hospital, they were like, ‘We’re gonna have to try and delay. He’s in a C-section right now,’” Karen recalled.
“They’d gotten [Lorene] out, and a nurse stuck her head in the door and said, ‘Dr. Ting, those twins are coming right now,’” Tara continued.
“He came rushing in, and immediately they performed my C-section,” Karen said.
“Then found out later that it was the Faucett boys, that Karen was in the hospital, and he was rushing out of my C-section to go deliver her twins,” Tara said.
“We put it together that I had interrupted Lorene’s delivery,” Karen said.
Doing the math, the odds of a soon-to-be married couple being born on the same day, minutes apart, in the same hospital, by the same doctor, are 1 in 514 billion.
Lorene has a memory from the day she was born written inside her baby book.
“[My mom] wrote, ‘Mommy’s friend Karen Faucett had twin boys on the same day I was born,’” Lorene read from the book.
“We were around each other a little bit as kids, because our moms were friends from high school,” Lorene said about their childhood. “But Brayden and his brother never wanted me to hang around with them.”
Brayden recalled never hanging out with her as children. “But I guess, from what she tells me, me and my brother always told her it was our birthday and not hers.”
They started dating after their 16th birthday and haven’t looked back. Brayden popped the question earlier this year on a piece of land where they’ll one day build their home and live happily ever after.
“I just feel like it is so important to find someone who’s truly your best friend,” Lorene said. “I mean, we’ll be joking around sometimes, and then I’ll just kind of sit there like, ‘Wow, we’re going to get married.’ Like, we’re going to get to spend the rest of our lives together.”
“She always says it’s like we’re just best friends,” Brayden said. “And I said, ‘Well, there’s nothing wrong with that.’”
Lorene and Brayden have their date set and it’s not on their birthday in July. Lorene said she doesn’t want a summer wedding.
They’re getting married on October 3rd.

title: Wife hid husband’s remains in freezer for up to 7 years to collect benefits, police say
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska. (KTUU/Gray News) - A woman in Alaska hid her late husband’s remains in a freezer for years in order to collect benefits, according to authorities.
Juneau police found the remains of Ross Pasquan inside a chest freezer on July 19. Police said he would have been 74 years old at the time of the discovery of his remains.
A family member had been cleaning out the property following the death of Pasquan’s wife, Sheryl Ann McDonald-Pasquan, who died on July 14, 2025, from natural causes.
Inside a storage shed, a family member discovered a locked freezer.
Police said the person found the key, opened the freezer and found a tarp-wrapped object that appeared to contain human remains. They closed the freezer and went directly to Juneau police.
The State Medical Examiner’s Office determined that Pasquan died of natural causes related to severe cardiovascular disease. Investigators believe Pasquan’s remains were placed in the freezer sometime between 2018 and 2025.
The investigation found that McDonald-Pasquan concealed his death and continued applying for and receiving benefits in his name until her death. Those benefits included Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend checks, Social Security benefits and retirement benefits.
Investigators also learned that a retirement benefit provider had not been notified of his death and was still depositing monthly payments into Pasquan’s account up until July 2026.
Investigators found no evidence that another person caused Pasquan’s death or helped McDonald-Pasquan in concealing his remains or collecting his benefits.
Witness interviews indicated that Pasquan had a history of significant health problems and that McDonald-Pasquan served as his primary caregiver. Witnesses said she explained his absence by telling them he had been moved to a care facility outside Juneau.
The investigation is now closed due to McDonald-Pasquan’s death.

FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Plenty of Sunshine Expected this Weekend, with Shower Chances Returning for the New Work Week
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Friday. After showers moved across the region earlier today, drier and cooler air is settling into northern Maine as we head into the weekend. High pressure builds into the region Saturday, setting us up for a great stretch of weather with plenty of sunshine both Saturday and Sunday. The tradeoff will be chilly temperatures, especially Saturday night when widespread frost is expected across northern Maine. Changes then return quickly for the new work week, with another round of rain possible Monday followed by increasingly gusty winds Tuesday.
Saturday will start off chilly, with some patchy fog possible early in the morning before plenty of sunshine takes over for the remainder of the day. Sunday looks very similar, with another good amount of sunshine expected after a frosty start. Clouds begin to increase later Sunday as our next system approaches, with rain chances returning Sunday night before becoming much more widespread Monday.
Despite all of the sunshine Saturday, temperatures will have a distinctly fall-like feel. Highs look to reach the mid to upper 50s across much of Aroostook County, including around 59 degrees in Presque Isle, Caribou and Houlton. Northwest winds around 5 to 10 mph will add a bit of a breeze during the day, but overall, Saturday is shaping up to be a great day to spend some time outdoors.
The bigger temperature story arrives Saturday night. Clear skies and light winds beneath strong high pressure will provide excellent conditions for radiational cooling, allowing temperatures to fall rapidly after sunset. Lows across much of northern Maine are expected to drop into the upper 20s, with some of our normally colder valleys potentially falling into the lower to mid 20s. Widespread frost is expected by Sunday morning.
Keep in mind, the National Weather Service’s frost and freeze program has ended for Aroostook County for the season, meaning a Frost Advisory or Freeze Warning will not be issued despite the cold temperatures. If you still have any sensitive vegetation outside, you’ll want to take steps to protect it Saturday night.
After the frosty start, temperatures rebound nicely Sunday afternoon. Highs look to reach the upper 50s across northern Aroostook County, with Presque Isle around 59 degrees and Houlton closer to the lower 60s. Sunshine will once again be plentiful during the morning before some additional cloud cover begins working into the region later in the day.
Our attention then turns toward the next system for Monday. A cold front approaching from Canada will interact with an area of low pressure moving north along the East Coast, bringing another opportunity for rain across the region. There remains quite a bit of uncertainty in exactly how these two systems interact, which will ultimately determine how much rain we receive.
The latest rainfall outlook does show additional accumulation across northern Maine through the end of next week, but confidence in Monday’s exact totals remains low. Rain is currently expected across much of Aroostook County Monday, with the National Weather Service carrying a 90 percent chance for much of the region.
Behind Monday’s system, attention quickly shifts from rain to wind. Confidence continues to increase in a period of gusty west to northwest winds Tuesday, with the latest guidance showing a good chance of gusts exceeding 35 mph across northern Maine and the possibility of some gusts exceeding 40 mph. With fall foliage at or near peak across portions of the region, those winds could also result in significant leaf loss.
For more details on the sunny weekend ahead, Saturday night’s frost and the changing weather pattern early next week, make sure to check out this evening’s First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great weekend!

title: Here’s why Troy Jackson speaks the way he does
text:
Mary M. Drymon, Ph.D., lives in Winslow.
I have been an avid supporter of Troy Jackson since I first heard him speak at the 2016 Maine State Democratic Party Convention. I believe strongly in the message that he has been articulating for years: support for Medicare for all, defending Social Security and protecting working-class values.
I not only support what he is saying, I love the way he says it.
What some see as not being “polished” enough, and speaking haltingly, I see as authenticity. As a historian specifically focused on the Scottish and Irish diaspora, I appreciate his “Allagash accent” and consider his patterns of speech unique. I couldn’t resist a bit of research into where it originates by looking at some of the surnames in his family.
Troy Jackson’s mother is a McBreairty. That surname may have origins on the islands of Arran and Bute in Western Scotland. The surname comes from the Gaelic Mac Muircheartaigh, which translates roughly to “son of the navigator or mariner.” This highlights their early history as skilled sea captains and sailors.
One branch of the McBreairtys migrated across the Irish Sea into the Ulster Plantations in Ireland. They concentrated in the seaport of Killybegs in the precinct of Boylagh and Bannagh in County Donegal, where they became deeply integrated into local Irish culture. During the early 1600s time period, the British fortified and planned the port town of Killybegs to prevent invasion by Spanish forces.
In around 1618, King James I also granted vast territories — which included the town of Killybegs as well as Kilcar, Ardara, the island of Inishkeel and Killymard — to John Murray. The McBreairtys were likely tenants of Murray.
By the mid-1700s, some McBreairtys were part of a group that migrated from Ireland to Nova Scotia, where they met and intermarried with people of French Canadian descent, creating an early fusion culture. Eventually some McBreairtys moved into Maine — lured by the abundantly available wood resources of the Allagash Valley. The residents of Allagash lived in deep geographical isolation at the edge of the Maine North Woods. This isolation created a linguistic time capsule. They retained a Donegal cadence of speech.
The Donegal accent belongs to the northern province of Ulster, which is heavily influenced by Scottish rhythms and vocabulary. The Allagash brogue mirrors this, sounding noticeably different from both the classic nasal “Boston/coastal Maine” accent and the neighboring Acadian French inflections. Listeners often note that the Allagash dialect features a distinct rhythmic “lilt,” clipped vowel sounds and subtle sentence-ending pitch changes reminiscent of the Ulster-Scots speech patterns found across County Donegal.
The speech pattern that is found deep within the Allagash Valley stands out as a unique, highly localized linguistic pocket that retains the speech patterns of its original settlers. Modern connectivity and standardized education have softened the accent.
Troy Jackson uses his accented speech to describe how we can navigate a better future together — not from the left or right but from the bottom up. He articulates new ideas with a very old way of speaking that unmistakably echoes history. It’s worth a listen.

title: Investigation reveals Russian connection to Medicare billing scheme
text:
COLLEGE GROVE, TN (InvestigateTV) - A WSMV4 investigation has uncovered a Medicare fraud scheme that billed the federal program tens of thousands of dollars for medical supplies that Tennessee recipients never needed or received.
Penny Vaughan, a retired nurse in College Grove, and her husband received their quarterly Medicare statements showing Medicare had been billed more than $11,000 for urinary catheters for both of them over five months.
“We did not need, did not buy, did not order,” Vaughan said. “The price was just extraordinary.”
The billing showed 300 catheters per month for five months.
“Three hundred a month would mean you were catheterizing yourself 10 times a day. Nobody does that. Nobody does that,” Vaughan said.
In Kingston Springs, Larry Welch’s mother-in-law received a similar quarterly report showing Medicare was billed for urinary catheters she never needed or received, totaling more than $11,000.
Several other Medicare recipients shared their quarterly reports, showing identical Medicare billing for hundreds of catheters they never needed.
“I knew it was fraud,” Vaughan said.
Despite the large number of catheters and high costs, Medicare paid the claims each time.
Russian citizen indicted
The billing for the catheters came from two medical equipment suppliers in Coral Springs, Florida, and Austin, Texas. In Texas, the billing came from Centurion Superior Medical.
Texas Secretary of State records show the company’s managing member is Nika Machutadze, a Russian citizen living in Austin.
Federal criminal complaints show Machutadze was indicted in federal court two-and-a-half weeks ago.
The complaint shows Machutadze’s company submitted claims to more than 221,000 Medicare beneficiaries across the United States, billing Medicare more than $3 billion, including for 752,281 urinary catheters.
“This could be pretty major,” Welch said.
Data breach may explain access
Questions remain about how Medicare recipients’ information in Tennessee reached the criminals.
Penny Vaughan recently received a letter from a billing service that works for health care providers stating there had been a data breach that may include identifying Medicare beneficiary identifiers.
Brandy Bauer with Senior Medicare Patrol, which helps Medicare recipients report fraud, said Medicare doesn’t have the ability to look at all 68 million enrollees and question claims.
“Medicare isn’t going to necessarily know what, on a day-to-day basis, what your prescribing physician has ordered for you,” Bauer said. “Medicare doesn’t have the ability to necessarily look at all 68 million enrollees and sort of question that. They’re going to sort of take the benefit of the doubt and go ahead and try and pay those claims until you realize, wait a second, I don’t need that supplies or I didn’t get those supplies.”
A spokesperson for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said in an emailed statement that they “do not confirm or comment on ongoing or potential investigations.”
Senior Medicare Patrol says all people interviewed for this story now need to reach out to Medicare to get new Medicare ID numbers.
Medicare recipients should review their quarterly reports to see what they were billed for and watch for notifications from hospitals and doctors about data breaches.
Experts also warn of scammers sending out fake plastic Medicare cards to Medicare recipients in Alabama. Activating one of these cards could give criminals access to your social security number, bank account, or allow them to make claims, according to AARP.
A real card you don’t need to activate nor pay for. These cards are never made of plastic, instead they are made with paper.

title: 2026 Fall Athlete of the Week: Week 4
Susan Collins votes conscientiously and gets results
text:
Sen. Susan Collins has taken years of criticism for her vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh. What her critics rarely mention is that she also voted to confirm Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan, nominated by President Obama, and Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, nominated by President Biden.
That record isn’t a contradiction. It reflects a principle. The Constitution gives senators the job of advising and consenting on a president’s nominees, and Sen. Collins has consistently treated that as a question of qualifications, character and respect for the law, not whether she agrees with a nominee’s politics. Voting only for judges who share your views would turn every confirmation into a partisan brawl. She has refused to do that, whether the president was a Republican or a Democrat, and she has refused to be moved by political campaigns built on accusations rather than evidence.
That same practical, steady approach shows up here at home. Sen. Collins secured $4.7 million in federal funding for a new Belgrade Fire and Rescue Station. For a small town like ours, that kind of investment would be nearly impossible to raise on our own. It means our firefighters and rescue personnel will have a safe, modern facility to serve residents and the thousands of visitors who come to the lakes every summer.
Mainers deserve a senator who does her homework, votes her conscience and gets results for our communities. Sen. Collins has done all three, and she has my support.
Penny Morrell
Belgrade

title: Susan Collins should drop out and step down
text:
A million years ago, by which I mean this past June, Graham Platner called Sen. Susan Collins “corrupt.” He took a lot of flak for that. But new reporting from ProPublica seems to prove him right.
That Collins reportedly played “pay to play” with Navatek demonstrates a lack of judgment and ethics. Offering government contracts in return for a campaign contribution is the very definition of bribery. We should hope that the next Democratic administration pulls the files and reopens the investigation.
Collins must drop out of the Senate race and resign immediately. She is clearly not fit to serve. Self-dealing and insider trading have no place in the Senate. I feel she’s an embarrassment to Maine, and she has to go.
They said there was zero tolerance for sexual misbehavior when Senate candidate Graham Platner was accused (without further adjudication). Shouldn’t there be zero tolerance for plausible allegations of bribery and corruption by a sitting senator?
Wayne Clark
Durham

title: Collins’ record on military affairs is distressing
text:
While the abandoned FBI investigation into Sen. Susan Collins — as reported by ProPublica and carried by this publication on Sept. 23 — is dismaying enough, there is considerably more reason to be dismayed by Collins’ record on military affairs.
Throughout the disastrous 2003-2011 Iraq War, Collins was a staunch supporter of the war, which, according to a Brown University report, will end up costing U.S. taxpayers a total of $2.9 trillion. That’s a staggering $8,457 for every man, woman and child in the country — and that’s about $12 billion right from the pockets of Maine taxpayers. All the while, 14 million American children face food insecurity.
In an emailed Sept. 22 “Tuesday Report,” Collins touted her having secured $42 million in Maine heating assistance. Not bad for one Tuesday Report, but at $42 million per year, Collins would need 285 years of heating assistance to equal the amount Maine taxpayers spent on her disastrous Iraq War — which killed 4,492 Americans and at least 733,000 Iraqis, and destabilized the entire Middle East.
Heating assistance for 285 years. Even Susan Collins would struggle to serve in Congress that long.
Lawrence Reichard
Belfast

title: Here’s why Troy Jackson speaks the way he does
text:
Mary M. Drymon, Ph.D., lives in Winslow.
I have been an avid supporter of Troy Jackson since I first heard him speak at the 2016 Maine State Democratic Party Convention. I believe strongly in the message that he has been articulating for years: support for Medicare for all, defending Social Security and protecting working-class values.
I not only support what he is saying, I love the way he says it.
What some see as not being “polished” enough, and speaking haltingly, I see as authenticity. As a historian specifically focused on the Scottish and Irish diaspora, I appreciate his “Allagash accent” and consider his patterns of speech unique. I couldn’t resist a bit of research into where it originates by looking at some of the surnames in his family.
Troy Jackson’s mother is a McBreairty. That surname may have origins on the islands of Arran and Bute in Western Scotland. The surname comes from the Gaelic Mac Muircheartaigh, which translates roughly to “son of the navigator or mariner.” This highlights their early history as skilled sea captains and sailors.
One branch of the McBreairtys migrated across the Irish Sea into the Ulster Plantations in Ireland. They concentrated in the seaport of Killybegs in the precinct of Boylagh and Bannagh in County Donegal, where they became deeply integrated into local Irish culture. During the early 1600s time period, the British fortified and planned the port town of Killybegs to prevent invasion by Spanish forces.
In around 1618, King James I also granted vast territories — which included the town of Killybegs as well as Kilcar, Ardara, the island of Inishkeel and Killymard — to John Murray. The McBreairtys were likely tenants of Murray.
By the mid-1700s, some McBreairtys were part of a group that migrated from Ireland to Nova Scotia, where they met and intermarried with people of French Canadian descent, creating an early fusion culture. Eventually some McBreairtys moved into Maine — lured by the abundantly available wood resources of the Allagash Valley. The residents of Allagash lived in deep geographical isolation at the edge of the Maine North Woods. This isolation created a linguistic time capsule. They retained a Donegal cadence of speech.
The Donegal accent belongs to the northern province of Ulster, which is heavily influenced by Scottish rhythms and vocabulary. The Allagash brogue mirrors this, sounding noticeably different from both the classic nasal “Boston/coastal Maine” accent and the neighboring Acadian French inflections. Listeners often note that the Allagash dialect features a distinct rhythmic “lilt,” clipped vowel sounds and subtle sentence-ending pitch changes reminiscent of the Ulster-Scots speech patterns found across County Donegal.
The speech pattern that is found deep within the Allagash Valley stands out as a unique, highly localized linguistic pocket that retains the speech patterns of its original settlers. Modern connectivity and standardized education have softened the accent.
Troy Jackson uses his accented speech to describe how we can navigate a better future together — not from the left or right but from the bottom up. He articulates new ideas with a very old way of speaking that unmistakably echoes history. It’s worth a listen.

title: Purple Iris Foundation's Fall Color Run Draws Hundreds To Bangor
text:
You Know What’s Pretty Cool: You Can Help Mainers With Cancer Just By Lacing Up Your Shoes To ‘Pound The Pavement!’
I'm not sure there's a place on Earth that cancer hasn't touched, and therefore, it more than likely that most people around have somehow directly or indirectly been affected by the disease.
Read More: Thomas Hill Standpipe In Bangor Remains Closed For Repairs
For those battling the illness, and their loved ones, support can be a crucial part of overcoming a negative outcome.
Christina Parrish knows that battle well, and personally, having been diagnosed with cancer over a decade ago. As a survivor, Parrish wanted to do something to help those going through similar situations, so she created the Purple Iris Foundation, an organization that helps supply resources and support to Mainers battling cancer.
Throughout the year, the Purple Iris Foundation raises funds to be able to fulfill the mission, the biggest of which is a fun fall color run called "Pound the Pavement."
"Our biggest year for Pound the Pavement was 2019 before covid. That year we had 504 total participants. This year we are trending to surpass that number. "
"At each kilometer mark, Pound the Pavement runners/walkers are doused from head to toe in a different colored powder. Participants wear white at the starting line and finish the race plastered in color."
"Once the run/walk is over, the fun continues at the finish line with a visit to the Sea Dog and two (2) complimentary beverages for all those 21 years of age and over! Don't miss the party with photo ops, friendship, and celebration!"
It's like a giant party on the waterfront for a great cause. There's music, food, prizes and fun!

There is a "PTP Junior Mad Dash Of Color" kid's run that takes place before the actual color run, so kids are absolutely invited to register and join in the fun and good vibes.
You can register as an individual or a team.

title: Store clerk and son charged with selling kratom linked to Ole Miss student death
text:
Store clerk and son charged with selling kratom linked to the death of Ole Miss student
Federal prosecutors have charged a store clerk and his son with selling kratom that authorities believe is linked to the death of a University of Mississippi student, prosecutors announced Friday.
Related video above: Ole Miss students react to deaths of two classmates
The U.S. attorney's office in Mississippi said authorities established a link between the kratom derivative found at the scene of the student's death and a local vape, tobacco and beer store.
They executed several search warrants and arrested the store clerk and his son.
Yahya Mosleh, 51, and his son, Islam Mosleh, 18, are charged with possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute. They appeared before a judge in Oxford on Thursday, where it was determined that there was probable cause to proceed with the case.
Both men were originally arrested following an investigation by the Lafayette County Metro Narcotics Unit into the alleged sale of illegal substances from Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer in Oxford.
During that investigation, agents recovered more than 500 units of synthetic kratom, along with THC cartridges, gummies and other suspected narcotics being sold at the store.
Law enforcement said there was packaging associated with kratom-related products found at each of the scenes where the two Ole Miss students died.
A drug task force in Mississippi had urged people to avoid kratom, an herbal extract that acts as a stimulant at low doses and a sedative at high doses, after authorities found packages of the substance while investigating the deaths of two University of Mississippi students.
Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said investigators are still waiting on official autopsy and toxicology findings from the Mississippi State Medical Examiner's Office to determine how Aidan Hamilton, a freshman from Englewood, Colorado, and Robert Strang, a junior from Atlanta, Georgia, died in late September.
It's still not clear whether kratom contributed to either death, but federal prosecutors said both deaths appear consistent with drug overdoses.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Man critically hurt after crashing into a tractor-trailer in Auburn
text:
Man critically hurt after crashing into a tractor-trailer in Auburn, Maine
A man from New Gloucester is in the hospital with what police say are life-threatening injuries after crashing into a turning tractor trailer truck in Auburn on Thursday evening.
Police say the crash happened at about 7:30 p.m. at the intersection of Washington Street and Kittyhawk Avenue. Police say the driver of the car, Jonah King, 29, was headed south on Washington Street when he went through a red light and hit the truck.
Police say the truck had a green light and was turning left from Kittyhawk Avenue onto Washington Street.
King was first taken to Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston and then transferred to MaineHealth Maine Medical Center in Portland.

title: Authorities release new details on death of Ken Urker, ﻿Gypsy Rose Blanchard's partner
text:
Authorities release new details on death of Ken Urker, Gypsy Rose Blanchard's partner
New information has been released on the death of Ken Urker, Gypsy Rose Blanchard's partner and father of her child.
According to the Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office in Louisiana, police were called to Urker's home on Oct. 1 around 6:18 p.m. to conduct a welfare check.
According to deputies, the welfare concern was due to Urker not answering his phone or the door.
Anita Blanchard told authorities that she and her husband, who is Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s half-brother, Urker was at church with them on Wednesday. They said Urker had made comments about being depressed and upset.
They also told deputies he was on TikTok Live around 11 p.m., driving without saying anything.
Due to his behavior on Wednesday and him not showing up for work, they went to check on him, while contacting LPSO.
Before deputies arrived, Anita, Dylan, and Justin Daigle were able to gain access to the home through a bedroom window that was unlocked, and were able to see Urker lying on his bed, unconscious.
Once they realized he was not answering, they made entry through the window and located Urker on the bed. They told officials Urker was cold to the touch and not breathing.
Authorities said drug paraphernalia, including syringes and a spoon in the bathroom next to a brown powdery substance, was located inside Urker's home. A syringe and a handgun were also found on the nightstand next to the bed.
Officials said Urker appeared to have been there for an extended period of time before police were called to the scene.
His face and arms were blue, and a paper towel was placed on his left arm with what appeared to be blotches of blood on the paper towel, according to deputies.
An official cause of death has yet to be released by officials.
An investigation remains ongoing.
Gypsy Rose Blanchard, 35, told People magazine that she is in disbelief following Urker's death, saying, "I've screamed until my throat burns."
"There are no words that can express the depth of this loss," she added. "I ask for privacy and compassion for our daughter, our families, and everyone grieving Ken during this incredibly painful time."
Gypsy Rose Blanchard became infamous due to her role in the killing of her abusive mother. She was released from prison in December 2023 after serving more than seven years of a 10-year prison sentence. Blanchard was the victim of Munchausen syndrome by proxy, in which a caregiver fakes their child’s illness or induces symptoms to make their child ill.
Blanchard met Urker while she was in prison. Urker had written a "supportive letter, not on any kind of romantic level" to Blanchard, and included his phone number, after watching "Mommy Dead and Dearest," which was released in 2017, Blanchard said on the "We Need to Talk" podcast in June.
Blanchard went on to marry Louisiana teacher Ryan Anderson in a prison wedding ceremony in July 2022, but they parted ways in 2023, and she rekindled her romance with Urker.
Urker and Blanchard share a daughter together named Aurora Raina Urker. The couple got engaged in October 2018 and then broke up. They reunited in April 2024, shortly after Blanchard's divorce from Ryan Anderson, and their daughter was born Dec. 28, 2024.
CNN contributed to this report.
