44 miles of I-295 will be repaved
text:
The 22-mile stretch of Interstate 295 between Portland and Topsham will be resurfaced with help from a federal grant.
The state received $27.8 million from the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Infrastructure for Rebuilding America grant program and will put it toward installing new asphalt and road layers on the northbound and southbound sides of the highway, a total of 44 miles.
Construction is expected to begin next summer, according to a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Transportation. Once the work begins, the department will provide more information and updates about traffic impacts such as lane closures and detours.
The grant was announced in a news release from Sen. Susan Collins’ office.
Crews will remove the existing asphalt down to the concrete, perform structural repairs, install two new road layers – including new asphalt – and add reflective pavement. The roadway’s surface drainage will be improved, as will the guardrails. The continuous vehicle count stations and weigh-in-motion infrastructure will also be replaced.
Including a state match of the grant, the total project funding is $46.3 million, official said.
“Interstate 295 is a vital corridor in Maine’s transportation network for residents, businesses, and visitors alike,” Collins said in the news release.

title: Bangor Mall owner must pay $1.1M in another lawsuit, judge rules
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A judge ruled against the owner of the Bangor Mall, saying it must pay more than $1 million after a malfunctioning sprinkler destroyed a store’s inventory.
Namdar Reality Group must pay just over $1.1 million to Tri-State Insurance Company of Minnesota to cover the cost of the destroyed inventory for Furniture, Mattresses & More.
The ruling comes after mall owner Namdar Realty Group failed to respond to multiple letters and did not show up in court for a Sept. 23 hearing for the lawsuit.
Namdar did not respond to a request for comment.
It’s the second million-dollar fine issued this year against Namdar concerning its ownership of the Bangor Mall. The company was supposed to pay the city of Bangor a $1.1 million fine and make repairs over code violations, including a leaky roof and a sewer line break, but had not paid by a July 31 deadline.
In February 2023, the furniture store alerted Bangor Mall ownership to a ceiling leak in the former Sears. The store was vacant at the time and was being used to store inventory for the furniture business. It took the mall two hours to shut off the water, according to the lawsuit.
A sprinkler pipe in the ceiling later burst, causing more damage, the lawsuit said.
The judgment does not include Maine Fire Protection Systems, which has shown up for court and responded to filings. The lawsuit between the insurance company and the sprinkler company is expected to continue.
Penobscot County Judge Bruce Mallonee signed the decision Sept. 24. The binding court order will mean the insurance company won against the New York-based mall owner.

title: Radio signal detected for the first time from a planet outside our solar system
text:
Radio signal detected for the first time from a planet outside our solar system
Astronomers say they have directly detected the first-ever radio emission from a planet outside the solar system. The signal, however, is evidence of a colossal magnetic field — not intelligent life.
“I know radio signals are associated with searches for extraterrestrial intelligence,” said Edo Berger, a professor of astronomy at Harvard University. “But this is something very different.”
Related video above | Astronomers discover how planets form
The discovery, described in a new paper awaiting publication in a peer-reviewed journal, traces repeating radio bursts that appear to come from the exoplanet Beta Pictoris b, located 63 light-years from Earth — a short distance, astronomically speaking. The gas giant, about 12 times the mass of Jupiter, is one of three planets orbiting a young star that is 1.75 times as massive as the sun.
Processes associated with the planet’s magnetic field produce the radio emission, according to Berger, a researcher at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Specifically, the detection involves auroras similar to Earth’s northern lights — the spectacular displays sparked by magnetic storms involving charged particles from the sun. “In order to see radio waves that extend all the way to the frequencies that we observed, you need an incredibly strong magnetic field,” added Berger, a coauthor of the paper posted September 15 to the preprint platform arXiv.
Not all planets have a magnetic field. Those that have one benefit from a natural shield that deflects disruptive energy. Earth’s magnetic field, for example, protects our atmosphere from being stripped away by solar wind, a continuous outflow of plasma that contains charged particles like protons and electrons.
“The magnetic field on this planet is at least 200 times stronger than the magnetic field of Jupiter,” Berger said, referring to Beta Pictoris b. Jupiter’s magnetic field, according to NASA, is powerful enough to generate a magnetosphere — the region of space influenced by the magnetic field — that ranks as the largest structure in our solar system, stretching up to 2 million miles (3 million kilometers) toward the sun.
Jupiter’s field also creates striking auroras, when electrically charged particles spewed from volcanoes on its moon Io become trapped around the field’s poles. As the gas giant rotates, the charged particles emit a glow but also a radio signal. “As these very high-energy particles are spiraling inside the magnetic field, along with the aurora they also produce radio waves,” Berger said.
Astronomers call this type of signal an auroral radio emission. The phenomenon has been previously observed from Jupiter, Saturn and the sun, as well as stars outside the solar system and cool objects known as brown dwarfs — intermediates between a star and a planet. This type of signal is what Berger and his colleagues detected from Beta Pictoris b, which ultimately points to the presence of an intense magnetic field that’s causing auroras and the radio emission.
Magnetic fields have implications for the structure of exoplanets and their atmospheres, according to Berger. “Radio observations can give us a completely new view on planets beyond our system,” he said.
A well-studied star system
There had been hints of radio emissions from exoplanets before, but none had been confirmed, largely because it couldn’t be ruled out that the source was actually the host star, said Joseph Callingham, an associate professor at the Anton Pannekoek Institute for Astronomy of the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands.
“What is unique for this study is that they localise the emission to the planet itself, separate from the star,” Callingham, who was not involved in the new research, wrote in an email.
The Beta Pictoris system is astronomically very young at about 23 million years old compared with our own solar system’s age of 4.5 billion years. Beta Pictoris b — the planet from which the radio signal potentially originates — was discovered in 2008. Two additional planets, Beta Pictoris c and Beta Pictoris d, were discovered in 2019 and 2026, respectively.
The planetary system is among the most studied in our galaxy, and its star is known to host 30 orbiting comets and a giant disk of dust and debris, which NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope photographed in detail in 2015. Some of the debris swirling in the rotating disk is a remnant from planetary formation.
The researchers used MeerKAT, an array of 64 radio telescope dishes in South Africa, to detect the signal, but they were highly surprised to see it coming from such a well-observed set of celestial bodies, Berger said. “My graduate student Kevin was going through the data. He came into my office one day with the detection and he said, ‘I don’t think you’re going to believe this,’” Berger recalled, referring to lead study author Kevin Ortiz Ceballos, a doctoral researcher at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. “This was really unexpected for us. We were doing the survey as a bit of a fishing expedition, knowing that we would only detect sources if the magnetic field was incredibly strong.”
The surprise stems from the fact that astronomers had assumed, according to Berger, that if exoplanets have magnetic fields, they should look roughly like Jupiter’s, and therefore their radio emissions would be at lower frequencies than what he and his colleagues found. Detecting the signal was the result of “going against the perceived wisdom in the field,” he said.
However, the researchers noted the report has not yet undergone peer review, the process in which independent experts assess a research paper before publication in a scientific journal. The review is underway and will be completed over the next few months.
Berger said he is confident about the quality of the detection. The research team pinpointed the radio emission’s source as Beta Pictoris b, ruling out an initial suspicion that it could be coming from the star instead. “We recorded it multiple times, at multiple frequencies. It’s there every single time,” he said.
Cautious enthusiasm for radio signal detection
Scientists who were not involved with the new research urged caution when interpreting the findings.
If the discovery holds up under the scrutiny of peer review, it would represent an incredibly exciting and key step forward in understanding the behavior of worlds beyond our solar system, according to Jonathan Nichols, a professor in planetary auroras at the University of Leicester in England. “Auroral radio emissions are important because they allow us to understand how an object interacts with its local space environment,” he wrote in an email.
“They allow us to infer properties of the planet that we cannot otherwise measure,” Nichols explained, referring to auroras, “and, importantly, they enable us to test theories and ideas developed for our own solar system in more extreme conditions.”
If confirmed, the results would show that exoplanets can have much stronger magnetic fields than expected, which would be a crucial learning, according to Callingham of the University of Amsterdam.
The authors have requested more telescope time to further study Beta Pictoris b and perhaps unlock some of its puzzles, such as why the planet’s magnetic field is so strong. “I think that’s going to be a question that occupies people for a while,” Berger said.

title: The Latest: Trump will campaign in Alabama ahead of the midterm elections
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
President Donald Trump is back on the campaign trail as he seeks to shore up lagging enthusiasm in the Republican Party ahead of next month’s midterm elections on Nov. 3. On Friday, he’ll attend a rally in Alabama, then travel to Ohio on Saturday. He could have his work cut out for him: Just 26% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low, according to a new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.
The Group of Seven industrial nations said Friday that they plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel recently hit record high prices in the United States. President Trump and the GOP face pressure to address surging prices ahead of the elections.
Meanwhile, Trump’s immigration policies are finding renewed attention in the Supreme Court, which agreed Thursday to review his administration’s denial of bond hearings for immigrants during its sweeping crackdown. The justices will consider whether immigrants who’ve been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation.
Here’s the latest:
Kelly says Hegseth’s Pentagon ‘focused on the wrong thing’
Sen. Mark Kelly has harsh words for Pete Hegseth and the changes he’s looking to bring to the Pentagon.
Asked about the defense secretary’s “ state of the force speech,” in which Heath rolled out a number of major shifts for the department he leads, the military veteran and former astronaut said Hegseth was “focused on giving speeches about killing people in lethality and insulting some service members” instead of “professionalism and training and improving our combat capability.”
Kelly is stumping for midterm Democrats this week in South Carolina, which holds the party’s first presidential primary, as he mulls a potential 2028 White House bid. He spoke to reporters Friday after an event in Mauldin.
Kennedy Center Honors to be held at Capital One Arena amid fight over adding Trump’s name
This year’s Kennedy Center Honors will be held at Washington’s Capital One Arena, not the riverfront building that’s been at the center of a legal fight over adding President Trump’s name to the building.
The 49th annual awards are set to take place at Washington’s downtown arena, a Kennedy Center spokesperson said Friday. Few other details were immediately available, and an explanation for the change wasn’t given.
The center’s board voted last month to close the iconic performing arts venue along the Potomac River waterfront after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning Trump’s name to the building.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth orders one day ‘stand-down’ to encourage military vote
Hegseth made the announcement in a video in which he said the move was “apolitical.” It’s his latest effort to encourage Republican-leaning military members to cast ballots ahead of what’s shaping up to be a challenging election for the party.
Earlier this week, Hegseth said that if every member of the military cast ballots, they could out-vote heavily Democratic cities like Boston and Detroit. His department was also sued Thursday by Democrats over a quiet change that makes it harder for Democratic-leaning overseas civilians to cast ballots. Earlier this year, the Army reduced the number of its voting assistance officers.
Hegseth has also announced that the Defense Department will provide cybersecurity for November’s election, a function previously done by a civilian agency that’s been gutted by Trump’s budget cuts after its prior leaders challenged Trump’s false claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen.
Iowa lawmakers to vote on raising tax incentive cap for a $15B steel plant
Iowa lawmakers returned to the Statehouse on Friday to consider expanding the ceiling on state tax incentives in an effort to secure a $15 billion steel plant project for the state.
President Trump announced the plant Monday alongside Iowa elected officials, heralding the project as a major economic and national security investment.
Five weeks before the midterm elections, Republicans seized on the promise of good-paying jobs and a central role for the heartland in the push for American steel manufacturing. It’s celebrated as an opportunity for southeast Iowa, an area along the Mississippi River that once thrived as a hub for industry but has since suffered from shuttered facilities and dwindled populations. Still, the deal and the tax abatements it could carry have also been met with some skepticism in rural Iowa and Des Moines alike.
Hiring slipped and unemployment rose last month in the final jobs report before midterms
U.S. businesses and other employers added just 29,000 job in September, down from a revised 133,000 in August and far fewer than economists had expected. The unemployment rate rose to a still-low 4.2% from 4.1%, the Labor Department said.
Job gains in July were revised lower to show employers shed 10,000 jobs that month. Average wages rose 3% in August from a year earlier, the slowest pace in five years. Americans’ paychecks are trailing inflation.
The jobs report underscores the political challenge for Trump and congressional Republicans: Unemployment is low and layoffs are rare, but stubbornly high inflation is eroding consumers’ ability to afford things like gas, food, and housing. A recent AP-NORC poll found just 17% of Americans approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living.
Trump: Europe agrees to release diesel reserves ‘immediately’ as fuel prices hover near record highs
President Trump said Friday that Europe has agreed to release some of its diesel reserves “immediately,” as the president and his Republican Party face pressure to address surging prices ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Trump announced the action on social media without offering details on which countries were releasing reserves or at what volumes. Trump writes, “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil.” Trump says, “The process will begin immediately.”
The president faces lagging approval ratings as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods.
Households will pay more for energy because of Trump’s policy changes, think tank says
Households in the contiguous United States will pay thousands of dollars more for energy through 2040 because of federal policy changes since Trump returned to office, according to modeling released Friday by a nonpartisan think tank.
The Energy Innovation analysis found that households will pay an average of $6,500 more for energy, cumulatively through 2040. In five states, households will pay roughly $9,000 more: Oregon, Mississippi, South Dakota, Virginia and Wyoming.
The California-based think tank says there’ll be more demand for natural gas for electricity because the administration is canceling new clean energy projects and there’ll be more demand for gasoline for transportation because Trump and Congress are revoking policies that encouraged or created incentives for more efficient and lower-emissions vehicles. Higher demand drives prices up.
Trump administration says it has no plans for ICE officers at polls. Activists are preparing, anyway
With early voting already underway, a question worrying some voters is what role — if any — immigration enforcement officers might have at polling places through Election Day.
Department of Homeland Security officials say they don’t plan to send immigration enforcement officers en masse to patrol the polls and dismissed concerns that they plan to do so as “fearmongering.” Election legal experts say federal law clearly prevents the government from deploying any armed troops, agents or officers to election sites except to “repel armed enemies of the United States,” a high bar to clear.
But organizations who represent Latino, Black and Asian American voters say the rhetoric and ICE’s own activity make them worried at a time the number of immigration arrests is soaring as President Trump carries out his mass deportation agenda.
Trump tried to make an ally out of fishermen. Some have started to turn on him
John Evich, a commercial fisherman in Washington and Alaska, has voted for President Donald Trump three times, viewing him as someone who would fight for his industry.
But these days, Evich is weary of the high cost of doing business at sea, with fuel prices rising and trade hostilities with Canada jeopardizing markets for the crabs that he pulls off the ocean floor.
“If somebody came along that was going to do a better job, I would vote for them in a heartbeat,” he said.
Evich’s sentiment, echoed throughout the U.S. seafood industry, is another piece of a political puzzle that’s working against Trump in the midterm elections. Dissatisfaction among commercial fishermen could cause collateral damage for Republicans in competitive races in Washington, Alaska and Maine.
Trump blitzes toward the midterms with campaign rallies across the country
President Donald Trump is back on the campaign trail as he seeks to shore up lagging enthusiasm in his party ahead of next month’s midterm elections.
He could have their work cut out for him, though.
A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.
Republicans have expressed growing pessimism about their chances in the election, which will determine control of Congress, as the president has repeatedly dismissed concerns about high costs and gas prices as his unpopular war in Iran drags on.
According to Trump, his party has merely done a poor job of public relations in promoting his administration’s accomplishments.
“Maybe we’re doing a bad job selling it,” Trump said while campaigning in Texas.

title: What to know about Christa Pike and her failed lethal injection execution attempt
text:
(AP) - Tennessee’s failed attempt at executing Christa Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug in the state’s death chamber has left her in critical condition, according to her attorneys.
Pike, 50, was still in the hospital Thursday and her lawyers said they did not know her long-term chance for recovery. Tennessee went forward with the lethal injection Wednesday eight hours after it was originally scheduled to have taken place, a delay caused by a court ruling that temporarily paused the execution.
What happened to Pike is “singular and unparalleled,” said Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. She said Pike was the only person who has remained alive after lethal injection drugs were administered in an execution.
Here’s what to know about Pike’s failed execution:
An execution delayed, prolonged then failed
Pike’s execution was supposed to start at 10 a.m., but a federal appeals court stopped it about an hour before. The state appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, and it took eight hours for the conservative majority to overrule the lower court and let the lethal injection with the barbiturate pentobarbital to proceed.
About 90 minutes later, prison officials raised the curtain to the execution chamber, where media witnesses saw Pike strapped to a gurney with an IV in her arm. She said she was leaving the world with love.
“I’m ready to be free,” she said. “This is a happy day.”
She sang a song with her spiritual adviser, looked around and after several minutes said her arm was hurting or burning and asked if it was supposed to feel that way.
The curtain to the witnesses was closed then opened again around the time a second dose of pentobarbital would be administered. Pike appeared to lose consciousness, but she continued breathing and at times made snoring-like noises for the next hour.
Prison officials closed the curtain for good about 40 minutes after they first opened it. Pike’s attorney demanded a telephone to ask a court to stop the execution.
It’s unknown what was happening to Pike from the time the curtain closed for good at 8:06 p.m. until her attorney was told an ambulance was coming and witnesses were told to leave around 8:50 p.m.
“We at this point do not know the ramifications of the chemical torture that she has endured,” Pike’s attorney Randy Spivey said.
Prison officials have not said when their attempt to execute Pike turned into life-saving efforts. They have only released a statement saying their lethal injection protocols were followed.
Tennessee governor stops December execution to investigate
Within hours, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee canceled the state’s last execution of 2026, scheduled for Dec. 3, and ordered a comprehensive third-party investigation into what went wrong with Pike.
“It needs to be done thoroughly and however long that takes, whatever process is required to make sure we get to the very end of it and all the questions are answered,” Lee said.
It’s not the first time Lee has ordered an investigation into capital punishment in Tennessee. Four years ago, an independent review found the state didn’t follow its own execution rules and failed to properly test lethal injection drugs. That probe came after an April 2022 execution was stopped because of mishandling of drugs.
In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after medical workers who got an IV into his right arm couldn’t get a secondary IV line after trying his other arm, his left hand and his left foot, then failing to establish a central line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute Carruthers again.
Pike’s lawyers called for the governor to now spare her life.
“Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa’s sentence now,” Spivey said.
Pike’s lawyers warned of medical conditions
Pike’s legal team has previously told courts and Tennessee prison officials that she had medical conditions that would make death by lethal injection agonizing.
They said Pike suffered from a condition with elevated platelets known as thrombocytosis. They argued the condition could cause issues with blood clotting at injection sites or bleeding that could affect her lungs.
Medical workers also had trouble drawing blood from her, and setting an IV line is a harder process, her lawyers said. Spivey said he counted at least seven spots where needles were put into her left arm Wednesday and that at least one needle bent on an unsuccessful attempt.
Pike’s biggest fear from being executed wasn’t “a fear of dying. It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death. And that’s what happened minus the death,” said Stephen Ferrell, an attorney for Pike.
Pike killed 19-year-old job corps classmate
Pike didn’t deny she killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. The two were classmates at Knoxville Job Corps.
Prosecutors said Pike feared Slemmer was a romantic rival and lured her to a secluded area where she and her boyfriend slashed Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. The case got widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body.
Pike said she was sexually abused starting from when she was a toddler and that she was raped at ages 11 and 17. Her lawyers said her death sentence was unfair because she was 18 at the time of the crime and the jury wasn’t told about the abuse and how that might have affected her behavior.
Slemmer’s mother witnessed the execution attempt and said her daughter didn’t get justice.
“I watched the whole thing. She was awake. She was laughing. She was moving her head, moving her feet. She was trying to sit up. Didn’t work the first time they gave her a shot. It didn’t work the second time so she’s in the hospital and alive,” May Martinez said by telephone.
Tadaryl Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into her body. He was 17 at the time of the killing and was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age.
___
Kim Chandler in Nashville and Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed to this report.

title: Line-dance instructor builds community while inspiring students
text:
PETERSBURG, Va. (Aging Untold) — Richard Caple leads a line dancing class at Club 17 in Petersburg, and he also gives back to the community through scholarships and fundraisers.
How the class started
Caple said he did not initially want to lead the class.
“So, a year ago, we had contemplated on him becoming a line dance instructor. And I asked him, would he do it? And he said yes,” Adrianne Green, a member of the group, said.
“And they set me up. I didn’t want to do it. I really didn’t want to do it. But after the response, I got twisted, twisted my arm,” Caple said.
Participants and the class
Most participants are members of Mount Olivet Baptist Church.
Caple said the class gives him joy when participants share their experiences.
“It gives me joy when I when they give me their testimonies like they’ve been to the doctor. The doctor said they have lost weight. They are doing good,” Caple said.
“I don’t know why I’m attached to them seniors, but them seniors, they got my heart, they got it and they know it too,” Caple said.
Community outreach
Caple has organized fashion shows to raise money for student scholarships. He keeps company with the sick and shut-in and raises money for the American Cancer Society. The group also helped one of its own members when she fell on hard times.
“Last week, one of the club members here asked up to help in a donation because a lady’s house was being condemned. So we were able to raise $500 that same evening,” Caple said.
Full-time job
Caple works a full-time job as a medical transport driver for seniors in addition to leading the class.
“I was told about it by a senior. She said, never change what you’re doing. You just ask God to give you the strength to make time to do what you like to do,” Caple said.

title: Federal court temporarily blocks Trump administration border wall in Texas' Big Bend region
text:
Federal court temporarily blocks Trump administration border wall in Texas' Big Bend region
A federal court in Texas on Friday issued a ruling temporarily blocking the Trump administration from building a border wall and other infrastructure across the state's Big Bend region.
Related video: DOJ files complaints against federal judges in Minnesota for their comments about immigration cases
The news marks a major win for landowners, businesses and environmentalists in the region who have united to oppose the planned infrastructure projects, which are part of a $46 billion effort by the Trump administration to line the southern border with a mix of 30-foot-tall steel walls, vehicle barriers, roads and surveillance technology.
Judge Kathleen Cardone said in her ruling that the plaintiffs were "likely to succeed on the merits of at least one of the claims in suit, that there is a likelihood that they will suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest weigh in their favor."
Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Collins’ record on military affairs is distressing
text:
While the abandoned FBI investigation into Sen. Susan Collins — as reported by ProPublica and carried by this publication on Sept. 23 — is dismaying enough, there is considerably more reason to be dismayed by Collins’ record on military affairs.
Throughout the disastrous 2003-2011 Iraq War, Collins was a staunch supporter of the war, which, according to a Brown University report, will end up costing U.S. taxpayers a total of $2.9 trillion. That’s a staggering $8,457 for every man, woman and child in the country — and that’s about $12 billion right from the pockets of Maine taxpayers. All the while, 14 million American children face food insecurity.
In an emailed Sept. 22 “Tuesday Report,” Collins touted her having secured $42 million in Maine heating assistance. Not bad for one Tuesday Report, but at $42 million per year, Collins would need 285 years of heating assistance to equal the amount Maine taxpayers spent on her disastrous Iraq War — which killed 4,492 Americans and at least 733,000 Iraqis, and destabilized the entire Middle East.
Heating assistance for 285 years. Even Susan Collins would struggle to serve in Congress that long.
Lawrence Reichard
Belfast

“Every cut to SNAP is really a cut to school meals as well. All of these federal programs work together, so every child enrolled in SNAP is automatically eligible for a free school meal. title: The breakup nobody talks about: Losing a friend as you age
text:
(Aging Untold) — Some friendships are built over decades of shared memories, routines and common ground. But as politics shift, priorities change and people grow in different directions, even the closest bonds can quietly come apart.
“It’s not talked about a lot”
Losing a friend later in life can hit just as hard as any other breakup, but friendship loss is often grieved in silence, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said.
“I think people grieve over lost friendships, and they don’t talk about it because it seems bad or wrong or uncommon, or they discount it,” O’Rourke said.
During a dinner with friends, the conversation drifted toward politics, O’Rourke said.
“We all agreed that that was a topic we were not going to bring up because our friendship meant more than a topic,” O’Rourke said. “I love the maturity of the friendships that we acknowledged it so it could be sustained.”
Why losing a friend can feel like a broken heart
“I don’t think people realize that not every broken heart comes from romance,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “There are a lot of really deeply broken hearts from severed families and severed friendships. We don’t give enough credence to it, and we certainly don’t allow people to normally grieve it.”
When someone loses a spouse or goes through a divorce, people rally around them. That support often doesn’t show up the same way when a friendship ends.
“Nobody’s bringing you casseroles or sending you flowers usually, and it can be really tough,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
Don’t put all your friendship “eggs in one basket”
O’Rourke said she isn’t a fan of relying on a single best friend.
“I like the idea of having friendships broader — broader in age, broader in number — so that you’re enhanced in all areas of your life,” O’Rourke said. “And if one friendship changes, you’re not completely unraveled.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, agreed, comparing close friendships to relationships that end the way marriages sometimes do.
“I see people as they grow as kind of like people who get divorced,” Rogers said. “They grow apart for whatever reason.”
When a friendship is one-sided
O’Rourke described watching a friendship where one person consistently gave and the other consistently took — until the giver stopped.
“The giver kind of woke up and thought, ‘I’m not going to give anymore,’” O’Rourke said. “And it ended. Those that were watching it thought, ‘Oh, a sigh of relief.’ But they both went through grief.”
Moving forward after a friendship ends
Ambrose shared how a recent friendship breakup affected her personally, including during a family vacation.
“I was so shocked to have this end that it devastated me, and it ruined a vacation that was very important to me with my husband and son,” Ambrose said.
Her advice: don’t let the loss take over.
“Don’t let people ruin your day, your vacation,” Ambrose said. “Just accept it for what it is. Embrace it and get over it. They’re doing things for their reasons, and it’s maybe none of your business. Stay out of judgment. Don’t try to figure them out — go on and just say next.”
Ambrose added that picking yourself back up opens the door to new connections.
“It can be really tough grief, but pick yourself up because you have the opportunity to find new joy, new happiness,” Ambrose said. “You never know when you’re going to meet your next friends. So give yourself that gift and get back out there.”
Key takeaways
- Friendship loss deserves real grief. Losing a close friend can be as painful as a romantic breakup, but it rarely comes with the same outside support.
- Talk about it before it breaks. Setting boundaries, like agreeing not to discuss divisive topics, can help sustain long-term friendships.
- Diversify your friendships. Having a broad circle of friends across different ages and backgrounds can soften the blow if one relationship ends.
- Watch for one-sided dynamics. Friendships where one person always gives and the other always takes often end — and both people grieve, even if outsiders feel relief.
- Don’t let the loss take over your life. Accept the friendship for what it was, resist the urge to over-analyze the other person’s reasons and keep moving forward.
- Stay open to new connections. New friendships can bring new joy, even after a painful loss.

title: The anti-bucket list: Why letting go might be a secret to aging well
text:
(Aging Untold) — A bucket list is about everything you still want to do. But what about an “anti-bucket list” — the things you’re finally ready to stop doing, stop caring about or stop apologizing for?
Saying no might be one of the most powerful tools for a freer, more joyful life after 60.
The problem with automatic “yes”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke kicked off the conversation with a true confession.
“I was asked to be on the HOA (homeowners association) board, and I said yes immediately,” O’Rourke said. “And then I went home and I was like, what did I say yes for? I don’t want to do that.”
O’Rourke said she had agreed out of guilt rather than genuine desire.
“I said it out of guilt that I should, that I can, that I would — afraid of what other people would think,” O’Rourke said. “So I reneged, and immediately I had better energy. I had better clarity. I got through the discomfort of saying no when I’m used to saying yes to everything.”
Subtraction as a privilege of aging
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose framed the shift as a kind of wisdom that comes with age.
“It’s a discernment. You hope as you get older, you become wiser and you make maybe more mature choices,” Ambrose said.
“One of the privileges of getting older is subtraction,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, added. “What can I do to subtract that’s going to give me more peace, more sleep, more joy. And it’s OK.”
Rogers said adding too many obligations creates stress that the body can’t distinguish from any other kind.
“Your body doesn’t realize the difference between types of stress, because it’s going to react the same,” Rogers said.
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck noted that saying yes isn’t always the wrong move.
“Sometimes yes is purpose,” Cradduck said. “Some people will say yes because it does give them the purpose, and we still need to feel that.”
Practicing the word “no”
Cradduck said the hardest habits to break are often the ones tied to people, boards and other obligations, like hosting Thanksgiving dinner year after year.
“I don’t want to fix Thanksgiving dinner anymore kind of thing,” Cradduck said, describing the kind of thought many people are afraid to say out loud. “I’ve done it for 35 years. Daughter, son, you can cook and it’s time for you to take it on.”
O’Rourke suggested starting small for anyone too anxious to say no to a big obligation right away.
“So maybe you start by saying something to someone other than a family member — say no and practice. Or if you’re really anxiety-ridden, say the words out loud to yourself. Kind of rehearse the conversation,” O’Rourke said.
Ambrose shared a story to illustrate the point, about a couple in their late 70s who had recently married.
“She was telling me about all the Thanksgivings and things that she’d hosted, what she could cook,” Ambrose said. “And he was so shocked. He said, ‘You told me you can’t cook.’ She said, ‘No, I didn’t say I can’t cook — I said I don’t cook.’”
“It can be very freeing,” Ambrose said. “I think as time becomes shorter, you start thinking about what I really want to do.”
Key takeaways
- An “anti-bucket list” is about subtraction, not addition.
- Guilt-driven “yes” answers can drain energy.
- The body reacts to different types of stress the same way.
- Not all “yes” answers are bad — some provide purpose.
- Practice saying no in low-stakes situations first.

title: Woman told Cornell investigators she 'felt like bait' during alleged gang rape
text:
A woman who says she was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity told the school’s investigators last year that she “felt like bait” as the attackers were “like lions around me,” according to records from the school’s disciplinary investigation.
The documents, reviewed Friday by The Associated Press, include excerpts of interviews Cornell’s investigators did with the woman and the men she accused and shed more light on the university’s handling of the case.
While heavily redacted, the records offer a fuller but sometimes conflicting timeline of events and a glimpse at how the men responded to the allegations. Some disputed the woman’s account and said they weren’t involved in any assault.
The woman, identified in court papers only as Jane Doe, sued Cornell and seven former students last month, alleging she was given ketamine and repeatedly assaulted at a fraternity house in October 2024.
She went to campus police three weeks after the encounter and gave a detailed account of what happened, but the local district attorney decided not to file criminal charges or push for more investigation after reviewing a police summary of her interview.
Only the school’s investigation, under the federal Title IX law, persisted, with a goal of deciding discipline for the students involved.
Lawsuit by one of the accused men reveals details on investigation
This week, a lawyer for one of the accused men filed documents from the school’s investigation in a lawsuit that seeks to overturn the university’s punishment and remove it from his academic record. They include a 99-page report on a campus hearing panel’s disciplinary findings and a summary of events submitted by the university’s lawyers.
Though only a fraction of the thousands of pages amassed in the investigation, the records show the breadth of the university’s inquiry — including 50 interviews with 32 witnesses and 12 days of hearings.
Late Thursday, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to lead a renewed criminal investigation, saying she had lost faith in Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.
According to the Title IX documents filed in court, which are only a portion of the entire investigation, the woman and several of the men gave investigators similar accounts of drug use and sexual activity that took place at the Chi Phi fraternity house — but differed sharply in how much of it was consensual.
Snapchat messages drew other men
The woman had been invited there by a fraternity member for whom she had long held strong romantic feelings and sexual interest, according to the disciplinary panel’s findings. The panel found that she initially consented to sex with that man and one of his friends, though she later alleged in her lawsuit that she had been pressured into taking ketamine, marijuana and alcohol and was too intoxicated to consent.
Then other men began showing up in the room, some drawn by a message one of the fraternity brothers sent to a Snapchat group at 1:42 a.m. using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman’s body was freely available. Later, another person in the chat asked if the “shop” was still open.
The woman told investigators that her intoxication had rendered her partly defenseless. She said she remembered smoking marijuana and said she knew she took ketamine, her first time doing so, but didn’t have an independent memory of it. The drug, she said, left her in a state of “vague consciousness.”
“You look like an operating human being,” she told school investigators at a hearing in May of 2025. “You don’t look dead or asleep necessarily. So, lights are on, but nobody’s home. Your brain is not functioning at its proper level.”
She said some of the men inhaled drugs off her unclothed body.
“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in,” she told investigators.
Accused student says he only entered room for a wellness check
One of the men the woman accused of snorting drugs off her body — but not participating in other elements of the assault — denied her account.
He told investigators he was in the room for no more than five minutes, and didn’t go there for sex.
“That was not our intentions at all. We were just checking out to see if everything” was OK, he said.
He insisted that he did not see the woman naked at any time — she was under bed coverings, he said — and did not partake in drug use. He said he sat on a couch and chatted for a few minutes, then left after the woman and another man there both indicated they were all right.
A Cornell disciplinary panel later cleared him of sexual assault or exploitation allegations, but found him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation because it didn’t believe his claim to have gone to the room for altruistic reasons.
The fraternity member, who is challenging Cornell’s disciplinary process in court, also posted in the Snapchat conversation, saying what was happening in the room was not a joke, adding: “Firsthand pov not a bit.” The student later told investigators he did not remember sending the message, according to Cornell’s account.
Woman’s lawsuit seeks tougher penalties
In her lawsuit, Jane Doe accused two of the other men who entered the room of performing sex acts on her without her consent, while she was partially incapacitated. She accused another man of kissing her without her consent. According to the Title IX documents, Jane Doe told investigators two other men stood at the foot of the bed acting “more like voyeurs than anything.”
The lawsuit seeks to hold all seven men liable for rape. She is asking for unspecified damages.
Cornell hasn’t detailed the results of its investigation, but said it resulted in some students being expelled.
The man who filed the lawsuit challenging his punishment was allowed to stay at Cornell, but he was ordered to stay away from the woman, take a class on sexual harassment and bystander intervention, and write a paper reflecting on the circumstances for which he was found responsible and include a proposal to train other students on preventing sexual harassment.

title: Mary Louise Weller of ‘Animal House’ dead at 79
text:
Mary Louise Weller of ‘Animal House’ dead at 79
Mary Louise Weller of ‘Animal House’ dead at 79
Mary Louise Weller, an actress best known for her role as Mandy Pepperidge in “Animal House,” has died, according to multiple reports.
She was 79.
Weller died Thursday, a day before her 80th birthday, after a brief illness. An official cause of death has not been released.
Related video above | Remembering those we lost in 2026
Weller’s breakout role came in John Landis’ 1978 comedy “National Lampoon’s Animal House,” in which she played Mandy Pepperidge, a member of the Pi House sorority and girlfriend of preppy fraternity leader Greg Marmalard.
She later won the affections of John Belushi’s Bluto, and the two rode off into the sunset together.
Weller also appeared in dozens of films and television shows in the 1970s and ’80s. Her film credits include “The Bell Jar,” “Q” and “Forced Vengeance.” She also had guest roles on “Kojak,” “Starsky & Hutch,” “Fantasy Island” and “CHiPs.”
Prior to her acting career, Weller was a prominent model in New York.

DEAR SUN SPOTS: It’s that time of year for making apple crisp and I’d like to hear from other Sun Spots fans. What’s your best recipe? I’m collecting tried and true homey recipes for my daughter’s upcoming bridal shower so if you have other old-timey recipes to share besides apple crisp, please send them to Sun Spots. (I asked Ms. Sun Spots ahead of time and she gave me the OK.)
I’ll then write the recipes out by hand and put them in a wooden recipe box made by my husband. This is what my parents did for me back in the ’70s and we’re excited to give our daughter this special gift. Thank you, Ms. Sun Spots, for helping to get the word out and agreeing that it would be fun to also share the recipes with the Sun Spots community. It will be fun to see what happens. — Margo, no town
ANSWER: I love this idea so much! I remember that for my bridal shower, each guest had taped a recipe card to their gifts then my mom gave me a cute recipe box to put them all in and yes, I still have these handwritten recipes and use them. They are very precious to me.
I’ll start this effort by sharing a crisp recipe that can be made with many different types of fruit besides apples, including pears, peaches, plums, cherries, rhubarb, strawberries and other berries, or any combination. You can also use canned fruit such as drained pineapple, peaches, or even cherry pie filling. I adjust the sugar amount and sometimes change the spices (pear with cardamom is delicious!)
Apple Crisp: Preheat the oven to 375 degrees and slice and pare about 6 medium-sized apples to make 4 cups. Place the apple slices in an 8-inch square or similar size buttered baking pan.
In a bowl, stir together 2/3 to 3/4 cup brown sugar (packed), 1/2 cup white or wheat flour, 1/2 cup old-fashioned oats, 1 teaspoon cinnamon, and 1 teaspoon nutmeg. Add 1/2 cup softened butter cut into small pieces. Mix with a fork until well combined. Spread over apple slices.
Bake for 35 minutes or until apples are tender and bubbling and topping is golden brown. Serve warm with vanilla ice cream or whipped cream. Makes 4-6 servings.
I encourage readers to write in with recipes they are willing to share with this bride, and with the rest of us! I don’t mind being the go-between one little bit.

title: Search continues for Hampden man missing nearly a year
Maine must not bring back Paul LePage
text:
Paul LePage is back, but there’s nothing new about him we haven’t already seen and nothing we want to revisit. He’s grossly insulting (believing he’s funny), calling himself “Trump before Trump,” making blatantly racist and sexist comments that don’t belong in political campaigns or polite conversations.
LePage was always an embarrassment for Maine, and he’d be happy to embarrass it again. I’ll never forget visiting friends in Massachusetts who were ready with cringeworthy questions about Maine’s infamous governor. (“Did he really say that?”) But, we’re never going back there.
LePage got into office by finding a third-party candidate who’d split the vote for him. A dishonest tactic, it drove Maine to embrace ranked-choice voting, which increases our choices and our power as voters. In Maine, our votes really do matter!
It’s highly ironic, but it’s thanks to Paul LePage’s awful record that we use RCV and why we’re not going to be cheated out of our best choice for Maine’s 2nd District: Matt Dunlap.
Toni Seger
Lovell

title: New treatment could drastically reduce sepsis death rate, researcher says
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Sepsis kills more than 350,000 adults and 1,800 children in the United States each year, according to the CDC. One in three adults who die in the hospital have sepsis.
A doctor in Kansas City, Missouri, has made a discovery that could drastically reduce that statistic.
What is sepsis?
Sepsis happens when the body’s immune system starts harming healthy tissues and organs in response to an infection, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
That can trigger a chain reaction throughout the body.
Early sepsis signs can start with a fever, chills and rapid breathing. Those symptoms then progress to confusion and difficulty breathing until it reaches the final stage, septic shock, which can lead to organ failure and death in as little as 12 hours, according to Sepsis Alliance.
A mother’s story
Two years ago, Brie Morgan Bauer was pregnant with her third child and excited to welcome him to a growing family. Everything about the pregnancy was normal until she felt flu-like symptoms at 27 weeks.
She went to her obstetrician’s office and that’s when the real emergency began.
“When they hooked me up, we were showing back-to-back contractions and I didn’t feel anything,” Bauer said. “But little did I know I was actually going septic.”
Bauer’s son, Bo, was delivered by emergency C-section. Her flu-like symptoms were strep throat. She went from bringing new life into the world to fighting for her own.
“By the third day that’s when they started looking at my toes, looking at my fingers and that they were turning purple and black,” Bauer said. “My hands were almost like mummified. They were black. And then I unwrapped my legs, and the legs were so crazy to see. The feet were definitely black.”
In her mind, Bauer thought there was no going back. “There’s no option to get blood flow back to a foot that is obviously dead.”
In the end, there was nothing she could have done to prevent what happened to her. She would have to live life as a quadruple amputee.
The current treatment for sepsis is antibiotics and IV fluids, which is sometimes not enough.
Researcher’s discovery
Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins has worked to find a solution to sepsis. He is the founder of Vivacell Bio Inc., where he has worked to find a solution to septic shock.
“There are 11 million cases around the world, and its mortality rate’s about 30%, 40%,” Simpkins said. “Depends on what stage you’re at, but if you’re at an advanced stage, it becomes almost 100%.”
Simpkins said during sepsis, the body makes too much nitric oxide, which leads to organ failure. His product, VBI-S, absorbs the nitric oxide, something Simpkins said has never been done before.
“It will act quickly, very quickly. You’ll see the blood pressure come up. You don’t have to wait to see its effect.”
He said that within 24 to 48 hours, “you’ll see the lungs get better, you’ll see the kidneys get better.”
In clinical trials, 80% of participants were expected to die from sepsis. VBI-S lowered that to 50%.
“They have shown that a high degree of efficacy in reversing failure of multiple organs,” Simpkins said.
He said the mortality rate would be even lower when the substance is given to patients early in their diagnosis. The clinical trials have concluded, and the product is awaiting FDA approval.
Other experts watching closely
Dr. Steven Simpson, a pulmonary and critical care doctor, is board chairman of the Sepsis Alliance, a group dedicated to finding a solution to sepsis.
“I am pleased that it seems to work as it’s intended to work,” Simpson said. “[It’s a] small study. We need a lot more patients treated. But very promising.”
Simpson said he sees patients in septic shock every day in the ICU.
He hopes, someday soon, no more will have to die from it. “It’s the reason that I work with Sepsis Alliance, it’s the reason for my entire career. It’s been 40 years, we haven’t found that solution yet.”
While Simpson doesn’t know if this will be a solution for sepsis, he is encouraged by the results.
“I don’t stick my neck out on what’s going to be the cure for sepsis. I am hopeful. I do believe that this is going to play a role, and I think it’s exciting,” he said.
Finding a new normal
Bauer was stunned to hear about the major discovery that could mean the end of sepsis.
I think that’s very promising," she said. “And I’m excited. I wish it was approved a while ago.”
VBI-S was not available for Bauer’s case. She has since found she has an interest in art and remains active in her sons’ lives.
“It’s been chaos. We live minute by minute,” Bauer said. “But my husband, he does everything. And I’m trying to do my best to find that more independence, more partnership with him to help reduce the chaos.”
“But that’s kind of what I’m showing my kids is what resilience looks like and to learn how to adapt,” Bauer said.
Bauer started a website, BriesHope.org, to offer support to survivors and families.
Simpkins said that with FDA approval, VBI-S could be in hospitals as soon as 2027.

title: Friday’s high school football: Biddeford rebounds, takes down Westbrook
text:
Estevao Lembissa rushed for two touchdowns and returned a kickoff 87 yards for the go-ahead score, leading Biddeford to a 31-14 win over Westbrook in a Class B South football game Friday night in Biddeford.
The teams combined for three touchdowns in the first two minutes. Biddeford (4-1) received the opening kickoff and quickly drove down the field and need just six plays to score, on a 7-yard run by Lembissa.
Cole Tanner returned the ensuing kickoff 70 yards to make it 7-7, but Biddeford needed just two plays to answer, with a 17-yard pass from Ernest Dore to Trey Coleman.
Westbrook (1-4) then grabbed a 14-13 lead on the final play of the first quarter when Beckett Griffin connected with Andre Hicks III for a 12-yard touchdown pass. But Lembissa opened the second quarter by returning the kickoff 87 yards, putting Biddeford ahead for good.
Cameron Bergeron extended the lead to 25-14 later in the second quarter when he broke a couple tackles and raced 61 yards with a screen pass.
Lembissa added a 53-yard TD run in the third quarter.
BONNY EAGLE 42, WINDHAM 6: Lucas Klehn accounted for all six Bonny Eagle touchdowns — four rushing and two passing — as the Scots (5-0) rolled past the Eagles (2-3) in Windham.
Klehn scored three times on power runs up the middle, twice from 16 yards and once from the 27. He also plunged in from 1.
Klehn’s first two TD runs were sandwiched around a 39-yard touchdown pass to Wes Pinkham as Bonny Eagle, the No. 2 team in the Varsity Maine Top 10, opened a 21-0 lead in the first quarter.
Windham got a 10-yard touchdown run from Jordan Pastore in the second quarter, but Klehn’s 1-yard TD made it 28-6 at halftime.
Ben Noe took a screen pass 43 yards for a touchdown in the third quarter. Klehn capped the scoring with his 27-yard run.
Klehn finished with 143 yards on 16 carries, and he completed 4 of 5 passes for 98 yards. Ben Havu ran for 76 yards on 10 carries. Noe and Pinkham each had an interception.
SOUTH PORTLAND 40, SANFORD 0: Christopher Salamone scored three touchdowns, Shea Healy ran for two and passed for two, and the Red Riots (3-2) rolled to a win over the Spartans (0-5) in Sanford.
Healy threw a 5-yard touchdown pass to Jacoby Jellow in the first quarter. In the second quarter, he scored on runs on 1 and 13 yards and threw a 59-yard touchdown pass to Salamone.
Salamone scored from 70 and 7 yards in the third quarter.
MARSHWOOD 42, FALMOUTH 16: Greg Castoras and the Hawks (5-0) ran past the Navigators (2-3) in a Class B South game in Falmouth.
Castoras rushed for four touchdowns and a 2-point conversion. All six of Marshwood’s scores were on the ground.
In the first quarter, Castoras recorded 6- and 4-yard touchdown runs for a 12-0 lead. Nate Goodwin scored from 2 yards out to make it 20-0.
After Marshwood recovered a bad snap on the Navigators’ 1-yard line, quarterback Michael Sbrizza scored as the Hawks extended their lead to 28-0 heading into halftime.
Castoras added 13- and 17-yard TD runs in the third quarter.
Falmouth quarterback Micah Derrig threw a 25-yard touchdown pass to Theo Roediger in the fourth quarter, and Alex Hau caught a 26-yard scoring pass.
WELLS 47, GARDINER 31: The Warriors (3-2) jumped out to a 21-0 lead in the first quarter and held on to beat the Tigers (3-2) in Wells.
Noah McDonough intercepted a pass on Gardiner’s first drive, and Wells capitalized on a 2-yard run by Mason Miles. Wyatt Mynes then forced and recovered a fumble on the Tigers’ next drive, and the Warriors went up 14-0 on a 3-yard run by Jameson Russell.
Gardiner turned the ball over on downs on its third possession, and Wells scored again, this time on a 35-yard run by Miles.
Quinn Finemore and Brady Godin ran for TDs in the second quarter as Wells went up 34-0. Jacob Barry added a 35-yard touchdown run in the third quarter.
Justin Doody scored on a 2-yard run in the second quarter and an 8-yard run in the fourth quarter for Gardiner. Isaac Madore threw an 18-yard TD pass to Colin McCormick.
MESSALONSKEE 28, FRYEBURG ACADEMY 20: Fin Minkel threw three touchdown passes to Malachi Cusano and rushed for a touchdown, leading the Eagles (3-2) past the Raiders (2-3) in a Class B North game in Oakland.
Messalonskee erased an early 7-0 deficit when Minkel and Cusano hooked up for 83 yards touchdown in the first quarter.
Cusano scored on receptions of 12 and 34 yards in the second quarter to make it 21-7.
Lars Bruhn’s second TD run of the game, from 3 yards out, cut the margin to 21-14. Minkel, though, answered with a 37-yard touchdown run.
A 12-yard run by Buk Awe later in the third pulled Fryeburg within 28-20, but the conversion kick was blocked.
The Raiders then threatened late in the fourth quarter, but Messalonskee held on downs to clinch the victory.
KENNEBUNK 34, DEERING 6: Ethan White rushed for five touchdowns and Kennebunk (4-1) intercepted four passes in a win over Deering (1-4) in Kennebunk.
White scored from the 5, 7 and 1 in the first half, then added 5- and 17-yard touchdowns in the second half.
Grisam Shields had two interceptions, while Charlie Pentland and Dominic Gaither each had one.
Matt Ciampi scored on a 40-yard run for Deering.

title: See the full interview with the man behind ‘Taking Care of Granny’
text:
(Aging Untold) — Caring for an aging loved one can reshape a family, and it’s a responsibility more men are shouldering than ever before. Today, an estimated 21 million men are in caregiving roles, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. They are navigating the daily challenges of aging and illness alongside their own jobs and children.
Dugan Meredith, who documents caring for his mother-in-law online through the “Taking Care of Granny” social media feeds, joined us to talk about what it’s really like to become a caregiver and how his family found their way through it.
Dugan Meredith joins us for the Aging Untold podcast
Dugan Meredith joined us for the Aging Untold podcast and spoke with Sam Cradduck. You can watch or listen to the podcast here.
How the family noticed something was wrong
Meredith’s mother-in-law, known online as Granny, was originally living with her oldest daughter in the Charleston, South Carolina, area. Meredith described the signs that led the family to seek a diagnosis.
“She was experiencing symptoms, showing signs, forgetting how to go pick up the grandchildren from school, getting lost,” Meredith said. “Talking to random strangers and inviting them back to the house.”
The turning point came when Granny tried to cook soup by putting it in a baking pan in the oven instead of putting it in a pot and placing it on the stove. Granny was later diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia, also known as FTD.
Dividing caregiving duties wasn’t planned — it just happened
When Granny moved in with Meredith and his wife, there wasn’t a formal plan for who would do what.
“I think it was decided for us,” Meredith said. The family originally intended to split time with another sister-in-law, but when she had to return to full-time work, “the responsibility fell squarely on our shoulders,” Meredith said.
For a time, Meredith’s wife took Granny to work with her during the day and Dugan took over caregiving duties in the evenings. Eventually, his wife’s employer could no longer accommodate the arrangement, prompting the family to hire outside help.
Learning to ‘meet her where she’s at’
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, asked Meredith to reflect on his experience as a man stepping into a caregiving role that required hiring help rather than “fixing” the problem himself.
“Granny coming to live with us was a struggle for me mentally,” Meredith said. “I was exhausted because I could not figure out why I could not get a 72-, 73-year-old woman to understand, you can’t do this — it will hurt you.”
Meredith described one moment when Granny wanted to cut her hair and used a lighter to try to burn off a piece of it after he took away her scissors and said they would take her to get her hair cut.
“I could not understand in my mind, why does this woman do this? Why can I not get her to understand she’s going to hurt herself?” he said.
Meredith said he came to the realization that he needed to meet Granny where she is.
“Sam taught me that very early on,” Meredith said, referring to Aging Untold expert and gerontologist Sam Cradduck. “You have to meet them where they are.”
Meredith emphasized that lesson for other men in a similar situation.
“For men out there, you’re not going to fix it. The only thing you can do to help the situation is to swallow your pride, swallow your ego and learn to meet them where they’re at,” Meredith said.
Decoding Granny’s signature word: ‘heavy’
Viewers of Meredith’s videos on TikTok and Facebook are familiar with Granny’s repeated word, “heavy.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, asked how the family figures out what she means.
“What is she trying to tell me? Is her stomach hurt? Is her food cold? Is her food too hot?” Meredith said. “When she says ‘my heavy is heavy,’ I keep reiterating, and eventually she’ll move a certain way, she’ll do something with her hands, she’ll nod with her head, and we’ll figure it out.”
Meredith said much of the communication comes down to body language and behaviors learned from living with Granny every day.
Why Meredith started sharing the journey online
Meredith said the decision to document his caregiving journey online came from feeling isolated.
“I felt like I was alone. I felt like nobody in the world understood what was going on within my mind and in my heart,” Meredith said.
He recalled sitting at his kitchen table with a cup of coffee, recording himself talking about his frustrations before posting the video to TikTok. That post led him to a community of other caregivers he didn’t know existed.
Meredith said he’s still learning to manage the volume of response, including tens of thousands of messages and comments.
“You go through a whirlwind of emotions just reading the comments or the messages that come in,” he said.
Meredith said the online community has helped his family tremendously.
“For every one negative person, there’s 500 positives,” he said, and people in that community provide tips, which Meredith uses.
“Not only are they helping us, but they are helping the others that are reading the comments,” Meredith said.
The ‘sandwich generation’ and the cost of care
O’Rourke noted that Meredith and his wife are also raising children while caring for Granny — a dynamic often called the “sandwich generation.”
“We are 100% the sandwich generation,” Meredith said.
In the beginning, he said, the couple struggled to give their children enough attention because of the protocols required to care for Granny. Hiring additional caregivers allowed them “to still be parents for our children and give them the attention that they need and that they deserve as well.”
Meredith also spoke about the cost of care. The family looked into memory care facilities before deciding on the private route, which he described as the more affordable option.
“You go look at nice memory care facilities — we’re talking $10,000 to $15,000 a month,” Meredith said.
He said monetizing the family’s social media content has helped cover the cost of keeping Granny comfortable at home.
“Everyone always asks, are you going to keep her here until her last breath. We will,” Meredith said.
Meredith is also the founder of a nonprofit, also called Taking Care of Granny, which he said is focused solely on helping caregivers.
He said the idea for a nonprofit came from a conversation with another caregiver who documents caring for his wife, who has Parkinson’s disease.
“He was the one that started the idea with me. He was like, ‘What about a nonprofit? You do a nonprofit to provide care to the caregivers,’” Meredith said. “I was like, I like that idea. I don’t know how I’m going to do it, but let me start digging into it.”
Where things stand today Asked how Granny is doing now, Meredith said the disease has progressed. The family now purees her food because of trouble swallowing, and he’s noticed her shuffling her feet while walking, so the family has removed rugs and other trip hazards from the house.
Hospice has also brought in a medical bed to help prevent falls.
“The disease has progressed, and we’re at that point now,” Meredith said. “But given what we’ve been through, I would say she’s doing well.”
How to follow Taking Care of Granny
Key takeaways
- Male caregiving. An estimated 21 million men are currently in caregiving roles for aging or ill loved ones, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving.
- Meet them where they are. Dugan Meredith emphasized that trying to reason with a loved one with dementia rarely works. Caregivers need to adapt to the person’s reality instead.
- The “sandwich generation” faces unique pressure. Balancing young children and an aging parent or relative at the same time requires intentional systems so neither gets neglected.
- Online communities can ease caregiver isolation. Sharing the caregiving journey publicly connected Meredith with a wider community of caregivers facing similar experiences.

title: Jay plans workshop on Walden solar project, possible TIF
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — The Jay Select Board plans to hold a separate workshop on Walden Renewables’ proposed solar development as board members seek more information about potential tax revenue, a possible tax increment financing agreement and questions raised during earlier public hearings.
The workshop is expected to include a general overview of tax increment financing, discussion of Walden Renewables’ proposal and the potential impact on local taxes.
Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere told the board Sept. 28 that discussions about a tax increment financing, or TIF, agreement would typically involve the town assessor, town attorney, Walden and members of the Select Board before a proposal would return to the full board for consideration.
“Ultimately, any TIF is approved by the residents,” LaFreniere said. “It has to go to a vote anyways.”
Board members debated whether those discussions should take place before voters decide the future of the project or afterward. Some questioned whether the town should devote time to developing a financial arrangement before knowing whether residents support the project, while others said voters should have more information about potential revenue before casting ballots.
LaFreniere said Walden has discussed using a structure modeled on a TIF in Sanford. Under her understanding of that arrangement, a TIF district would capture the project’s added taxable value so it would not count against the municipality in calculations involving state revenue sharing and school funding, while payments from the developer would provide revenue to the town.
“I don’t even want to say this because I don’t know enough to make sure that this is correct,” LaFreniere said before explaining her understanding of the Sanford arrangement.
Questions at the meeting included whether payments would be based on the project’s proposed generating capacity or its actual annual production, along with the eventual number of solar panels, acreage involved, buffer zones and screening.
“And that’s part of those discussions,” LaFreniere said. “These are important questions.”
In a follow-up email Wednesday, LaFreniere said she expects the workshop to cover TIFs more broadly as well as the Walden proposal.
“I believe the workshop will be a complete overview of TIFs in general as well as the Walden proposal,” she said.
The board ultimately favored a separate workshop rather than adding the discussion to a regular Select Board meeting. It was noted that a dedicated workshop would be more beneficial to the public.
No date has been set. LaFreniere said Walden is coordinating possible dates with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection and an attorney.
Separately, Walden Renewables will hold a public informational meeting from 5:30-7 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 13, at LaFleurs Restaurant, 224 Main St. The meeting is intended for residents who want information about the proposed solar project directly from the developer.

NASA telescope expected to fall to Earth soon. Here’s where it could land
text:
(CNN) — A large NASA telescope is about to fall to Earth.
The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has been observing asteroids, comets and gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, for 22 years.
The 3,200-pound observatory has fallen to about 200 miles above Earth. An effort to lift it back into a stable orbit failed.
The telescope is expected to enter Earth’s atmosphere in a couple of weeks. Most of it will burn up, but a few chunks might survive and rain down.
Experts say if that happens, the debris will almost definitely fall into the ocean or onto uninhabited land.

title: "Ensure the safety and comfort of Maine people." Gov. Mills urges Congress to boost LIHEAP funding
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
"Ensure the safety and comfort of Maine people." Gov. Mills urges Congress to boost LIHEAP funding
Gov. Janet Mills, D-Maine, is calling on Congress to approve more funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP).
In a letter to Maine's Congressional delegation on Friday, Mills said that the current funding is not enough to meet the growing need caused by the significantly higher home heating costs, compared to last heating season.
The average cost for a gallon of home heating oil in Maine reached an all-time record of $6.02 in late September, before dropping slightly to $5.96, as of Sept. 28. The record was an 81% increase from the same time a year ago.
Maine is the most heating oil-dependent state in the nation, with approximately half of all homes relying on oil as their primary heat source.
“Maine people should not be forced to choose between staying warm and putting food on the table because the President chose to drag the country into a needless war,” Mills wrote in her letter. “Congress should significantly increase these funds to ensure the safety and comfort of Maine people heading into the winter season.”
Mills said in her letter that the money already appropriated did not fully factor in the impacts of the war in Iran.
“I urge you to work with your colleagues to provide a supplemental appropriation for LIHEAP to ensure that Maine people are not left to shoulder the burden of the President’s blunder,” she wrote.
Mills urged eligible Mainers to apply for heating assistance for this winter as soon as possible. The application window for the program opened in August and will continue until funds are exhausted.
Local community action groups that help administer the money say they have been very busy.
“Every year seems to be a little bit of a new challenge, a new curveball thrown to us as the heating season approaches. This year, definitely the high costs are on everybody’s mind. Right now, we are having more phone calls than we have ever experienced this early in the season, and I think it’s just sheer panic and worry with the cost of fuel," said Heidi Rackliffe, Chief Program Officer of Avec Community Action. "Fuel tanks are low now and people are already in a position where they’re not able to financially put fuel in their tanks."
On Sept. 17, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and dozens of other senators sent a letter to U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to release funds for LIHEAP swiftly and at the highest level possible once funding became available on October 1.
Last year, Maine households received more than $42 million in LIHEAP funds.
After the Administration proposed zeroing out funding for LIHEAP in its fiscal year 2027 budget plan, the Senate Appropriations Committee, which Collins chairs, pushed to protect LIHEAP and continue funding for the program at more than $4 billion this year.
The Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (P.L. 119-103) requires the Department of Health and Human Services to distribute no less than 90% of its total LIHEAP allotment by Nov. 1, 2026.
In late September, Democratic candidate for governor in Maine Hannah Pingree called on Congress and the Trump Administration to double Maine's LIHEAP funding allocation.
Republican candidate for governor Bobby Charles has also called for doubling Maine's LIHEAP funding as part of his Emergency 207 plan, which he released on Sept. 28.
During Thursday's debate with the candidates for Maine's Second Congressional District on WMTW, Republican Paul LePage said LIHEAP needs to be fully funded and that the Trump Administration needs to make sure the money is released quickly.

title: Aging Untold: How to spot the signs you need to step back from caregiving
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, explore how to recognize when family caregiving demands have become too overwhelming and why stepping back can be the healthiest choice for everyone involved.
Plus, find out how to safely navigate physical intimacy and rebuild confidence after a serious health scare like a heart attack or stroke.
Then, we introduce a Virginia medical transport driver using line-dancing classes and community outreach to inspire local seniors.
Providing care for a loved one can be an honor, but it can also wear you down over time.
If you are experiencing caregiver burnout, it might be time to step back.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing how to admit you’re struggling, handle the conflicting emotions, get a break and find support.
Fear of another major health event like a heart attack or stroke can affect more than your routine — it can affect your relationship and your sex life.
“So many times people are so afraid of that fear of, if I do something, especially intercourse, I’m going to have another heart attack,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “You have to realize you’re going to have a new normal now. It’s not that you’re going back to where you were, but it’s a new norm, and you just have to talk with a physician. Cardiac rehab is a big deal.”
The Aging Untold experts are sharing how couples can navigate intimacy during recovery, from getting medical clearance and easing anxiety to finding a new normal together.
Many consumers, including older shoppers, are seeking out pre-owned and sustainable products, retail experts say.
Stephanie Hernandez, a secondhand stylist based in Washington, D.C., helps her clients build a one-of-a-kind, sustainable wardrobe — because many want to shop more responsibly but don’t have the time to do it themselves.
Richard Caple says he didn’t want to teach the line-dancing class at Club 17, but he said yes. Now he’s attached to the seniors in his class, and it brings him joy when they share how it is helping them.
