title: ‘Learn from Lutz’: Sharing his son’s traffic death to encourage safe-driving
text:
GEORGIA (InvestigateTV) — Mike Lutzenkirchen is sharing his son’s story with teens and young adults in hopes of preventing fatal crashes caused by unsafe driving.
Both had blood alcohol levels above the legal limit.
“It’s just like that. There’s a crash last night. Your son is dead,” Mike Lutzenkirchen said, recalling a conversation with a coroner the day after Philip’s death.
“We went to a black hole for two weeks. We’re trying to figure out what do you do in life,” Lutzenkirchen said.
A new foundation
Lutzenkirchen created the Lutzie 43 Foundation after his son’s death. The foundation works with schools, government agencies and law enforcement to address the more than 42,000 annual traffic deaths in the United States.
The foundation holds summits, including one at Georgia Military College, where students take part in breakout sessions.
The foundation’s message asks drivers to take 43 seconds when they get in a car — a reference to Philip’s jersey number at Auburn — to make sure they have a clear head, clear hands, clear eyes, and to buckle their seat belt.
The summit also covers sharing the road with truckers and demonstrates how state transportation professionals and first responders work the scene of a crash.
School and law enforcement response
Georgia Military College Assistant Principal Jennifer Deason said students attending the summit are distracted by their phones and the freedom of driving, which leads them to ignore safety.
“Every student that attends here, I see them as my children. And so to know that they are in danger, if every time they get on the highway, whether or not they are distracted or not,” Deason said.
Capt. Maurice Raines, deputy director of the Georgia Governor’s Office of Highway Safety, said fatal crashes are 100% preventable.
“Hopefully by educating, the word will get out that we need to change our behavior. And if that doesn’t work, law enforcement will work to try to change that behavior,” Raines said.
Raines said more than 200 traffic deaths have occurred in Georgia so far this year.
Nationwide goal
Lutzenkirchen’s goal is a recognizable nationwide campaign sharing his son’s story.
“We’re trying to take the mistakes that Philip and his friend made that weekend and just make a difference. Live like Lutz, love like Lutz, and learn from Lutz,” Lutzenkirchen said.
The Lutzie 43 Foundation’s safe driving summit also demonstrates how state transportation professionals and first responders work a crash scene, allowing students to learn from multiple perspectives why driving is both dangerous and a privilege.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports seat belts can reduce the risk of death or injury by nearly half.

title: Iowa lawmakers to vote on raising tax incentive cap for a $15B steel plant
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Iowa lawmakers returned to the Statehouse Friday to consider expanding the ceiling on state tax incentives in an effort to secure a $15 billion steel plant project for the state.
President Donald Trump announced the plant Monday alongside Iowa elected officials, heralding the project as a major economic and national security investment.
Five weeks before the midterm elections, Republicans seized on the promise of good-paying jobs and a central role for the heartland in the push for American steel manufacturing. It’s celebrated as an opportunity for southeast Iowa, an area along the Mississippi River that once thrived as a hub for industry but has since suffered from shuttered facilities and dwindled populations. Still, the deal and the tax abatements it could carry have also been met with some skepticism in rural Iowa and Des Moines alike.
And while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the “deal is done,” state action and local officials in the days since suggest otherwise.
Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds on Tuesday called lawmakers back for the special session, saying “reasonable and limited updates” to the state’s economic development program were needed to advance the project proposed by Mesabi Metallics, a Minnesota company owned by the India-based conglomerate Essar Group.
The terms of an agreement between the state and Mesabi Metallics have been outlined in a memorandum of understanding; neither provided a copy when asked for one.
While the specific location remains undisclosed, elected officials have indicated the project is set for Lee County. Still, the chair of the county board of supervisors said this week that the company has not yet committed to the project site.
Mesabi Metallics “looks forward to breaking ground in the near future,” Jesse Harris, a spokesperson for the company, said in a statement Tuesday. He said the company is “optimistic” that changes to the law will be enacted based on conversations with legislators and elected officials.
The White House said Thursday that the Iowa project is only possible because of the president’s policies.
“President Trump has a proven record of securing historic investments, creating high-paying jobs, and bringing manufacturing back to the United States,” spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
The pivot to Iowa seems to have moved quickly
Iowa state Rep. Matthew Rinker said he joined conversations on a potential project in his district several months ago.
Still, as recently as July, job listings on Mesabi’s website for the steel plant were based in Paducah, Kentucky, according to a version saved in the web archive. Jobs are now listed for Iowa, though the job responsibilities for a government relations manager still include interfacing with Kentucky’s economic development team.
While the company had been in discussion with Kentucky officials, the scale of the project “more than doubled over the negotiation period,” spokesperson Brandon Mattingly said in an email.
Iowa “did get kind of into the mix late,” said Rinker, a Republican. “I think once they got here, they realized this is where they needed to be.”
First, though, changes in state law are necessary for Iowa to compete against other states for the project, Reynolds said in her proclamation. She is asking lawmakers to modify the economic development program so that tax credits on eligible projects can be worth up to 10% of investments, an increase from the current 5%, and paid out over 10 years instead of five.
For a $15 billion project, that could mean up to $1.5 billion in kickbacks payable over 10 years once the plant is running and contingent on jobs.
A major investment opportunity could carry risks for local communities
Lee County does not have any zoning or permitting ordinances that would be required for the project itself. The company would need a permit for hauling on the county’s secondary roads.
The scale of an investment such as this one is asymmetrical with the legal and administrative capacity of a small, rural community, said Anthony Pipa, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who studies development and policy in rural areas.
While there’s a lot of potential upside to a project of this scale, that asymmetry also leaves those communities vulnerable and without significant leverage, he said. Pipa also pointed to examples of massive proposed investments that didn’t come to fruition.
In neighboring Wisconsin, for example, Trump announced a Foxconn Technology Group display screen manufacturing facility and its promise of 13,000 jobs, saying it would be the “eighth wonder of the world.” The state Legislature, at the urging of then-Republican Gov. Scott Walker, approved up to $3 billion in state tax breaks for the Taiwanese manufacturing company if it hit employment and investment benchmarks, though those were significantly scaled back by Walker’s successor, Democratic Gov. Tony Evers.
Foxconn has since dramatically reduced the scope of the project and now says it will employ about 2,600 people by the end of 2029.
Wisconsin Democrat Gordon Hintz, a leading opponent of the Foxconn project when he was a state lawmaker, said he sees parallels with what’s promised in Iowa.
“The idea of having domestic production in an Upper Midwest, post-industrial economy has a lot of appeal,” said Hintz, who is now a county executive. “The devil’s in the details.”
The Lee County Economic Development Board, which Rinker said was pivotal in bringing the Mesabi project to Iowa, said the plant brings “extraordinary opportunity,” while acknowledging the ongoing questions that need to be addressed “about workforce, infrastructure, housing, and community services.”
“We take both seriously,” board CEO and President Emily Benjamin said in a statement. “Our job is to help make sure growth like this benefits the people who live and work here.”
___
Associated Press reporter Scott Bauer contributed from Madison, Wisconsin.

title: Obituary: Rosemarie (Rowell) Granger
text: AUGUSTA – Rosemarie Rowell Granger, 83, of Woolwich and China, passed away peacefully on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, after a brief illness. “Ree” was born on Oct. 13, 1942, in Hartford, Conn., to William Clogston Rowell and Margaret O’Brien Rowell. She attended St. Joseph’s Roman Catholic Academy, Deering High School, and Westbrook College in Portland before earning her bachelor’s and master’s degrees from the University of New Hampshire. A lifelong Roman Catholic, Ree was a devout communicant of St. Mary’s Church in Bath. Ree’s greatest passion was Morgan horses, and she devoted many joyful years to showing and caring for them. She competed in and won Morgan Horse shows throughout the East, notably earning second place at Nationals with her beloved horse, Jack McNary. She also showed dogs, and adored her childhood Dalmatian, Bonnie. Rosemarie met Clark Granger of Lee, N.H., while attending UNH. They were married on Aug. 31, 1965, in Portland, and settled in Woolwich in 1969. Together, they shared over six decades of marriage, family, hard work, and cherished memories. Ree began her teaching career in 1965, dedicatedly serving as an elementary school teacher in Bath for 40 years and touching the lives of generations of children. She had a special gift for knowing exactly what students needed and supporting their success. Ree and Clark raised their children, Kym and Greg, built a home, and established a farm together. She was a constant support in her children’s endeavors, even becoming a certified gymnastics judge. Her family was always at the heart of her life, and she gave generously of her time and energy to everyone around her. In 2024, Clark and Ree built a home and moved full-time to South China to live on the farm that Clark and Greg had nurtured for many years, bringing her closer to her son and grandchildren. Rosemarie was known for her perseverance, determination, and high standards. She believed deeply in doing things well and encouraged those around her to always give their best. Beneath her trademark strength was a deep sense of responsibility and a steadfast love for her family. Rosemarie was preceded in death by her parents; and her brother, Michael Rowell.She is survived by her loving husband, Clark, of China; her daughter, Kimberly Ann Granger, of Bath, her son, Gregory Granger, of China; and her cherished grandchildren, Seamus and Keagan Gethicker, of Bath, and Katherine and William Granger of China. She is also survived by her sister, Peggy Ann Keaney, of Portland; Kym’s partner, Gaetan Breton; her close friend, Donna Smith; five nieces and nephews; and three grandnieces. The family wishes to express gratitude to MaineGeneral Health and Augusta Rehab for the compassionate care they provided to Rosemarie during the last 11 weeks of her life. A Celebration of Life will be held at Montsweag Restaurant in Woolwich on Sunday, Oct. 25, from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m. All are welcome.Arrangements have been entrusted to Plummer Funeral Home, 983 Ridge Rd., Windsor, ME 04363. Condolences, stories and photos may be shared by visiting http://www.plummerfh.com. In lieu of flowers, memorial contributions may be made to a charity of one’s choice.

title: Collamore Wants to Finish What He Started in House District 45
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After serving in local government for several decades, Clinton Collamore hopes to help Mainers across the state in his bid for House District 45.
Collamore, I-Waldoboro, faces Rebecca Stephens, R-Waldoboro, in the race in the race for the district, which consists of Bremen, Friendship, Louds Island Township, Waldoboro, and Washington.
If elected, Collamore hopes to lead with empathy and be a bipartisan voice for the constituents of House District 45.
“We don’t need any more partisan bickering,” he said. “We need real answers to help Mainers.”
A Waldoboro native, Collamore attended Medomak Valley High School and the University of Maine, graduating in 2009 with degrees in science, public administration, and business. He said growing up in a family that farmed and fished exposed him to working on the water. Collamore works as a lobsterman today after starting in 1969.
Collamore worked for several decades at Bath Iron Works, where he said he got involved in the labor movement and eventually became president of the shipbuilders’ union. During his time in leadership, his work enshrined his belief that “we should be taking care of the working class,” he said.
“I found out what that long table was going to be about, negotiations and whatnot,” he said.
Collamore has also served several stints on the Waldoboro Select Board, beginning in 1987. He said the experiences allowed him to work closely with and learn from five different town managers, as well as countless other select board members.
He has also served on the Waldoboro Planning Board and the town’s shellfish and comprehensive planning committees.
Collamore was previously state representative for House District 45, elected in 2022. He resigned in February 2023 after being found guilty for a violation of the Maine Clean Election Act and signature forgery. He served three days in jail and performed 100 hours of community service.
Looking back on the events, Collamore said he made a mistake and had not intended to violate the rules about donations when running as a clean elections candidate.
Collamore ran for office in 2022 as a Democrat. This election, he is on the ballot as an independent, a decision he said he made after feeling that intense partisanship was infringing on elected officials’ ability to make meaningful change.
“When I was in another party, I said, ‘This isn’t working,’ and it’s got worse and worse and worse,” Collamore said. “I’m hoping, as an independent, we can do the people over parties, support local fisheries and farms and small businesses. We’ve got to do what we can for them.”
Collamore said affordability is one of the top concerns of voters in District 45.
“Fuel is out of sight now, all (those) things are triple,” he said.
Collamore praised the Waldoboro Food Pantry and Free Clothing Closet. He said the work of their volunteers has been “really successful” in supporting the community as costs have risen.
“Things like that really help people out,” he said.
Collamore believes decreases in funding from the federal government are negatively affecting many areas of policy, including education budgets.
“That’s a trickle down, you know, once you start cutting it all trickles down to the states, and then eventually, to even keep the status quo, it’s going to be more on the taxpayers,” Collamore said.
In regard to education, he said he supports the recent changes to the state subsidy formula for schools. He said there are concerns about residents on fixed incomes who can no longer afford to stay in their homes because of rising property taxes, and that he wants to ensure the state meets its funding obligations.
“I don’t know if it’s a broken system or not, but I think it’s something that the education committee ought to really sit down, and put a group of concerned people together, and come up with a vision,” Collamore said.
Improving Maine schools is a campaign priority for Collamore, especially regarding the maintenance of facilities and attracting teachers to the state. He pointed to Medomak Valley High School in Waldoboro as an example of the importance of putting resources into schools early on to prevent more costly work later. In June, RSU 40 voters approved a $24.9 million capital improvement bond to improve upgrades at Medomak that the school district said could no longer be delayed.
“The school really needed work, and it takes a long time when you find something, to save up for something,” Collamore said.
Encouraging qualified teachers to come to and stay in the state by offering competitive salaries and professional resources was another one of Collamore’s goals. .
“We’ve just got to keep hiring and trying to find the right people,” he said.
In conjunction with one of his other campaign priorities – supporting local fisheries and farms – Collamore said he would support nutrition programs and the Farm and Sea to School initiative, which brings local food into Maine school cafeterias.
Another substantial challenge facing Maine residents is finding affordable housing, Collamore said. If elected, he said he would pursue the organization of a “housing group” of various organizations dedicated to collaborating on building more housing units.
Collamore cited an influx of out-of-state residents purchasing property in Maine as one reason for the jump in prices.
“It’s a dream for a rich person from out of state, I guess, and that’s who’s buying them all, but there’s no one local buying them,” he said.
When it comes to waterfront regulations, Collamore said the state should have a smaller role, citing varying environments and needs across the state. He said that along the Medomak River, industry and recreation find balance and don’t require legislative intervention.
“It’s just ingrained in us,” he said. “It’s probably how we’ve adjusted over the years. That’s just how it is, we share.”
Regarding infrastructure, Collamore said he supports allocating more money into improving it. He emphasized a prioritization of roads because of their daily importance. He referenced Route 220, where he said he gives road crews who try to keep them patched credit.
“I’ve destroyed a part in the front of my truck,” he said. “The roads are miserable.”
Collamore has been endorsed by the Maine AFL-CIO.
For more information, go to collamoreforhouse.com or find the Clint Collamore for Maine House District 45 Facebook page.
The general election takes place Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: Trump heads to Alabama: 'I go there because they want to see me there'
text:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. (AP) — President Donald Trump will continue his midterm campaign swing with a rally in deep red Alabama Friday, returning to the place where he drew his first mega crowd.
Trump will be stumping for Republican candidates, including Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who is running against former Democratic Sen. Doug Jones for Alabama governor, and state Rep. Rhett Marques, who is seeking to flip Alabama’s newly redrawn 2nd Congressional District. The rally will also give Trump the chance to be surrounded by some of his most loyal supporters as he confronts dismal poll numbers and growing pessimism from his party about their chances of holding onto the House and Senate in November.
“I’m going because you have to thank these states that are with you 1,000% and I haven’t been there in a while and I want to just thank ’em,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House Thursday. “I go there because they want to see me there.”
Trump held his first mega-rally in Mobile more than a decade ago, drawing what some estimated to be 30,000 people to a college football stadium. The huge crowd made clear that Trump was more than a celebrity candidate and had the potential to make waves in the 2016 primary.
Trump is planning an aggressive travel schedule between now and November, with trips to the most competitive battlegrounds including Ohio and Texas. But his decision to start his tour in deep red states that have garnered relatively little attention this election cycle underscores the challenges he faces.
Alabama is friendly turf as voters have soured on Trump
While Trump maintains a loyal base of supporters who turn out when he is on the ballot, he has become increasingly toxic. A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research this week found that only about 3 in 10 U.S. adults approve of how Trump is handling his job as president. And when it comes to the economy, most blame him for rising prices.
Trump, however, has repeatedly dismissed concerns about high costs and gas prices as his unpopular war in Iran drags on.
Friday night’s rally will offer Republicans the optics of a large, cheering crowd as they try to build enthusiasm. Speakers will include Tuberville and Republican Rep. Barry Moore, who is running for Tuberville’s seat, and said the president’s rally “will be the jet fuel we need to win big in Alabama.”
While Republicans remain the heavy favorites in Alabama’s statewide campaigns, they face a more challenging political landscape this year, despite redistricting efforts.
Mobile is near Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, where Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures is trying to fend off a challenge from Trump-backed Marques after its lines were redrawn to be more red as part of a larger effort to help the party keep control of the U.S. House.
The district is one of several Democratic-leaning districts across the South that were reshaped to Republican advantage after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling this year that severely weakened the Voting Rights Act, a Civil-Rights era law that has increased minority representation in Congress and elsewhere. Figures was first elected to the House in 2024, giving Alabama two Black representatives for the first time in its history.
Trump’s rally will also reach Florida voters
Mobile is also next to Florida’s panhandle, a Republican stronghold. Party officials hope the rally will help to bolster Trump-backed candidates there, including Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who is running for governor.
In a meeting on Capitol Hill this week, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles told GOP senators that Trump would be campaigning aggressively until the Nov. 3 midterms, with events almost every day.
Friday’s rally is also expected to highlight the recent approval of the $3.2 billion Mobile River Bridge and Bayway project. U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is appearing with Gov. Kay Ivey at a groundbreaking earlier in the day.
Ivey’s office called the project the largest transportation project in Alabama history and necessary to support Alabama’s Gulf Coast region and beyond.
___
Colvin reported from New York.

title: Scammers are using everyday tech tools to flood your phone
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Scam calls and texts have become the top way scammers reach their victims, outpacing overall scam growth, according to a new report from the Better Business Bureau.
Josh Planos, a spokesperson for the Better Business Bureau, said the scale of the problem continues to grow.
“This is a very lucrative industry for scammers, and they really seem to be interested in growing and scaling their efforts in ways that we’ve never seen before,” Planos said.
The BBB’s International Investigations Initiative analyzed nearly 440,000 Scam Tracker reports since 2022. Planos said scammers are frequently relying on legitimate digital services to reach victims.
“In a lot of cases, they are exploiting legal services like virtual or VOIP phone numbers, bulk texting platforms, website builders, AI voice and video generation and social media ad platforms, all of which have very low barriers to entry,” Planos said.
Planos said the report found regulators are struggling to keep up with how scammers operate.
“The study really does argue that the current telecom rules were written for the landline era of phones,” Planos said. “We outline a number of fixes. We should expand two existing FCC rules, which are the telemarketing sales rule and the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, that limit telemarketing calls. We would recommend that it be brought in to explicitly cover text messages, which currently have weaker protection than calls.”
Planos said there is one simple step every consumer can take immediately: turning on a phone’s spam filter.
He also noted that a new or unfamiliar phone number does not necessarily mean a new scam. Scammers can change phone numbers quickly and often do so as part of the same ongoing scheme.
The BBB also recommends being suspicious of texts offering jobs or loans that were never applied for. If such a text arrives, the BBB recommends ending the conversation and avoiding any links sent by an unknown sender.

title: G7 nations to release ‘substantial’ amounts of diesel as prices hover near record highs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Group of Seven industrial nations said they agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel recently hit record prices in the United States, where President Donald Trump said the diesel release would happen “immediately.”
Trump and his Republican Party face pressure to address surging prices ahead of November’s midterm elections. Trump announced the action Friday on social media, saying, “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately.”
The president faces lagging approval ratings as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods.
Gas prices in the U.S. and abroad have soared during the eight-month-long war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. Trump has insisted prices will come down after the war, though there’s no end in sight.
The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.
Trump had a conversation overnight with French President Emmanuel Macron, the chair of the G7, about the need to address rising fuel prices and the availability of petroleum products, according to the French Embassy in the U.S. Macron on Friday then chaired a videoconference of G7 leaders to discuss the issue.
France holds the rotating presidency of the G7 group and made the announcement in a statement released after video-conference talks that Macron presided over. The International Energy Agency will coordinate the effort to combat soaring fuel prices. “We will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels (MB) to begin immediately over 4 months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners,” the statement said.
A new AP-NORC poll found that a majority of U.S. adults blame Trump for higher prices, and approval on his handling of the economy hit a new low.
Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a disconnect between his achievements and the public’s view of his work. Trump this week gave himself an A-plus for his work on the economy but said “we’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion.”

title: What to know about Kennebunk’s plans for a new cell tower
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The town of Kennebunk is planning for the development of a new cell tower to improve service coverage downtown.
At a planning board meeting on Sept. 14, the town hosted a public hearing where residents could voice their concerns and ask questions about the project.
Attorney Michael Dolan spoke on behalf of Wireless Edge Towers, the applicant proposing the cell tower plan. He said the proposed location, on Factory Pasture Lane, was chosen by the town in part because of its location in the town’s industrial zone and its tree coverage.
The proposal calls for a 176-foot monopole antenna tower with a fenced equipment compound. Dolan said tree height on Factory Pasture Lane averages about 70 feet.
Christopher Osterrieder, Kennebunk director of community development, said the project is nearing the tail end of the planning process. Here’s what residents should know.
THE TIMELINE
Osterrieder said the project is in such early stages that it’s hard to pinpoint an exact timeline, but that the town has granted final conditional approval. As long as conditions are met, Osterrieder said, the project should not need further planning board discussion.
The conditions include additional performance guarantees to the town and an updated landscaping plan.
Osterrieder said depending on the timing from Wireless Edge, construction could begin as early as this winter or spring.
THE LOOK
At the Sept. 14 hearing, one resident voiced concerns about the visibility of the tower from Water Street, asking for a deeper explanation into the necessary height for the tower.
Dolan explained that, while some towers can reach up to 200 feet in height, Wireless Edge aimed to keep it as low as possible while still managing to fill the gaps in coverage provided by carriers like Verizon and AT&T.
Osterrieder said his hope is that — especially for businesses and residents close by — the tower won’t be as great an eyesore as some fear.
Along with tree cover, he said, the company is also considering ways to mitigate aesthetic issues, like making the tower a neutral color that would make it easier on the eyes.
THE COST
The tower construction costs will be covered by Wireless Edge, Osterrieder said.
Stephen Houdlette, Kennebunk’s director of economic vitality, said the town is not incurring any costs. The town owns the land and is leasing the plot to Wireless Edge, which will provide financial compensation to the town.
Houdlette said the project will also contribute to a regional network of public safety operators in York County while improving connection throughout the region.

title: "Cannot mistake progress for the end." Fatal overdoses in Maine are down, but concerns continue
text:
"Cannot mistake progress for the end of the crisis." Fatal overdoses in Maine are down, but concerns continue
The number of deadly overdoses in Maine is down this year compared to last year, while the number of non-fatal overdoses is up.
According to the monthly overdose report from the Maine Drug Data Hub for July, which is the most recent report available, the total number of confirmed and suspected fatal overdoses for January to July 2026 is 209, 10.3% lower than the total confirmed fatal overdoses for January to June 2025.
The total number of nonfatal overdoses for January to July 2026 is 4,343, 2.3% higher than the reported nonfatal overdoses for January–June 2025.
That report shows that Portland had 36 confirmed and suspected fatal overdoses from January to July of this year, compared to 50 during the same time period last year. The number in Lewiston dropped from 28 during that time frame last year to nine this year. In Bangor, the number dropped from 35 to 24.
Joanne Grant, Chief Growth Officer at Sweetser, spoke with Maine's Total Coverage on Friday about the data and needs facing Mainers.
How should we understand this mixed picture in Maine's overdose data?
Any reduction in lives lost is meaningful, and it reflects years of work across prevention, treatment, recovery support, and the wider availability of naloxone. But we cannot mistake progress for the end of the crisis. Each number represents a person, a family, and often another chance to connect someone with care.
The rise in nonfatal overdoses is an important reminder that recovery is rarely a straight line. Someone may interact with an emergency responder, clinician, case manager, peer supporter, educator, or family member at a critical moment. How that person responds can help open the door to treatment and recovery - or unintentionally make someone less willing to ask for help again.
What does effective support look like for someone living with a substance use disorder?
It starts with seeing the person, not defining them by a diagnosis or a difficult moment. Effective support is compassionate, evidence-based, and free of shame. It also meets people where they are. A person who is unsure about change needs a different conversation than someone who is actively building a recovery plan.
Professionals need practical skills: understanding how substances affect the brain and behavior, recognizing how substance use can look different across populations, using motivational interviewing, and connecting people with treatment, peer support, and other recovery resources. Those skills build trust, and trust can be the bridge to the next step in someone's recovery journey.
Why is continuing education for substance use professionals so important in this work?
Substance use care continues to evolve. The drug supply changes, research advances, and the language we use can either reduce stigma or reinforce it. Even experienced professionals benefit from revisiting their approach and learning alongside people in other roles.
This is not only for specialists in addiction treatment. Substance use can surface in primary care, behavioral health, schools, hospitals, housing programs, corrections, and community services. The more prepared those professionals are, the more likely a person is to encounter informed support wherever they reach out.
What new learning opportunity is Sweetser making available?
Sweetser's Training Institute now offers a Substance Use Disorder professional development certificate built around five workshops. Participants must complete four required workshops:
- Treating Substance Use Disorder
- Substance Use: Effects and Awareness
- Understanding Substance Use Disorders in Special Populations
- Motivational Interviewing and Stage of Change
Then they get to choose an elective. The elective options focus on either recovery planning and self-help and peer resources, or the neuroscience of addiction and the impact of substance use disorder on the brain. Together, the workshops give professionals a stronger, more practical foundation for supporting people with dignity throughout recovery.
How can people learn more or register?
The full professional development catalog and registration information are available at Sweetser.org/Training. Whether you work directly in substance use treatment or support people in another setting, continuing to learn is one way each of us can help sustain Maine's progress and ensure more people find hope and healing.

title: AARP Poll: Older Maine voters show sharp ticket-splitting in Senate, governor races
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - AARP has released its annual poll of Maine voters 50 and older.
Turnout is expected to be high once again among older voters, but pollsters report notable ticket-splitting among the nearly 1,000 Mainers surveyed.
While Sen. Susan Collins holds a 6-point lead over Troy Jackson among voters 50 and older, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree is polling strongly across all age groups against Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett.
Survey respondents ranked affordability, protecting Social Security, healthcare costs, and Medicare as their top concerns, with 60% of older Mainers reporting that they are worried about personal finances.
Voters 50 and older make up about 44% of Maine’s population, but casted 59% of all ballots in the 2024 presidential election.
Pollsters say that outsized turnout, paired with Maine’s status as both the nation’s oldest state and a key battleground, makes this voting bloc critical.
“Maine had the biggest gap between the Senate and gubernatorial votes, and it’s really 50+ voters that are driving that gap,” explained Matt Hogan, an AARP pollster partner from Impact Research. “We see a 10-point gap overall between the Senate margin and the gubernatorial margin, but among 50+, that gap grows to 16 points. Among seniors, it grows to 21 points, which I think just really, again, underscores the critical importance of the 50+ vote.“
Ultimately, AARP found a strong majority want candidates who pledge to protect Social Security from cuts for those who paid into it and take immediate action to lower healthcare costs.

title: Do you need to step back from caregiving? How to spot the signs
text:
(Aging Untold) — Caregiving is often called an act of love, but over time it can wear down your mind, your body and your relationships.
The Aging Untold experts explain the warning signs of caregiver burnout, why stepping back can actually be the safer choice and how to make the transition without falling into guilt.
“It’s OK if you’re even deliberating quitting”
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, says the first step is giving yourself permission to admit you’re struggling.
“The first thing I would say is, it’s OK if you’re even deliberating quitting. And it’s very understandable,” O’Rourke said. “If you’re really, really tired, you’re not sleeping, everybody’s making you mad, and you’re getting burnt out — the first thing I would do is do whatever you need to do to get unburned out. Don’t make a decision in the middle of that stress.”
O’Rourke recommends caregivers step back, let someone else fill in and let their nervous system settle before making any long-term decision.
“Get your central nervous system kind of dialed back a bit, and then make the decision,” she said. “If you’re going to make the decision — I want to quit — then have a plan. What’s the transition plan? Is it a community? Is it a relative? Is it a paid caregiver, whatever it is.”
Expect “buyer’s remorse” after the decision
O’Rourke said caregivers who do step back should prepare for a wave of conflicting emotions afterward.
“Be fully prepared to what I call buyer’s remorse,” O’Rourke said. “You make the decision and then you regret it, and you’re back and forth. ‘I’m a bad daughter.’ ‘I couldn’t do it.’ So there’s some back-and-forth emotions. I’ve had clients do this and they end up quitting. And then I have others — they got the rest they needed, and then they went back and did it differently.”
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, compared unmanaged caregiver stress to a fire waiting to happen.
“We often love to tell caregivers, don’t let yourself get burnout. But listen, guys — the match is lit, the kindling’s sitting there, and there’s literally gasoline on it,” Cradduck said. “And there’s not oftentimes water in the area to put the fire out. We fail to tell people how not to burn out.”
Respite care can offer a reset
Cradduck pointed to hospice respite care as one option for families whose loved one has reached that stage of care.
“If your loved one has reached the stage of hospice, hospice respite care is part of that program,” Cradduck said. “You can have your loved one, if they’re in the home, transported to a community for a week to 10 days. And they can do this every quarter. It can give you that reset and that break. And then you can go, ‘OK, I can do this a little longer.’ Or maybe you’re like, ‘You know what, I can’t.’”
O’Rourke added that respite care isn’t limited to hospice situations.
“If they’re not terminal, communities have respite care. Home health has respite care too,” O’Rourke said. “I love the idea of just saying, temporarily, I’m taking a leave of absence.”
Love doesn’t mean you have the ability to do the job
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said one of the hardest parts of caregiving is separating love for a person from the physical and emotional capacity to care for them.
“Being a caregiver takes away from your identity over time,” Rogers said. “One of the hardships is understanding that love doesn’t mean ability. When you recognize that you’re at a crossroad, I think that’s really empowering, because if you continue to do what you know is not working out, you’re going to take it out on your body physically as well. And then the resentment comes in, and then that fight-or-flight — you’re stuck in this mode and you just can’t heal. It becomes detrimental to both parties.”
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose shared what she has seen.
“I see people that say, ‘I loved my mom all the way to heaven. It was the greatest honor of my life,’” Ambrose said. “And then I see other people that say, ‘I can’t put my husband in a home. My children are ready to support me doing that, but I just can’t do it, and I don’t know what to do.’”
Ambrose noted that overwhelmed caregivers sometimes reach a point of hopelessness.
“Sometimes caregivers don’t outlive the person they’re caring for,” Ambrose said. “That’s sad when people are so overwhelmed that they may hope that they just pass away in their sleep, and that’s the way they see the burden being lifted.”
Caregiving doesn’t have to mean hands-on, 24/7 work
Ambrose said families should remind caregivers that stepping back from hands-on duties doesn’t mean stepping away from the relationship.
“Maybe mom needs even more than just, ‘Mom, we’re ready to support you when you’re ready,’” Ambrose said. “Maybe she needs to be rescued, because many caregivers do not outlive the spouse or the parent they’re caring for. But here’s the deal: Caregiving doesn’t have to be 24/7 hands-on. It can be advocacy and still being the spouse, still being the mom, still being the daughter.”
Ambrose described leverage as the key to sustainable caregiving.
“How can you use leverage? Leverage is three things: it’s systems, people and tools,” Ambrose said. “You may not know what those are, but you can reach out to people that work in home care, home health, the doctor’s office, the social worker at the hospital. Just keep asking questions, and you’ll find the resource to the resources. You’ll find your answers.”
Give yourself permission to get help
Cradduck said many caregivers stay in unsustainable situations because of a sense of duty tied to marriage vows or family roles.
“The problem that I see so frequently is the duty – It’s my duty. ‘Sickness and in health, better or worse — and this is the worst, and this is the sickness,’” Cradduck said. “I say you can still live those out as the spouse and not be the one that’s doing all the work. Try your darndest to find somebody that can help you out and give you that break. And then if that break’s what you need on a permanent level, go ahead and have somebody else step into the role. Give yourself permission. This is the hardest job you will ever do.”
Key takeaways
- Love doesn’t automatically equal capacity. Being the closest emotionally or geographically doesn’t mean you’re the one who has to have the skills or ability to provide hands-on care.
- Burnout harms both people — the caregiver and the person receiving care — through resentment, stress and physical health decline.
- Stepping away may be the healthiest choice.
- You can exit in planned stages — rest to clear your head, plan finances and arrange who will fill gaps in coverage.
- Caregiving can mean advocacy, not just hands-on labor. Using “leverage” — systems, people and tools — can let you stay involved without doing everything yourself.

title: Every Marvel Cinematic Universe Movie Since ‘Endgame,’ Ranked From Worst to Best
text:
Every Marvel Cinematic Universe Movie Since ‘Avengers: Endgame,’ Ranked From Worst to Best
Officially, there are six phases of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. There were six movies in Phase One (which started with Iron Man and ended with The Avengers), six in Phase Two (from Iron Man 3 to Ant-Man), 11 in Phase Three (Captain America: Civil War to Spider-Man: Far From Home), seven in Phase Four (Black Widow to Black Panther: Wakanda Forever), six in Phase Five (Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania to Thunderbolts*), and four in the current Phase Six.
But realistically, you can boil all of those films down to two distinct eras: Before and after Avengers: Endgame. Canonically, Marvel refers to that first era as “The Infinity Saga,” and that second one as “The Multiverse Saga.” After that, no doubt, will be “The Mutant Saga,” anchored by the studio’s already-announced X-Men movie.
Even a hardcore Marvel zombie would have to admit: So far, the Multiverse Saga has failed to match the Infinity Saga. The highs are lower, and the lows are way more frequent. That could all change once we get to Avengers: Secret Wars, but it’s been years since the MCU generated the sort of rabid fan excitement that was a regular occurrence back in that pre-Endgame era.
As this second era reaches its climax with Avengers: Doomsday and Secret Wars, it’s instructive to look at everything that’s come so far. When you lay it all out, and rank all these post-Endgame Marvel movies from worst to best, you can see that the company may need some heroes of its own to come to their rescue. (Perhaps the X-Men will fit the bill.)

title: Father of four with stage 4 cancer gets liver transplant from surprise donor
text:
Father of four with stage 4 cancer gets liver transplant from a stranger
Kyler Hess is a father of four battling stage 4 colorectal cancer. Doctors told him a liver from a living donor will give him a chance at a cure. Then a surprise donor stepped up.
Father of four with stage 4 cancer gets liver transplant from a stranger
Kyler Hess is a father of four battling stage 4 colorectal cancer. Doctors told him a liver from a living donor will give him a chance at a cure. Then a surprise donor stepped up.
Throwing the football in the yard with his kids is not something Kyler Hess takes for granted. It's the small moments that carry a lot of meaning for the Iowa dad battling stage 4 colorectal cancer.
"When it came to giving us the odds, my wife immediately said, 'Absolutely not. We're not going to put that in his head,'" the father of four told sister station KCCI.
Kyler's wife Emilie says the family has strived to maintain a positive outlook since receiving the diagnosis in July 2025.
"We would be a statistic at that point. It was, 'Let us have our own story and see what we can do from there,'" said Emilie Hess.
A CT scan revealed the cancer had spread to Kyler's liver with more than 15 tumors. The Hess family says doctors in Des Moines told them there wasn't much they could do, so the family sought treatment at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota.
"After a couple of months of treatment and nutritional changes and all the other things we did, things started to turn around, and things started to shrink," said Kyler Hess.
With the cancer under control, Kyler says the doctors at Mayo Clinic told him he was eligible for a liver transplant, but the liver needed to come from a living donor. The liver is made up of two lobes, and one lobe has the ability to grow and regenerate in another person.
Kyler's brother immediately underwent extensive testing, but was not able to donate because of his liver anatomy.
"I felt awful for them, but then it was that moment where I was like, 'It's meant to be me,'" said Abby Conley.
Want more content like this? Subscribe to our News We Love newsletter here.
Abby Conley didn't know Kyler, but she followed his journey online because their kids attend the same school in Polk City, Iowa. Abby decided to quietly travel to Mayo Clinic to go through three days of extensive testing to see if her liver was a match. She says she felt called to do this in honor of her father, who died in 2021 while awaiting a bone marrow transplant after battling leukemia.
"When my dad was in his final days, he wrote his family a letter, and in that letter he said, 'I have lived a fairy tale life ... keep it going,'" Conley said.
Now, Conley hopes her donation will allow Kyler many more years with his kids.
"In order to continue on for the future years of watching my kids graduate, walk my daughter down the aisle, see all the big moments in life with them, I had to have that piece I can't do on my own," Kyler said.

title: Florida officer let impaired driver go. Minutes later, driver killed 2 people, chief says
text:
Florida officer let an impaired driver go. Minutes later, that driver killed a mom and son, chief says
A mother and her son were killed on Tuesday in Florida after being hit by a driver who was allowed on the road despite showing signs of impairment just minutes prior.
They were identified by the police department as Eric Derick Maurice McGill, 31, and De Lawn Marshall Duncan, 50.
Ocala Police Chief Mike Balken said the department has taken immediate steps to launch a full-scale investigation into the crash, which he described as "devastating" and preventable.
The crash happened around 2:45 a.m. in Ocala, Florida, police said.
'Y’all are good to go, Y'all can head on out'
The chief said what's "troubling" is that the lead officer had just interacted with the driver and his brother, who the chief said were no doubt impaired.
"There's no way to sugarcoat this," he said.
Police body camera footage shows the two brothers arguing on a sidewalk near their van, which was parked in the middle of the road.
“It's his birthday, it's his birthday ... we just beef, bro,” the brothers can be heard saying. 
An officer saw that the van was in the middle of the road and had stopped to see why.
“Y’all are good to go. Y'all can head on out,” the officer says in the bodycam footage.
Minutes later, the chief says the brothers were involved in the crash that killed a 50-year-old mother and her 31-year-old son.
The police officer has been placed on paid administrative leave. 
The brothers, aged 33 and 24, were taken to a local hospital, one of whom was listed as a trauma alert, according to police.
"There are indications, unfortunately, that both had been drinking earlier in the night and may have been impaired," Balken said. "Unfortunately, and really for reasons I can't fully yet explain, the officers failed to investigate a possible DUI or even question the driver's level of intoxication. Instead, the brothers were allowed to drive away, and within minutes their vehicle struck and killed our victims."
New to the department
Balken said the officer involved is new to the department and had been out of field training for about 30 days. Two other officers also responded to the initial interaction with the brothers.
"You know, I really just can't express how deeply disappointed and saddened I am with this situation," Balken said. "I really want the community to know that we are taking every necessary step to investigate thoroughly and address any mistakes."
Balken said he has met with the victims' family, shown them the body camera footage, and is working to provide them with resources.
"They're frankly in shock right now," he said. "We owe it to the families involved and this community to address these failures head-on and ensure mistakes like this never, ever happen again. To the family that have lost their loved ones, I am profoundly sorry. I only wish we had done more to prevent this tragedy."
The chief said that the incident is not being attributed to a failure in training but rather a failure to act on a probable impairment issue. The identities of the officers and the victims have not been released, and charges are pending.

title: NASA telescope expected to fall to Earth soon. Here’s where it could land

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has been observing asteroids, comets and gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, for 22 years.

The telescope is expected to enter Earth’s atmosphere in a couple of weeks. Most of it will burn up, but a few chunks might survive and rain down.
Experts say if that happens, the debris will almost definitely fall into the ocean or onto uninhabited land.

title: Van Buren Completes Town Mural
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
VAN BUREN, Maine (WAGM) - A 60-foot wall in downtown Van Buren is telling the story of the town. This Sunday, the community celebrates the finished mural. A yearlong project built by hundreds of volunteers.
14 organizations, and over 450 community members have worked for the last year to complete Van Buren’s community mural. The mural is 60 feet long and 14 feet high and features 20 unique locations in town. Each stamp displayed has mileage on it to tell visitors how far each landmark is from the mural. Leah Cook, who started the project, says it’s highlighted Van Buren’s community spirit.
“We came up with this idea for designs that look like oversized postage stamps that are featuring different places in town. After that first set that we made that I did the design and the painting for then we did a second phase that was a community design process and with that we asked people in the community to give us ideas of different places we should feature and that turned into our final 9 designs that people came and painted with me,” said Leah Cook, the artist who started the project.
The project was funded by the town along with Maine Creates, which encourages artists to offer solutions to local problems and increase community engagement. The community mural has been part of Van Buren’s revitalization plan.
“Van Buren has been rebuilding itself since going through some economic decline when the international bridge was relocated and so there’s been a lot of effort put into reviving the Main Street. There have been a lot of studies that show that if you have an art attraction in your town it increases spending in local businesses. As soon as you get people out of cars and on foot, you’re driving foot traffic and that becomes an economic multiplier. One thing that has been really wonderful about this project is that this is all things that are in the right here right now. So, as you look at the wall and you see these 20 different designs that literally fill an entire wall it’s just a joyful celebration of like, “Wow, look how much there is in this town,” continued Cook.
Cook says she’s happy to have started the project but is even happier to see how many people have stepped in to help. “It feels pretty amazing. It’s humbling in some ways. To have folks come and actually paint with me, it’s just so fun. So, to be reaching this point I’m beyond thrilled and happy. We were letting out some pretty happy yips and giggles when we were installing stuff on the wall. It’s really been a whole project of partnership from end to end.”
Van Buren will host a celebration in honor of the completion of the community art project Sunday, Oct. 4, at noon at 52 Main St. Cook says they will be handing out postcards based on the mural to attendees. County residents are encouraged to drop by and celebrate the completion of the mural with the town.

text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A cold front will continue to cross the state this afternoon pushing rain southward towards the coast this afternoon. Rain is expected to be light... although there could be a few heavier downpours here and there but overall rain will be light with most areas only seeing a tenth of an inch or less. Otherwise expect mostly cloudy skies for our Friday with temperatures staying on the milder side despite the clouds and rain in the forecast. Temperatures will hold steady in the mid-60s across northern locales where the rain arrives first but areas further south will see temperatures climbing to the upper 60s to mid-70s before the rain arrives this afternoon. Showers are expected to move out this evening followed by clearing skies as the night progresses. There is an upper-level disturbance forecast to cross the state behind the cold front tonight. This may bring a few more showers to mainly northern parts of Aroostook County between about 8pm tonight through 2-3am Saturday. Cooler air will move in behind the front with low temperatures dropping to the 40s tonight.
High pressure will build in and bring us a fantastic day Saturday with plenty of sunshine and highs in the upper 50s to mid-60s. At the same time... strong low pressure over the Maritimes combined with high pressure over the Eastern Great Lakes Region will result in a tight pressure gradient over the region leading to a gusty west/northwest wind that may gust in excess of 40 MPH at times... especially over northern locales. Temperatures on Tuesday will be in the mid-40s to around 50° north and mainly low to mid-50s elsewhere and with the gusty wind on top of that... it’s going to feel very fall-like.

title: Former GOP Rep. David Rivera sentenced to prison for secret Venezuela lobbying
text:
Former GOP Rep. David Rivera sentenced to prison for secret Venezuela lobbying
A former Miami congressman and longtime friend of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was sentenced Friday to 10 years in prison in connection with a secret $50 million lobbying campaign on Venezuela's behalf during the first Trump administration.
Republican David Rivera has been jailed since jurors found him guilty in May on all counts, including failing to register as a foreign agent and conspiracy to commit money laundering as part of his work for former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro's government.
Rivera, 61, appeared stone-faced as Judge Melissa Damian denounced him for betraying his life's mission, saying he would surely have been judged harshly if his many friends and the millions of dollars came from the Cuban regime instead of its allies in Caracas.
"Nobody would accept that's OK, and I don't think this is different," the judge said. "There's no dispute this money came from the Maduro regime."
The seven-week trial offered a rare glimpse into Miami's role as a crossroads for foreign influence campaigns aimed at shaping U.S. policy toward Latin America, highlighting the city's reputation as a magnet for both anti-communist crusaders and corruption among its sizable exile population.
It included testimony from President Donald Trump's secretary of state, Rep. Pete Sessions of Texas and a top Washington lobbyist — all of whom testified they felt betrayed when learning of Rivera's mammoth consulting contract with a U.S.-based affiliate of Venezuela's state oil company, PDVSA.
Attorneys for Rivera plan to appeal and in June applied for a presidential pardon. Rivera faces additional federal charges in Washington, D.C., in a related foreign lobbying case.
Prosecutors said betrayal featured coded figures — 'Sombrero' and 'Miss Clairol'
In an indictment unsealed in 2022, prosecutors alleged that Rivera was tapped by then Foreign Minister Delcy Rodríguez — now Venezuela's acting president — to work Republican connections to get the first Trump administration to abandon its hard line and crippling sanctions on Venezuela.
As part of the charm offensive, Rivera and a co-defendant, political consultant Esther Nuhfer, sought to manipulate influential friends, including Rubio and Sessions. Their goal was to normalize relations with the new Trump administration even as the Maduro government faced sanctions over serious accusations of human rights violations.
But Rivera and Nuhfer didn't disclose their lobbying work as required, for fear it would have ended Rivera's political career as an anti-communist stalwart, prosecutors argued at trial.
"The United States and the public were the true victims of this fraud," Assistant U.S. Attorney Roger Cruz said in urging a stiff sentence. "He used his position of trust — and betrayed it consistently and repeatedly."
To hide his work, prosecutors allege, Rivera also set up an encrypted chat group called MIA — for Miami — with his main conduit to the Maduro government: Venezuelan media tycoon Raúl Gorrín, who was subsequently charged in the U.S. with bribing top Venezuelan officials.
Members of the group used playful code words to discuss their activities: Maduro was the "bus driver," Sessions "Sombrero," Rodríguez "The Lady in Red," and their windfall payments "La Luz," Spanish for "The Light," according to copies of text messages presented to the jury. Rubio was known as "Miss Clairol," because rubio means blond in Spanish.
Defense said only missing paperwork made the $50 million contract illegal
At Friday's sentencing, attorneys for Rivera repeated their trial argument that the former congressman believed he was under no requirement to disclose the work. The three-month, $50 million contract with Rivera's one-man consulting firm, they said, was focused on luring oil giant ExxonMobil back to Venezuela — commercial work that is generally exempt from the Foreign Agents Registration Act.
"David Rivera does not deserve to die in prison because he failed to file a FARA registration," defense attorney Ed Shohat said at Friday's hearing. "If he had filed that paper, that form, everything he did, including the $50 million contract, which totally distorted this case, is perfectly legal."
Wholly distinct from that consulting work, they say, were Rivera's meetings with Rubio and Sessions, which were focused on ushering in leadership in Venezuela that would be less hostile to the U.S. – not supporting Maduro in normalizing relations with the U.S.
"There's not one word in any chat, not one document, not one thing he did to help Nicolás Maduro," said Shohat.
Prosecutors said Rivera used the contract with the affiliate, New York-based PDV USA, as cover for illegal lobbying.
"This is a classic money laundering case," the judge said Friday in rejecting Rivera's motion to lower the federal guidelines range.
Where did the money go? A luxury yacht, among other things
The partners tried to hide the work — backdating documents and coming up with sham agreements, like one to justify a wire transfer of $3.75 million to a South Florida company that maintained Gorrín's luxury yacht, prosecutors said.
The political activity included setting up meetings for Rodríguez in New York, Caracas, Washington and Dallas. As part of the effort, Rivera roped in Sessions, who later tried to broker a meeting for Rodríguez with the ExxonMobil executive who took over as CEO when Rex Tillerson became Trump's first-term secretary of state. After a secret meeting in Caracas with Maduro, Sessions also agreed to deliver a letter from the Venezuelan president to Trump.
The outreach quickly unraveled, however. Within six months of taking office, Trump sanctioned Maduro and labeled him a "dictator," launching a "maximum pressure" campaign to unseat the president.
And now, nearly a decade later, Rodríguez has emerged as the second Trump administration's trusted partner after the U.S. military's ousting of Maduro.
Rubio's former housemate faced scandal before, but Cuban Americans support him
Before being elected to Congress in 2010, Rivera was a high-ranking Florida legislator and shared a Tallahassee home with Rubio, who eventually became the Florida House speaker.
Rivera faced earlier controversy, including allegations that he secretly funded a Democratic spoiler candidate in a 2012 congressional race. Last year, federal prosecutors dropped that case after an appeals court threw out a sizable fine imposed by a lower court. Rivera was also investigated — but never charged — for alleged campaign finance violations and a $1 million contract with a gambling company while serving in the Florida Legislature.
Despite all that, Rivera remains popular among Miami's Cuban American establishment.
Friends of the former congressman, including the former president of Florida International University and Miami-Dade County's supervisor of elections, packed the courtroom to show their support.
Sessions, in a letter seeking leniency that was read into the record by his chief of staff, said his former congressional colleague devoted decades to public service, much of it focused on defending liberty and democracy.
"I don't think it's productive for society by sending David away for a long, long time," testified Liliana Ros, a longtime Miami GOP committee member.

title: Hymn for Her to kick off fifth concert season at The Underground Lounge
text:
BELFAST — The Underground Lounge in Belfast is launching its fifth season on Thursday, Oct. 8 with indie duo Hymn for Her.
Hymn for Her (Lucy Tight and Wayne Waxing) is a roaming folk duo whose sound feels pulled from back roads, front porches, and long stretches of open highway. Blending Americana, country folk and a touch of old-time grit, they weave rich harmonies, acoustic textures and foot-powered rhythms into something both intimate and alive. Their songs carry stories of travel, love and resilience. Whether under festival lights or in a field at sunset, Hymn for Her creates a warm, magnetic atmosphere that draws people in and stays with them long after the music fades.
Don’t let the words “folk” and “acoustic” fool you: Hymn for Her’s sound is raucous, intensely rhythmic and powerful. Vintage Guitar Magazine described Hymn for Her as “White Stripes meet Country Joe McDonald, with things just psychedelic enough to keep everyone interested and on their toes. The humor is good. The music even better.” To learn more about Hymn and Her, visit www.hymnforher.com
Located just under the Basil Burwell Community Theatre (the “Bazz”) at 17 Court St. in Belfast, The Underground Lounge is a volunteer-led music series that aims to keep live music flowing during the Maine off-season. Doors open at 6:30 p.m. and the music starts at 7 p.m. Admission is $10 to $ 20 (cash only at the door), and food and beverages will be available by donation. A season’s membership for all 12 shows can be purchased in advance on a sliding scale of $100 to $200 at https://tinyurl.com/43hb7kyx.

title: New York’s governor says state’s AG will oversee Cornell rape investigation
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) — New York’s governor appointed a special prosecutor Thursday to oversee an investigation into a woman’s allegations that she was gang raped at a Cornell University fraternity house, saying she had lost faith in the local district attorney’s ability to handle the case.
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she had signed an executive order appointing the office of New York Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the investigation, which had initially been closed without charges in 2024.
The woman’s allegations got a rush of new attention when she filed a civil lawsuit last month. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation Monday, but has been battered by criticism that he’d abandoned the original investigation too quickly.
“Newly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute an alleged sexual assault on Cornell University’s campus in October 2024,” Hochul said.
“This has, in turn, undercut my faith, and the public’s faith, in the District Attorney’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time.”
Hochul said the attorney general would oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury.
“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said. ”This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.”
Messages left for Van Houten were not immediately returned late Thursday. Hochul, James and Van Houten are all Democrats.
A campus roiled by continued revelations
Hochul’s announcement came shortly after dozens of students and community members spent hours demanding transparency and accountability from university leaders at a forum sponsored by Cornell’s student government. The case has roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about its response and the larger issue of how sexual assaults are handled on college campuses.
The woman, identified only as Jane Doe in court documents, reported the alleged assault to campus police in November of 2024, then discussed it with the university’s internal investigators as part of Cornell’s disciplinary process.
The lawsuit against seven fraternity brothers, the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and others, alleges that she was plied with drugs and alcohol, then subjected to sex acts by a group of men while she was partially or entirely incapacitated. One of the men sent a social media message to other fraternity members alerting them to what was happening, and inviting people to take part, according to the lawsuit.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they participated in a sexual assault. One said his client hadn’t touched the woman. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful.
When he reopened the investigation earlier this week, Van Houten said he would review new information in the woman’s lawsuit. But he also issued a statement defending his initial decision not to prosecute, maintaining the woman’s first account to police didn’t include allegations that she was drugged against her will, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex.
Under pressure from the public and politicians, including Hochul, Cornell agreed Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations.
Students, community call for change
Over more than 2 1/2 hours Thursday, students and other members of the Cornell community expressed anger, frustration and grief over the school’s handling of sexual assault allegations in general, with several speakers sharing their own experiences of sexual violence.
Many criticized Cornell President Michael I. Kotlikoff and the university’s administration, calling for greater transparency and accountability in the handling of the case, stronger sexual assault prevention efforts and changes to Greek life.
Jane Wang, a sophomore, said at the forum that when she reported being sexually assaulted on campus a year ago, she was met with a slew of paperwork and little guidance or follow-up. After an initial email chain about starting the investigation, she got few updates and had to prod for answers, she said. The process left her feeling an “overall sense of helplessness within a broader institution.”
“My main message for Cornell here is that we can’t be treating these cases only with care and attention after it catches national news,” Wang said, calling for the university to improve the “seriousness and timeliness” of its response to sexual assault allegations.
There was no immediate response to a message seeking comment about the forum and Wang’s case sent to the university late Thursday.
Cornell has said it took a series of actions after the woman identifying as Jane Doe reported being raped at the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024.
It announced publicly that it had opened an investigation, condemned the alleged behavior, indefinitely suspended the fraternity, and convened a university task force to study ways to more effectively protect students against sexual assault.
It also conducted a monthslong investigation, which ended with some students being disciplined or expelled, though it has declined to provide specifics, citing student privacy rules. The university issued a statement Monday saying it supported reopening the criminal investigation.
“I think what happened here is an American problem,” said Hayden Watkins, an undergraduate and executive vice president of the Student Assembly, which hosted the forum.
“People kind of put Cornell on this pedestal because we are an elite institution,” he added. “But if it’s happening at places like Cornell, it’s happening on college campuses all across the country.”
___
Associated Press reporter Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this report.

title: USDA considers adapting farm-style safety net for fishermen
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Top federal agriculture officials visited Maine this week to evaluate whether crop insurance can be expanded to protect the state’s multimillion dollar lobster industry.
The visit by U.S. Department of Agriculture Undersecretary Richard Fordyce and Risk Management Agency Administrator Pat Swanson comes as the agency increasingly looks to integrate seafood producers into traditional agricultural safety nets.
Federal crop insurance allows farmers to buy government-subsidized policies that pay out in weeks to months after natural disasters or market drops cause severe revenue losses. In contrast, lobstermen rely on federal fishery disaster declarations that can take three to five years to distribute aid, which industry analysts call far too slow for small operators.
“We are a small-boat, owner-operated fishery made up of thousands of independent businesses, so programs designed for agriculture or other food-producing sectors will not necessarily translate neatly to lobster,” said Patrice McCarron, director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association.
However, McCarron called the visit “an important first step” toward determining whether existing USDA programs can be adapted or new approaches developed to better support Maine lobstermen in their role as food producers for the world.
During a dockside roundtable in Stonington on Tuesday, industry leaders emphasized that lobstermen face severe market swings and price crashes rather than physical catch loss alone. Fordyce, a corn and soybean farmer from Missouri, noted that lobstermen favored revenue protection over simple yield guarantees.
“Just talking with the lobstermen, I think they were probably more inclined to try to find a product or try to find a path forward that would be more supportive of total revenue,” Fordyce said. “I was quite surprised by the data that’s available as far as supporting catch numbers.”
Last year’s lobster catch was valued at $461.4 million — 7.5% below the 10-year average, and, when adjusted for inflation, 20% down from 2024, state data shows.
Curt Brown, president of Bold Coast Seafood in Prospect Harbor, hosted the delegation and highlighted the shared reality between ocean and land harvesters.
“I was struck by how many of the same challenges we face in seafood are also challenges that farmers across the country face every day,” Brown said. “There is a lot we can learn from each other.”
Seafood industry consultant Noah Oppenheim said bringing Midwest agricultural leaders to coastal Maine provided crucial perspective, especially the similarities between the rural fishing communities in Maine and the rural farming communities in the Midwest.
While the visit was focused on ways to manage the industry’s risks, representatives also used the time to drive home other ways the agency can help water-based food producers like they support land-based farmers, including equal access to loan, grant, purchasing and marketing programs.
“The agency seems wide open to focus on all of this at once,” Oppenheim said. “Congress knows this is a bipartisan feel-good issue. We need to be eating more domestic seafood. It’s the right thing to do to have seafood be an equal part of our food system.”
Oppenheim said opportunities for fishermen have expanded since the USDA created its Office of Seafood in April. One of its top priorities is to find ways for fishermen to tap into the same federal programs and safety nets as the nation’s potato and dairy farmers.
Addressing expectations regarding a timeline, Fordyce cautioned that any official expansion must ultimately be approved by the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation board. However, because local advocates have worked on the issue for several years, he said “a lot of that preliminary work has been kind of done.”
While a full rollout for lobster insurance remains down the road, Fordyce emphasized that establishing direct working relationships between Washington officials and Maine coastal leaders was the immediate, vital outcome of the trip.

title: Happy to be ‘stuck’ in central Maine, thanks
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I was disappointed by a recent news report (“As life in Maine gets more expensive, young people struggle to keep up,” Sept. 18). As a proud Augusta resident who left Portland years ago due to — go figure — rising costs and lack of opportunity, I thought it quite rich to ascribe to my neighbor the feeling that he was “stuck in central Maine.”
The report itself makes clear my neighbor was attributing that sentiment to his friends in — I guess, to the reporter — more desirable locales, not necessarily speaking about his own feelings.
Some people want to live in Maine, even up here in the scary boondocks of central Maine, because it’s a great place to live, with great people. It’s disappointing that the reporting ignores that possibility.
Honestly, that last line (“Maybe, for now, he is [stuck].”) angered and offended me.
“Maybe,” indeed.
Stanley Abraham
Augusta
