title: ‘The Debut’ Review: A Comedy About Acting With Two of the Best Performances of the Year
text:
‘The Debut’ Review: This Comedy About Acting Contains Two of the Best Performances of the Year
I’m not much of a gambler, but I’m willing to make this wager. I’ll bet that if you go see The Debut in a theater, there will come a moment when the audience breaks into spontaneous applause. It happened at my screening of the film attended by a bunch of jaded film critics, and I’ve already heard from one colleague who said the same thing happened when they saw it too.
I won’t go into specifics about this moment, but it involves both of The Debut’s leads — Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti — locked in an intense back-and-forth exchange that gets to the heart of what this movie is all about: Art, self-expression, and the power of acting. You’ll know it when you see it — because odds are you’ll be clapping too.
That scene is certainly a highlight, but it’s far from the only memorable sequence in The Debut, which is written and directed by Jesse Eisenberg, a very good actor and talented director who here takes a major step forward as a filmmaker with a comedy that is as moving as it funny. It’s one of the most surprising things I’ve seen in a long time.
READ MORE: The Best Movies of the Year So Far
Its early scenes disarm you with perceptive but familiar satire about the quirky characters and rituals that populate every community theater. Then right around the scene that earns spontaneous applause, The Debut blindsides you with an earnest consideration of the nature of performance, not just on stage but also in people’s day-to-day lives, where they don proverbial masks to navigate a world full of disappointment and compromise. Suddenly, an amusing if predictable spoof of small-town weirdos — a modern, less jokey Waiting for Guffman — transforms into something far more ambitious and far more interesting.
That transformation mirrors the one undertaken in the film by Moore’s character, Mona. For reasons that initially seem unclear to both the audience and to her, she decides to audition for a musical mounted at the Brook Theatre in her small New Jersey town. Mona is downright terrified to sing for the first time since her days as a choir girl, and her audition for the theater’s imposing director Jerry (Giamatti) does not go well. She doesn’t deserve the part, and she doesn’t get it — but then circumstances change and Jerry reluctantly drafts Mona into service.
Mona’s stage work is as tentative as the rest of her existence, which is largely defined by her unhappy marriage to a man who seems to spend as much time as possible in their bathroom doing the crossword puzzle in order to minimize his contact with his ife. With Mona’s fumbling line delivers and hushed singing voice, Jerry recognizes Mona could be a major problem for his show, a Manhattan-set musical called Nosy Neighbors. Jerry explains that the play is a decades-old theatrical staple; in fact, the whole show — right down to its peppy musical numbers — was written by Eisenberg himself.
Given the enormous cult of personality in this troupe around Jerry, we expect The Debut to turn into a battle of wills between he and Mona; we assume, given the way these types of stories typically go in movies about wacky eccentrics, that he will try break her down and Whiplash her into doing Nosy Neighbors at his tempo. But Eisenberg’s lively and sensitive script is full of surprises; about Jerry’s skills as a director, about Eisenberg’s own feelings about Method performers, and about what happens to Mona’s private life after she begins to blossom under Jerry’s guidance.
Mona’s gradual evolution gives Moore one of her best and biggest showcases in quite some time. Eisenberg sets several scenes in the alley beside the Brook Theatre, where the wall is adorned with the image of the masks of tragedy and comedy. They feel emblematic of The Debut as a whole; some scenes contain the funniest work that Moore’s ever done. (Wait until you see her awful dancing during her first one-on-one session with the Brook’s musical director.) Others let her tap into her full range of emotions; Moore’s reaction to Mona’s big debut is nothing short of jaw-dropping. And some scenes — like the one that drew spontaneous applause at my screening — shift between the two modes so seamlessly it’s almost supernatural. There is zero chance Moore isn’t nominated for an Academy Award for this movie.
Giamatti’s role isn‘t as flashy as Moore’s, but his work in The Debut is no less committed. The film only works if we understand why the members of this little theater revere Jerry — and we do. It also only works if we fear him the way Mona does — and we do. And the movie only transcends the limitations of its somewhat clichéd premise if Giamatti keeps showing us more dimensions of this man, which he does over and over again. In a career that includes movies like Sideways, Cinderella Man, Win Win, and The Holdovers, this might be the best thing he’s ever done.
The Debut impressed me. It defies easy categorization; it’s one of the funniest movies of 2026 and also one of the saddest. It’s also one of the best depictions I’ve ever seen of dead-end life in suburban New Jersey; only a Jersey native like Eisenberg, who grew up in Middlesex County, could so adroitly capture the visual essence of this land of drab Asian restaurants and expansive but lifeless homes. The poignance and dark humor of Mona’s plight instantly puts Eisenberg in the pantheon of great artists of Garden State ennui alongside the likes of Bruce Springsteen and David Chase.
RATING: 9/10
Reviewed at the New York Film Festival.

title: Stephens Brings Healthcare Background to House District 45 Race
text:
A desire to serve a larger population is the motivation behind Rebecca Stephens’ campaign for House District 45.
Stephens, R-Waldoboro, faces Clint Collamore, I–Waldoboro, in the race for the district, which consists of Bremen, Friendship, Louds Island Township, Waldoboro, and Washington.
“I grew up with parents who really instilled in me that you should give back to your community, and this is a way to give back to a broader community than what I’ve done in the past,” Stephens said.
Stephens grew up in the Midcoast and has lived in Waldoboro for the past six years. After graduating from Kennebec Valley Community College in Fairfield in 1994, she earned a bachelor’s degree in applied science and a minor in geriatric human services from the University of Maine at Augusta in 2007 and a Ph.D. in physical therapy from the University of Maine in 2010.
Stephens worked for over 30 years at MaineHealth Pen Bay Hospital in Rockport and has spent the past four years working as the physical therapist for RSU 40. She said her career has provided valuable knowledge of the healthcare industry and of local schools.
Stephens currently serves on the Waldoboro Select Board and previously served on the Lincolnville School Board. She coaches basketball at the Coastal Christian School in Waldoboro and has served as a court–appointed special advocate for children for the Maine Department of Health and Human Services.
Taxes and rising electricity costs are among the top concerns of voters in District 45, Stephens said. If elected, she hopes to see a “deep dive” into the state’s budget to potentially alleviate affordability.
Stephens said audits help to increase effectiveness of future initiatives and provide more transparency to the public.
“My experience looking at school and municipal budgets has taught me that you have to look line item by line item,” she said. “There’s only a couple ways to modify a budget, if you think about your household budget. You only can increase revenue or decrease spending.”
Stephens said she supports reevaluating bureaucratic regulations and rolling back some taxes to help Mainers with cost-of-living worries. She said this would also encourage people to move to or stay in the state.
“Everything’s being taxed, and that’s discouraging,” Stephens said.
According to Stephens, schools are one area where more transparency is needed. She said it should be easier to find education budgets and curriculums digitally, and this is something she would work on if elected.
“We need to create streamlined websites where things are not difficult to find, (where) the non-tech-savvy person can get there, find it, and not have to dig to find curriculum, to find the budget,” Stephens said. “People fear what they don’t know.”
Stephens would also like to see a reduction of technology in schools. She said while devices have educational benefits for some students, they “decrease interaction” among students and teachers and have other negative effects.
“Having an iPad instead of a book is not creating diverse pathways in your brain,” Stephens said.
Sometimes local municipalities are better equipped to respond to a challenge than the state, Stephens said. One issue that came to mind for her was access to waterways and the balance of the usage of it.
Stephens said towns understand their working waterfronts better than someone in the state would because something that might work for Waldoboro might not work for Machias.
“Sometimes the state tends to put their hand in a place where it doesn’t necessarily need to be in order for the system to work better,” Stephens said.
Natural resources are something the state “absolutely” needs to protect, Stephens said. However, she said some initiatives intended to reduce environmental impacts, such as the expansion of solar energy, have caused ecological harm and should be reconsidered.
Stephens said she would also like to explore other energy options, including small-scale nuclear power. She said she would like to look at micronuclear options after seeing how it has served other states.
“If you look at solar and the byproducts of making a solar panel and the byproducts of disposing of a solar panel, they’re not terribly environmentally friendly,” Stephens said. “Unfortunately, some of the more recent initiatives have looked good on paper and not looked good in implementation.”
If elected, Stephens hopes to bring her knowledge of the healthcare industry to discussions of reform to the MaineCare system. She said expanding MaineCare had benefits but also created financial challenges for hospitals. According to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ website, MaineCare provides health care coverage for Maine’s children and adults who are elderly, disabled, or have low income.
“It’s great to make sure that when people have a need, that we’re as a society meeting that need,” she said. “If you increase the number of people on MaineCare and then hospitals who are also not being reimbursed, but if they were being reimbursed at the rates that are currently being paid by MaineCare, it’s still very low.”
Lower reimbursement rates through MaineCare put pressure on hospitals that, unlike private practices, must accept MaineCare patients, Stephens said. This then leads to a lack of providers.
With her stance on healthcare, Stephens said she supports raising the rates for MaineCare.
“If we’re going to cover people, then the government needs to pay out enough to at least cover a hospital’s cost,” she said.
For more information, go to beckyformaine.com or find the Rebecca Stephens for House District 45 Facebook page.
The election is on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

Recall roundup: Meat, cheeses, cinnamon, toys and more recalled across U.S.
text:
Recall roundup: Meat, cheeses, cinnamon, toys and more recalled across U.S.
Dozens of products have been recalled across the U.S. over the past two weeks, from food products to everyday household items.
The recalls include cheeses that may contain E. coli, pasta that may be contaminated with Listeria, and blood pressure medication that may not work as intended.
Above video | Check your fridge: Recalled foods could already be in your home
Everyday items like mattresses, hand warmers and toys are also on the list, along with several Ford, GM and Land Rover vehicles.
Here’s what to know and how to check whether something you own is affected.
FOOD ITEMS
- Raw meat products | Star Meat Delivery recalled about 167,639 pounds of A&D Foods raw pork, beef and goat products distributed to retailers and restaurants nationwide because the meat was produced without federal inspection and carried a false USDA inspection mark. Click here to view the full recall.
- Raw milk cheeses | Sierra Nevada Cheese Company recalled Graziers raw milk cheeses distributed nationwide because they may be contaminated with E. coli. Click here to view the full recall.
- Stuffed pasta | Deano’s Pasta recalled its Pear and Pecorino Triangoli Ravioli sold in Massachusetts because it may contain undeclared lobster. Click here to view the full recall.

title: New treatment could drastically reduce sepsis death rate, researcher says
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Sepsis kills more than 350,000 adults and 1,800 children in the United States each year, according to the CDC. One in three adults who die in the hospital have sepsis.
A doctor in Kansas City, Missouri, has made a discovery that could drastically reduce that statistic.
What is sepsis?
Sepsis happens when the body’s immune system starts harming healthy tissues and organs in response to an infection, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
That can trigger a chain reaction throughout the body.
Early sepsis signs can start with a fever, chills and rapid breathing. Those symptoms then progress to confusion and difficulty breathing until it reaches the final stage, septic shock, which can lead to organ failure and death in as little as 12 hours, according to Sepsis Alliance.
A mother’s story
Two years ago, Brie Morgan Bauer was pregnant with her third child and excited to welcome him to a growing family. Everything about the pregnancy was normal until she felt flu-like symptoms at 27 weeks.
She went to her obstetrician’s office and that’s when the real emergency began.
“When they hooked me up, we were showing back-to-back contractions and I didn’t feel anything,” Bauer said. “But little did I know I was actually going septic.”
Bauer’s son, Bo, was delivered by emergency C-section. Her flu-like symptoms were strep throat. She went from bringing new life into the world to fighting for her own.
“By the third day that’s when they started looking at my toes, looking at my fingers and that they were turning purple and black,” Bauer said. “My hands were almost like mummified. They were black. And then I unwrapped my legs, and the legs were so crazy to see. The feet were definitely black.”
In her mind, Bauer thought there was no going back. “There’s no option to get blood flow back to a foot that is obviously dead.”
In the end, there was nothing she could have done to prevent what happened to her. She would have to live life as a quadruple amputee.
The current treatment for sepsis is antibiotics and IV fluids, which is sometimes not enough.
Researcher’s discovery
Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins has worked to find a solution to sepsis. He is the founder of Vivacell Bio Inc., where he has worked to find a solution to septic shock.
“There are 11 million cases around the world, and its mortality rate’s about 30%, 40%,” Simpkins said. “Depends on what stage you’re at, but if you’re at an advanced stage, it becomes almost 100%.”
Simpkins said during sepsis, the body makes too much nitric oxide, which leads to organ failure. His product, VBI-S, absorbs the nitric oxide, something Simpkins said has never been done before.
“It will act quickly, very quickly. You’ll see the blood pressure come up. You don’t have to wait to see its effect.”
He said that within 24 to 48 hours, “you’ll see the lungs get better, you’ll see the kidneys get better.”
In clinical trials, 80% of participants were expected to die from sepsis. VBI-S lowered that to 50%.
“They have shown that a high degree of efficacy in reversing failure of multiple organs,” Simpkins said.
He said the mortality rate would be even lower when the substance is given to patients early in their diagnosis. The clinical trials have concluded, and the product is awaiting FDA approval.
Other experts watching closely
Dr. Steven Simpson, a pulmonary and critical care doctor, is board chairman of the Sepsis Alliance, a group dedicated to finding a solution to sepsis.
“I am pleased that it seems to work as it’s intended to work,” Simpson said. “[It’s a] small study. We need a lot more patients treated. But very promising.”
Simpson said he sees patients in septic shock every day in the ICU.
He hopes, someday soon, no more will have to die from it. “It’s the reason that I work with Sepsis Alliance, it’s the reason for my entire career. It’s been 40 years, we haven’t found that solution yet.”
While Simpson doesn’t know if this will be a solution for sepsis, he is encouraged by the results.
“I don’t stick my neck out on what’s going to be the cure for sepsis. I am hopeful. I do believe that this is going to play a role, and I think it’s exciting,” he said.
Finding a new normal
Bauer was stunned to hear about the major discovery that could mean the end of sepsis.
I think that’s very promising," she said. “And I’m excited. I wish it was approved a while ago.”
VBI-S was not available for Bauer’s case. She has since found she has an interest in art and remains active in her sons’ lives.
“It’s been chaos. We live minute by minute,” Bauer said. “But my husband, he does everything. And I’m trying to do my best to find that more independence, more partnership with him to help reduce the chaos.”
“But that’s kind of what I’m showing my kids is what resilience looks like and to learn how to adapt,” Bauer said.
Bauer started a website, BriesHope.org, to offer support to survivors and families.
Simpkins said that with FDA approval, VBI-S could be in hospitals as soon as 2027.

title: How geography plays a role in overwhelmed animal shelters
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (InvestigateTV) — Many animal shelters across America are overwhelmed, and where animals are located is a big reason why.
In regions like the South, shelters are under-resourced and over-capacity, packed with dogs and cats waiting for adoption. For many, that wait can be fatal. In 2024, U.S. shelters euthanized more than 600,000 animals.
Experts say homes often exist for these animals, but the animals are in the wrong place.
It’s a geographic mismatch the ASPCA and other groups are working to fix by moving pets hundreds of miles by land and air.
A new addition at home
Inside Johnny Hunter’s home, it’s clear he has a hobby. Over the years, he’s put together more than 100 Lego sets, with his apartment packed wall to wall.
Now he’s making room for someone new.
In early 2025, Hunter adopted a dog named Abby from Wayside Waifs in his hometown of Kansas City.
“It’s been awesome. I mean, she’s really changed my life,” Hunter said. “She’s kind of like a celebrity in my life.”
Abby, a 3-year-old pit bull mix, likely never would have become Hunter’s pet because she’s not from Missouri.
Abby ended up in Kansas City from Arkansas. The ASPCA brought her as part of a program that moves pets to places with more space and more adopters.
Hunter believes that relocating Abby “probably did” save her life.
How the program works
Casey Waugh has worked at Wayside Waifs for more than a decade and knows Abby’s story well.
“Her life completely changed because of this program and because of Wayside Waifs,” Waugh said.
Wayside Waifs has been part of the ASPCA’s national relocation network since 2010.
“We knew that there were homeless animals outside of Kansas City. We could reach our arms a little bit further and help those animals,” Waugh said.
Wayside Waifs is a destination shelter, meaning animals are transported from other shelters that may not have the resources to care for them.
In 2025, it took in about 850 animals through the program.
“Unfortunately, a lot of these animals wouldn’t make it,” Waugh.
While shelter euthanasia rates have declined over the last decade, shelters in many communities still take in more adoptable dogs and cats than they can place locally.
“There are often animals at source shelters that are at the end of opportunities that people have utilized all of the foster homes they can possibly utilize in their community,” said Karen Walsh, the ASPCA’s senior director of relocation.
Walsh said the relocation program has been operating since 2014 and partners with more than 140 shelters nationally.
She said shelters around the country are dealing with overpopulation, especially in the South and Midwest. Weather in those regions is more conducive to longer breeding seasons, and robust spay and neuter programs are less readily available.
“Our country is really out of balance in that area,” Walsh said.
Restoring that balance is a massive logistical challenge, according to Walsh.
It starts with more than 20 vehicles on the road seven days a week, along with locations across the country where animals can stay overnight during longer trips. Vehicles never travel more than 650 miles without stopping.
“We want to make sure that the drivers are safe and that the animals are safe,” Walsh said.
The program also relocates animals by plane. Flights take off weekly, sometimes carrying as many as 100 pets.
“I’ve never been on a runway where a flight was taking off where everybody wasn’t crying,” Walsh said.
Over the last decade, more than 300,000 animals have been moved through the program.
“This program absolutely saves lives,” Walsh said.
Health and safety standards
To ensure the health of the animals and prevent the spread of disease, Walsh said the ASPCA requires source and destination shelters to meet guidelines established by the Association of Shelter Veterinarians and the American Veterinary Medical Association.
“You always have to take the pet’s health and well-being in concern, no matter what you do,” said Dr. Michael Bailey, former president of the American Veterinary Medical Association.
The organization does not oversee relocation programs, but he said he believes the ASPCA is trying to carry out the work responsibly, and the details matter.
“Regular stops, making sure that they have time to exercise, that they have time to relieve themselves so that they do not get stressed in the movement so they do not become overheated,” Bailey said.
Bailey cautioned that moving animals can come with risks.
“The stress can lower their immune system. So, they are susceptible to new diseases,” Bailey said. “It also means that they can get hurt in the transport process themselves.”
He said veterinarian-issued health certificates can help confirm whether animals are healthy enough to travel, and many states require them across state lines. Beyond that, he said oversight varies widely.
Walsh has seen issues with some transfers conducted outside of the ASPCA’s program.
“We see some people driving from Texas to Canada and things like that, not being able to stop. Just switching over, switching over,” she said. “That’s so dangerous that we really try to encourage people not to do that.”
Walsh said the organization also educates on safe relocation and advocates for broader changes that address the root cause of shelter overpopulation.
“It’s just the beginning of a safety net program that allows the pop-off valve to open and the animals to leave so that people can be like, okay, now what are we doing this week to make a change?” Walsh said.
She stressed the importance of programs that prioritize low-cost spay and neuter practices, community engagement, and progressive adoption and foster services.
A new chapter
Since adopting Abby, Hunter has started volunteering at Wayside Waifs. “The more dogs we could save, the better.”
Hunter said he’ll always have a passion for building worlds, brick by brick, and now, one animal at a time.
“She really is my best friend. She’s just made every aspect of my life better,” Hunter said.
States are slowly adopting stricter regulations for animal shelters and rescue transfers.
In December 2025, New York began enforcing a law that requires licensing, health evaluations and transport safety standards for animal relocations into the state. Similar oversight exists in states including Oregon and Massachusetts.
The ASPCA said this relocation pipeline works because willing adopters are waiting at the other end.

title: This is why regular eye exams matter as vision changes with age
text:
(Aging Untold) — Vision changes can be easy to brush off until everyday tasks — such as reading small print or seeing clearly at night — become more difficult.
Changes may be common with age, but eye exams can reveal more than vision problems and protecting your eyesight can help preserve independence.
Night vision changes and glare can be early warning signs
“Some of the symptoms that people will get will be like changes in the vision at nighttime,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Others experience difficulty with reading or glare.
“Or they have to adjust the distance from which they’re reading, either too close or too far. And there’s something that’s changing.” Rogers said.
Rogers said people may assume these changes are simply a normal part of getting older, but don’t dismiss vision changes as an inevitable part of aging. Some eye diseases can offer early signs of what is happening elsewhere in the body.
Eye exams can offer clues about overall health
Rogers said the eyes are among the body’s most energy-demanding organs.
Conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure can increase oxidative stress, which Rogers described as damage to the mitochondria — the cells’ powerhouses.
Damage to mitochondria can contribute to deterioration in the eyes, Rogers said.
She recommends at least one regular eye exam once a year — at a minimum.
An exam might also reveal signs associated with diabetes, autoimmune diseases and blood pressure issues, gerontologist Sam Cradduck said. That means an exam is not only about checking whether someone needs a stronger prescription or reading glasses.
Amy shares a personal story
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a personal story of how an eye exam prompted by difficulty with headlights led doctors to find a mole in the back of her eye that they are monitoring.
“I would encourage anybody to get regular eye exams because you just don’t know what’s going on,” O’Rourke host said.
The major eye conditions
Rogers said glaucoma, cataracts and macular degeneration are three major eye conditions to watch for.
Medicare coverage for vision care can be limited, but cataract treatment is covered, O’Rourke said.
Family history can also be important, especially for people whose relatives have had macular degeneration or glaucoma.
“If you’ve got a family history, your eye issues like macular degeneration and glaucoma, then you for sure ought to be very active in your eye care,” O’Rourke said.
The potential consequences of losing vision make eye care an important investment.
“You lose so much if you lose your vision,” O’Rourke said.
Protecting vision can help preserve independence
Vision affects more than the ability to read a label or drive at night. Ambrose said losing vision can affect a person’s ability to remain in their own home as well as everyday independence.
“This is really about independence,” Ambrose said. “Because when you lose vision, it can affect your ability to stay in your own home. It can affect just absolutely everything.”
Ambrose encouraged people to consider what steps they can take when changes begin.
5 key takeaways about aging and eye health
- Do not assume every change is normal aging. Some changes in vision may be connected to broader health concerns.
- Schedule regular eye exams. Dr. Rhea Rogers recommends exams at least once a year, while noting that people with conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure may need particular attention to eye care.
- Know your family history. A family history of glaucoma or macular degeneration can make it especially important to be proactive about eye care.
- Think about independence. Protecting vision can help support everyday activities and the ability to remain in your own home.

title: Obituary: Ronald “Ron” Pottle
text:
DURHAM – Ronald “Ron” Pottle, 82, of Durham, passed away peacefully on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, with family members at his bedside. He was also under the compassionate care of hospice. For the past three years, Ron lived in Durham with his niece, Renee, and nephew, John, who lovingly supported him throughout his illness.
Born on July 24, 1944, in Lewiston, Ron was the son of Rita Curtis and Fred Pottle. From a young age, he possessed a natural curiosity and a talent for fixing things – skills that guided him into a long and dedicated career as an HVAC technician. He took great pride in his work, and his strong work ethic, reliability, and willingness to lend a hand earned him the respect of coworkers and friends alike. Ron was often the first to offer help, whether someone needed a repair, a ride, or simply a good laugh.
Outside of his profession, Ron was an avid outdoorsman. He found joy in photography, bicycling, camping, and motorcycling – activities that reflected his appreciation for nature, adventure, and quiet moments of reflection.
Ron is survived by two siblings; several nieces and nephews; and many lifelong friends.
He was preceded in death by his parents; and his sister, Mary.
A celebration of life will be held on 1 p.m., Oct. 17, at 21 Penney Lane in Durham. Friends and family are invited to gather, share memories, and honor Ron’s life.
Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.

title: Quicksand won’t swallow you whole, here’s how to escape
text:
(InvestigateTV) — As kids playing outside, a lot of us were afraid of running into quicksand. But as it turns out, quicksand is not a bottomless pit like in the movies. It is a mixture of sand and water that appears solid.
According to Scientific American, quicksand can look solid, but the moment a person steps on it, the sand grains lose their grip and the ground turns “soupy.”
Quicksand then flows like liquid, and sand starts sinking to the bottom. The more a person struggles, the more fluid quicksand becomes. Research shows it will not swallow a person whole.
Matt Bloomfield, a professional guide based in Phoenix, got stuck in quicksand last year during a canyoneering trip with friends at Grand Staircase Escalante in Utah.
“It’s one of my favorites, for sure,” Bloomfield said.
In Bloomfield’s videos, the canyon floor becomes bouncy, like jello.
“So then we started to, like, kind of squish around in it and noticed that there was a lot of quicksand around,” Bloomfield said.
Bloomfield said he recognized the quicksand immediately because he had encountered it before.
“No, that was a big surprise,” Bloomfield said. “It kind of shocked me at first because it was up to my waist when I first fell in. But then once you start to struggle a little bit more, you start to sink. You can get stuck if you don’t know the proper way to free yourself. It can be very, very difficult to pull your legs out.”
In quicksand, the more a person struggles, the deeper they sink.
Bloomfield sank to his chest at one point.
“At this point, I had been, like, struggling to keep my cameras out of the mud,” Bloomfield said. “So I was staying upright, which is exactly what I shouldn’t have been doing. So I was sinking in a little bit deeper.”
Bloomfield said he flattened himself and leaned forward to get his arms out in front of him.
“I was able to kind of wiggle my legs and get them closer to the surface and then just kind of army crawl my way out,” Bloomfield said.
The current quicksand alert applies just south of the Grand Staircase Escalante area at the Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. The area spans more than a million acres of Arizona and Utah and includes Lake Powell, where dropping water levels are exposing more areas to explore on foot.
The quicksand alert is intended to raise awareness rather than alarm. The danger comes from getting stuck for hours and becoming exhausted, rather than from sinking completely underground.
Bloomfield said sinking stops before a person goes fully underwater.
“Yeah, it feels like that’s going to happen, but generally I think you get to like your lungs and you have more buoyancy where you actually can’t go any further,” Bloomfield said.
Bloomfield was with other people during his encounter. Park rangers recommend hiking with someone else in case of encountering quicksand in the area.
If a person gets stuck, officials recommend staying calm and applying the methods described to escape.

title: See the full interview with the man behind ‘Taking Care of Granny’
text:
(Aging Untold) — Caring for an aging loved one can reshape a family, and it’s a responsibility more men are shouldering than ever before. Today, an estimated 21 million men are in caregiving roles, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. They are navigating the daily challenges of aging and illness alongside their own jobs and children.
Dugan Meredith, who documents caring for his mother-in-law online through the “Taking Care of Granny” social media feeds, joined us to talk about what it’s really like to become a caregiver and how his family found their way through it.
Dugan Meredith joins us for the Aging Untold podcast
Dugan Meredith joined us for the Aging Untold podcast and spoke with Sam Cradduck. You can watch or listen to the podcast here.
How the family noticed something was wrong
Meredith’s mother-in-law, known online as Granny, was originally living with her oldest daughter in the Charleston, South Carolina, area. Meredith described the signs that led the family to seek a diagnosis.
“She was experiencing symptoms, showing signs, forgetting how to go pick up the grandchildren from school, getting lost,” Meredith said. “Talking to random strangers and inviting them back to the house.”
The turning point came when Granny tried to cook soup by putting it in a baking pan in the oven instead of putting it in a pot and placing it on the stove. Granny was later diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia, also known as FTD.
Dividing caregiving duties wasn’t planned — it just happened
When Granny moved in with Meredith and his wife, there wasn’t a formal plan for who would do what.
“I think it was decided for us,” Meredith said. The family originally intended to split time with another sister-in-law, but when she had to return to full-time work, “the responsibility fell squarely on our shoulders,” Meredith said.
For a time, Meredith’s wife took Granny to work with her during the day and Dugan took over caregiving duties in the evenings. Eventually, his wife’s employer could no longer accommodate the arrangement, prompting the family to hire outside help.
Learning to ‘meet her where she’s at’
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, asked Meredith to reflect on his experience as a man stepping into a caregiving role that required hiring help rather than “fixing” the problem himself.
“Granny coming to live with us was a struggle for me mentally,” Meredith said. “I was exhausted because I could not figure out why I could not get a 72-, 73-year-old woman to understand, you can’t do this — it will hurt you.”
Meredith described one moment when Granny wanted to cut her hair and used a lighter to try to burn off a piece of it after he took away her scissors and said they would take her to get her hair cut.
“I could not understand in my mind, why does this woman do this? Why can I not get her to understand she’s going to hurt herself?” he said.
Meredith said he came to the realization that he needed to meet Granny where she is.
“Sam taught me that very early on,” Meredith said, referring to Aging Untold expert and gerontologist Sam Cradduck. “You have to meet them where they are.”
Meredith emphasized that lesson for other men in a similar situation.
“For men out there, you’re not going to fix it. The only thing you can do to help the situation is to swallow your pride, swallow your ego and learn to meet them where they’re at,” Meredith said.
Decoding Granny’s signature word: ‘heavy’
Viewers of Meredith’s videos on TikTok and Facebook are familiar with Granny’s repeated word, “heavy.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, asked how the family figures out what she means.
“What is she trying to tell me? Is her stomach hurt? Is her food cold? Is her food too hot?” Meredith said. “When she says ‘my heavy is heavy,’ I keep reiterating, and eventually she’ll move a certain way, she’ll do something with her hands, she’ll nod with her head, and we’ll figure it out.”
Meredith said much of the communication comes down to body language and behaviors learned from living with Granny every day.
Why Meredith started sharing the journey online
Meredith said the decision to document his caregiving journey online came from feeling isolated.
“I felt like I was alone. I felt like nobody in the world understood what was going on within my mind and in my heart,” Meredith said.
He recalled sitting at his kitchen table with a cup of coffee, recording himself talking about his frustrations before posting the video to TikTok. That post led him to a community of other caregivers he didn’t know existed.
Meredith said he’s still learning to manage the volume of response, including tens of thousands of messages and comments.
“You go through a whirlwind of emotions just reading the comments or the messages that come in,” he said.
Meredith said the online community has helped his family tremendously.
“For every one negative person, there’s 500 positives,” he said, and people in that community provide tips, which Meredith uses.
“Not only are they helping us, but they are helping the others that are reading the comments,” Meredith said.
The ‘sandwich generation’ and the cost of care
O’Rourke noted that Meredith and his wife are also raising children while caring for Granny — a dynamic often called the “sandwich generation.”
“We are 100% the sandwich generation,” Meredith said.
In the beginning, he said, the couple struggled to give their children enough attention because of the protocols required to care for Granny. Hiring additional caregivers allowed them “to still be parents for our children and give them the attention that they need and that they deserve as well.”
Meredith also spoke about the cost of care. The family looked into memory care facilities before deciding on the private route, which he described as the more affordable option.
“You go look at nice memory care facilities — we’re talking $10,000 to $15,000 a month,” Meredith said.
He said monetizing the family’s social media content has helped cover the cost of keeping Granny comfortable at home.
“Everyone always asks, are you going to keep her here until her last breath. We will,” Meredith said.
Meredith is also the founder of a nonprofit, also called Taking Care of Granny, which he said is focused solely on helping caregivers.
He said the idea for a nonprofit came from a conversation with another caregiver who documents caring for his wife, who has Parkinson’s disease.
“He was the one that started the idea with me. He was like, ‘What about a nonprofit? You do a nonprofit to provide care to the caregivers,’” Meredith said. “I was like, I like that idea. I don’t know how I’m going to do it, but let me start digging into it.”
Where things stand today Asked how Granny is doing now, Meredith said the disease has progressed. The family now purees her food because of trouble swallowing, and he’s noticed her shuffling her feet while walking, so the family has removed rugs and other trip hazards from the house.
Hospice has also brought in a medical bed to help prevent falls.
“The disease has progressed, and we’re at that point now,” Meredith said. “But given what we’ve been through, I would say she’s doing well.”
How to follow Taking Care of Granny
Key takeaways
- Male caregiving. An estimated 21 million men are currently in caregiving roles for aging or ill loved ones, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving.
- Meet them where they are. Dugan Meredith emphasized that trying to reason with a loved one with dementia rarely works. Caregivers need to adapt to the person’s reality instead.
- The “sandwich generation” faces unique pressure. Balancing young children and an aging parent or relative at the same time requires intentional systems so neither gets neglected.
- Online communities can ease caregiver isolation. Sharing the caregiving journey publicly connected Meredith with a wider community of caregivers facing similar experiences.

title: Investigation reveals Russian connection to Medicare billing scheme
text:
COLLEGE GROVE, TN (InvestigateTV) - A WSMV4 investigation has uncovered a Medicare fraud scheme that billed the federal program tens of thousands of dollars for medical supplies that Tennessee recipients never needed or received.
Our investigation found the billing is connected to a Russian citizen living in Texas, accused in a $3 billion Medicare fraud scheme.
Penny Vaughan, a retired nurse in College Grove, and her husband received their quarterly Medicare statements showing Medicare had been billed more than $11,000 for urinary catheters for both of them over five months.
“We did not need, did not buy, did not order,” Vaughan said. “The price was just extraordinary.”
The billing showed 300 catheters per month for five months.
“Three hundred a month would mean you were catheterizing yourself 10 times a day. Nobody does that. Nobody does that,” Vaughan said.
In Kingston Springs, Larry Welch’s mother-in-law received a similar quarterly report showing Medicare was billed for urinary catheters she never needed or received, totaling more than $11,000.
Several other Medicare recipients shared their quarterly reports, showing identical Medicare billing for hundreds of catheters they never needed.
“I knew it was fraud,” Vaughan said.
Despite the large number of catheters and high costs, Medicare paid the claims each time.
Russian citizen indicted
The billing for the catheters came from two medical equipment suppliers in Coral Springs, Florida, and Austin, Texas. In Texas, the billing came from Centurion Superior Medical.
Texas Secretary of State records show the company’s managing member is Nika Machutadze, a Russian citizen living in Austin.
Federal criminal complaints show Machutadze was indicted in federal court two-and-a-half weeks ago.
The complaint shows Machutadze’s company submitted claims to more than 221,000 Medicare beneficiaries across the United States, billing Medicare more than $3 billion, including for 752,281 urinary catheters.
“This could be pretty major,” Welch said.
Data breach may explain access
Questions remain about how Medicare recipients’ information in Tennessee reached the criminals.
Penny Vaughan recently received a letter from a billing service that works for health care providers stating there had been a data breach that may include identifying Medicare beneficiary identifiers.
Brandy Bauer with Senior Medicare Patrol, which helps Medicare recipients report fraud, said Medicare doesn’t have the ability to look at all 68 million enrollees and question claims.
“Medicare isn’t going to necessarily know what, on a day-to-day basis, what your prescribing physician has ordered for you,” Bauer said. “Medicare doesn’t have the ability to necessarily look at all 68 million enrollees and sort of question that. They’re going to sort of take the benefit of the doubt and go ahead and try and pay those claims until you realize, wait a second, I don’t need that supplies or I didn’t get those supplies.”
A spokesperson for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said in an emailed statement that they “do not confirm or comment on ongoing or potential investigations.”
Senior Medicare Patrol says all people interviewed for this story now need to reach out to Medicare to get new Medicare ID numbers.
Medicare recipients should review their quarterly reports to see what they were billed for and watch for notifications from hospitals and doctors about data breaches.
Experts also warn of scammers sending out fake plastic Medicare cards to Medicare recipients in Alabama. Activating one of these cards could give criminals access to your social security number, bank account, or allow them to make claims, according to AARP.
A real card you don’t need to activate nor pay for. These cards are never made of plastic, instead they are made with paper.

title: Some low-income Mainers to see automatic discount on their CMP, Versant bills
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Some low-income Mainers will soon see automatic discounts on their electric bills.
Governor Mills announcing Thursday under a new state initiative called “support-link,” the Department of Health and Human Services will use existing data from programs like SNAP, TANF and Mainecare to enroll eligible residents automatically.
That information will be shared with utilities—including CMP and Versant, to apply discounts amounting to 40-million dollars through the state’s Low-income Assistance Program.
Governor Mills spoke on the new discounts, saying, “Maine families are being pushed to the brink by the President’s whipsaw tariffs and his reckless war in Iran. At a time when every dollar matters, my administration is making it easier for vulnerable Mainers to lower their electric bills without unnecessary paperwork or bureaucratic hurdles,” Mills said.
To qualify, households must be at or below 150 percent of the federal poverty level, or eligible for federal home heating assistance.
Residents not already enrolled in a state assistance program can apply through their local community action agency.

title: Babies after 40: How having babies later alters roles for parents, grandparents
text:
(Aging Untold) — More women are waiting until their 40s to have children, and the numbers show it.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, total U.S. births fell 14% from 1990 to 2023. During that same period, births among women 40 and older rose by more than 96,000 — a 200% increase.
The health risks are real, but manageable
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down why birth rates among women 40 and older have surged and what that shift means for health, family planning and the generations in between.
“It’s going to depend on the health state,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “At the foundation, it’s build your foundation, a healthy foundation, because they’re going to be more risks and complications in advanced maternal ages.”
Rogers said pregnancy after 40 is classified as advanced maternal age and can carry a higher risk for high blood pressure, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and chromosomal abnormalities. Physicians who specialize in high-risk pregnancies are available to help manage those risks, she added.
“With the resources that we have nowadays, it’s really, really important that you look at your foundation, your health, your sleep and all that,” Rogers said.
She added that paternal health matters just as much as maternal health.
“A lot of times we’re looking at the woman, but don’t forget the man,” Rogers said. “The fathers, their health as well has an influence on the sperm, just like the mothers on the egg.”
Why women are waiting longer
Rogers said many women now have more wisdom, resources and financial stability by the time they decide to have children.
“After age 40, for women, their wisdom is really leading their biology, but they’re doing it with intent,” she said. “They have better resources, more tools and probably are financially more stable.”
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, connected that shift to how this generation of women grew up.
“I think a lot of this age group grew up with single moms that were struggling because they didn’t put their education first, and they didn’t build those careers,” she said. “And so now they’re like, I’m not going to be in those shoes. I’m going to wait. I’m going to have all of that stability and all that financial security, and then I’m going to have my children.”
The trade-off: a changing generational gap
What’s lost when people wait longer to have children is time with grandparents, Cradduck said.
“My grandmother was my world,” Cradduck said. “I can’t imagine not having that in my life. Because of those influences, that’s how we build our empathy. So how are we reaching these smaller children when we’re losing that aged generation?”
Katherine Ambrose, an aging well coach, tied the concern back to the importance of healthy aging.
“That’s why healthy longevity is so important,” Ambrose said. “If you want to be around for grandchildren that are coming later, you’ve got to stay healthy and keep your energy up. So you can run around the theme parks with them.”
Older parents may bring more patience — and a new “sandwich generation”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared firsthand observations of children raised by older parents.
“My godson’s parents are older, and they were so much more patient,” she said. “They had less energy, so they asked for more help faster.”
O’Rourke said there was a crew of people, including herself, who helped.
The children were exposed to more people as a result and “seemed to mature faster,” she said.
O’Rourke also pointed to new financial and caregiving pressures that come with having children later in life.
“I would really put that thought in before I even had the child, because that’s a real concern,” O’Rourke said. “If you plan for it, it’s very, very possible. But it’s something to really think about.”
Cradduck said waiting to have kids can also mean caring for aging parents and raising children at the same time.
“There is that sandwich generation 2.0 that goes on here by being older,” Cradduck said. “You know your parents are in their 60s, likely by the time you’re having your children. So when your kids are teenagers, now your parents are in their advanced years. You may be caring for both at the same time, which we know is difficult.”
Wisdom over energy
Despite the challenges, the experts agreed that having children later in life comes with its own rewards.
“I’m so much calmer and wiser than I was as a young mom,” Cradduck said. “Maybe this waiting game — the wisdom replaces the energy. The patience replaces the frustration.”
“Every season of life has different strengths and trade-offs,” Ambrose said. “Every individual and family is different.”
Key takeaways
- Pregnancy after 40 carries a higher risk of high blood pressure, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and chromosomal abnormalities, Dr. Rhea Rogers said, so your health foundation matters.
- Paternal health and sperm quality matter just as much as maternal health when planning a pregnancy later in life.
- Women who wait often bring more financial stability, patience and life experience to parenting.
- Having children later can mean simultaneously caring for aging parents and raising kids — a “sandwich generation 2.0.”

Partners for Peace to host several events, fundraisers for Domestic Violence Awareness Month
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month.
Serving Penobscot and Piscataquis counties, Partners for Peace has been a resource for victims of domestic violence and those who support survivors since 1973.
To celebrate survivorship and raise awareness of domestic violence, they will be hosting two events in the area.
On Oct. 8 in Lincoln, there will be an awareness walk and vigil to honor those affected by and the lives lost to domestic violence. Events begin at noon with the walk starting at 5 p.m.
Then there will be a family movie day at the Center Theatre in Dover-Foxcroft on Oct. 25 for a 3 p.m. showing of Hotel Transylvania: Transformania.
Both events are free to attend.
Partners for Peace says involving entire communities in these events speaks to the prevalence and widespread personal, familial, and community impacts of domestic violence.
“It’s important to involve the whole family because we know that this issue affects whole families, including pets and definitely children,” explained Casey Faulkingham Bixy, director of development and engagement at Partners for Peace. “We want our name to be known by our community. We want people to know that we are here and we’ve been here for over 50 years.“
If you can’t make it to these events, there are still ways you can support Partners for Peace.
Dream Charm Bar in Bangor is donating all proceeds from their $5 purple ribbon charm to the nonprofit all year.
On Oct. 22, Moe’s Original BBQ on Broadway will donate a portion of profits to them as well.
There are more fundraisers and events for Domestic Violence Awareness Month, which can be found here.
Partners for Peace has a 24/7 hotline for those in need of support, which they say is personalized to fit the needs of the victim: 1-800-863-9909

title: Here’s how experts map Maine’s drought — and how you can help
text:
Do you know how to measure soil moisture levels or have a deep understanding of your region’s hydrology?
No?
Well, it doesn’t matter — if you want to help inform those responsible for analyzing drought conditions across Maine and the country, all you need is your own observations.
It doesn’t take a scientist to tell you that your lawn is turning brown, the pond you frequent is low, or your well is drying up. In fact, that’s where you’re the expert.
During a drought, one can’t help but feel a little helpless. It’s not like we can make it rain.
But you can help, because the public’s input is taken into account when the weekly U.S. Drought Monitor maps are put together. The maps and data are used to analyze drought impacts, and federal agencies consider them when they weigh whether to declare drought-related disasters.
Here’s how it all works — and where the average Mainer fits into the equation:
ONE NATION, UNDER DROUGHT
Those yellow, orange and red drought maps of Maine don’t really end at the state line.
The U.S. Drought Monitor was formed in 1999 by the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Meteorologists and climatologists from those entities take turns as the lead author of the national map, usually rotating every two weeks.
Precipitation is a major factor in analyzing a drought, but far from the only one. Streamflow, reservoir levels, temperatures, soil moisture, evaporation and vegetation health all play a role as well.
The author will compile that data (much of it obtained via satellite) and come up with a draft of that week’s map.
But numbers don’t tell the full story, nor can one meteorologist or climatologist. That’s where regional and local experts step in.
LOCAL EXPERTS
Sarah Jamison, senior service hydrologist with the National Weather Service office in Gray, is one of those experts.
Every week, she and other members of the Northeast Drought Early Warning System review the Drought Monitor’s draft and weigh in with their knowledge of the region.
“They’re getting not just their own assessment, not just the raw numbers, but they’re getting the more localized feedback,” Jamison said. “We don’t define what it should be for New England, but we recommend some changes.”
Local experts are necessary because the data isn’t one-size-fits-all.
“The same kind of dryness in Utah may reflect completely different impacts as it would to Cumberland County,” Jamison said. “There is climatology that’s also weighed into this.”
The Drought Monitor says it consults hundreds of regional and local experts. The weekly maps are, essentially, a (very) well-educated guess.
“It’s definitely a consolidation of a lot of contributors and a lot of information, balanced by the impact reports that they do solicit,” Jamison said.
HOW TO CONTRIBUTE
There’s no way for the experts who contribute to the weekly Drought Monitor maps to be everywhere at once, which is where Condition Monitoring Observer Reports come in. Anyone (18 or older, in most states) can find and fill out the form at droughtimpacts.unl.edu or drought.gov, or via the ArcGIS Survey123 app.
The observer report starts by asking for some basic information, like your location, familiarity with the area and general observations.
Then, there are over a dozen optional questions pertaining to a wide range of topics, from livestock and crop production to home and garden impacts. There are also questions on community health, water supply, hydropower, fish spawning and tourism impacts.
“My wetland pond has dried up, my well has gone dry, my lawn has turned brown, the trees are stressed and dropping acorns,” Jamison said, rattling off examples of various reports that help the experts. “It doesn’t matter exactly what magnitude of impact. Any kind of impacts that are driven by drought are all weighed.”
At the end, you can type in any additional comments and upload photos.
HOW THAT HELPS
The color of your backyard on the next week’s map isn’t just going to change because you made a submission. Conditions can vary from lawn to lawn and farm to farm, even in the same town or neighborhood.
“That’s one of the most unique things about drought,” Jamison said. “If we have a snowstorm with 8 inches, the impacts are relatively uniform across much of the area. With a drought … they’re going to vary, and that’s just natural.”
What can catch experts’ eyes are common reports that actually go against what the data is saying.
“If we believe, for example, it’s not a very significant drought, but then we start to see reports of ‘wells are going dry,’ ‘ponds are drying up,’ ‘crops are failing,’” Jamison said, “those kinds of things really can help be the checks and balances or the gut check on what we’re processing and evaluating.
“We don’t have people literally walking the area to make these designations,” Jamison added. “We have to rely on the tools in our arsenal, and then the reports that we get from people in the field.”

title: Obituary: Edison “Ed” C. Henderson Sr.
text:
HARTFORD – Edison “Ed” C. Henderson Sr., 87, of Hartford, died Sept. 22, 2026, at the Maine Veterans’ Home in South Paris, where he had spent the previous two months. His wife, Rosemary, and their daughters were at his bedside.
Ed was born in Norway, Maine, on Dec. 15, 1938, to the late Jack Henderson and Anna (Holt) Henderson. He grew up in Welchville, Paris, Sumner and Woodstock. As a teenager, he worked with his father peeling pulp. He lived with his Aunt Dolly and attended his first year of high school in Paris. He then lived with and worked for Alvah Hendrickson, graduating from Woodstock High School in 1957.
After high school, Ed enlisted in the Army and was stationed in Germany for two years. Following his discharge, he served for two years in the National Guard in Norway.
Ed began his career as a truck driver after his Army service. He met Rosemary Bragg, and they married on June 15, 1962. Ed and Rosie were married for 64 years and had six children. He tried working for himself as a pulp truck driver but decided it was not for him. He later drove a log truck for Timberlands and Irving. His CB radio handle was “Henhouse” after he once showed up at the mill with a chicken in his load. After retiring, he drove a dump truck for David Bragg.
Ed enjoyed playing baseball during his high school years and was an avid Red Sox fan. He also enjoyed Westerns, reading, fishing, feeding the birds and scratching an occasional lottery ticket.
In his final days, Ed appreciated his many visitors, especially the little ones. His family admired the patience and courage with which he faced his many health challenges.
He is survived by his wife, Rosemary; his son David Heath; and the children he shared with Rosemary: Stephanie Buswell and her husband, Gerald, Stephen Henderson and his wife, Beverly, Edison Henderson Jr., Shawn Henderson and his wife, Karen, and Suzanne Rowe. He is also survived by his grandchildren, Danielle, Justin, Jamison, Alyssa, Lindsay, Brigette, Caitlin, Marissa, Crosby, Lauren, Michael, Gunnar, Kathryn, Max and Autumn; 16 great-grandchildren; his brothers, Fred and his wife, Carole, Quentin and his wife, Glenice, and Dennis and his wife, Nancy; his sister Dona Brown; and many nieces and nephews.
He was predeceased by his son Stewart Henderson; his grandson Jared Henderson; his brothers, Tom and Paul; and his sisters, Sara “Sally” and Martha.
The family would like to thank the staff at the Maine Veterans’ Home and Andwell Hospice for their compassionate care.
A celebration of Ed’s life will be held Saturday, October 10, at 1 p.m. at the East Sumner Congregational Church, followed by a graveside committal service at the Elmwood Cemetery in Sumner.
Arrangements are in the care of Cliff Gray Cremations where condolences and memories may be shared with the family at http://www.cliffgraycremations.com.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to the Maine Veterans’ Home Activities Department,

title: Here’s what to know about flu, Covid-19 and RSV vaccines this fall
text:
Respiratory virus season has arrived. Here’s what to know about flu, Covid-19 and RSV vaccines this fall
There’s a bit of a chill in the air, pumpkin spice in your coffee and children back to school — which means the threat of respiratory viruses like Covid-19, influenza and RSV is looming.
Some respiratory illnesses have arrived already. Seasonal influenza activity is still low at the national level, data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows.
But certain flu metrics are inching up – especially in the West. Health officials in Washington state’s King County note that since mid-August there has been an increase in people with flu visiting emergency departments in the area.
Related video above | When is the best time to get your flu shot?
Vaccines that help prevent illness and reduce the risk of serious infections and hospitalization are now available, and for some people, this is the right time to roll up their sleeves.
Typically, the CDC launches a fall campaign around this time of year, recommending seasonal immunizations such as the flu shot and Covid-19 vaccines. But after sweeping changes to the agency’s vaccine advisory committee during the second Trump administration and ongoing lawsuits, the CDC recently posted guidance online to follow last year’s recommendations for flu and Covid-19.
Meanwhile, the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project launched their own independent reviews of this fall’s vaccines – including those for flu, Covid and RSV – which were published in September in the medical journal JAMA.
The review papers helped inform 2026-27 respiratory virus immunization recommendations released by several medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.
“For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP,” Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a news briefing.
“Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter,” Gellin said.
“Clinicians will still have patients to care for. Parents will still have decisions to make for their children, and older Americans, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions will still need to know how best to protect themselves,” he said. “We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance.”
The US Department of Health and Human Services has not responded to CNN’s request for comment on the groups’ recommendations.
Flu, Covid-19 and RSV immunizations are now available at most major pharmacies.
“And really reassuringly, insurers have indicated to the major groups that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations,” Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in a news briefing.
Ordering through Vaccines for Children, the federal program that provides routine immunizations at no cost to children who are uninsured or underinsured or whose families may not otherwise be able to afford them, has also started. About half of US children are eligible for the program.
“Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives,” Nosal said in a news release. “As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients.”
RSV immunization
Who should get it
The groups eligible for RSV immunizations include older adults, pregnant people and infants.
“People age 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75 years old, should get one dose,” Nosal said. “This is not an annual vaccine. If you got one before, you do not need a new one this year. Getting one should protect you throughout the entire season.”
During pregnancy, RSV vaccination is recommended in the third trimester, between weeks 32 and 36.
Children younger than 8 months should be immunized against RSV using a monoclonal antibody unless their mother got an RSV vaccination during pregnancy, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.
“If the mother’s immunization status is unknown, that child should be immunized,” Racine said in the briefing. He added that children between 8 months and 19 months of age who are in certain high-risk groups for severe disease are also recommended to get the RSV monoclonal antibody.
And a single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for adults who have weakened immune systems.
“Immunosuppressed individuals are at higher risk for severe disease than immunocompetent individuals,” Dr. Dan Barouch, director of the Center for Virology and Vaccine Research at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, who was not involved in the new recommendations, said in an email. “The vaccines are also generally less effective in immunosuppressed individuals compared with immunocompetent individuals.”
When to get it
For older adults, RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall.
The advice slightly changed this year for pregnant people.
“ACOG now recommends that pregnant individuals receive a single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, from September 1 through March 1 instead of only through January 31,” Dr. Christina Davidson, chief medical officer of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said in the news briefing.
“We made this change because the RSV disease season is now occurring later in the spring, and it is also more severe than it used to be,” Davidson said. “The extension of the eligibility window will help provide pregnant patients and their infants with additional protection.”
For infants, the RSV monoclonal antibody is typically recommended around virus season, from October through March.
Seasonal flu shots
Who should get it
Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu shot.
“On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to go to the doctor by 30% to 60%,” Nosal said.
“Adults 65 years and older should get an enhanced flu vaccine, one that is high-dose, adjuvanted or recombinant, when it’s available,” she said. “But do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available.”
And for the first time, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for use in adults 50 and older.
The flu vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy, but pregnant people should avoid the nasal spray version, according to the recommendations.
“Pregnant and postpartum people still have a significantly higher risk of developing serious complications from infection compared with non-pregnant people,” Davidson said.
“The inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccines remain the only vaccines that are recommended for use in pregnancy in any trimester, so please work with your OB care clinician or pharmacist to get these,” she said. “Most importantly, if you are able to get the vaccine while you are pregnant, the immunity will also, in part, pass on to your baby.”
When to get it
October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, Nolan said, because “protection wanes throughout the season.”
Some providers use the slogan “flu before boo” to remind people to get a flu shot before Halloween.
Updated Covid-19 vaccines
Who should get it
Getting an updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for adults.
“If you’re older than 19, we recommend getting the Covid-19 vaccine,” Nosal said.
“This is especially important for people who are 65 years and older, at increased risk for severe Covid infection and those who’ve never received a Covid-19 vaccine,” she said. “For those adults 65 years and older, they should receive a second dose of the updated Covid-19 vaccine six months after that season’s initial dose to help maintain protection as immunity wanes over time.”
The vaccine is also recommended for infants between 6 months and 23 months of age, and children in certain high-risk groups or those whose families request vaccination.
And for people who are immunocompromised, the annual updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for ages 6 months and older.
Last year, the CDC recommended Covid-19 vaccines based on conversations with the patient’s healthcare provider, known as shared decision-making, Barouch noted, but the agency “also emphasized that the risk-benefit of the vaccines is most favorable for individuals who are at higher risk of severe disease.”
Davidson, of ACOG, said the vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy.
“The most important message is this: If you are pregnant, considering pregnancy or are a new or breastfeeding parent, please get your vaccine or your annual booster. All four of the available Covid vaccines are safe for you,” Davidson said.
Moderna offers two mRNA shots, Pfizer and BioNTech have another, and Sanofi and Novavax offer a more traditional protein-based version.
“A recommendation for the Covid vaccine is based on more than five years of research and millions of administered doses,” Davidson said. “I want to emphasize that the evidence has found no increased risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth or birth defects. The risks of complications from Covid for pregnant people and their babies, however, are high. So please get the vaccine.”
When to get it
It’s recommended to get the updated vaccine now, but if you have been recently infected with Covid, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the vaccine.
The updated Covid-19 vaccine “targets the most recent strain that’s been circulating, and so if you want to update your protection, that’s the best way to do it,” Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, president-elect of the American Medical Association, said in a news briefing.
“You know, your computer constantly needs to be updated. Well, your immune system, your immunity needs to be constantly updated too,” she said. “You’re going to get your most protection in those first few months after the vaccine. So if you have a big event – if you have to go to a wedding, or if you’re going on some fabulous trip, or you’re going to a fabulous birthday party, or just any birthday party or get-together – think about getting that vaccine a couple of weeks before that event, so you’ll stay healthy and well.”

title: Maine must not bring back Paul LePage
text:
Paul LePage is back, but there’s nothing new about him we haven’t already seen and nothing we want to revisit. He’s grossly insulting (believing he’s funny), calling himself “Trump before Trump,” making blatantly racist and sexist comments that don’t belong in political campaigns or polite conversations.
LePage was always an embarrassment for Maine, and he’d be happy to embarrass it again. I’ll never forget visiting friends in Massachusetts who were ready with cringeworthy questions about Maine’s infamous governor. (“Did he really say that?”) But, we’re never going back there.
LePage got into office by finding a third-party candidate who’d split the vote for him. A dishonest tactic, it drove Maine to embrace ranked-choice voting, which increases our choices and our power as voters. In Maine, our votes really do matter!
It’s highly ironic, but it’s thanks to Paul LePage’s awful record that we use RCV and why we’re not going to be cheated out of our best choice for Maine’s 2nd District: Matt Dunlap.
Toni Seger
Lovell

title: Joe Gatto Is Bringing His Comedy Tour to Maine This December
text:

title: Portland homicide suspect who was shot by police has died
text:
A man suspected in a Portland homicide who was shot by responding officers has died, the police department announced Friday afternoon.
Police said they were notified Thursday that Brian Oliver, 41, had died while being treated at Maine Medical Center.
Oliver was shot Sept. 21 by officers who were responding to calls for an assault at a home on Colonial Road. Police say Oliver did not comply with officers’ commands to drop a weapon before officers shot him.
It’s unclear what weapon Oliver allegedly failed to drop or how many times he was shot. Authorities have so far declined to release further details about the incident. Police have referred questions to the Office of the Maine Attorney General, which has declined to share more information while it investigates and did not immediately respond to emailed questions Friday afternoon.
The victim in the alleged assault, 69-year-old Mark Tschamler, was pronounced dead at the scene. Police said Oliver had been expected to face a murder charge in connection with Tschamler’s death.
Better Business Bureau filings indicate that Tschamler was the owner of a business, One Call Craftsmen, founded in 1984. Tschamler told a Portland Press Herald reporter in 1996 that he was a “jack-of-all-trades” who worked on general home maintenance projects such as landscaping and carpentry. Tschamler’s next-door neighbor said last month that he occasionally helped her with home projects.
Officers Joseph Lowe and David Moore, who shot Oliver, were placed on administrative leave following the shooting.
It’s the second time Portland police have fatally shot a man in roughly a month.
Jacob Hastings, 37, was shot and killed by officers Aug. 27 following a chaotic, late-night chase across the city that ended near the Casco Bay Lines terminal.
The attorney general’s office is reviewing both cases; the office reviews all fatal police shootings in the state and hasn’t found one to be unjustified since at least 1990.
