title: Susan Collins votes conscientiously and gets results
text:
Sen. Susan Collins has taken years of criticism for her vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh. What her critics rarely mention is that she also voted to confirm Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan, nominated by President Obama, and Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, nominated by President Biden.
That record isn’t a contradiction. It reflects a principle. The Constitution gives senators the job of advising and consenting on a president’s nominees, and Sen. Collins has consistently treated that as a question of qualifications, character and respect for the law, not whether she agrees with a nominee’s politics. Voting only for judges who share your views would turn every confirmation into a partisan brawl. She has refused to do that, whether the president was a Republican or a Democrat, and she has refused to be moved by political campaigns built on accusations rather than evidence.
That same practical, steady approach shows up here at home. Sen. Collins secured $4.7 million in federal funding for a new Belgrade Fire and Rescue Station. For a small town like ours, that kind of investment would be nearly impossible to raise on our own. It means our firefighters and rescue personnel will have a safe, modern facility to serve residents and the thousands of visitors who come to the lakes every summer.
Mainers deserve a senator who does her homework, votes her conscience and gets results for our communities. Sen. Collins has done all three, and she has my support.
Penny Morrell
Belgrade

title: Maine Credit Unions kick off $100,000 challenge to support hunger relief
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WESTBROOK – Maine credit unions are once again asking for the public’s help this October to provide food for neighbors in need through the 7th Annual $100,000 Ending Hunger Challenge.
Throughout the month, Maine Credit Unions’ Campaign for Ending Hunger is working to raise $100,000 to help provide funding for 200,000 healthy meals across the state. Anyone can donate, including individuals and businesses, and you do not need to be a credit union member to participate.
“Maine credit unions always step up when our neighbors need help,” Elise Baldacci, president of the Maine Credit Union League, said. “A few months ago, we contributed $100,000 to Good Shepherd Food Bank through our 48 to Feed the State initiative, and now we’re asking the public to join us in supporting our October fundraiser. Demand for food assistance continues to grow and every donation our campaign receives this month will help put food on the table for more people in need.”
Food insecurity remains a serious concern across Maine. One in five Maine children experience food insecurity; 14.5% of households struggle to consistently put food on the table, and more than 31,000 seniors are at risk of hunger. Maine also has the highest rate of childhood food insecurity in New England. Those challenges are especially significant in a rural state like Maine, where access to food assistance can be more difficult. Washington County, for example, has a food insecurity rate of 18.8% — the highest in New England!
Funds raised in October will support hunger relief efforts across Maine, with 25% of online donations directly benefiting Good Shepherd Food Bank. Remaining funds will support local food pantries, meal programs, schools, and other organizations addressing hunger.
“I’m incredibly proud of the way Maine’s credit unions carry out our People Helping People philosophy through this Campaign,” added Baldacci. “They see the impact of hunger in their communities every day, and that makes this work personal. It’s why credit unions across Maine continue to give so generously to this cause, and why we hope others will feel compelled to join us.”
To support the $100,000 Ending Hunger Challenge through an online donation, visit www.campaignforendinghunger.org. You can also check with your local credit union for opportunities to donate at a branch near you.
The Maine Credit Union League is a nonprofit, professional trade association that exists to serve Maine’s credit unions. Founded in 1938, the League’s mission is to help credit unions succeed and improve the financial lives of their members. As the trade association for Maine’s credit unions, the League provides advocacy, education, and other resources designed to assist credit unions in meeting the needs of their membership. For more information, visit www.mainecul.org.

title: ‘I was fighting for my life.’ Flydubai pilot recounts moments when he was attacked
text:
NEW DELHI (AP) — The Indian airline captain who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a FlyDubai flight described Friday how he fought for his life in the minutes after his co-pilot stabbed him and the plane began a steep descent.
Capt. Smit Machchhar, recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a televised video call that he knew he had to get back on his feet to save his passengers.
“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” he said from the hospital, his head bandaged and tubes in his nose, before breaking down as he recalled the attack.
“I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realized that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives,” he told Modi.
Machchhar, who is from Mumbai, was seriously injured in Wednesday’s attack but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and restrain the attacker as the Boeing 737 descended sharply, witnesses and Israeli authorities said. He has been hailed as a hero, with world leaders saying he helped avert a disaster.
The flight, carrying 182 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was diverted to Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia for an emergency landing. FlyDubai said Wednesday that the jet was secured by on-duty crew members “who diverted and landed the aircraft safely.” A regional official said the crew members were pilots in training.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the attacker, an Omani national, was arrested in Saudi Arabia and was undergoing interrogation there. The motive for the attack was not immediately clear.
Modi told Machchhar his “courage, patience, and presence of mind” saved many lives.
Machchhar said his flying experience allowed him to sense the plane’s steep descent even after he was knocked down by the attacker.
“I have been flying planes for 17 years and serving as a captain for the last 11 years. I can sense exactly what is happening with the aircraft even with my eyes closed. When I was down, I could feel that the aircraft was plummeting,” he said.
Machchhar said that during those difficult moments, he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a Hindu devotional hymn dedicated to Lord Hanuman, the monkey god, and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” he told Modi.
Machchhar, who is married and has two children, has worked for FlyDubai for about four years, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before joining the airline, he spent 11 years with SpiceJet, an Indian low-cost carrier, where he served as a senior commander and line training captain. He logged more than 9,750 flying hours with SpiceJet.
Philip Kean, CEO of Mainland Air, the New Zealand flight school where Machchhar trained, said pilots are taught how to take over if a fellow crew member becomes incapacitated. But the training does not typically prepare them for a stabbing attack by a colleague, he told The Associated Press on Friday.
“I don’t think there’s much in the handbook for being stabbed,” Kean said.
“You’re friends and you’re flying together,” he said. “Nobody would expect … a person to have a go at you like that.”
___
Associated Press journalist Charlotte Graham-McLay in Wellington, New Zealand, contributed to this report.

title: Bangor City Council candidate wants to eliminate affordable housing
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Bangor Daily News is profiling all 12 Bangor City Council candidates ahead of the election this fall. Read more coverage of Bangor’s local election here.
One Bangor City Council candidate sees drugs as the primary problem in the city and wants to eliminate affordable housing, syringe exchange programs and the public health department.
Michael Furrow, 67, has lived in Bangor for nearly 30 years. He’s retired from the military and from a job at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.
Furrow’s top priority is addressing drug use and he believes substances are the root of many other issues in the city. “Drugs are causing homelessness, they’re causing robberies and, of course, drug addiction,” he said.
He also wants to stop the construction of low-income housing and said at a candidate forum event last week that he thinks affordable homes are “bringing in the wrong type of people.”
Furrow does not believe that there is a housing shortage in Bangor, nor does he believe the results of the BangorHousing Study, he said. The study, commissioned by the city and carried out by an outside consultant, found that Bangor is short 700 affordable units.
The candidate thinks the City Council needs more people who think outside the box, and is running because “when good men do nothing, bad things happen.”
Furrow is involved with the Penobscot County Conservation Association and the Disabled American Veterans, and he’s an archery range instructor, he said.
The candidate declined to share his political party, saying the party system is “just designed to divide us,” although many of his policy positions are some of the most conservative in the council race.
He told the Bangor Daily News he wants to cease operating a city public health department and “let the state run it.”
Furrow sees Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center as a key part of the city’s homelessness response and wants judges to send people there for involuntary treatment.
The aging state-run treatment facility is one of two psychiatric hospitals run by the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. It houses about 60 to 70 patients, and the state eventually plans to rebuild it but doesn’t have the funds to do so in the near future, City Manager Carollynn Lear reported in a recent workshop. The council does not have any jurisdiction over the facility, although its legislative committee is investigating ways to encourage speedier progress.
In order to expand the facility, Furrow wants to see the state funding allocated to permanent supportive housing projects like Bangor’s Yellen Pines redirected to mental hospitals.
Furrow doesn’t think the syringe exchange programs in the city are working and thinks banning those programs would help address the ongoing Penobscot County HIV outbreak and coinciding surge of hepatitis C.
HIV is often transmitted by sharing needles, and programs that give out sterile ones are proven to reduce HIV and hepatitis C transmission rates by around 50%, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Furrow also would like to require local syringe service programs to label each needle they pass out and fine agencies if someone litters their syringes on the ground.
Similarly, he wants to fine grocery stores if someone abandons their shopping carts.
The candidate said he’s completely opposed to Yellen Pines because he believes housing first programs don’t work. Furrow said he expects that none of the people who live there will recover from addiction because the housing placements don’t mandate treatment, and that he believes the facility will be a “pipeline from Portland” wherein homeless people in Portland will be sent to Bangor and housed there.
Furrow’s doubts about social services extend beyond just public programs; he said he wants to get rid of some of the nonprofits in the city and believes some of the money from their budgets should be put toward the Dorothea Dix facility. This likely would not be possible or legal because nonprofits are private organizations.
“There’s a lot of them. They have so many overlapping services. Don’t need it,” he said of Bangor’s nonprofits.
Instead of funding most social programs, Furrow wants the city to focus on bringing in more jobs because a lack of them makes it hard for young people to stay here and leads to brain drain.
He thinks that homelessness and public drug use discourage businesses from moving to Bangor because they see that “Bangor’s a mess,” he said. Addressing drug-related issues, he said, would encourage people to stay.
“Bangor has to be a family-friendly, family-oriented city,” he said.
At the candidate forum last week, he raised an idea for combating drug use in the city: sending drug dogs into every homeless encampment, hourly. Sheriff Troy Morton, who was in the audience, said that would not be possible.
Furrow also wants to offer tax breaks to businesses, in order to create jobs, tax revenue and economic development.
One social program he does support is heating assistance for elderly residents.
“They’re spending so much money on the homeless, i.e. the drug problem,” Furrow said of the council. “What about the elderly?”
He noted the affordability concerns shared by many older residents, especially given rising heating oil costs. He’d like the city to provide heating assistance to those constituents and address their property tax affordability concerns.
Like some of the more liberal candidates running this year, Furrow is staunchly opposed to artificial intelligence data centers and automatic license plate readers, such as Flock cameras.
He’d like to ban those cameras and said he’d make the temporary data center ban that is already in place permanent, noting that electric and water bills often go up when a data center is built nearby.
In terms of the way the council conducts its business, Furrow noted widespread concerns about bickering among councilors and said he thinks too many sitting councilors are political activists.
“You cannot have political activism on a city council. City council is a business. It has to be run like a business. We have to bring businesses here. We have to bring industry here. We can’t be worrying about ICE,” he said, alluding to a monthslong debate earlier this year regarding how the city should regulate cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
Furrow said he’s attended almost all of the council meetings this year.
